tests.name: Reading Through Ideas 1
tests.source: Original RC passages written for LSAT Trainer from real scholarship (philosophy, epistemology, etymology, poetry, literature, history, mathematics, Islamic thought, law, economics and politics), with sources for further reading on every passage. Every key was confirmed by a blind solver and every passage checked for accuracy. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

sections.title: Reading Through Ideas 1: Was the Gate of Ijtihad Closed? · Hallaq's Impossible State · Saussure's coefficients and Hittite · Roots, stems and the Semitic word

passages.title: Was the Gate of Ijtihad Closed?
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
For decades, Western scholarship told the history of Islamic law as a story of early creativity followed by long stagnation. Its most influential version, in Joseph Schacht's An Introduction to Islamic Law (1964), runs as follows. By about the beginning of the tenth century, jurists of all the schools felt that the essential questions had been settled, and a consensus gradually took hold that no one thereafter possessed the qualifications for ijtihad, the independent reasoning by which a qualified jurist derives rulings from the law's sources. What remained was taqlid, the acceptance of established authorities' doctrines: later jurists could explain and apply the law, and at most interpret it, but not rethink it.

Wael Hallaq's 1984 article "Was the Gate of Ijtihad Closed?" answered no. From a systematic, chronological study of the original legal sources, Hallaq judged the prevailing views of ijtihad's later history "entirely baseless and inaccurate." His evidence was of two kinds. In legal theory, jurists continued to treat ijtihad as indispensable: because new cases kept arising, the law required jurists able to reason from the sources, and some theorists insisted that no age could be without such a jurist. The qualifications they specified were demanding but attainable, not set impossibly high, as the older account supposed. In practice, jurists in nearly every century after the tenth were recognized as mujtahids, and some claimed the rank for themselves. Even the language of closure, Hallaq observed, enters the sources only centuries after the date assigned to it, and amid controversy rather than consensus. The gate, he concluded, "was not closed in theory nor in practice."

Hallaq's article has largely carried the day; few specialists now defend the closure thesis in its original form. Yet later research suggests that refuting it was only a first step, because the debate had been framed by an assumption the older thesis supplied: that ijtihad measures a legal system's vitality and taqlid marks its decline. Mohammad Fadel, studying later Maliki jurisprudence, argued that taqlid answered a demand for uniform rules and limited the discretion of judges and muftis, especially those of lower rank; the school's authoritative abridgments of doctrine functioned, on his account, something like a codified common law. Hallaq himself, in Authority, Continuity, and Change in Islamic Law (2001), described taqlid not as blind acquiescence but as a reasoned defense of established doctrine, within which change could still occur.

These refinements do not rehabilitate Schacht. They show, rather, that both sides of the controversy shared a premise that neither examined: to prove that mujtahids existed in every century was to concede that their existence was what mattered. If taqlid was itself a disciplined form of legal reasoning, then the question of whether the gate was closed is less false than misposed. The law's capacity to adapt lay not only in the rare jurist who reasoned directly from the sources but in the ordinary work of interpreting, ranking, and extending a school's settled doctrine. Hallaq's 1984 article remains indispensable precisely because, by dismantling the closure story on its own terms, it cleared the ground on which a better question could be asked.

sources.author: Joseph Schacht
sources.title: An Introduction to Islamic Law
sources.note: The classic statement of the closure thesis: by about 900 CE jurists of all schools held that essential questions were settled and that no one thereafter was qualified for ijtihad, leaving taqlid (paraphrased in the passage, not quoted).

sources.author: Wael B. Hallaq
sources.title: Was the Gate of Ijtihad Closed?
sources.note: International Journal of Middle East Studies 16(1): 3-41; argues from legal theory and the record of later jurists that ijtihad never ceased. Source of both quotations: the views on ijtihad's history after the second/eighth century are "entirely baseless and inaccurate" and "the gate of ijtihad was not closed in theory nor in practice."

sources.author: Mohammad Fadel
sources.title: The Social Logic of Taqlid and the Rise of the Mukhtasar
sources.note: Islamic Law and Society 3(2): 193-233; reads post-6th/12th-century Maliki taqlid as a demand for uniform rules that limited officials' discretion, with the mukhtasar functioning like a codified common law.

sources.author: Wael B. Hallaq
sources.title: Authority, Continuity, and Change in Islamic Law
sources.note: Hallaq's own later reframing: taqlid is not blind acquiescence but a reasoned defense of established doctrine, and continuity and change both run through school authority.

passages.title: Hallaq's Impossible State
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
Passage A

"The argument of this book is fairly simple," Wael Hallaq writes at the opening of The Impossible State (2013): "The 'Islamic state,' judged by any standard definition of what the modern state represents, is both an impossibility and a contradiction in terms." Hallaq does not ask whether particular Islamist programs are prudent; he compares two paradigms. The modern state, in his account, is a European creation defined by sovereignty, by a will to legislate, by a bureaucracy that penetrates society, and by its power to fashion the very subjects it governs. Its law expresses the sovereign's will, and that law, like modernity generally, rests on a separation of what is from what ought to be.

Premodern sharia, by contrast, was not the command of any ruler. It was elaborated by jurists who emerged from society rather than from government, and rulers, who held executive power, were themselves bound by a law they did not make. In this order the legal was an instrument of the moral: law belonged to a wider set of practices through which Muslims cultivated themselves as moral persons. Measured against those practices, the state's own technologies of the self appear morally thin. To attach sharia to the modern state, Hallaq concludes, is not to revive it but to subordinate it to an alien sovereign will. Yet he does not counsel despair. Modernity's moral predicament is shared, he suggests, and the sharia tradition offers resources for a critique that some Western thinkers have also begun.

Passage B

Few reviewers of The Impossible State doubted Hallaq's command of his sources, and nothing in the strongest criticism of the book requires denying that the modern state is a historically specific, European-made form, or that sharia enacted as the legislation of such a state ceases to be what it was. The objection concerns method. The legal scholar Lama Abu-Odeh observes that Hallaq treats the two sides of his comparison in radically different ways. The Islamic order appears as a norm, a paradigm whose essential features stand prior to its history. The modern state, by contrast, "is nothing but history, saturated by it through and through, and its history is the history of Europe."

Hallaq turns the historical-critical tools of modern theory on the state with devastating effect, but he declines to turn them on the premodern Islamic model, so the distance between that model's ideal and the conduct of actual dynasties stays obscure. Andrew March, reviewing the book in Political Theory, pressed a similar complaint. The result, in Abu-Odeh's phrase, is a "Huntington-in-reverse": a clash of civilizations in which the Islamic side wins. A comparison of one order's ideal with another's record can show that the two differ, which no one disputes; it cannot show that one of them is impossible. And a form that is nothing but history may yet be remade by history.

sources.author: Wael B. Hallaq
sources.title: The Impossible State: Islam, Politics, and Modernity's Moral Predicament
sources.note: Columbia University Press (released late 2012, dated 2013); argues that the modern state and the sharia's moral-legal paradigm are structurally incompatible. Source of passage A's opening quotation, "The argument of this book is fairly simple... is both an impossibility and a contradiction in terms."

sources.author: Lama Abu-Odeh
sources.title: Review of The Impossible State: Islam, Politics, and Modernity's Moral Predicament, by Wael B. Hallaq
sources.note: International Journal of Middle East Studies (online February 2014); charges that Hallaq treats the Islamic order as a norm prior to history and the modern state as pure history. Source of passage B's quotations: the modern state "is nothing but history, saturated by it through and through, and its history is the history of Europe," and "Huntington-in-reverse."

sources.author: Andrew F. March
sources.title: What Can the Islamic Past Teach Us about Secular Modernity?
sources.note: Political Theory 43(6): 838-849; review essay on Hallaq's The Impossible State and Hussein Agrama's Questioning Secularism, critical of how Hallaq treats the premodern Islamic model (paraphrased, not quoted).

passages.title: Saussure's coefficients and Hittite
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
In a monograph dated 1879, the Mémoire sur le système primitif des voyelles dans les langues indo-européennes, the twenty-one-year-old Ferdinand de Saussure proposed that the Indo-European parent language had contained sounds attested in none of its known descendants. His reasoning was structural. Many roots alternate between a full grade containing the vowel e and a reduced grade lacking it, and when e drops out, a following resonant such as r or n becomes the vowel of its syllable. Roots with long vowels, such as the root meaning "stand" (Greek histāmi, Latin stāre), seemed to break this pattern. Saussure proposed that they, too, consisted of e plus an element, a member of a class he called "coefficients sonantiques," which combined with e to yield a long vowel and which, he wrote, "ne pourront apparaître à nu que dans l'état réduit de la racine": they could appear on their own only in the reduced grade of the root. He specified what these units did, not how they were pronounced.

For nearly half a century the proposal was largely neglected. Leading scholars of the day, Hermann Osthoff among them, received the Mémoire with open hostility, and one of its few defenders, Hermann Möller, linked the posited elements to the laryngeal consonants of the Semitic languages, thereby giving the theory its name. The situation changed after Bedřich Hrozný deciphered Hittite, an Indo-European language preserved on cuneiform tablets, in 1915. In a short 1927 article titled "ə indo-européen et ḫ hittite," Jerzy Kuryłowicz showed that the Hittite consonant written ḫ stood in positions where Saussure's analysis required one of his coefficients: Hittite ḫant- "front," beside Greek antí and Latin ante, preserves at the beginning of the word a consonant that the other languages had lost.

The episode is often told as a vindication comparable to the sighting of a planet whose existence had been calculated before anyone observed it: a method working entirely from regularities among known forms posited an unseen entity, and new evidence later revealed it. Some go further, treating the episode as proof that the comparative method, rigorously applied, reliably recovers the prehistory of languages.

The first of these claims is justified; the second outruns the evidence. Hittite confirmed that at least some of Saussure's units had been real consonants, which is more than his critics had allowed. But on most accounts Hittite ḫ reflects only some of them; the laryngeal now usually written *h1 leaves no consonantal trace there, so its existence still rests on the very internal reasoning that Hittite was supposed to have checked. Nor did the confirmation settle what Saussure had left open. Most scholars now work with three laryngeals, but some have argued for fewer and others for more, and their phonetic values, whether glottal stops or fricatives produced far back in the throat, remain disputed. What the episode shows is that a method attentive to systematic patterns can detect that something must have been present; it does not show that the same method can determine, without further help, exactly what that something was.

sources.author: Ferdinand de Saussure
sources.title: Mémoire sur le système primitif des voyelles dans les langues indo-européennes
sources.note: The founding text of the laryngeal theory, positing 'coefficients sonantiques' from patterns of vowel alternation; the quotation 'ne pourront apparaître à nu que dans l'état réduit de la racine' is from it (as transcribed in the Wikisource Recueil and the Huma-Num Corpus de textes linguistiques fondamentaux). The title page is dated 1879, though copies circulated at the end of 1878.

sources.author: Jerzy Kuryłowicz
sources.title: ə indo-européen et ḫ hittite (in Symbolae grammaticae in honorem Ioannis Rozwadowski, vol. 1)
sources.note: The short article showing that Hittite ḫ appears where Saussure's theory requires a coefficient, the turning point in the theory's acceptance; its title is quoted in the passage.

sources.author: Winfred P. Lehmann
sources.title: Proto-Indo-European Phonology
sources.note: A classic account of PIE phonology with a long chapter on the laryngeal theory, its history from Saussure and Möller to the Hittite evidence, and the competing proposals about the laryngeals' number.

sources.author: James Clackson
sources.title: Indo-European Linguistics: An Introduction
sources.note: A modern Cambridge textbook that treats Saussure's laryngeals as a model case of internal reconstruction and sets out what is and is not agreed about them today.

passages.title: Roots, stems and the Semitic word
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
The grammarians who founded the Arabic linguistic tradition in eighth-century Basra, where the study of language was bound up with the effort to understand and preserve the Arabic of the Qur'an, analyzed words as built from a consonantal root combined with a pattern of vowels and affixes. Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad organized the Kitāb al-ʿAyn, usually counted the first Arabic dictionary, by roots rather than by whole words, listing each set of radical consonants together with its possible permutations, though the work may have been completed by his student al-Layth ibn al-Muẓaffar. Al-Khalil's pupil Sibawayh, in his grammar known simply as al-Kitāb, described word forms by matching them to templates built on the consonants f-ʿ-l, so that kātib, "writer," belongs to the pattern fāʿil. On this analysis the root k-t-b carries a core meaning of writing that kataba, "he wrote," kitāb, "book," and maktab, "office," share, while each pattern contributes a grammatical meaning of its own.

Some modern linguists have argued that this analysis, however useful descriptively, misrepresents how words are actually formed. Outi Bat-El, studying Modern Hebrew verbs derived from nouns, observed that such verbs often keep consonant clusters of the source noun: praklit, "lawyer," yields priklet, "practiced law," preserving the noun's initial pr, an arrangement that pouring the bare consonants into a verbal template would not predict. Bat-El called the phenomenon "cluster transfer" and concluded that new words are formed by modifying existing stems, so that the consonantal root can be dispensed with in the grammar. Adam Ussishkin extended the argument in a 1999 paper pointedly titled "The inadequacy of the consonantal root."

Psycholinguists have approached the question differently. Ram Frost, Kenneth Forster and Avital Deutsch began a 1997 study from the premise that "All Hebrew words are composed of 2 interwoven morphemes: a triconsonantal root and a phonological word pattern." Using masked priming, in which a prime word is flashed too briefly to be consciously read, they found that a prime sharing its root with a target noun speeded recognition of the target, whereas a prime sharing only its nominal pattern did not. Words related in meaning but not sharing a root produced no priming, so the root effect could not be reduced to similarity of meaning. Sami Boudelaa and William Marslen-Wilson later reported comparable root effects in Arabic, along with pattern effects that the Hebrew noun studies had not found.

Defenders of the traditional analysis treat such results as decisive: whatever theorists say, the mind treats roots as units. That inference is too quick in one respect but not in another. The experiments show that readers track recurring consonant sets; they do not show that every word is produced by inserting a root into a pattern, and stem-based theorists need not deny that speakers register the consonants their stems share. Yet the findings do tell against any version of the stem-based view holding that roots have no psychological standing whatever. The grammarians' root, it seems, is a real unit of the mental lexicon, even if its role in forming new words is narrower than the tradition assumed.

sources.author: Outi Bat-El
sources.title: Stem modification and cluster transfer in Modern Hebrew
sources.note: Natural Language and Linguistic Theory 12: argues from denominal verbs that preserve the source noun's clusters that Hebrew words are formed from stems and that the consonantal root can be eliminated from the grammar; the term 'cluster transfer' is quoted from its title.

sources.author: Adam Ussishkin
sources.title: The inadequacy of the consonantal root: Modern Hebrew denominal verbs and output-output correspondence
sources.note: Phonology 16: extends Bat-El's case in Optimality Theory, arguing that roots are not needed to derive Hebrew denominal verbs; the passage quotes the first part of its title.

sources.author: Ram Frost, Kenneth I. Forster and Avital Deutsch
sources.title: What can we learn from the morphology of Hebrew? A masked-priming investigation of morphological representation
sources.note: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition 23: finds root but not nominal-pattern priming in Hebrew, independent of semantic similarity; the quotation 'All Hebrew words are composed of 2 interwoven morphemes: a triconsonantal root and a phonological word pattern' is the first sentence of its abstract (PubMed 9265076).

sources.author: Sami Boudelaa and William D. Marslen-Wilson
sources.title: Morphological units in the Arabic mental lexicon
sources.note: Cognition 81: cross-modal and masked priming experiments on Arabic testing the triconsonantal root as a unit of lexical representation, the start of a research program that later also found word-pattern priming in Arabic.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Hallaq's evidence that jurists continued to practice ijtihad after the tenth century shows that Schacht's account of Islamic legal history should be rejected in favor of an account centered on taqlid.
Although later scholars have refined Hallaq's 1984 argument, the closure thesis remains defensible if it is understood as a claim about the decline of the most independent forms of legal reasoning.

Hallaq persuasively refuted the claim that ijtihad ceased, but later research suggests that the debate rested on a questionable assumption about where a legal system's capacity to adapt is to be found.
The closure thesis arose because Western scholars mistook the spread of authoritative abridgments of school doctrine for evidence that independent legal reasoning had been abandoned.
Taqlid, rather than ijtihad, was the principal means by which Islamic law adapted to new circumstances, as both Fadel and the later Hallaq have demonstrated.
questions.explanation: The passage reports the closure thesis, presents Hallaq's refutation as having 'largely carried the day,' then argues in the last two paragraphs that both sides shared an unexamined premise (that ijtihad is what measures vitality), so the question was 'misposed.' C captures both halves. E is the near-miss: the author says the capacity to adapt lay 'not only' in the rare mujtahid but also in ordinary doctrinal work, which is not the claim that taqlid was the principal means, and the author never says Fadel or Hallaq 'demonstrated' that.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the claim the whole passage builds toward, including the author's own position in the last paragraph.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, first two sentences; paragraph 4, first three sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Map: P1 the older thesis (Schacht); P2 Hallaq's refutation and evidence; P3 the refutation succeeded, but the debate assumed ijtihad = vitality, and Fadel and the later Hallaq treat taqlid as reasoned; P4 author: both sides shared that premise, so the question was misposed, though Hallaq's article was the indispensable first step. Prephrase: Hallaq was right that the gate wasn't closed, but the better question is about how the law adapted through ordinary doctrinal work too. Watch for answers that keep only one half, or that inflate 'not only' into 'principally.'

choices.note: Half right and distorted. The passage does say Schacht's thesis is no longer defended, but it never claims Hallaq's evidence of continuing ijtihad leads to a 'taqlid-centered' account; that reframing comes from later research, and it doesn't replace ijtihad.
Opposite. The author says the refinements 'do not rehabilitate Schacht.' Nothing in the passage defends a modified closure thesis.

CORRECT. Paragraph 3: Hallaq's article 'has largely carried the day,' yet the debate 'had been framed by an assumption' that ijtihad measures vitality. Paragraph 4 says both sides shared this premise and locates adaptation also in ordinary doctrinal work.

Out of scope. The passage mentions abridgments only in Fadel's account of what taqlid did; it never explains how the closure thesis arose or attributes a mistake about abridgments to Western scholars.

Too strong. The author says adaptation lay 'not only' in the rare mujtahid, which keeps ijtihad in the picture; 'principal means' and 'demonstrated' overstate both the author's claim and what is reported of Fadel and Hallaq. It also omits Hallaq's refutation, half the passage.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Hallaq's evidence against the closure thesis included which one of the following?
choices: the fact that abridgments of school doctrine were consulted by judges of lower rank
the fact that later legal theorists lowered the qualifications for ijtihad that earlier theorists had set
the fact that Schacht relied on sources composed long after the tenth century
the fact that jurists of the tenth century explicitly denied that the gate of ijtihad had been closed
the fact that jurists in nearly every century after the tenth were recognized as mujtahids
questions.explanation: The second paragraph lists Hallaq's evidence 'of two kinds,' and the practical kind is that 'jurists in nearly every century after the tenth were recognized as mujtahids.' E restates it. A belongs to Fadel's later account, not Hallaq's 1984 evidence. B distorts the point about qualifications: Hallaq found them attainable, not lowered over time.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Locate the list of Hallaq's evidence and match one item.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, third through sixth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 2 gives two kinds of evidence: theory (ijtihad treated as indispensable; some theorists said no age could lack a mujtahid; qualifications attainable) and practice (mujtahids recognized in nearly every century; some claimed the rank). Plus the observation that the language of closure appears centuries late. The right answer will be one of these, possibly paraphrased.

choices.note: Wrong position-holder. Abridgments and lower-ranking judges come from Fadel's account in paragraph 3, research that followed Hallaq's article.

Distortion. The passage says the qualifications were 'demanding but attainable,' contrasting Hallaq's reading with the older account's; it says nothing about later theorists lowering earlier standards.
Not stated. The passage never discusses which sources Schacht used.
Not stated, and it runs against the passage: the language of closure 'enters the sources only centuries after' the tenth century, so tenth-century jurists would not be discussing it at all.
CORRECT. Paragraph 2: 'In practice, jurists in nearly every century after the tenth were recognized as mujtahids.'

questions.stem: The author mentions Fadel's comparison of a school's authoritative abridgments to a codified common law (third paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: suggest that Islamic law developed independently the same institutions as European legal systems
illustrate how a practice that the older thesis treated as a sign of decline could serve recognizable legal purposes
show that Fadel's conclusions contradict those Hallaq reached in his 1984 article
provide evidence that the qualifications for ijtihad were attainable in later centuries
concede that the closure thesis was correct about the rigidity of later Maliki law
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the debate assumed 'taqlid marks [a legal system's] decline,' and then presents Fadel's view that taqlid served uniformity and limited officials' discretion, with the abridgments working 'something like a codified common law.' The comparison shows taqlid doing familiar legal work, which is B. E is the trap for a reader who hears 'codified' as 'rigid': the author introduces Fadel to challenge, not concede, the decline reading.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the comparison is there: what claim it supports.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, second and third sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The sentence before Fadel names the assumption to be challenged: ijtihad = vitality, taqlid = decline. Fadel's account then gives taqlid a positive function (uniform rules, limits on discretion), and the common-law comparison makes that function recognizable. Prephrase: to show taqlid as a working legal mechanism, not a symptom of stagnation.

choices.note: Too strong and out of scope. The comparison is an analogy 'something like,' used to describe a function; the passage makes no claim about parallel independent development of institutions.

CORRECT. The preceding sentence identifies the assumption that 'taqlid marks its decline'; Fadel's account, capped by the common-law comparison, shows taqlid securing uniform rules and limiting discretion.
Distortion. The passage presents Fadel and the later Hallaq as moving in the same direction; it never says Fadel contradicts Hallaq's 1984 finding that ijtihad continued.
Wrong part. The attainability of the qualifications is Hallaq's evidence in paragraph 2; the abridgments concern taqlid, not ijtihad.
Opposite. A reader may hear 'codified' as 'rigid,' but the author uses Fadel to question the decline story, and paragraph 4 says these refinements 'do not rehabilitate Schacht.'

questions.stem: By saying that the question of whether the gate was closed is "less false than misposed" (fourth paragraph, third sentence), the author most probably means that the question
choices: has been answered incorrectly by most scholars who have addressed it
is meaningful only when applied to jurists of the highest rank
cannot be answered, because the relevant legal sources have not survived
rests on an assumption that directs attention away from much of what explains the law's capacity to adapt
was posed in bad faith by scholars who wished to portray Islamic law as stagnant
questions.explanation: The sentence follows the claim that both sides 'shared a premise that neither examined,' and it is followed by the claim that adaptation lay 'not only in the rare jurist' but in ordinary doctrinal work. A misposed question is one built on an assumption that misdirects inquiry, which is D. A takes 'false' literally; the author actually agrees with Hallaq's answer.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Interpret the phrase from its surroundings.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, second through fourth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: 'Less false than misposed' contrasts two ways a question can go wrong: having the wrong answer, or being badly framed. The surrounding sentences show the framing problem: the question assumes the existence of mujtahids is 'what mattered,' when adaptation also happened through interpreting, ranking, and extending doctrine. Prephrase: its premise points us at the wrong place.

choices.note: Distortion. The author accepts that Hallaq's answer ('no') was right; the problem is the framing, not that scholars answered incorrectly.

Shell game. The passage does contrast 'the rare jurist' with ordinary work, but it doesn't say the question makes sense for top-ranked jurists only; the point is that the question leaves out the ordinary work.
Out of scope. The passage says Hallaq studied 'the original legal sources'; nothing suggests the question is unanswerable for lack of evidence.

CORRECT. The shared premise was that mujtahids' existence 'was what mattered'; the author then says adaptation lay 'not only' in the rare mujtahid but in ordinary doctrinal work, which the question ignores.
Unsupported motive. The author attributes an unexamined assumption to both sides, Hallaq included; there's no charge of bad faith.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Hallaq's 1984 article would have been more persuasive had it argued that taqlid rather than ijtihad was the source of later Islamic law's vitality.
Evidence that later jurists claimed the rank of mujtahid more often than Hallaq reported would settle the questions the passage regards as most important.
Schacht was correct that later jurists confined themselves to explaining and applying the law, though wrong to regard this as stagnation.
A study of how jurists who followed a school's settled doctrine dealt with new cases would bear on whether later Islamic law could adapt.
The term taqlid was introduced by later scholars to describe a practice that earlier jurists had regarded as a form of ijtihad.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says the law's capacity to adapt lay 'not only in the rare jurist who reasoned directly from the sources but in the ordinary work of interpreting, ranking, and extending a school's settled doctrine.' So evidence about how doctrine-following jurists handled new cases is relevant to adaptability: D. B is the trap: the author says proving mujtahids existed 'was to concede that their existence was what mattered,' so more such evidence would not settle what the author thinks matters. C is the outside-knowledge trap: the passage nowhere endorses Schacht's description.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the author's own view, in the last paragraph, supports.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, especially the second and fourth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The author's view: (1) Hallaq was right; (2) both sides assumed ijtihad's presence is what matters; (3) adaptation also happened through ordinary work on settled doctrine. Prephrase a consequence: evidence about doctrine-following jurists counts when we ask whether the law adapted. Wrong answers will overstate, reverse the author's stance on Schacht, or add history the passage doesn't give.

choices.note: Too strong and against the passage. The author calls the article 'indispensable precisely because' it dismantled the closure story 'on its own terms'; nothing says it would have been better arguing for taqlid instead, and 'rather than ijtihad' exceeds the author's 'not only.'
Opposite of the author's point. Counting mujtahids is exactly what the author says concedes the shared premise; more of the same evidence wouldn't settle the better question.

Distortion. The author says the refinements 'do not rehabilitate Schacht' and describes later law as 'interpreting, ranking, and extending' doctrine, not merely explaining and applying it. Some readers know the revisionist literature and import this view; the passage doesn't state it.

CORRECT. Paragraph 4 locates the law's capacity to adapt partly in 'the ordinary work of interpreting, ranking, and extending a school's settled doctrine,' so a study of that work bears directly on adaptability.
Out of scope. The passage gives no history of the term taqlid or of how earlier jurists classified it.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Hallaq's 1984 article can most accurately be described as
choices: appreciation of its achievement, combined with the view that its framing of the question was limited
admiration for its evidence, tempered by doubt about whether its central conclusion is correct
skepticism about its methods, offset by approval of its influence on later scholarship
unqualified endorsement of both its conclusions and its framing of the debate
polite disagreement, on the grounds that later research has overturned its findings
questions.explanation: The author says the article 'largely carried the day' and 'remains indispensable,' but also that it shared with Schacht 'a premise that neither examined.' Appreciation plus a limit on its framing: A. B is the trap: the author never doubts Hallaq's conclusion that the gate wasn't closed, only the way the question was posed.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize the author's view of the 1984 article, including its degree.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, first sentence; paragraph 4, first, second, and last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Positive markers: 'largely carried the day,' 'remains indispensable,' 'cleared the ground.' Qualifying marker: both sides 'shared a premise that neither examined.' So: positive about the result, critical of the framing, and specifically not doubting the conclusion. Look for an answer that keeps the praise and puts the reservation on the framing.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Remains indispensable' and 'largely carried the day' are the appreciation; the shared, unexamined premise is the limitation on its framing.
Half right. The reservation is in the wrong place: the author accepts that the gate was not closed and calls the question 'misposed,' not wrongly answered.
Wrong target. The author never criticizes Hallaq's methods; the 'systematic and chronological study' is reported without objection.
Too extreme. The author explicitly faults the framing the article shared with Schacht.
Opposite. Later research 'refined' the debate and the author says refuting the thesis was 'a first step'; nothing says the findings were overturned.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim about where the law's capacity to adapt lay (fourth paragraph)?
choices: Several jurists of the fourteenth century claimed the rank of mujtahid, although some of their contemporaries disputed those claims.
Legal theorists in later centuries described the qualifications for ijtihad in greater detail than earlier theorists had.
Jurists who professed to follow a school's doctrine devised rules for new commercial practices by extending its earlier opinions.
Judges of lower rank in later centuries frequently departed from the doctrine set out in their school's authoritative abridgments.
Some Western scholars before Schacht had already argued that ijtihad continued after the tenth century.
questions.explanation: The claim is that adaptation lay 'not only in the rare jurist who reasoned directly from the sources but in the ordinary work of interpreting, ranking, and extending a school's settled doctrine.' C supplies such a case: professed followers of doctrine adapting the law to something new. A supports Hallaq's 1984 point about mujtahids, which the author says leaves the shared premise in place; it doesn't touch the claim about ordinary doctrinal work.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most supports the claim that adaptation occurred through ordinary work on settled doctrine.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, fourth sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The claim has a specific content: jurists working within settled doctrine (not mujtahids) still adapted the law. The strongest support is a case of exactly that: self-described followers of doctrine producing new rules. Watch for evidence about mujtahids (Hallaq's question, not the author's) and for facts that cut against the uniformity Fadel described.

choices.note: Irrelevant to this claim. Evidence about mujtahids bears on the 1984 question; the author's claim is about the work of jurists who did not reason directly from the sources.
Irrelevant. More detailed qualifications for ijtihad say nothing about how doctrine-following jurists adapted the law.

CORRECT. Professed followers of a school's doctrine producing rules for new practices by extending its earlier opinions is precisely 'interpreting, ranking, and extending a school's settled doctrine' as a source of adaptation.
Off target, and it cuts against Fadel's account that abridgments limited lower officials' discretion. Departing from doctrine is not adapting through it.
Out of scope. Who first argued against closure has no bearing on where adaptation happened.

questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with
choices: the historical process by which European states imposed codified law on Muslim societies
an argument that the modern state and premodern sharia are incompatible
the question of whether Islamist political movements have pursued prudent programs
the methods by which premodern jurists cultivated the moral character of Muslims
the reception of Western critical theory among scholars of Islamic law
questions.explanation: Passage A sets out Hallaq's argument that an Islamic state is 'an impossibility and a contradiction in terms'; passage B evaluates that argument's method. Both are about B's subject. C is drawn from passage A's remark that Hallaq does not ask whether Islamist programs are prudent, so it's a topic both passages set aside.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Name the topic common to both passages.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, first two sentences; passage B, first two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Passage A: Hallaq's thesis and its supports. Passage B: a methodological objection to that thesis. Common ground: Hallaq's incompatibility argument. Eliminate anything only one passage mentions, or that neither discusses at length.

choices.note: Out of scope. Neither passage narrates a historical process of imposition; passage A says only that the state is a 'European creation.'
CORRECT. Passage A presents the argument; passage B assesses it.
Shell game. Passage A mentions Islamist programs only to say Hallaq does not ask about them.
Too narrow, and passage A only. Moral self-cultivation is one feature of Hallaq's description of premodern sharia; passage B doesn't discuss it.
Too narrow. Passage B mentions 'the historical-critical tools of modern theory' in passing; neither passage is about the reception of critical theory.

questions.stem: According to passage A, Hallaq holds that rulers in the premodern sharia order
choices: derived their authority from the jurists, who appointed them
legislated only in matters that the jurists had left unsettled
fashioned the moral character of their subjects through the courts
were subject to a law whose authors were not themselves rulers
had no executive power independent of the jurists
questions.explanation: Passage A: sharia 'was elaborated by jurists who emerged from society rather than from government, and rulers, who held executive power, were themselves bound by a law they did not make.' D paraphrases that. E reverses the passage's statement that rulers 'held executive power.' A and B add claims a reader with background knowledge might supply but the passage never makes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what passage A says about premodern rulers.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, second paragraph, first and second sentences.

breakdown.analysis: One sentence carries the answer: rulers held executive power and were bound by a law made by jurists rooted in society. Prephrase: rulers were under a law they didn't author. Reject anything that adds a mechanism (appointment, residual legislation) the passage doesn't give.

choices.note: Unsupported. The passage says jurists made the law; it says nothing about jurists appointing rulers.
Unsupported. The passage says rulers were bound by 'a law they did not make'; it never describes a sphere where rulers legislated.
Wrong position-holder. Moral self-cultivation is something Muslims did through a wider set of practices; the passage says the modern state, not the premodern ruler, fashions its subjects.
CORRECT. Rulers were 'bound by a law they did not make,' a law elaborated by jurists who 'emerged from society rather than from government.'
Opposite. Passage A says rulers 'held executive power.'

questions.stem: The author of passage B quotes Abu-Odeh's statement that the modern state "is nothing but history" (first paragraph of passage B) primarily in order to
choices: show that Hallaq's account of the modern state is historically inaccurate
support the claim that the modern state may yet be remade
illustrate one side of a difference in method that the author goes on to criticize
concede that Hallaq's description of the modern state is correct in all respects
contrast Abu-Odeh's view of the state with that of Andrew March
questions.explanation: Passage B says 'The objection concerns method' and that Hallaq 'treats the two sides of his comparison in radically different ways': the Islamic order as a norm prior to history, the modern state as 'nothing but history.' The quotation fills in the second side of the asymmetry the author then criticizes: C. B is the trap: the final sentence does reuse the phrase, but that's a later application, not why the quotation is introduced.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what job the quotation does in passage B's argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, first paragraph, third through last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Read the sentence before the quotation: 'The modern state, by contrast,...' It completes a contrast with the preceding sentence about the Islamic order. The contrast is the 'radically different' treatment that is the methodological objection. Prephrase: it describes how Hallaq treats one side of the comparison.

choices.note: Distortion. Passage B says nothing in the critique 'requires denying' that the state is a historically specific European form; the complaint is about asymmetric treatment, not inaccuracy.
Shell game. The last sentence of passage B echoes 'nothing but history,' but the quotation is introduced to describe Hallaq's method, as the surrounding 'by contrast' shows.
CORRECT. The quotation gives the second half of the 'radically different' treatment: the Islamic order as a norm prior to history, the state as nothing but history.
Too extreme. Passage B grants that the state is historically specific, but 'nothing but history' is presented as a flaw in Hallaq's approach, not something conceded 'in all respects.'
Opposite. Passage B says March 'pressed a similar complaint,' so there's no contrast.

questions.stem: Hallaq, as presented in passage A, and the author of passage B would be most likely to disagree over whether
choices: the modern state is a political form that originated in Europe rather than elsewhere
the jurists who elaborated premodern sharia were learned in the law they developed
the modern state's law rests on a separation of what is from what ought to be
sharia enacted as the legislation of a modern state is changed by that enactment
contrasting the premodern sharia order with the modern state can establish that an Islamic state is impossible
questions.explanation: Hallaq reaches his conclusion that an Islamic state is 'an impossibility' by comparing two paradigms; passage B says such a comparison 'can show that the two differ... it cannot show that one of them is impossible.' That's E. D is the trap: it sounds like the crux, but passage B grants that sharia enacted by such a state 'ceases to be what it was,' which matches Hallaq's claim that attaching sharia to the state subordinates it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim on which the two hold opposed views. Both views must be supported.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, first and last paragraphs; passage B, first sentence and the last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Passage B is careful about what it concedes: the state is European-made and historically specific; enacting sharia changes it. What it denies: that comparing one order's ideal with another's record can show impossibility. Hallaq draws exactly that conclusion from the comparison. Answers B's author concedes are agreements, not disagreements.

choices.note: Agreement. Passage A calls the state 'a European creation'; passage B grants it is 'European-made.'
Agreement or not addressed. Passage B says few reviewers doubted Hallaq's command of his sources, and neither passage questions the jurists' learning.
Not disputed. Passage B never contests Hallaq's description of the state's law; its objection is to the asymmetric treatment of the two sides.
Agreement. Passage B concedes that sharia enacted as a state's legislation 'ceases to be what it was'; passage A says attaching sharia to the state subordinates it to an alien will.
CORRECT. Hallaq infers impossibility from the paradigm comparison; passage B says that comparison 'cannot show that one of them is impossible.'

questions.stem: The author of passage B would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about the argument presented in passage A?
choices: It is correct in its conclusion but relies on an inaccurate description of the premodern jurists.
It shows that the modern state and sharia differ, but its conclusion requires more than that difference.
It errs chiefly in describing the modern state as a European creation.
It fails because it draws on modern theory to criticize the modern state.
It establishes that an Islamic state is undesirable, though not that it is impossible.
questions.explanation: Passage B ends: a comparison of one order's ideal with another's record 'can show that the two differ, which no one disputes; it cannot show that one of them is impossible.' So B grants the difference and denies that it suffices for 'impossible': B. E is the near-miss for readers who know the reviews: some critics recast Hallaq's claim as one about undesirability, but passage B never says the argument establishes undesirability; it only says the comparison shows difference.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Determine passage B's overall assessment of Hallaq's argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, first two sentences and the last two sentences of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Passage B's verdict has two parts: (1) concession: the state is historically specific and European-made, and enacted sharia changes; the comparison shows difference; (2) denial: the comparison of ideal with record can't show impossibility. Prephrase: right that they differ, wrong that difference proves impossibility. Watch for answers that move the criticism to a point B concedes, or that credit the argument with a conclusion B never grants.

choices.note: Reversed. Passage B denies that the conclusion follows, and it criticizes Hallaq for not examining the premodern model historically, not for describing jurists inaccurately.
CORRECT. 'It can show that the two differ, which no one disputes; it cannot show that one of them is impossible.'
Opposite. Passage B says the critique doesn't require denying the state is 'European-made.'
Distortion. Passage B faults Hallaq for not turning the historical-critical tools on the Islamic model as well; using them on the state is described as effective ('devastating effect').
Outside knowledge trap. Passage B never says the argument establishes undesirability; 'Huntington-in-reverse' criticizes the comparison, not a narrower conclusion it grants.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?
choices: Passage B accepts much of passage A's account of the modern state but disputes that passage A's comparison supports its conclusion.
Passage B offers historical evidence that contradicts the account of premodern sharia given in passage A.
Passage B extends the argument of passage A by applying it to a case that passage A does not consider.
Passage B argues that the conclusion stated in passage A is true for reasons other than those passage A gives.
Passage B rejects both the account of the modern state in passage A and the conclusion that passage A draws from it.
questions.explanation: Passage B concedes that the state is a historically specific, European-made form and that enacted sharia changes, then objects that comparing one order's ideal with another's record cannot show impossibility. A says that. B is the trap: passage B complains that Hallaq doesn't test the premodern model against 'the conduct of actual dynasties,' but it doesn't supply such evidence itself.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how passage B stands to passage A as a whole.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, first two sentences, and the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Passage B's moves: concede (command of sources; state is historical and European; enacted sharia changes), then object on method (asymmetry), then conclude (difference, not impossibility). So partial acceptance plus a challenge to the inference. Reject answers that make B reject everything, supply its own counter-evidence, or agree with the conclusion.

choices.note: CORRECT. Passage B grants the state is 'historically specific, European-made' and that enacted sharia 'ceases to be what it was,' then argues the comparison 'cannot show that one of them is impossible.'
Distortion. Passage B says the gap between ideal and practice 'stays obscure' in Hallaq's account; it doesn't present historical evidence of its own.
Wrong relationship. Passage B criticizes rather than extends passage A's argument.
Opposite. Passage B denies that the comparison shows impossibility; it doesn't endorse the conclusion on other grounds.
Too strong. Passage B explicitly accepts key parts of passage A's account of the state.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the objection raised by the author of passage B?
choices: Some premodern rulers were praised by the jurists of their own time for submitting to the law in disputes with their subjects.
Several Western philosophers have criticized modernity's separation of what is from what ought to be, as Hallaq does.
Modern states differ considerably from one another in how deeply their bureaucracies penetrate the societies they govern.
Many premodern jurists lived far from the capital cities and held no official position under any ruler.
Hallaq's picture of sharia comes mainly from jurists' accounts of how law should work, and his picture of the state from how states have actually behaved.
questions.explanation: Passage B's objection is an asymmetry: the Islamic order is treated as a norm, the modern state as history, so the argument compares 'one order's ideal with another's record.' E confirms that asymmetry in the sources themselves. C is the tempting trap: it might suggest the state is treated too monolithically, a criticism some reviewers make, but passage B's objection is about ideal versus record, not variation among states.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify passage B's objection and find the fact that most supports it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, the sentences on 'radically different ways' and the sentence comparing 'one order's ideal with another's record.'

breakdown.analysis: The objection: Hallaq evaluates sharia by its norms and the state by its history. Support would show the comparison really is ideal-versus-record. Watch for facts that support Hallaq instead (rulers bound by law, jurists independent of government) and for a different criticism than the one B makes.

choices.note: Opposite tendency. Praise for law-abiding rulers supports passage A's picture of rulers bound by law; it does nothing to show an asymmetric method.
Irrelevant. This fits passage A's remark that some Western thinkers share Hallaq's critique; it doesn't touch B's objection.
A different criticism. Variety among states might suggest Hallaq treats the state too uniformly, but passage B's objection concerns comparing an ideal with a record, not variation among states.
Supports passage A's claim that jurists 'emerged from society rather than from government'; irrelevant to B's objection about method.

CORRECT. If the sharia side comes from jurists' accounts of how law ought to work and the state side from how states actually behaved, the comparison is exactly 'one order's ideal with another's record.'

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Saussure's hypothesis was ignored until Kuryłowicz showed that the comparative method can recover the pronunciation of sounds no descendant language preserves.
Hittite evidence showed that some of Saussure's posited units were real, without showing that internal analysis can fix their number or pronunciation.
The Hittite confirmation of Saussure's hypothesis demonstrates that the comparative method, rigorously applied, reliably recovers the prehistory of languages.
Because Hittite preserves only some of Saussure's coefficients, the laryngeal theory is no better supported now than it was before Kuryłowicz's article.
Saussure's coefficients sonantiques are best understood as the laryngeal consonants of Semitic, as Möller was the first to recognize.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph gives the author's verdict: the vindication claim 'is justified' but the claim about the method's reliability 'outruns the evidence,' since Hittite confirmed some units while their number and phonetics 'remain disputed.' B states both halves. C is the view the author attributes to 'some' and rejects; D overstates the author's qualification into a denial of any confirmation.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall conclusion about what the Hittite evidence shows.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraphs 3 and 4, especially the first and last sentences of paragraph 4.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraphs 1 and 2 tell the story; paragraph 3 gives two popular readings; paragraph 4 accepts the first and rejects the second. Prephrase: Hittite proved something was there, not exactly what. Expect a trap that adopts the stronger popular reading and one that turns the qualification into total rejection.

choices.note: Distortion. The author says the confirmation said little about phonetics, and the passage says Saussure 'specified what these units did, not how they were pronounced.' The answer credits the method with the very thing the author denies.
CORRECT. It keeps both sides of the author's qualified view: 'at least some' units were real consonants, but number and phonetic values remain unsettled by internal reasoning.
Wrong position-holder. This is the second claim in paragraph 3, held by 'some,' which the author says 'outruns the evidence.'
Too extreme. The author says Hittite confirmed 'more than his critics had allowed'; the qualification limits the confirmation, it doesn't cancel it.
Detail, and distorted. Möller's link to Semitic is a background fact in paragraph 2, not the passage's point, and the passage never says the Semitic identification is correct.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Saussure posited the coefficients sonantiques because
choices: certain sounds in Greek and Latin had no counterparts in the other Indo-European languages
the Semitic languages contained consonants that the Indo-European languages appeared to lack
a consonant appeared in Hittite in positions where the other languages had none
they let long-vowel roots be analyzed as following the same alternation as other roots
the reduced grade of most roots contained a vowel that could not be traced to a resonant
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says long-vowel roots 'seemed to break this pattern' of e-alternation, and Saussure 'proposed that they, too, consisted of e plus an element.' D paraphrases that. C is the later Hittite evidence, which came decades after the Mémoire; B is Möller's later linkage.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the reason the passage gives for Saussure's proposal.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph, sentences 3–5.

breakdown.analysis: This is a detail question, but the traps borrow facts from later in the story. Saussure's motive is in paragraph 1: the long-vowel roots didn't fit the e/zero pattern unless they contained a hidden element. Anything about Hittite or Semitic belongs to other people and later dates.

choices.note: Distortion. Greek and Latin are cited only as examples of a long-vowel root; the passage never says they had unique sounds.
Wrong position-holder. Linking the elements to Semitic laryngeals was Möller's later contribution, not Saussure's reason.
Wrong time. Hittite was deciphered in 1915 and Kuryłowicz wrote in 1927; this is the later confirmation, not Saussure's motive in 1879. A reader who knows the story's ending is drawn here.
CORRECT. Positing e plus a coefficient let the long-vowel roots fit the same full-grade/reduced-grade alternation as roots with resonants.
Distortion. The passage says that in the reduced grade a resonant becomes the vowel; it never claims most reduced grades had an unexplained vowel.

questions.stem: The author's reference to a planet whose existence had been calculated before it was observed (third paragraph) primarily serves to
choices: suggest that hypotheses in historical linguistics, like those in astronomy, can be confirmed only by direct observation
introduce a comparison that the author goes on to reject as overstating what the Hittite evidence showed
convey a characterization of the episode that the author accepts as accurate in its basic outline
contrast the precision of the physical sciences with the uncertainty that attends linguistic reconstruction
indicate that Saussure modeled his reasoning on methods developed in the natural sciences
questions.explanation: The planet comparison belongs to the first of the two claims in paragraph 3: a method posited an unseen entity and new evidence revealed it. The fourth paragraph opens, 'The first of these claims is justified.' So the comparison expresses a view the author accepts. B is the trap: the author does reject an overstatement, but it is the second claim ('Some go further'), not the planet comparison.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify what the planet comparison does in the argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, first sentence; fourth paragraph, first sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 3 has two claims, and paragraph 4 sorts them: the first is justified, the second outruns the evidence. Ask which claim the planet image belongs to. It's attached to the first sentence, the vindication story. The common error is to lump both claims together because the author is qualified overall.

choices.note: Distortion. The passage never says confirmation requires direct observation; in fact Hittite spelling, not observation of the parent language, supplied the evidence.
Shell game. The author rejects the second claim in paragraph 3, the one introduced with 'Some go further.' The planet comparison goes with the first claim, which the author calls 'justified.'
CORRECT. The comparison frames the episode as a prediction later confirmed by new evidence, and the author says that claim 'is justified,' while disputing only the broader lesson some draw from it.
Out of scope. No contrast between physical and linguistic science is drawn; the comparison likens the two.
Out of scope. The passage says nothing about where Saussure got his method; the comparison is the later tellers', not Saussure's.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following statements about the laryngeal now usually written *h1?
choices: Its existence rests more on internal analysis of the other languages than on Hittite evidence.
Most scholars now doubt that it existed, since Hittite preserves no consonant corresponding to it.
Kuryłowicz identified it as the source of the Hittite consonant written ḫ.
Hittite evidence shows that it was pronounced as a glottal stop rather than as a fricative.
Saussure explicitly included it among the coefficients he described in the Mémoire.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says *h1 'leaves no consonantal trace' in Hittite, 'so its existence still rests on the very internal reasoning that Hittite was supposed to have checked.' A says just that, hedged. B ignores the statement that most scholars 'work with three laryngeals'; E requires outside knowledge the passage doesn't supply.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage supports about *h1 specifically.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, sentences 3–5.

breakdown.analysis: Only one sentence mentions *h1: it leaves no trace in Hittite, so the case for it rests on internal reasoning. The traps will either overread that (scholars doubt it) or import knowledge from outside the passage (what Saussure himself said, how it was pronounced).

choices.note: CORRECT. The passage says its existence 'still rests on the very internal reasoning' rather than on Hittite, which leaves no consonantal trace of it.
Contradicted. Most scholars 'work with three laryngeals'; lacking Hittite support makes *h1 less directly confirmed, not widely doubted.
Opposite. Hittite ḫ reflects only some laryngeals, and *h1 is singled out as the one that leaves no trace there.
Unsupported. The passage lists glottal stops and fricatives only as disputed possibilities, and says Hittite shows nothing of *h1 at all.

Outside knowledge. The passage never says which of Saussure's coefficients corresponds to *h1, or how many he described; a reader who knows the history might assume an answer the passage doesn't give.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the view that the Hittite confirmation proves the reliability of the comparative method can most accurately be described as
choices: enthusiastic agreement tempered by regret that the theory was so long neglected
dismissive rejection of the comparative method as a source of knowledge about prehistory
neutral reporting of a view the author neither endorses nor criticizes
cautious acceptance, on the grounds that Hittite confirmed most of Saussure's specific claims
doubt that the evidence warrants so broad a conclusion, with acceptance of a narrower one
questions.explanation: The author says this claim 'outruns the evidence' and ends by saying what the episode does show: the method 'can detect that something must have been present.' That is doubt about the broad conclusion plus acceptance of a narrower one. B is too extreme; the author credits the method with real success.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize the author's attitude toward the 'proof of reliability' view.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, last sentence; the whole of the fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Locate the view (paragraph 3, 'Some go further') and the author's response (paragraph 4, 'outruns the evidence'). But the author isn't anti-method: the last sentence grants it real power. Look for skeptical-but-measured.

choices.note: Opposite. The author rejects this view; 'enthusiastic agreement' fits neither the view nor the tone.
Too extreme. The author says the method 'can detect that something must have been present'; that is a limit on the method, not a dismissal of it.
Wrong. The author takes a clear position: the claim 'outruns the evidence.'
Distortion. The author does not accept the view, and the passage says Hittite left 'open' the very matters Saussure had not specified while confirming only some units.
CORRECT. The author rejects the sweeping conclusion but accepts that the method can show 'that something must have been present.'

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most call into question the author's conclusion in the last sentence of the passage?
choices: Several other sounds that scholars posited for the Indo-European parent language on the basis of internal patterns have never been confirmed by any later evidence.
Hittite ḫ occurs in a number of words for which no laryngeal has been reconstructed in the parent language.
Saussure privately believed that his coefficients were consonants, although he did not say so in the Mémoire.
Some scholars who accept three laryngeals regard the phonetic values assigned to them as provisional.
Pronunciations assigned to the laryngeals by internal analysis alone, before Hittite was deciphered, were later borne out by new evidence.
questions.explanation: The last sentence says the method can detect 'that something must have been present' but cannot determine 'without further help, exactly what that something was.' E shows the method, unaided, did determine what the sounds were, which undercuts the second half. B targets the confirmation itself (the first claim of paragraph 3), not the conclusion about the method's limits; D is consistent with the author.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most undermines the author's final conclusion.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Break the conclusion into its parts: (1) the method can detect that something was there; (2) it cannot, unaided, say what. The likeliest target is (2): show the method, without outside help, correctly fixed the phonetics. Watch for answers that attack the Hittite confirmation instead, which is a different claim.

choices.note: Opposite. Failed predictions elsewhere would, if anything, support the author's caution about the method.

Wrong conclusion. This might weaken the claim that Hittite confirmed the theory, but the author's last sentence is about what the method can and can't determine, not about how strong the Hittite match is. It's the trap for readers who attack the nearest evidence.
Irrelevant. Saussure's private belief about the units' nature is not a result of the method, and it isn't shown to be correct.
Consistent with the author, who says the phonetic values 'remain disputed.'

CORRECT. If internal analysis alone had correctly fixed the laryngeals' pronunciation before Hittite, the method would have determined 'exactly what that something was' without further help, contrary to the author's claim.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to Saussure's reasoning as described in the first paragraph?
choices: A mathematician posits an unrecorded quantity in the few terms that break a sequence's rule, specifying its effect but not its nature.
An epigrapher deciphers a newly discovered inscription and finds in it a letter that appears in no other known text of the language.
A biologist explains an unusual trait in one species by comparing it with a similar trait in an unrelated family of species.
A historian reconstructs the content of a lost letter by collecting the replies that its recipients wrote.
A chemist predicts the atomic weight of an undiscovered element and later confirms the prediction by isolating the element in the laboratory.
questions.explanation: Saussure noticed that long-vowel roots broke the alternation pattern, posited a hidden element that would make them regular, and 'specified what these units did, not how they were pronounced.' A matches each feature. E is the trap: it captures the later confirmation, which belongs to Kuryłowicz and Hittite, not to Saussure's reasoning in paragraph 1.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the structure of Saussure's reasoning to a new case.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph, sentences 2–6.

breakdown.analysis: Abstract the reasoning: a regular pattern; exceptions; a posited hidden element that restores regularity; its function specified but not its nature. Note that confirmation isn't part of Saussure's reasoning; that comes in paragraph 2. Eliminate cases built on new evidence or on borrowing from another family.

choices.note: CORRECT. Regular pattern, exceptions, a posited unseen element defined by its effect and not its nature: the same structure as Saussure's coefficients.
Wrong part of the story. Finding a new sign in newly deciphered material parallels Hrozný and Kuryłowicz, not Saussure's reasoning from known forms.
Wrong method. Explaining by comparison with an unrelated family resembles Möller's link to Semitic, not Saussure's internal analysis.
Partial match. It reconstructs something unseen, but from direct responses to it rather than from irregularities in a pattern, and nothing is defined by function alone.
Half right. The prediction resembles Saussure's, but it specifies a property he left open and adds a confirmation step that belongs to the later episode.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Priming experiments in Hebrew and Arabic have vindicated the Arab grammarians' view that every word is formed by inserting a consonantal root into a pattern.
Studies of Modern Hebrew denominal verbs show that the consonantal root, though descriptively useful, has no place in an account of how words are formed.
Experimental evidence gives the root a real place in the mental lexicon without establishing that words are formed as the traditional analysis holds.
The traditional root-and-pattern analysis applies to Arabic but not to Hebrew, since only Arabic shows priming from word patterns.
The Arab grammarians anticipated modern psycholinguistics by recognizing that speakers store roots separately from patterns.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says the inference that the mind treats roots as units, so words are built from them, is 'too quick in one respect but not in another,' and concludes that the root 'is a real unit of the mental lexicon, even if its role in forming new words is narrower than the tradition assumed.' C states that. A is the defenders' view the author calls too quick; B is the stem theorists' view, which the author partly rejects.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall conclusion.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, especially its last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Three views: the traditional analysis (paragraph 1), the stem-based challenge (paragraph 2), and the priming evidence (paragraph 3). The author speaks in paragraph 4, splitting the difference: roots are psychologically real; the claim that all words are built from them isn't shown. Expect one trap for each side's full position.

choices.note: Wrong position-holder. This is the defenders' inference, which the author says is 'too quick' because the experiments 'do not show that every word is produced by inserting a root into a pattern.'
Wrong position-holder, and too strong for the author. This is Bat-El's conclusion; the author says the findings tell against any view denying roots psychological standing.
CORRECT. It keeps both halves of the author's verdict: roots are a real unit of the mental lexicon, but their role in forming words may be narrower than the tradition assumed.
Distortion. Pattern effects differed between the Arabic and the Hebrew noun studies, but root effects appeared in both, and the passage never confines the traditional analysis to Arabic.
Out of scope. The passage does not claim the grammarians made claims about mental storage; it applies their analysis to a modern question.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Frost, Forster and Deutsch found that
choices: primes sharing only a nominal pattern with a target noun speeded its recognition
root priming occurred only when the prime was presented long enough to be consciously read
primes sharing a root with a target speeded recognition only when the two words were close in meaning
Hebrew verbs and nouns derived from the same root were recognized equally quickly
words related in meaning but not sharing a root did not speed recognition of the target
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says, 'Words related in meaning but not sharing a root produced no priming.' E restates it. A reverses the noun-pattern finding, and C contradicts the point that the root effect 'could not be reduced to similarity of meaning.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage reports about the 1997 study.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, sentences 2–4.

breakdown.analysis: Straight retrieval. The passage reports three results: root primes helped; nominal-pattern primes didn't; meaning-related primes without a shared root didn't. Match one of these and watch for reversals.

choices.note: Opposite. A prime sharing 'only its nominal pattern did not' speed recognition. Pattern effects are reported for Arabic, by other researchers.
Opposite. Masked priming flashes the prime 'too briefly to be consciously read,' and the effect was found under those conditions.
Opposite. The passage says the root effect 'could not be reduced to similarity of meaning.'
Out of scope. The passage reports no comparison of recognition speed for verbs and nouns.
CORRECT. This is the finding that showed the root effect is not a meaning effect.

questions.stem: The author mentions praklit and priklet (second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: illustrate a feature of derived words that stem-based theorists say a root analysis fails to predict
show that Modern Hebrew has abandoned the root-and-pattern system described by the Arab grammarians
provide evidence that Hebrew speakers treat consonant clusters as psychological units
suggest that verbs derived from borrowed nouns are exceptions that the traditional analysis can safely ignore
illustrate the use of templates built on f-ʿ-l to classify the forms of words
questions.explanation: The pair shows a derived verb 'preserving the noun's initial pr, an arrangement that pouring the bare consonants into a verbal template would not predict,' which is the basis for Bat-El's conclusion that words are formed from stems. A captures that role. B overstates; the example concerns how some verbs are formed, not the whole system.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify the role of the Hebrew example.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, sentences 2–3.

breakdown.analysis: The example sits inside the stem-based argument: it's the data (cluster transfer) that the root analysis supposedly can't predict. So its job is evidence for the challenge. Traps will overstate it, attach it to the psycholinguistic studies, or assign it to the grammarians.

choices.note: CORRECT. It is the stem theorists' evidence: the verb keeps a cluster that inserting a bare root into a template would not produce.
Too strong. The example concerns one class of derived verbs; neither Bat-El nor the author is said to claim Hebrew has abandoned roots and patterns altogether.
Wrong part of the passage. The example is linguistic data about word formation, not a psycholinguistic finding about mental units.
Outside knowledge and opposite in effect. The passage never mentions borrowing, and the example is offered as a problem for the traditional analysis, not one it can ignore.
Shell game. The f-ʿ-l templates belong to Sibawayh in the first paragraph; the Hebrew pair is used to challenge that kind of analysis.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Priming results show that Modern Hebrew speakers form new verbs by inserting roots into verbal templates.
Bat-El's argument rests on a misreading of the analysis developed by al-Khalil and Sibawayh.
The root is best regarded as a convenient label for a family of words related in meaning.
A stem-based account of word formation could be consistent with evidence that readers register shared roots.
The traditional analysis has no bearing on the study of Modern Hebrew, which differs fundamentally from Classical Arabic.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says the experiments 'do not show that every word is produced by inserting a root into a pattern, and stem-based theorists need not deny that speakers register the consonants their stems share.' D paraphrases that compatibility. A is the defenders' overreach; C contradicts the finding that the root effect is not a meaning effect.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the author's own view supports.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, sentences 3–5.

breakdown.analysis: Separate the author from the defenders and the stem theorists. The author grants the stem theorists one thing (roots registered in reading need not mean roots build words) and the defenders another (roots have psychological standing). The key will likely be a modest compatibility claim.

choices.note: Wrong position-holder. This is the defenders' inference; the author says the experiments 'do not show' that words are produced this way.
Out of scope. The author never evaluates whether Bat-El understood the medieval grammarians.
Opposite. Priming from meaning alone didn't occur, so the root effect 'could not be reduced to similarity of meaning'; the author treats the root as a real unit, not a label.
CORRECT. The author says stem-based theorists 'need not deny that speakers register the consonants their stems share,' so stem formation and root effects in reading can coexist.
Too extreme and unsupported. The passage applies the root analysis to Hebrew throughout; it draws no such contrast.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim that the findings tell against any version of the stem-based view holding that roots have no psychological standing?
choices: Hebrew words that share a root are usually also similar in meaning.
Primes sharing three consonants in order with a target, but not its root, produced no priming in the same experiments.
Hebrew speakers who are asked to identify the root of a given word often cannot do so reliably.
Priming effects from shared roots are larger for Hebrew verbs than for Hebrew nouns.
New denominal verbs in Hebrew preserve the clusters of their source nouns more consistently in informal speech than in writing.
questions.explanation: The passage rules out meaning as the source of the root effect but not mere letter overlap; if shared consonants alone produced the priming, roots as such would have no special standing.
