B removes that alternative, so the effect must reflect the root as a unit. C looks like a weakener but concerns conscious judgment, whereas masked priming works below awareness.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most supports the claim that roots have psychological standing.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, sentences 3–4; fourth paragraph, sentence 4.

breakdown.analysis: The author's evidence is root priming that isn't explained by meaning. What other explanation is left open? Overlap of form: root-sharing words also share letters. A good strengthener closes that gap. Watch for answers about consciousness (irrelevant to masked priming) or about word formation (a different claim).

choices.note: Weakens if anything. If root-sharing words are usually similar in meaning, the effect might seem to be about meaning, though the passage already reports it isn't.
CORRECT. If sharing the same consonants in order without sharing a root yields no priming, the effect can't be mere letter overlap; it tracks the root itself.

Irrelevant. Masked priming measures processing 'too brief to be consciously read'; failure at conscious root identification doesn't bear on that. This is the trap for readers who take it as a weakener and then reverse.
Irrelevant comparison. A difference in size between verbs and nouns leaves the existence of root effects unchanged.
Out of scope. This concerns how verbs are formed, the stem theorists' topic, not whether roots have psychological standing.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?
choices: A traditional analysis is described, a challenge to it is shown to rest on a misunderstanding, and the traditional analysis is then reaffirmed.
Two rival theories are described, and experimental evidence is presented that decisively favors one of them.
A historical account of a grammatical tradition is given, and the author argues that modern linguists have neglected it.
An experimental finding is described, two theories that attempt to explain it are compared, and both are rejected.
A traditional analysis is described, a challenge to it is presented, relevant evidence is summarized, and the evidence's limits are assessed.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 gives the grammarians' analysis, paragraph 2 the stem-based challenge, paragraph 3 the priming studies, and paragraph 4 the author's verdict that the evidence is 'too quick in one respect but not in another.' E tracks all four. B is the trap: the author explicitly denies the evidence is decisive.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe the sequence of the passage's paragraphs.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First sentence of each paragraph; the whole of paragraph 4.

breakdown.analysis: Label each paragraph: tradition; challenge; evidence; assessment. The key will name all four, with the assessment mixed. Reject answers in which anything is 'decisive,' 'refuted' or 'rejected' outright.

choices.note: Distortion. The challenge is not shown to rest on a misunderstanding, and the author says the root's role in forming words may be 'narrower than the tradition assumed.'
Too strong. The author says treating the results as decisive is 'too quick'; the evidence favors neither side wholesale.
Out of scope. Paragraph 1 is background, and the passage never says modern linguists neglected the tradition; they engage it directly.
Wrong order and wrong verdict. The passage starts with the analysis, not an experiment, and the author accepts part of each position.
CORRECT. It names all four stages, and 'the evidence's limits are assessed' fits the author's mixed verdict: the evidence shows roots are real units but not that every word is built from one.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the position the author takes in the last paragraph?
choices: A historian argues that because a guild's records were destroyed, nothing can be known about its role in the town.
A historian concludes that a guild was real to its members, while doubting that it controlled every stage of production in its town.
A historian argues that a guild controlled every stage of production in its town, since its members recognized it as a real institution.
A historian concludes that a guild was an invention of later chroniclers, since production in the town was organized household by household.
A historian argues that two rival accounts of a guild's role are equally well supported and that the question cannot be settled.
questions.explanation: The author holds that the root 'is a real unit of the mental lexicon, even if its role in forming new words is narrower than the tradition assumed.' B has the same shape: real and recognized, but not as all-encompassing as claimed. C is the defenders' inference (real unit, so it does everything), which the author calls 'too quick.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the author's final position to a case in another field.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Abstract the author's view: X is real (against the strongest skeptics), but its role is narrower than its champions claim (against the strongest defenders). Look for the same two-sided structure, and reject answers that copy one side's inference.

choices.note: Wrong structure. The author doesn't reason from missing evidence to total ignorance; the evidence here is substantial.
CORRECT. Real and recognized, like the root in the mental lexicon, but with a role narrower than the strongest claim, like the root in word formation.
Analogous to the wrong position. This mirrors the defenders' leap from 'real unit' to 'the source of every word,' which the author rejects.
Analogous to the wrong position. This mirrors the strongest stem-based view, which the author says the findings tell against.
Wrong attitude. The author does not call the question unsettleable; the author reaches a definite, qualified conclusion.

sections.title: Reading Through Ideas 2: Wigner's puzzle and its critics · Gödel and the mechanical mind · Al-Ghazali and Hume on causal connection · Plantinga, Ibn Taymiyya, and belief without proof

passages.title: Wigner's puzzle and its critics
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
In 1960 the physicist Eugene Wigner published "The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Mathematics in the Natural Sciences." Wigner's puzzle was not that mathematics is useful, which no one disputes, but that concepts mathematicians develop for reasons of their own, such as elegance and generality, so often turn out to be exactly what physics requires. Complex numbers, which no physical observation suggested, prove indispensable to the formulation of quantum mechanics; Newton's law of gravitation, framed on rather crude observations, later proved accurate to better than a ten-thousandth of a percent. Wigner called the appropriateness of mathematics to physical law "a wonderful gift which we neither understand nor deserve."

Twenty years later the mathematician Richard Hamming offered several deflationary explanations. We see what we look for: the concepts and instruments we bring to nature already impose a mathematical form on what we find. We select the mathematics that fits and quietly discard what does not. And science answers comparatively few questions; much of human experience has never yielded to mathematical treatment at all. Philosophers of a naturalist bent have extended the point: if mathematics originated in abstraction from counting, measuring, and the shapes of things, and has grown into a general science of structure, then its fit with a world full of structure is no more surprising than a map's fit with the terrain from which it was drawn. Hamming himself, however, concluded that his explanations, even taken together, were not enough to account for what he had set out to explain.

Others have argued that the puzzle points beyond naturalism. Mark Steiner contended in 1998 that twentieth-century physicists repeatedly made discoveries by following what he called Pythagorean analogies, purely formal ones guided by notation and mathematical beauty, as when Dirac's equation for the electron led to the prediction of antimatter. Naturalism, Steiner argued, gives no reason to expect that such humanly parochial strategies would succeed. Alvin Plantinga has developed the thought in an explicitly theistic direction: if the physical world and the human mind both issue from a single rational Creator, then what he calls a deep concord between the mathematics we find compelling and the structure of nature is what one should expect, whereas the naturalist must regard it as a happy accident.

Neither the deflationary nor the theistic account settles the matter. Selection explains why physicists use the mathematics that fits; it does not explain why mathematics developed long before, and with no thought of, its eventual application was already available to be selected. On this point Wigner's puzzle survives Hamming's reply, as Hamming himself acknowledged. Yet the theistic reading is better understood as an inference to the best explanation than as a proof, and its force depends on comparative judgments that are hard to make precise: how often formal analogies have failed, and how much of their apparent success is the residue of a historical record that remembers its triumphs. The effectiveness of mathematics is best treated as a genuine datum that any account of the world must accommodate, one that sits more comfortably with some worldviews than with others, rather than as a demonstration of any of them.

sources.author: Eugene P. Wigner
sources.title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Mathematics in the Natural Sciences
sources.note: The founding essay (Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics 13): mathematical concepts chosen for their beauty keep fitting physical law; source of the quotation 'a wonderful gift which we neither understand nor deserve.'

sources.author: Richard W. Hamming
sources.title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Mathematics
sources.note: Reply in the American Mathematical Monthly offering partial explanations (we see what we look for, we select the mathematics that fits, science answers comparatively few questions, evolution) and conceding they leave the question essentially unanswered.

sources.author: Mark Steiner
sources.title: The Applicability of Mathematics as a Philosophical Problem
sources.note: Harvard University Press; argues that discovery by 'Pythagorean' formal analogies (e.g. Dirac and antimatter) succeeded in ways naturalism gives no reason to expect.

sources.author: Alvin Plantinga
sources.title: Where the Conflict Really Lies: Science, Religion, and Naturalism
sources.note: Oxford University Press; argues for 'deep concord' between theism and science, citing Wigner's puzzle as something theism expects and naturalism must treat as luck.

passages.title: Gödel and the mechanical mind
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Passage A

In 1961 the philosopher J. R. Lucas argued that Gödel's first incompleteness theorem shows that "minds cannot be explained as machines." The theorem states that any consistent formal system whose theorems can be generated mechanically, and which contains a modest amount of arithmetic, includes a sentence that the system can neither prove nor refute. This sentence, constructed so that in effect it asserts its own unprovability, is true if the system is consistent. Any machine that produces mathematical claims, Lucas reasoned, embodies such a system; so for any machine proposed as a model of a mind, there is a sentence that the machine cannot produce as true but that the mind can see to be true. Hence no machine can be an adequate model of the mind.

Roger Penrose revived and refined the argument in The Emperor's New Mind (1989) and Shadows of the Mind (1994). His emphasis falls on mathematical understanding. When a mathematician grasps that the rules of a formal system are sound, Penrose holds, she thereby grasps that its Gödel sentence is true, and this grasp is not itself an output of the system. If human mathematical insight were the product of a knowably sound algorithm, we could apply Gödel's construction to that algorithm and see the truth of a sentence it cannot prove. Penrose concluded that human understanding is not algorithmic, and he speculated that its noncomputable element has a physical basis in a yet-undiscovered theory uniting quantum mechanics and gravity.

Passage B

Most logicians have rejected the Lucas-Penrose argument, largely because of what it must assume about the mind. The theorem does not say that a system's Gödel sentence is true outright; it says that if the system is consistent, the sentence is unprovable in it and therefore true. The system can itself prove that conditional. What the human reasoner is supposed to add is knowledge that the system is consistent, and, as Hilary Putnam observed, nothing guarantees that we possess such knowledge for an arbitrary complicated system, least of all for the system, if there is one, that describes our own reasoning. Gödel's second theorem shows that a consistent system of this kind cannot prove its own consistency; a mind that was a machine would be in just this position, and the argument offers no evidence that we are not. Penrose's appeal to knowable soundness shifts but does not remove the difficulty: the argument shows at most that our reasoning cannot be captured by any algorithm we could know to be sound.

Gödel himself drew a more cautious conclusion. In his 1951 Gibbs Lecture he argued that his results establish a disjunction: either the human mind "infinitely surpasses the powers of any finite machine," or there exist absolutely unsolvable problems in number theory of a certain kind. Gödel was inclined to believe the first disjunct, but he did not claim that the theorems alone decide between the two.

sources.author: J. R. Lucas
sources.title: Minds, Machines and Gödel
sources.note: Philosophy 36: the original anti-mechanist argument from incompleteness; its opening sentence is the source of the quotation 'minds cannot be explained as machines.'

sources.author: Roger Penrose
sources.title: Shadows of the Mind
sources.note: Penrose's fullest version (after The Emperor's New Mind, 1989): human mathematicians do not use a knowably sound algorithm, with speculation about noncomputable physics.

sources.author: Kurt Gödel
sources.title: Some basic theorems on the foundations of mathematics and their implications (Gibbs Lecture, 1951)
sources.note: Published in Collected Works vol. III; states the disjunction, source of the quotation 'infinitely surpasses the powers of any finite machine.'

sources.author: Solomon Feferman
sources.title: Penrose's Gödelian Argument
sources.note: Review of Shadows of the Mind in Psyche 2: a logician's detailed account of where Penrose's use of the theorems goes wrong; Putnam's review in Bull. AMS 32 (1995) makes the parallel point about knowing consistency.

passages.title: Al-Ghazali and Hume on causal connection
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Passage A

The seventeenth discussion of al-Ghazali's The Incoherence of the Philosophers (c. 1095) opens with a thesis aimed at the Aristotelian philosophers, Avicenna foremost among them: "The connection between what is habitually believed to be a cause and what is habitually believed to be an effect is not necessary, according to us." When cotton is brought into contact with fire, al-Ghazali argues, observation shows only that the burning occurs together with the contact, not that it occurs by means of the fire. Nor is there any contradiction in supposing the contact without the burning. The regularity on which we rely reflects God's habitual course (ʿāda), which God may suspend, as when Abraham was cast into the fire and was not burned.

For much of the twentieth century this was read as straightforward occasionalism: God, not fire, is the only true agent of burning. Yet al-Ghazali goes on to offer a second account, one that allows fire a nature to burn while God retains the power to alter that nature or the cotton that receives it. Michael Marmura read al-Ghazali as an occasionalist; Richard Frank argued that he accepted secondary causes. Frank Griffel's 2009 study proposes that the seventeenth discussion deliberately leaves the question open. What al-Ghazali denies, on this reading, is not that causes operate but that their connection is necessary. Nor does the denial leave him a skeptic: God, he holds, creates in us the knowledge that the possible but extraordinary will not ordinarily occur.

Passage B

David Hume's analysis of causation, set out in A Treatise of Human Nature (1739–40) and recast in An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), begins from a question about ideas. Every idea, Hume held, is copied from some impression; from what impression, then, is the idea of necessary connection copied? Not from the objects themselves. When one billiard ball strikes another, we observe the first ball's motion, the contact, and the second ball's motion, but no power binding them. "One event follows another; but we never can observe any tie between them. They seem conjoined, but never connected." What experience supplies is constant conjunction: like events repeatedly followed by like events. After enough repetitions, the mind is carried by custom from the appearance of the one to the expectation of the other, and this felt determination is the impression from which the idea of necessity is copied. Necessity, on this account, is felt in the mind rather than perceived in objects.

It would be a mistake to read this as a debunking of causal belief. Hume denies that reason can justify the inference from past to future, but he treats custom as the indispensable guide of practical life and never suggests that anyone could do without it. The same reliance on uniform experience later grounds his argument, in the Enquiry's section on miracles, that testimony to a violation of the laws of nature can rarely if ever outweigh the experience that established those laws.

sources.author: al-Ghazali (trans. Michael E. Marmura)
sources.title: The Incoherence of the Philosophers (Tahāfut al-falāsifa): A Parallel English-Arabic Text
sources.note: The seventeenth discussion argues that the connection between habitual cause and effect is not necessary (cotton and fire, God's habitual course, Abraham); Passage A's opening quotation is the discussion's first sentence in Marmura's translation, as quoted in the Journal of the History of Philosophy (doi 10.1353/hph.2008.1685).

sources.author: Frank Griffel
sources.title: Al-Ghazali's Philosophical Theology
sources.note: Oxford University Press study arguing that the seventeenth discussion leaves al-Ghazali uncommitted between occasionalism and secondary causality, mediating between Marmura's occasionalist and Richard Frank's secondary-causes readings.

sources.author: David Hume
sources.title: An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding
sources.note: Section VII ('Of the Idea of Necessary Connexion') traces the idea of necessity to custom; Passage B's quotation ('One event follows another; but we never can observe any tie between them. They seem conjoined, but never connected.') is from that section; Section X is the argument on miracles. First published as Philosophical Essays Concerning Human Understanding.

sources.author: David Hume
sources.title: A Treatise of Human Nature
sources.note: Book 1, Part 3 gives the first version of the analysis of causation as constant conjunction plus the mind's customary transition (Books 1–2 in 1739, Book 3 in 1740).

passages.title: Plantinga, Ibn Taymiyya, and belief without proof
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
In "Reason and Belief in God" (1983), Alvin Plantinga challenged the evidentialist objection to theism: the claim that belief in God is irrational unless it is supported by adequate argument. The objection, he contended, rests on classical foundationalism, which counts a belief as properly basic—rightly held without being inferred from other beliefs—only if it is self-evident, incorrigible, or evident to the senses. Yet that criterion is itself none of these things, and no one appears to have inferred it from beliefs that are; by its own standard, the classical foundationalist ought not to accept it. Freed from it, Plantinga proposed that belief in God can be properly basic, much as perceptual and memory beliefs are: not groundless, since it arises in characteristic circumstances, such as beholding the starry heavens or feeling guilt, but not inferred from those circumstances either. In Warranted Christian Belief (2000) he developed the idea through what Calvin called the sensus divinitatis, "a kind of faculty or a cognitive mechanism" that, functioning properly, produces beliefs about God.

Critics answered with what Plantinga himself called the Great Pumpkin objection: if belief in God may be basic, why not the belief that the Great Pumpkin returns every Halloween? Plantinga replied that the Reformed epistemologist need not accept every belief as basic, since there is no natural tendency to believe in the Great Pumpkin as there is to believe in God. Critics have pressed that this reply succeeds only if the theist is already right about which tendencies are natural.

A strikingly similar position had been developed more than six centuries earlier by Ibn Taymiyya (1263–1328). In his Darʾ taʿāruḍ al-ʿaql waʾ l-naql, written against Fakhr al-Din al-Razi's rule that rational proofs take precedence whenever they appear to conflict with scripture, Ibn Taymiyya rejected the view of many theologians that knowledge of God must be acquired through rational reflection. Such knowledge, he held, is necessary for anyone whose fitra—the original disposition with which, according to a well-known hadith, every child is born—remains intact; it is upbringing and corrupting influence, not the lack of a proof, that turn people away from it. The philosopher Jamie Turner has argued that the resulting model can be seen as "wholly ‘Plantingan.’"

The parallel is real, but it should not be overstated. Plantinga's central claim is permissive and defensive: belief in God can be rational without argument, and if theism is true, such belief is probably warranted. Whether theism is true he leaves largely to other inquiries. Ibn Taymiyya makes no such conditional retreat; fitra belongs to an account of human nature that he takes revelation to have disclosed, and it orients a person not only toward assent but toward the love and worship of God. Interpreters also disagree about whether fitra contains knowledge at all or is instead a capacity that yields knowledge when unimpeded; on the latter reading, the comparison with Plantinga's faculty-based model is, if anything, closer. What the two share is less a doctrine than a refusal: neither grants that a believer who has never followed a proof therefore believes without warrant.

sources.author: Alvin Plantinga
sources.title: Reason and Belief in God
sources.note: Essay in Faith and Rationality (ed. Plantinga and Wolterstorff, University of Notre Dame Press) arguing that classical foundationalism is self-referentially incoherent, that belief in God can be properly basic, and answering the Great Pumpkin objection.

sources.author: Alvin Plantinga
sources.title: Warranted Christian Belief
sources.note: Oxford University Press; develops the Aquinas/Calvin model in which the sensus divinitatis, 'a kind of faculty or a cognitive mechanism' (the passage's quotation), produces beliefs about God, and argues that if Christian belief is true it is probably warranted.

sources.author: Jamie B. Turner
sources.title: An Islamic Account of Reformed Epistemology
sources.note: Philosophy East and West 71(3): critiques Erik Baldwin's 'Islamic externalism' and builds a Taymiyyan model of knowledge of God that, in the abstract's words (quoted in the passage), 'can be seen as wholly ‘Plantingan’.'

sources.author: Carl Sharif El-Tobgui
sources.title: Ibn Taymiyya on Reason and Revelation: A Study of Darʾ taʿāruḍ al-ʿaql wa-l-naql
sources.note: Brill (open access) study of the Darʾ taʿāruḍ, written against al-Razi's 'universal rule' giving reason priority over revelation, with an extended account of fitra in Ibn Taymiyya's epistemology.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Wigner's puzzle about the effectiveness of mathematics is fully dissolved once one recognizes that scientists select the mathematics that fits the phenomena they study.
The success of mathematics in physics shows that the physical world and the human mind must issue from a single rational Creator.
Deflationary accounts leave part of Wigner's puzzle unexplained, but the puzzle is better treated as evidence any worldview must accommodate than as a proof of one.
Because mathematics arose by abstraction from counting and measuring, its fit with the physical world is no more surprising than a map's fit with its terrain.
Theistic and naturalist interpretations of Wigner's puzzle are equally well supported, since neither can be stated with any precision.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph is the author's verdict: selection 'does not explain' the prior availability of the mathematics, so the puzzle 'survives Hamming's reply,' yet the theistic reading is 'an inference to the best explanation' rather than 'a proof,' and the effectiveness of mathematics is 'a genuine datum' rather than 'a demonstration.' C captures both halves. B gives Plantinga's view more force than the author allows; D is the naturalists' view, not the author's.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: State the author's overall conclusion about Wigner's puzzle and the two families of response.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, especially its first and last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraphs 1-3 lay out Wigner's puzzle, the deflationary replies, and the anti-naturalist and theistic readings. Paragraph 4 is the author: the deflationary replies do not explain everything (the puzzle 'survives'), and the theistic reading is not a proof. Prephrase: a real puzzle, partly but not fully explained away, that counts as evidence but proves nothing. Expect traps that keep only one half.

choices.note: Opposite of the author's view. The author says selection 'does not explain' why the mathematics was already available, so the puzzle 'survives Hamming's reply.'
Too strong. This is Plantinga's position pushed to a demonstration; the author says the theistic reading is 'an inference to the best explanation' and not 'a proof.'
CORRECT. It keeps both halves of paragraph 4: the deflationary replies leave something unexplained, and the effectiveness of mathematics is 'a genuine datum' rather than 'a demonstration.'
Wrong position-holder. This is the naturalist extension in paragraph 2, which the author never endorses and partly undercuts in paragraph 4.
Distortion. The author says the datum 'sits more comfortably with some worldviews than with others,' which denies that the views are equally supported.

questions.stem: The author mentions that Hamming concluded his explanations were not enough to account for what he had set out to explain (last sentence of the second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: note that a proponent of the deflationary explanations conceded that they leave something unexplained
show that Hamming ultimately came to share Wigner's view that the fit of mathematics to physics is an undeserved gift
suggest that Hamming rejected as overreaching the naturalist extension that philosophers made of his points
introduce the theistic interpretation as the alternative that Hamming himself preferred
indicate that the several explanations Hamming offered are, on reflection, inconsistent with one another
questions.explanation: The sentence reports that Hamming, who offered the deflationary explanations, judged them insufficient. The author returns to it in paragraph 4: the puzzle survives Hamming's reply 'as Hamming himself acknowledged.' A states that role. B over-reads the concession into agreement with Wigner's 'gift' language, which the passage never attributes to Hamming.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the author reports Hamming's concession.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last sentence of paragraph 2 ('however') and the third sentence of paragraph 4.

breakdown.analysis: 'However' marks a turn against the deflationary explanations just listed, and the author cites the same concession in paragraph 4 to support the claim that the puzzle survives. The function is to show that even the deflationist admitted the explanations fall short.

choices.note: CORRECT. Hamming offered the deflationary explanations and still judged them 'not enough'; the author later invokes this ('as Hamming himself acknowledged').
Too strong. Conceding that one's explanations are incomplete is not adopting Wigner's view that the fit is 'a wonderful gift'; the passage says nothing of Hamming's view of that phrase.
Shell game. The concession concerns Hamming's own explanations, not the naturalist philosophers' extension of them; nothing says Hamming rejected that extension.
Out of scope. The theistic reading appears only in paragraph 3 and is attributed to Plantinga; nothing links Hamming to it.
Distortion. 'Even taken together' implies the explanations are insufficient in combination, not that they conflict.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Steiner's argument against naturalism rests on which one of the following?
choices: the claim that complex numbers were suggested by no physical observation
the observation that much of human experience has never yielded to mathematical treatment
the premise that the human mind and the physical world have a common source
the imprecision of the observations on which Newton based his law of gravitation
the success of discovery strategies guided by notation and mathematical beauty
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says Steiner pointed to discoveries made by following 'Pythagorean analogies, purely formal ones guided by notation and mathematical beauty,' and argued that naturalism gives no reason to expect such strategies to succeed. E paraphrases that. A and D are Wigner's examples; C is Plantinga's premise.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says Steiner's argument depends on.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, first two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Detail questions punish attaching the right kind of fact to the wrong person. Steiner's evidence is the success of formal, human-flavored analogies (Dirac and antimatter); his claim is that naturalism does not predict that success.

choices.note: Shell game: Wigner's example in paragraph 1, not part of Steiner's argument as the passage presents it.
Wrong position-holder: this is Hamming's third point in paragraph 2, which if anything works against the puzzle.
Wrong position-holder: the common-Creator premise belongs to Plantinga, who 'developed the thought in an explicitly theistic direction.' The passage does not give it to Steiner.
Shell game: Wigner's Newton example from paragraph 1.
CORRECT. Steiner's evidence is discovery by 'Pythagorean analogies, purely formal ones guided by notation and mathematical beauty,' whose success naturalism gives 'no reason to expect.'

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the deflationary explanations described in the second paragraph is best described as
choices: dismissive, because they ignore the history of how and why mathematics developed as it did
partly receptive, because they explain why fitting mathematics is used but not why it was already on hand
wholly approving, because they show that the fit between mathematics and nature is unsurprising
skeptical, because they rest on speculative and untestable claims about the course of human evolution
receptive only to the naturalist extension, which the author regards as answering Wigner fully
questions.explanation: In paragraph 4 the author grants that 'Selection explains why physicists use the mathematics that fits' but adds that 'it does not explain why mathematics developed long before ... was already available to be selected.' That is partial acceptance, B. A is too extreme, and E credits the author with an endorsement the passage never gives.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pin down the author's precise degree of acceptance of Hamming-style explanations.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, second and third sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The author's sentence has a concession and a limit: selection does explain use; it does not explain availability. The attitude is qualified acceptance. Watch for answers that are too extreme in either direction, and for an answer that brings in evolution, which this passage never mentions.

choices.note: Too extreme. The author grants that selection explains something; 'dismissive' ignores the concession.
CORRECT. It mirrors the author's concession ('Selection explains why physicists use the mathematics that fits') and its limit (it 'does not explain' the prior availability).
Opposite. The author says the puzzle 'survives Hamming's reply.'
Out of scope. The passage mentions no evolutionary explanation; a reader who knows Hamming's essay might supply it, but the passage does not.
Distortion. The author never endorses the naturalist map analogy, and the objection about prior availability applies to it as well.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously undermine the author's reason for holding that Wigner's puzzle survives Hamming's reply?
choices: Several branches of mathematics that were first developed for physical applications later proved unexpectedly fruitful within pure mathematics itself.
Dirac regarded the beauty of an equation as more important than its agreement with the experimental results available at the time.
Wigner knew, when he wrote his essay, of sciences in which mathematics had been of little use.
Mathematicians have devised so many structures that nearly any regular pattern physicists find will match one already in existence.
Many physicists who rely on advanced mathematics in their daily work do not know the purposes for which that mathematics was originally developed.
questions.explanation: The author's reason is that selection cannot explain why suitable mathematics 'was already available to be selected.' If mathematicians have produced so much structure that almost any pattern will match something already on hand, prior availability is just what selection would predict, and the author's objection loses its force. A reverses the direction of application; the others leave the availability point untouched.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most damages the author's specific reason, not the puzzle in general.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, second and third sentences.

breakdown.analysis: First isolate the reason: selection explains use, not prior availability. To undermine it, show that prior availability is unsurprising, for example because the stock of available mathematics is so large that a match is nearly guaranteed. The traps are about mathematics and physics but miss that one link.

choices.note: Irrelevant: it concerns application running from physics to pure mathematics, the reverse of the puzzle the author discusses.
Irrelevant to the author's reason; at most it bears on Steiner's claim that beauty guided discovery.
Echoes Hamming's third point, but Wigner's knowledge has no bearing on whether selection explains prior availability.
CORRECT. If almost any pattern would match some existing structure, then suitable mathematics being 'already available to be selected' is what selection predicts, and the author's objection fails.
Irrelevant: what physicists know about the history of their tools does not affect whether those tools were available beforehand.

questions.stem: By "the residue of a historical record that remembers its triumphs" (fourth sentence of the fourth paragraph), the author most probably refers to
choices: the fact that the early triumphs of mathematical physics were later refined and absorbed into more accurate and general theories
the possibility that the apparent success of formal analogies is inflated because their failures are forgotten
the theistic view that the success of mathematics is what remains of a divine design
the tendency of historians of science to credit mathematicians rather than physicists with major discoveries
the claim that mathematics developed long before its physical application remains available to physicists long afterward
questions.explanation: The phrase is paired with 'how often formal analogies have failed' as a judgment the theistic inference depends on. A record that 'remembers its triumphs' preserves successes and forgets failures, so success may look more common than it was. That is B, a selection worry. C borrows the word 'residue' and attaches it to the theistic view the sentence is qualifying.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Interpret the phrase in its sentence.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth sentence of paragraph 4, after the colon.

breakdown.analysis: The sentence lists two hard comparative judgments: how often formal analogies have failed, and how much of their 'apparent success' is a residue of selective memory. Prephrase: some of the success may be an artifact of remembering only the wins.

choices.note: Distortion. Refinement of theories is not what a record that 'remembers its triumphs' suggests; the point is selective memory, not later improvement.
CORRECT. 'Apparent success' plus a record that 'remembers its triumphs' means the successes may be overcounted because the failures drop out.
Shell game. 'Residue' is attached here to the theistic view, which the sentence is qualifying, not describing.
Out of scope. Credit between mathematicians and physicists is never discussed.
Shell game. This is the author's prior-availability point from the second sentence of paragraph 4, not the meaning of this phrase.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the explanation, described in the second paragraph, that we select the mathematics that fits and quietly discard what does not?
choices: A key opens a lock because a locksmith cut it specifically to match that lock's pins.
A scholar finds that an unknown script can be read with a dictionary compiled centuries earlier for another language.
A gardener's plants thrive because she waters them on a strict schedule.
A photographer's pictures all look blue because she always shoots through a blue filter.
A shopper tries on dozens of ready-made jackets and buys only the one that fits, leaving the rest on the rack.
questions.explanation: The selection explanation says the fit results from choosing among many candidates and discarding the misfits. E matches that: many ready-made options, one kept because it fits. D is the trap: it matches Hamming's other explanation (we see what we look for, because our instruments impose the form), and B describes Wigner's puzzle itself.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the structure of the selection explanation to a new case.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, second through fourth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Get the structure down before reading the choices: many things already exist, we try them, we keep what fits, and the misfits are forgotten. Paragraph 2 gives several different explanations, and the traps match the others.

choices.note: Wrong mechanism. The key is made to order for the lock; selection explains fit by choosing among things already made, not by making something for the case.
Opposite: this is Wigner's puzzle, something developed for another purpose that unexpectedly fits, not an explanation of it.
Simple causation with no selection among candidates.
Tempting, but this matches 'we see what we look for' (the observer's tools impose the form), a different explanation in the same paragraph.
CORRECT. Many ready-made candidates, the one that fits is kept, and the misfits stay on the rack, which is the structure of 'we select the mathematics that fits and quietly discard what does not.'

questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with
choices: explaining the method by which Gödel constructed a sentence that asserts its own unprovability
defending the claim that human mathematical understanding is not algorithmic
assessing whether consciousness has a physical basis in quantum gravity
whether Gödel's incompleteness results show that the human mind is not a machine
tracing the influence of Gödel's own philosophy of mind on Lucas and Penrose
questions.explanation: Passage A presents the Lucas-Penrose argument that Gödel's theorem shows minds are not machines; passage B presents objections and Gödel's more cautious disjunction. Both are about whether the theorems support that conclusion, D. B is the conclusion of passage A only.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the topic common to both passages.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First sentence of each passage.

breakdown.analysis: A comparative main-point answer has to cover both passages without taking one side. A argues yes, B argues the theorems alone do not show it. The shared question is whether incompleteness refutes mechanism.

choices.note: Too narrow. Both passages describe the sentence briefly as background; neither explains how it is constructed.
Covers only passage A. Passage B argues the case has not been made.
A detail from the end of passage A; passage B never discusses physics.
CORRECT. A argues that the theorems show 'minds cannot be explained as machines'; B argues they do not show this by themselves.
Distortion. Gödel's view appears only in B's last paragraph, and neither passage claims it influenced Lucas or Penrose.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is mentioned in passage B but not in passage A?
choices: a result establishing that a consistent formal system of the relevant kind cannot prove its own consistency
the claim that the Gödel sentence of a formal system is true provided that the system is consistent
the notion of an algorithm that is knowably sound
the requirement that the formal system in question be able to express at least a modest amount of arithmetic
a proposed physical basis, in a theory not yet discovered, for the noncomputable element of human thought
questions.explanation: Only passage B mentions Gödel's second theorem ('a consistent system of this kind cannot prove its own consistency'). B is the trap: passage A also says the sentence 'is true if the system is consistent,' so the conditional appears in both, though only B makes it the center of an objection.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find an item that appears in B and is absent from A.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Scan both passages for each choice.

breakdown.analysis: Check each choice against both passages. Items in both, or only in A, are out. The second theorem is the only item that appears in B and nowhere in A.

choices.note: CORRECT. Passage B: 'Gödel's second theorem shows that a consistent system of this kind cannot prove its own consistency.' Passage A mentions only the first theorem.
In both passages. Passage A says the sentence 'is true if the system is consistent'; B only stresses that the claim is conditional.
In both: A says 'a knowably sound algorithm,' and B refers to 'Penrose's appeal to knowable soundness.'
Only in passage A ('contains a modest amount of arithmetic').
Only in passage A (Penrose's speculation about quantum mechanics and gravity).

questions.stem: The author of passage B would most likely regard Lucas's claim, as reported in passage A, that the mind can see to be true the sentence a machine cannot produce as true as
choices: mistaken, because the Gödel sentence of a consistent system is in fact false
correct, because human reasoners can verify the consistency of any formal system
warranted only if the mind knows that the system in question is consistent
irrelevant, because Gödel's theorem applies only to systems that contain no arithmetic
acceptable for simple systems but refuted by Gödel's second theorem for every system
questions.explanation: Passage B says the theorem shows only that the sentence is true 'if the system is consistent,' and that what the human must add is 'knowledge that the system is consistent,' which 'nothing guarantees.' So B's author would accept Lucas's claim only on that condition, C. E overstates: B says the argument 'offers no evidence that we are not' in the machine's position, not that the second theorem refutes Lucas for every system.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply passage B's objection to the specific claim in passage A.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, fourth sentence; passage B, second through fourth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: B's objection is conditional: the mind can see that the Gödel sentence is true only if it knows the system is consistent. So B does not deny the claim outright; it makes the claim depend on a condition. Prephrase: true only given knowledge of consistency.

choices.note: Distortion of the mathematics. Both passages say the sentence is true if the system is consistent.
Opposite. B says 'nothing guarantees that we possess such knowledge for an arbitrary complicated system.'
CORRECT. B: what the reasoner must add is 'knowledge that the system is consistent,' so Lucas's claim holds only where that knowledge is available.
Contradicts both passages: the theorem applies to systems that do contain arithmetic.
Too strong. B uses the second theorem to show that a machine-mind could not establish its own consistency, not to refute the claim 'for every system.'

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken the argument presented in the first paragraph of passage A?
choices: Some formal systems that contain arithmetic have been proved consistent by mathematicians using methods that go beyond the resources of those systems themselves.
Accomplished mathematicians have sincerely accepted as consistent formal systems that were later shown to be inconsistent.
Some true arithmetical statements that are unprovable in standard formal systems are of genuine mathematical interest rather than mere curiosities.
Penrose's proposed physical theory uniting quantum mechanics and gravity has not been confirmed.
Lucas first presented his argument to philosophers rather than to logicians.
questions.explanation: Lucas's argument needs the mind to 'see' that a machine's Gödel sentence is true, which, as passage B makes explicit, requires seeing that the system is consistent. If capable mathematicians have confidently judged inconsistent systems to be consistent, the mind's supposed ability to see this is in doubt, B. D is aimed at the second paragraph, not the first.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most damages Lucas's argument as stated in paragraph 1 of passage A.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, paragraph 1; passage B makes the hidden premise explicit.

breakdown.analysis: Lucas's argument has a hidden premise: the mind can recognize the truth of the Gödel sentence, which (given the theorem's conditional form) means recognizing consistency. Evidence that people misjudge consistency attacks that premise. Make sure the choice targets paragraph 1, not Penrose.

choices.note: Neutral at best. That some systems are known consistent does not show the mind can see the consistency of the system that is supposed to model it; if anything it slightly helps Lucas.
CORRECT. If skilled mathematicians accept inconsistent systems as consistent, the mind's ability to 'see' the truth of Gödel sentences, which depends on seeing consistency, is called into question.
Irrelevant truth: whether the unprovable truths are interesting has no bearing on whether minds can recognize them.
Wrong target: this bears on Penrose's speculation in paragraph 2, not on Lucas's argument in paragraph 1.
Irrelevant: who first heard an argument has no bearing on whether it is sound.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by passage B's account of Gödel's 1951 position?
choices: Gödel held that if the human mind surpasses every finite machine, then every number-theoretic problem of the relevant kind must be solvable by it.
Gödel believed that his incompleteness theorems by themselves show that some problems in number theory are absolutely unsolvable.
Gödel regarded his theorems alone as sufficient to show that the mind surpasses every machine.
Gödel allowed that both alternatives in his disjunction might turn out to be false.
Gödel was committed to holding that if no problem of the specified kind is absolutely unsolvable, the mind surpasses every finite machine.
questions.explanation: Gödel held that his results establish 'either' the mind 'infinitely surpasses the powers of any finite machine,' 'or' there are absolutely unsolvable problems. If the second alternative is false, the first must be true, which is E. A reverses the inference: a disjunction lets you go from denying one side to affirming the other, not from affirming one side to denying the other.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Draw a valid inference from Gödel's disjunction as passage B states it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, final paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Treat the disjunction as 'M or U.' What follows validly is 'if not U, then M' and 'if not M, then U.' What does not follow is 'if M, then not U' (both could hold), that either one is established on its own, or that both could fail. Gödel leaned toward M, but the theorems alone do not decide.

choices.note: Invalid inference. 'Either M or U' does not imply that M rules out U; both alternatives could hold, and the passage gives Gödel no such claim.
Too strong. That is only one alternative of the disjunction, and the passage says Gödel 'was inclined to believe the first.'
Contradicts the passage: he 'did not claim that the theorems alone decide between the two.'
Contradicts the passage: he held that his results 'establish' the disjunction, so at least one alternative is true.
CORRECT. Given 'either the mind surpasses any finite machine or there are absolutely unsolvable problems,' denying the second alternative commits one to the first.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between passage A and passage B?
choices: Passage A presents a mathematical theorem and its consequences, and passage B argues that the theorem itself was never validly proved.
Passage A presents an argument, and passage B offers further considerations in support of its conclusion.
Passage A presents an argument, and passage B questions a premise it requires and offers a more guarded conclusion.
Passage A presents two incompatible arguments about the mind, and passage B shows that only the earlier of the two is sound.
Passage A defends a view about the mind, and passage B argues that the mind is in fact a machine.
questions.explanation: Passage B accepts the theorems as stated, identifies what the Lucas-Penrose argument 'must assume about the mind' (knowledge of consistency), questions that assumption, and ends with Gödel's 'more cautious conclusion.' That is C. E is the tempting overstatement: B says the argument 'offers no evidence that we are not' machines, which is not an argument that we are.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how passage B responds to passage A.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First and last sentences of passage B.

breakdown.analysis: B does not dispute the mathematics; it disputes an assumption ('what it must assume about the mind') and then offers Gödel's disjunction as a more limited conclusion. Watch for answers that turn 'the argument fails' into 'the opposite is true.'

choices.note: Distortion. B accepts the theorems; it disputes what they show about the mind.
Opposite. B says most logicians 'have rejected' the argument.
CORRECT. B targets the assumption of 'knowledge that the system is consistent' and closes with Gödel's 'more cautious conclusion.'
Distortion. Penrose's version is presented as a refinement of Lucas's, not as incompatible with it, and B says Penrose's version also fails to remove the difficulty.
Too strong. B argues that the case against mechanism is not made, not that mechanism is true.

questions.stem: The author of passage B regards Penrose's appeal to knowable soundness as
choices: a decisive improvement that answers the objections raised against Lucas
flawed chiefly because it misstates the content of Gödel's first theorem
irrelevant to Lucas's argument because it concerns physics rather than logic
a reformulation that relocates the central difficulty without resolving it
successful in showing that no algorithm whatever could capture human reasoning
questions.explanation: Passage B says Penrose's appeal 'shifts but does not remove the difficulty,' since the argument then shows 'at most that our reasoning cannot be captured by any algorithm we could know to be sound.' D paraphrases 'shifts but does not remove.' E is the trap: it drops 'we could know to be sound' and states the stronger conclusion B denies.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find B's specific assessment of Penrose's refinement.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, last sentence of the first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The key sentence has two parts: the refinement 'shifts' the difficulty (so it does something) but 'does not remove' it, and the most it shows is limited to knowably sound algorithms. An unknowable algorithm is left open.

choices.note: Opposite: B says the refinement 'does not remove the difficulty.'
Out of scope. B never says Penrose misstates the theorem; a reader who knows the reviews might bring this in, but the passage does not.
Distortion. 'Knowable soundness' is a logical notion; physics enters only in Penrose's separate speculation in passage A.
CORRECT. 'Shifts but does not remove the difficulty': the refinement moves the problem without solving it.
Too strong. B says the argument shows 'at most' that no algorithm 'we could know to be sound' captures our reasoning, which leaves open an algorithm we cannot know to be sound.

questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with
choices: explaining how a philosopher's denial of necessary connection was shaped by his views about miracles
assessing competing interpretations of a thinker's account of how causes produce their effects
presenting a thinker's view that observation reveals no necessary link between an event and what follows it
tracing the idea of necessary connection to the feeling produced in the mind by its experience of repeated sequences of events
contrasting a theological explanation of natural regularity with a psychological one
questions.explanation: Passage A presents al-Ghazali's thesis that observation shows burning only 'together with' the contact, not 'by means of' the fire; passage B presents Hume's claim that we 'never can observe any tie' between events. Each passage's subject is such a thinker's denial, so (C). (E) describes the relationship a reader sees between the two passages, not what either passage is about; (B) and (D) each fit one passage only.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the subject common to both passages.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The opening sentences of each passage and each passage's central claim.

breakdown.analysis: Passage A: al-Ghazali denies that the connection between habitual cause and effect is necessary; the second paragraph discusses how to read him. Passage B: Hume finds no impression of necessary connection in objects and traces the idea to custom. The shared core is the denial that experience reveals a necessary link. Test every choice against both passages.

choices.note: Miracles appear in both passages, but as consequences or illustrations (Abraham in A; Hume's later argument in B), not as the main subject. And in B, the miracles argument follows from the analysis rather than shaping it. Distortion.
This is passage A's second paragraph only. Passage B reports no competing interpretations of Hume. Half right.

CORRECT. A: observation shows the burning occurs 'together with the contact, not that it occurs by means of the fire.' B: 'we never can observe any tie between them.' Both passages are built around this position.
This is passage B's account exactly, but passage A grounds regularity in God's habitual course, not in the mind's response to repetition. One passage only.

Tempting because it names the real difference between the two thinkers. But neither passage contrasts the two; each presents one thinker. The choice describes the pair, not what each passage is concerned with.

questions.stem: Passage A's reference to God's "habitual course" (last sentence of the first paragraph) and passage B's use of the word "custom" (first paragraph) differ in that
choices: the former belongs to the one who produces a regular sequence of events, the latter to one who observes it
the former is said to explain why fire burns cotton, whereas the latter is said to be insufficient to explain any expectation about the future
the former is presented as a source of certain knowledge, whereas the latter is presented as a source of mere opinion
the former is derived from repeated observation, whereas the latter is copied from an impression of external objects
the former is the philosophers' term for a necessity in nature, whereas the latter is Hume's term for constant conjunction
questions.explanation: In A the regularity 'reflects God's habitual course,' which 'God may suspend': the habit belongs to the agent who produces the events. In B 'the mind is carried by custom' from one appearance to the expectation of the other: the habit belongs to the observer. That is (A). (D) reverses the passages' terms, and (E) gives al-Ghazali's term to his opponents.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Compare what the two 'habit' words refer to in their own passages.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: A, first paragraph, last sentence; B, first paragraph, the sentence beginning 'After enough repetitions'.

breakdown.analysis: Read each word in context. A: 'The regularity on which we rely reflects God's habitual course, which God may suspend.' Whose habit? God's, the one who makes fire and burning go together. B: 'the mind is carried by custom from the appearance of the one to the expectation of the other.' Whose habit? The mind's, the one watching. Prephrase: same word, different bearer. A reader who knows that both thinkers 'appeal to habit' may miss this.

choices.note: CORRECT. A: the regularity 'reflects God's habitual course' and 'God may suspend' it, so the habit is the producer's. B: 'the mind is carried by custom,' so the habit is the observer's.
Half right at best. A says the regularity reflects God's habit, but B never says custom fails to explain expectation; it says custom produces the expectation. Distortion of B.

A says God creates in us knowledge that the extraordinary will not ordinarily occur, but it does not call the habitual course itself a source of certain knowledge, and B never calls custom's product 'mere opinion'; it calls custom 'the indispensable guide of practical life.' Out of scope.

Reversal and shell game. In B, the idea of necessity is copied from an impression, and that impression is in the mind, not of external objects; nothing in A derives God's habitual course from observation.

Wrong position-holder. 'Habitual course' is al-Ghazali's term, used against the philosophers, who held the connection necessary. And custom in B is the mind's transition, not constant conjunction, which is what experience supplies.

questions.stem: Al-Ghazali, as described in passage A, and Hume, as described in passage B, would be most likely to disagree over whether
choices: observing fire in contact with cotton reveals that the fire produces the burning
contact between fire and cotton has regularly been followed by burning in past experience
reason can demonstrate that future events will resemble past ones
there exists a being capable of suspending the regular course of nature
nature's regularity makes it unreasonable to credit a report that it was once suspended
questions.explanation: Al-Ghazali accepts that Abraham 'was cast into the fire and was not burned,' a reported suspension of the habitual course; Hume holds that testimony to a violation of the laws of nature 'can rarely if ever outweigh the experience that established those laws.' They would disagree over (E). They agree on (A) and (B); the passages say nothing that sets them against each other on (C) or (D).

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim one thinker would accept and the other reject, on the evidence of the passages alone.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: A, first paragraph, last sentence (Abraham); B, last sentence (miracles).

breakdown.analysis: First list where they agree: neither thinks observation shows a necessary tie, and both accept that the regularity holds. The disagreement lies in what each makes of the regularity. For al-Ghazali it is a habit God may suspend, and he credits the report about Abraham. For Hume, uniform experience nearly always outweighs testimony to a violation. Watch for choices that rely on what you know about Hume's religion rather than what passage B says.

choices.note: Both deny it: al-Ghazali says observation shows only that the burning occurs 'together with the contact'; Hume says 'we never can observe any tie.' They agree.
Both accept the regularity: al-Ghazali speaks of 'the regularity on which we rely'; Hume of 'constant conjunction.' Agreement, not disagreement.

Passage B says Hume 'denies that reason can justify the inference from past to future,' but passage A says nothing about whether al-Ghazali thinks reason can demonstrate it. No basis for a disagreement.
The outside-knowledge trap. A reader who knows Hume's reputation as a religious skeptic may pick this, but passage B says nothing about whether Hume believed in such a being. Out of scope for B.

CORRECT. Al-Ghazali credits the report that Abraham 'was not burned'; Hume holds that testimony to a violation of the laws of nature 'can rarely if ever outweigh the experience that established those laws.'

questions.stem: According to passage A, Griffel's reading of the seventeenth discussion holds that al-Ghazali
choices: regarded God as the only true agent of the burning of cotton
accepted that created things act as secondary causes
gave up, in his second account, the thesis that the connection between cause and effect is not necessary
left unresolved whether events come about through God alone or also through secondary causes
regarded our knowledge of the regularity of nature as uncertain
questions.explanation: Passage A says Griffel's 2009 study 'proposes that the seventeenth discussion deliberately leaves the question open,' the question being the one on which Marmura (occasionalism) and Frank (secondary causes) divide. That is (D). (A) is the older and Marmura's reading, (B) is Frank's.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage attributes to Griffel specifically.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, third through sixth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The paragraph lines up three readings: occasionalism (the twentieth-century reading, and Marmura's), secondary causes (Frank's), and Griffel's: the question is left open. The trap is assigning the other scholars' readings to Griffel.

choices.note: Wrong position-holder. This is the twentieth-century occasionalist reading, which the passage attributes to Marmura, not Griffel.
Wrong position-holder. This is Richard Frank's reading.
Distortion. On Griffel's reading what al-Ghazali denies throughout is that the connection is necessary; the second account keeps that denial while allowing fire a nature.
CORRECT. Griffel 'proposes that the seventeenth discussion deliberately leaves the question open,' the question dividing occasionalism from secondary causes.
Opposite. The passage says the denial does not 'leave him a skeptic': God creates in us the knowledge that the extraordinary will not ordinarily occur.

questions.stem: The author of passage B mentions Hume's argument about miracles (last sentence of the passage) primarily in order to
choices: suggest that Hume's analysis of causation was motivated by a wish to discredit religious testimony
illustrate that Hume relied on expectations grounded in experience though he denied that reason could justify them
concede that Hume's analysis has a skeptical consequence that the author elsewhere denies
identify an inconsistency between Hume's account of the origin of necessity and his later treatment of testimony about miracles
explain why Hume concluded that necessity is felt in the mind rather than perceived in objects
questions.explanation: The second paragraph argues that Hume's analysis is not 'a debunking of causal belief': he relies on custom as 'the indispensable guide of practical life.' The miracles sentence begins 'The same reliance on uniform experience,' showing Hume himself putting that reliance to work in an argument. That is (B). (D) and (C) read tension into a sentence offered as support.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the last sentence does for the second paragraph's claim.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, first sentence (the claim) and the phrase 'The same reliance on uniform experience.'

breakdown.analysis: The paragraph's claim: reading Hume as debunking causal belief is a mistake. Support: he treats custom as indispensable. Then the miracles argument, introduced as 'the same reliance': further evidence that Hume trusts experience-based expectation, even using it to weigh testimony. Prephrase: an example of Hume leaning on custom-based expectation.

choices.note: Out of scope, and a trap for readers who know Hume's reputation. The passage says nothing about his motives; it presents the miracles argument as growing out of the analysis ('later grounds'), not as its motive.

CORRECT. 'The same reliance on uniform experience' links the miracles argument to the preceding claim that Hume, though he 'denies that reason can justify the inference from past to future,' treats custom as indispensable.
Opposite. The sentence supports the author's denial that the analysis is a debunking; it concedes nothing.
The author presents no inconsistency; the miracles argument is said to rest on 'the same reliance' the analysis describes.
Wrong part. The mind-not-objects conclusion is drawn in the first paragraph from the billiard-ball argument, not from the miracles sentence.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by passage A?
choices: Al-Ghazali held that it would be contradictory to suppose fire in contact with cotton without the cotton's burning.
Avicenna maintained that God could suspend the burning of cotton brought into contact with fire.
Griffel's reading settles the dispute between Marmura and Frank in Frank's favor.
Al-Ghazali regarded the extraordinary events he counted as possible as ones that frequently occur.
On Griffel's reading, denying necessary connection is compatible with fire's having a nature to burn.
questions.explanation: On Griffel's reading 'what al-Ghazali denies... is not that causes operate but that their connection is necessary,' and al-Ghazali's second account 'allows fire a nature to burn' while keeping God's power to alter it. So the denial and a burning nature can go together: (E). (A) is the opposite of the passage's third sentence; (C) misreads 'leaves the question open.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the statement the passage supports without going beyond it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, second sentence (the second account) and fifth sentence (what is denied).

breakdown.analysis: Combine two statements: the second account gives fire a nature to burn; and Griffel says al-Ghazali denies only that the connection is necessary, not that causes operate. Together: denying necessity doesn't require denying fire's nature. Eliminate choices that reverse the passage or assign views to the wrong person.

choices.note: Opposite: 'Nor is there any contradiction in supposing the contact without the burning.'
Wrong position-holder. The thesis that the connection is not necessary is aimed at the philosophers, 'Avicenna foremost among them'; nothing says Avicenna allowed that God could suspend the burning.
Distortion. Griffel's study 'proposes that the seventeenth discussion deliberately leaves the question open,' which favors neither side.
Opposite: God creates in us the knowledge that 'the possible but extraordinary will not ordinarily occur.'
CORRECT. The second account 'allows fire a nature to burn,' and on Griffel's reading the denial is 'not that causes operate but that their connection is necessary.'

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the origin of the idea of necessary connection as Hume explains it in passage B?
choices: A traveler who has crossed a bridge many times without incident comes to believe that it is well built, and a later inspection confirms that it is.
A child who sees a coin appear suddenly from behind her ear concludes, from that one performance, that the magician has a special power.
A listener who has heard a melody many times feels that its last note must follow the one before, and takes this necessity to be in the melody rather than in himself.
A researcher who finds that two quantities rise and fall together concludes that one causes the other, though both are in fact effects of a third.
A cook who follows a recipe exactly expects the dish to match the photograph because the recipe's author has promised that it will.
questions.explanation: Hume's account has three steps: repeated sequences, a felt determination of the mind produced by custom, and an idea of necessity copied from that feeling, which is 'felt in the mind rather than perceived in objects.' The listener in (C) has all three, including a feeling produced by repetition that he mistakes for a property of the thing. (D) is the classic causal flaw, but Hume's point is not about mistaking which thing is the cause.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the structure of Hume's explanation to a new case.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph, last three sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Abstract the account: (1) like followed by like, many times; (2) the mind is carried by custom to expect the second; (3) that felt determination is the source of the idea of necessity, which belongs in the mind, not the objects. The right analogue needs repetition, a felt expectation, and necessity located in the mind though seemingly in the thing.

choices.note: Repetition and a belief, but the belief is about a property that inspection can confirm. Hume's point is that no inspection finds the necessary tie, and nothing here puts the necessity in the mind.
One performance, not repetition, and an inference to a hidden power rather than a feeling produced by custom.
CORRECT. Repetition, an expectation that feels compulsory, and necessity that is felt in the listener though taken to be in the melody, matching 'felt in the mind rather than perceived in objects.'
A genuine reasoning error (a common cause), but Hume's account is not that we pick the wrong cause; it is about where the idea of necessity itself comes from.
The expectation rests on a promise (authority), not on custom formed by repeated experience.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Ibn Taymiyya anticipated Plantinga's reformed epistemology so closely that Plantinga's work adds little to the earlier account.
Ibn Taymiyya's account of fitra, like Plantinga's view, denies that warranted belief in God requires proof, though the two differ significantly.
Plantinga's reply to the Great Pumpkin objection fails, but Ibn Taymiyya's account of fitra escapes the difficulty that reply faces.
Disagreement among interpreters about the nature of fitra makes any comparison between Ibn Taymiyya and Plantinga premature.
Plantinga answered the evidentialist objection to theism by showing that the classical foundationalism on which it rests does not meet its own standard.
questions.explanation: The passage sets out Plantinga's view, finds 'a strikingly similar position' in Ibn Taymiyya, and then says 'The parallel is real, but it should not be overstated,' ending on what the two share: neither grants that a believer without proof 'therefore believes without warrant.' (B) captures parallel plus qualification. (E) is accurate but is only the first paragraph.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: State the passage's overall point, including the author's qualification.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, first sentence; fourth paragraph, first and last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Structure: Plantinga's position (P1), an objection and reply (P2), Ibn Taymiyya's similar position (P3), the author's qualified comparison (P4). The main point must carry both the similarity and the limits. Watch for choices that keep only one half, or one paragraph.

choices.note: Too strong. The author calls the parallel 'real' but says it 'should not be overstated' and never ranks the two thinkers' contributions.
CORRECT. 'The parallel is real, but it should not be overstated,' with the shared ground being that neither grants a believer without proof 'therefore believes without warrant.'
The author reports the critics' doubt about Plantinga's reply without endorsing it, and never says Ibn Taymiyya's account escapes it.
Opposite. The author says the interpretive disagreement leaves the comparison 'if anything, closer' on one reading; it does not make comparison premature.
True to the first paragraph, but that is only the starting point; it leaves out Ibn Taymiyya and the comparison that occupies the rest of the passage.

questions.stem: The primary function of the second paragraph is to
choices: argue that Plantinga's position would license belief in arbitrary objects
show that Plantinga revised his account of properly basic belief in response to his critics
explain why Ibn Taymiyya's account of fitra is not exposed to an objection that Plantinga's account of properly basic belief faces
present an objection to Plantinga's view, his reply, and a doubt raised about that reply
illustrate the evidentialist objection to theism by means of an example
questions.explanation: The paragraph gives the Great Pumpkin objection, Plantinga's reply ('there is no natural tendency to believe in the Great Pumpkin'), and the critics' rejoinder that the reply 'succeeds only if the theist is already right about which tendencies are natural.' That is (D). (A) assigns the critics' argument to the author.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe what the second paragraph does.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: All three sentences of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Three sentences, three moves: objection, reply, doubt about the reply. The author takes no side here. The right answer describes all three without attributing the objection to the author.

choices.note: Wrong position-holder. The paragraph reports that critics raised this objection; the author does not argue for it.
Out of scope. Plantinga's reply defends his view; the paragraph says nothing about a revision.
Ibn Taymiyya does not appear until the third paragraph, and the passage never says his account escapes the objection.
CORRECT. Objection ('why not the belief that the Great Pumpkin returns'), reply ('no natural tendency'), and doubt ('succeeds only if the theist is already right').
The evidentialist objection, that belief in God needs argument, is set out in the first paragraph. The Great Pumpkin objection is a different objection, aimed at Plantinga's answer to it.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Plantinga argued that classical foundationalism
choices: does not meet the standard it sets for beliefs that may properly be accepted
wrongly counts perceptual and memory beliefs as properly basic
was first formulated as an objection to Calvin's account of the sensus divinitatis
requires that belief in God be produced by a properly functioning faculty
allows belief in the Great Pumpkin to be properly basic
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says the classical foundationalist criterion 'is itself none of these things, and no one appears to have inferred it from beliefs that are; by its own standard, the classical foundationalist ought not to accept it.' That is (A). (E) borrows the Great Pumpkin from the next paragraph, where it is aimed at Plantinga, not at classical foundationalism.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what Plantinga says about classical foundationalism.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph, second and third sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The criterion: a belief is properly basic only if self-evident, incorrigible, or evident to the senses. Plantinga's point: the criterion fails its own test. Paraphrase: it doesn't meet its own standard.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'By its own standard, the classical foundationalist ought not to accept it.'
Distortion. Plantinga appeals to perceptual and memory beliefs as models for properly basic belief; he doesn't fault classical foundationalism for counting them.
Out of scope. Calvin is mentioned only as the source of the term sensus divinitatis.
Shell game. The properly functioning faculty is Plantinga's own model from 2000, not a requirement of classical foundationalism.
Shell game. The Great Pumpkin objection is raised against Plantinga's view in the second paragraph.

questions.stem: By "no such conditional retreat" (fourth paragraph), the author most probably means that Ibn Taymiyya
choices: does not concede that any theologians held that knowledge of God requires rational reflection
does not allow that a person's fitra can be corrupted by upbringing
does not make his claim depend on a supposition whose truth he leaves for others to settle
does not defend his account of fitra against the charge that it would license belief in arbitrary objects such as the Great Pumpkin
does not abandon the view that rational proofs should take precedence over scripture
questions.explanation: The phrase answers the preceding sentences: Plantinga's claim is that 'if theism is true, such belief is probably warranted,' and 'Whether theism is true he leaves largely to other inquiries.' Ibn Taymiyya makes no claim of that conditional form; he takes fitra to belong to an account of human nature disclosed by revelation. That is (C). (D) borrows the Great Pumpkin, which the passage never connects to Ibn Taymiyya.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out what 'such' refers back to.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, second through fourth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: 'Such' points back to Plantinga's move: claim warrant if theism is true, and leave whether it is true to others. A 'retreat' to that conditional form is what Ibn Taymiyya doesn't make. Prephrase: he doesn't hedge his claim on an assumption he leaves unsettled.
