choices.note: Contradicts the third paragraph: Ibn Taymiyya 'rejected the view of many theologians that knowledge of God must be acquired through rational reflection,' which acknowledges that they held it.
Contradicts the third paragraph: 'upbringing and corrupting influence... turn people away from it.'
CORRECT. Plantinga's claim is conditional ('if theism is true') and leaves the truth question 'largely to other inquiries'; Ibn Taymiyya's account of fitra is not hedged this way.
Shell game. The Great Pumpkin objection is raised against Plantinga, and the passage never says how Ibn Taymiyya would answer it.
Reversal. That rule is al-Razi's, which the Darʾ taʿāruḍ was written against.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Fitra, properly understood, contains knowledge of God rather than merely a capacity that yields such knowledge.
Plantinga holds that belief in God is warranted whether or not theism is true.
Plantinga's sensus divinitatis, unlike Ibn Taymiyya's fitra, orients a person toward love and worship as well as toward belief.
The most important difference between the two thinkers is that Ibn Taymiyya wrote against theologians whereas Plantinga wrote against evidentialist critics of theism.
On either reading of fitra the passage mentions, Ibn Taymiyya's account remains comparable to Plantinga's.
questions.explanation: The author reports the dispute over whether fitra 'contains knowledge at all or is instead a capacity' without settling it, and says that on the capacity reading the comparison is 'if anything, closer.' 'If anything, closer' presupposes the comparison already holds on the other reading, and the closing sentence names what the two share. So the author would accept (E). (A) asks the author to settle a dispute the author leaves open.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the author's own claims support.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, fifth and sixth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Separate the interpreters' dispute from the author's verdict. The author doesn't choose between the readings; the author says one of them makes the comparison closer still. Combine with 'The parallel is real': the comparison survives either way. Choices that pick a side in the dispute go beyond the passage.

choices.note: The author reports that interpreters disagree and takes no side. Too strong: it settles an open question.
Opposite: Plantinga's claim is that 'if theism is true, such belief is probably warranted,' which is conditional on truth.
Reversal: the passage says it is fitra that 'orients a person not only toward assent but toward the love and worship of God.'

The passage mentions al-Razi and the theologians, and the evidentialist objection, but never ranks differences. The differences it stresses are the conditional form and the account of human nature. Unsupported.
CORRECT. 'On the latter reading, the comparison... is, if anything, closer' implies the comparison already stands on the former reading, and 'The parallel is real.'

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the doubt that critics have raised about Plantinga's reply to the Great Pumpkin objection (second paragraph)?
choices: Belief in the Great Pumpkin is held by very few adults in any society.
People's judgments about which of their belief-forming tendencies are natural follow whatever beliefs they already hold.
Plantinga developed his account of the sensus divinitatis further in later work.
Some beliefs held without inference, such as memory beliefs, are widely regarded as rational.
Many people who once held belief in God as basic later came to support that belief with arguments drawn from natural theology.
questions.explanation: The critics' doubt is that Plantinga's reply 'succeeds only if the theist is already right about which tendencies are natural.' If judgments of naturalness simply follow whatever beliefs a person already holds, the theist's judgment that belief in God is natural gives no independent support, which deepens the doubt: (B). (A) and (D) help Plantinga.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Critics: Plantinga's reply succeeds only if the theist is already right about which tendencies are natural.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Plantinga's reply depends on there being a natural tendency to believe in God and none to believe in the Great Pumpkin.

breakdown.analysis: The doubt is that the judgment 'this tendency is natural' cannot be made independently of the belief it is supposed to support. Strengthen it by showing that judgments of naturalness are driven by prior belief.

choices.note: Opposite. If almost no one believes in the Great Pumpkin, that tends to support Plantinga's claim that there is no natural tendency to such belief.

CORRECT. If judgments of naturalness follow 'whatever beliefs they already hold,' the theist's judgment that belief in God is natural depends on already holding that belief, which is the critics' worry.
Irrelevant. Later development of the account says nothing about whether the reply avoids depending on prior belief.
Opposite. This supports the analogy between belief in God and memory beliefs that Plantinga uses.
Irrelevant. People later adding arguments says nothing about whether judgments of naturalness depend on prior belief.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Turner's claim that the Taymiyyan model can be seen as "wholly ‘Plantingan’" (third paragraph) is most accurately described as
choices: unqualified endorsement of the claim as an account of how the two thinkers relate
doubt that any meaningful parallel between the two thinkers exists
neutrality, since the author reports the claim without evaluating whether it accurately describes the relationship
acceptance of the parallel it identifies, with a caution that differences limit it
disapproval, on the grounds that the claim ignores the disagreement among interpreters about fitra
questions.explanation: The sentence after Turner's claim is the author's verdict: 'The parallel is real, but it should not be overstated,' followed by the differences in aim and account of human nature. That is acceptance with a caution: (D). (C) misses that the fourth paragraph evaluates the claim; (E) misreads the interpretive dispute, which the author says makes the comparison closer on one reading.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize the author's response to Turner's claim.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: End of the third paragraph and first sentence of the fourth.

breakdown.analysis: Turner's claim closes paragraph 3; paragraph 4 opens 'The parallel is real, but it should not be overstated.' 'Wholly' is exactly the kind of overstatement the author cautions against, but the author keeps the parallel. Look for mixed, qualified wording.

choices.note: Too extreme. The author immediately says the parallel 'should not be overstated' and lists differences.
Too extreme the other way. The author says 'The parallel is real.'
The fourth paragraph evaluates the claim directly, so the author is not neutral.
CORRECT. 'The parallel is real, but it should not be overstated,' with the differences (Plantinga's conditional, defensive claim; fitra's place in a revealed account of human nature) as the limits.
Distortion. The author raises the interpretive dispute but says that on one reading it makes the comparison 'if anything, closer'; it is not offered as a reason to reject Turner's claim.

sections.title: Reading Through Ideas 3: The unity of the classical Arabic qasida · Hopkins, Scotus, and sprung rhythm · Gutas and the Graeco-Arabic translation movement · Gettier cases and the inescapability argument

passages.title: The unity of the classical Arabic qasida
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
The ninth-century scholar Ibn Qutayba, in his Book of Poetry and Poets, passed on an account, which he credited to an unnamed man of learning, of how the classical Arabic ode, the qasida, proceeds. The poet begins at an abandoned campsite, weeps over its traces, and recalls the beloved who once lived there; this amatory prelude, the nasib, is meant to win the listener's attention, since love touches every heart. Next comes the rahil, the desert journey, in which the poet describes his sleepless night travel and his exhausted camel, and so establishes his claim on the patron. Only then does he turn to the madih, praise that urges the patron to be generous. In many pre-Islamic odes the closing place is held instead by fakhr, the poet's boast on behalf of himself and his tribe.

To a number of nineteenth- and early twentieth-century European scholars, the qasida looked like a string of loosely joined episodes, its sections held together by convention and by a single rhyme and meter rather than by any developing idea. Later scholarship complicated the charge without simply refuting it. Geert Jan van Gelder's study of the medieval Arab critics, Beyond the Line, found that they judged poetry chiefly verse by verse and gave comparatively little attention to the coherence of the whole poem. If that is right, to demand organic unity of the qasida is to impose a standard foreign to its own tradition.

Suzanne Pinckney Stetkevych has argued that the sequence is not a mere juxtaposition but a ritual progression. In The Mute Immortals Speak (1993), drawing on Arnold van Gennep's analysis of rites of passage, she reads the nasib as a phase of separation, in which the poet is cut off from the beloved and from a way of life now in ruins; the rahil as a liminal phase, in which he crosses a desert outside the social order; and the closing boast or praise as reaggregation, his return to the community in a new status. In The Poetics of Islamic Legitimacy (2002) she extended the model to the court panegyric, using Marcel Mauss's account of gift exchange to treat the ode as an offering answered by the patron's reward, and argued that such poetry "created, encoded, and promulgated a myth and ideology of legitimate Arabo-Islamic rule."

The ritual reading's chief merit is that it gives the parts a direction: the ode moves from loss through ordeal to restored belonging, explaining why the sections come in this order. Yet caution is warranted. Ibn Qutayba's sequence describes a norm, not a law; many surviving odes omit the journey or lack a closing boast or praise, and a model that makes them incomplete rites risks treating variation as failure. Moreover, Ibn Qutayba's own explanation was rhetorical: each section prepares the listener for the next. That account, too, finds coherence in the sequence, but locates it in the poet's design on an audience rather than in a ritual pattern. The ritual reading is best taken as a powerful interpretation of the many odes that realize the full pattern, not as a key to every qasida.

sources.author: Suzanne Pinckney Stetkevych
sources.title: The Mute Immortals Speak: Pre-Islamic Poetry and the Poetics of Ritual
sources.note: Cornell University Press; reads the pre-Islamic qasida as ritual in form and function, mapping nasib, rahil and closing boast onto van Gennep's phases of the rite of passage, beginning with Labid's Mu'allaqa.

sources.author: Suzanne Pinckney Stetkevych
sources.title: The Poetics of Islamic Legitimacy: Myth, Gender, and Ceremony in the Classical Arabic Ode
sources.note: Indiana University Press; extends the ritual model to the panegyric ode as ritual exchange (after Mauss); source of the quotation 'created, encoded, and promulgated a myth and ideology of legitimate Arabo-Islamic rule' (p. ix).

sources.author: Michelle Hartman
sources.title: Review of The Poetics of Islamic Legitimacy, American Journal of Islamic Social Sciences 21:2
sources.note: A review that quotes the book's thesis sentence from p. ix verbatim (used to verify the passage's quotation) and assesses its case against reading panegyric as mere flattery.

sources.author: Geert Jan van Gelder
sources.title: Beyond the Line: Classical Arabic Literary Critics on the Coherence and Unity of the Poem
sources.note: Brill; the standard study of how medieval Arab critics treated coherence beyond the single verse, finding that whole-poem unity was not their central concern.

passages.title: Hopkins, Scotus, and sprung rhythm
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Gerard Manley Hopkins called the meter of his mature poems "sprung rhythm." In the preface he later wrote for his manuscript poems, he explained that it is measured by stresses alone: each foot has a single stress, falling on its first syllable, and may consist of that stressed syllable by itself or with as many as three unstressed ones. Strong syllables can therefore collide, as conventional meter seldom allows. Hopkins did not claim to have invented the device; he pointed to precedents in nursery rhymes, in Greek and Latin lyric, and in old English verse such as Piers Plowman. Yet writing to R. W. Dixon in 1878 about The Wreck of the Deutschland, the first poem he composed throughout in the new meter, he recalled that he had "long had haunting my ear the echo of a new rhythm."

Hopkins is equally known for two coinages. "Inscape" names the distinctive, unified pattern that makes a thing the thing it is; "instress" names both the energy that holds that pattern together and the force with which it strikes a perceiver. Many critics have linked these ideas to John Duns Scotus, the medieval Franciscan whose term for the principle of individuation, haecceitas, means "thisness": whatever makes this thing this one rather than merely an instance of its kind. Hopkins came upon Scotus's commentary on the Sentences in 1872, and a journal entry from that summer records that whenever he took in an inscape of sky or sea he now thought of Scotus. In 1879 he praised Scotus in the sonnet "Duns Scotus's Oxford" as "Of realty the rarest-veinèd unraveller," and in "As Kingfishers Catch Fire" each mortal thing announces its own selfhood: "myself it speaks and spells."

Skeptics object that this genealogy runs backward. Hopkins was already using both "inscape" and "instress" in notes on Parmenides in 1868, four years before he read Scotus, so Scotus cannot have supplied the concepts. Even Christopher Devlin, the Jesuit editor who explored the affinity, cautioned against simply identifying inscape with haecceitas. Sprung rhythm, too, has a sufficient ancestry without any theology: the precedents Hopkins himself named, the strong-stress verse of Old English, and the Welsh poetic craft whose chiming consonants he studied in north Wales after 1874. On this view, to read the meter as an expression of haecceity is to mistake a metaphor for an explanation.

The skeptics are right about origins, but origins do not settle meaning. Scotus gave Hopkins neither his terms nor his meter. What he seems to have given was a warrant: an account on which a creature's distinctness is no accident of matter but something positively real and willed by God, so that attending to it becomes a kind of praise. The same may hold for the verse. A meter that counts only stresses, letting them crowd together when the sense demands, allows each strong syllable its own weight instead of leveling it into regular alternation; it is hardly accidental that "stress" reappears inside "instress." The theology does not explain how the lines scan, but it may explain why Hopkins thought scanning them so was worth the trouble.

sources.author: Gerard Manley Hopkins (ed. Robert Bridges)
sources.title: Poems of Gerard Manley Hopkins
sources.note: The first collected edition, with Hopkins's Author's Preface on sprung rhythm; source of the quotations from 'Duns Scotus's Oxford' ('Of realty the rarest-veinèd unraveller') and 'As Kingfishers Catch Fire' ('myself it speaks and spells').

sources.author: Claude Colleer Abbott (ed.)
sources.title: The Correspondence of Gerard Manley Hopkins and Richard Watson Dixon
sources.note: Contains Hopkins's October 1878 letter on the origin of The Wreck of the Deutschland's meter, the source of 'long had haunting my ear the echo of a new rhythm.'

sources.author: Humphry House and Graham Storey (eds.)
sources.title: The Journals and Papers of Gerard Manley Hopkins
sources.note: Prints the 1868 notes on Parmenides, where 'inscape' and 'instress' first appear, and the 1872 journal entry recording Hopkins's discovery of Scotus.

sources.author: Christopher Devlin (ed.)
sources.title: The Sermons and Devotional Writings of Gerard Manley Hopkins
sources.note: Devlin's edition and commentary, the classic exploration of the Hopkins–Scotus affinity, which also warns against simply equating inscape with haecceitas.

passages.title: Gutas and the Graeco-Arabic translation movement
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
For much of the twentieth century, the passage of Greek learning into Arabic was told as a story about patrons. Between the eighth and tenth centuries, most of the secular Greek philosophy, medicine, astronomy and mathematics then available was rendered into Arabic in Baghdad, often by way of Syriac, and accounts of this achievement credited it chiefly to a few enlightened caliphs, above all al-Ma'mun (r. 813–833), and to the Bayt al-Hikma, or House of Wisdom, which they pictured as a state academy where scholars gathered to translate. A related account, associated with historians such as De Lacy O'Leary, emphasized the Syriac-speaking Christian scholars who had preserved the Greek texts and who supplied many of the translators.

In Greek Thought, Arabic Culture (1998), Dimitri Gutas argues that such accounts mistake the occasion for the cause. A movement that lasted more than two centuries, and that was financed not only by caliphs but by courtiers, military commanders, physicians and scholars, cannot rest on the tastes of individual rulers; it must have answered needs widely felt across Abbasid society. Some of those needs were practical: astrology for timing decisions of state, medicine, and arithmetic and geometry for administration and surveying. Others were ideological. Al-Mansur, the founder of Baghdad, took over, on Gutas's account, the Zoroastrian imperial ideology of the Sasanians, holding that the sciences had once been Persian and had been scattered abroad, so that recovering them was a mark of legitimate rule; later, under al-Ma'mun, the Byzantines were portrayed as Christians who had abandoned the learning of their Greek ancestors, leaving the Abbasids its rightful heirs, a pairing of anti-Byzantinism with philhellenism. His treatment of the House of Wisdom is deflationary: the evidence points to a palace library on the Sasanian model, associated chiefly with translations from Persian rather than Greek, and it "was certainly also not an 'academy'" for teaching the ancient sciences.

Gutas's central negative claim is persuasive. No single patron could have sustained so long and so costly an enterprise, and the image of a translation academy does not survive scrutiny of the sources. Yet "needs" explains less than it seems to. Demand for astrology and medicine accounts well for which texts were translated first; it accounts less well for the standards the ninth-century translators came to hold themselves to. Hunayn ibn Ishaq reports searching Mesopotamia, Syria, Palestine and Egypt for a manuscript of Galen's On Demonstration, and he revised earlier translations by collating several Greek copies, labors that went well beyond anything a patron's practical purposes required. George Saliba, for his part, has proposed that the impetus came from rivalry among bureaucrats after the Umayyad decision to convert the administrative registers into Arabic; his account is no less social than Gutas's, but it locates the pressure in professional competition rather than imperial ideology.

Gutas was right to ask what Abbasid society wanted from Greek learning. The answer is perhaps best pictured as a demand that the scholarly culture it called into being soon outgrew, so that the translators' own standards became, in time, part of the cause.

sources.author: Dimitri Gutas
sources.title: Greek Thought, Arabic Culture: The Graeco-Arabic Translation Movement in Baghdad and Early 'Abbasid Society (2nd-4th/8th-10th centuries)
sources.note: Argues that the translation movement answered social, political and ideological needs across the Abbasid elite (including al-Mansur's Sasanian imperial ideology and al-Ma'mun-era anti-Byzantinism), and that the Bayt al-Hikma was a library, not a translation academy; the quotation "was certainly also not an 'academy'" is from Gutas's discussion of the Bayt al-Hikma, as quoted on historyofinformation.com and elsewhere.

sources.author: George Saliba
sources.title: Islamic Science and the Making of the European Renaissance
sources.note: Challenges the 'classical narrative' and roots the rise of Arabic science in competition among administrators after the Umayyad Arabization of the diwan.

sources.author: De Lacy O'Leary
sources.title: How Greek Science Passed to the Arabs
sources.note: An older survey that traces the transmission of Greek learning through Syriac-speaking Christian scholarship, representative of the view Gutas revised.

passages.title: Gettier cases and the inescapability argument
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Many mid-twentieth-century philosophers accepted the view that knowledge is justified true belief: a person knows a proposition if it is true, she believes it, and she is justified in believing it. In a 1963 paper, "Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?", Edmund Gettier argued that these conditions "do not constitute a sufficient condition for the truth of the proposition that S knows that P." In one case, Smith has strong evidence that Jones will get a certain job and that Jones has ten coins in his pocket, and he infers that the man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket. In fact Smith gets the job, and Smith, unknowingly, also has ten coins. His belief is true and justified, yet it seems not to be knowledge, since it is true only by luck. Such cases were not new; the eighth-century Buddhist philosopher Dharmottara described a traveler who mistakes a mirage for water and then finds water hidden under a rock at that very spot.

The first responses sought a fourth condition. Some required that the belief not be inferred from any falsehood, as Smith's is; others, that no unknown truth would defeat the believer's justification; Alvin Goldman proposed that the fact believed must cause the belief in an appropriate way. Each met new counterexamples. In one, a man driving through a district filled with convincing barn facades looks at the only real barn and believes, truly, that it is a barn. He infers nothing false, and the barn itself causes his belief, yet most readers judge that he does not know.

Linda Zagzebski argued in 1994 that the pattern is no accident. So long as the condition added to true belief can be satisfied by a false belief, a recipe is available: take a justified belief that bad luck has made false, then add a stroke of good luck, unrelated to the believer's grounds, that makes it true after all. In such cases, she wrote, "an accident of bad luck is cancelled out by an accident of good luck." A fourth condition either leaves the gap open, inviting a new case, or closes it by guaranteeing truth, in which case the truth condition does no independent work. Her own later proposal, like Ernest Sosa's, belongs to virtue epistemology: knowledge is a belief that is true because of the believer's intellectual virtue or competence, or in Sosa's term an apt belief, as an archer's shot is apt when it hits because of her skill rather than a lucky gust.

Zagzebski's argument is the most illuminating result of the debate, because it shows that the difficulty is structural rather than a product of carelessly drafted conditions. Virtue accounts, however, relocate the problem more than they dissolve it. Whether a belief is true "because of" competence calls for judgments of credit that are as contested as the original cases; Sosa concludes that the barn viewer has a lower, "animal" grade of knowledge while lacking a higher, reflective grade. Still, the relocation is progress: it makes the role of luck explicit instead of hiding it inside a list of conditions.

sources.author: Edmund L. Gettier
sources.title: Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?
sources.note: The three-page Analysis paper (vol. 23, no. 6) with the ten-coins and Barcelona cases; the quoted phrase "do not constitute a sufficient condition for the truth of the proposition that S knows that P" is from its statement of thesis.

sources.author: Linda Zagzebski
sources.title: The Inescapability of Gettier Problems
sources.note: Philosophical Quarterly 44 (174): 65-73; argues that any analysis whose added condition does not entail truth permits Gettier cases, in which, as she puts it (p. 66), "an accident of bad luck is cancelled out by an accident of good luck."

sources.author: Ernest Sosa
sources.title: A Virtue Epistemology: Apt Belief and Reflective Knowledge, Volume I
sources.note: Develops knowledge as apt belief (true because competent), with the archer analogy and the distinction between animal and reflective knowledge applied to the fake-barn case.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The qasida's apparent lack of unity results from a classical critical tradition that judged poems verse by verse rather than as wholes.
Stetkevych's ritual model has shown that the qasida's tripartite sequence derives from rites of passage practiced in pre-Islamic Arabia.
The ritual reading shows how the qasida's sections can form a progression, though it fits best the odes that display the full sequence.
Ibn Qutayba's rhetorical account of the qasida is more faithful to the poems than Stetkevych's ritual account, since it was written by a classical critic.
Because so many surviving odes depart from Ibn Qutayba's sequence, no general account of the qasida's structure can succeed.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph carries the author's view: the ritual reading's 'chief merit' is that it 'gives the parts a direction,' but it is 'best taken as a powerful interpretation of the many odes that realize the full pattern, not as a key to every qasida.' C states both halves. B is the trap for a reader who knows Stetkevych's work: it upgrades her interpretive model into a historical claim about origins that the passage never makes, and it drops the author's caution.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: State the author's overall claim about the qasida's structure and the ritual reading of it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, first and last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 1 describes the form, paragraph 2 gives the old charge of disunity and van Gelder's complication, paragraph 3 gives Stetkevych's ritual model, and paragraph 4 is the author's verdict: real merit, limited scope. Prephrase: the ritual reading explains the order of the parts well, but not for every ode.

choices.note: Van Gelder's finding is a supporting detail from paragraph 2, and the passage never says the critics' method caused the appearance of disunity. Too narrow and distorted.
Wrong claim and too strong. The passage presents a model that 'reads' the sections as phases, not a proof that the form came from actual rites, and it omits the author's caution.
CORRECT. It keeps both the 'chief merit' (a direction from loss through ordeal to belonging) and the limit ('not as a key to every qasida').
The author says Ibn Qutayba's account 'too, finds coherence' but never ranks it above Stetkevych's, and certainly not because of who wrote it. Unsupported comparison.
Too extreme. The author calls the ritual reading 'a powerful interpretation' of many odes; variation limits its reach, it does not defeat every general account.

questions.stem: The author mentions Ibn Qutayba's own explanation of the sequence (fourth paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that classical critics regarded the qasida as a loosely joined series of episodes
provide evidence that the ritual pattern Stetkevych describes was recognized by medieval Arab scholars
argue that the rhetorical account should replace the ritual account as an interpretation of the qasida
suggest that the nasib was more important to the success of an ode than the rahil or the closing praise
indicate that the order of the qasida's sections can be explained without appeal to ritual
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says Ibn Qutayba's rhetorical account 'too, finds coherence in the sequence, but locates it in the poet's design on an audience rather than in a ritual pattern.' Its role is to show an alternative source of coherence, which tempers the claim that the ritual model is needed. C is the trap: the author offers the rhetorical account as an alternative to keep in view, not as a replacement, and ends by affirming the ritual reading as 'a powerful interpretation.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the author brings in Ibn Qutayba's rhetorical explanation in paragraph 4.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, the fourth and fifth sentences ('Moreover...' and 'That account, too...').

breakdown.analysis: The sentence is introduced by 'Moreover,' so it is a second reason for caution about the ritual model. The next sentence spells out the point: the rhetorical account also finds coherence, located elsewhere. Prephrase: to show that the order of the parts can be explained another way.

choices.note: Opposite. Ibn Qutayba's explanation finds coherence (each section 'prepares the listener for the next'); the loose-episodes view belongs to the European scholars of paragraph 2.
Distortion. The passage contrasts Ibn Qutayba's rhetorical account with a ritual pattern; it does not say he recognized the rites of passage.
Too strong. The author uses it to limit the ritual model's reach, then calls that model 'a powerful interpretation' of many odes. No replacement is proposed.
Out of scope. The passage says the nasib wins attention, but the author never ranks the sections by importance.
CORRECT. The account 'too, finds coherence' but locates it 'in the poet's design on an audience rather than in a ritual pattern,' so ritual is not the only way to explain the sequence.

questions.stem: According to the passage, The Poetics of Islamic Legitimacy differs from The Mute Immortals Speak in that the later book
choices: applies the ritual model to court panegyric and draws on an account of gift exchange
abandons van Gennep's three phases in favor of a purely rhetorical account of the ode
argues that the nasib is a phase of separation rather than a phase of liminality
concludes that the qasida lacks unity when judged by the standards of its own tradition
treats the poet's boast on behalf of himself and his tribe as the ode's central section
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says that in the 2002 book Stetkevych 'extended the model to the court panegyric, using Marcel Mauss's account of gift exchange to treat the ode as an offering answered by the patron's reward.' A restates that. C uses the passage's own words but assigns to the later book a reading of the nasib that the passage attributes to the 1993 book.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says the 2002 book adds to or changes from the 1993 book.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, second and third sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Detail questions reward going back to the sentence. The 1993 book: van Gennep, separation, liminality, reaggregation. The 2002 book: 'extended the model' (so it keeps it) to court panegyric, with Mauss's gift exchange. Watch for answers that say she abandoned the model.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Extended the model to the court panegyric, using Marcel Mauss's account of gift exchange.'
Opposite. 'Extended the model' means she kept it. The rhetorical account is Ibn Qutayba's, not hers.
Shell game. Reading the nasib as separation is the 1993 book's claim; the passage reports no change on that point.
Wrong position-holder. The point about standards foreign to the tradition comes from the author's comment on van Gelder in paragraph 2.
Unsupported. Neither book is said to make the boast the central section; the 2002 book concerns praise of a patron.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly suggests that van Gelder's findings bear on the charge described in the second paragraph in which one of the following ways?
choices: They show that the medieval Arab critics shared the European scholars' low opinion of the qasida as a form.
They demonstrate that the qasida does in fact possess organic unity when it is read as a whole.
They show that the qasida's sections were originally composed as independent poems and only later joined.
They suggest the charge relies on a standard that the qasida's own tradition did not treat as central.
They confirm that rhyme and meter were the only features that held the qasida's sections together.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says van Gelder's study 'complicated the charge without simply refuting it': the medieval critics gave 'comparatively little attention to the coherence of the whole poem,' so demanding organic unity 'is to impose a standard foreign to its own tradition.' D is that inference. B is the trap a sympathetic reader picks: it turns 'complicated without refuting' into a refutation, and the passage never says van Gelder found organic unity.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Infer how van Gelder's findings relate to the charge that the qasida is a string of loosely joined episodes.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, third through fifth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The key phrase is 'complicated the charge without simply refuting it.' So the right answer neither confirms nor refutes the disunity claim; it changes how we should judge it. The last sentence of the paragraph says how: the demand for organic unity is a foreign standard.

choices.note: Distortion. Paying little attention to whole-poem coherence is not the same as holding the qasida in low esteem; the passage reports no such opinion.
Opposite of 'without simply refuting it.' The finding questions the standard; it does not show the standard is met.
Out of scope. The passage says nothing about how the sections were originally composed.
CORRECT. Little critical attention to whole-poem coherence implies that organic unity is 'a standard foreign to its own tradition.'
Wrong position-holder and too strong. 'Convention and... a single rhyme and meter' is how the European scholars described the binding, and even they did not say 'only' rhyme and meter.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Stetkevych's ritual interpretation of the qasida can most accurately be described as
choices: skeptical dismissal of a model imported into literary study from anthropology
appreciation of its explanatory power, tempered by doubt about its scope
enthusiastic endorsement of it as the key to understanding every qasida
neutral reporting without any evaluation of its merits
reluctant acceptance of it in the absence of any alternative account
questions.explanation: The author credits the reading with a 'chief merit' and calls it 'a powerful interpretation,' but says 'caution is warranted' and that it is 'not... a key to every qasida.' B captures both. E is the trap: the author's acceptance is not reluctant, and the passage itself supplies an alternative (Ibn Qutayba's rhetorical account).

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize the author's view of the ritual reading.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4: 'chief merit,' 'caution is warranted,' 'a powerful interpretation... not as a key to every qasida.'

breakdown.analysis: Collect the evaluative words. Positive: 'chief merit,' 'powerful interpretation.' Negative: 'caution is warranted,' 'risks treating variation as failure,' 'not as a key to every qasida.' Mixed and specific: good where the full pattern appears, overextended elsewhere.

choices.note: Too negative. The author praises the model's 'chief merit' and never objects to its anthropological source.
CORRECT. Real praise ('chief merit,' 'powerful interpretation') with a limit on scope ('not as a key to every qasida').
Too positive. 'Not as a key to every qasida' rejects exactly this.
The author plainly evaluates in paragraph 4.
The passage offers an alternative account of coherence (Ibn Qutayba's), and nothing in the tone is reluctant.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the risk the author attributes to the ritual model in the fourth paragraph?
choices: A critic reads a tragedy's five acts as a single movement from prosperity to catastrophe and concludes that the play was performed as part of a religious festival.
A folklorist classifies folktales by their opening formulas and finds that tales with the same opening often have very different endings.
A biographer explains a composer's late style by his deafness, ignoring the influence of the composers he studied in his youth.
A historian who describes pilgrimage as penance ending in absolution treats pilgrimages made partly for trade as failed pilgrimages.
An editor arranges a poet's short lyrics into a sequence and argues that the arrangement reveals a story the poet never intended.
questions.explanation: The author's worry is that a model built on the full three-part pattern 'makes [odes that depart from it] incomplete rites' and so 'risks treating variation as failure.' D has the same structure: a pattern abstracted from some cases becomes a standard by which differing cases count as failures. A is the trap: it echoes the ritual theme and the idea of a single movement, but its error is inferring a historical origin, a different overreach from the one the author describes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the case that matches the specific risk the author names for the ritual model.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, third sentence: 'a model that makes them incomplete rites risks treating variation as failure.'

breakdown.analysis: Abstract the risk first: a descriptive model drawn from typical cases is used as a norm, so atypical cases are judged defective rather than different. Then look for the answer with that structure, ignoring answers that merely share the subject matter (ritual, sequence, poems).

choices.note: Topic match, structure mismatch. The error here is a leap to historical origins, not the judging of variant cases as failures.
No model is used to judge cases as defective; the folklorist simply notices variation.
This is a neglected alternative cause, a different error.
CORRECT. A model built from the typical case (penance to absolution) is turned into a standard, so variant cases become 'failed' instances, just as variant odes become 'incomplete rites.'
This imposes a unity on separate poems, closer to the critics' demand for unity in paragraph 2 than to the risk in paragraph 4.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's reason for caution about the ritual model?
choices: Classical audiences regularly praised as complete and accomplished many odes that contain no desert journey.
Labid's celebrated ode moves clearly from a ruined campsite through a desert crossing to a boast on behalf of his tribe.
Van Gennep's analysis of rites of passage has been widely applied to literary forms other than the qasida.
Ibn Qutayba attributed his account of the qasida's sequence to an unnamed man of learning rather than presenting it as his own.
Some court panegyrics of the Islamic period were composed for patrons who rewarded poets with gifts.
questions.explanation: The author's worry is that odes lacking parts of the pattern would be wrongly treated as 'incomplete rites,' 'treating variation as failure.' If classical audiences praised journey-less odes as complete and accomplished, then such variation was not failure by the tradition's own lights, which supports the worry. B is the trap for a reader who knows the scholarship: Labid's ode is a strong case for the model where the full pattern appears, which the author already grants, so it does nothing for the caution.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that best supports the author's reason for caution about the ritual model.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, third sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The caution rests on two things: many odes depart from the pattern, and the model would make them failures. A strengthener should show that such departures were legitimate. Answers that support the model's fit to full-pattern odes, or that concern Stetkevych's sources, miss the reason.

choices.note: CORRECT. If the tradition itself treated journey-less odes as complete, then reading them as 'incomplete rites' does treat legitimate variation as failure.
Opposite direction. A full-pattern ode supports the model within the range the author already grants.
Irrelevant. How widely van Gennep is applied elsewhere says nothing about odes that depart from the sequence.
True to paragraph 1 but irrelevant. Who first described the sequence does not bear on whether varying odes are failures.
Irrelevant. It fits Stetkevych's gift-exchange reading but does not touch the problem of odes that depart from the pattern.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Hopkins's concepts of inscape and instress were derived from Scotus's doctrine of haecceitas, which also shaped the design of sprung rhythm.
Because Hopkins coined his key terms before reading Scotus, critics who connect his work with Scotus's philosophy have been mistaken.
Sprung rhythm is best explained by its precedents in nursery rhymes, classical lyric, Old English verse, and Welsh poetic craft.
Though Scotus originated neither Hopkins's key concepts nor his meter, Scotus's thought may help explain the value Hopkins found in both.
Hopkins's poems about Scotus show that his theology and his prosody were inseparable from the time he first began writing verse.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph concedes that 'Scotus gave Hopkins neither his terms nor his meter' but argues that Scotus gave him 'a warrant,' and that the theology 'may explain why Hopkins thought scanning them so was worth the trouble.' D states that qualified thesis. B is the skeptics' conclusion, which the author accepts only about origins ('origins do not settle meaning').

setup.label: Task
setup.text: State the author's overall position on how Scotus relates to Hopkins's ideas and meter.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, especially its first three sentences and its last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraphs 1 and 2 present sprung rhythm, inscape, and the Scotus connection; paragraph 3 gives the skeptics; paragraph 4 is the author: right about origins, wrong to think origins settle meaning. Expect traps that take either the strong-influence view (A) or the skeptics' view (B, C) as the main point.

choices.note: The strong-influence view the author rejects: 'Scotus gave Hopkins neither his terms nor his meter.'
Wrong position-holder and too broad. The skeptics are 'right about origins,' but the author denies that this shows the connection is mistaken.
This is part of the skeptics' case in paragraph 3, not the author's conclusion, which goes beyond origins.
CORRECT. It keeps the concession (neither terms nor meter came from Scotus) and the claim (a warrant that may explain why he valued them).
Unsupported and contradicted by the chronology: the passage dates the Scotus encounter to 1872, after the 1868 notes.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a foot in sprung rhythm can consist of
choices: two stressed syllables followed by one unstressed syllable
a single stressed syllable with no unstressed syllables
an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable
a stressed syllable followed by four or more unstressed syllables
any number of syllables, provided that none of them is stressed
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says each foot 'has a single stress, falling on its first syllable, and may consist of that stressed syllable by itself or with as many as three unstressed ones.' A lone stressed syllable is therefore a foot (B). D overshoots the limit of three; C puts the stress second.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Use the passage's definition of a sprung-rhythm foot.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Three rules: one stress per foot, the stress comes first, and zero to three unstressed syllables follow. Check each choice against all three.

choices.note: Violates 'a single stress.'
CORRECT. 'That stressed syllable by itself.'
Violates 'falling on its first syllable.'
Violates 'as many as three unstressed ones.'
Violates 'a single stress'; every foot has one.

questions.stem: The author mentions Hopkins's notes on Parmenides (third paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that Hopkins's interest in philosophy began with the study of Greek rather than medieval thinkers
suggest that Parmenides rather than Scotus was the true source of Hopkins's sprung rhythm
illustrate the difficulty of assigning dates to Hopkins's unpublished writings
indicate that Hopkins had abandoned the concepts of inscape and instress before he read Scotus
present evidence for the claim that Scotus could not have supplied Hopkins with his concepts
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says Hopkins used both terms 'in notes on Parmenides in 1868, four years before he read Scotus, so Scotus cannot have supplied the concepts.' The notes are the skeptics' evidence for that conclusion (E). B is a shell-game trap: the passage never proposes Parmenides as a source, of the concepts or of the meter.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the 1868 notes on Parmenides are mentioned.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, second sentence, which ends 'so Scotus cannot have supplied the concepts.'

breakdown.analysis: The sentence contains its own conclusion indicator ('so'). The notes are a premise about chronology, used to support the skeptics' claim that the concepts came before Scotus.

choices.note: Out of scope. The passage draws no conclusion about how Hopkins's interest in philosophy began.
Shell game. Parmenides is the subject of the notes, not a proposed source, and the paragraph's point about the meter appeals to verse traditions.
The date is offered as firm; no difficulty in dating is mentioned.
Distortion. He was 'already using' the terms in 1868, and the passage shows him still using 'inscape' in 1872.
CORRECT. Earlier use of the terms is the premise for 'Scotus cannot have supplied the concepts.'

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: That Hopkins formed his concepts before reading Scotus is compatible with Scotus's having shaped how Hopkins valued them.
Hopkins's references to Scotus in his journal and his poems show that the concepts of inscape and instress were Scotist from the start.
The precedents that Hopkins named for sprung rhythm were cited mainly to disguise the theological motive behind the meter.
A full account of how Hopkins's lines scan would require an understanding of Scotus's doctrine of haecceitas.
Critics who trace sprung rhythm to Old English and Welsh verse have overstated the importance of those traditions for Hopkins.
questions.explanation: The author grants the skeptics' chronology ('right about origins') but holds that 'origins do not settle meaning' and that Scotus supplied 'a warrant' for valuing distinctness. A later influence on how Hopkins valued existing ideas is exactly what that combination allows. D is the trap for a reader who takes the author as pro-Scotus: the last sentence says the theology 'does not explain how the lines scan.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the author's qualified view commits the author to.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, first three sentences and last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Separate the author's claims: (1) the skeptics' facts about origins stand; (2) Scotus gave a warrant, a reason for valuing; (3) theology explains why the meter mattered, not how it scans. The right answer should fit all three; traps will push the author toward either camp.

choices.note: CORRECT. The author accepts the later date ('right about origins') yet assigns Scotus the role of 'a warrant,' a reason for valuing what Hopkins already had.
Contradicts the concession that Scotus 'cannot have supplied the concepts,' which the author accepts.
Unsupported and too strong. Nothing suggests Hopkins's precedents were a disguise.
Opposite of the last sentence: 'The theology does not explain how the lines scan.'
The author concedes that sprung rhythm 'has a sufficient ancestry' and never disputes the role of these traditions.

questions.stem: By "a warrant" (third sentence of the fourth paragraph), the author most probably means
choices: an official authorization that permitted Hopkins to publish his poems
a guarantee that Hopkins's descriptions of nature were accurate
a justification for valuing something Hopkins already attended to
a technical method by which Hopkins composed his lines
an argument that compelled Hopkins to abandon his earlier views
questions.explanation: The colon after 'a warrant' explains it: an account on which distinctness is 'positively real and willed by God, so that attending to it becomes a kind of praise.' The warrant is a reason that makes Hopkins's existing attention to distinct things worthwhile (C). D is tempting because the next sentences turn to the meter, but the author has just said Scotus gave Hopkins 'neither his terms nor his meter,' so the warrant is not a method.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Determine what 'a warrant' means in this sentence.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, second and third sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Meaning-in-context answers are fixed by the surrounding sentences. The preceding sentence rules out terms and meter. The colon defines the warrant as an account that makes attending to distinctness a form of praise. Prephrase: a reason to value what he was already doing.

choices.note: The everyday legal sense, with no support in context. Publication is never discussed.
Wrong kind of support. The warrant concerns the value of attending to distinctness, not the accuracy of description.
CORRECT. Distinctness 'positively real and willed by God, so that attending to it becomes a kind of praise' justifies valuing what he already noticed.
Contradicted by the preceding sentence: Scotus gave him 'neither his terms nor his meter.'
Opposite. The warrant supports views Hopkins already held; nothing is abandoned.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the skeptics described in the third paragraph can most accurately be described as
choices: wholehearted agreement with their conclusion about the relation between Scotus and Hopkins's verse
dismissal of their evidence as resting on a misdating of Hopkins's notes
indifference to the question of origins that they raise
suspicion that their argument is motivated by hostility to theology
acceptance of their factual claims, with doubt that those claims settle the larger issue
questions.explanation: 'The skeptics are right about origins, but origins do not settle meaning.' The author accepts their chronology and genealogy but denies that this shows the meter has no theological significance (E). A is the near miss: the author agrees with their premises and their claim about origins, not with their conclusion that reading the meter theologically 'is to mistake a metaphor for an explanation.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize the author's stance toward the skeptics.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, first sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The first sentence of paragraph 4 is both a concession and a rebuttal. A good answer has two parts: agreement on facts or origins, disagreement on what follows.

choices.note: Too strong. The author resists their final step, that a theological reading mistakes 'a metaphor for an explanation.'
Opposite. The author says they are 'right about origins' and never questions the dates.
The author engages origins directly and concedes them; that is not indifference.
Unsupported. No motive is attributed to the skeptics.
CORRECT. 'Right about origins' (acceptance), 'but origins do not settle meaning' (doubt about what follows).

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously undermine the author's suggestion in the last sentence of the passage?
choices: Hopkins had written several poems with clustered stresses before he first read Scotus's commentary in 1872.
Scotus's doctrine of haecceitas was little discussed by the other English poets and critics of Hopkins's time.
Hopkins defended sprung rhythm solely as true to natural speech and denied that it held religious meaning for him.
Hopkins's knowledge of Welsh poetic craft was far more extensive than earlier scholars of his work had recognized.
Some readers of Hopkins's poems find the clustered stresses of sprung rhythm difficult to read aloud.
questions.explanation: The last sentence suggests that the theology 'may explain why Hopkins thought scanning them so was worth the trouble,' a claim about Hopkins's reasons for valuing the meter. If Hopkins himself defended it solely on other grounds and denied any religious meaning, that suggestion loses its footing (C). A is the strongest trap: it would undermine a claim that Scotus originated the meter, but the author already concedes that Scotus gave Hopkins 'neither his terms nor his meter.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most weakens the claim that theology may explain why Hopkins valued sprung rhythm.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, last sentence, with its first two sentences for what the author has already conceded.

breakdown.analysis: Pin down exactly what is claimed: not that theology produced the meter (conceded away), but that it supplied Hopkins's reason for valuing it. The best weakener attacks that reason; evidence about origins only repeats the skeptics' point, which the author accepts.

choices.note: Attacks origins, which the author has already conceded; it leaves the claim about Hopkins's reasons untouched.
Irrelevant. What other poets discussed says nothing about Hopkins's reasons.
CORRECT. If Hopkins's own reasons were entirely non-theological, and he denied religious meaning, theology is a poor explanation of why he valued the meter.
Strengthens the account of origins, which the author already accepts; it does not show theology was no part of his reasons.
Irrelevant. Readers' difficulty does not bear on why Hopkins valued the meter.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Gutas has shown that the Graeco-Arabic translation movement was driven by the ideological needs of the Abbasid court rather than by any scholarly motive.
The House of Wisdom, long pictured as an academy of translators, was in fact a palace library associated chiefly with translations from Persian.
Gutas rightly rejects patron-centered explanations, but social demand alone does not explain a movement whose scholarly standards became part of its cause.
Saliba's account of rivalry among bureaucrats explains the translation movement more satisfactorily than does Gutas's account of imperial ideology.
The translation movement is best explained by the interests of caliphs such as al-Ma'mun together with the preservation of Greek texts by Syriac-speaking Christians.
questions.explanation: The author grants Gutas's 'central negative claim' (paragraph 3) but says 'needs' explains less than it seems, concluding that the translators' standards 'became, in time, part of the cause.' C captures both halves. A is Gutas's view pushed further than even Gutas goes and is rejected by the author; B is one detail from paragraph 2.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall claim about Gutas's explanation of the translation movement.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3's first sentences and the final paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 1 gives the older patron-centered view; paragraph 2 gives Gutas; paragraph 3 is the author: agree with the negative claim, doubt the positive one is complete; paragraph 4 sums up. Prephrase: Gutas is right against the patron story, but demand doesn't explain everything; the scholars' own standards mattered.

choices.note: Wrong position-holder and too strong. The author argues the opposite: the translators' standards exceeded what patrons' purposes required.
True according to the passage's report of Gutas, but it is only one supporting detail, not the point of the whole passage.
CORRECT. It keeps the author's agreement ('Gutas was right to ask...') and the qualification ('a demand that the scholarly culture it called into being soon outgrew').
The author presents Saliba as another social account but never ranks it above Gutas's.
This is the earlier view from paragraph 1, which both Gutas and the author reject.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Gutas holds that the Bayt al-Hikma
choices: served as a state academy in which Greek works were translated under the direction of al-Ma'mun
was founded by al-Mansur in order to recover sciences that had once been Persian
housed the manuscripts that Hunayn ibn Ishaq gathered in his search for Galen's On Demonstration
had little in common with the royal libraries of the Sasanian period
was associated chiefly with translations from Persian rather than with the translation of Greek works
questions.explanation: The last sentence of the second paragraph says the evidence points to 'a palace library on the Sasanian model, associated chiefly with translations from Persian.' E restates this. B splices al-Mansur's ideology onto the library, which the passage never says he founded; A is the earlier view Gutas rejects.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Locate what the passage attributes to Gutas about the House of Wisdom.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last sentence of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: A pure retrieval question, but the passage mentions the House of Wisdom in two places with opposite views. Make sure the answer comes from Gutas's 'deflationary' account, not from the older picture in paragraph 1.

choices.note: This is the older account from paragraph 1, which Gutas denies: the library 'was certainly also not an "academy"'.
Shell game. Al-Mansur and the recovery of Persian sciences appear in the same paragraph, but the passage never says he founded the library or why.
Out of scope. Hunayn's search is in paragraph 3 and is never connected to the library.
Opposite. Gutas calls it a library 'on the Sasanian model.'
CORRECT. A direct paraphrase of 'a palace library on the Sasanian model, associated chiefly with translations from Persian,' together with Gutas's denial that it was an academy.

questions.stem: The author mentions Hunayn ibn Ishaq's search for a manuscript of Galen's On Demonstration (third paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: illustrate something that an explanation in terms of patrons' needs accounts for less well than it does the choice of texts
provide evidence that the translation movement depended on the enthusiasm of a few enlightened patrons
show that the translators were largely indifferent to the practical purposes of the caliphs, courtiers and physicians who financed them
support Saliba's claim that rivalry among officials supplied the impetus for the translation movement
suggest that the ideological needs identified by Gutas mattered more than the practical needs
questions.explanation: The example follows the claim that demand 'accounts less well for the standards the ninth-century translators came to hold themselves to,' and the author says Hunayn's labors 'went well beyond anything a patron's practical purposes required.' It illustrates that limit, as A says. C is the near-miss: 'went beyond' what patrons required is not 'indifferent' to their purposes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what job the Hunayn example does in the author's argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, sentences three through five.

breakdown.analysis: Read the sentence before the example: 'needs' explains which texts were translated first, but not the translators' standards. The example is evidence for that second half. Prephrase: it shows scholarly standards exceeding what demand explains.

choices.note: CORRECT. It matches the contrast drawn just before the example: demand explains which texts came first but 'accounts less well for the standards.'
Opposite of the author's direction. The example concerns translators' own standards, not patrons' enthusiasm.
Too extreme. Exceeding patrons' purposes is not indifference to them; the passage never says translators ignored those purposes.
Wrong position-holder. Saliba's thesis comes after the example and is presented separately ('for his part').
Irrelevant comparison. The example does not weigh ideological against practical needs.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Gutas's account of the translation movement can most accurately be described as
choices: unqualified endorsement of both its rejection of earlier explanations and its positive explanation of the movement
skepticism about its claim that no single patron could have sustained the movement
reluctant acceptance of its conclusions in the absence of any plausible alternative explanation
agreement with its critique of earlier explanations, combined with doubt that its positive explanation is complete
dismissiveness toward its emphasis on ideology, which the author regards as less important than professional competition
questions.explanation: The author calls Gutas's 'central negative claim' persuasive and endorses that 'No single patron could have sustained' the enterprise, then says '"needs" explains less than it seems to.' D captures that split. E gives Saliba's emphasis to the author, who only reports it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize the author's stance toward Gutas, including any qualification.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraphs 3 and 4.

breakdown.analysis: Mixed attitude: yes to the negative thesis (no patron story, no academy), partial no to the positive thesis (needs don't explain the translators' standards). Look for an answer with both halves and no extreme wording.

choices.note: Too strong. The author explicitly limits the positive account: 'needs' explains less than it seems.
Opposite. The author affirms this very claim: 'No single patron could have sustained so long and so costly an enterprise.'
Distortion. The author does not accept Gutas reluctantly, and the passage itself presents an alternative (Saliba's).
CORRECT. Agreement ('central negative claim is persuasive') plus qualification ('explains less than it seems to').
Wrong position-holder. Professional competition is Saliba's emphasis; the author never ranks it above ideology.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly suggests that Saliba's account and Gutas's account
choices: disagree about whether the House of Wisdom served as a center for translating Greek scientific and philosophical works
agree that the movement's impetus lay in conditions across society rather than in the tastes of individual rulers
agree that the earliest translations were prompted chiefly by demand for astrology
disagree about whether the Umayyad administration converted its registers into Arabic
share a failure to account for the exacting standards that ninth-century translators such as Hunayn ibn Ishaq adopted
questions.explanation: The passage says Saliba's account 'is no less social than Gutas's, but it locates the pressure in professional competition rather than imperial ideology.' Both, then, explain the movement by social conditions rather than by the tastes of individual rulers, which Gutas explicitly rejects. E is the trap: the author makes that objection to Gutas's 'needs' explanation only and never applies it to Saliba.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Infer how the two accounts relate, using only what the passage says about each.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph's first two sentences; third paragraph's last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: 'No less social' signals common ground; 'but ... rather than' signals the difference. The common ground is a social explanation, which Gutas defines against 'the tastes of individual rulers.' Anything beyond that (about the library, astrology, the diwan, or Hunayn) goes past what the passage reports about Saliba.

choices.note: Out of scope. The passage says nothing about Saliba's view of the House of Wisdom.
CORRECT. Supported by 'no less social than Gutas's,' read with Gutas's contrast between social needs and 'the tastes of individual rulers.'
The astrology point is attributed only to Gutas; nothing is said about Saliba's view of the first translations.
No disagreement is reported. The passage mentions the Arabic registers only as part of Saliba's account.
Tempting but unsupported. The author raises the problem of translators' standards against Gutas's 'needs' and does not say whether it applies to Saliba.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the author's objection to Gutas's account in the third paragraph?
choices: Hunayn ibn Ishaq's search across several regions failed to turn up a complete manuscript of Galen's On Demonstration.
Works on astrology were among the first Greek texts to be translated in Baghdad.
Many patrons of translations were physicians rather than caliphs or courtiers.
Translators working before Hunayn's generation rarely consulted more than one Greek manuscript of the work they were translating.
Patrons paid more for translations based on collated manuscripts, because medical practice and disputation required exact texts.
questions.explanation: The objection is that the translators' standards 'went well beyond anything a patron's practical purposes required.' If patrons paid extra for collated texts because their practice needed precision, those standards were themselves a response to demand, as E says. B is consistent with what the author already grants, and D at most supports the author.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify the author's objection and find the fact that undercuts it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, sentences three to five.

breakdown.analysis: The objection: demand explains which texts were chosen, not the translators' rigor. To weaken it, show that the rigor was demanded too, that patrons' purposes did require it.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Whether the search succeeded doesn't bear on why Hunayn undertook it.
Already granted. The author concedes that demand 'accounts well for which texts were translated first'; this does not touch the objection about standards.
Irrelevant. The objection concerns standards exceeding patrons' purposes, whoever the patrons were; the passage already lists physicians among them.
If anything this supports the author's picture of standards rising over time; it does not tie those standards to demand.
CORRECT. It makes the translators' rigor a product of patrons' practical purposes, removing the gap the author points to.

questions.stem: By saying that earlier accounts "mistake the occasion for the cause" (first sentence of the second paragraph), the author most probably means that, in Gutas's view, those accounts
choices: confused the period in which the translation movement began with the later period in which it was most productive and best funded
treated the circumstances of translation, such as particular caliphs' patronage, as though they explained why the movement arose
credited the Abbasid caliphs with a movement that had in fact been begun earlier by Syriac-speaking Christian scholars
mistook ideological motives for the practical needs that actually drove the movement
overlooked the role of the House of Wisdom as an occasion for gatherings of scholars
questions.explanation: The next sentence explains the phrase: a movement this long and broadly funded 'cannot rest on the tastes of individual rulers; it must have answered needs widely felt.' Particular patrons were the setting in which translation happened, not its explanation, as B says. E reverses Gutas, who denies the academy picture.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Interpret the quoted phrase using the sentences that follow it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, first two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: 'Occasion' is where and through whom something happens; 'cause' is why. The sentence right after it says what Gutas puts in place of patrons: society-wide needs. So the earlier accounts took the patrons (the occasion) for the explanation (the cause).

choices.note: Out of scope. Nothing in the passage concerns dating the movement's phases.
CORRECT. It matches the contrast between 'the tastes of individual rulers' and 'needs widely felt across Abbasid society.'
Distortion. The passage reports O'Leary's emphasis on Syriac scholars but never says Gutas thinks they began the movement.
Shell game. Gutas counts both practical and ideological needs as causes; the phrase isn't about confusing the two.
Opposite. Gutas's account of the House of Wisdom is 'deflationary'; he does not fault others for neglecting it.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Gettier showed that knowledge cannot be analyzed at all, since every proposed set of conditions, however carefully drafted, faces counterexamples.
Gettier cases stem from the structure of analyses that permit justified false beliefs; virtue accounts do not escape this but do make luck's role explicit.
Virtue epistemology solves the Gettier problem by requiring that a belief be true because of the believer's competence rather than because of luck.
The fourth conditions proposed after Gettier failed only because they were carelessly drafted, a defect that the virtue accounts of Zagzebski and Sosa avoid.
Gettier cases were described centuries before 1963, which shows that the justified-true-belief analysis was never as widely accepted as is often said.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph calls Zagzebski's argument 'the most illuminating result' because the difficulty is 'structural,' says virtue accounts 'relocate the problem more than they dissolve it,' and adds that 'the relocation is progress.' B has all three parts. C omits the author's reservation; D reverses 'structural rather than a product of carelessly drafted conditions.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: State the author's overall conclusion about the Gettier debate.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The final paragraph, read against paragraph 3.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraphs 1 and 2 narrate Gettier and the failed repairs; paragraph 3 gives Zagzebski's diagnosis and the virtue proposal; paragraph 4 is the author's verdict: Zagzebski is right about the structure, virtue theory does not solve the problem, but it is progress. Expect traps that drop the qualification in either direction.

choices.note: Too strong, and wrong position-holder. Gettier argued only that the three conditions are not sufficient; neither he nor the author says knowledge can't be analyzed.
CORRECT. It covers the structural diagnosis, the 'relocate ... more than ... dissolve' reservation, and 'the relocation is progress.'
Too strong. The author denies that virtue accounts dissolve the problem.
Opposite. The author says the difficulty is 'structural rather than a product of carelessly drafted conditions.'
Distortion. Dharmottara's case is a side note; the passage says the analysis was widely 'accepted' in the mid-twentieth century.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the case of the man who sees the only real barn presents a difficulty for the proposal that the fact believed must cause the belief because
choices: the man infers his belief from a false assumption about the other barns in the district
the man's belief, though caused by the barn, turns out to be false
the man lacks any justification for believing that he sees a barn
the real barn does cause the man's belief, and yet he is judged not to know
the man's belief is caused by the facades rather than by the barn he looks at
questions.explanation: The passage says 'the barn itself causes his belief, yet most readers judge that he does not know.' So Goldman's causal condition is met in a case of non-knowledge, as D says. A contradicts 'He infers nothing false'; E contradicts 'the barn itself causes his belief.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says the barn case shows against the causal proposal.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, last three sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Match the condition to the case: the causal proposal requires that the fact cause the belief. The passage says it does. If the condition holds and knowledge is still absent, the condition is not sufficient.

choices.note: Contradicted: 'He infers nothing false.' (This would be relevant to the no-false-inference proposal, not the causal one.)
Contradicted: he 'believes, truly, that it is a barn.'
Unsupported. Nothing suggests the man is unjustified; Gettier cases assume justification.
CORRECT. Restates 'the barn itself causes his belief, yet most readers judge that he does not know.'
Contradicted: 'the barn itself causes his belief.'

questions.stem: The primary function of the second paragraph is to
choices: describe attempts to repair the analysis that Gettier criticized and indicate that those attempts met further counterexamples
present evidence that the justified-true-belief analysis was widely accepted before Gettier's paper appeared
introduce the argument that a Gettier case can be constructed against any analysis permitting justified false beliefs
defend the requirement that a known belief not be inferred from a falsehood against the objection raised by the barn case
show that Goldman's causal proposal succeeded where proposals based on undefeated justification failed
questions.explanation: The paragraph opens 'The first responses sought a fourth condition,' lists three, says 'Each met new counterexamples,' and gives the barn case. A describes that. C belongs to the third paragraph, which explains why the pattern recurs.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the second paragraph contributes to the passage.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph as a whole, with the first sentence of the third.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 2 is a survey of repairs plus a counterexample. Paragraph 3 then says the pattern 'is no accident.' So paragraph 2 sets up the pattern that paragraph 3 explains.

choices.note: CORRECT. Matches 'The first responses sought a fourth condition ... Each met new counterexamples.'
Out of place. The acceptance of the analysis is mentioned in paragraph 1, and the second paragraph offers no evidence for it.
That is the job of the third paragraph ('the pattern is no accident').
Opposite. The barn case is used against the proposals, including the no-false-inference one ('He infers nothing false').
Contradicted. The barn case counts against the causal proposal too.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, Zagzebski would be most likely to agree with which one of the following claims about a proposed condition that, added to true belief, could be satisfied only by true beliefs?
choices: It would remain open to a counterexample constructed by the recipe she describes.
It would need to require a causal connection of the kind that Goldman proposed.
It would show that Gettier's original cases were not genuine counterexamples.
It would make the requirement that the belief be justified unnecessary.
It would leave the truth requirement with no work of its own to do.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says a fourth condition either leaves the gap open 'or closes it by guaranteeing truth, in which case the truth condition does no independent work.' A condition satisfiable only by true beliefs guarantees truth, so E follows. D is the trap: it is the truth condition, not the justification condition, that becomes idle; A fails because the recipe applies only when the added condition 'can be satisfied by a false belief.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply Zagzebski's dilemma, as the passage reports it, to a truth-guaranteeing condition.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, second and fourth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Two steps: the recipe needs a condition a false belief can meet (sentence 2); a condition that guarantees truth makes the truth condition redundant (sentence 4). The hypothetical condition is the second horn. Watch which condition becomes redundant.

choices.note: Opposite. The recipe works only 'So long as the condition added to true belief can be satisfied by a false belief.'
Out of scope. Nothing in the passage ties the truth-guaranteeing horn to a causal condition; the barn case shows causation does not guarantee knowledge.
Unsupported. Zagzebski treats Gettier cases as genuine and widespread.
Shell game. The passage says the truth condition, not the justification condition, 'does no independent work.'
CORRECT. Directly from 'closes it by guaranteeing truth, in which case the truth condition does no independent work'; the 'truth requirement' is that condition.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the structure that, according to Zagzebski, Gettier cases share?
choices: A student who studies the wrong chapter by mistake fails the examination she had spent weeks preparing for.
A forecaster using reliable models predicts rain for the afternoon, and it rains at the time the models indicated.
A hiker trusts a trail sign that vandals have turned the wrong way, but the wrong path, by a link she knew nothing of, reaches her goal.
A gambler picks a lottery number at random, with no reason to favor it, and wins the prize.
A navigator relies on a compass that is faulty without her knowing it, and her ship ends up far off course.
questions.explanation: Zagzebski's structure: a well-grounded belief that bad luck would make false, rescued by unrelated good luck, so 'an accident of bad luck is cancelled out by an accident of good luck.' In C the hiker reasonably trusts the sign (good grounds), vandals mislead her (bad luck), and an unknown trail rescues her (good luck). D has good luck but no grounds; A and E have bad luck with nothing to cancel it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match a new case to the double-luck structure the passage attributes to Zagzebski.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, sentences two and three.

breakdown.analysis: Three ingredients: (1) reasonable grounds, (2) bad luck that would defeat success, (3) separate good luck that restores success. Check each choice for all three.

choices.note: Bad luck only, and no success to cancel it.
No luck at all: success comes from reliable grounds, like knowledge.
CORRECT. Good grounds (a sign), bad luck (vandals), unrelated good luck (an unknown connecting trail) that cancels it.
Good luck without any grounds; nothing bad is cancelled.
