Reasonable reliance plus bad luck, but no good luck to restore success.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward virtue-epistemological responses to Gettier cases can most accurately be described as
choices: qualified approval: they do not dissolve the problem, but they represent an advance
enthusiastic endorsement of them as a solution to the problem Zagzebski identified
dismissal of them as restatements of the fourth conditions that had already failed
neutrality, since the author reports them without evaluating them
skepticism grounded in the view that Sosa's distinction between grades of knowledge is incoherent
questions.explanation: The author says virtue accounts 'relocate the problem more than they dissolve it' and then 'Still, the relocation is progress.' A captures both. E treats the author's example of a contested judgment (Sosa's verdict on the barn viewer) as a charge of incoherence, which the author never makes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize the author's evaluation of virtue accounts.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Final paragraph, second through last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Two signals: 'however' (a reservation) and 'Still' (a concession back). The attitude is mixed and positive on balance.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'relocate the problem more than they dissolve it' plus 'the relocation is progress.'
Too positive; the author denies they dissolve the problem.
Too negative; the author calls them progress and never equates them with the failed conditions.
The author clearly evaluates them in the last paragraph.
Distortion. Sosa's two grades are cited to show the judgments are contested, not to call them incoherent.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim that virtue accounts "relocate the problem more than they dissolve it"?
choices: Most epistemologists now agree that the barn viewer's belief is true because of his perceptual competence.
On a virtue account, Dharmottara's traveler would not count as knowing that there is water at the spot.
Analogies between knowing and skilled performance, like Sosa's archer, have a long history in philosophy.
Virtue epistemologists have devised a precise test for whether a belief is true because of competence, and it classifies every familiar Gettier case without dispute.
Philosophers who accept the same virtue account still disagree about whether the beliefs in familiar Gettier cases are true because of competence.
questions.explanation: The author's reason is that judging whether a belief is true 'because of' competence calls for judgments 'as contested as the original cases.' E shows that even agreement on the account leaves the cases contested, so the problem has moved into the 'because of' judgment. D is the opposite: an uncontested test would mean the problem was dissolved.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the support for the author's reservation about virtue accounts.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Final paragraph, second and third sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The author's support for 'relocate' is that the old disputes about cases reappear as disputes about credit. A strengthener shows continuing disagreement located in the 'because of competence' judgment.

choices.note: Weakens, if anything: consensus on the barn case would suggest the account settles the case.
Shows the account gets one case right; it does not bear on whether its judgments are contested.
Irrelevant. The age of the analogy says nothing about whether the account resolves Gettier cases.
Opposite. A test that settles every case without dispute would mean the problem had been dissolved.
CORRECT. Disagreement among those who share the account places the dispute in the 'because of' judgment, the relocation the author describes.

tests.name: Reading Through Ideas 2
tests.source: Original RC passages written for LSAT Trainer from real scholarship (philosophy, epistemology, etymology, poetry, literature, history, mathematics, Islamic thought, law, economics and politics), with sources for further reading on every passage. Every key was confirmed by a blind solver and every passage checked for accuracy. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

sections.title: Reading Through Ideas 4: Hallaq on taqlid · Verner's law and exceptionless sound change · Wine and the tavern in Hafez · Rumi in English

passages.title: Hallaq on taqlid
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
For much of the twentieth century, Western scholarship told the later history of Islamic law as a story of decline. In the account given its most influential form by Joseph Schacht, by about the year 900 jurists of every school had come to believe that the essential questions were settled; the door of ijtihad, or independent legal reasoning, was considered closed, and what followed was taqlid, the following of established doctrine, a term commonly rendered in English as imitation. On this view the law's later stability was a symptom of intellectual exhaustion, and its failure to keep pace with social change was the price of that stability.

Wael Hallaq's Authority, Continuity and Change in Islamic Law (2001) builds on his earlier argument that the gate of ijtihad was never in fact closed, but its more ambitious claim concerns taqlid itself. Taqlid, Hallaq argues, was not "blind" or "mindless acquiescence to the opinions of others" but "the reasoned and highly calculated insistence on abiding by a particular authoritative legal doctrine." Such insistence presupposed an authority to abide by, and Hallaq shows that this authority was itself constructed. The doctrine of each school, or madhhab, accumulated over generations, came to be attributed to the school's eponymous founder, who was retrospectively cast as an absolute mujtahid whose reasoning later jurists could defend but not rival. Taqlid of the founder was what bound a dispersed mass of opinions into a single tradition, allowing a judge in one century to rely on rulings formulated in another.

The same mechanism, Hallaq argues, made change possible. New problems came first to the jurisconsult, or mufti, whose fatwas answered particular cases. The decisive figure, however, is the author-jurist, who composed the treatises that recorded school doctrine. Using the school's operative terminology, by which one opinion was declared the sound one or the one on which fatwas were to be given, an author-jurist could raise a formerly minority view, often one supported by recent fatwas, to authoritative status while presenting it as the school's own. Continuity and change thus appear not as opposites but as two products of a single practice: the reasoned defense of a doctrine.

Hallaq's account has largely displaced the image of a frozen law, and rightly so, for it explains what the stagnation thesis cannot: how a system that disclaimed innovation nonetheless absorbed new rulings for centuries. Yet it would be a mistake to conclude that the older critics saw nothing at all. What Hallaq's evidence establishes is that taqlid was reasoned, not that it was independent. The jurist practicing taqlid reasoned about which opinion carried the school's authority rather than about whether the founder's reasoning was correct, and change entered the law precisely by being presented as continuity. This is the distinction pressed by critics of taqlid within the tradition itself, such as the Yemeni jurist al-Shawkani, who urged jurists to return to the scriptural evidence. The stagnation thesis misdescribed the intellectual quality of taqlid; its question about where authority finally resided remains open.

sources.author: Wael B. Hallaq
sources.title: Authority, Continuity and Change in Islamic Law
sources.note: Argues that taqlid was a reasoned defense of an authoritative school doctrine whose founder's absolute authority was constructed later, and that muftis and author-jurists used this structure to absorb legal change. Source of both quotations in the second paragraph ('blind' or 'mindless acquiescence to the opinions of others'; 'the reasoned and highly calculated insistence on abiding by a particular authoritative legal doctrine').

sources.author: Wael B. Hallaq
sources.title: Was the Gate of Ijtihad Closed?
sources.note: International Journal of Middle East Studies 16; Hallaq's earlier argument that ijtihad continued after the formative period and that the 'closing of the gate' was not the settled consensus later scholarship assumed.

sources.author: Joseph Schacht
sources.title: An Introduction to Islamic Law
sources.note: The classic statement of the view that by about A.D. 900 jurists regarded the 'door of ijtihad' as closed, leaving later law to explanation and application of fixed doctrine; the position Hallaq set out to revise.

passages.title: Verner's law and exceptionless sound change
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
By the 1870s philologists knew that the Germanic languages are set apart from their Indo-European relatives by a series of consonant changes, the first sound shift described by Rasmus Rask and Jacob Grimm. The voiceless stops p, t and k of Proto-Indo-European became the fricatives f, th and h in Germanic. The correspondences had exceptions. Gothic broþar, "brother," shows the expected th where Sanskrit bhrātar has t, but Gothic fadar, "father," has d where Sanskrit pitar also has t. The same inherited consonant, in what seemed the same position, had developed differently. Grimm had treated the shift as a general tendency that admitted such exceptions.

Karl Verner's solution, set out in a paper completed in 1875 under the title "Eine Ausnahme der ersten Lautverschiebung" ("An Exception to the First Sound Shift"), located the cause in a feature Germanic no longer displayed: the position of the Indo-European accent, preserved in Sanskrit and Greek. In the Sanskrit word for "brother" the accent falls on the root syllable, immediately before the t; in the word for "father" it falls on the final syllable, after it. Verner showed that a fricative produced by the shift inside a word, between voiced sounds, stayed voiceless only if the accent immediately preceded it; otherwise it became voiced, and s likewise became z. Because Germanic later fixed the accent on the first syllable, the conditioning factor had been erased, and the outcome looked arbitrary. The rule also explained alternations within a single verb, such as Old English cweþan, "to say," beside the past plural cwǣdon.

The Neogrammarians of Leipzig took Verner's result as a vindication. If even the most stubborn exceptions to Grimm's law dissolved once their condition was found, perhaps no sound law had genuine exceptions. In 1878 Hermann Osthoff and Karl Brugmann made this the programmatic principle of their school: all sound change, "so weit er mechanisch vor sich geht" (insofar as it proceeds mechanically), follows laws that admit no exceptions. The Ausnahmslosigkeit der Lautgesetze, the exceptionlessness of sound laws, became an axiom of historical linguistics; opponents such as Hugo Schuchardt objected that it was a dogma rather than a finding, since no one had checked every word.

Admirers who took Verner's result as proof of the doctrine and critics who dismissed it as unverified, however, share a misreading of what it claims. Its qualifying clause is not a loophole but its substance. The Neogrammarians openly allowed that words could escape a sound law through analogy with related forms or through borrowing from another dialect; what they denied was that a mechanical change could apply to one word and simply skip another in the same phonetic environment. The doctrine is thus less a report of observations than a rule of method: an apparent exception is never accepted as brute fact but treated as a sign that the environment has been misdescribed or that some other process intervened. Verner's discovery did not prove that rule; no single success could. It showed that the rule was fruitful: refusing to accept an exception had led to a real fact, the old accent, that no one would otherwise have sought.

sources.author: Karl Verner
sources.title: Eine Ausnahme der ersten Lautverschiebung
sources.note: Zeitschrift für vergleichende Sprachforschung 23, 97–130 (worked out in 1875, often cited with that date); shows that the Germanic voiced reflexes of Indo-European voiceless stops depend on the position of the old accent. The passage quotes its title.

sources.author: Hermann Osthoff and Karl Brugmann
sources.title: Morphologische Untersuchungen auf dem Gebiete der indogermanischen Sprachen, vol. 1 (Vorwort)
sources.note: The Neogrammarian manifesto, stating that all sound change, 'so weit er mechanisch vor sich geht', follows exceptionless laws; source of the passage's quoted qualifying clause.

sources.author: Hugo Schuchardt
sources.title: Über die Lautgesetze: Gegen die Junggrammatiker
sources.note: The best-known contemporary attack on the doctrine of exceptionless sound laws.

sources.author: Winfred P. Lehmann (ed.)
sources.title: A Reader in Nineteenth-Century Historical Indo-European Linguistics
sources.note: English translations of Grimm, Verner, and the Osthoff–Brugmann preface, with introductions; the most accessible way to read the primary texts.

passages.title: Wine and the tavern in Hafez
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
For six centuries readers have disagreed about what the wine, the tavern and the beloved mean in the ghazals of Hafez of Shiraz. The disagreement is not idle. Hafez's pen name designates one who has memorized the Qur'an, he is honored as Lisan al-Ghayb, the "Tongue of the Unseen," and his Divan is still opened at random for guidance. Yet the same poems praise the wine-house, bid the reader stain his prayer mat with wine if the Magian elder commands it, and mock the ascetic and the inspector of public morals.

The oldest answer is mystical. Long before Hafez's century, Persian poets had used the vocabulary of drinking and erotic longing to speak of the soul's love for God, and commentators read Hafez accordingly: wine is divine love, the tavern is the Sufi lodge, the Magian elder is the spiritual master. Wilberforce Clarke's 1891 English translation glosses the elder as just such a guide. Against this reading, a number of modern scholars insist on the literal and the social. The translator Dick Davis has argued that the wine in these poems is very often simply wine. Hafez's attacks on the morals inspector, moreover, had a historical target: the Muzaffarid ruler Mubariz al-Din, who closed the taverns of Shiraz and whom Hafez is reported to have called by that title. On this view the poems' hero, the rend, a word that Franklin Lewis notes has been rendered "rake, ruffian, pious rogue, brigand, libertine," is a figure of defiance against official piety rather than a symbol of the mystic.

A third group of scholars denies that one must choose. Persian pronouns do not mark gender, so the beloved addressed in a ghazal may be a youth, a royal patron or God, and Julie Scott Meisami has traced how court poetry cast the poet as lover and the ruler as beloved. Davis himself observes that ambiguity was a quality Persian poets of the period were admired for achieving, and Lewis suggests that Hafez's ambiguity may have been deliberate, a weapon in his campaign against hypocrisy. On this view the double meaning is not a puzzle awaiting solution but the substance of the poems.

This third position seems to me the most persuasive, but it is sometimes stated in a form that goes too far: as though Hafez's poems were indifferent to what their images refer to, so that any reading is as good as another. The ambiguity works only because two determinate codes were available to his first audience at once. The mystical code was centuries old; the closed taverns were a fact of the city's life. When Hafez mocks the self-satisfied ascetic, the pious reader hears the Sufi rebuke of merely outward observance and the worldly reader hears a defense of pleasure, and the poem draws its force from the friction between them. Readers who settle on one meaning do not err in finding a meaning; they err in supposing that the poem asks them to choose.

sources.author: Franklin Lewis
sources.title: Hafez viii. Hafez and Rendi (Encyclopaedia Iranica)
sources.note: Surveys the rend, the impious 'rogue' hero of Hafez's ghazals, and Hafez's war on religious hypocrisy, suggesting his ambiguity may be deliberate; source of the quoted list of English renderings of rend ("rake, ruffian, pious rogue, brigand, libertine"), from the entry's opening sentence.

sources.author: Dick Davis
sources.title: Faces of Love: Hafez and the Poets of Shiraz
sources.note: Verse translations of Hafez and two Shiraz contemporaries; the introduction argues that the wine is often literal wine and that ambiguity was a prized quality of fourteenth-century Persian poetry.

sources.author: Julie Scott Meisami
sources.title: Medieval Persian Court Poetry
sources.note: Argues that Persian court poets were moral instructors as well as entertainers and analyzes the court lyric's casting of poet as lover and ruler as beloved.

sources.author: Annemarie Schimmel
sources.title: A Two-Colored Brocade: The Imagery of Persian Poetry
sources.note: A survey of the conventional images of Persian poetry, wine, tavern and beloved among them, as a web of symbols embedded in Islamic culture; background for the mystical code described in the second paragraph.

passages.title: Rumi in English
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Jalal al-Din Rumi, the thirteenth-century Persian poet who taught and preached in Konya, is often described as the best-selling poet in the United States, and most Americans who know him know him through Coleman Barks. Barks never learned Persian. Beginning in 1976, when the poet Robert Bly handed him a volume of A. J. Arberry's scholarly translations and told him, by Barks's account, that the poems "need to be released from their cages," Barks recast the literal English of Arberry and R. A. Nicholson, together with cribs prepared by his collaborator John Moyne, into loose American free verse. He called the results versions rather than translations.

The scholarly objection received its fullest statement in Franklin Lewis's Rumi: Past and Present, East and West (2000). Lewis credits Barks, more than anyone else, with creating Rumi's American audience, but he argues that Barks has fashioned a Rumi who fits comfortably into contemporary American poetry: a serene sage dispensing wisdom, his Islamic setting largely out of view. The historical Rumi was trained in Islamic law and theology, and his Masnavi is so dense with allusions to the Qur'an and the sayings of the Prophet that Nicholson devoted two volumes of commentary to tracing them. The writer Rozina Ali pressed the point in 2017. Barks's lines "Out beyond ideas of wrongdoing and rightdoing, there is a field. I'll meet you there," she noted, render a quatrain whose Persian speaks not of right and wrong but of Islam and infidelity.

Barks's defenders reply that he never claimed scholarly fidelity, that the accurate translations had for decades found few readers, and that what a translation must carry across is a poem's life, which no amount of annotation can preserve.

Both sides, I think, assume too simple an account of what a translation owes its source. No rendering carries everything; selection is unavoidable, and the label "versions" is an honest acknowledgment that Barks selects freely. What a translation owes is narrower and more demanding: it must not present its selection as the whole, and above all it must not reverse the direction of what it keeps. The quatrain shows the difference. When Rumi gestures beyond the opposition of Islam and infidelity, he does so in a vocabulary that Sufism had developed within Islam; to pass beyond outward religious categories is itself a recognizably Islamic mystical move. Rendered as a field beyond moral ideas, the same gesture appears to come from outside religion altogether, and the reader is told, in effect, that Rumi's depth lies in his distance from his faith. That is not a loss of detail but an inversion of the poem's frame. The remedy, though, is not to dismiss the versions, which have led many readers to Rumi, but to read them beside translations that keep the frame in view.

sources.author: Franklin D. Lewis
sources.title: Rumi: Past and Present, East and West: The Life, Teachings and Poetry of Jalal al-Din Rumi
sources.note: The standard scholarly study of Rumi's life, works and reception; credits Barks with Rumi's American popularity while arguing that his Rumi is shaped to fit contemporary American poetry.

sources.author: Coleman Barks (with John Moyne)
sources.title: The Essential Rumi
sources.note: The best-known collection of Barks's free-verse versions; source of the quoted lines "Out beyond ideas of wrongdoing and rightdoing, there is a field. I'll meet you there." Bly's remark that the poems "need to be released from their cages" is Barks's own recollection of their 1976 meeting, as quoted in the Wikipedia article on Robert Bly and in interviews.

sources.author: Rozina Ali
sources.title: The Erasure of Islam from the Poetry of Rumi (The New Yorker)
sources.note: Argues that popular English versions, chiefly Barks's, detach Rumi from Islam, using the 'field' quatrain, whose Persian speaks of Islam and infidelity, as an example.

sources.author: Reynold A. Nicholson
sources.title: The Mathnawi of Jalalu'ddin Rumi
sources.note: The critical edition, literal translation and two-volume commentary (published 1925-1940) that traces the Masnavi's Qur'anic and hadith allusions; one of the scholarly translations Barks reworked.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Hallaq has shown that the gate of ijtihad was never closed, so that Islamic law continued to develop chiefly through independent reasoning after the year 900.
The stagnation thesis rightly identified taqlid as a source of rigidity in Islamic law, although it exaggerated how little the law actually changed.
Hallaq is right that taqlid was a reasoned practice sustaining continuity and change, but a question raised by the older critique remains open.
Hallaq's account of the author-jurist shows that change in Islamic law was introduced openly, through the explicit rejection of the founders' doctrines.
Because the founders' authority was constructed later, the doctrine that jurists defended through taqlid had no genuine connection to the founders themselves.
questions.explanation: The passage lays out the stagnation thesis, presents Hallaq's account of taqlid as the mechanism of both continuity and change, and ends with the author endorsing that account ('rightly so') while insisting that the older critics' question 'about where authority finally resided remains open.' C captures both halves. A rests on Hallaq's earlier argument and shifts the engine of change from taqlid to ijtihad; B gives the author too much sympathy for the stagnation thesis.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall claim about Hallaq's account of taqlid and the older view it replaces.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, its first two sentences and its last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 1 is the old view, paragraphs 2 and 3 are Hallaq's view, and paragraph 4 is the author: Hallaq is right that taqlid was reasoned and enabled change, but the older critics' question about authority 'remains open.' Prephrase: Hallaq is largely right, with one reservation.

choices.note: Shell game. The gate argument is Hallaq's earlier work, mentioned in passing, and the passage locates change in taqlid and the author-jurist, not in independent reasoning.

Too close to the old view. The author says the stagnation thesis 'misdescribed the intellectual quality of taqlid' and that Hallaq 'rightly' displaced the image of a frozen law; the author grants only that one question it raised is still open.
CORRECT. It joins the author's endorsement ('rightly so') to the reservation in the last sentence, that the question 'about where authority finally resided remains open.'
Opposite. Change entered 'precisely by being presented as continuity'; the author-jurist presented a new view 'as the school's own.'
Too extreme. The passage says the founder's absolute authority was constructed retrospectively; it never says the doctrine had no connection to the founders, and this is not the passage's main point.

questions.stem: The author's discussion of the attribution of each school's doctrine to its eponymous founder (second paragraph) serves primarily to
choices: cast doubt on Hallaq's claim that taqlid was a reasoned and calculated practice
provide evidence for the older view that later jurists merely imitated their predecessors without reasoning
explain why later jurists came to regard the door of ijtihad as closed
suggest that the founders' own reasoning was less rigorous than later jurists supposed
identify the authority that, on Hallaq's account, taqlid presupposed and that held the tradition together
questions.explanation: The discussion follows directly from 'Such insistence presupposed an authority to abide by, and Hallaq shows that this authority was itself constructed,' and ends by saying taqlid of the founder 'bound a dispersed mass of opinions into a single tradition.' So it identifies the authority taqlid needed and shows how it produced continuity: E. C borrows the 'closed door' from the first paragraph, but the founder discussion is part of Hallaq's account, not Schacht's.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the founder discussion does in the argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, sentences 3 to 5.

breakdown.analysis: The sentence just before the discussion says taqlid 'presupposed an authority to abide by.' The discussion then names that authority (the founder, cast as an absolute mujtahid) and says what it did (bound opinions into a single tradition). Prephrase: it supplies the authority that taqlid rests on and explains continuity.

choices.note: Opposite. The discussion is part of Hallaq's case for taqlid as a reasoned system, not an objection to it.
Wrong position-holder. The older view is in paragraph 1; this discussion belongs to Hallaq's revision of it.
Shell game. The closed door is Schacht's account in paragraph 1; the founder discussion does not explain why anyone believed it.
Out of scope. The passage says the founder was 'retrospectively cast' as an absolute mujtahid; it never evaluates how rigorous his reasoning actually was.
CORRECT. It names what taqlid 'presupposed' and shows how taqlid of the founder 'bound a dispersed mass of opinions into a single tradition.'

questions.stem: According to the passage, Hallaq holds that the author-jurist
choices: could give a formerly minority opinion authoritative standing while presenting it as the doctrine of the school
was ordinarily the first to address the new legal problems that arose when particular cases came before the school
set aside the authority of the school's founder whenever recent fatwas conflicted with it
confined the school's doctrine to the opinions that the founder himself had expressly held
was regarded by later jurists as an absolute mujtahid equal in standing to the school's founder
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says that by using operative terminology 'an author-jurist could raise a formerly minority view, often one supported by recent fatwas, to authoritative status while presenting it as the school's own.' That is A. B describes the mufti: 'New problems came first to the jurisconsult, or mufti.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says the author-jurist did.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, sentences 2 to 4.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 3 has two figures. The mufti answers particular cases first; the author-jurist writes the treatises and uses operative terminology to raise a minority view to authority, presenting it as the school's own. Watch for answers that give the mufti's job or the founder's status to the author-jurist.

choices.note: CORRECT. Nearly a paraphrase of the fourth sentence of paragraph 3: he could 'raise a formerly minority view... to authoritative status while presenting it as the school's own.'
Shell game. 'New problems came first to the jurisconsult, or mufti'; the author-jurist comes later.
Distortion. The author-jurist presented the change 'as the school's own'; nothing says he set aside the founder's authority.
Opposite. He elevated views 'often... supported by recent fatwas,' so he did not restrict doctrine to the founder's own opinions.
Shell game. 'Absolute mujtahid' describes how the founder was cast; later jurists could 'defend but not rival' him.

questions.stem: In saying that Hallaq's evidence establishes that taqlid was "reasoned, not that it was independent" (third sentence of the fourth paragraph), the author most probably means that
choices: jurists who practiced taqlid could not reason about new legal questions without first obtaining the guidance of a mufti
the textual sources on which Hallaq relies were not composed independently of one another but drew on earlier works
the reasoning involved in taqlid was less rigorous than the reasoning involved in ijtihad
the reasoning in taqlid sought the school's authoritative view rather than judging the founder's arguments on their merits
taqlid could not have produced legal change unless jurists had departed from the doctrine of their school
questions.explanation: The next sentence explains the phrase: the jurist practicing taqlid 'reasoned about which opinion carried the school's authority rather than about whether the founder's reasoning was correct.' 'Independent' therefore means reasoning that judges the merits for itself rather than deferring to the school, which is D. B takes 'independent' in a different sense, the independence of sources, which the passage never discusses; C turns a difference in kind into a difference in rigor.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out what 'independent' means in this sentence.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, sentences 3 and 4.

breakdown.analysis: The sentence right after the phrase defines it: taqlid reasoned about 'which opinion carried the school's authority' rather than 'whether the founder's reasoning was correct.' So reasoned = careful argument; not independent = the final ground is the school's authority, not the jurist's own judgment of the merits.

choices.note: Shell game. The mufti appears in paragraph 3 as the first to answer new cases; the contrast in paragraph 4 is between deferring to school authority and judging the merits, not between jurists and muftis.
Wrong sense of 'independent.' The author is describing taqlid itself, not how Hallaq's sources relate to one another.
Distortion. The author does not say taqlid was less rigorous; the point is about what the reasoning was directed at, and the author grants it was 'reasoned.'

CORRECT. The following sentence supplies this meaning almost word for word: reasoning 'about which opinion carried the school's authority rather than about whether the founder's reasoning was correct.'
Opposite. On the passage's account change came through taqlid's own machinery and was 'presented as continuity,' not through departures from the school.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the stagnation thesis described in the first paragraph can most accurately be described as
choices: complete rejection, on the grounds that it misdescribed both the character of taqlid and the place where authority lay
rejection of its picture of taqlid, together with acknowledgment that it raised a legitimate question
cautious endorsement, since Hallaq's evidence confirms that taqlid kept the law from changing
indifference, since the author regards every question about taqlid as settled by Hallaq's work
strong approval of its explanation of how new rulings entered the law
questions.explanation: The author says Hallaq 'rightly' displaced the image of a frozen law and that the stagnation thesis 'misdescribed the intellectual quality of taqlid,' but also that 'it would be a mistake to conclude that the older critics saw nothing at all' and that 'its question about where authority finally resided remains open.' That is B, rejection with a concession. A is the near-miss: it rejects the thesis on the very point (authority) that the author says it got right.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pin down how far the author goes in rejecting the old view.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, sentences 1, 2 and the last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Two signals pull in different directions: 'rightly so' and 'misdescribed' (rejection), against 'saw nothing at all' and 'remains open' (concession). The right answer must be mixed, and the concession is about where authority lay.

choices.note: Too extreme. The author faults the thesis only on the 'intellectual quality of taqlid'; on the location of authority the author says its question 'remains open.'
CORRECT. It rejects the picture of taqlid as mindless and keeps the concession of the last sentence.
Opposite. Hallaq's evidence shows the law 'absorbed new rulings for centuries'; the author agrees.
Distortion. The author explicitly says one question 'remains open,' so the author does not treat everything as settled.
Opposite. The stagnation thesis held that the law failed to keep pace with social change; explaining how new rulings entered is what it 'cannot' do.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the means by which, according to the passage, author-jurists brought about legal change?
choices: A legislature repeals an old statute and openly enacts a new one in its place, explaining that the old rule no longer fits current conditions.
A judge declines to follow an established precedent she regards as mistaken and decides the case by appeal directly to the original constitutional text.
A high court adopts a rule first proposed by a lower court in a recent case, openly crediting that court with an innovation in the law.
A committee keeps an organization's founding charter exactly as written and declines to address situations that its drafters did not foresee.
A guild's rulebook compiler, drawing on arbiters' recent rulings, labels a long-disfavored reading the preferred one and calls it settled practice.
questions.explanation: Hallaq's author-jurist uses the school's own labels to raise a minority view, 'often one supported by recent fatwas,' to authoritative status 'while presenting it as the school's own.' E has every element: a standard compilation, input from practitioners' recent rulings, a disfavored view promoted by labeling, and presentation as established practice. C is the half-right trap: it has the recent rulings from below, but the change is openly credited as an innovation.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the structure of the author-jurist's method to a new case.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, sentences 3 and 4; paragraph 4, sentence 4.

breakdown.analysis: List the features: (1) a writer of authoritative doctrine, (2) draws on recent case rulings, (3) raises a minority view by declaring it the sound one, (4) presents the change as the tradition's own rather than as new. The analogue needs (3) and (4) above all.

choices.note: Opposite of feature (4). The change is announced openly as a replacement.
Shell game. Returning to the original source over accumulated precedent resembles the critics' demand, such as al-Shawkani's, not the author-jurist's method.
Half right. Recent rulings from below feed the change, but it is 'openly' credited as an innovation, while the author-jurist presented change 'as the school's own.'
Out of scope. This is the frozen law of the stagnation thesis, with no change at all.
CORRECT. Recent rulings feed in, a disfavored reading is promoted by labeling, and the change is described as settled practice, just as the author-jurist presented a new view 'as the school's own.'

questions.stem: Based on the passage, the author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: A jurist could reason with real sophistication in practicing taqlid while still deferring, in the end, to the school's authority.
Al-Shawkani's critique of taqlid depended on the assumption that the door of ijtihad had in fact been closed around the year 900.
Hallaq's account would be seriously undermined if it were shown that author-jurists sometimes elevated formerly minority opinions.
Legal change that is presented as continuity is for that reason less legitimate than change that is openly acknowledged.
The older critics of taqlid were correct that Islamic law failed to keep pace with the social changes of later centuries.
questions.explanation: The author holds that taqlid was 'reasoned' but not 'independent': its practitioner 'reasoned about which opinion carried the school's authority rather than about whether the founder's reasoning was correct,' and the question 'about where authority finally resided remains open.' A follows: sophistication and deference to the school's authority are compatible. D is the strong trap: the author notes that change was 'presented as continuity' and treats where authority lies as an open question, but never says such change is less legitimate.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the author's own view supports, as distinct from Hallaq's or the critics'.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, sentences 3 to 6.

breakdown.analysis: The author's distinctive claim: reasoned is not the same as independent. Taqlid can involve real reasoning while its final ground is the school's authority. The right answer applies that distinction; expect traps that turn the author's open question into a verdict.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the 'reasoned, not... independent' distinction: the reasoning concerns 'which opinion carried the school's authority,' not the jurist's own judgment of the merits.
Out of scope. The passage says al-Shawkani urged a return to 'the scriptural evidence'; it attributes no view on the closing of the door to him.
Opposite. Elevating minority opinions is the very mechanism Hallaq uses to explain change, so showing it happened would support his account.
Too strong. The author observes that change entered 'by being presented as continuity' and leaves the authority question 'open'; no judgment of legitimacy is made.
Contradicts the author, who credits Hallaq 'rightly' with explaining how the law 'absorbed new rulings for centuries.'

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Verner's explanation of the exceptions to Grimm's law proved that sound laws admit no exceptions, as the Neogrammarians maintained.
Schuchardt was right that the Neogrammarian doctrine of exceptionless sound laws was a dogma rather than a finding.
Verner showed that Grimm's law was mistaken in treating the Germanic consonant changes as regular correspondences.
Verner's solution did not prove the exceptionlessness of sound laws, but it showed the value of that doctrine understood as a rule of method.
The position of the Indo-European accent, rather than the first sound shift, accounts for most of the consonant differences between Gothic and Sanskrit.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph gives the author's view: both admirers and critics misread the doctrine, which is 'less a report of observations than a rule of method'; Verner's discovery 'did not prove that rule' but 'showed that the rule was fruitful.' D states that. A is the admirers' reading the author rejects, and B is the critics' reading the author also rejects.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: State the passage's overall claim, including where the author stands.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, especially sentences 1, 4, 5 and 6.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraphs 1 to 3 are history: the exceptions, Verner's accent rule, the Neogrammarians' doctrine and Schuchardt's objection. Paragraph 4 is the author: both sides misread the doctrine; it is a rule of method that Verner did not prove but did show to be fruitful.

choices.note: Wrong position-holder. This is the admirers' reading; the author says 'Verner's discovery did not prove that rule; no single success could.'
Wrong position-holder. The author says the critics who dismissed the doctrine 'share a misreading' of it.
Distortion. Verner explained the exceptions within the sound shift; he did not show that the correspondences were not regular.
CORRECT. It joins the author's two claims: Verner 'did not prove' the doctrine, and the doctrine, read as 'a rule of method,' proved 'fruitful.'
Distortion. The accent decides only between voiceless and voiced outcomes of the shift; the shift itself still accounts for the consonant changes.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Gothic fadar has d rather than th because
choices: the word entered Gothic as a borrowing from another dialect
in its Indo-European form the accent did not immediately precede the consonant
Germanic fixed the accent on the first syllable of the word before the sound shift began
the word was reshaped by analogy with the Gothic word for "brother" and its related forms
Sanskrit pitar preserves an inherited d that Gothic kept unchanged
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says that in the word for 'father' the accent 'falls on the final syllable, after' the t, and that a fricative 'stayed voiceless only if the accent immediately preceded it; otherwise it became voiced.' So the th of the shift became voiced, giving d: B. Borrowing and analogy (A, D) are the escape routes mentioned in paragraph 4, not Verner's explanation.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the passage's explanation of the d in fadar.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, sentences 2 and 3.

breakdown.analysis: Combine two sentences: the accent in 'father' comes after the t, and a fricative inside a word stays voiceless only if the accent immediately precedes it. Not preceded, so voiced.

choices.note: Shell game. Borrowing appears in paragraph 4 as one way words escape a sound law, not as the explanation of fadar.
CORRECT. The accent fell 'after' the consonant, so it did not 'immediately' precede it, and the fricative 'became voiced.'
Reversed order. The accent was fixed on the first syllable 'later,' which is why the condition became invisible.
Shell game. Analogy is mentioned in paragraph 4 in general terms, never as the explanation of fadar.
Contradicts the passage, which says Sanskrit pitar 'has t.'

questions.stem: The author mentions that Germanic later fixed the accent on the first syllable (second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: introduce a second sound law that operated alongside the one Verner discovered
show that the accent played no part in the development of the Germanic consonants
account for Grimm's view that the first sound shift was only a general tendency with exceptions
suggest that Gothic preserves the Indo-European accent more faithfully than Sanskrit does
explain why the condition on the change could not be seen in Germanic forms alone
questions.explanation: The sentence says that because of the later accent shift 'the conditioning factor had been erased, and the outcome looked arbitrary,' which is why Verner had to look to the accent 'preserved in Sanskrit and Greek,' a feature 'Germanic no longer displayed.' That is E. C is tempting because the erasure helps explain why the irregularities looked real, but the author never ties the sentence to Grimm's view.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the author brings up the later accent shift.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, sentences 1 and 4.

breakdown.analysis: Verner found the cause in 'a feature Germanic no longer displayed,' preserved instead in Sanskrit and Greek. The accent-shift sentence explains why Germanic no longer displays it: the condition was erased, so the outcome 'looked arbitrary.'

choices.note: Out of scope. The passage treats the accent shift only as what hid Verner's condition; it is not presented as a second law or analyzed.
Opposite. The accent is the very condition Verner found.
Shell game. Grimm's view appears at the end of paragraph 1; this sentence explains why the condition was hidden, not why Grimm held his view.
Opposite. The old accent is 'preserved in Sanskrit and Greek'; Germanic erased it.
CORRECT. The fixed initial accent erased 'the conditioning factor,' so the condition had to be recovered from Sanskrit and Greek.

questions.stem: In asserting that the doctrine's qualifying clause "is not a loophole but its substance" (second sentence of the fourth paragraph), the author most probably means that
choices: the restriction to mechanical change states what the doctrine actually asserts, rather than serving as a way to escape counterevidence
the Neogrammarians added the qualification only after critics such as Schuchardt began pointing to words that the sound laws did not fit
the qualification makes the doctrine so weak that no possible observation could count against it
analogy and borrowing account for most of the sound changes that the Neogrammarians studied
the clause was the part of the doctrine that Verner's discovery most directly confirmed
questions.explanation: The clause is 'so weit er mechanisch vor sich geht' (insofar as it proceeds mechanically). The author then explains it: the Neogrammarians allowed analogy and borrowing, and 'what they denied was that a mechanical change could apply to one word and simply skip another in the same phonetic environment.' So the clause defines the claim instead of hedging it: A. C is the critics' kind of complaint, and the author's next sentences show the doctrine does forbid something definite.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Interpret 'not a loophole but its substance.'

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, sentence 3 (the quoted clause); paragraph 4, sentences 2 and 3.

breakdown.analysis: A loophole is a way out of an obligation; substance is the content of the claim. The author's point: the clause is what the doctrine says (no mechanical change skips a word in the same environment), not an excuse for evading exceptions. The next sentence spells out what is still forbidden.

choices.note: CORRECT. The clause sets the doctrine's content: mechanical change never skips a word in the same environment, while analogy and borrowing are a separate matter.
Contradicts the passage. The clause is in the 1878 statement itself, and the passage says Schuchardt's objection came after the doctrine was an axiom.
Opposite. The author says the doctrine denies something definite, a mechanical change that skips a word 'in the same phonetic environment'; a loophole reading is what the author rejects.
Out of scope. Analogy and borrowing are named as ways words 'could escape' a sound law; nothing says how much change they account for.
Distortion. Verner's discovery concerned the conditioning environment; the author says it 'did not prove' the rule, and nothing ties it to the clause in particular.

questions.stem: Which one of the following situations would be inconsistent with the doctrine of exceptionless sound laws as the author interprets it?
choices: Speakers reshape a word to match related forms in which a sound change did not apply, so that the word escapes the change.
A word from a dialect that never underwent a sound change is borrowed by a neighboring dialect after that dialect's change has run its course.
Two words with the same sound in the same environment, untouched by analogy or borrowing, show different results of one mechanical change.
A sound change applies only to consonants that follow a stressed vowel and leaves the same consonants unchanged everywhere else.
A change that once applied regularly is later obscured in many words because a subsequent change removes the condition on which it depended.
questions.explanation: On the author's reading the doctrine allows analogy and borrowing and denies only 'that a mechanical change could apply to one word and simply skip another in the same phonetic environment.' C describes exactly that. D is the trap for readers who treat any limit on a change as an exception: a change conditioned by stress is regular, as Verner's accent rule shows.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply the author's reading of the doctrine to new cases and find the one it forbids.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, sentence 3; paragraph 2, sentences 3 and 4 for conditioned change.

breakdown.analysis: The doctrine forbids one thing: a mechanical change skipping a word in the same environment with no other process to blame. Allowed: analogy, borrowing, changes conditioned by environment (Verner), and conditions later obscured (the accent shift).

choices.note: Allowed. The Neogrammarians 'openly allowed' escape 'through analogy with related forms.'
Allowed. Borrowing 'from another dialect' is one of the named escape routes.
CORRECT. Same sound, same environment, no analogy or borrowing, different outcomes: what the doctrine denies, that a mechanical change could 'skip another in the same phonetic environment.'
Consistent. A change limited by its environment is regular; Verner's rule is exactly this kind of conditioned change.
Consistent. This mirrors the later Germanic accent shift, which erased the condition so that 'the outcome looked arbitrary' without being irregular.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Schuchardt's objection would have been decisive had the Neogrammarians claimed only that sound change usually proceeds regularly.
The title Verner gave his paper shows that he rejected the view that sound laws admit no exceptions.
The doctrine could prove fruitful for inquiry even if it could never be established by surveying the relevant words.
Verner's discovery showed that Grimm was right to treat the first sound shift as a general tendency rather than a law.
Schuchardt's objection is answered by the fact that Verner's law, unlike Grimm's, has no exceptions of its own.
questions.explanation: The author calls the doctrine 'a rule of method,' says 'no single success could' prove it, and says Verner's result showed it 'fruitful' because refusing to accept an exception led to a real fact. Schuchardt's complaint that 'no one had checked every word' is thus beside the point for the author: the doctrine's value does not depend on such a survey. C follows. E is the strong trap: it answers Schuchardt with another empirical success, which the author says cannot prove the rule.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the claim that follows from the author's reading of the doctrine.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, last sentence; paragraph 4, sentences 4 to 6.

breakdown.analysis: Connect three things: the critics' complaint (no one checked every word), the author's reply (it is a rule of method, not a report of observations), and its payoff (fruitful even though no success proves it). The right answer separates the doctrine's value from its being verified word by word.

choices.note: Out of scope and confused. The author never considers a weaker 'usually' version, and nothing suggests Schuchardt's objection would be decisive against it.
Distortion. The title names the problem Verner solved; the passage says his solution was taken as support for the doctrine, not that he rejected it.
CORRECT. The doctrine is 'less a report of observations than a rule of method,' it cannot be proved by successes, and it was still 'fruitful.'
Opposite. Verner explained away the apparent exceptions Grimm had tolerated, and the author shows no sympathy for the tendency view.
Contradicts the author: 'Verner's discovery did not prove that rule; no single success could.' Answering Schuchardt with another success misses the author's point.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Mystical readings of Hafez's ghazals, though long established, have been discredited by historical evidence that his poems responded to the closing of the taverns of Shiraz by a strict ruler.
Hafez's ghazals are ambiguous in a way that depends on two specific interpretive codes known to his audience, not in a way that leaves their meaning indeterminate.
Because Persian pronouns do not mark gender, the identity of the beloved addressed in Hafez's ghazals can never be determined with confidence.
Scholars who read Hafez's wine imagery literally have correctly identified the historical targets of his satire, while mystical readers have not.
Hafez's ghazals are best understood as court poetry whose beloved is, in most cases, the royal patron on whom the poet depended for his position and livelihood.
questions.explanation: The author endorses the third (ambiguity) position but rejects its strong form: the ambiguity 'works only because two determinate codes were available to his first audience at once.' B states exactly that. D gives the literal readers' view to the author, and C promotes a supporting detail from paragraph 3 into the thesis and overstates it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall claim about how Hafez's imagery should be read.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, where the author speaks in the first person ('seems to me').

breakdown.analysis: Paragraphs 2 and 3 lay out three positions: mystical, literal/social, and deliberate ambiguity. Paragraph 4 gives the author's verdict: the ambiguity view is right, but not in the form that makes the poems 'indifferent to what their images refer to.' Prephrase: Hafez is ambiguous between two definite meanings, not open to any meaning. Expect traps that adopt one of the rival positions.

choices.note: Too strong and the wrong position. The author never says the mystical reading is discredited; paragraph 4 treats the mystical code as one of the two that make the poems work.
CORRECT. It captures both halves of the author's view: the endorsement of ambiguity and the qualification that the ambiguity rests on two 'determinate codes' rather than indeterminacy.

A detail from paragraph 3 turned into the main point, and overstated. The pronoun fact supports the ambiguity view; the passage never says the beloved can 'never' be identified, and the author's thesis is about how ambiguity works, not about the beloved's identity.
Wrong position-holder. This sides with the literal/social readers of paragraph 2; the author holds that both the literal and the mystical meanings are live.
Distortion of Meisami's point. Paragraph 3 says the beloved 'may be' a patron among other possibilities; the author does not claim the poems are mainly court poetry.

questions.stem: The author mentions Wilberforce Clarke's 1891 English translation (second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that nineteenth-century English translators were the first readers to propose a mystical interpretation of Hafez's imagery of wine and the tavern
cast doubt on the reliability of nineteenth-century English translations of Persian poetry
illustrate how the mystical interpretation has shaped the way Hafez's imagery is rendered and explained
provide evidence that the wine in Hafez's poems is very often simply wine
suggest that the mystical interpretation was unknown to Hafez's first audience
questions.explanation: The sentence follows the account of how 'commentators read Hafez accordingly' (wine as divine love, elder as spiritual master) and notes that Clarke's translation 'glosses the elder as just such a guide.' It is an example of the mystical reading's reach into translation. A is the trap: the passage says the mystical reading is 'the oldest answer,' long predating any English translator.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the author brings up Clarke's translation.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, sentences 2-3, and the sentence that follows ('Against this reading...').

breakdown.analysis: Read the sentence before: commentators decoded the elder as a spiritual master. Clarke's gloss does the same thing in an English translation. So the mention is an illustration of the mystical reading at work. The very next sentence turns to the opposing view, which tells you Clarke belongs to the mystical side.

choices.note: Not what the passage says. The mystical reading is 'the oldest answer,' used by commentators long before 1891; nothing suggests Clarke originated it.
Out of scope. The author does not evaluate Clarke's reliability or that of nineteenth-century translations generally.
CORRECT. Clarke's gloss shows the mystical decoding (elder = spiritual guide) built into how the poems were translated and explained.
Wrong position. That claim belongs to Davis, in the literal reading introduced after the Clarke sentence ('Against this reading...').
Opposite. The author says the mystical code 'was centuries old' and available to Hafez's first audience.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Franklin Lewis suggests that
choices: the rend in Hafez's ghazals should be understood primarily as a symbol of the mystic
Persian poets of Hafez's period were admired chiefly for achieving ambiguity
the beloved addressed in Hafez's ghazals was usually a royal patron
Mubariz al-Din was the first ruler to close the taverns of Shiraz
Hafez's ambiguity may have served his opposition to hypocrisy
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'Lewis suggests that Hafez's ambiguity may have been deliberate, a weapon in his campaign against hypocrisy.' E paraphrases that with the same hedge. B is the wrong-person trap: the point about poets being admired for ambiguity is Davis's, in the same sentence.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage attributes to Lewis specifically.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Lewis appears twice: paragraph 2 (the renderings of rend) and paragraph 3, second-to-last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Track names. Paragraph 2 cites Lewis only for the English renderings of rend. Paragraph 3 joins Davis and Lewis in one sentence: Davis on ambiguity being admired; Lewis on deliberate ambiguity against hypocrisy. Pick the one tied to Lewis.

choices.note: Opposite. In paragraph 2 the rend, on the literal reading, is 'a figure of defiance against official piety rather than a symbol of the mystic,' and Lewis is cited only for how the word has been translated.
Wrong person and too strong. The observation about poets being admired for ambiguity is Davis's, and the passage does not say 'chiefly.'
Not Lewis's claim, and too strong. Paragraph 3 says the beloved 'may be' a youth, patron or God; the court-poetry point is Meisami's.
Not stated. The passage says Mubariz al-Din closed the taverns, not that he was the first to do so, and does not attribute this to Lewis.
CORRECT. Paragraph 3: Lewis suggests Hafez's ambiguity 'may have been deliberate, a weapon in his campaign against hypocrisy.'

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: A reader who takes Hafez's wine to signify divine love has identified a meaning that the poems genuinely carry.
The mystical reading of Hafez is less defensible than the literal reading, since it ignores the history of Shiraz.
Hafez's first audience was largely unaware that his images could be understood in more than one way.
The value of Hafez's ghazals lies chiefly in their indifference to what their images refer to.
Scholars who stress the ambiguity of Hafez's poems have generally ignored the circumstances of his city.
questions.explanation: The last sentence says readers who settle on one meaning 'do not err in finding a meaning; they err in supposing that the poem asks them to choose.' So the mystical meaning is real, though not the whole. A says no more than that. D is the strong ambiguity thesis the author rejects, and E overgeneralizes 'sometimes stated in a form that goes too far.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the statement the author's own view supports.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, especially its first and last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The author holds that both codes are determinate and both are live. A one-meaning reader is half right: right that the meaning is there, wrong to exclude the other. Look for an answer that credits a single reading with finding something real, without saying it is complete.

choices.note: CORRECT. The final sentence: such readers 'do not err in finding a meaning.' The mystical code is one of the 'two determinate codes' the poems rely on.
The author ranks neither reading above the other; both codes are needed for the poem's 'friction.'
Opposite. The ambiguity works because both codes 'were available to his first audience at once.'
This is the overstated form of the ambiguity thesis that the author says 'goes too far.'
Too strong. The author says the thesis is 'sometimes' stated too strongly, not that its proponents 'generally' ignore history; paragraph 3's scholars in fact cite court and social contexts.

questions.stem: By "two determinate codes" (second sentence of the fourth paragraph), the author most probably means
choices: two rival schools of commentators, each of which insisted that the poems have a single correct meaning that the other school had missed
two sets of formal rules governing the meter and rhyme of the Persian ghazal
two audiences, one courtly and one religious, for whom Hafez composed separate poems
two established systems of reference through which the poems' images could be specifically understood
two meanings between which the poems remain wholly indifferent
questions.explanation: The next sentence names the two codes: 'The mystical code was centuries old; the closed taverns were a fact of the city's life.' These are two definite frames of reference, the Sufi symbolism and the social world, each giving the images a specific sense. E reverses the author's point: 'determinate' is set against the claim that the poems are 'indifferent to what their images refer to.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out what 'two determinate codes' refers to.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The sentence right after it in paragraph 4, and the first sentence, which the phrase answers.

breakdown.analysis: 'Determinate' is the author's answer to the overstated thesis that any reading is as good as another. The following sentence identifies the codes as the mystical symbolism and the lived reality of the closed taverns. Prephrase: two known frameworks that give the images definite meanings.

choices.note: Shell game. The codes are frames of meaning the audience shared, not groups of commentators; and the author denies that the poem asks readers to pick one.
Out of scope. The passage never discusses meter or rhyme.
Distortion. The author describes one poem heard two ways by different readers, not separate poems for separate audiences.
CORRECT. The mystical code and the social facts of Shiraz are each established, and each gives the images a definite sense.
Opposite. 'Determinate' is contrasted with the view that the poems are 'indifferent to what their images refer to.'

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously undermine the author's argument against the strong form of the ambiguity thesis?
choices: Many of Hafez's ghazals were first recited at court, before mixed audiences that included both religious scholars and worldly courtiers.
Many modern readers who know nothing of Sufi symbolism nevertheless find Hafez's ghazals deeply moving.
Most of Hafez's contemporaries in Shiraz were unfamiliar with the convention of reading wine as a figure for divine love.
Mubariz al-Din's closing of the taverns of Shiraz was also criticized by poets other than Hafez.
Later commentators disagreed with one another about which of Hafez's ghazals should be read mystically.
questions.explanation: The author argues that the ambiguity 'works only because two determinate codes were available to his first audience at once,' supporting this with 'The mystical code was centuries old.' If most contemporaries did not know the mystical convention, one of the two codes was not available to the first audience, and the argument loses its premise. B is the trap: it concerns modern readers, whom the argument never addresses.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The ambiguity is not indifference to meaning; it depends on two determinate codes.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Both the mystical code and the social facts of Shiraz were available to Hafez's first audience at once.

breakdown.analysis: To weaken, attack the premise that both codes were live for the first audience. An answer showing one code was not available then does it. Watch for answers about later or modern readers, which change the time frame.

choices.note: This fits the author's picture of a mixed audience hearing both meanings; if anything it supports the argument.
Out of scope. The argument concerns Hafez's first audience; whether modern readers are moved says nothing about which codes his contemporaries knew.
CORRECT. It denies that the mystical code was available to the first audience, removing one of the two codes the author's argument requires.
Irrelevant, or a slight strengthener: it confirms that the closed taverns were a live social fact.
Consistent with the author's view. Disagreement among later commentators is what one expects if the poems carry two meanings at once.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the way the author believes Hafez's ambiguity functions?
choices: A painter leaves a canvas largely unfinished so that each viewer is free to complete the image in whatever way he or she wishes.
A diplomat drafts a communiqué in deliberately vague terms so that no party can later hold her government to any particular commitment.
A playwright writes a scene that audiences in two different centuries interpret differently because their customs have changed.
A satirist under censorship writes a fable that loyal readers take as a moral tale and dissenters take as an attack on the regime.
A translator renders an obscure term in two different ways in successive editions after scholars dispute its meaning.
questions.explanation: For the author, one text carries two definite meanings, each drawn from a convention its first audience knew, and its force comes from the 'friction' between them; the meanings also differ in their stance toward authority, much as the pious and worldly hearings of the ascetic poem do. D matches: one fable, two contemporaneous audiences, each reading through a recognizable code. A is the strong ambiguity thesis the author rejects ('any reading is as good as another'); C spreads the two meanings across centuries rather than one audience 'at once.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the case whose structure matches the author's account of Hafez's ambiguity.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4: 'two determinate codes,' 'available to his first audience at once,' 'friction between them.'

breakdown.analysis: List the features: (1) one work, (2) two definite meanings, not an open field, (3) both available to the same original audience at the same time, (4) the effect depends on both. Test each answer against all four. Answers that offer indeterminacy, vagueness, or meanings that arise at different times each fail a feature.

choices.note: This is the strong form of the thesis the author rejects: meaning left open for 'any reading,' rather than two determinate meanings.
Vagueness designed to avoid commitment is the opposite of two definite meanings each fully available to its readers.
Two meanings, but separated in time by changing customs; the author stresses that both codes were available to the first audience 'at once.'
CORRECT. One text, two determinate readings drawn from conventions the same contemporary audience recognizes, with the work's force depending on that doubleness.
Two renderings in two editions reflect a scholarly dispute about one meaning, not a single text deliberately carrying two.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Barks's versions of Rumi should be set aside in favor of the scholarly translations that preserve the poet's many allusions to the Qur'an and to the sayings of the Prophet.
The great popularity of Barks's versions shows that a translation owes its source a poem's life rather than its doctrinal content.
Selection is unavoidable, but Barks's versions at times invert the Islamic frame of Rumi's poems, a fault best addressed by reading them beside fuller translations.
Franklin Lewis's critique of Barks is misplaced, since Barks has never claimed that his versions are translations of Rumi's Persian.
Rumi's poetry cannot be rendered into English without the loss of the religious meaning that is essential to it.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 holds that selection is unavoidable, that what a translation must not do is 'reverse the direction of what it keeps,' that Barks's quatrain is 'an inversion of the poem's frame,' and that the remedy is 'not to dismiss the versions' but to read them beside other translations. C carries all three parts. A is the near-miss: it takes the critics' side and contradicts the author's remedy.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: State the author's overall position on Barks and what a translation owes.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, from 'Both sides, I think' to the last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraphs 1-3 set up Barks, the scholarly critique, and the defense. Paragraph 4 rejects both sides' assumption, then states a narrower duty, applies it to the quatrain, and ends with a remedy. A good answer needs the concession (selection is fine), the charge (inversion of frame), and the remedy (read alongside), or at least nothing that contradicts them.

choices.note: Too strong. The author explicitly says the remedy 'is not to dismiss the versions.'
This is the defenders' view from paragraph 3, which the author says assumes 'too simple an account.'
CORRECT. It keeps the concession, the specific charge of inversion, and the author's remedy.
Wrong conclusion. The author grants the honesty of the 'versions' label but still finds a real fault, so Lewis's concern is not dismissed.
Too strong. The author holds that a translation can keep the frame in view and recommends reading such translations.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Barks's versions of Rumi are based on
choices: Barks's own reading of the Persian text of the Masnavi, which he checked line by line against Nicholson's commentary
translations of Rumi that Robert Bly prepared during the 1970s
the translations that Franklin Lewis included in his study of Rumi
earlier English translations by Arberry and Nicholson, together with cribs prepared by John Moyne
recitations of the Masnavi that Barks heard during his travels in Konya
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: Barks 'recast the literal English of Arberry and R. A. Nicholson, together with cribs prepared by his collaborator John Moyne.' D restates this. A contradicts 'Barks never learned Persian'; B confuses Bly, who handed Barks Arberry's book, with a translator.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says Barks worked from.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph, sentences 2-3.

breakdown.analysis: A straight retrieval. The passage names three sources: Arberry, Nicholson, and Moyne's cribs. Eliminate any answer that has Barks reading Persian or names someone the passage casts in a different role.

choices.note: Contradicts the passage: 'Barks never learned Persian.'
Shell game. Bly handed Barks a volume of Arberry's translations; the passage does not say Bly translated Rumi.
Wrong role. Lewis is the critic of paragraph 2; the passage does not say Barks used Lewis's translations.
CORRECT. Paragraph 1 names Arberry, Nicholson and Moyne's cribs as Barks's materials.
Out of scope. The passage mentions Konya only as where Rumi taught and preached.

questions.stem: The primary function of the third paragraph is to
choices: present a response that has been offered to the criticism described in the second paragraph
set out the author's own account of what a translation owes its source
provide evidence that Barks's versions are in fact more accurate renderings of the Persian than his critics have claimed
concede that Lewis's account of Rumi's religious learning is overstated
explain why the scholarly translations by Arberry and Nicholson are difficult to read
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 begins 'Barks's defenders reply' and lists their answers to the scholarly objection of paragraph 2. A says this. B is the wrong-paragraph trap: the author's own account comes in paragraph 4, which opens by saying 'Both sides' are mistaken.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what paragraph 3 does in the passage's structure.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3 and the first sentence of paragraph 4.

breakdown.analysis: The structure is: background (1), objection (2), reply (3), author's resolution (4). Paragraph 3 is the reply. Its voice is the defenders', not the author's: paragraph 4 begins by faulting 'both sides.'

choices.note: CORRECT. It gives the defenders' reply to the objection stated by Lewis and Ali.
Wrong position-holder. The author's view comes in paragraph 4, which criticizes the defenders as well.
Distortion. The defenders concede that Barks 'never claimed scholarly fidelity'; they argue about what matters, not that he is more accurate.
Not in the passage. Neither the defenders nor the author disputes Rumi's training in Islamic law and theology.
Distortion. Paragraph 3 says the accurate translations 'found few readers'; it does not explain why they are hard to read.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Barks's versions of Rumi can most accurately be described as
choices: unqualified admiration for their success in bringing Rumi to American readers
dismissive contempt for their departures from the literal sense of the Persian
neutrality, since the author declines to judge between Barks and his critics
reluctant approval, tempered only by regret that Barks does not read the Persian in which Rumi wrote
critical of a specific distortion they introduce, while granting that they have real value
questions.explanation: The author calls the quatrain's rendering 'an inversion of the poem's frame' but calls the 'versions' label 'an honest acknowledgment' and says the versions 'have led many readers to Rumi' and should not be dismissed. E captures that mix. D is the trap: it is mildly positive, but the author's criticism is of inversion, not of Barks's lack of Persian, which the author never treats as a fault in itself.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize the author's attitude toward Barks's versions.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4: 'honest acknowledgment,' 'inversion of the poem's frame,' 'not to dismiss the versions.'

breakdown.analysis: Collect the author's evaluative words. Positive: 'honest acknowledgment,' 'have led many readers to Rumi.' Negative: 'reverse the direction,' 'inversion of the poem's frame.' So the attitude is mixed, with a precise criticism. Eliminate extremes and any answer that names the wrong fault.

choices.note: Too positive. The author charges the versions with 'an inversion of the poem's frame.'
Too negative. The author defends the label 'versions' as honest and says the versions should not be dismissed.
Wrong. The author takes a clear position, faulting 'both sides.'
Wrong fault. The author never treats Barks's not reading Persian as the problem; the criticism is the reversal of what the versions keep.
CORRECT. Critical of one distortion (inverting the poem's Islamic frame), while granting the versions' honesty and their value in leading readers to Rumi.

questions.stem: By "reverse the direction of what it keeps" (third sentence of the fourth paragraph), the author most probably means
choices: alter the order in which the lines of the original poem appear
retain an element of the original while making it point away from what it pointed toward in the original
omit those elements of the original that the translator finds least congenial
change the meanings of individual words in the original while preserving the poem's overall structure and form
translate a poem back into its original language from an intermediate version
questions.explanation: The author illustrates the phrase with the quatrain: Rumi's gesture beyond Islam and infidelity is kept, but 'rendered as a field beyond moral ideas, the same gesture appears to come from outside religion altogether' and becomes 'an inversion of the poem's frame.' The element is kept but turned to face the opposite way. C is the trap: omission is the selection the author says is 'unavoidable,' and the phrase is about what is kept, not what is left out.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Interpret the phrase from its use in paragraph 4.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The phrase and the sentences after it ('The quatrain shows the difference...').

breakdown.analysis: The phrase is contrasted with mere selection. It concerns 'what it keeps.' The quatrain example shows the kept gesture (going beyond religious categories) recast so that it seems to lead away from religion, though in the original it is an Islamic mystical move. Prephrase: keep something but make it mean the opposite of its original orientation.

choices.note: Too literal. 'Direction' refers to orientation of meaning, not the sequence of lines.
CORRECT. The gesture beyond Islam and infidelity is retained, but it is made to point away from religion when in the original it was a move within Islam.
This describes omission, which the author treats as unavoidable selection; the phrase concerns what is kept.
Out of scope. The example concerns the orientation of a whole gesture, not word meanings within a preserved structure.
Too literal and unsupported. No back-translation is discussed.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: A translator who cannot read a poem's original language cannot produce a legitimate rendering of that poem.
Most readers who first encountered Rumi through Barks's versions have been misled about Rumi's beliefs.
Lewis's account of Rumi's training in Islamic law and theology overstates the role of religion in Rumi's poetry.
By calling his renderings versions rather than translations, Barks fully discharges whatever obligations a translator owes to a source.
A rendering of Rumi that omitted many of his Qur'anic allusions would not, for that reason alone, fail in what it owes its source.
questions.explanation: The author holds that 'No rendering carries everything; selection is unavoidable,' and that what a translation owes is 'narrower': not to present its selection as the whole and not to reverse what it keeps. So omission by itself is not the failing. E says exactly this, hedged with 'for that reason alone.' D is the trap: the author calls the label 'an honest acknowledgment' of selection but still finds the inversion a fault, so the label does not discharge every obligation.

setup.label: Task
