setup.text: Find the statement the author's account of a translation's duties supports.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, sentences 2-3.

breakdown.analysis: The author separates two things: selection (unavoidable, acceptable) and inversion or false wholeness (a real fault). An answer that treats omission alone as acceptable fits; answers that make the author more severe (A, B) or more lenient (D) than paragraph 4 do not. The key sounds modest; that is typical.

choices.note: Too strong. The author treats Barks's method as legitimate in principle and faults a specific inversion, not his lack of Persian.
Too strong. The author identifies a distortion in at least one rendering but makes no claim about what most readers believe, and credits the versions with leading readers to Rumi.
Unsupported. The author accepts Lewis's account of Rumi's learning and builds on it.
Too strong. The label honestly acknowledges selection, but the author says a translation must also 'not reverse the direction of what it keeps,' which Barks's quatrain does.
CORRECT. Since 'selection is unavoidable,' omitting allusions is not in itself a breach; the duties are not to present the selection as the whole and not to invert what is kept.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, which one of the following renderings would the author regard as failing in the same way that the author believes Barks's version of the quatrain fails?
choices: A translator renders a medieval Christian mystic's passage about passing beyond all images of God, which the mystic grounds in Christian teaching, as a call to leave belief behind.
A translator of a Hebrew psalm omits several allusions to earlier scripture in order to preserve the rhythm of the psalm in English.
A translator of a classical Chinese poem adds footnotes explaining its Buddhist references for readers unfamiliar with them.
A translator of a classical Arabic ode replaces its desert imagery with familiar English landscapes of hedge, meadow and field while faithfully keeping the ode's praise of the poet's tribe.
A translator who reads no Sanskrit renders a Sanskrit hymn from an earlier literal English version, clearly labeling the result an adaptation rather than a translation.
questions.explanation: The author's charge is that Barks keeps Rumi's gesture beyond outward religious categories, a move made within Islam, but renders it so that it 'appears to come from outside religion altogether.' A is the same pattern: a mystical transcendence grounded in a faith is turned into a call to leave that faith. B and D are losses of detail, which the author calls unavoidable selection, and E describes Barks's method, which the author does not fault in itself.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the case that commits the specific fault the author identifies in the quatrain.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, from 'The quatrain shows the difference' to 'an inversion of the poem's frame.'

breakdown.analysis: Name the fault precisely: not omission, not freedom, not working from cribs, but keeping a religious mystic's move beyond religious categories while recasting it as a move out of religion. Find the answer with that inversion.

choices.note: CORRECT. A faith-grounded mystical gesture is kept but made to point away from the faith, the inversion of frame the author finds in Barks's quatrain.
Omission for the sake of form is selection, which the author calls 'unavoidable'; nothing is inverted.
Opposite. Explaining religious references keeps the frame in view, which is what the author recommends.
A substitution of imagery is a loss of detail; the ode's orientation (praise of the tribe) is kept, not reversed.
This is Barks's working method, which the author treats as honest when labeled; it is not the fault the author identifies.

sections.title: Reading Through Ideas 5: Cantor and the infinite past · Ibn Khaldun and his modern readers · Barr and the Root Fallacy · Chains of Testimony

passages.title: Cantor and the infinite past
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Among the arguments that Muslim theologians of the kalam tradition advanced for the creation of the world, one has enjoyed an unusual modern afterlife. If the world had no beginning, the argument runs, the past would contain an actually infinite series of events, and no such series can exist. In The Incoherence of the Philosophers, al-Ghazali pressed this point against philosophers such as Ibn Sina, who held the world to be eternal. Saturn, he observed, completes a revolution in thirty years and Jupiter in twelve. Over a beginningless past each would have completed infinitely many revolutions, yet Jupiter's must be more than twice as numerous as Saturn's; and the total would be neither even nor odd, though every number must be one or the other.

The philosophers had a reply: past revolutions no longer exist, and what is impossible is only an infinity of things existing together. Al-Ghazali answered that on the philosophers' own view human souls survive death, so an eternal world would now contain infinitely many souls. In 1979 William Lane Craig revived the argument in The Kalam Cosmological Argument, recasting it with the help of a later illustration, Hilbert's hotel. A hotel with infinitely many rooms, all occupied, can admit a new guest by moving each occupant up one room; and if the guests in every odd-numbered room depart, infinitely many guests have left, yet the hotel holds as many guests as before. Craig contends that such consequences show that an actual infinite, whatever its standing as an idea, cannot exist in reality.

Critics answer that Georg Cantor's set theory has settled the matter. Cantor showed how to reason consistently about completed infinite collections: an infinite collection is precisely one that can be matched one-to-one with a part of itself, so the hotel displays the defining property of infinity, not a contradiction. Al-Ghazali's puzzles fare no better, since in Cantor's arithmetic Jupiter's revolutions and Saturn's form collections of the same size, and the parity dilemma assumes that every collection has a finite count.

This reply, I think, settles less than its proponents suppose, though more than Craig allows. It establishes that the concept of an actual infinite is not self-contradictory, and so it defeats any version of the argument, the parity dilemma included, that treats a completed infinity as impossible as a matter of logic. But Craig does not deny that Cantor's system is consistent; his premise concerns reality, and mathematics, which tells us what can be consistently described, does not by itself tell us what concrete things can do. Hilbert himself, Cantor's most celebrated defender, concluded that the infinite "neither exists in nature nor provides a legitimate basis for rational thought." Yet the same distinction limits Craig. If the hotel is consistent, then calling it absurd means only that it offends intuitions formed on finite collections, and those are exactly the intuitions one would expect to fail when applied to the infinite. What Cantor leaves open is a question of metaphysics, whether successive concrete events can compose a completed infinity, and on that question neither party may simply appeal to the mathematics.

sources.author: al-Ghazali (trans. Michael E. Marmura)
sources.title: The Incoherence of the Philosophers (Tahafut al-falasifa)
sources.note: The First Discussion attacks the philosophers' (chiefly Ibn Sina's) claim to have demonstrated the world's eternity, including the Saturn-Jupiter revolutions argument, the even-or-odd dilemma and the argument from infinitely many surviving souls; Marmura's parallel Arabic-English edition is the standard translation.

sources.author: William Lane Craig
sources.title: The Kalam Cosmological Argument
sources.note: Revives the medieval kalam argument, defending the premise that an actual infinite cannot exist in reality (illustrated by Hilbert's hotel) while granting that transfinite set theory is consistent as a mathematical system.

sources.author: David Hilbert
sources.title: On the Infinite (Uber das Unendliche)
sources.note: Hilbert's 1925 Munster lecture defending Cantor's set theory while denying that the infinite is found in physical reality; the passage's quotation is from the English translation by Erna Putnam and Gerald J. Massey in Benacerraf and Putnam, eds., Philosophy of Mathematics.

sources.author: Wes Morriston
sources.title: Craig on the Actual Infinite (Religious Studies 38)
sources.note: Argues that Craig's case against an actually infinite collection of real things fails and that the Hilbert's-hotel 'absurdities' do not show such a collection to be impossible.

passages.title: Ibn Khaldun and his modern readers
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
In 1377, in a fortress in what is now Algeria, Ibn Khaldun completed the first draft of the Muqaddimah, the introduction to a universal history. In it he proposed what he called a new science, the science of 'umran, a term usually rendered "civilization" or "human social organization." Its purpose, as he stated it, was critical: historians had repeated absurd reports because they did not know what the nature of social life makes possible, and a science of that nature would let them test reports against it.

The engine of his account is 'asabiyya, which Franz Rosenthal translated as "group feeling": the solidarity that binds people who share descent or long association. It is strongest among desert peoples, whose harsh life demands mutual reliance, and it enables such a group to seize royal authority. Once in power, however, the dynasty settles into sedentary life; luxury softens its members, its rulers come to depend on paid troops and clients rather than kinsmen, and within roughly three generations it grows weak enough to be displaced by a group whose solidarity is still intact. Religion, in his account, can greatly strengthen group feeling but cannot replace it: a religious movement that lacks such backing, he held, will fail.

Modern readers have found the Muqaddimah strikingly familiar. Writers in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries hailed Ibn Khaldun as a founder of sociology, and economists have pointed to his passages on the division of labor and on taxation ("At the beginning of the dynasty, taxation yields a large revenue from small assessments") as anticipations of their own discipline. Other scholars caution against such claims. Muhsin Mahdi, in Ibn Khaldun's Philosophy of History (1957), argued that the new science can be understood only within the philosophical tradition that Muslim thinkers inherited from Plato and Aristotle, in which to know a thing scientifically is to grasp its nature and causes, and that to read it as an early version of modern sociology is to miss the questions it was meant to answer. More recently, Robert Irwin has stressed how much of the Muqaddimah, from its treatment of Sufism to its discussions of magic and divination, modern admirers quietly set aside.

These cautions are well taken, but they are sometimes pressed further than they will go. It is true that to call Ibn Khaldun a sociologist is to credit him with a discipline whose aims, chief among them a study of society detached from any account of the good life, he did not share; his science was meant to serve the historian, and he regularly presented the regularities he described as God's way with His creatures. But a reading can be anachronistic in its framing without being mistaken in what it notices. The mechanism by which solidarity wins power and comfort erodes it is a genuine causal argument, drawn from observation and stated with a generality that invites testing against cases he never knew. To recognize this is not to make him a modern; it is to grant that the questions he asked belong to no single century, even if the answers he would accept do.

sources.author: Ibn Khaldun (trans. Franz Rosenthal)
sources.title: The Muqaddimah: An Introduction to History
sources.note: The standard complete English translation, which renders 'asabiyya as 'group feeling'; source of the quotation on taxation ('At the beginning of the dynasty, taxation yields a large revenue from small assessments') in the chapter on the dynasty.

sources.author: Muhsin Mahdi
sources.title: Ibn Khaldun's Philosophy of History: A Study in the Philosophic Foundation of the Science of Culture
sources.note: Argues that Ibn Khaldun's new science of culture rests on the philosophy of Plato, Aristotle and their Muslim followers, and must be read in that light rather than as proto-modern sociology.

sources.author: Robert Irwin
sources.title: Ibn Khaldun: An Intellectual Biography
sources.note: A deliberately 'de-modernizing' portrait of Ibn Khaldun as a Maliki jurist, Sufi sympathizer and man of his age, stressing the parts of the Muqaddimah (magic, divination, mysticism) that modern admirers neglect.

passages.title: Barr and the Root Fallacy
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
In The Semantics of Biblical Language (1961), James Barr attacked a style of argument then common in biblical theology. Its practitioners held that Hebrew and Greek embodied distinct ways of thinking, so that the structure of a biblical word could disclose the theology of those who used it. Thorleif Boman had contrasted a dynamic Hebrew mentality with a static Greek one, reading the contrast off features of the two languages, and many contributors to Gerhard Kittel's Theological Dictionary of the New Testament treated a single word as the bearer of a whole theological concept. Barr argued that both habits rested on mistakes about how language works. Differences of linguistic structure, he contended, do not license conclusions about differences of thought, and what a word means is settled by its use in particular contexts, not by the history behind it.

Two of Barr's diagnoses have become standard terms. The "root fallacy" is the assumption that a root carries a basic sense present in every word derived from it. Against it, Barr insisted that "the etymology of a word is not a statement about its meaning but about its history." The Hebrew words for bread and for war share a root, but no reader supposes that a mention of bread evokes battle. The second error, which Barr called "illegitimate totality transfer," occurs when the full range of senses a word bears across a body of literature is "read into a particular case as its sense and implication there." The Hebrew dabar can mean "word" or "matter," but in a given sentence it does not ordinarily mean both at once.

Barr's critique is now often invoked as a blanket prohibition, and here some qualification is needed. Barr himself never held that etymology is worthless. In Comparative Philology and the Text of the Old Testament (1968) he examined the practice of clarifying obscure Hebrew words through their cognates in Arabic, Ugaritic, and other Semitic languages, criticizing its excesses while granting it a place. The Hebrew Bible contains many words that occur only once or twice, and for such words the evidence of use that Barr's method requires is too thin to fix a meaning. Etymology is weak evidence, but where it is nearly the only evidence it is not negligible. Moreover, biblical writers sometimes exploit etymology themselves, as when Genesis links the first human, adam, to the ground, adamah; to notice such wordplay is to describe the text's own usage, not to impose a history on it.

The lesson of Barr's book, then, is not that etymology must be ignored but that it must be given its proper evidential weight. Moisés Silva's Biblical Words and Their Meaning (1983), largely endorsing Barr, likewise allows that a word's history may at times serve interpretation, provided it does not override what context shows. What Barr overturned was the inference from a word's origin, or from a language's structure, to a theology; what he left standing was the ordinary philological use of origins as one clue among others. Those who cite him to dismiss every appeal to origins credit him with a stricter position than he defended.

sources.author: James Barr
sources.title: The Semantics of Biblical Language
sources.note: The founding critique of arguing from etymology and from Hebrew versus Greek linguistic structure to theology, aimed at Boman and Kittel's Theological Dictionary; source of both quotations: 'the etymology of a word is not a statement about its meaning but about its history' (p. 109) and the definition of illegitimate totality transfer, where a word's total meaning 'is read into a particular case as its sense and implication there' (p. 218).

sources.author: James Barr
sources.title: Comparative Philology and the Text of the Old Testament
sources.note: Barr's study of using Arabic, Ugaritic and other cognates to explain rare Hebrew words: it criticizes the excesses of cognate-based guessing while putting the method on a firmer footing.

sources.author: Moisés Silva
sources.title: Biblical Words and Their Meaning: An Introduction to Lexical Semantics
sources.note: An accessible introduction to lexical semantics for Bible readers that builds on Barr, warning against letting a word's history override context while allowing that etymology can sometimes help (revised edition 1994).

passages.title: Chains of Testimony
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Passage A

When Sunni scholars of the second and third Islamic centuries asked whether a report attributed to the Prophet Muhammad was authentic, they did not, for the most part, try to verify its contents directly. They examined its isnad, the chain of named transmitters through whom it had passed, asking of each link whether he was upright and accurate and whether he could actually have heard the report from the person he cited. The resulting science of the men, 'ilm al-rijal, produced vast biographical dictionaries grading thousands of narrators. As Jonathan A. C. Brown explains in Hadith (2009), a narrator's accuracy was gauged largely by comparison: critics gathered the versions of a report transmitted by different students of the same teacher, and a narrator whose versions regularly diverged from those of his peers was judged weak. A transmitter whose standing was unknown could not make a report sound, however plausible its content.

Western skeptics doubted that this procedure could reach the truth. Joseph Schacht, in The Origins of Muhammadan Jurisprudence (1950), argued that chains were often fabricated along with the reports they carried and tended to be extended backward, so that a doctrine first held by later jurists acquired an ever more authoritative pedigree. A flawless chain, on this view, proves little. Brown grants that forgery was widespread, as the critics themselves acknowledged, but argues that the skeptics underestimated the critics, who also rejected reports whose content was objectionable, often expressing that judgment in the vocabulary of isnad criticism. Checking a chain was never merely checking names.

Passage B

How can we be justified in believing what others tell us? David Hume, in the section on miracles in his Enquiry (1748), answered that our reliance on testimony rests on experience: we have observed that people's reports usually match the facts, and we trust testimony to the degree that this observed conformity warrants. On this reductionist view, testimony is a derivative source of knowledge, justified by perception, memory, and induction. Thomas Reid (1764) objected that children believe what they are told long before they could have gathered such evidence, and he posited instead an innate "disposition to confide in the veracity of others, and to believe what they tell us."

C. A. J. Coady's Testimony (1992) renewed Reid's case. Coady argued that no individual has observed nearly enough agreement between reports and facts to ground the vast body of testimony each of us accepts; much of what we might cite as a check, from maps to scientific findings, is itself testimony. He argued further that we could not even recognize a community's utterances as reports unless most of them were true.

Anti-reductionism is not credulity, however. On this view we are entitled to accept testimony by default, but the entitlement can be defeated: we withdraw trust from a speaker shown to be careless or dishonest, or whose report conflicts with what others tell us. We assess sources; we do not, and could not, verify every claim for ourselves.

sources.author: Jonathan A. C. Brown
sources.title: Hadith: Muhammad's Legacy in the Medieval and Modern World
sources.note: A clear introduction to how Sunni critics assessed isnads and narrators ('ilm al-rijal), and to the Western debate begun by Goldziher and Schacht; Brown argues the critics also judged content, a case he develops in his 2008 Islamic Law and Society article on early matn criticism.

sources.author: Joseph Schacht
sources.title: The Origins of Muhammadan Jurisprudence
sources.note: The classic skeptical study arguing that legal hadith largely arose after the Prophet's time and that isnads tended to grow backwards toward more authoritative figures.

sources.author: Thomas Reid
sources.title: An Inquiry into the Human Mind on the Principles of Common Sense
sources.note: Reid's case that trust in testimony is an original principle of human nature, not a conclusion from experience; source of the quotation defining the principle of credulity as 'a disposition to confide in the veracity of others, and to believe what they tell us.'

sources.author: C. A. J. Coady
sources.title: Testimony: A Philosophical Study
sources.note: The modern anti-reductionist classic: argues that Hume's attempt to justify testimony by each person's observed correlations between reports and facts fails, since we have far too little first-hand evidence of speakers' reliability.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Cantor's set theory shows that the kalam argument against an infinite past, in both its medieval and its modern forms, rests on a logical confusion.
Al-Ghazali's argument from planetary revolutions anticipated in nearly every respect the version of the kalam argument that Craig later defended.
Cantor's work shows that an actual infinite is not self-contradictory but does not by itself settle whether a beginningless series of concrete events is possible.
Craig's version of the kalam argument succeeds where al-Ghazali's failed, because Craig's premise concerns what can exist in reality rather than what is possible as a matter of logic.
Because intuitions formed on finite collections are unreliable, the question whether the past had a beginning cannot be answered.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says Cantor's reply 'settles less than its proponents suppose, though more than Craig allows': it shows the actual infinite is not self-contradictory, but 'What Cantor leaves open is a question of metaphysics.' C states both halves. A is the critics' view, which the author rejects; D keeps the author's point against the critics but drops 'Yet the same distinction limits Craig.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall claim about what Cantor's set theory does and does not settle in the kalam debate.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, first two sentences and last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraphs 1-2 present the argument (al-Ghazali, then Craig); paragraph 3 gives the critics' Cantorian reply; paragraph 4 is the author's verdict, a two-sided one: Cantor defeats the logic-based versions but leaves the metaphysical question open, and that limits both sides. Prephrase: 'Cantor proves consistency, not real possibility.' Expect one trap that sides wholly with the critics and one that sides wholly with Craig.

choices.note: Wrong position-holder. This is the critics' claim that Cantor 'has settled the matter'; the author says it 'settles less than its proponents suppose' and that Craig's premise survives it.

Distortion. The passage presents Craig as reviving and recasting the argument with a new illustration; it never says the two versions match in nearly every respect, and the author treats them differently (the parity dilemma is defeated, Craig's premise is not).

CORRECT. 'Not self-contradictory' is taken from the paragraph's second sentence, and 'What Cantor leaves open is a question of metaphysics, whether successive concrete events can compose a completed infinity' becomes the second half.
Half right. The author agrees that Craig's premise concerns reality and escapes the logical objection, but says 'the same distinction limits Craig' and never says his argument succeeds.
Too extreme. The author says only that neither party 'may simply appeal to the mathematics'; the question is left to metaphysics, not declared unanswerable.

questions.stem: The author quotes Hilbert's conclusion about the infinite (fourth sentence of the fourth paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that even the most celebrated defender of Cantor's theory had doubts about whether the theory was internally consistent
provide decisive evidence that Craig's premise about what can exist in reality is true
suggest that the critics have misunderstood the purpose for which Cantor developed his set theory
explain why the illustration Craig uses to support his argument bears Hilbert's name
illustrate that accepting Cantor's mathematics is compatible with denying that the infinite exists in reality
questions.explanation: The sentence before the quotation says mathematics 'does not by itself tell us what concrete things can do'; Hilbert, 'Cantor's most celebrated defender,' nonetheless held that the infinite 'neither exists in nature.' The example shows the two positions can be held together, as E says. B overstates: the very next sentence, 'Yet the same distinction limits Craig,' shows the author is not endorsing Craig's premise.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the author brings in Hilbert at this point in the argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, sentences 3-5: the sentence before the quotation and the 'Yet' sentence after it.

breakdown.analysis: Function questions are answered by context. Sentence 3 separates what is consistent from what concrete things can do. Hilbert is then introduced as someone who championed Cantor yet denied the infinite in nature: a living example of the gap. Sentence 5 ('Yet the same distinction limits Craig') shows the author is not using Hilbert to prove Craig right. Prephrase: 'to show you can accept Cantor and still deny a real infinite.'

choices.note: Distortion. Calling Hilbert Cantor's 'defender' implies he accepted the theory; the quotation concerns nature, not the theory's consistency.
Too strong. The author uses Hilbert to show that the real-world question is open, not settled in Craig's favor; the next sentence turns the distinction against Craig.
Out of scope. Nothing in the passage concerns the purpose for which Cantor developed the theory.
Irrelevant. The passage names 'Hilbert's hotel' but never explains the name, and the quotation is not about the hotel.
CORRECT. Hilbert both defended Cantor and denied that the infinite 'exists in nature,' which is exactly the compatibility the author's distinction in the preceding sentence requires.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the philosophers' reply to al-Ghazali's argument from planetary revolutions relied on the claim that
choices: what is impossible is an infinity of things existing together, and past revolutions do not now exist
the revolutions completed by Saturn and those completed by Jupiter over an infinite past are equal in number
human souls do not survive the death of the bodies they inhabit
the distinction between even and odd numbers applies only to finite collections
the motions of the heavens began at a definite moment in the past
questions.explanation: The second paragraph's first sentence gives the reply: 'past revolutions no longer exist, and what is impossible is only an infinity of things existing together.' A restates it. D is the trap for readers who know the Tahafut debate: in this passage the point about parity and finite counts is made by the modern Cantorian critics in the third paragraph, not by the philosophers.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Locate the philosophers' reply and match it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, first sentence; compare paragraph 3 for the critics' separate reply.

breakdown.analysis: A pure retrieval question with a shell-game risk: the passage contains two different replies to al-Ghazali's puzzles, the philosophers' (paragraph 2) and the modern critics' (paragraph 3). The stem asks for the philosophers'. Prephrase: 'past revolutions are gone; only a coexisting infinite is impossible.'

choices.note: CORRECT. A close paraphrase of paragraph 2, sentence 1.
Shell game. Equal size is what the Cantorian critics say 'in Cantor's arithmetic' (paragraph 3), not the philosophers' reply.
Opposite. Al-Ghazali's counter rests on the philosophers' 'own view' that 'human souls survive death.'

Wrong position-holder. The passage attributes the point that the parity dilemma 'assumes that every collection has a finite count' to the modern critics, not to the medieval philosophers, whatever a reader may know of the original debate.
Opposite. The philosophers 'held the world to be eternal'; a beginning of the heavens' motion is al-Ghazali's side of the dispute.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Al-Ghazali's argument from the survival of souls is immune to the objection that the critics raise against his argument from the parity of numbers.
The critics are mistaken in claiming that Cantor's theory dissolves the parity dilemma.
Mathematics is irrelevant to the question whether the past had a beginning.
Craig's appeal to Hilbert's hotel shows at most that an actual infinite of real things would be counterintuitive, not that it is impossible.
Craig's argument fails chiefly because Craig denies that Cantor's system of transfinite arithmetic is internally consistent.
questions.explanation: The author writes: 'If the hotel is consistent, then calling it absurd means only that it offends intuitions formed on finite collections.' D paraphrases that verdict. C is the tempting overstatement: the author says mathematics 'does not by itself' settle the question and that neither side may 'simply' appeal to it, which leaves mathematics relevant (it defeats the logical versions of the argument).

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the author's own claims support, as distinct from Craig's or the critics'.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, especially sentences 2-3 and 5-6.

breakdown.analysis: The author makes three moves: Cantor defeats logic-based versions (including the parity dilemma); Craig's premise concerns reality, so it escapes; but Craig's hotel then shows only an offense to finite intuitions. Answers that contradict any of these, or that inflate 'not by itself' into 'irrelevant', are out.

choices.note: Out of scope. The author never evaluates the souls argument; nothing says it escapes the critics' objection.
Opposite. The author says the reply 'defeats any version of the argument, the parity dilemma included,' that treats a completed infinity as logically impossible.
Too strong. 'Does not by itself tell us' and 'neither party may simply appeal to the mathematics' limit mathematics' role; they do not make it irrelevant, since it does defeat the logical versions.
CORRECT. 'Calling it absurd means only that it offends intuitions formed on finite collections' is the 'counterintuitive, not impossible' point.
Contradicts the passage. 'Craig does not deny that Cantor's system is consistent.'

questions.stem: In saying that the critics' reply 'settles less than its proponents suppose, though more than Craig allows' (first sentence of the fourth paragraph), the author most probably means that Cantor's theory
choices: answers the question whether an actual infinite can exist in reality but leaves open the question whether the concept of one is coherent
does not decide whether an infinite past is possible, yet it weakens the case for taking the hotel's oddities as signs of impossibility
refutes al-Ghazali's version of the argument while confirming Craig's
has been accepted by fewer working mathematicians than the critics claim, though by more of them than Craig is willing to acknowledge
is less consistent than the critics believe but more consistent than Craig believes
questions.explanation: The rest of the paragraph unpacks the phrase. 'Less than its proponents suppose': Cantor leaves the metaphysical question open. 'More than Craig allows': if the hotel is consistent, calling it absurd 'means only that it offends intuitions.' B captures both. E is the trap for readers who expect Craig to dispute the mathematics; the passage says he 'does not deny that Cantor's system is consistent.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Decode a compressed phrase from the rest of the paragraph.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, whole paragraph: sentences 2-3 explain the 'less', sentences 5-6 the 'more'.

breakdown.analysis: 'Proponents' are the critics, who think Cantor ends the debate; the author says it doesn't, because the real-world question remains. 'More than Craig allows' must name something Cantor does against Craig: it shows the hotel's oddities are consistent, so they are not absurdities. Prephrase: 'it doesn't end the debate, but it does take the sting out of the hotel.'

choices.note: Reversal. Cantor settles the coherence question and leaves the real-world question open, not the other way around.
CORRECT. Both halves are drawn from the paragraph's own development of the phrase.
Half right. It does defeat the parity dilemma, but the author never says it confirms Craig; the hotel is weakened by it.
Misreads 'proponents' as supporters of the theory among mathematicians; the passage says nothing about how widely the theory is accepted.
Distortion. The author treats the theory's consistency as established ('not self-contradictory'), and Craig 'does not deny' it.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, the author would most likely regard Cantor's work as sufficient by itself to defeat which one of the following arguments?
choices: An infinite past is impossible, because it would require a collection the same size as a part of itself, and logic guarantees that a whole exceeds each of its parts.
An infinite past is impossible, because a collection that included every event up to the present could never have been completed by adding one event after another.
An infinite past is impossible, because the physical evidence indicates that the universe began a finite time ago.
An infinite past is impossible, because concrete events, unlike the objects of mathematics, cannot compose a collection that matches one-to-one with a part of itself.
An infinite past is impossible, because whatever exists must have a cause, and a world without a beginning would have none.
questions.explanation: The author says Cantor's reply 'defeats any version of the argument... that treats a completed infinity as impossible as a matter of logic,' because an infinite collection is 'precisely one that can be matched one-to-one with a part of itself.' A rests its case on a claimed truth of logic that Cantor shows a consistent infinite violates. D is the near-miss: it states the same property but as a claim about what concrete things can do, which is exactly what the author says Cantor 'leaves open.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply the author's line between what Cantor settles (logical impossibility) and what he leaves open (whether concrete things can form an actual infinite) to five new arguments.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, second sentence; paragraph 4, sentences 2-3 and the last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Sort each argument by the kind of premise it uses. Only a premise claiming logical contradiction falls to Cantor alone. Premises about successive addition or concrete events are metaphysical (left open); empirical and causal premises are outside the dispute entirely. Watch for an answer that uses Cantor's own vocabulary (one-to-one correspondence) attached to a metaphysical claim.

choices.note: CORRECT. Its key premise is a purported logical truth that a consistent infinite collection violates; per the author, Cantor defeats any version that treats a completed infinity as impossible 'as a matter of logic.'
This is the question the author says Cantor 'leaves open': 'whether successive concrete events can compose a completed infinity.'
Out of scope. An empirical premise about the universe's age is untouched by a result about the consistency of infinite sets.
Shell game. It borrows the language of one-to-one matching, but its premise is about what concrete events can do, which 'mathematics... does not by itself tell us.'
Out of scope. A causal premise is a different argument; nothing in Cantor's work bears on it.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Craig's argument can most accurately be described as
choices: unreserved endorsement, because the argument correctly separates the question of logical possibility from that of real possibility
dismissive rejection, because the argument rests throughout on a basic misunderstanding of what Cantor's set theory establishes
studied neutrality, because the author declines to assess the argument's merits
partial agreement mixed with doubt: it survives a prominent objection, but its central illustration does less for it than Craig supposes
reluctant acceptance: the author regards the argument's conclusion as established while disliking its heavy reliance on intuition
questions.explanation: The author defends Craig against the critics ('Craig does not deny that Cantor's system is consistent; his premise concerns reality') and then turns on him ('Yet the same distinction limits Craig'), saying the hotel shows only an offense to finite intuitions. D captures the mix. A and E overstate the agreement; B overstates the disagreement.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize the author's attitude toward Craig, specifically.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, sentences 3 and 5-7.

breakdown.analysis: Attitude answers live or die on degree. The author gives Craig something (his premise escapes the Cantorian reply) and takes something away (the hotel doesn't prove impossibility; Craig may not 'simply appeal to the mathematics' either). Prephrase: 'mixed: right about the critics, overreaching with the hotel.'

choices.note: Too extreme. The author grants the distinction but says it 'limits Craig.'
Too extreme, and wrong on the reason: the author says Craig does not deny Cantor's consistency, so no misunderstanding of Cantor is alleged.
Wrong. The author takes clear positions ('I think'), assessing both sides.
CORRECT. 'Survives a prominent objection' = the Cantorian reply fails against his reality premise; 'does less than Craig supposes' = the hotel shows only that it 'offends intuitions.'
Distortion. The author never treats Craig's conclusion as established; the metaphysical question is left open.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Modern scholars have shown that Ibn Khaldun's science of 'umran has nothing of significance in common with the modern discipline of sociology.
Although calling Ibn Khaldun a sociologist misdescribes his science's aims, his account of dynastic rise and fall is a genuine causal argument.
Ibn Khaldun's theory of 'asabiyya shows that religion is the decisive factor in the rise of dynasties.
Mahdi's philosophical interpretation of the Muqaddimah has been superseded by Irwin's attention to its religious material.
Ibn Khaldun's account of taxation anticipated modern economics more closely than his account of dynasties anticipated modern sociology.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph grants that the cautions 'are well taken' (calling him a sociologist credits him with aims 'he did not share') but adds that a reading 'can be anachronistic in its framing without being mistaken in what it notices,' since the dynastic mechanism 'is a genuine causal argument.' B states both halves. A takes the cautions further than the author says they will go.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify the author's overall conclusion about modern claims for Ibn Khaldun.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, first three sentences and last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraphs 1-2 are exposition (the new science; 'asabiyya and dynastic cycles). Paragraph 3 sets out the modern claims and the cautions. Paragraph 4 is the author's verdict: the cautions are right about framing but overreach. Prephrase: 'Not a sociologist, but his causal argument is real.'

choices.note: Too extreme. The author says the cautions are 'pressed further than they will go' and affirms that the readings notice something real.
CORRECT. The concession ('credit him with a discipline whose aims... he did not share') and the claim ('a genuine causal argument') are both here.
Distortion. Religion 'can greatly strengthen group feeling but cannot replace it'; the decisive factor is group feeling.
Out of scope. The passage presents Mahdi and Irwin as complementary cautions and never ranks them.
Out of scope comparison. The passage mentions both claims but never compares how closely each anticipated a modern discipline.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?
choices: A theory is presented, two modern interpretations of it are compared, and the author shows that one interpretation rests on a mistranslation.
A theory is presented, the evidence against it is surveyed, and the author concludes that it has been refuted by later historical research.
A work and its key concept are described, modern claims about it and scholarly cautions are presented, and the cautions are assessed with a qualification.
Modern claims about a work are described, the work's central concept is then explained, and the author defends the modern claims against all of the criticism they have received.
A work is described, its influence on later social science is traced, and the author argues that this influence has been overstated.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 introduces the Muqaddimah and its new science, paragraph 2 explains 'asabiyya, paragraph 3 gives modern claims and the cautions of Mahdi and Irwin, and paragraph 4 says 'These cautions are well taken, but they are sometimes pressed further than they will go.' C tracks that order. D gets the order wrong and overstates the author's defense; E confuses modern claims about Ibn Khaldun with his influence on modern thinkers.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the sequence of the four paragraphs.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of each paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Map: (1) the work and the new science; (2) 'asabiyya and the dynastic cycle; (3) moderns claim him as sociologist or economist, scholars caution; (4) author: cautions right but overextended. Check each choice's order and the strength of its last clause.

choices.note: Distortion. Mahdi and Irwin are not compared as rivals, and no mistranslation is alleged.
Wrong. The author never treats the theory as refuted; the author calls it a genuine causal argument.
CORRECT. Each clause matches a paragraph, and 'with a qualification' matches 'well taken, but... pressed further than they will go.'
Wrong order, and too strong: the author concedes that the cautions 'are well taken.'
Shell game. The passage discusses what modern readers have claimed for him, not his influence on later social science, and the author does not argue that any influence was overstated.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Ibn Khaldun held which one of the following about religion and group feeling?
choices: Religion is the original source from which group feeling arises.
Religion weakens group feeling by encouraging the settled life of cities.
Group feeling and religion are rival bonds, so that the growth of one diminishes the other.
Religion can take the place of group feeling once a dynasty has grown accustomed to luxury.
A religious movement cannot succeed unless it is backed by group feeling.
questions.explanation: The last sentence of the second paragraph says religion 'can greatly strengthen group feeling but cannot replace it: a religious movement that lacks such backing, he held, will fail.' E restates the second clause. D is the opposite of 'cannot replace it'; C contradicts 'can greatly strengthen.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage reports Ibn Khaldun said about religion's relation to group feeling.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: One sentence answers this. Two claims: religion strengthens group feeling; it cannot substitute for it, so a movement without group feeling fails. Prephrase: 'religion needs group feeling behind it.'

choices.note: Distortion. Group feeling 'binds people who share descent or long association'; religion strengthens it but is not said to be its source.
Shell game. Sedentary life and luxury weaken group feeling in paragraph 2, but religion is not the cause.
Contradicts the passage: religion 'can greatly strengthen group feeling.'
Opposite. Religion 'cannot replace' group feeling.
CORRECT. 'A religious movement that lacks such backing... will fail.'

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following statements about the decline of a dynasty as Ibn Khaldun describes it?
choices: It results primarily from attacks by groups whose religious commitment is stronger than the dynasty's.
It occurs in part because the rulers cease to rely mainly on those bound to them by kinship.
It can be prevented if the dynasty's rulers keep taxes low.
It is completed in exactly three generations in every case.
It begins among the desert peoples whom the dynasty displaced when it seized power.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 lists the causes of decline: 'luxury softens its members, its rulers come to depend on paid troops and clients rather than kinsmen.' B follows, hedged with 'in part.' D is the over-literal trap for readers who know the three-generation rule; the passage says 'within roughly three generations.' C reads a modern policy lesson into a passage that links taxation only to modern economists' interest.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage's account of decline supports, without going beyond it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, third sentence; paragraph 3, second sentence for the taxation material.

breakdown.analysis: The decline sentence gives three linked factors: sedentary life, luxury, dependence on paid troops and clients instead of kinsmen. The new group wins because its 'solidarity is still intact', not because of religion. Prefer the hedged answer that restates one listed factor.

choices.note: Distortion. The displacing group is distinguished by intact 'solidarity,' not stronger religion.
CORRECT. Dependence on 'paid troops and clients rather than kinsmen' is one of the listed causes; 'in part' keeps it within limits.
Out of scope. The passage quotes the taxation remark only as something economists have pointed to; it never links taxes to preventing decline.
Too strong. 'Within roughly three generations' is neither exact nor universal.
Distortion. Decline begins in the dynasty's own sedentary life; desert peoples are where group feeling is strongest.

questions.stem: By the statement that a reading 'can be anachronistic in its framing without being mistaken in what it notices' (third sentence of the fourth paragraph), the author most probably means that a reading of Ibn Khaldun can
choices: misidentify the kind of inquiry his work belongs to while correctly identifying something real in his analysis
accurately describe his historical circumstances while misstating the conclusions he reached
be mistaken in all its particulars while still proving useful to modern readers
correctly describe the aims of his science while also detecting features of his work that he deliberately concealed
rest on a mistranslation of some of his key vocabulary while still reaching true conclusions about his theory
questions.explanation: The sentence before says calling him a sociologist credits him with 'a discipline whose aims... he did not share' (the anachronistic framing); the sentence after says the dynastic mechanism 'is a genuine causal argument' (what the reading correctly notices). A pairs those. B reverses which part is right and which is wrong.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Decode the contrast between 'framing' and 'what it notices'.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, sentences 2-4.

breakdown.analysis: Context defines both terms. 'Framing' = the label 'sociologist,' which imports aims he did not have. 'What it notices' = the solidarity-and-luxury mechanism, which the author calls genuine. Prephrase: 'wrong label, real insight.'

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Kind of inquiry' paraphrases the discipline label; 'something real in his analysis' is the causal mechanism the author affirms.
Reversal. The anachronism concerns the framing, and the author says the observation is correct; nothing is said about misstating conclusions.
Too strong. The author says the reading is right about what it notices, not mistaken in all particulars.
Out of scope. Nothing in the passage concerns concealed features; the framing is the part that misdescribes his aims.
Shell game. Rosenthal's translation is mentioned in paragraph 2, but the author's point concerns disciplinary framing, not translation.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim that Ibn Khaldun's account of dynasties is stated with a generality that 'invites testing against cases he never knew' (fourth sentence of the fourth paragraph)?
choices: Ibn Khaldun knew the works of Aristotle through Arabic translations and commentaries.
Several nineteenth-century writers who called Ibn Khaldun a founder of sociology had read only parts of the Muqaddimah.
Ibn Khaldun's discussions of magic and divination occupy a substantial portion of the Muqaddimah.
Historians applying Ibn Khaldun's model to dynasties far from North Africa have found its claims checkable against the record and sometimes borne out.
Ibn Khaldun drew most of his examples of dynastic decline from North African dynasties whose history he had observed at first hand during his career.
questions.explanation: The claim is that the mechanism is general enough to be tested on cases outside Ibn Khaldun's experience. D supplies such tests on distant dynasties, showing the model can be checked against them. E is the trap: it fits 'drawn from observation' but concerns the cases he knew, not ones he never knew; A and C support Mahdi's and Irwin's cautions rather than the author's claim.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that best supports the claim that the dynastic model is general enough to test on new cases.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, fourth sentence; paragraph 3 for Mahdi and Irwin.

breakdown.analysis: Pin the claim down: generality plus testability beyond Ibn Khaldun's own cases. The strengthener must involve cases he never knew, or show the model's claims can be checked. Facts about his sources, his reception or his other interests are irrelevant to this claim, however true.

choices.note: Irrelevant truth. This bears on Mahdi's reading of the science's philosophical basis, not on whether the dynastic model can be tested on new cases.
Out of scope. It concerns how well his nineteenth-century admirers read him, not the generality of his argument.
Irrelevant. This supports Irwin's point about what admirers set aside, not the testability of the dynastic account.
CORRECT. It shows the model applied to and checked against cases 'he never knew,' which is precisely what the author says its generality invites.
Tempting because it echoes 'drawn from observation,' but it concerns cases he knew; it does nothing to show the account reaches beyond them.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, the author would be most likely to regard which one of the following as an anachronistic description of Ibn Khaldun's science of 'umran?
choices: a science intended to help historians judge which reports are credible
a science that seeks the nature and causes of human social organization
a science that studies society independently of any account of how human beings ought to live
a science that treats the regularities of social life as expressions of God's way with His creatures
a science whose explanations are general enough to be tested against cases outside its author's experience
questions.explanation: The author says calling him a sociologist credits him with a discipline whose aims, 'chief among them a study of society detached from any account of the good life, he did not share.' C paraphrases that aim. E is the strongest trap because it sounds like modern social science, but the author affirms it: the account is 'stated with a generality that invites testing against cases he never knew.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Use the author's own criteria to sort accurate descriptions of the science from an anachronistic one.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, last sentence; paragraph 3, Mahdi sentence; paragraph 4, sentences 2 and 4.

breakdown.analysis: Four choices are things the passage affirms of the science: its critical purpose for historians (paragraph 1), knowing a thing through 'its nature and causes' (Mahdi, paragraph 3), God's way with His creatures (paragraph 4), and testable generality (paragraph 4). One is the aim the author says he did not share. Don't pick by which answer 'sounds modern'; check each against the text.

choices.note: Accurate per paragraph 1: the science would let historians 'test reports against it,' and 'his science was meant to serve the historian.'
Accurate per Mahdi's account in paragraph 3, which the author calls 'well taken': to know a thing scientifically is 'to grasp its nature and causes.'
CORRECT. Detachment 'from any account of the good life' is named as an aim of modern sociology that Ibn Khaldun 'did not share,' so ascribing it to him is anachronistic.
Accurate: 'he regularly presented the regularities he described as God's way with His creatures.'
Sounds modern, but the author explicitly affirms it; this is what the reading correctly 'notices,' not its anachronistic framing.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Barr showed that etymology is a statement about a word's history rather than its meaning, and so etymological evidence has no legitimate role in interpreting biblical texts.
Barr's attack on arguments from etymology, though persuasive in 1961, was later qualified by Barr himself and by Silva, who restored etymology to a central place in biblical interpretation.
The errors Barr identified in Boman and in Kittel's dictionary arose because those scholars ignored the evidence of cognate languages such as Arabic and Ugaritic.
Barr rightly rejected inferring meaning or theology from a word's origin or a language's structure, but his critique leaves room for a carefully weighted use of etymology.
Because many Hebrew words occur only once or twice, interpreters of the Hebrew Bible must rely primarily on etymology rather than on the contexts in which words are used.
questions.explanation: The passage presents Barr's critique and its two named fallacies with approval (paragraphs 1 and 2), then qualifies the way it is now used: etymology is weak evidence but 'not negligible' where little else exists, and Barr 'left standing' the use of origins as 'one clue among others' (paragraphs 3 and 4). D captures both halves. A is the trap: it takes Barr's quoted line and turns it into the blanket prohibition the author rejects. B invents a reversal: the passage says Barr's 1968 book was consistent with his critique, and Silva 'largely' endorses Barr.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify the main point of the whole passage, including the author's qualification.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, first sentence ('here some qualification is needed'), and paragraph 4, first and last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Map: P1 what Barr attacked; P2 his two named fallacies; P3 the qualification (etymology is weak but not negligible for rare words; wordplay); P4 the lesson: proper weight, not ignoring. The author agrees with Barr's diagnoses but objects to treating them as a ban. Prephrase: Barr was right about the errors, but etymology keeps a modest role. Expect a trap that states only the first half, and one that overstates the second.

choices.note: Half right and too strong. The quotation is Barr's, but the passage's point is that this does not mean etymology has 'no legitimate role'; that is exactly the 'blanket prohibition' the author qualifies.

Distortion. Barr's 1968 book is presented as consistent with his earlier view ('Barr himself never held that etymology is worthless'), and Silva 'largely' endorses Barr and allows etymology only 'at times.' Nothing restores etymology to a 'central place.'
Out of scope. The passage diagnoses Boman's and Kittel's errors as mistakes about how language works, not as neglect of cognates; cognates come up only in paragraph 3.
CORRECT. The first half matches paragraphs 1 and 2 and the 'What Barr overturned' sentence; the second half matches 'given its proper evidential weight' and 'one clue among others.'

Too strong. The passage says etymology is 'weak evidence' that is 'not negligible' where it is nearly the only evidence. It never says interpreters must rely 'primarily' on etymology, and Barr's method still privileges use.

questions.stem: The author mentions Thorleif Boman (third sentence of the first paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: illustrate one of the kinds of argument that Barr's book criticized
identify the scholar whose work first described the root fallacy
provide an example of a scholar who used cognate languages responsibly
suggest that the contrast between Hebrew and Greek thought has been confirmed by later scholarship
contrast a scholar Barr admired with the contributors to Kittel's dictionary
questions.explanation: The first paragraph describes a 'style of argument' Barr attacked, and the sentence about Boman gives an instance: a contrast between Hebrew and Greek mentalities read off features of the languages. The next sentence says 'both habits' rested on mistakes, so Boman is an example of one habit. E is wrong because Boman and the Kittel contributors are paired as targets, not contrasted.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why Boman is mentioned.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, sentences 2 to 4.

breakdown.analysis: The sentence before sets up a general claim (practitioners thought language structure revealed theology). The Boman sentence gives a concrete case, and 'both habits' in the next sentence confirms that Boman and Kittel's contributors are the two examples of what Barr attacked. Prephrase: an example of the target.

choices.note: CORRECT. Boman's dynamic-versus-static contrast, read off the languages, is one of the 'habits' Barr argued 'rested on mistakes about how language works.'
Wrong position-holder. The root fallacy is Barr's diagnosis (paragraph 2), not something Boman described; Boman is one of those Barr criticized.
Out of scope. Cognate languages enter only in paragraph 3, in connection with Barr's 1968 book; Boman is not linked to them.
Opposite. The passage presents the contrast as resting on a mistake; nothing suggests later confirmation.
Distortion. Boman and the Kittel contributors are joined by 'and' and then called 'both habits'; Barr criticized both.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the error Barr called "illegitimate totality transfer" consists in
choices: assuming that every word derived from a root retains the root's basic sense
inferring differences in ways of thinking from differences in the structure of two languages
treating the whole range of senses a word has across a body of writings as present in one particular use of it
assigning a meaning to a rare word on the basis of a cognate word in a related language
reading a later meaning of a word back into an earlier text in which the word occurs
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 defines the error: 'the full range of senses a word bears across a body of literature' is 'read into a particular case as its sense and implication there,' and the dabar example shows it (a word that can mean 'word' or 'matter' does not mean both at once). C paraphrases this. A is the trap: it is the root fallacy, defined two sentences earlier in the same paragraph.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the passage's definition of illegitimate totality transfer.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 2 defines two fallacies back to back, so the main danger is swapping them. Root fallacy: a root's sense carries into every derivative. Totality transfer: all of a word's senses get loaded into one occurrence. Paraphrase the second before reading choices.

choices.note: Shell game. This is the passage's definition of the root fallacy, the first of the two diagnoses in paragraph 2.
Wrong error. This describes the Boman-style argument from paragraph 1 that Barr also rejected, not illegitimate totality transfer.

CORRECT. 'The full range of senses a word bears across a body of literature' becomes 'the whole range of senses ... across a body of writings,' and 'read into a particular case' becomes 'treating ... as present in one particular use.'
Out of place. Cognate-based interpretation is discussed in paragraph 3 as a practice with a legitimate if limited role, not as this fallacy.
Plausible but not stated. Anachronism is a real interpretive error, but the passage's definition concerns piling many senses into one occurrence, not moving a later sense into an earlier text.

questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments commits the error that the passage calls the root fallacy?
choices: Because a Hebrew word that occurs only once has a cognate in Ugaritic meaning "storehouse," the Hebrew word probably meant something similar, though the conclusion is tentative.
Because a Greek word can mean both "spirit" and "wind" elsewhere in the New Testament, a writer who uses it in a given verse must be alluding to both senses there.
Because Hebrew verbs differ in structure from Greek verbs, the ancient Hebrews must have experienced time differently from the ancient Greeks.
Because a narrative explicitly explains a character's name by a pun on a similar-sounding word, the pun is part of how the narrative uses that name.
Because a Greek word for the church is formed from a verb meaning "to call out," each New Testament use of that word implies that the church is called out of the world.
questions.explanation: The passage defines the root fallacy as 'the assumption that a root carries a basic sense present in every word derived from it.' E assumes that the sense of the verb from which the word is formed ('call out') is present in every use of the derived word. B is the strongest trap: it commits illegitimate totality transfer, the other fallacy in paragraph 2. C is Boman's kind of argument from paragraph 1.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply the passage's definition of the root fallacy to new arguments.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, second and third sentences; contrast paragraph 1 and paragraph 3.

breakdown.analysis: The choices are built to match each idea in the passage: one root fallacy (E), one totality transfer (B), one Boman-style structural argument (C), and two practices the author accepts (A, cognates for a rare word held tentatively; D, wordplay the text itself makes). Look for the argument that moves a root's sense into every use of a derivative.

choices.note: A practice the author accepts. Paragraph 3 says etymology is weak but 'not negligible' for words that occur only once or twice, and the argument is explicitly tentative.
Wrong fallacy. Loading two senses a word has elsewhere into one verse is illegitimate totality transfer (the dabar example), not the root fallacy.
Wrong error. Inferring differences of thought from differences of linguistic structure is the Boman-style argument of paragraph 1. It is a mistake Barr attacked, but not the root fallacy.
A practice the author accepts. When the text itself exploits an etymology, noticing it is 'to describe the text's own usage, not to impose a history on it.'
CORRECT. The sense of the source verb is assumed to be present in every use of the derived word, regardless of context: the root fallacy exactly as paragraph 2 defines it.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Barr's critique is best described as
choices: unreserved agreement with its conclusions and approval of the way it is now applied
agreement with its central diagnoses, combined with concern that others apply it more sweepingly than Barr did
respect for its historical influence, combined with doubt that its central diagnoses are correct
agreement with its criticism of Kittel's dictionary, combined with rejection of its criticism of Boman
approval of its aims, combined with the view that Barr undermined it by later defending cognate-based etymology
questions.explanation: The author presents Barr's two diagnoses without dissent and in paragraph 4 restates what Barr 'overturned' as genuinely overturned. The reservation is aimed at others: the critique 'is now often invoked as a blanket prohibition,' and those who use it this way 'credit him with a stricter position than he defended.' B fits. E is the trap: it sees tension between 1961 and 1968, but the author presents the later book as consistent with Barr's view ('Barr himself never held that etymology is worthless').

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize the author's attitude toward Barr's critique, not toward its later users.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, first two sentences; paragraph 4, last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The author has two attitudes: toward Barr (approving) and toward people who invoke Barr as a ban (critical). The right answer must keep these apart. Watch for choices that move the criticism onto Barr himself.

choices.note: Too extreme. The author explicitly objects to how the critique is 'now often invoked,' so the author does not approve of the way it is applied.
CORRECT. Agreement: the diagnoses are presented as correct and what Barr 'overturned' stays overturned. Concern: the 'blanket prohibition' and the 'stricter position than he defended.'
Opposite. The author never doubts the diagnoses; the qualification concerns how far they reach.
Distortion. The author treats Boman and Kittel's contributors as 'both habits' resting on mistakes and does not side with Boman.
Wrong position-holder. The author's reservation is about later users, not Barr, and the 1968 book is presented as consistent with Barr's view, not as undermining it.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following about an interpreter faced with a Hebrew word that occurs only once in the Bible?
choices: The interpreter should treat the meaning of the word's cognate in a related language as settling the question, since there is no evidence of use to override it.
The interpreter may take the word's cognates into account, while recognizing that such evidence is weak and can be outweighed by context.
The interpreter should decline to assign the word any meaning, since a single occurrence cannot provide the evidence of use that Barr's method requires.
The interpreter would commit the root fallacy by consulting any cognate of the word in another Semitic language.
The interpreter should assume that the word bears all the senses its cognates have in the related languages.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says that for words occurring 'only once or twice' the evidence of use is 'too thin to fix a meaning,' and that 'Etymology is weak evidence, but where it is nearly the only evidence it is not negligible.' Paragraph 4 adds that a word's history may serve interpretation 'provided it does not override what context shows.' B combines these. A is the trap: it turns 'not negligible' into 'settling,' which is too strong for 'weak evidence.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply what the author says about rare words to an interpreter's practice.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, sentences 4 and 5; paragraph 4, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The author's position has two limits: etymology counts when little else is available, and it is still weak and subordinate to context. A correct answer must stay within both limits. Eliminate choices that make it decisive, forbid it, or abandon interpretation.

choices.note: Too strong. 'Weak evidence' that is 'not negligible' does not 'settle' anything, and the author says history should not 'override what context shows,' which implies context can outweigh it.
CORRECT. 'Not negligible' licenses taking cognates into account; 'weak evidence' and 'provided it does not override what context shows' supply the caution.
Too extreme. The passage says thin evidence of use cannot 'fix' a meaning, but it then says etymology helps in exactly this case. Nothing calls for declining to interpret.
Distortion. The root fallacy is assuming a root's sense is present in every derivative; paragraph 3 presents cautious use of cognates as legitimate, granted 'a place' even by Barr.
Reverse use of a named error. Loading every available sense into one word resembles illegitimate totality transfer, which the passage rejects.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that etymology "is not negligible" where it is nearly the only evidence for a word's meaning (fifth sentence of the third paragraph)?
choices: Where Hebrew words' meanings are well established by use, their cognates' meanings predict those meanings no better than chance.
Biblical writers play on the etymologies of words far less often than some commentators on the Hebrew Bible have claimed.
Fewer words in the Hebrew Bible occur only once or twice than scholars of the mid-twentieth century believed.
Some meanings that scholars proposed for rare Hebrew words on the basis of cognates were later confirmed by ancient texts discovered after the proposals were made.
Many of the contributors to Kittel's dictionary relied on cognates when discussing rare New Testament words.
questions.explanation: The claim is that etymology has some real evidential value when little else is available. If, in cases where the truth can be checked, a cognate's meaning predicts the Hebrew meaning no better than chance, then etymology has essentially no evidential value, and being the only evidence does not give it any. A undercuts this directly. C is the strongest trap: it shrinks the number of cases where the claim matters but leaves the claim about those cases intact. D strengthens.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most undercuts the claim that etymology has real, if weak, evidential value.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, sentences 4 and 5.

breakdown.analysis: The claim is about evidential value: weak but more than nothing. To weaken it, show that etymology tracks meaning no better than guessing. A test case would be words whose meanings are known from use, where we can see whether cognates would have pointed the right way. Choices about how often the situation arises, or about other uses of etymology, miss the claim.

choices.note: CORRECT. If cognates are no better than chance where we can check them, there is no reason to think they carry weight where we cannot, so etymology would be negligible even as the only evidence.
Irrelevant to this claim. Wordplay is the author's separate point ('Moreover...'); undermining it leaves the claim about rare words untouched.
Scope trap. Fewer rare words means the claim applies less often, but the claim is that etymology has value in those cases, and this choice says nothing about that.
Opposite. Confirmation by new evidence shows that cognate-based proposals can be right, which supports the claim.
Irrelevant. Who used cognates, and in which corpus, says nothing about whether cognate evidence has value.

questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with
choices: defending the authenticity of a body of reports against skeptical objections
how the reliability of reports received from others can be assessed
whether knowledge gained through testimony is reducible to knowledge gained through perception
the historical origins of a method for evaluating chains of transmission
the reasons that trust in testimony is a natural feature of human psychology
questions.explanation: Passage A describes how hadith critics judged reports by evaluating their transmitters, and the skeptics' challenge to that method; passage B describes rival philosophical accounts of when we are justified in believing testimony and ends 'We assess sources.' B covers both. C is the trap: it is passage B's central debate, but passage A never takes up reductionism.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the concern the two passages share.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, first two sentences and last sentence; passage B, first sentence and last paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: A is historical (Sunni hadith criticism, Schacht, Brown); B is philosophical (Hume, Reid, Coady). The common ground is assessing reports from others. Choices that fit only one passage are the traps.

choices.note: Too narrow, and only A. Passage A reports Brown's response to the skeptics; passage B defends no particular body of reports.

CORRECT. A: how critics judged transmitted reports by their narrators and content. B: what justifies believing what others tell us and when trust is withdrawn. Both concern assessing reports from others.
Passage B only. Reductionism is B's subject; A never asks whether testimony reduces to perception.
Passage A only, and too narrow. B is about epistemology, not the history of a method, and even A is not mainly about origins.
Passage B only, and only part of it. Reid's innate disposition is one view in B; A says nothing about human psychology.

questions.stem: According to passage A, the hadith critics judged a narrator's accuracy largely by
choices: examining whether the content of each report he transmitted was plausible on its face
determining whether he had lived in the same city and period as the person he cited
consulting the opinions that his own students and later transmitters held of him
checking whether the doctrines in his reports were held by earlier jurists
comparing his versions of reports with those of other students of his teacher
questions.explanation: Passage A says that 'a narrator's accuracy was gauged largely by comparison: critics gathered the versions of a report transmitted by different students of the same teacher, and a narrator whose versions regularly diverged from those of his peers was judged weak.' E paraphrases this. A is the trap: passage A does say critics also rejected reports with objectionable content, but that is Brown's point about reports, not the stated way of judging a narrator's accuracy, and the first paragraph says plausible content could not save a report from an unknown transmitter.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what passage A says was the main way of judging a narrator's accuracy.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, fourth sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The answer is stated: 'gauged largely by comparison.' Match that to the choice. Be wary of choices drawn from elsewhere in the passage.

choices.note: Shell game. Content appears later (critics 'also rejected reports whose content was objectionable'), and 'however plausible its content' appears in the first paragraph, but neither is how accuracy was 'largely' gauged.

Not stated. The critics asked whether a narrator 'could actually have heard the report from the person he cited,' but the passage does not say this was how accuracy was judged, or that it was tested by city of residence.
Not stated. The comparison was with the narrator's peers, students of the same teacher, not with what his students or later transmitters thought of him.
Wrong position-holder. Doctrines of later jurists figure in Schacht's account of how chains were forged, not in the critics' method.
CORRECT. A paraphrase of 'critics gathered the versions of a report transmitted by different students of the same teacher,' with divergence from peers marking a narrator as weak.

questions.stem: In passage A, the statement that forgery was widespread "as the critics themselves acknowledged" (third sentence of the second paragraph) serves primarily to
choices: show that the skeptics' central claim was first advanced by the critics they opposed
concede that the critics' methods were unable to detect most forged reports
suggest that Brown accepts Schacht's account of how chains were extended backward
indicate that the critics themselves recognized a problem that the skeptics emphasize
imply that the critics' biographical dictionaries are unreliable as evidence about narrators
questions.explanation: The sentence has Brown grant a point ('forgery was widespread') and then argue the skeptics 'underestimated the critics.' The clause noting that the critics themselves acknowledged forgery shows that the skeptics' key fact was not hidden from the critics; it was the problem their method was built to handle. D says this. A is the trap: the critics acknowledged that forgery existed, but the skeptics' central claim (that chains were fabricated and extended backward, so a flawless chain 'proves little') is not attributed to the critics.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain what the parenthetical acknowledgment contributes to Brown's reply.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, second paragraph, sentences 2 to 4.

breakdown.analysis: Structure: Schacht's objection, then Brown's concession ('grants'), then his counterargument ('but argues'). The clause about the critics' acknowledgment sits in the concession and blunts it: the critics knew about forgery, so its existence does not show they were naive. Prephrase: it shows the critics were aware of the problem the skeptics stress.

choices.note: Too strong / distortion. That forgery existed is common ground; the skeptics' distinctive claim is that chains were fabricated with their reports and extended backward, which the passage does not attribute to the critics.
Unsupported. Brown argues the critics were better than the skeptics thought; nothing concedes that they missed most forgeries.
Distortion. Brown grants that forgery was widespread, not Schacht's account of backward growth, and he goes on to argue against the skeptics.
