CORRECT. Pointing out that the critics themselves said forgery was common shows they recognized the problem the skeptics stress; the rest of the sentence describes how they addressed it, including through content criticism.
Out of scope. Nothing in the clause or the passage questions the dictionaries' reliability.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is a way of evaluating testimony that is described in both passages?
choices: comparing a source's report with reports about the same matter from other sources
verifying the content of each report through one's own observation
relying on an innate disposition to trust what one is told
rejecting any report whose content conflicts with the hearer's prior beliefs
tracing a report back to an eyewitness through a chain of named transmitters
questions.explanation: Passage A: critics compared a narrator's versions with those of 'different students of the same teacher.' Passage B: we withdraw trust from a speaker 'whose report conflicts with what others tell us.' Both describe checking a source against other sources. B is the trap: passage A says the critics did not 'try to verify its contents directly,' and passage B says we 'could not' verify every claim for ourselves.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the method that appears in both passages.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, first paragraph, sentences 1 and 4; passage B, last paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Take each choice and check it against both passages. Cross-checking against other reports appears in A (comparison among students) and in B (a report that 'conflicts with what others tell us'). Each other choice appears in one passage at most, or in neither.

choices.note: CORRECT. A: comparing a narrator's versions with his peers'. B: a report that 'conflicts with what others tell us' defeats trust.
Opposite of both. A's critics 'did not, for the most part, try to verify its contents directly'; B says we 'could not' verify every claim for ourselves.
Passage B only. This is Reid's view; A says nothing about innate dispositions.
In neither as stated. A mentions rejecting objectionable content, but neither passage says a conflict with the hearer's prior beliefs is enough; B speaks of conflict with what others report.
Passage A only. The isnad is A's subject; B never mentions chains of transmitters.

questions.stem: The practice described in passage A of refusing to accept a report from a transmitter whose standing was unknown is most clearly in tension with which one of the following views discussed in passage B?
choices: the view that trust in testimony is justified only by observed agreement between reports and facts
the view that much of the evidence one might use to check testimony is itself testimony
the view that a hearer may accept testimony unless there is a specific reason to doubt it
the view that a speaker shown to be dishonest should no longer be trusted
the view that a community's utterances could not be recognized as reports unless most of them were true
questions.explanation: Passage B's anti-reductionists hold that 'we are entitled to accept testimony by default,' and trust is withdrawn only when defeated, for instance by a speaker 'shown to be careless or dishonest.' A transmitter of unknown standing has not been shown to be either, so default entitlement would accept his report; the hadith critics did not. C names this view. A is the trap: Hume's reductionism requires positive evidence of reliability, which fits the critics' practice rather than conflicting with it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the view in passage B that the critics' treatment of unknown transmitters conflicts with.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, first paragraph, last sentence; passage B, last paragraph and first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: In A, a report needs a transmitter of established good standing; unknown standing is enough to fail. In B, the anti-reductionist position is that trust is the default and needs a specific defeater to be withdrawn. An unknown transmitter offers no defeater, so the two clash. Hume's demand for positive evidence agrees with the critics. This is where the passages differ beneath their agreement that sources, not every claim, are assessed.

choices.note: Reversal trap. Requiring positive evidence of reliability before trusting is consistent with refusing unknown transmitters, so this is the view in B closest to the critics' practice, not in tension with it.
No tension. The critics checked transmitters largely through other transmitters' reports, which fits the idea that checks on testimony are themselves testimony.
CORRECT. Default entitlement means accepting testimony absent a defeater; refusing someone merely because his standing is unknown denies that default.
Consistent with A. The critics also stopped trusting unreliable narrators ('judged weak'); both sides agree that shown dishonesty defeats trust.
No clear bearing. Coady's claim is about testimony as a whole, not about whether any particular unknown speaker should be believed.

questions.stem: The author of passage B would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Children's tendency to believe what they are told shows that testimony is generally reliable.
A hearer is justified in accepting testimony only after confirming the speaker's past record of accuracy.
Because most checks on testimony are themselves testimony, no report can be shown to be false.
The anti-reductionist view implies that a hearer should believe every report that is not self-contradictory.
One can be justified in believing a report without personally confirming its source's reliability.
questions.explanation: The author of passage B endorses the anti-reductionist position: 'we are entitled to accept testimony by default,' and 'We assess sources; we do not, and could not, verify every claim for ourselves.' Default entitlement means belief can be justified without first confirming the speaker's track record, as E says. B is the trap: it is Hume's reductionist view, which the author presents as rejected.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify a claim the author of passage B would accept.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, last paragraph; also Reid's and Coady's arguments.

breakdown.analysis: The author speaks in the first person plural in the last paragraph and so endorses default, defeasible trust. Correct answers must not slip into credulity (the author says 'Anti-reductionism is not credulity') or into Hume's demand for a confirmed track record.

choices.note: Distortion. Reid's point about children is that their trust comes before any evidence, so it cannot rest on observed reliability. The passage does not say children's credulity shows testimony is reliable.
Wrong position-holder. This is roughly Hume's reductionism, which the passage presents only to report the objections to it.
Too extreme. Coady's point is that we cannot ground testimony without relying on testimony; the author says reports can conflict with others and that such conflict defeats trust.
Opposite. The author stresses that 'Anti-reductionism is not credulity' and lists defeaters well beyond self-contradiction.
CORRECT. Default entitlement means justification without prior personal confirmation of the source's reliability; it remains defeasible.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen Brown's position against the skeptics as it is described in passage A?
choices: Many of the narrators graded in the biographical dictionaries were active in the second Islamic century, before the major collections were compiled.
Schacht's account of backward-growing chains was later refined by scholars who accepted its basic premise that many chains were fabricated.
Medieval Muslim scholars wrote treatises defending the importance of the isnad against rationalist critics who questioned its value.
Reports early critics faulted only in terms of their transmitters largely coincide with reports later rejected explicitly for their content.
Skeptical Western scholars have generally conceded, as Brown does, that forged reports were common in the early Islamic period.
questions.explanation: Brown's position is that the skeptics 'underestimated the critics, who also rejected reports whose content was objectionable, often expressing that judgment in the vocabulary of isnad criticism.' If the reports early critics faulted on the transmitter level largely coincide with reports later rejected explicitly for content, that suggests the early isnad-language verdicts were tracking content too, which is just what Brown claims. E is the trap: it repeats a point both sides already accept and does nothing for Brown's distinctive claim.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most supports Brown's claim that the critics also judged content while speaking in isnad terms.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, second paragraph, last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Brown's specific claim has a hidden part: content criticism stated 'in the vocabulary of isnad criticism.' Evidence for it would show that verdicts phrased as attacks on transmitters line up with content-based rejection. Answers that rest on agreed facts or that bear on neither side miss the point.

choices.note: Irrelevant. When the narrators lived, relative to the collections, does not bear on whether the critics evaluated content.
Opposite. A refinement of Schacht by scholars who share his premise supports the skeptics' side, and it says nothing about whether the critics judged content.
Weak and possibly opposite. Defending the isnad's importance is consistent with critics who looked only at chains, which is the picture Brown argues against.
CORRECT. A high correspondence suggests that early verdicts phrased in terms of transmitters reflected judgments about content, supporting Brown's claim that the skeptics underestimated the critics.
Premise restatement. Passage A already says Brown 'grants that forgery was widespread.' Agreement on that point does not show that the critics' methods were better than the skeptics thought.

sections.title: Reading Through Ideas 6: MacIntyre on the rationality of traditions · The Tusi couple and Copernicus · Al-Ghazali and Descartes on doubt · Hallaq's restatement of Orientalism

passages.title: MacIntyre on the rationality of traditions
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Much of modern moral philosophy has hoped that rival positions could be judged by standards that any rational person must accept, whatever his or her history. Alasdair MacIntyre's Whose Justice? Which Rationality? (1988) is a sustained attack on that hope. Extending the argument of After Virtue (1981), where he described a living tradition as "an historically extended, socially embodied argument," MacIntyre contends that standards of rational justification are themselves developed within particular traditions of inquiry, among them the Aristotelian, the Augustinian, the Scottish Enlightenment, and modern liberalism. There is, he writes, "no standing ground, no place for enquiry" apart from what some particular tradition provides. Rationality, on this view, is tradition-constituted.

Critics have pressed an obvious objection. If every standard belongs to some tradition, then any judgment between traditions must be made from within one of them, and each tradition, it seems, will simply vindicate itself. MacIntyre's position, they charge, collapses into relativism: no tradition can be shown rationally superior to another. Martha Nussbaum, reviewing the book in 1989, went further, arguing that his turn to tradition amounted to a retreat from critical reason toward the acceptance of authority.

MacIntyre's reply turns on the idea of an epistemological crisis. A tradition can fail by its own lights: its accepted methods of inquiry may become sterile, its central problems may resist every solution its resources allow, and its internal conflicts may go unresolved. Such a crisis is overcome only when new concepts are found that solve the problems previously intractable, explain why the tradition had failed before acquiring them, and do so while preserving continuity with what came before. Sometimes those concepts come from a rival tradition. If the rival can explain, in terms the troubled tradition itself accepts, why that tradition failed, its adherents have reason, by their own standards, to acknowledge the rival's superiority. MacIntyre's central example is Aquinas, whose integration of Augustinian theology with the newly recovered Aristotle succeeded, on his account, because it resolved difficulties that neither tradition could resolve alone. Defeat, then, is not imposed from some neutral standpoint; it is recognized from within.

This reply is more successful than MacIntyre's critics allow, though narrower than he sometimes suggests. It shows that tradition-constituted rationality need not be closed: a tradition can be defeated and can know that it has been. But the vindication it permits is local and retrospective. A tradition is shown superior only to a rival that has already entered crisis, and only once that rival's adherents have learned the victor's idiom well enough to see their failure in its terms. Where two traditions are both flourishing, the account yields no verdict at all. That is not relativism, since MacIntyre denies that all traditions are equally warranted. It does mean, however, that the rational standing of a tradition depends on its history of meeting crises, a standard that can be applied only as that history unfolds.

sources.author: Alasdair MacIntyre
sources.title: Whose Justice? Which Rationality?
sources.note: Argues that standards of rational justification are constituted within traditions of inquiry and that a tradition can be rationally defeated through an epistemological crisis; source of the quotation "no standing ground, no place for enquiry" (ch. 18, p. 350).

sources.author: Alasdair MacIntyre
sources.title: After Virtue: A Study in Moral Theory
sources.note: Diagnoses the fragmentation of modern moral discourse and defines a living tradition as "an historically extended, socially embodied argument" (ch. 15), the conception the later book develops.

sources.author: Martha C. Nussbaum
sources.title: Recoiling from Reason (review of Whose Justice? Which Rationality?), The New York Review of Books
sources.note: A sharp critical review charging that MacIntyre's turn to tradition retreats from critical reason toward authority; reprinted in her Philosophical Interventions (2012).

passages.title: The Tusi couple and Copernicus
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
Ptolemy's Almagest accounted for the planets' motions with impressive accuracy, but at a philosophical cost. To fit the observations, Ptolemy made the center of a planet's epicycle move uniformly not about the center of the circle that carried it but about a separate point, the equant, thereby violating his own principle that celestial motions are compounded of uniform circular motions. From the eleventh century, astronomers writing in Arabic within the discipline of hay'a, or theoretical astronomy, treated this as a defect to be repaired rather than tolerated; Ibn al-Haytham catalogued such inconsistencies in his Doubts Concerning Ptolemy. In his Tadhkira, completed around 1260, Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, director of the new observatory at Maragha, set out a remedy he had first sketched in an earlier Persian work: a small circle rolling inside a circle twice its diameter, so that a point on the small circle moves back and forth along a straight line. This device, now called the Tusi couple, produces straight-line motion from uniform circular motions alone, and it allowed astronomers to approximate Ptolemy's results without the equant. In the fourteenth century the Damascus astronomer Ibn al-Shatir built lunar and planetary models free of equants altogether.

Copernicus's De revolutionibus (1543) employs the same device, and his lunar model is essentially identical to Ibn al-Shatir's. Noel Swerdlow and Otto Neugebauer concluded that the question is "not whether, but when, where, and in what form" Copernicus learned of Maragha theory. Willy Hartner had already observed that the letters marking points on Copernicus's diagram of the couple largely correspond to those on Tusi's, and Byzantine Greek manuscripts describing the device are known to have reached Italy. George Saliba, in Islamic Science and the Making of the European Renaissance (2007), and F. Jamil Ragep have since extended the case, Ragep arguing that Copernicus's debts may include not only devices but arguments by the fifteenth-century astronomer Ali Qushji about whether astronomy must depend on Aristotelian natural philosophy.

Skeptics, notably Viktor Blåsjö, reply that no Arabic text is known to have been in Copernicus's hands, that he probably could not read Arabic, and that anyone seeking equant-free models built from uniform circles might well arrive at similar constructions; the lettering argument, Blåsjö contends, is less telling than it appears.

Both sides, however, frame the matter too narrowly, as a choice between copying and invention. The skeptics are right that no single route of transmission has been documented, but the case does not rest on any one item. An identical lunar model, the same device, and a shared diagram convention could each be coincidence; that all three should be is far less likely than that some channel, as yet unidentified, existed. What crossed that channel, though, were solutions to a problem Copernicus already shared with the Maragha astronomers, namely their commitment to uniform circular motion. The Maragha devices address the irregularities in a planet's motion around the zodiac, not the retrograde loops that heliocentrism explains. Copernicus most probably inherited tools, not the revolution itself.

sources.author: George Saliba
sources.title: Islamic Science and the Making of the European Renaissance
sources.note: Traces the hay'a tradition's critique of Ptolemy, the Maragha-school models of Tusi and Ibn al-Shatir, and the evidence that Copernicus drew on them.

sources.author: N. M. Swerdlow and O. Neugebauer
sources.title: Mathematical Astronomy in Copernicus's De Revolutionibus
sources.note: The standard technical study of Copernicus's models; source of the quotation that the question is "not whether, but when, where, and in what form" Copernicus learned of Maragha theory (part 1, p. 47).

sources.author: F. Jamil Ragep
sources.title: Copernicus and His Islamic Predecessors: Some Historical Remarks (History of Science 45)
sources.note: Reviews the case for transmission, covering both the Tusi couple and Ibn al-Shatir's models and Ali Qushji's arguments on astronomy's independence from Aristotelian physics.

sources.author: Viktor Blåsjö
sources.title: A Critique of the Arguments for Maragha Influence on Copernicus (Journal for the History of Astronomy 45)
sources.note: The leading skeptical reply, arguing that independent discovery is plausible and that the lettering and other arguments for transmission are weaker than claimed.

passages.title: Al-Ghazali and Descartes on doubt
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Passage A

In al-Munqidh min al-Dalal (Deliverance from Error), written late in his life, the theologian al-Ghazali (d. 1111) recounts how a thirst to know things as they really are led him to test his convictions. The senses failed first. Sight looks at a shadow and judges it motionless, though it is later seen to have moved; it sees a star as no larger than a coin, though geometrical proofs show the star to be larger than the earth. Reason, acting as judge, convicts the senses. But might there be, al-Ghazali asks, another judge beyond reason, whose verdict would expose reason's errors as reason exposed those of the senses? In dreams we accept what we imagine and see its baselessness only on waking; perhaps waking life stands to some further state as dreams stand to waking.

He could not argue his way out, since any argument would have to be built from the very first principles of reason that were now in doubt. For nearly two months, he reports, he was a skeptic in fact though not in what he professed. Then the malady passed, and the necessary truths of reason were again accepted as certain. This came about, in W. Montgomery Watt's translation, "not by systematic demonstration or marshalled argument, but by a light which God most high cast into my breast." After examining the theologians, the philosophers and the Ismaili advocates of an infallible teacher, he concluded that the Sufis possessed what the others only described: their distinctive knowledge came by direct experience, which he called tasting (dhawq), not by words. In 1095 he left his professorship in Baghdad to follow their path.

Passage B

Descartes's Meditations (1641) also begins by demolishing belief. The senses sometimes deceive; there are no sure signs by which waking can be distinguished from dreaming; and for all the meditator yet knows, an omnipotent deceiver might make him err even when he adds two and three. The Second Meditation finds the one belief such doubt cannot touch: the proposition "I am, I exist, is necessarily true whenever it is put forward by me or conceived in my mind." From the idea of a perfect being in his mind, the Third Meditation argues that God exists and cannot be a deceiver, "since it is manifest by the natural light that all fraud and deception depend on some defect." Whatever the meditator clearly and distinctly perceives may therefore be trusted. Antoine Arnauld objected that this is circular: the proof of God relies on clear and distinct perceptions that only God's existence was supposed to certify.

In 1966 Sami Najm argued that al-Ghazali's handling of doubt is profoundly comparable to Descartes's and that their solutions are essentially the same, though he claimed no evidence of influence. The first half of this claim holds: both thinkers doubt the senses, both use the dream to unsettle waking certainty, and both entertain a power that might overturn reason itself. The second half does not. Descartes reasons his way back; whatever one makes of Arnauld's circle, it is a difficulty that only an argument can have. Al-Ghazali says that argument could not restore him and that certainty returned as a gift. The parallel lies in how the two lost certainty, not in how they regained it.

sources.author: al-Ghazali (tr. W. Montgomery Watt)
sources.title: The Faith and Practice of al-Ghazali (translation of al-Munqidh min al-Dalal)
sources.note: Al-Ghazali's own account of his crisis of doubt, its cure and his turn to Sufism. The quotation 'not by systematic demonstration or marshalled argument, but by a light which God most high cast into my breast' is Watt's rendering (p. 25 in later printings).

sources.author: René Descartes (tr. John Cottingham)
sources.title: Meditations on First Philosophy
sources.note: The method of doubt, the cogito and the non-deceiving God. Quotations are from the Cottingham translation in The Philosophical Writings of Descartes, vol. II (1984): Second Meditation (AT VII 25) and Third Meditation (AT VII 52).

sources.author: Sami M. Najm
sources.title: The Place and Function of Doubt in the Philosophies of Descartes and al-Ghazali
sources.note: Philosophy East and West 16: argues that the two thinkers' treatments of doubt are profoundly comparable and their solutions essentially the same, while disclaiming any evidence of influence.

passages.title: Hallaq's restatement of Orientalism
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
When Edward Said published Orientalism in 1978, he characterized his subject, among other things, as "a Western style for dominating, restructuring, and having authority over the Orient." His achievement was to show that a body of learned writing about Arab and Islamic societies, long presented as disinterested scholarship, had been bound up with European imperial rule; its representations of the Orient helped make that rule seem natural. The book became a founding text of postcolonial studies. Many of its early critics charged that it went too far, indicting a whole field for the failings of some of its members.

Wael Hallaq's Restating Orientalism: A Critique of Modern Knowledge (2018) argues the reverse: Said did not go far enough. On Hallaq's reading, Said treated Orientalism as a discrete field and located its fault chiefly in misrepresentation serving power. That diagnosis implies a remedy, more accurate representation, and leaves untouched the knowledge from which Orientalism grew. Hallaq contends instead that Orientalism is one expression of structural features of modern knowledge as such. The habits of thought that made the Orient an object to be known and governed operate as well in modern law, philosophy, economics and the sciences, and they are tied to the sovereign state and to colonial projects. What kept Said from seeing this, Hallaq argues, was his own secular liberal humanism, which shared the premises he would have needed to question. Hallaq therefore shifts attention from the individual scholar to the paradigm within which scholars work, a paradigm organized around what he had called, in The Impossible State (2013), modernity's central domains. The question becomes less whether a given Orientalist was prejudiced than what the discipline's premises made thinkable. Against Said's focus on individual authors Hallaq sets the figure of the subversive author, exemplified by the French metaphysician René Guénon, who rejected modernity's founding premises rather than merely its abuses.

The book has drawn sharp responses. Lahouari Addi contends that Said, drawing on philosophy and the social sciences, analyzed Orientalism better than Hallaq does, and that "by rejecting both the social sciences, and their Kantian underpinning, Hallaq strengthens the intellectual hegemony of orientalism." Other reviewers, while admiring the rigor of the argument, have found its polemic frustrating.

Whatever the merits of these objections, Hallaq's reframing explains something Said's cannot: why decades of correcting stereotypes have left largely intact the institutions and habits of thought that produced them. Yet in its strongest form the thesis strains. If modern knowledge is structurally bound to domination, then Hallaq's own critique, written within the modern university and in its idiom, needs an account of how it escapes. His appeal to subversive authors supplies the beginning of one, for it concedes that the paradigm admits dissent from within its own era. The argument is most persuasive when read as a claim about the paradigm's dominant tendencies rather than about everything modern knowledge can do.

sources.author: Wael B. Hallaq
sources.title: Restating Orientalism: A Critique of Modern Knowledge
sources.note: Argues that Said's critique was too narrow because Orientalism expresses structural features of modern knowledge tied to sovereignty and colonialism; contrasts Said with René Guénon as 'the subversive author.'

sources.author: Edward W. Said
sources.title: Orientalism
sources.note: The founding critique of Western scholarship on the Orient; the quoted definition, 'a Western style for dominating, restructuring, and having authority over the Orient,' is from the introduction (p. 3).

sources.author: Lahouari Addi
sources.title: Review of Restating Orientalism (Reading Religion)
sources.note: A critical review defending Said's use of philosophy and the social sciences; source of the quotation 'By rejecting both the social sciences, and their Kantian underpinning, Hallaq strengthens the intellectual hegemony of orientalism.'

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: MacIntyre's account of epistemological crises answers the charge of relativism by showing that rival traditions can be judged from a neutral standpoint once one of them has entered crisis.
Because MacIntyre holds that all standards of rational justification are developed within traditions, his position cannot avoid the conclusion that no tradition is rationally superior to another.
MacIntyre's appeal to epistemological crises frees his view of rationality from relativism, but only by making a tradition's superiority something established case by case over its history.
MacIntyre's analysis of Aquinas shows that a tradition in crisis can rationally adopt a rival tradition's concepts without abandoning continuity with its own past.
MacIntyre's reply to his critics succeeds completely, since it establishes that every tradition can eventually be shown superior or inferior to each of its rivals.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph is the author's verdict: the crisis reply 'is more successful than MacIntyre's critics allow, though narrower than he sometimes suggests'; it is 'not relativism,' but vindication is 'local and retrospective' and depends on a tradition's 'history of meeting crises.' C states both halves. B is the critics' view, which the author rejects; E drops the author's qualification and contradicts 'the account yields no verdict at all.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall claim about MacIntyre's reply to the relativism charge.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, especially its first sentence and its last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 1 gives MacIntyre's thesis, paragraph 2 the relativism objection, paragraph 3 MacIntyre's reply, and paragraph 4 the author's evaluation, which is where the main point lives. Prephrase: the crisis reply really does avoid relativism, but the vindication it allows is limited, one rival at a time and after the fact. Expect traps that give the critics' view as the author's and traps that drop 'narrower.'

choices.note: Distortion. The passage says defeat 'is not imposed from some neutral standpoint; it is recognized from within.' A reader who expects any answer to relativism to need neutral ground picks this.
Wrong position-holder. This is the critics' charge from paragraph 2. The author says the reply shows tradition-constituted rationality 'need not be closed' and that the result 'is not relativism.'

CORRECT. 'Frees his view... from relativism' matches 'more successful than... critics allow' and 'That is not relativism'; 'only by making... case by case over its history' matches 'local and retrospective' and the closing sentence.
Too narrow. Aquinas is MacIntyre's example in paragraph 3, a supporting detail, and the answer omits the author's evaluation entirely.
Too extreme. The author calls the reply 'narrower than he sometimes suggests' and says that where two traditions flourish 'the account yields no verdict at all.'

questions.stem: According to the passage, Nussbaum contended that MacIntyre's turn to tradition
choices: relied on a misreading of the synthesis that Aquinas achieved
was inconsistent with the argument MacIntyre had made in After Virtue
failed to recognize that modern liberalism is itself a tradition
ignored the possibility that a tradition could enter an epistemological crisis
amounted to a retreat from critical reason toward accepting authority
questions.explanation: The last sentence of the second paragraph says Nussbaum argued 'that his turn to tradition amounted to a retreat from critical reason toward the acceptance of authority.' E restates it. D borrows the term at the center of MacIntyre's reply in paragraph 3 and attaches it to his critic.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Retrieve what the passage says Nussbaum argued.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: A pure detail question: find Nussbaum's name and read her claim. The passage gives exactly one claim to her. Every other choice either uses words from elsewhere in the passage or brings in something a reader who knows the debate might expect.

choices.note: Out of scope. Aquinas appears only as MacIntyre's example in paragraph 3; the passage attributes no view about him to Nussbaum.
Out of scope. After Virtue is mentioned in paragraph 1 as a work MacIntyre extended; no one is said to find the two books inconsistent.
Shell game. Paragraph 1 lists modern liberalism among MacIntyre's traditions; the passage never says Nussbaum denied or missed this.
Shell game. 'Epistemological crisis' is MacIntyre's reply in paragraph 3, not something Nussbaum is said to have discussed.
CORRECT. A close paraphrase of 'a retreat from critical reason toward the acceptance of authority.'

questions.stem: The author mentions Aquinas (third paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: give an example MacIntyre offers of a tradition overcoming difficulties by drawing on resources from another tradition
show that the problems of medieval theology were resolved from a standpoint neutral between the Augustinian and Aristotelian traditions
illustrate the author's claim that the vindication MacIntyre's account permits is local and retrospective
suggest that MacIntyre's account of epistemological crises applies chiefly to theological traditions
provide evidence against Nussbaum's claim that MacIntyre's position amounts to a retreat toward authority
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says new concepts 'sometimes... come from a rival tradition' and then offers 'MacIntyre's central example,' Aquinas, whose integration of Augustinian theology with Aristotle 'resolved difficulties that neither tradition could resolve alone.' A names that role. C moves the example to the author's paragraph 4 point; E invents a link to Nussbaum the passage never draws.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the Aquinas sentence is there.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, the sentences just before and after the Aquinas example.

breakdown.analysis: Read the context: the sentence before says crisis-resolving concepts sometimes come from a rival tradition; the Aquinas sentence is introduced as 'MacIntyre's central example'; the next sentence draws the moral, defeat 'recognized from within.' So it is MacIntyre's illustration of his own reply. Watch for answers that reassign it to the author or to the dispute with Nussbaum.

choices.note: CORRECT. It is introduced as 'MacIntyre's central example' of the claim that crisis-resolving concepts 'sometimes... come from a rival tradition.'
Opposite. The paragraph ends by insisting defeat 'is not imposed from some neutral standpoint.'
Wrong position-holder. The 'local and retrospective' claim is the author's, made in paragraph 4; Aquinas is MacIntyre's example, offered in paragraph 3.
Out of scope. Nothing suggests the account is limited to theology; the traditions in paragraph 1 include the Scottish Enlightenment and liberalism.
Irrelevant link. Nussbaum's objection is reported in paragraph 2, but the passage never presents Aquinas as an answer to it; the example serves the relativism reply.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward MacIntyre's reply to the charge of relativism can most accurately be described as
choices: enthusiastic endorsement of its claim to settle the dispute between any two traditions of inquiry
reluctant agreement that it leaves MacIntyre's position indistinguishable from relativism
skepticism about whether it shows that a tradition can ever be defeated by a rival
qualified approval, crediting it with answering the charge while finding its reach limited
detached neutrality, reporting it without assessing whether it succeeds
questions.explanation: The author says the reply 'is more successful than MacIntyre's critics allow, though narrower than he sometimes suggests,' that the result 'is not relativism,' and that it yields no verdict between flourishing traditions. That is approval with a limit, as D says. C reverses the author's explicit concession that 'a tradition can be defeated and can know that it has been.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize the author's evaluation of MacIntyre's crisis reply.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, first two sentences and the sentence beginning 'That is not relativism.'

breakdown.analysis: The attitude is mixed in a specific way: positive on whether the reply defeats the relativism charge, limiting on how much the reply can decide. A correct answer needs both a positive component and a restriction. Eliminate any choice that is all-for, all-against, or neutral.

choices.note: Too extreme. The author says the account gives 'no verdict at all' where two traditions are both flourishing, so it does not settle disputes between any two traditions.
Opposite. The author states, 'That is not relativism.'
Opposite. The author grants that the reply 'shows... a tradition can be defeated and can know that it has been'; the doubt concerns scope, not possibility.
CORRECT. 'More successful than MacIntyre's critics allow' and 'not relativism' are the approval; 'narrower than he sometimes suggests' and 'local and retrospective' are the qualification.
Wrong attitude. Paragraph 4 is explicitly evaluative ('more successful,' 'narrower').

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: A tradition that has never undergone an epistemological crisis is, for that reason, rationally inferior to one that has overcome such a crisis.
MacIntyre's account gives no basis for ranking two traditions if neither faces problems it cannot solve with its own resources.
Critics who charge MacIntyre with relativism are correct that, on his view, each tradition can rationally vindicate only itself.
On MacIntyre's account, the adherents of a defeated tradition must abandon every belief they held before their tradition's crisis.
Nussbaum's objection to MacIntyre's position is more damaging than the charge of relativism that other critics have made.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4: 'A tradition is shown superior only to a rival that has already entered crisis,' and 'Where two traditions are both flourishing, the account yields no verdict at all.' A tradition that faces no problems it cannot solve is a tradition not in crisis, so B follows. A is the tempting overreach: the author makes a tradition's standing depend on its 'history of meeting crises' but never says an untested tradition is inferior.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the author's own claims support.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, third through fifth sentences; paragraph 3, first two sentences for what a crisis is.

breakdown.analysis: The author's limits on MacIntyre's account are the place to look. Paragraph 3 defines a crisis as a tradition's central problems resisting 'every solution its resources allow.' Paragraph 4 says superiority is shown only over a rival in crisis, and that flourishing traditions get no verdict. Combine them and you get B. Traps will stretch 'history of meeting crises' into a ranking, or hand the critics' or Nussbaum's claims to the author.

choices.note: Too strong. The final sentence ties standing to a 'history of meeting crises,' but the author says flourishing traditions get 'no verdict at all,' not that untested ones lose.
CORRECT. 'Neither faces problems it cannot solve with its own resources' describes two traditions not in crisis, i.e., 'both flourishing,' for which 'the account yields no verdict at all.'
Wrong position-holder. This is the critics' claim; the author says the reply shows a tradition 'can be defeated and can know that it has been.'
Distortion. Resolution of a crisis must preserve 'continuity with what came before,' and the passage never says a defeated tradition's adherents give up every belief.
Unsupported comparison. The author reports Nussbaum's objection but never weighs it against the relativism charge.

questions.stem: Which one of the following scenarios most closely conforms to the account of rational defeat that the passage attributes to MacIntyre?
choices: Scholars from two rival schools of legal interpretation adopt a set of rules that neither school's members had accepted but that both agree are neutral, and by those rules they judge one school superior.
A school of medicine loses most of its adherents after a rival school gains the patronage of a powerful ruler who forbids the older school's teaching.

Adherents of a school of astronomy, unable to resolve certain anomalies with their own methods, adopt a rival school's methods, which resolve the anomalies but offer no account of why the older methods failed.

Adherents of a school of astronomy, unable to resolve certain anomalies with their own methods, come to see that a rival school resolves them and explains, by standards they accept, why their methods failed.
Two schools of ethics, after long debate, conclude that their standards of justification differ so deeply that neither school can be judged superior to the other.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 requires a crisis (problems that resist the tradition's resources) and a rival that can 'explain, in terms the troubled tradition itself accepts, why that tradition failed'; then adherents acknowledge superiority 'by their own standards.' D has every element. C is the near-miss: it has the crisis and the solved problems but lacks the explanation of failure, which both the crisis criteria and the defeat condition require.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match a new case to MacIntyre's conditions for one tradition's rational defeat of another.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, second through fifth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: List the conditions first. (1) The defeated tradition is in crisis by its own lights. (2) The rival supplies what resolves the crisis. (3) The rival explains why the troubled tradition failed. (4) That explanation is in terms the troubled tradition accepts, so the defeat is recognized from within, not from neutral ground. Then check each scenario against all four; a scenario that has three is still wrong.

choices.note: Contradicts the account. MacIntyre denies a neutral standing ground, and the passage says defeat 'is not imposed from some neutral standpoint.'
No rational defeat. Losing adherents through a ruler's patronage involves no crisis and no explanation by the school's own standards; it is closer to the authority Nussbaum mentions.
Half right, and the trap. It has the crisis and the solution, but the account also requires that the rival 'explain... why that tradition failed,' and this rival offers no such account.
CORRECT. Crisis by the school's own methods, a rival that resolves it, and an explanation of the failure 'by standards they accept,' so the defeat is recognized from within.
This is the relativist conclusion the passage says MacIntyre's reply is meant to block, not his account of defeat.

questions.stem: By "local and retrospective" (third sentence of the fourth paragraph), the author most probably means that the vindication MacIntyre's account permits
choices: applies only to traditions that arose within a single region and can be confirmed only by historians writing later
holds only against a particular rival already in crisis, and only after that rival's failure has occurred
rests on the personal judgments of individual adherents rather than on any standards those adherents share
is valid within the victorious tradition but cannot be acknowledged by adherents of the defeated rival
concerns secondary doctrines of a tradition rather than its fundamental commitments
questions.explanation: The next two sentences explain the phrase: a tradition is 'shown superior only to a rival that has already entered crisis' (local: one rival at a time) and 'only once that rival's adherents have learned the victor's idiom' to see their failure (retrospective: after the fact). B paraphrases both. D contradicts the passage's point that defeat 'is recognized from within' by the defeated tradition.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Determine what 'local and retrospective' means in context.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, the phrase and the two sentences that follow it.

breakdown.analysis: The author defines the phrase immediately: 'only to a rival that has already entered crisis' and 'only once that rival's adherents have learned the victor's idiom.' So 'local' means pairwise, tradition against a particular rival; 'retrospective' means after the crisis and its recognition. Watch for literal readings of 'local' (geographic) and answers that contradict 'recognized from within.'

choices.note: Literal misreading. 'Local' here concerns which rival a tradition is measured against, not geography, and the passage says nothing about later historians.
CORRECT. 'A particular rival already in crisis' is 'a rival that has already entered crisis'; 'only after that rival's failure has occurred' is the retrospective element.
Distortion. The passage stresses the troubled tradition's own shared standards ('in terms the troubled tradition itself accepts'), not private judgment.

Opposite. The defeated tradition's adherents 'have reason, by their own standards, to acknowledge the rival's superiority,' and the author grants that a tradition 'can know that it has been' defeated.
Out of scope. The passage never distinguishes secondary from fundamental doctrines in this connection.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Copernicus's planetary models were derived from those of the Maragha astronomers, as the identical lunar model and the shared diagram lettering conclusively demonstrate.
Copernicus very probably drew on Maragha devices, which solved a problem he shared with their inventors but did not give him heliocentrism.
Skeptics have shown that Copernicus could have devised his models independently, so the question of Maragha influence on his work cannot be settled.
The Maragha astronomers anticipated the central elements of the Copernican revolution, including its explanation of the planets' retrograde motion.
Tusi's device repaired a philosophical defect in Ptolemy's astronomy that astronomers writing in Arabic had recognized since the eleventh century.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph holds that convergent evidence makes it far more likely 'that some channel, as yet unidentified, existed,' but that what crossed it were 'solutions to a problem Copernicus already shared,' so that he 'most probably inherited tools, not the revolution itself.' B states both. A drops the author's hedges ('most probably,' 'as yet unidentified') and the tools-not-revolution limit.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall claim about Copernicus and the Maragha astronomers.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, especially its third, fourth and last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraphs 1-3 lay out the background, the case for transmission and the skeptics' reply; paragraph 4 is the author's resolution. Prephrase: transmission probably happened even though the route is unknown, but what was transmitted was tools for a shared problem, not heliocentrism. Traps will overstate the case or give the skeptics' view.

choices.note: Too strong. The author treats each item as something that 'could... be coincidence' and argues only that transmission is far more likely; 'conclusively demonstrate' and 'planetary models were derived' overreach.
CORRECT. It keeps the probabilistic conclusion ('very probably') and the limit ('tools, not the revolution itself').
Wrong position-holder. This is closer to the skeptics; the author answers them and judges transmission 'far' more likely than coincidence.
Opposite. The author says the Maragha devices 'address the irregularities in a planet's motion around the zodiac, not the retrograde loops that heliocentrism explains.'
Too narrow. True of paragraph 1, but it says nothing about Copernicus, the subject of the debate the passage resolves.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the Tusi couple
choices: was first proposed by Ibn al-Haytham in his Doubts Concerning Ptolemy
enabled astronomers to account for the retrograde loops of the planets
yields straight-line motion from uniform circular motions
was used by Ibn al-Shatir but not by Copernicus
reproduced Ptolemy's results more accurately than the equant had
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'This device, now called the Tusi couple, produces straight-line motion from uniform circular motions alone.' C restates it. B is a shell game with the final paragraph, which says the Maragha devices do not address the retrograde loops.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Retrieve what the passage says about the Tusi couple.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, fourth and fifth sentences; paragraph 2, first sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Locate the device's description in paragraph 1. The passage says it is two circles, one rolling inside the other; a point oscillates along a straight line; it 'produces straight-line motion from uniform circular motions alone' and lets astronomers 'approximate' Ptolemy's results without the equant. Check each choice against those words.

choices.note: Shell game. Ibn al-Haytham 'catalogued such inconsistencies'; the device is credited to Tusi in his Tadhkira.
Opposite. The last paragraph says the Maragha devices address motion around the zodiac, 'not the retrograde loops that heliocentrism explains.'
CORRECT. Matches 'produces straight-line motion from uniform circular motions alone.'
Contradicts paragraph 2: 'Copernicus's De revolutionibus (1543) employs the same device.'
Distortion. The passage says the device allowed astronomers to 'approximate Ptolemy's results'; it claims no gain in accuracy.

questions.stem: The primary function of the third paragraph is to
choices: present evidence casting doubt on the claim that Copernicus's lunar model resembles Ibn al-Shatir's
give the author's own reasons for doubting that any transmission occurred
explain how Byzantine manuscripts might have carried Maragha theory to Italy
concede that the correspondence between the two diagrams has been misreported
set out objections to the case for transmission that the author then evaluates
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 reports 'Skeptics, notably Viktor Blåsjö,' and their objections; paragraph 4 opens 'Both sides, however, frame the matter too narrowly' and grants that 'The skeptics are right that no single route... has been documented' before answering them. E names that role. B gives the skeptics' view to the author.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify what paragraph 3 does in the passage's structure.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3 and the first two sentences of paragraph 4.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 2 builds the case for transmission; paragraph 3 introduces opponents ('Skeptics... reply'); paragraph 4 evaluates both sides. So paragraph 3 is the counterposition the author goes on to weigh. Watch for answers that make it the author's view or that attribute specific claims the skeptics do not make.

choices.note: Distortion. The skeptics dispute how the resemblance arose (independent arrival 'at similar constructions'), not whether it exists.
Wrong position-holder. The views are attributed to 'Skeptics, notably Viktor Blåsjö'; the author answers them in paragraph 4.
Shell game. The Byzantine manuscripts appear in paragraph 2, as part of the case for transmission.
Distortion. Blåsjö says the lettering argument 'is less telling than it appears,' an objection to its weight, not a claim that it was misreported, and the author concedes nothing of the kind.
CORRECT. The paragraph lays out the skeptics' objections; paragraph 4 grants one ('no single route... documented') and answers the rest.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the skeptics' position described in the third paragraph can most accurately be described as
choices: partial agreement, granting one of their points but denying that it defeats the case
complete rejection, regarding each of their objections as entirely without foundation
full endorsement of their view that independent invention is the likelier explanation
indifference, since the author considers the question they address unanswerable
admiration for their success in identifying the actual route of transmission
questions.explanation: 'The skeptics are right that no single route of transmission has been documented, but the case does not rest on any one item.' The author grants a point and then argues that convergence makes transmission far more likely. That is A. B misses the explicit concession; C reverses the author's conclusion.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize the author's stance toward the skeptics.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, first three sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Look for the author's direct words about the skeptics: 'Both sides... frame the matter too narrowly' and 'The skeptics are right that... but.' A concession followed by 'but' signals partial agreement. The right answer needs both elements.

choices.note: CORRECT. The author grants that 'no single route of transmission has been documented' but holds that the convergence of evidence makes some channel far more likely than coincidence.
Too extreme. The author explicitly says 'The skeptics are right' about one point.
Opposite. The author judges coincidence across all three items 'far less likely' than transmission.
Unsupported. The author reaches a definite probabilistic conclusion ('most probably inherited tools'), so does not regard the question as unanswerable.
Distortion. The route is 'as yet unidentified,' and the skeptics' point is precisely that none has been documented.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the passage?
choices: Copernicus learned of the Tusi couple from the Byzantine Greek manuscripts that reached Italy.
Ibn al-Shatir's models were the first to make use of the Tusi couple.
Swerdlow and Neugebauer doubted that Copernicus had any knowledge of Maragha theory.
Copernicus, like the Maragha astronomers, objected to Ptolemy's use of the equant.
Ragep considers Copernicus's debts to Ali Qushji more important than his debts to Tusi.
questions.explanation: The equant is objectionable because it violates the principle of uniform circular motion (paragraph 1); the Maragha devices solve that problem, and the author says they were 'solutions to a problem Copernicus already shared with the Maragha astronomers, namely their commitment to uniform circular motion.' So Copernicus, too, saw the equant as a defect. A is the attractive overreach: the manuscripts are evidence that a route was possible, but the author calls the channel 'as yet unidentified.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the claim the passage best supports.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, second sentence; paragraph 4, fourth sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Link the two ends of the passage. Paragraph 1: the equant violates uniform circular motion, and hay'a astronomers treated it as 'a defect to be repaired.' Paragraph 4: Copernicus shared their 'commitment to uniform circular motion,' and the devices were solutions to that shared problem. The inference is that he too found the equant objectionable. Beware answers that turn possible routes into actual ones or invent comparisons.

choices.note: Too strong. Paragraph 2 says such manuscripts 'are known to have reached Italy,' but paragraph 4 says the channel is 'as yet unidentified.'
Unsupported, and contrary to the chronology given: Tusi proposed the device around 1260, and Ibn al-Shatir worked in the fourteenth century.
Opposite. They concluded the question is 'not whether, but when, where, and in what form' he learned of it, which presupposes that he did.
CORRECT. The problem the Maragha devices solve is the equant's violation of uniform circular motion, and Copernicus 'already shared' that problem through his 'commitment to uniform circular motion.'
Unsupported comparison. Ragep is said to argue that the debts 'may include not only devices but arguments' by Qushji; no ranking is given.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously undermine the author's reasoning in the fourth paragraph concerning the likelihood that some channel of transmission existed?
choices: None of the books known to have belonged to Copernicus, including those he annotated, was written by an astronomer who wrote in Arabic.
Several of the Byzantine Greek manuscripts describing the Tusi couple were copied in Italy during the fifteenth century, before Copernicus studied there.
Geometry leads anyone building an equant-free lunar model from uniform circles to both the Tusi couple and Ibn al-Shatir's model.
Ibn al-Shatir's lunar model predicted the moon's positions more accurately than Ptolemy's had.
Copernicus's arguments for the motion of the earth owed nothing to the work of Ali Qushji.
questions.explanation: The author argues that the lunar model, the device and the diagram convention 'could each be coincidence,' but 'that all three should be is far less likely' than transmission. That reasoning treats the three matches as independent. If the problem's geometry leads anyone to both the couple and the lunar model, two of the three are not separate coincidences at all, and the improbability of their joint occurrence collapses. A restates a point the author has already conceded ('no single route... has been documented').

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most damages the author's argument from converging evidence.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, second and third sentences; paragraph 3 for the skeptics' related point.

breakdown.analysis: Identify the structure: three matches, each possibly coincidental; together, coincidence is unlikely; therefore a channel probably existed. The hidden assumption is that the three are independent, so their probabilities multiply. A weakener should show they are linked, so that one cause (the constraints of the problem) would produce them together. Facts about missing books restate a conceded point; facts about accuracy or Qushji are off the argument.

choices.note: Premise restatement. The author already grants that 'no single route of transmission has been documented' and argues that the case does not rest on any one item.
Irrelevant, or a slight strengthener: manuscripts circulating in Italy shortly before Copernicus would make a channel more available, not less.

CORRECT. It shows that two of the three matches would follow from the same constraint rather than being independent coincidences, undercutting the claim that their joint occurrence is 'far less likely' than transmission.
Irrelevant truth. The accuracy of the lunar model bears on its merit, not on whether Copernicus's identical model is evidence of transmission.
Out of scope. The author's convergence argument concerns the lunar model, the device and the lettering; Qushji's arguments are Ragep's further claim and are not among its premises.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the relationship that the author believes most probably held between Copernicus and the Maragha astronomers?
choices: An architect, without acknowledgment, copies in every detail the entire design of a cathedral built a century earlier by a rival architect.
A composer who shares an earlier school's rule of harmony adopts its techniques for honoring that rule and uses them in a new kind of music.
An engineer invents a bridge design that, unknown to her, had been devised centuries earlier by builders working in a distant country.
A novelist adopts an earlier writer's revolutionary narrative form but uses it only to tell conventional stories of the kind long familiar.
A scientist who rejects the founding principles of an earlier school nonetheless borrows its instruments in order to refute its theories.
questions.explanation: The author's picture has three elements: a shared commitment (to uniform circular motion), borrowed solutions serving that commitment ('tools'), and a new achievement the predecessors did not make ('not the revolution itself'). B has all three. D reverses what was inherited: there the revolutionary element is borrowed and the use is conventional.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the author's view of the Copernicus-Maragha relationship to a parallel case.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, fourth through last sentences, and the first sentence's rejection of 'copying' vs. 'invention.'

breakdown.analysis: Abstract the relationship first: (1) the later figure shares the earlier group's governing commitment; (2) he very probably takes over their techniques for satisfying it; (3) he puts them to use in something new that is his own. The author explicitly rejects framing it as either copying or independent invention, so answers that model pure plagiarism or pure independent discovery fail.

choices.note: Too strong. Wholesale copying is the 'copying' side of the choice the author says frames the matter 'too narrowly'; and Copernicus did not inherit 'the revolution itself.'
CORRECT. Shared commitment (the rule / uniform circular motion), inherited techniques (the tools), and a new achievement of his own (heliocentrism / the new kind of music).
This models independent rediscovery, the skeptics' alternative, which the author judges far less likely than transmission.
Reversal. Here the revolutionary element is what is borrowed; the author says Copernicus inherited tools, 'not the revolution itself.'
Distortion. Copernicus shared the Maragha astronomers' governing commitment rather than rejecting their principles, and he did not use their tools to refute them.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?
choices: Passage A presents an argument that the senses are unreliable, and passage B refutes that argument by identifying a belief that survives even the most radical doubt.
Passage A describes one thinker's turn from philosophy to mysticism, and passage B argues that a later thinker made the same turn by a more rigorous route.
Passage A recounts a crisis of doubt and its resolution, and passage B argues that a later philosopher borrowed that resolution while concealing his source.
Passage A recounts one thinker's crisis of doubt and its end, and passage B recounts a similar crisis and assesses a claim that both ended the same way.
Passage A defends a religious resolution of skepticism, and passage B defends a philosophical resolution of skepticism against an objection raised to it.
questions.explanation: Passage A narrates al-Ghazali's doubt and how it ended; passage B narrates Descartes's doubt and then evaluates Najm's claim that the two solutions are 'essentially the same', accepting half of it. D captures both halves. C is the trap for readers who know the old influence legend: passage B says Najm 'claimed no evidence of influence', and nobody in the passage alleges borrowing.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe what each passage does and how B relates to A.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A as a whole; passage B, second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Passage A is narrative: doubt, failed escape, light, Sufism. Passage B narrates Descartes's doubt and recovery, then turns to Najm's comparison, endorsing its first half and rejecting its second. The right answer has to mention that B evaluates a comparison. Check the verbs: 'refutes', 'defends' and 'borrowed' all overstate.

choices.note: Passage A doesn't argue that the senses are unreliable; it reports al-Ghazali's doubts. And passage B never tries to refute passage A. It treats the two thinkers as parallel.
Half right at most. A does end with al-Ghazali turning to the Sufis, but B never says Descartes turned to mysticism, and it doesn't call his route 'more rigorous'.

Out of scope. B notes that Najm 'claimed no evidence of influence', and it says nothing about borrowing or concealment. This trap tempts readers who have heard the old story that Descartes read al-Ghazali.

CORRECT. A tells al-Ghazali's story. B tells Descartes's and then weighs Najm's claim that their 'solutions are essentially the same', accepting the claim about doubt and rejecting the claim about its resolution.

Too strong in both halves. A reports al-Ghazali's account without defending it. B reports Arnauld's objection and then sets it aside ('whatever one makes of Arnauld's circle') instead of defending Descartes against it.

questions.stem: According to passage A, al-Ghazali could not argue his way out of his doubt because
choices: the theologians and philosophers whose views he examined had never seriously tested the reliability of reason
any argument he built would have had to rest on first principles that his doubt had called into question
his senses had shown him that geometrical proofs about the size of the stars could not be trusted
the Sufis taught that knowledge acquired through words is inferior to knowledge acquired by tasting
he had concluded that waking life is in fact a dream from which some further state will awaken us
questions.explanation: Passage A gives the reason directly: 'any argument would have to be built from the very first principles of reason that were now in doubt.' B paraphrases it. D is the trap: the Sufi preference for tasting over words comes later in the story, and the passage never offers it as the reason argument failed.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the reason passage A gives for al-Ghazali's inability to argue his way out.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, second paragraph, first sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The sentence uses 'since': 'He could not argue his way out, since any argument would have to be built from the very first principles of reason that were now in doubt.' Prephrase: arguments need premises, and the premises were what he doubted.

choices.note: Out of scope. The passage says he examined these groups after his recovery, and it says nothing about their failing to test reason.
CORRECT. Paraphrases 'any argument would have to be built from the very first principles of reason that were now in doubt.'
Reversal. In the passage, geometrical proofs correct the senses ('geometrical proofs show the star to be larger than the earth'), not the other way round.
Shell game. Tasting (dhawq) appears in the last part of the passage, as what al-Ghazali concluded about the Sufis after his recovery. It isn't given as the reason argument failed.
Too strong. The passage says only 'perhaps waking life stands to some further state as dreams stand to waking.' A possibility he couldn't rule out isn't a conclusion he reached.

questions.stem: In passage B, the discussion of Arnauld's objection contributes to the author's argument primarily by
choices: showing that Descartes's resolution of doubt fails, so that only a resolution like al-Ghazali's could restore certainty
establishing that Descartes, like al-Ghazali, ultimately relied on something other than argument to restore certainty
suggesting that Najm overlooked the influence that al-Ghazali's work had on Descartes's seventeenth-century critics
illustrating the claim that both thinkers entertained the possibility of a power capable of overturning reason
providing a sign that Descartes's way back to certainty proceeded by reasoning, which sets it apart from al-Ghazali's
questions.explanation: The author returns to Arnauld in the second paragraph: 'Descartes reasons his way back; whatever one makes of Arnauld's circle, it is a difficulty that only an argument can have.' The objection is therefore evidence that Descartes's recovery was an argument, which is the difference from al-Ghazali's 'gift'. A is the trap: the author explicitly declines to judge whether the objection succeeds.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what role Arnauld's objection plays in passage B's argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, last sentence of the first paragraph, and the fourth sentence of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: An objection can be mentioned to refute a view, to concede a weakness, or to make some other point. Here the author says 'whatever one makes of Arnauld's circle', which sets aside whether it succeeds, and then 'it is a difficulty that only an argument can have'. So the objection's being possible is what matters: it shows Descartes argued his way back. That supports rejecting the second half of Najm's claim.

choices.note: Too strong. 'Whatever one makes of Arnauld's circle' leaves open whether the objection succeeds, and the author never says only al-Ghazali's resolution could work.
Opposite. The author uses the circle to show that Descartes did rely on argument: 'it is a difficulty that only an argument can have.'
Out of scope. Passage B mentions influence only to say Najm 'claimed no evidence of influence', and it never connects al-Ghazali to Descartes's critics.
Shell game. The 'power that might overturn reason' belongs to the list of what the two thinkers' doubts share. Arnauld's objection concerns how Descartes got out of doubt.
CORRECT. Only an argument can be circular, so the objection marks Descartes's recovery as argued, unlike al-Ghazali's, which 'returned as a gift'.

questions.stem: The author of passage B would be most likely to regard which one of the following details in passage A as the strongest support for rejecting Najm's view that the two thinkers' solutions are essentially the same?
choices: al-Ghazali's report that certainty returned not by demonstration but by a light God cast into his breast
al-Ghazali's suggestion that waking life might stand to some further state as dreams stand to waking life
al-Ghazali's conclusion that the distinctive knowledge of the Sufis came by direct experience rather than by words
al-Ghazali's observation that sight judges a shadow to be motionless even though the shadow has in fact moved
al-Ghazali's decision, after his recovery, to leave his professorship in Baghdad and follow the path of the Sufis
questions.explanation: Passage B rejects the second half of Najm's claim because 'Descartes reasons his way back' while al-Ghazali 'says that argument could not restore him and that certainty returned as a gift.' The detail in passage A that shows this is the quotation: 'not by systematic demonstration or marshalled argument, but by a light which God most high cast into my breast.' C is the trap. It contrasts experience with words, but it concerns the Sufis' knowledge later on, not how al-Ghazali's certainty in reason was restored.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the detail in passage A that best supports B's rejection of 'essentially the same solutions'.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, second paragraph; passage A, second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: First pin down B's reason: Descartes recovers by argument, al-Ghazali by a gift that argument couldn't supply. Then look in A for the matching detail. Details about the senses and dreams belong to the half of Najm's claim B accepts, the doubt, so they can't support rejecting the other half.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the 'gift' that passage B contrasts with Descartes's reasoning: certainty came 'not by systematic demonstration or marshalled argument'.
This belongs to the doubt, which passage B says the two share ('both use the dream to unsettle waking certainty'). It supports the half of Najm's claim B accepts.

Tempting, since it contrasts experience with words. But it describes what al-Ghazali concluded about the Sufis after his recovery, not how his certainty in reason's first principles came back. Shell game.
Part of the shared doubt about the senses, which B accepts as a genuine parallel. It doesn't bear on how certainty was regained.
A biographical consequence. It says nothing about whether his certainty was restored by argument, which is B's point of contrast.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is attributed both to al-Ghazali in passage A and to Descartes in passage B?
choices: testing the reports of the senses against the results of geometrical proof
a period of doubt that, by his own report, lasted for nearly two months
an appeal to dreaming to unsettle confidence in waking beliefs
the discovery that his own existence was beyond the reach of his doubt
the hypothesis that an omnipotent deceiver might make him err in simple sums
questions.explanation: Passage A: in dreams we accept what we imagine and see its baselessness only on waking, so waking life may be like a dream. Passage B: 'there are no sure signs by which waking can be distinguished from dreaming', and the author adds that 'both use the dream to unsettle waking certainty.' D is the trap for readers who know Descartes: the certainty of one's own existence appears only in passage B.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the feature both passages attribute to their thinker.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, first paragraph, last sentence; passage B, first sentence of the first paragraph and second sentence of the second.

breakdown.analysis: Check each choice against both passages. Most choices appear in only one. Passage B even lists what the two share: the senses, the dream, and a power that might overturn reason. Of those, only the dream appears here in wording that fits both passages.

choices.note: Passage A only. The star example uses geometry to correct sight. Passage B says only that 'the senses sometimes deceive.'
Passage A only ('For nearly two months'). Passage B gives no length for Descartes's doubt.
CORRECT. Both passages describe the dream used this way, and passage B says so explicitly: 'both use the dream to unsettle waking certainty.'
Passage B only (the Second Meditation's 'I am, I exist'). Passage A never says al-Ghazali found his own existence indubitable.
Passage B only. Al-Ghazali's counterpart in passage A is a 'judge beyond reason', not a deceiver, and sums are never mentioned. Shell game.

questions.stem: In passage A, the phrase "another judge beyond reason" (first paragraph) most probably refers to
choices: the infallible teacher whose authority the Ismaili advocates urged al-Ghazali to accept
the Sufi masters whose direct experience al-Ghazali eventually came to trust
God, whose light finally restored al-Ghazali's confidence in the first principles
the senses, whose reports reason had been unable to confirm or to correct
a faculty standing to reason as reason stands to the senses, able to expose its errors
questions.explanation: The sentence defines the phrase itself: a judge 'whose verdict would expose reason's errors as reason exposed those of the senses.' That is a faculty above reason, as E says. C is the trap: God does restore al-Ghazali's certainty, but the light confirms reason's first principles instead of convicting them of error. A tempts readers who know about the Ismailis' infallible teacher, who appears in the passage only later and in a different role.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out what 'another judge beyond reason' means where it occurs.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, first paragraph, fourth and fifth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Read the phrase together with the sentence before it. 'Reason, acting as judge, convicts the senses.' Then: 'another judge beyond reason, whose verdict would expose reason's errors as reason exposed those of the senses.' It's a proportion: senses are to reason as reason is to this further judge. The dream sentence that follows makes the same comparison. Prephrase: a higher faculty that might show reason to be wrong.

choices.note: Outside-knowledge trap. The Ismaili advocates appear later, among the groups examined after the recovery, and the passage never makes their teacher a judge of reason.
Shell game. The Sufis enter at the end, as possessors of experiential knowledge, not as a possible tribunal over reason.
Tempting, because God's light ends the doubt. But the light restores 'the necessary truths of reason' instead of exposing their errors, so it isn't the judge al-Ghazali feared.
Reversal. The senses are what reason judged. The new judge would stand above reason.
CORRECT. The passage defines the judge by the proportion: its verdict 'would expose reason's errors as reason exposed those of the senses.'

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen Najm's claim, as described in passage B, that the two thinkers' solutions to doubt are essentially the same?
choices: A Latin translation of a work by al-Ghazali was among the books Descartes owned when he wrote the Meditations, though he never cited it.
Descartes held that he saw his own existence by the natural light, a faculty he took to be God's gift, rather than inferring it.
Most of Descartes's seventeenth-century readers accepted Arnauld's objection as showing that the proof of God in the Meditations is circular.
Al-Ghazali's period of doubt ended suddenly and against his expectations, whereas Descartes undertook and ended his doubt by deliberate method.
Al-Ghazali's later works criticize the philosophers for claiming that their proofs about metaphysical matters reached demonstrative certainty.
questions.explanation: Passage B rejects Najm's second claim on one ground: Descartes 'reasons his way back' while al-Ghazali's certainty 'returned as a gift' that argument could not supply. B narrows exactly that gap: if Descartes's founding certainty was seen, not inferred, by a God-given light, his recovery also rests on something received rather than argued. A is the trap. Evidence of influence speaks to a claim Najm expressly did not make, and borrowing a source doesn't make two solutions the same.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that would best support 'essentially the same solution' against passage B's objection.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, second paragraph; passage A, second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: To strengthen a claim the author has criticized, attack the criticism. B's one ground is the contrast between argument and gift. So look for something that makes Descartes's recovery less a matter of argument, or al-Ghazali's more of one. Facts about influence, about Arnauld's success, or about later works don't touch how certainty was restored.

choices.note: Influence trap. B says Najm 'claimed no evidence of influence'; his claim concerns similarity of solution, which owning a book doesn't show.
CORRECT. It weakens B's contrast at its root. Descartes's first certainty would be seen rather than argued, by a light given by God, much like al-Ghazali's.
Irrelevant to the comparison. Whether the circle is fatal doesn't change the fact that Descartes's route was an argument, which is B's point.
Opposite. A sudden, unplanned recovery set against a deliberate method widens the difference between the two solutions.
Doesn't bear on how al-Ghazali's own certainty was restored. If anything, it fits his distrust of argument and so leaves B's contrast intact.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Said's Orientalism went too far in condemning an entire field of scholarship for the failings of some of the scholars who belonged to it.
Hallaq has demonstrated that all modern knowledge serves domination, and Said's narrower critique of Orientalism should therefore be set aside.
