Hallaq's account of Orientalism as an expression of modern knowledge improves on Said's, though it is more defensible in a less sweeping form.
Addi is right that Hallaq, by rejecting the social sciences, strengthens the very Orientalism that Restating Orientalism sets out to criticize.
The survival of Orientalist institutions shows that Said's call for more accurate representations of the Orient has gone largely unheeded.
questions.explanation: The passage presents Said, then Hallaq's claim that Said 'did not go far enough', then critics, and ends with the author's verdict. Hallaq's reframing 'explains something Said's cannot', but 'in its strongest form the thesis strains', and it is 'most persuasive' as a claim about 'dominant tendencies'. C states that qualified verdict. B is the trap: it takes Hallaq's strongest form, which the author says strains, and makes the author endorse it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the passage's main point, which is the author's own conclusion.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last paragraph, read against the second.

breakdown.analysis: In a passage built from several positions, the main point is usually the author's verdict, often near the end. Here it has two parts: Hallaq improves on Said, and his thesis works best in a moderated form. The right answer needs both parts. Answers that give someone else's view (early critics, Addi) are wrong position-holders.

choices.note: Wrong position-holder. This is the view of Said's 'early critics', which Hallaq 'reverses' and the author does not adopt.
Too extreme. The author says the strongest form of the thesis 'strains' and needs an account of how Hallaq's critique 'escapes'. 'Demonstrated' and 'all' overstate.
CORRECT. 'Explains something Said's cannot' is the improvement; 'most persuasive when read as a claim about the paradigm's dominant tendencies' is the less sweeping form.
Wrong position-holder. The author reports Addi's objection and then moves past it ('Whatever the merits of these objections'), without endorsing it.
Distortion. The author does say institutions survived decades of correcting stereotypes, but uses that to support Hallaq's diagnosis, not to say Said's call was ignored.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Hallaq faults Said for
choices: treating Orientalism as a discrete field whose fault lay chiefly in misrepresentation serving power
condemning an entire field of scholarship because of the prejudices of a relatively small number of its members
relying so heavily on philosophy and the social sciences that he could not see the premises of Orientalism
rejecting the founding premises of modernity when he should have confined himself to criticizing its abuses
denying that European learning about Arab and Islamic societies had any real connection with imperial rule
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says that, on Hallaq's reading, 'Said treated Orientalism as a discrete field and located its fault chiefly in misrepresentation serving power.' A restates this. B is the trap: it is the early critics' charge, which runs opposite to Hallaq's.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says Hallaq criticizes in Said.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, first three sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Hallaq's complaint is that Said 'did not go far enough'. The passage explains how: Said treated Orientalism as discrete and put its fault in misrepresentation. Expect a paraphrase of that sentence, and be careful not to pick up the opposite complaint ('went too far') made by others.

choices.note: CORRECT. Restates 'treated Orientalism as a discrete field and located its fault chiefly in misrepresentation serving power.'
Wrong position-holder. This is what Said's early critics charged. Hallaq argues the reverse.
Shell game. Philosophy and the social sciences appear in Addi's defense of Said, as resources Said drew on well. Hallaq blames Said's 'secular liberal humanism', not his use of those disciplines.
Reversal. Rejecting modernity's founding premises is what Hallaq praises in the subversive author, Guénon. He faults Said for not doing it.
Opposite. The passage credits Said with showing that this learning 'had been bound up with European imperial rule.'

questions.stem: Based on the passage, Hallaq would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: The chief defect of Orientalist scholarship was that its practitioners were personally hostile to the societies they studied.
The problems Said identified could be remedied by replacing distorted representations of the Orient with accurate ones.
Modern law and economics, unlike Orientalism, developed largely independently of the sovereign state and colonial projects.
A study of Arab societies free of factual distortion could still share the premises that made Orientalism possible.
Said's critique failed because he rejected the secular humanism that the Orientalists he studied took for granted.
questions.explanation: Hallaq holds that Orientalism expresses 'structural features of modern knowledge as such', that Said's remedy of 'more accurate representation' leaves the underlying knowledge 'untouched', and that 'the question becomes less whether a given Orientalist was prejudiced than what the discipline's premises made thinkable.' So accuracy alone doesn't free a study from those premises, which is D. B is the trap: it states the remedy that the passage says Said's diagnosis implies and Hallaq finds insufficient.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement Hallaq, as the passage presents him, would accept.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Collect Hallaq's commitments: the problem is structural, not just misrepresentation; accurate representation doesn't reach it; what matters is premises and the paradigm, not individual prejudice; modern law, economics and so on share the problem. The answer should follow from these without adding anything. Watch for answers that give Hallaq Said's view.

choices.note: Opposite of Hallaq's shift: 'less whether a given Orientalist was prejudiced than what the discipline's premises made thinkable.'
Wrong position-holder. More accurate representation is the remedy the passage says Said's diagnosis 'implies', and Hallaq argues it 'leaves untouched the knowledge from which Orientalism grew.'
Contradicts Hallaq's claim that the same habits of thought 'operate as well in modern law, philosophy, economics and the sciences, and they are tied to the sovereign state and to colonial projects.'

CORRECT. If the problem lies in premises and not only in misrepresentation, a study with no distortions can still carry those premises. This follows from 'leaves untouched the knowledge from which Orientalism grew.'
Reversal. Hallaq says Said's 'own secular liberal humanism' shared the premises he needed to question. Said didn't reject humanism; he held it.

questions.stem: The author refers to Hallaq's appeal to subversive authors (last paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: illustrate Hallaq's claim that individual authors matter less than the paradigm within which they carry out their work
point out that Hallaq's own account allows for a kind of dissent that counts against the strongest form of his thesis
show that Guénon's metaphysics supplies the alternative to modern knowledge that Hallaq's critique ultimately requires
support Addi's charge that Hallaq abandons the social sciences in favor of a metaphysical approach to Orientalism
explain why decades of correcting stereotypes have left the institutions that produced those stereotypes largely intact
questions.explanation: The last paragraph raises a problem: if modern knowledge is structurally bound to domination, how does Hallaq's own critique escape? The appeal to subversive authors 'supplies the beginning of one, for it concedes that the paradigm admits dissent from within its own era.' That concession supports reading the thesis as about 'dominant tendencies', not as a total claim. A is the trap: it gives the role the idea plays in the second paragraph, not in the last.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the author brings up subversive authors in the last paragraph.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last paragraph, third and fourth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The same idea plays different roles in different paragraphs. In the second paragraph, subversive authors are part of Hallaq's case. In the last, the author uses them against the strongest version of that case: dissent is possible within the era, so the paradigm isn't total. The question asks about the last paragraph.

choices.note: Shell game. That's the idea's role in Hallaq's argument in the second paragraph. In the last paragraph the author uses it to show the paradigm 'admits dissent'.
CORRECT. 'It concedes that the paradigm admits dissent from within its own era' is what makes the author prefer the 'dominant tendencies' reading over the strongest form.
Too strong. The author says the appeal 'supplies the beginning of' an account, and says nothing about Guénon's metaphysics as the alternative Hallaq needs.
Wrong position-holder, and a distortion. Addi's objection comes in the third paragraph and concerns the social sciences. The author doesn't use subversive authors to support it.
Shell game. That's the job of the last paragraph's first sentence, which credits Hallaq's reframing. The subversive authors come in later, to answer a different question.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Hallaq's argument can most accurately be described as
choices: skeptical dismissal of its central claim about Orientalism
unreserved endorsement of its account of modern knowledge
detached neutrality that avoids judging its strengths
impatience with the polemical manner of its presentation
qualified appreciation with doubt about its broadest form
questions.explanation: The author credits Hallaq's reframing with explaining 'something Said's cannot' but says that 'in its strongest form the thesis strains' and is 'most persuasive' in a narrower reading. That is qualified appreciation with a reservation about scope. D is the trap: the frustration with the polemic belongs to 'other reviewers', not to the author.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe the author's attitude toward Hallaq's argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Look for the author's evaluative words: 'explains something Said's cannot' (positive); 'strains', 'needs an account' (reservation); 'most persuasive when read as...' (qualified endorsement). Mixed but more positive than negative, and with a specific reservation about how far the claim reaches.

choices.note: Too negative. The author says the reframing 'explains something Said's cannot' and endorses a version of the central claim.
Too positive. 'In its strongest form the thesis strains' rules out 'unreserved'.
The author does judge, in the last paragraph, both a strength and a weakness.
Wrong position-holder. 'Other reviewers' found the polemic frustrating. The author says nothing about the book's tone.
CORRECT. Appreciation ('explains something Said's cannot') plus a reservation about the broadest form ('in its strongest form the thesis strains').

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to Hallaq's criticism of Said, as that criticism is described in the passage?
choices: A critic charges that a historian of a lost war unfairly blamed an entire officer corps for the errors of a few of its generals.
A critic argues that a museum's biased exhibit about a community should be corrected by consulting members of that community.
A critic contends that an economist's forecast went wrong because the data on which the economist relied were inaccurate.
A critic praises a reformer for exposing abuses within an institution while leaving the institution's founding purposes intact.
A critic faults a report on one newspaper's bias for missing that the bias stems from assumptions the report shares.
questions.explanation: Hallaq's criticism has three parts: Said exposed real bias in one field; the bias comes from premises shared across modern knowledge; and Said himself shared them ('his own secular liberal humanism ... shared the premises he would have needed to question'). E maps all three: bias in one paper, assumptions shared beyond it, and the report's author sharing them. A is the trap. It is the early critics' charge, that Said went too far, which is the reverse of Hallaq's.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the situation whose structure matches Hallaq's criticism of Said.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Strip the criticism to its structure: an exposé of a local fault misses that the fault is structural, and it misses this because the exposer shares the underlying assumptions. Then test each choice for all parts. Choices that fault inaccuracy or recommend better information match Said's diagnosis, not Hallaq's criticism of it.

choices.note: Reversal. This matches the early critics, who said Said 'went too far, indicting a whole field for the failings of some of its members.' Hallaq says he didn't go far enough.
Matches the Said-style remedy, correcting the representation, that Hallaq says 'leaves untouched' the deeper problem.
Locates the fault in inaccurate data, which parallels misrepresentation. Hallaq's point is that accuracy isn't the issue.
Opposite attitude. Hallaq faults Said for criticizing within the frame instead of questioning its premises. This critic praises that.
CORRECT. Local bias, a structural source and a critic who shares the assumptions: the shape of 'did not go far enough' plus the charge about Said's humanism.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken Hallaq's criticism of Said as the passage presents it?
choices: Said's book traced Orientalism's distortions to premises shared with other modern disciplines and challenged those premises too.
Several of the Orientalist scholars whom Said criticized had a deep and sympathetic interest in Islamic mysticism and its literature.
Hallaq's own critique, like Said's, was published by a university press and written in the idiom of modern academic scholarship.
Many readers of Said's book concluded that the proper response to Orientalism was more accurate and better-informed scholarship.
Said's book became a founding text of postcolonial studies despite strong objections from many established Orientalists of the day.
questions.explanation: Hallaq's criticism, as the passage gives it, is that Said 'treated Orientalism as a discrete field', put its fault in misrepresentation, and so 'leaves untouched the knowledge from which Orientalism grew.' If Said in fact traced the distortions to premises shared with other modern disciplines and challenged them, that criticism misdescribes him. C is the trap: it bears on the author's own reservation about Hallaq's thesis in the last paragraph, not on Hallaq's criticism of Said.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most undermines Hallaq's case against Said.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph; compare the last paragraph to see what the trap is aimed at.

breakdown.analysis: Identify the target precisely: Hallaq's claim about what Said did (treated Orientalism as discrete, put its fault in misrepresentation, didn't question modern knowledge). The strongest weakener shows Said did what Hallaq says he didn't. Be careful: the passage also contains the author's objection to Hallaq, and an answer aimed at that is a different conclusion.

choices.note: CORRECT. It directly contradicts the claim that Said treated Orientalism as 'a discrete field' and left 'untouched the knowledge from which Orientalism grew.'

Irrelevant to the criticism. Hallaq's complaint concerns the scope of Said's diagnosis, not whether some Orientalists admired Islamic traditions. If anything it fits Hallaq's shift away from individual prejudice.

Wrong conclusion. This supports the author's worry that Hallaq's critique, 'written within the modern university and in its idiom', must explain how it escapes. It doesn't show that Hallaq misread Said.
Opposite. If readers drew the remedy of more accurate scholarship from Said, that supports Hallaq's claim that Said's diagnosis 'implies' that remedy.
Irrelevant. Said's influence and his opponents' objections don't bear on whether his critique reached beyond Orientalism to modern knowledge.

sections.title: Reading Through Ideas 7: Foreign words in an Arabic scripture · Benacerraf's dilemma · Convivencia in al-Andalus · Hume, Miracles, and Probability

passages.title: Foreign words in an Arabic scripture
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
The Qur'an describes itself repeatedly as Arabic. "Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an that you might understand," runs one verse (12:2), and others speak of revelation in a clear Arabic tongue. Yet early exegetes identified a number of its words as having come from Persian, Syriac, Ethiopic, Hebrew, or Greek, and whether a scripture so described could contain foreign vocabulary became a recurring question in classical Islamic scholarship.

Its most uncompromising answer came from al-Shafi'i (d. 820). In al-Risala, his treatise on the foundations of jurisprudence, he denied that the Qur'an contains any word that is not Arabic. Those who claimed otherwise, he argued, had mistaken the limits of their own knowledge for the limits of the language. Arabic is the most extensive of tongues in its range of expression, and no one but a prophet commands the whole of it; a word unfamiliar to one scholar may be known to other Arabs, and a word found in another language may simply be shared by both. For al-Shafi'i the stakes were not merely lexical. His legal theory rests on the Qur'an's bayan, its clear declaration to those it addressed, and that clarity presupposed that the text be wholly in the language of its first hearers.

Later scholars were less reluctant. Al-Suyuti (d. 1505) compiled, in al-Muhadhdhab, a catalogue of more than a hundred Qur'anic words of reputed foreign origin, drawing heavily on earlier authorities. He also reported a reconciling view that he traced to the philologist Abu 'Ubayd (d. 838): both parties were correct, since the words were foreign in origin but had been taken into Arabic, adapted to its forms, and used by Arabs before the revelation, so that by the time the Qur'an employed them they were Arabic words.

Modern philology reopened the question. Arthur Jeffery's The Foreign Vocabulary of the Qur'an (1938) applied comparative Semitic scholarship to more than two hundred and fifty terms and concluded that much of the Qur'an's religious vocabulary had non-Arabic sources, Syriac prominent among them. Jeffery's etymologies remain a standard point of departure, though many have since been revised. But he sometimes moved from the origin of a term to claims about the communities from which the Prophet's teaching derived, and that step outruns the evidence: an etymology establishes where a word came from, not what it meant to those who heard it. Here the reconciling view proves more discerning than either its classical opponents or its modern successor. By separating a word's history from its membership in a language, it anticipates a distinction linguists now take for granted. It does not, however, simply defeat al-Shafi'i. His concern was intelligibility, and on that question the reconciling view largely concedes his point: words already Arabized were, for the Qur'an's first audience, as clear as any others.

sources.author: Arthur Jeffery
sources.title: The Foreign Vocabulary of the Qur'an
sources.note: Gaekwad's Oriental Series 79 (Baroda: Oriental Institute; reprinted by Brill, 2007): a lexicon of the Qur'an's non-Arabic vocabulary built on comparative Semitic philology, whose introduction surveys the classical Muslim debate, including al-Suyuti's al-Muhadhdhab.

sources.author: Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafi'i (trans. Majid Khadduri)
sources.title: Al-Shafi'i's Risala: Treatise on the Foundations of Islamic Jurisprudence
sources.note: The earliest surviving work of Islamic legal theory; its opening chapters on bayan and the Arabic tongue contain the denial that the Qur'an holds any non-Arabic word (paraphrased in the passage, not quoted).

sources.author: Saheeh International (trans.)
sources.title: The Qur'an: Arabic Text with Corresponding English Meanings
sources.note: Source of the passage's quotation of Qur'an 12:2, "Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an that you might understand," verified against the Sahih International text at quran.com.

passages.title: Benacerraf's dilemma
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
In "Mathematical Truth" (1973), Paul Benacerraf argued that two demands on any account of mathematics, each reasonable on its own, cannot easily be met together. The first is semantic: we want "a homogeneous semantical theory," one on which a claim about numbers has the same logical form, and is made true in the same way, as a parallel claim about cities. The second is epistemic: the account of truth must "mesh with a reasonable epistemology." The difficulty is that a uniform semantics makes mathematical sentences true in virtue of objects, such as numbers and sets, that exist outside space and time, while the causal theory of knowledge Benacerraf accepted required that knowers stand in some causal relation to what they know. Abstract objects cause nothing. Accounts that instead identify mathematical truth with provability in a formal system make knowledge easy to explain but leave it unclear why provable sentences deserve to be called true in the ordinary sense.

Platonists accept the semantics and contest the epistemology. Kurt Gödel held that, despite their remoteness from sense experience, "we do have something like a perception also of the objects of set theory," as is shown by the way the axioms force themselves upon us as true. Critics reply that an analogy with perception explains nothing until it says how a faculty could put us in contact with objects that act on nothing.

Others relocate the problem. Structuralists such as Stewart Shapiro hold that mathematics describes structures rather than freestanding objects: the number 2 is simply a position in the structure of the natural numbers. We grasp small structures by abstracting from patterns in concrete systems and reach infinite ones by describing them. Critics answer that the structures Shapiro posits exist independently of any instance and so are no less abstract than numbers were. Hartry Field, in Science Without Numbers (1980), instead denied the objects. Mathematical existence claims, on his view, are literally false; mathematics earns its place in science by being conservative, meaning that adding it to a theory of the physical world yields no conclusions about that world that could not in principle be drawn without it. He supported the claim by reformulating Newtonian gravitational theory without reference to numbers. The price is a reconstruction program not yet carried out for modern physics, and the verdict that "2 + 2 = 4" is not true.

The causal theory of knowledge that powered the original argument has since been largely abandoned, and one might conclude that the dilemma went with it. That would be too quick. Field himself later restated the challenge without the causal theory: the platonist owes an explanation of how mathematicians' beliefs could reliably track facts about objects that make no difference to them. So restated, the problem is less a refutation of platonism than a standing demand for explanation, and none of the replies fully meets it. Gödel's answer names the explanation rather than giving it; the structuralist's supplies it only for the finite; Field's comes closest only by denying that there is any mathematical truth to explain.

sources.author: Paul Benacerraf
sources.title: Mathematical Truth
sources.note: Journal of Philosophy 70: 661-679; sets out the conflict between a uniform semantics for mathematics and a causal theory of knowledge. Source of the quoted phrases "a homogeneous semantical theory" and "mesh with a reasonable epistemology" (p. 661).

sources.author: Kurt Gödel
sources.title: What Is Cantor's Continuum Problem? (revised version)
sources.note: Revised for Benacerraf and Putnam's Philosophy of Mathematics; source of the quotation "we do have something like a perception also of the objects of set theory," the classic platonist appeal to mathematical intuition.

sources.author: Hartry Field
sources.title: Science Without Numbers: A Defence of Nominalism
sources.note: Founding statement of mathematical fictionalism: argues that mathematics is dispensable and conservative, and reformulates Newtonian gravitational theory without numbers.

sources.author: Stewart Shapiro
sources.title: Philosophy of Mathematics: Structure and Ontology
sources.note: Defends ante rem structuralism, on which numbers are places in structures, and offers an epistemology of structures that begins with pattern recognition and abstraction.

passages.title: Convivencia in al-Andalus
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
Passage A

In 1948 the Spanish philologist Américo Castro gave historians a word for what he believed set Spain apart from the rest of Europe: convivencia, the "living together" of Christians, Muslims, and Jews through the centuries of the Middle Ages. For Castro, Spanish identity itself had been forged in that long proximity, out of the rivalry and mutual borrowing of three peoples he called castes. The literary historian María Rosa Menocal carried the idea to a wide readership in The Ornament of the World (2002), whose subtitle states her thesis: that Muslims, Jews, and Christians created a "culture of tolerance" in medieval Spain. Her title borrows the praise that a tenth-century German canoness, Hrotsvitha of Gandersheim, bestowed on Umayyad Córdoba.

Menocal's evidence is chiefly cultural. Under the Umayyad caliphs a Jewish physician and diplomat, Hasdai ibn Shaprut, rose to prominence at court and patronized Hebrew scholarship; Hebrew poets adopted the meters and themes of Arabic verse; and Arabic learning later passed, often through Jewish intermediaries, to translators working in Christian Toledo. Menocal does not claim that the three communities were equals or that violence was absent. Her claim is that, at its best, Andalusi culture made room for its own contradictions, and that its most enduring achievements came from people who borrowed freely across confessional lines while remaining loyal to their own faiths. The tolerance she describes is less a legal regime than a habit of cultural life, and its lesson, she suggests, is that deep religious conviction and openness to others need not be at odds.

Passage B

Critics reply that this picture rests on a selective reading of the sources. In The Myth of the Andalusian Paradise (2016), Darío Fernández-Morera argues that al-Andalus was shaped by Maliki jurists whose rulings kept Christians and Jews in a legally inferior position, and that its rulers relied on war and coercion far more than admirers acknowledge. Critics in this vein point to the massacre of Granada's Jews in 1066 as a reminder of how precarious a minority's position could be. Even Hrotsvitha's praise of Córdoba, they observe, appears in a poem celebrating a Christian youth executed at the court of Córdoba's ruler.

Other historians, less polemical, locate the difficulty in the concept of tolerance itself. Under the dhimma, the arrangement by which Islamic law protected Christian and Jewish subjects, those communities kept their worship, property, and internal courts in exchange for a special tax and restrictions meant to mark their subordinate status, terms whose enforcement varied with rulers and regions and grew harsher under the Almohads. Mark R. Cohen, comparing the Jews of Islam with those of Christendom, has argued that such an arrangement could provide considerable security precisely because it fixed each group's place in a hierarchy. This was toleration as a superior extends it to an inferior, not the equal standing the modern word implies. On this view the cultural exchange that admirers celebrate is real; what is mistaken is the inference from exchange to equality.

sources.author: María Rosa Menocal
sources.title: The Ornament of the World: How Muslims, Jews, and Christians Created a Culture of Tolerance in Medieval Spain
sources.note: The best-known modern case for a medieval Iberian culture of tolerance and exchange; the quoted phrase "culture of tolerance" is from the book's subtitle, and its title borrows Hrotsvitha of Gandersheim's praise of Córdoba (decus orbis).

sources.author: Darío Fernández-Morera
sources.title: The Myth of the Andalusian Paradise: Muslims, Christians, and Jews under Islamic Rule in Medieval Spain
sources.note: A polemical critique arguing that the tolerant al-Andalus of modern scholarship is a myth, stressing Maliki jurisprudence, the legal inferiority of dhimmis and the regime's reliance on coercion.

sources.author: Mark R. Cohen
sources.title: Under Crescent and Cross: The Jews in the Middle Ages
sources.note: Compares Jewish life under Islam and Christendom and argues that the dhimma's fixed, hierarchical place for non-Muslims helps explain the relative security of Jews in the Islamic world, rejecting both utopian myth and lachrymose countermyth.

sources.author: Kenneth Baxter Wolf
sources.title: Convivencia in Medieval Spain: A Brief History of an Idea
sources.note: Religion Compass 3/1: traces the term from Américo Castro's España en su historia (1948) to its later popular sense, tempering both romantic and hostile readings; good on how the word changed meaning.

passages.title: Hume, Miracles, and Probability
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
In "Of Miracles," the tenth section of his Enquiry concerning Human Understanding (1748), David Hume begins from an uncontroversial principle: "A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence." A miracle, he holds, is a violation of the laws of nature, and since those laws rest on uniform experience, that experience amounts to a full proof against any miracle. Hence his maxim: no testimony can establish a miracle unless "its falsehood would be more miraculous, than the fact, which it endeavours to establish." In the essay's second part he adds that no actual miracle report has met that standard.

An early probabilistic reply came from Richard Price, the dissenting minister who in 1763 had seen Thomas Bayes's essay on chance into print. In Four Dissertations (1767), Price observed that it is common for "the slightest testimony to overcome an almost infinite improbability": the antecedent odds against many particulars we accept on others' word are enormous. He also denied that past uniformity testifies against the unprecedented, since a miracle is "more properly an event different from experience than contrary to it."

John Earman's Hume's Abject Failure (2000) renews Price's case in Bayesian terms, and its title announces its verdict. Read one way, Earman argues, Hume's maxim says only that testimony makes a miracle more probable than not when the falsehood of the testimony is less probable than the miracle—true but trivial, a consequence of the probability calculus that tells us nothing about how improbable either is. Read as assigning a miracle zero probability, he continues, the maxim makes the miracle unconfirmable by any evidence, which is not weighing evidence but refusing to. Hume himself seems to resist that reading, for he grants that unanimous testimony could establish eight days of total darkness over the earth. And Earman stresses that the concurring reports of independent witnesses, each only moderately reliable, can in principle overcome any prior probability that is not zero.

Defenders of Hume such as Robert Fogelin and Peter Millican reply that this attacks a position Hume did not hold. His question, they argue, is not whether miracles occur, but whether it is reasonable to believe the reports of them we have, and his case depends on the typical reliability of the kinds of testimony that report miracles (the subject of the essay's second part) rather than on the probability of any single report.

Probability theory, I think, clarifies this dispute without settling it. Earman is right that the maxim cannot serve as an a priori refutation of every possible miracle report; the defenders are right that Hume need not be read as offering one. What Bayes's theorem shows is that the disagreement turns on quantities the calculus cannot supply: the prior probability of the event and the reliability and independence of the witnesses. A theist who regards divine action in history as antecedently credible and a naturalist who does not may both reason impeccably and reach opposite conclusions. The formalism contributes a discipline rather than a verdict: it forbids treating a prior as zero while claiming to weigh evidence, and it forbids counting dependent witnesses as independent ones.

sources.author: David Hume
sources.title: An Enquiry concerning Human Understanding, Section X: Of Miracles
sources.note: The argument itself; quotations ("A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence" and the maxim's "its falsehood would be more miraculous, than the fact, which it endeavours to establish") checked against the Enquiry's text as edited in the Early Texts corpus (section 10, paragraphs 4 and 13).

sources.author: Richard Price
sources.title: Four Dissertations
sources.note: Dissertation IV answers Hume: testimony routinely overcomes enormous prior improbability, and a miracle is different from rather than contrary to experience; both quotations as given in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on Price (D 402, D 406).

sources.author: John Earman
sources.title: Hume's Abject Failure: The Argument Against Miracles
sources.note: A Bayesian critique arguing that Hume's maxim is trivial on one reading and untenable on others, and that independent witnesses can overcome any nonzero prior; the passage quotes only the book's title phrase.

sources.author: Robert J. Fogelin
sources.title: A Defense of Hume on Miracles
sources.note: A reply to Earman and others contending that Hume's question is whether belief in reported miracles is reasonable and that Part II is integral to the argument.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Modern philology has shown that al-Shafi'i was mistaken in denying that the Qur'an contains words of foreign origin, and the classical debate has accordingly been settled in favor of his opponents.
Jeffery's study of the Qur'an's vocabulary, though once influential, has been so extensively revised that it no longer offers a reliable guide to the origins of Qur'anic terms.

The classical view that some Qur'anic words were foreign in origin but Arabic in use is more defensible than certain inferences from modern etymology, and it accommodates al-Shafi'i's central concern.
Al-Shafi'i's denial that the Qur'an contains non-Arabic words, rightly understood, is the position best supported by both classical and modern scholarship on the Qur'an's vocabulary.
Classical Muslim scholars disagreed about whether the Qur'an contains foreign words, and their disagreement was resolved only when modern scholars applied comparative philology to the question.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph carries the author's view: the reconciling view 'proves more discerning than either its classical opponents or its modern successor,' and it 'does not, however, simply defeat al-Shafi'i' but 'largely concedes his point' on intelligibility. C states both halves. A is the trap for a reader who knows Jeffery's work and assumes philology settled the matter; the author says the reconciling view does not simply defeat al-Shafi'i.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall claim about the debate over foreign words in the Qur'an.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, especially its last four sentences, where the author judges the positions laid out in paragraphs 2 and 3.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraphs 1 to 3 lay out the question and two classical positions: al-Shafi'i's denial and Abu 'Ubayd's reconciling view. Paragraph 4 adds Jeffery and then evaluates: Jeffery's etymologies are useful but one of his inferences outruns the evidence; the reconciling view is the most discerning; yet it accommodates al-Shafi'i's concern rather than refuting him. Prephrase: the reconciling view is the best position, and it leaves al-Shafi'i's real concern standing.

choices.note: Too strong and against the passage. The author says the reconciling view 'does not, however, simply defeat al-Shafi'i,' and nothing says philology settled the debate. A reader who knows the modern consensus on loanwords may pick this.
Distortion. The author calls Jeffery's etymologies 'a standard point of departure, though many have since been revised.' Revised in part is not unreliable.

CORRECT. It captures the author's preference for the reconciling view over both rivals ('more discerning than either its classical opponents or its modern successor') and the qualification that it 'largely concedes' al-Shafi'i's point about intelligibility.
Wrong position. The author defends the concern behind al-Shafi'i's denial, not the denial itself, and prefers the reconciling view.
Half right. The first clause is background; the second misdescribes the passage, which does not say philology resolved the dispute and in fact faults one of Jeffery's inferences.

questions.stem: According to the passage, al-Shafi'i held that a word in the Qur'an that a particular scholar takes to be foreign
choices: may be one that other speakers of Arabic know
must have been adopted into Arabic before the revelation
is best explained by consulting the language from which it seems to come
was used in the Qur'an in order to address listeners who were not Arabs
would be fully understood only by a prophet
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says al-Shafi'i argued that such scholars 'had mistaken the limits of their own knowledge for the limits of the language' and that 'a word unfamiliar to one scholar may be known to other Arabs.' A paraphrases that. E is the trap: the passage says no one but a prophet commands the whole language, not that each unfamiliar word is understood only by a prophet. B gives Abu 'Ubayd's view to al-Shafi'i.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage reports al-Shafi'i saying about words that seem foreign.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, the third and fourth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: This is a detail question, but the paragraph has several claims close together. Al-Shafi'i says (1) critics confuse their own ignorance with the language's limits, (2) only a prophet commands all of Arabic, (3) an unfamiliar word may be known to other Arabs, (4) a word in another language may be shared by both. The answer should restate one of these exactly, not blend them.

choices.note: CORRECT. A direct paraphrase of 'a word unfamiliar to one scholar may be known to other Arabs.'
Wrong position-holder. Adoption into Arabic before the revelation is the reconciling view the passage traces to Abu 'Ubayd in paragraph 3. Al-Shafi'i denies the words are foreign at all.
Out of scope, and close to the opposite of al-Shafi'i's view. He says the word may simply be Arabic or shared with the other language; he never recommends tracing it to another language.
Opposite. For al-Shafi'i the Qur'an's clarity depends on its being wholly in the language of its first hearers, the Arabs.

Distortion. The passage says no one but a prophet commands 'the whole of' Arabic. That is a claim about the language as a whole, not about who can understand any particular unfamiliar word, which other Arabs may know.

questions.stem: The author states that "an etymology establishes where a word came from, not what it meant to those who heard it" (fourth paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: suggest that Jeffery's etymologies are unreliable because they ignore how Arabic speakers used the words
support al-Shafi'i's claim that no word in the Qur'an has an origin outside Arabic
explain why al-Suyuti's catalogue contained fewer words than Jeffery's later study
introduce the reconciling view as a position that Jeffery had misunderstood
identify why one inference Jeffery drew from his evidence goes beyond what that evidence shows
questions.explanation: The clause follows a colon after 'that step outruns the evidence,' where 'that step' is Jeffery's move 'from the origin of a term to claims about the communities from which the Prophet's teaching derived.' The quoted clause gives the reason the step outruns the evidence, so E is right. A is the main trap: the author criticizes an inference from the etymologies, not the etymologies, which remain 'a standard point of departure.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Determine what job the quoted clause does in the fourth paragraph.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, the third and fourth sentences: what comes before the colon, and what 'that step' refers to.

breakdown.analysis: Function questions turn on what a sentence is attached to. The clause explains why 'that step outruns the evidence.' 'That step' is the move from where a word came from to where the Prophet's teaching came from. So the clause names the gap in one inference of Jeffery's. It does not attack the etymological work itself, which the author praises a sentence earlier.

choices.note: Distortion. The author calls Jeffery's etymologies 'a standard point of departure.' The criticism is aimed at a further inference, not at the etymologies.
Shell game. The clause separates origin from meaning, which actually allows that words have foreign origins; it gives no support to the claim that no Qur'anic word has an origin outside Arabic.
Out of scope. The passage gives the sizes of the two lists but never compares them or explains the difference, and the clause is not about counts.
Distortion. The reconciling view is introduced in paragraph 3, and the author compares it favorably with Jeffery but never says Jeffery misunderstood it.
CORRECT. The clause is the reason, given after the colon, that Jeffery's move from a term's origin to claims about the sources of the Prophet's teaching 'outruns the evidence.'

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Jeffery's work can most accurately be described as
choices: unqualified admiration for its method and its conclusions
respect for its etymological contribution combined with doubt about one kind of conclusion drawn from it
skepticism about its etymologies combined with acceptance of its account of the sources of the Prophet's teaching
neutral detachment, since the author reports Jeffery's findings without evaluating them
disapproval of its attempt to apply comparative philology to a sacred text
questions.explanation: The author says Jeffery's etymologies 'remain a standard point of departure,' then faults his move from word origins to claims about the sources of the Prophet's teaching: 'that step outruns the evidence.' B captures both. C reverses the two halves.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize how the author regards Jeffery's study.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, the second through fourth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Look for evaluative language. Positive: 'remain a standard point of departure.' Negative: 'he sometimes moved... and that step outruns the evidence.' So the attitude is mixed, and it is split along a particular line: the etymologies are valued, one kind of inference from them is not.

choices.note: Too extreme. The author explicitly faults one step in Jeffery's reasoning.
CORRECT. Respect ('a standard point of departure') plus a specific doubt about moving from a word's origin to the sources of the Prophet's teaching ('that step outruns the evidence').
Reversed. The author values the etymologies and doubts the claims about the sources of the Prophet's teaching, not the other way round.
Wrong. The author evaluates Jeffery directly ('outruns the evidence').

Out of scope and too extreme. The author never objects to applying philology to the Qur'an; the objection is to one inference, and the author even relies on the linguistic distinction between origin and membership.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Al-Shafi'i's position that the Qur'an contains no non-Arabic words has been refuted by Jeffery's findings.
Most of the words that al-Suyuti catalogued as foreign were in fact native Arabic words that some scholars did not recognize.
The reconciling view was a concession that classical scholars made only after philologists had established the foreign origins of Qur'anic words.
That a word entered Arabic from another language is compatible with its having been fully intelligible to the Qur'an's first audience.
The question of the Qur'an's foreign vocabulary is of interest chiefly to philologists and has little bearing on legal theory.
questions.explanation: The author endorses the reconciling view, which holds the words were 'foreign in origin' yet Arabic by the time of the Qur'an, and says 'words already Arabized were, for the Qur'an's first audience, as clear as any others.' So foreign origin and full intelligibility can go together: D. A is the trap for a reader who assumes modern loanword research settles the matter; the author says the reconciling view 'does not... simply defeat al-Shafi'i' and treats his concern as one about intelligibility.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the author's own claims support.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, the last four sentences, read alongside the reconciling view in paragraph 3.

breakdown.analysis: The author's position combines two ideas: a word's history is separate from its membership in a language, and Arabized words were clear to the first hearers. Put together: foreign origin does not prevent intelligibility. Watch for answers that turn the author's partial agreement with al-Shafi'i into either full agreement or refutation.

choices.note: Too strong, and against the author. The author grants Jeffery's etymologies but says the reconciling view 'does not, however, simply defeat al-Shafi'i,' because his concern was intelligibility. Nothing says Jeffery refuted him.
Unsupported. This applies al-Shafi'i's argument to al-Suyuti's list; the author never judges how many of those words were really native.
Wrong time. The passage traces the reconciling view to Abu 'Ubayd (d. 838), centuries before modern philology.
CORRECT. The reconciling view, which the author favors, treats the words as foreign in origin, and the author says Arabized words were 'as clear as any others' to the first audience.
Against the passage. Paragraph 2 says al-Shafi'i's 'legal theory rests on the Qur'an's bayan,' so the question did bear on legal theory.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the reconciling view as the passage describes it?
choices: A linguist holds that a term long thought to be borrowed is in fact native and merely happens to resemble a word in a neighboring language.
A legal historian holds that a foreign doctrine absorbed into domestic case law over generations is rightly called both foreign in origin and part of the domestic law.
A legal historian holds that a term coined abroad becomes part of a nation's legal vocabulary as soon as a court first uses it in a ruling, whether or not anyone had used it before.
A critic argues that because a poem's central images derive from earlier poets, the poem must express the religious outlook of those poets.
An editor holds that a text intended for a general audience should replace every borrowed term with a native equivalent so that all readers can understand it.
questions.explanation: The reconciling view says the words were foreign in origin but had been 'taken into Arabic, adapted to its forms, and used by Arabs before the revelation,' so that 'both parties were correct.' B has the same structure: foreign origin, prior absorption, both descriptions true. C is the near miss: it drops the requirement that the term be in use before the text that employs it, which is exactly what made the words Arabic 'by the time the Qur'an employed them.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the situation whose logic matches the reconciling view.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, the second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Break the view into parts: (1) the item comes from outside, (2) it was absorbed and adapted before the text in question used it, (3) so both 'foreign' and 'native' are correct descriptions, of its origin and of its status. The analogue needs all three. Expect traps that match al-Shafi'i (it was native all along), Jeffery's criticized inference (origin determines meaning), and one that keeps (1) and (3) but loses the timing in (2).

choices.note: This matches al-Shafi'i's argument that a word found in another language may simply be shared, not the reconciling view, which grants the foreign origin.
CORRECT. Foreign origin, absorption over time before the present use, and the conclusion that both descriptions are correct: the three parts of the reconciling view.

Near miss. It grants a foreign origin and native status, but makes the status arise at the moment of first use with no prior absorption. The reconciling view requires that the words had been adapted and 'used by Arabs before the revelation.'
This mirrors the inference the author criticizes in Jeffery, moving from where something came from to what it expresses.
Out of scope. The reconciling view does not recommend removing borrowed words; it holds that Arabized words were already intelligible.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that the reconciling view largely concedes al-Shafi'i's point about intelligibility?
choices: Several of Jeffery's etymologies have been rejected by later scholars, who traced the words to different languages.
Al-Shafi'i was familiar with at least one of the languages from which Qur'anic words were later said to derive.
Al-Suyuti included in al-Muhadhdhab some words that no earlier authority had identified as foreign.
Many of the words that the reconciling view treats as Arabized had changed considerably in pronunciation and form when they were first taken into Arabic.
Several words the reconciling view counts as Arabized were, at the time of the revelation, unfamiliar to most of the Qur'an's first audience.
questions.explanation: The author's claim depends on the premise that 'words already Arabized were, for the Qur'an's first audience, as clear as any others.' If some words counted as Arabized were unfamiliar to most first hearers, adoption into Arabic did not guarantee intelligibility, and the concession weakens: E. D is the trap: change in pronunciation is part of being 'adapted to its forms' and, if anything, fits the reconciling view.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most undercuts the claim that the reconciling view accommodates al-Shafi'i's concern about intelligibility.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, the last two sentences; paragraph 3 for what 'Arabized' means.

breakdown.analysis: The author's reasoning: al-Shafi'i cared about intelligibility; the reconciling view holds the words were Arabized before the revelation; Arabized words were clear to the first audience; so the view concedes his point. The weakest link is the step from 'Arabized' to 'clear to the first audience.' Attack it.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Which foreign language a word came from does not bear on whether Arabized words were intelligible to the first audience.
Irrelevant. Al-Shafi'i's own linguistic knowledge does not touch whether the first hearers understood the words.
Irrelevant to the claim. The extent of al-Suyuti's list says nothing about whether Arabized words were understood.
Opposite or irrelevant. Adaptation in form is part of what the reconciling view means by Arabization ('adapted to its forms'); it does not show the words were unclear.
CORRECT. It breaks the link between being Arabized and being clear to the first audience, which is the premise the author's claim relies on.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: argue that fictionalism, despite its costs, offers the only satisfactory resolution of a long-standing dilemma about the relation between mathematical truth and mathematical knowledge
show that a dilemma about mathematical knowledge depended on a theory of knowledge that has since been abandoned
explain why accounts that identify mathematical truth with provability are preferable to platonist accounts
present a dilemma about mathematical truth and knowledge and several responses to it, and argue that the dilemma persists in a modified form that none of those responses fully answers
defend Gödel's view of mathematical perception against the objections raised by structuralists and fictionalists
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 sets out Benacerraf's dilemma, paragraphs 2 and 3 give the platonist, structuralist and fictionalist responses, and paragraph 4 argues the dilemma survives, restated, as 'a standing demand for explanation, and none of the replies fully meets it.' D covers all of this. B is the trap: the passage raises that conclusion only to reject it ('That would be too quick').

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the purpose of the passage as a whole.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, its first three sentences, together with the structure of paragraphs 1 to 3.

breakdown.analysis: Map the passage: dilemma (P1), platonist reply and objection (P2), structuralist and fictionalist replies and objections (P3), author's verdict (P4). The verdict: the causal theory is gone but the problem survives as a demand for explanation that no reply meets. The right answer describes both the survey and the verdict.

choices.note: Too strong. The author says Field's view 'comes closest only by denying that there is any mathematical truth to explain,' which is not an endorsement.
Opposite. The author raises this conclusion and rejects it: 'That would be too quick.'
Out of scope. Provability accounts appear once in paragraph 1, with a cost noted, and are not defended.
CORRECT. It names the dilemma, the survey of responses, and the author's conclusion that the restated problem is one 'none of the replies fully meets.'
Wrong. The author says Gödel's answer 'names the explanation rather than giving it,' and the objection in paragraph 2 is from unnamed critics, not structuralists or fictionalists.

questions.stem: According to the passage, accounts that identify mathematical truth with provability in a formal system
choices: require that knowers stand in a causal relation to mathematical objects
make it easy to explain how mathematical knowledge is possible
provide the homogeneous semantics that Benacerraf sought
were defended by Gödel as an alternative to platonism
show that mathematics is conservative over theories of the physical world
questions.explanation: The last sentence of the first paragraph says such accounts 'make knowledge easy to explain but leave it unclear why provable sentences deserve to be called true in the ordinary sense.' B restates the first half. C is the reverse: these accounts give up the ordinary, uniform sense of truth.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about provability accounts.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, the last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: One sentence answers this. Provability accounts: knowledge is easy to explain; the cost is that their 'truth' may not be truth in the ordinary sense. Pick the answer that restates the first half.

choices.note: Wrong theory. The causal requirement belongs to the theory of knowledge in paragraph 1, which provability accounts are meant to sidestep.
CORRECT. 'Make knowledge easy to explain.'
Reversed. The passage says these accounts leave it unclear why provable sentences are 'true in the ordinary sense,' which is the uniform semantics they give up.
Wrong position-holder. Gödel is presented as a platonist who accepts the semantics and appeals to perception.
Shell game. Conservativeness is Field's claim about mathematics in paragraph 3, unrelated to provability accounts.

questions.stem: By saying that Gödel's answer "names the explanation rather than giving it" (last sentence of the passage), the author most probably means that Gödel's answer
choices: credits knowledge to a faculty without saying how that faculty reaches its objects
identifies the axioms of set theory that force themselves upon us but does not explain why those axioms are true
offers an explanation that is probably correct but that Gödel never proved
relies on the authority of mathematicians rather than on philosophical argument
explains how mathematical beliefs are reliable but not why they are true
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says Gödel appeals to 'something like a perception' of set-theoretic objects, and critics reply that the analogy 'explains nothing until it says how a faculty could put us in contact with objects that act on nothing.' To name the explanation without giving it is to call the source of knowledge a kind of perception without saying how it works: A. E is the trap: it says Gödel did explain reliability, which is exactly what the author denies.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Interpret the phrase in light of what the passage says about Gödel.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last sentence of paragraph 4, and paragraph 2, especially the critics' reply.

breakdown.analysis: The restated challenge asks how beliefs could reliably track facts about objects that make no difference to us. Gödel's answer: by something like perception. The critics in paragraph 2 say that analogy explains nothing until it says how the faculty makes contact. So 'names the explanation' means he labels the faculty; 'rather than giving it' means he does not say how it works.

choices.note: CORRECT. Calling the faculty 'something like a perception' names a source of knowledge; the objection is that it does not say how that faculty could 'put us in contact with' its objects.
Distortion. The passage says the axioms 'force themselves upon us as true'; the complaint is not that Gödel failed to explain their truth but that he did not explain the faculty.
Unsupported. The author does not suggest the answer is probably correct, and the issue is not proof.
Out of scope. Nothing in the passage says Gödel appealed to the authority of mathematicians.
Opposite. Explaining how beliefs are reliable is exactly what the restated challenge demands and what the author says Gödel's answer fails to supply.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the critics of Shapiro's structuralism mentioned in the third paragraph would most likely hold that
choices: structuralism gives up the uniform semantics that Benacerraf required
no one can grasp even small structures by abstracting from patterns in concrete systems
Benacerraf's epistemic difficulty arises for instance-independent structures just as it did for numbers
the number 2 cannot be a mere position in a structure, because it is a freestanding abstract object
structuralism would succeed only if it also denied, as Field does, that mathematical existence claims are literally true
questions.explanation: The critics 'answer that the structures Shapiro posits exist independently of any instance and so are no less abstract than numbers were.' The problem in paragraph 1 is that abstract objects 'cause nothing' and so seem unknowable; if structures are just as abstract, the same problem arises for them: C. B is the trap: the critics target the abstractness of the structures, and the author himself grants that structuralism 'supplies' an explanation 'for the finite.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Infer what the critics of structuralism are committed to.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, the fourth sentence; paragraph 1 for why abstractness is a problem.

breakdown.analysis: The critics say structures are 'no less abstract than numbers were.' Why does that matter? Because the original problem was that abstract objects cause nothing and so cannot be known on a causal theory. So the critics' point is that structuralism relocates the difficulty without removing it. Stay within that: they object to the abstractness, not to the account of finite structures.

choices.note: Unsupported. The critics say nothing about semantics; their complaint is about abstractness, which is an epistemic problem.
Too strong and not their point. The critics do not deny abstraction from patterns; the author even says structuralism supplies an explanation 'for the finite.'
CORRECT. Saying the structures are 'no less abstract than numbers were' amounts to saying the problem abstract objects posed for knowledge carries over to them.
Distortion. The critics do not defend numbers as freestanding objects; they claim structures are as abstract as numbers.
Out of scope. The passage does not suggest the critics favor Field's approach or any remedy at all.

questions.stem: Which one of the following statements is most strongly supported by the passage?
choices: Of the responses the passage discusses, fictionalism provides the most satisfactory account of how mathematicians come to know mathematical truths.
Field's restatement of the challenge shows that the platonist view of mathematical objects is false.
Benacerraf's original argument remains decisive in the form in which he first stated it.
Structuralism fails to explain knowledge of any mathematical structure, finite or infinite.
Abandoning the causal theory of knowledge does not by itself free platonists from having to explain the reliability of mathematical belief.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph says that concluding the dilemma vanished with the causal theory 'would be too quick,' because Field restated it without that theory: the platonist 'owes an explanation' of how beliefs could reliably track the relevant facts. That is E. A is the trap built from 'comes closest': the author says Field's view comes closest 'only by denying that there is any mathematical truth to explain,' so it offers no account of knowing mathematical truths at all.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the author's reasoning supports.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, all four sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The author's moves: (1) the causal theory is abandoned; (2) it would be too quick to think the dilemma went with it; (3) the restated challenge demands that platonists explain reliability; (4) it is a demand, not a refutation, and no reply fully meets it. Answers that turn the demand into a refutation, or 'closest' into 'satisfactory,' overreach.

choices.note: Distortion of 'comes closest.' Field 'comes closest only by denying that there is any mathematical truth to explain,' so fictionalism gives no account of knowing mathematical truths, satisfactory or not.
Too strong. The author says the restated problem is 'less a refutation of platonism than a standing demand for explanation.'
Against the passage. The original version relied on the causal theory, which 'has since been largely abandoned'; the author defends a restated version, not the original.
Too strong. The author says the structuralist explanation is supplied 'only for the finite,' which grants it for finite structures.
CORRECT. 'That would be too quick': the challenge survives without the causal theory, and 'the platonist owes an explanation' of reliability.

questions.stem: The author mentions Field's later restatement of the challenge (last paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that the problem Benacerraf raised does not depend on the theory of knowledge he originally relied on
indicate that Field eventually abandoned the fictionalism he had defended in Science Without Numbers
suggest that Field misunderstood the argument Benacerraf originally made
concede that the dilemma lost most of its force once philosophers abandoned the causal theory of knowledge it relied on
establish that fictionalism is the only response capable of meeting Benacerraf's challenge
questions.explanation: The author raises the idea that the dilemma 'went with' the causal theory, calls that 'too quick,' and then cites Field's restatement 'without the causal theory.' The restatement shows the problem survives without that theory: A. D is the opposite: it states the conclusion the restatement is used to reject.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Determine why the author brings in Field's restatement.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, the first three sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Read the sequence: the causal theory is abandoned; one might think the dilemma went with it; 'That would be too quick'; Field restated it without the causal theory. The restatement is the evidence against the 'too quick' conclusion.

choices.note: CORRECT. The restatement is offered as the reason it 'would be too quick' to think the dilemma fell with the causal theory.
Out of scope. The passage says nothing about Field abandoning fictionalism.
Unsupported. The passage presents the restatement as a reformulation, not a misreading.
Opposite. This is the conclusion the author rejects as 'too quick.'
Too strong. The author says no reply fully meets the challenge, Field's included.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the critics' objection to Gödel's position as the passage describes it?
choices: Many mathematicians report that the axioms of set theory strike them as obviously true.
Sense perception sometimes produces false beliefs about the objects it represents.
Gödel made major contributions to mathematical logic as well as to philosophy.
Every faculty known to yield reliable beliefs about a domain works through interaction with that domain's objects.
Some philosophers have described a faculty that could yield reliable beliefs about objects with which it has no causal contact of any kind.
questions.explanation: The critics say an analogy with perception 'explains nothing until it says how a faculty could put us in contact with objects that act on nothing.' If every known reliable faculty works through interaction with its objects, a faculty that reliably tracks objects that act on nothing would be unlike anything known, and the analogy loses its support: D. A is the trap: it supports Gödel's evidence that axioms 'force themselves upon us,' the opposite of what is asked.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most supports the critics' complaint about Gödel's appeal to perception.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, the second and third sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Gödel: we have something like perception of set-theoretic objects. Critics: perception-like faculties need contact with their objects, and abstract objects act on nothing, so the analogy explains nothing. To strengthen the critics, show that reliable faculties in general depend on interaction with their objects.

choices.note: Opposite. This supports Gödel's claim that the axioms 'force themselves upon us as true.'
Irrelevant. That ordinary perception sometimes errs does not bear on whether a perception-like faculty could make contact with abstract objects.
Irrelevant. Gödel's achievements do not touch the critics' point; appealing to them would be an appeal to authority.
CORRECT. If reliable faculties always work through interaction with their objects, a faculty tracking 'objects that act on nothing' has no model, which is the critics' complaint.
Opposite. A reliable faculty without causal contact, if it exists, would weaken the critics' objection, not strengthen it.

questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with
choices: explaining how Arabic learning came to be available to translators working in Christian Toledo
tracing the changes in the meaning of the term "convivencia" since Castro introduced it
comparing the treatment of Jews under Islamic rule with their treatment under Christian rule
assessing whether tolerance accurately describes interfaith relations in al-Andalus
determining whether the massacre of 1066 was typical of the policies of Andalusi rulers
questions.explanation: Passage A presents Castro's and Menocal's picture of a culture of tolerance; passage B presents critics who doubt that "tolerance" fits a legally hierarchical society. Both are about whether tolerance is the right description, as D says. C is the trap: the comparison is Cohen's, mentioned in one sentence of passage B only.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the topic both passages are mainly about.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The thesis sentences: Menocal's subtitle claim in passage A and the opening sentences of each paragraph of passage B.

breakdown.analysis: Passage A: convivencia, Menocal's 'culture of tolerance', cultural evidence, tolerance as a habit of cultural life. Passage B: critics say the picture is selective; moderates say the very concept of tolerance misleads. Common ground: is 'tolerance' an accurate description of interfaith relations in al-Andalus? Test each answer against both passages; wrong answers cover a detail found in only one.

choices.note: Toledo's translators appear in one clause of passage A as part of Menocal's evidence; passage B never mentions them. Too narrow, and one passage only.
Passage A mentions Castro's coinage, but neither passage traces the word's later changes in meaning. Out of scope (and a reader who knows the historiography might expect it).
Tempting because Cohen compares Jews of Islam and Christendom, but that is one sentence of passage B; passage A makes no such comparison. One passage only.
CORRECT. Passage A defends describing al-Andalus as a 'culture of tolerance'; passage B argues that the description is selective (paragraph 1) or that the concept itself misleads (paragraph 2).
The 1066 massacre is one example offered by critics in passage B; passage A never mentions it, and neither passage asks whether it was typical. Too narrow.

questions.stem: Menocal, as she is described in passage A, and the historians discussed in the second paragraph of passage B would both be likely to accept which one of the following statements?
choices: Members of different religious communities in al-Andalus borrowed from one another's cultural traditions.
Christians and Jews in al-Andalus enjoyed a legal standing equal to that of their Muslim neighbors.
The dhimma gave Christians and Jews in al-Andalus more security than Christian rulers gave Jews elsewhere.
The word "tolerance" can be applied to Andalusi society only in the sense that it has in modern usage.
Hrotsvitha's description of Córdoba reflects her approval of the caliphs' treatment of their Christian subjects.
questions.explanation: Passage A says Andalusi achievements came from people who "borrowed freely across confessional lines"; passage B's moderate historians grant that "the cultural exchange that admirers celebrate is real." So both accept A. C is the trap: it imports the conclusion a reader might expect from Cohen's comparison, but the passage reports only that the arrangement could provide considerable security, and Menocal says nothing about it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim both Menocal and the moderate historians would accept.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, second paragraph; passage B, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Agreement questions: look for the concession. Passage B's last sentence concedes that the cultural exchange is real and objects only to the inference from exchange to equality. Passage A's second paragraph makes exchange Menocal's central evidence. Each wrong answer is either held by only one side or by neither.

choices.note: CORRECT. Menocal: people 'borrowed freely across confessional lines'. Moderate historians: 'the cultural exchange that admirers celebrate is real.' Both accept it.
Opposite of the moderates' view (subordinate status, no 'equal standing'), and passage A says Menocal does not claim the communities were equals.

Tempting from outside knowledge of Cohen. The passage reports only that the arrangement 'could provide considerable security'; it gives no comparative result, and Menocal is not said to hold any view of the dhimma. Out of scope.
The moderates say the opposite: medieval toleration was 'not the equal standing the modern word implies'. Opposite.
Neither group addresses Hrotsvitha's attitude; the critics in passage B's first paragraph imply that her poem complicates any such reading. Out of scope.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is mentioned in passage B but not in passage A?
choices: the praise that Hrotsvitha of Gandersheim gave to Córdoba
the part played by Jewish intermediaries in passing on Arabic learning
the court of the caliphs who ruled from Córdoba
Castro's view of the origins of Spanish identity
a special tax paid by Christian and Jewish subjects
questions.explanation: Only passage B, describing the dhimma, mentions "a special tax" paid by Christian and Jewish subjects. A and C are in both passages (Hrotsvitha's praise; the caliphs' court), and B and D are in passage A only.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the item that appears in passage B and is absent from passage A.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Scan each passage for each choice; eliminate anything in both or in A only.

breakdown.analysis: Check each answer twice: is it in B? Is it absent from A? Items in both passages (Hrotsvitha, the caliph's court) are the usual trap, as are items only in A.

choices.note: In both: passage A says Menocal's title borrows Hrotsvitha's praise of Córdoba; passage B's critics discuss the same praise.
In passage A only ('often through Jewish intermediaries, to translators working in Christian Toledo').
In both: passage A has Hasdai ibn Shaprut rising 'at court' under the Umayyad caliphs; passage B mentions the youth executed 'at the caliph's court'.
In passage A only (Castro's view that Spanish identity was forged in proximity among three castes).
CORRECT. Passage B: communities kept their worship, property and courts 'in exchange for a special tax'. Passage A never mentions taxation.

questions.stem: The critics' observation about the subject of Hrotsvitha's poem (last sentence of the first paragraph of passage B) primarily serves to
choices: show that Hrotsvitha's information about life at the caliph's court in Córdoba was unreliable
suggest that a source cited by admirers comes from a context that complicates their picture
establish that Christians living under the caliphs were routinely executed for their faith
argue that Menocal mistranslated the Latin phrase from which her book takes its title
illustrate one of the restrictions that marked the subordinate status of Christian subjects
questions.explanation: Menocal's title borrows Hrotsvitha's praise; the critics note that the praise sits in a poem celebrating a Christian youth executed at the court of Córdoba's ruler. The point is that the very source admirers invoke comes from a context of persecution, which complicates the picture, as B says. D tempts readers who know the scholarly debate over what Hrotsvitha's phrase meant, but the passage says nothing about translation.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the critics mention what Hrotsvitha's poem is about.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, last sentence of paragraph 1 (Menocal's title borrows Hrotsvitha's praise); passage B, last sentence of paragraph 1.

breakdown.analysis: Function questions ask what a detail does in the argument. The paragraph's claim is that the tolerant picture 'rests on a selective reading of the sources'. 'Even' signals that this is the most pointed example: the praise admirers cite comes from a poem about a martyrdom. Prephrase: it turns the admirers' own source against them.

choices.note: The critics do not question the accuracy of Hrotsvitha's information; they question what her praise can be taken to show. Distortion.
CORRECT. The praise is the source of Menocal's title (passage A); 'Even' marks it as a case where the admirers' own source, read in context, cuts against their picture of a selective reading.
One execution is cited; nothing in the passage supports 'routinely'. Too strong.
Tempting for readers who know the scholarship on Hrotsvitha's phrase, but the passage never raises translation. Outside knowledge, out of scope.

Shell game: restrictions marking subordinate status come up in the second paragraph under the dhimma; an execution is not presented as one of those legal terms, and the first paragraph's point is about the sources.

questions.stem: By "toleration as a superior extends it to an inferior" (fourth sentence of the second paragraph of passage B), the author most probably means a toleration that
choices: was granted only by rulers who personally favored the religious minorities in their realms
was offered reluctantly and withdrawn whenever it ceased to serve the rulers' interests
let subject communities live and worship within a ranked order that denied them equality
required minority communities to give up their own internal courts in return for legal protection
was later extended by Christian rulers to the Muslims living in the territories they conquered
questions.explanation: The sentence sums up the dhimma just described: protection of worship, property and courts, in exchange for a tax and restrictions marking subordinate status, giving each group a fixed "place in a hierarchy" and "not the equal standing the modern word implies." That is C. B is the trap: it sounds like a skeptical gloss but contradicts the claim that the arrangement could provide "considerable security."

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Paraphrase the phrase as the passage uses it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The two sentences before it (the dhimma and Cohen's hierarchy argument) and the contrast at the end of the same sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Meaning-in-context: use the surrounding sentences, not the phrase's everyday connotations. 'Superior' and 'inferior' pick up 'subordinate status' and 'hierarchy'; the contrast is with 'equal standing'. The phrase is descriptive, not a charge of bad faith.

choices.note: Nothing ties the toleration to rulers' personal sympathies; it was a legal arrangement. Out of scope.
Tempting because 'superior' sounds grudging, but the passage says the arrangement 'could provide considerable security'. Distortion.
CORRECT. Protected worship within a fixed 'place in a hierarchy', 'not the equal standing the modern word implies'.
Contradicts the passage: the communities kept their 'internal courts'.
The passage never discusses Christian rulers' treatment of Muslims. Out of scope.

questions.stem: Based on passage A, which one of the following most accurately describes how Menocal's position is related to the inference criticized in the last sentence of passage B?
