choices.note: Opposite. Latin precedents strengthen the opponents' point that 'medieval Latin verse' supplies native sources for fin'amor.
CORRECT. It answers the objection that no early troubadour is known to have read Arabic, and it shows actual contact with Andalusian poetry, not mere possibility.
If anything this weakens A's case by suggesting limited circulation of the treatise; it does nothing to show transmission to France.
More parallels. Passage B already grants that 'The parallels are real' and argues that parallels alone can't decide the question, so this leaves the objection untouched.
Opposite. Conventions without Andalusian counterparts make the resemblance less complete and so weaken passage A's position.

questions.stem: The author of passage B would most likely characterize the Arabist thesis as
choices: an explanation undermined by the absence of any genuine resemblance between the two traditions
a hypothesis that has been confirmed by the evidence of contact after the siege of Barbastro
a theory whose defenders have mistaken Latin sources for Arabic ones
a claim less plausible than the rival view that the troubadours devised their conventions without any outside model
a position still open, though not established by the resemblances its defenders cite
questions.explanation: Passage B's author says 'None of this refutes the Arabist case' and that the resemblances 'cannot by themselves decide between borrowing and independent invention.' Open, but not established by parallels alone: E. D is the near-miss: it ranks independent invention above borrowing, but the author declines to decide between them.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pin down the passage B author's own stance on the Arabist thesis.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, second paragraph, first two and last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Separate the author from the opponents. The opponents give objections; the author concludes that the objections don't refute the thesis but that the parallels can't decide the matter alone. Prephrase: not proven, not disproven. Reject anything that tips the balance either way.

choices.note: Contradicts the author, who says 'The parallels are real.'
Distortion. The Barbastro captives are cited as contact that shows 'at most that transmission was possible,' and even that report is hedged ('reportedly').
Out of scope. The opponents say Latin verse offers native sources; no one says the Arabists confused Latin with Arabic sources.
Too strong. The author says the resemblances 'cannot by themselves decide between borrowing and independent invention,' so neither is ranked above the other.
CORRECT. 'None of this refutes the Arabist case' (still open) plus resemblances 'cannot by themselves decide' (not established by the evidence its proponents chiefly cite).

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Stern's publication of Romance kharjas in 1948 showed that a popular Romance lyric existed in al-Andalus before the troubadours.
Jones and Hitchcock have shown that the kharjas were composed by the Arabic and Hebrew poets themselves rather than quoted from popular songs.
Doubts about the kharjas' texts weaken the case for an older Romance lyric without showing that the poets invented the kharjas.
The muwashshah differs from the classical qasida chiefly in closing with a kharja in colloquial Arabic or Romance.
Because the scripts of the kharjas omit vowels, no reading of a kharja can be trusted, and the debate over their origin is idle.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph states the author's view: 'Both sides, I think, claim more than the evidence allows.' The skeptics have undercut a lost tradition built on reconstructed texts, but 'showing that readings are uncertain is not showing that the poets invented the kharjas.' C states both halves. B is the trap: it is the skeptics' strongest conclusion, which the author says has not been shown.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall conclusion.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last paragraph, first three sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Map: P1 the form and the kharja; P2 Stern's discovery and the Romance-lyric thesis; P3 the textual problem, Jones and Hitchcock; P4 the author: both sides overclaim; the kharjas show vernacular speech in learned poems, not whether that speech had songs of its own. The answer must be qualified in both directions.

choices.note: Wrong position-holder. This is what the Romance philologists took the discovery to show; the author says the thesis 'built a lost tradition on texts whose wording is often reconstructed.'
Too strong, and the author denies it: 'showing that readings are uncertain is not showing that the poets invented the kharjas.'
CORRECT. It keeps the author's two-sided verdict: the Romance thesis claims too much, and so does the conclusion that the poets invented the kharjas.
A true detail from the first paragraph, but the passage is about the debate over the kharjas, not a comparison of forms.
Too extreme. The author draws a 'modest and still remarkable' conclusion from the kharjas, which would be impossible if no reading could be trusted.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which one of the following is true of the qufl in a muwashshah?
choices: Its rhyme recurs unchanged throughout the poem.
It is built of the units called aghsan.
Its rhyme changes from one strophe to the next.
It is always in the colloquial Arabic of the poem's audience.
It precedes the bayt within each strophe.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says the qufl, 'built of asmat ("strings"), keeps one rhyme throughout the poem.' That is A. B and C describe the bayt, the other half of the strophe, a classic swap; D attaches what is said of the last qufl, the kharja, to every qufl.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about the qufl.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph, third and fourth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The passage contrasts two halves of each strophe: bayt = aghsan, rhyme changes; qufl = asmat, one rhyme for the whole poem. The last qufl is the kharja. Read carefully: the traps swap the two halves or generalize from the kharja.

choices.note: CORRECT. The qufl 'keeps one rhyme throughout the poem.'
Swap. The bayt is 'built of units called aghsan'; the qufl is built of asmat.
Swap. It is the bayt that 'changes its rhyme from strophe to strophe.'
Shell game. Only the last qufl, the kharja, 'may abandon the classical language,' and even then it may be in Romance; the body of the poem is in literary Arabic.
The passage never says which part comes first within a strophe.

questions.stem: The author mentions Ibn Sana' al-Mulk's advice in the last paragraph primarily in order to
choices: confirm the Romance philologists' view that the kharjas were quoted from popular songs
show that muwashshah poets regarded the kharja as the least important part of the poem
explain why many kharjas are in colloquial Arabic rather than in Romance
support the claim that one conclusion drawn by the skeptics goes beyond their evidence
cast doubt on Jones's finding that the published texts were not accurate transcriptions
questions.explanation: The advice that 'it was better to borrow a good kharja than to compose a weak one' 'presupposes that kharjas could come from elsewhere,' which counts against the skeptics' conclusion that the kharjas are 'the poets' own compositions.' So it supports D. A is the trap the author blocks directly: 'if not necessarily from popular song.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the author brings up Ibn Sana' al-Mulk in the last paragraph.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last paragraph, third sentence; first paragraph, last sentence; third paragraph, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The sentence pairs two points against the skeptics: uncertain readings don't prove invention, and Ibn Sana' al-Mulk assumes kharjas could be borrowed. But the author hedges: borrowed from somewhere, 'if not necessarily from popular song.' So the advice limits the skeptics without vindicating the Romance thesis.

choices.note: The author explicitly stops short of this: kharjas could come from elsewhere, 'if not necessarily from popular song.'
Opposite. Ibn Sana' al-Mulk taught that poets 'composed the poem out of the kharja,' which makes it central.
Out of scope. The advice concerns borrowing, not the choice between colloquial Arabic and Romance.
CORRECT. Some skeptics concluded the kharjas are the poets' own compositions; advice that presupposes borrowing shows that conclusion outruns the evidence of uncertain readings.
Irrelevant. The advice has no bearing on whether García Gómez's printed texts matched the manuscripts.

questions.stem: Jones's remark quoted in the third paragraph most strongly suggests that, before his examination of the manuscripts, scholars of the kharjas had generally
choices: rejected most of García Gómez's Romance readings as implausible
doubted some of García Gómez's readings but trusted the texts he printed
checked García Gómez's transcriptions against facsimiles of the manuscripts
regarded the kharjas in Hebrew poems as more reliable than those in Arabic poems
concluded that the supposedly Romance kharjas were in fact colloquial Arabic
questions.explanation: Jones says 'some' of García Gómez's readings 'had raised doubts' but that 'it does not appear to have crossed anyone's mind that the transcriptions he printed might not be accurate.' Scholars doubted some interpretations but trusted the printed texts: B. A overstates 'some' as 'most.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Infer what Jones's remark implies about earlier scholarship.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, third sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Two layers: readings (how the letters are interpreted as Romance) and transcriptions (what the manuscript letters are). Earlier scholars doubted some readings but never questioned the transcriptions. The answer should keep that distinction and the word 'some.'

choices.note: Too strong. Jones says 'some' of the readings raised doubts, not that most were rejected.
CORRECT. Doubts about 'some' readings, but no one thought 'the transcriptions he printed might not be accurate.'
Opposite. If they had checked against the manuscripts, the possibility of inaccurate transcriptions would have crossed their minds.
Out of scope. The remark concerns the Arabic series and García Gómez; it makes no comparison with the Hebrew kharjas.
Wrong position-holder. That is Hitchcock's later contention, not the general view before Jones.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the view that the kharjas preserve fragments of an older Romance lyric can most accurately be described as
choices: firm conviction that the view has been decisively refuted
qualified endorsement of the view's central claim
dismissiveness toward the evidence on which the view was first based
confidence that the view will be vindicated by better editions
doubt that the kharjas can establish the view, without rejecting it
questions.explanation: The author says the skeptics 'have shown that the Romance thesis built a lost tradition on texts whose wording is often reconstructed,' but ends: 'Whether that speech already had songs of its own, the kharjas alone cannot tell us.' The view is unproven, not refuted: E. A is the trap for readers who stop at the skeptics' success; the author also says the skeptics claim too much.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize the author's view of the Romance-lyric thesis.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last paragraph, all sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The author's verdict: 'Both sides... claim more than the evidence allows.' Against the Romance thesis: it rests on reconstructed texts. But the final sentence leaves the existence of Romance songs open. Prephrase: skeptical about the evidence, agnostic about the conclusion.

choices.note: Too extreme. The final sentence leaves open whether Romance speech 'already had songs of its own.'
Too positive. The author says the thesis claims more than the evidence allows.
Distortion. The author calls what the kharjas establish 'remarkable' and doubts only how far they reach, not the evidence's value.
Out of scope. The author never predicts that better editions will vindicate the thesis.
CORRECT. The kharjas 'alone cannot tell us' whether such songs existed: doubt that they establish the view, without denying it.

questions.stem: Which one of the following discoveries would bear most directly on the question that, according to the author, the kharjas alone cannot answer?
choices: an independent, datable record of Romance-speaking women in al-Andalus singing love songs of their own
a better manuscript of an Arabic muwashshah that confirms, letter by letter, García Gómez's Romance reading of its kharja
a treatise by another Andalusian theorist that, like Ibn Sana' al-Mulk's, recommends borrowing a good kharja
a Hebrew muwashshah whose kharja is in colloquial Arabic rather than in Romance
evidence that the audiences of Andalusian muwashshahs included many speakers of Romance
questions.explanation: The unanswered question is 'Whether that speech already had songs of its own.' Only an independent record of Romance-speaking women singing their own songs bears directly on it: A. B is the strong trap: confirming a Romance reading shows a kharja is in Romance, which the author already grants is possible, but not that a Romance song tradition stood behind it. E restates what the author says the kharjas already establish.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify the open question and pick the discovery that addresses it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last paragraph, last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The author separates what the kharjas show (vernacular speech in learned poems, heard by mixed audiences) from what they can't show (whether that speech had its own songs). The right discovery must come from outside the kharjas and concern Romance song itself. Better readings or more theory about borrowing stay inside the kharjas.

choices.note: CORRECT. It is independent of the muwashshahs and directly concerns whether Romance speech 'already had songs of its own.'
Tempting, but a secure Romance reading shows only that a kharja is in Romance. It still could be the poet's own composition, so the question of an older song tradition stays open.
Borrowing could be from other poets, as the author notes ('if not necessarily from popular song'), so another such treatise doesn't touch the question.
Irrelevant. A kharja in Arabic tells us nothing about Romance songs.
Shell game. The author already takes it as established that audiences were expected to hear 'the Romance-speaking household'; this adds nothing on the open question.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken Hitchcock's position as the passage describes it?
choices: Many kharjas in Arabic muwashshahs are written entirely in colloquial Arabic and contain no Romance words at all.
The scripts in which the kharjas were copied omit vowels even in poems composed in literary Arabic.
Read in facsimile without emendation, most supposedly Romance kharjas show Romance grammar that cannot be construed as Arabic.
Some kharjas in Hebrew muwashshahs contain Arabic words such as habib alongside Romance ones.
García Gómez's readings of the Arabic series depend on considerably more emendations than Stern's readings of the Hebrew series do.
questions.explanation: Hitchcock contends that 'many supposedly Romance kharjas are better read as a highly colloquial Arabic marked by Romance influence.' If unemended manuscript texts show Romance grammar that cannot be read as Arabic, that reading fails: C. D is the trap: mixed Arabic and Romance wording fits Hitchcock's picture of Arabic with Romance influence as well as the Romance thesis.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most undercuts Hitchcock's reading of the kharjas.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Hitchcock's claim is about the language of the supposedly Romance kharjas: colloquial Arabic with Romance influence. To weaken it, show that the texts, read without emendation, are genuinely Romance and not construable as Arabic. Facts about other kharjas or about emendation counts elsewhere miss the claim.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Kharjas already in colloquial Arabic are not the 'supposedly Romance' ones Hitchcock reinterprets; if anything they show the register he proposes was available.
Irrelevant. A general feature of the scripts doesn't favor one reading of the Romance kharjas over another.
CORRECT. Unemended texts whose grammar is Romance and cannot be construed as Arabic contradict the claim that they are better read as colloquial Arabic.
Consistent with Hitchcock: Arabic words mixed with Romance fit his 'colloquial Arabic marked by Romance influence' as well as the opposing view.
Compares two editors' methods; it says nothing about whether the Romance kharjas are really colloquial Arabic.

sections.title: Reading Through Ideas 9: Poems of the Ruined Place · Al-Jurjani and the Grammar of Eloquence · The Rose, the Nightingale, and Originality · FitzGerald's Rubaiyat and Its Persians

passages.title: Poems of the Ruined Place
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Passage A

The classical Arabic ode, the qasida, customarily opens with a nasib, an elegiac prelude, and the nasib very often opens at the atlal, the traces of an abandoned desert encampment. The most famous instance begins the Mu'allaqa of the sixth-century poet Imru' al-Qays with the words qifa nabki, "stop, let us weep." The verb is a dual imperative, addressed to two companions, and the halt it commands, the wuquf, became the scene's defining gesture. The poet names the site exactly, between al-Dakhul and Hawmal, observes that the winds have not yet effaced its traces, and weeps at the memory of a beloved and of a dwelling. Other poets likened such traces to the remains of a tattoo or to faded writing.

Jaroslav Stetkevych has argued that the nasib is best understood as a poetics of nostalgia, and the argument is persuasive. The abandoned camp is not chiefly an emblem of decay; it is the place where memory begins, where a particular woman, a season of union and a precisely named landscape are recovered in the act of mourning them. That is why the convention could outlive the desert. In Abbasid Baghdad, Abu Nuwas mocked poets who halted at ruins and asked instead after the tavern, yet his parody kept the old frame. Mystical poets turned the encampment into a station of the soul's longing for God, and in the twentieth century a poem titled al-Atlal, sung by Umm Kulthum, could name the ruins of a love affair. In each case the ruin matters for what it makes the poet remember.

Passage B

The Old English elegies survive in the Exeter Book, a manuscript copied in the later tenth century. In The Wanderer, a solitary exile who has lost his lord and companions surveys walls where the old work of giants stands empty, and then asks: Hwaer cwom mearg? Hwaer cwom mago? (literally, "Where has the horse gone? Where the young man?"). The questions follow the ubi sunt formula, from the Latin "where are they who were before us?", which Old English writers knew from Latin homiletic prose. The poem's answer is that here wealth, friends, men and kin are all laene, lent and fleeting, and it closes by declaring it well for one who seeks mercy from the Father in heaven, where all our stability stands. The Ruin, by contrast, has no speaker who mourns and no ubi sunt questions; it marvels at the masonry of a fallen city, perhaps Roman Bath, whose walls, it says, wyrd, or fate (the ancestor of our word weird), has broken.

Some earlier critics treated the Christian close of The Wanderer as a late addition to a pagan lament. Yet the poem's ruins are never anyone's in particular: the walls go unnamed, and the horse and the young man are types rather than remembered individuals. Such anonymity is the point. The ruin in these poems is evidence for a general truth, that everything under heaven is transitory, and the lament over it is completed only by turning toward what does not decay. Even The Ruin, which makes no such turn, offers its fallen city as an example of what fate does to all human work.

sources.author: Jaroslav Stetkevych
sources.title: The Zephyrs of Najd: The Poetics of Nostalgia in the Classical Arabic Nasib
sources.note: A comparatist study (University of Chicago Press) that reads the nasib's abandoned campsite as a site of nostalgia for lost places of bliss, and follows the motif into mystical poetry and the Najd-Arcadia comparison. Passage A's 'qifa nabki' ('stop, let us weep') is the opening phrase of Imru' al-Qays's Mu'allaqa in its standard literal gloss, not a particular translator's wording.

sources.author: Philip F. Kennedy
sources.title: The Wine Song in Classical Arabic Poetry: Abu Nuwas and the Literary Tradition
sources.note: The standard English study of Abu Nuwas's wine poetry, including his parodic rejection of the atlal in favor of the tavern.

sources.author: Anne L. Klinck
sources.title: The Old English Elegies: A Critical Edition and Genre Study
sources.note: Edition of the nine Exeter Book elegies, including The Wanderer and The Ruin, with a study of the genre. The Old English quoted in passage B is the standard text of these lines, as printed in editions such as this one, and was checked against online editions (The Wanderer 92: 'Hwaer cwom mearg? Hwaer cwom mago?', with the line's standard glosses mearg 'horse' and mago 'young man'; The Ruin's 'wyrde gebraecon', 'fates broke [it]'; The Wanderer 115, 'thaer us eal seo faestnung stondeth').

sources.author: J. E. Cross
sources.title: 'Ubi Sunt' Passages in Old English: Sources and Relationships
sources.note: Published in the Lund Vetenskaps-Societetens Arsbok; it traces Old English ubi sunt passages to their Latin homiletic sources.

passages.title: Al-Jurjani and the Grammar of Eloquence
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
In the eleventh century, Arabic critics had long disputed whether excellence in speech lies in its wording or in its meaning. Al-Jahiz had famously held that meanings lie in the road, known to Arab and non-Arab, villager and Bedouin alike, so that the poet's merit lies in wording and craft. The question mattered to theologians as well, because the Qur'an challenges its hearers to produce anything like it; if its inimitability (i'jaz) is linguistic, one must say where in the language it resides. 'Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani (d. 1078 or 1081) answered, in Dala'il al-I'jaz, that both parties had looked in the wrong place.

Single words, he argued, are not ranked as bare words: the same word that delights in one verse burdens another, as al-akhda', a sinew of the neck, pleases in a line of al-Buhturi and grates in a line of Abu Tammam. Nor does merit lie in a bare idea that any paraphrase could carry. It lies in nazm, construction (literally, the stringing of pearls on a thread): "laysa al-nazmu illa an tada'a kalamaka al-wad'a alladhi yaqtadihi 'ilmu al-nahw" (construction is nothing but placing your speech in the position the science of grammar requires). By grammar he meant not rules of correctness but the meanings that syntactic choices carry: "Zayd muntaliq" and "al-muntaliq Zayd" differ in what they assert. Readers who credited the power of the Qur'anic "wa-shta'ala al-ra'su shayban" ("and the head blazes with white hair") to its metaphor alone, he observed, overlooked its construction: the verb belongs in meaning to the white hair but is attached in form to the head, which conveys that whiteness has spread through all of it, as "the white hair of the head blazes" does not. The order of sounds within a word is arbitrary, he added; the order of words follows the order of meanings in the mind.

Modern readers have found much here that sounds familiar. Kamal Abu-Deeb, who had earlier applied structural analysis to pre-Islamic poetry, set al-Jurjani in conversation with modern Western linguistics and criticism in Al-Jurjani's Theory of Poetic Imagery (1979), and others have compared his view that a word's value depends on its relations to Saussure's account of the linguistic sign. A reader of the New Critics may hear in his refusal to locate merit in paraphrasable content an anticipation of what Cleanth Brooks called the heresy of paraphrase.

These resemblances are real, but Margaret Larkin was right to read al-Jurjani within the theological and linguistic debates of his own century. Saussure's relations belong to an impersonal system; al-Jurjani's belong to an utterance shaped by a speaker's intended meanings. And his comparisons of formulations served an end no structuralist would share: to show why one construction is superior to another, and ultimately why the Qur'an's construction exceeds what human speakers can match. To call him a structuralist before his time is to keep his method while discarding the question it was built to answer.

sources.author: 'Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani
sources.title: Dala'il al-I'jaz, ed. Mahmud Muhammad Shakir (Cairo: Maktabat al-Khanji)
sources.note: The primary text. The quoted definition ('laysa al-nazmu illa an tada'a kalamaka al-wad'a alladhi yaqtadihi 'ilmu al-nahw') and the analyses of 'Zayd muntaliq', al-akhda', Qur'an 19:4, al-Jahiz's dictum and the order of sounds versus words were checked against the Arabic text (OpenITI, Shamela 22664); the English rendering is literal.

sources.author: Kamal Abu-Deeb
sources.title: Al-Jurjani's Theory of Poetic Imagery
sources.note: Approaches to Arabic Literature 1 (Warminster: Aris & Phillips); the major English study of al-Jurjani's poetics, which brings his thought into conversation with modern Western linguistics and criticism. Abu-Deeb's earlier article 'Towards a Structural Analysis of Pre-Islamic Poetry' appeared in IJMES in 1975.

sources.author: Margaret Larkin
sources.title: The Theology of Meaning: 'Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani's Theory of Discourse
sources.note: American Oriental Series 79; it reads al-Jurjani's theory of nazm within eleventh-century theological (kalam) and linguistic debates over the Qur'an's inimitability, resisting readings that detach him from that context.

passages.title: The Rose, the Nightingale, and Originality
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Few images in Persian lyric poetry are more persistent than the pairing of the rose (gul) and the nightingale (bulbul). Its elements are fixed: the bird sings its longing through the brief season of bloom; the rose, perfect and proud, answers with indifference; and the thorn wounds whoever reaches for it. A poet could summon the whole drama merely by announcing its season, as Hafiz does in a line Gertrude Bell rendered as "The rose has flushed red, the bud has burst." Annemarie Schimmel, in her studies of the imagery of Persian poetry, showed that the pair works on several levels at once. It is lover and beloved, but in mystical verse the nightingale can also be the soul and the rose the divine beauty it glimpses in the world. In Attar's Conference of the Birds, the nightingale declines the journey to the Simurgh, the king the birds seek, because love of the rose is enough for it; the hoopoe replies that the rose's beauty is brief and that the rose returns none of its love.

The nightingale of English Romanticism seems to belong to a different order. In 1819 a nightingale nesting near the house where John Keats lodged in Hampstead became the occasion for his "Ode to a Nightingale," a poem less about the bird than about the experience of hearing it: the listener's numbness, his wish to fade with the song into the forest, his longing to share the happiness of a creature untouched by mortality. "Thou wast not born for death, immortal Bird!" he exclaims, and the poem ends on a question about his own state: "Do I wake or sleep?" Readers have often drawn the contrast sharply: the Persian poet manipulates a shared code, while the Romantic poet records an experience no one else has had. Some European literary historians turned the contrast into a verdict, dismissing much later Persian poetry as merely derivative.

The contrast is real, but it is misdrawn if it implies that convention excludes originality. Paul Losensky's study of the later Persian ghazal shows that poets routinely composed replies to predecessors' poems, keeping their meter and rhyme, and that individuality was measured in what a poet did within that shared frame. Originality, on this view, is a relation to precedent rather than an escape from it. Nor was the Romantic bird as unprecedented as it appears. Coleridge's "The Nightingale" had argued with the melancholy bird of literary tradition before Keats wrote, and Keats's ode itself is thick with inherited material, from Ruth "amid the alien corn" to the classical fountain of the Muses.

What differs, then, is less the presence of convention than its acknowledgment. The Persian poet displays mastery by turning a known image so that readers who know it notice the turn; the Romantic poet must make an inherited image seem to rise from his own experience. Something of the older contrast survives even so. The Persian rose carries meanings settled before any poem begins, while Keats's bird means only what his poem makes it mean.

sources.author: Annemarie Schimmel
sources.title: A Two-Colored Brocade: The Imagery of Persian Poetry
sources.note: Schimmel's survey of the stock images of Persian, Ottoman and Indo-Muslim poetry, including the rose, the nightingale and the garden, and of how each image works at once on worldly and mystical levels.

sources.author: Paul E. Losensky
sources.title: Welcoming Fighani: Imitation and Poetic Individuality in the Safavid-Mughal Ghazal
sources.note: Argues that poetic imitation, including 'reply' poems in a predecessor's meter and rhyme, was the medium in which later Persian poets asserted individuality, against older histories that dismissed the period as derivative.

sources.author: Hafiz (trans. Gertrude Lowthian Bell)
sources.title: Poems from the Divan of Hafiz
sources.note: Bell's verse translation; the quoted line 'The rose has flushed red, the bud has burst' opens poem VIII of the collection.

sources.author: John Keats
sources.title: Ode to a Nightingale
sources.note: Composed in May 1819 at Hampstead and first printed in the Annals of the Fine Arts that July; source of the quoted lines 'Thou wast not born for death, immortal Bird!', 'Do I wake or sleep?' and 'amid the alien corn'.

passages.title: FitzGerald's Rubaiyat and Its Persians
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
In 1859 the London bookseller Bernard Quaritch published, without the translator's name, a pamphlet of seventy-five quatrains titled Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám, the Astronomer-Poet of Persia. It did not sell, and its remaining copies were eventually offered for a penny. In 1861 a copy reached Dante Gabriel Rossetti, who passed it to Swinburne, and within a few decades Edward FitzGerald's poem had become one of the most quoted in English. Its stanza is the Persian ruba'i, a self-contained quatrain in which the first, second, and fourth lines rhyme and the third usually does not, so that the last line, returning to the rhyme, delivers the poem's turn. FitzGerald kept the scheme in iambic pentameter: "The Moving Finger writes; and, having writ, / Moves on: nor all thy Piety nor Wit / Shall lure it back to cancel half a Line, / Nor all thy Tears wash out a Word of it."

Yet what FitzGerald was translating is less certain than it appears. Omar Khayyam, who died around 1131, was remembered by his contemporaries as a mathematician and astronomer; quatrains are attributed to him only in sources written decades after his death, and later manuscripts credit him with hundreds. In 1897 the Russian scholar Valentin Zhukovsky identified "wandering quatrains," poems ascribed to Khayyam in some manuscripts and to other poets in others, and later scholars such as Ali Dashti tried to recover a small core of authentic poems by testing each against what can be known of the man. The manuscripts FitzGerald worked from, supplied by his friend and teacher E. B. Cowell, already represented an accumulated tradition rather than a single author.

FitzGerald, moreover, did not translate quatrain by quatrain. He fused some poems, added stanzas with no clear Persian source, and arranged the whole into a sequence that moves from dawn to nightfall. In an 1857 letter to Cowell he wrote, "It is an amusement to me to take what Liberties I like with these Persians," who, he added, "really do want a little Art to shape them." Readers have since divided over what he produced. Some treat it as a translation, unusually free but largely traceable to Persian originals; others, such as the editor Daniel Karlin, read it as an English poem, attending to its many affiliations with English, classical, and biblical literature; and critics of Orientalism see in that letter's condescension an appropriation that remade a Persian poet to suit Victorian taste.

Each verdict captures something, but none is adequate alone. The charge of appropriation is strongest when directed at the letter and weakest when directed at the poem's effects, since it was largely through FitzGerald that English readers came to know Khayyam at all. And the problem of authenticity complicates any simple opposition between a faithful original and its English distortion: the Khayyam FitzGerald reshaped was already a composite that generations of copyists had enlarged. In that sense FitzGerald became one more contributor to a wandering tradition, though, unlike those copyists, he worked from outside it and from a position of cultural power they did not share.

sources.author: Edward FitzGerald
sources.title: Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám, the Astronomer-Poet of Persia
sources.note: The first edition (Quaritch, 250 copies, 75 quatrains, anonymous); the quoted 'Moving Finger' stanza is quatrain LI of this edition.

sources.author: André Lefevere (ed.)
sources.title: Translation/History/Culture: A Sourcebook
sources.note: Collects statements on translation as rewriting shaped by ideology and poetics, including FitzGerald's 1857 letter to E. B. Cowell, source of the quoted 'It is an amusement to me to take what Liberties I like with these Persians' and 'really do want a little Art to shape them'.

sources.author: Ali Dashti (trans. L. P. Elwell-Sutton)
sources.title: In Search of Omar Khayyam
sources.note: Dashti reconstructs Khayyam's character from reliable sources and uses it to sift the attributed quatrains down to a core of roughly a hundred he judges consistent with the man.

sources.author: Daniel Karlin (ed.)
sources.title: Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám (Oxford World's Classics)
sources.note: Karlin's edition and introduction document FitzGerald's treatment of his Persian sources and the poem's affiliations with English, classical and biblical literature.

questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with
choices: explaining how poets writing in two different languages came to share a single convention for lamenting ruined places
describing how a poetic tradition treats ruined places and arguing for a particular view of what those ruins signify
tracing the history of a poetic convention from its earliest surviving instance to its uses in the twentieth century
defending a religious reading of poems that some earlier critics had interpreted as essentially secular laments
contrasting poems that name the places they describe with poems that leave those places deliberately unnamed
questions.explanation: Each passage introduces a tradition's ruin poetry (the atlal in A, the Exeter Book elegies in B) and then argues for what the ruin means: for A, 'what it makes the poet remember'; for B, 'evidence for a general truth.' B fits both. C and D each describe only one passage, and E is a contrast a reader draws between the passages, not what either one is about.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the purpose the two passages share, stated generally enough to fit both.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first paragraph of each passage (the description) and the last sentences of each (the claim about meaning).

breakdown.analysis: Map A: P1 describes the atlal opening of the qasida; P2 endorses Stetkevych's nostalgia reading and traces later transformations. Map B: P1 describes The Wanderer and The Ruin; P2 rejects the interpolation view and argues that the ruin stands for universal transience. Both describe, then interpret. Prephrase: each describes one tradition's ruin poems and argues for what the ruin means. Eliminate any choice that fits only one passage.

choices.note: Out of scope. Neither passage claims the two traditions borrowed from each other or share an origin. Passage B mentions Latin borrowing, but Latin is not Arabic.

CORRECT. Both passages describe a tradition's ruin poems and then argue for a meaning: A's last sentence says the ruin 'matters for what it makes the poet remember'; B says the ruin 'is evidence for a general truth.'
Half right, passage A only. A follows the atlal down to Umm Kulthum, but B traces no history beyond noting the Latin source of a formula.
Passage B only. Only B mentions the earlier critics and the Christian close; A argues against reading the atlal as chiefly about decay, which has nothing to do with a religious reading.
Shell game. Named places (A) and unnamed ruins (B) are details a reader can contrast across the passages, but neither passage is about that contrast; each discusses only one kind of poem.

questions.stem: The author of passage A mentions Abu Nuwas's mockery of poets who halted at ruins (second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that the atlal convention was abandoned once Arabic poetry moved from the desert to the cities of the caliphate
illustrate a contrast between pre-Islamic and Abbasid attitudes toward the value of nostalgia
suggest that the convention had always contained an element of irony that later poets made explicit
give an instance in which even a rejection of the convention kept its form, as evidence that it outlived its setting
cast doubt on Stetkevych's view that the nasib is best understood as a poetics of nostalgia for lost places
questions.explanation: The sentence before the example says the convention 'could outlive the desert,' and the example ends: Abu Nuwas 'asked instead after the tavern, yet his parody kept the old frame.' It is the first of several cases (mystical poets, al-Atlal) offered as support. A is the opposite of the point, and E has the author attacking a view the author calls 'persuasive.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the author brings up Abu Nuwas: what claim the example supports.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, sentences 3 and 4, and the sentences that follow.

breakdown.analysis: Read the sentence that sets up the example: 'That is why the convention could outlive the desert.' Then come three cases in a row, Abu Nuwas, the mystics, and al-Atlal, ending with 'In each case the ruin matters for what it makes the poet remember.' The word 'yet' in 'yet his parody kept the old frame' is the hinge: even mockery kept the convention going. Prephrase: evidence that the convention survived outside the desert, even in parody.

choices.note: Opposite. The example shows the convention surviving the move to Baghdad; the passage says the parody 'kept the old frame.'
Distortion. The passage contrasts no attitudes toward nostalgia between periods; it uses Abu Nuwas to show continuity of form, not a change in values.
Out of scope. The passage never says the convention was ironic from the start; the parody is Abu Nuwas's own.
CORRECT. The example follows 'the convention could outlive the desert' and ends 'yet his parody kept the old frame': a rejection that still used the form, offered as the first piece of evidence.
Opposite of the author's stance. The author calls Stetkevych's argument 'persuasive,' and the Abu Nuwas example is offered in support of the claim that follows from it.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a difference between the accounts the two authors give of the poems they discuss?
choices: Passage A's author holds that the traces at the ruined site have already been effaced, whereas passage B's author holds that the ruined walls are still standing.
Passage A's author treats the lament at the ruin as a formal gesture without real feeling, whereas passage B's author treats it as an expression of genuine grief.
Passage A's author regards religious meaning as foreign to the convention discussed, whereas passage B's author regards it as essential to the poems discussed.
Passage A's author traces the convention to a single originating poem, whereas passage B's author traces the formula to a large body of earlier writing.
Passage A's author locates the ruin's significance in the particular people and places it recalls; passage B's author, in a condition shared by all earthly things.
questions.explanation: A says the camp 'is not chiefly an emblem of decay' but 'the place where memory begins,' where 'a particular woman' and 'a precisely named landscape' are recovered. B says the ruins 'are never anyone's in particular' and are 'evidence for a general truth, that everything under heaven is transitory.' E states that contrast. C is the strongest trap: B does stress the Christian turn, but A mentions mystical poets who made the encampment 'a station of the soul's longing for God,' so A does not treat religious meaning as foreign.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a difference between the two authors' interpretations that each passage actually supports.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, paragraph 2, sentences 2 and 6; passage B, paragraph 2, sentences 2 through 4.

breakdown.analysis: Each author ends with a thesis about what the ruin means. A: memory of a particular beloved and named place ('not chiefly an emblem of decay'). B: anonymity is 'the point'; the ruin is evidence of universal transience. Prephrase: particular memory vs. general transience. Check each half of every choice against its passage; several traps get one half right.

choices.note: Shell game with A's detail. A says the winds 'have not yet effaced' the traces, so its first half is the reverse of the text.
Out of scope. Neither author questions whether the feeling is sincere; A calls the weeping an 'act of mourning.'

Half right. B does stress the turn toward heaven, but A's mystical poets made the encampment 'a station of the soul's longing for God,' so A does not treat religious meaning as foreign to the convention.
Distortion. A calls Imru' al-Qays's ode 'the most famous instance,' not the origin; B names one source tradition (Latin homiletic prose), not a large body of writing.

CORRECT. A: the camp is 'not chiefly an emblem of decay' but where 'a particular woman' and 'a precisely named landscape' are recovered. B: the ruins 'are never anyone's in particular' and are 'evidence for a general truth.'

questions.stem: Which one of the following is mentioned in passage B but not in passage A?
choices: a formula taken over from writing in another language
a poem whose speaker addresses companions at the ruined site
a convention later used to describe the end of a love affair
a comparison of the traces at a ruined site to faded writing
a poet who mocked a convention while still using its frame
questions.explanation: Passage B says the ubi sunt formula comes 'from the Latin' and that Old English writers 'knew [it] from Latin homiletic prose.' Passage A never says the atlal came from writing in another language. Every other choice appears in passage A, not B: the dual imperative addressed to two companions, al-Atlal, the comparison to 'faded writing,' and Abu Nuwas.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: For each choice, check whether it appears in passage B and whether it is absent from passage A. Only one passes both tests.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, paragraph 1, sentence 3; passage A throughout.

breakdown.analysis: Detail-pairing questions reward a quick inventory. Passage A has the two companions, the tattoo and faded-writing comparison, Abu Nuwas, the mystics and al-Atlal. Passage B has the Exeter Book, ubi sunt and its Latin source, laene, the Christian close, and The Ruin's wyrd. Only the Latin source is a borrowing from another language. Watch for choices that sound like B's material (writing, ruins) but come from A.

choices.note: CORRECT. B: the ubi sunt formula comes 'from the Latin,' which 'Old English writers knew from Latin homiletic prose.' A traces nothing to another language.
Passage A, not B. Imru' al-Qays's 'qifa nabki' is 'a dual imperative, addressed to two companions.' B's Wanderer speaks alone, as a 'solitary exile.'
Passage A, not B. A says al-Atlal, sung by Umm Kulthum, 'could name the ruins of a love affair.'
Passage A, not B. A: 'Other poets likened such traces to the remains of a tattoo or to faded writing.' B mentions Latin prose as a source, not as a comparison for ruins.
Passage A, not B. Abu Nuwas 'mocked poets who halted at ruins,' 'yet his parody kept the old frame.' B mentions no parody.

questions.stem: Suppose a poem opens with a speaker halting at an unnamed ruined fortress, asks where its warriors and their horses have gone, and concludes that only the kingdom of heaven endures. Based on passage A, its author would most likely regard this poem as
choices: an example of the atlal in its original pre-Islamic form, before later poets in the cities transformed it
a parody of the atlal convention comparable to the one written by Abu Nuwas in Baghdad
sharing the atlal's halt and lament but lacking what, for the author, gives the atlal its meaning
evidence that the atlal convention, like the ubi sunt formula, derived from religious prose
a mystical transformation of the encampment into a station of the soul's longing for God
questions.explanation: The imagined poem has passage B's pattern: an anonymous ruin, typical figures, and a turn to heaven. Passage A's author says the atlal's force lies in recovering 'a particular woman, a season of union and a precisely named landscape,' and that 'in each case the ruin matters for what it makes the poet remember.' A poem with a halt and a lament but no particular memory shares the gesture and lacks the core, so C. E is the near-miss: the poem is religious, but it concludes that the world is transient, not that the soul longs for God, and it has no encampment or beloved.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply passage A's criterion for what makes the atlal meaningful to a new poem built on passage B's pattern.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, paragraph 1, sentences 3 and 4; paragraph 2, sentences 2 and 7.

breakdown.analysis: First identify what passage A says matters: a halt (wuquf) and weeping, but above all memory of a particular beloved and a 'precisely named' place. Then score the new poem: it has a halt and a lament; it has an unnamed site, generic warriors, and no beloved. So it shares the gesture but not what A treats as the substance. Prephrase: 'same gesture, missing the heart of it.'

choices.note: Distortion. The pre-Islamic atlal in A names its site exactly and mourns a beloved; this poem does neither.
Out of scope. Nothing in the poem mocks the convention; Abu Nuwas's parody replaced the ruin with a tavern.

CORRECT. The poem has the halt and the lament, but A says the atlal matters because it recovers 'a particular woman' and 'a precisely named landscape.' An unnamed fortress and generic warriors supply neither.
Out of scope. Passage A says nothing about where the atlal came from, and the Latin source belongs to passage B's formula.
Shell game. A's mystics kept the encampment and made it a station of longing; this poem has no encampment, and it concludes that the world is transient, not that the soul longs.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the position taken by the author of passage B regarding the close of The Wanderer?
choices: The Exeter Book was copied in a monastery by scribes who also copied a range of Latin religious works.
The opening lines of The Wanderer already describe the solitary man as waiting for God's mercy.
Several pre-Christian Germanic poems lament fallen halls without any mention of the divine.
Ubi sunt passages occur in a number of Old English sermons and saints' lives as well as in poetry.
The Ruin, preserved in the same manuscript, ends without any reference to heaven or mercy.
questions.explanation: Against 'earlier critics' who treated the Christian close 'as a late addition to a pagan lament,' the author argues that the lament 'is completed only by turning toward what does not decay.' If the poem already speaks of God's mercy at its start, the religious frame runs through the whole poem and is much less likely to be a later addition at the end. A could even help the interpolation view (monastic scribes might add such lines), and C supports the 'pagan lament' reading.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Christian close is integral to The Wanderer, not a late addition: the lament is completed by turning toward what does not decay.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The ruins are anonymous and typical, which makes them evidence for a general truth (everything under heaven is transitory) that calls for that turn.

breakdown.analysis: The opposing view is that the close was tacked onto a pagan lament. The best support shows that the religious perspective belongs to the poem as composed, not only to its last lines. Prephrase: evidence of Christian framing elsewhere in the poem. Avoid answers that support the interpolation view or are about other poems.

choices.note: Opposite tendency. Monastic copyists who knew religious works are exactly who might have added a pious ending; this fits the interpolation view at least as well.
CORRECT. If the poem opens with the exile awaiting God's mercy, the religious frame is present from the start, which undercuts the claim that the close is 'a late addition to a pagan lament.'
Weakens. Pagan laments over fallen halls with no divine reference make the 'pagan lament' reading more plausible.
Irrelevant. That the formula also appears in sermons bears on its sources, not on whether The Wanderer's close is original.

Irrelevant or weakening. The author already grants that The Ruin 'makes no such turn'; another poem's ending says nothing about whether The Wanderer's close is original, and if anything suggests elegies could do without one.

questions.stem: The author of passage B would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about The Ruin?
choices: Its lack of ubi sunt questions indicates that it was composed earlier than The Wanderer.
Its attribution of the city's destruction to fate shows that its outlook is pagan rather than Christian.
Like The Wanderer, it completes its lament by turning toward what does not decay.
Its city is presented less as a particular place to be remembered than as an illustration of a general fate.
Its probable identification with Roman Bath shows that, unlike The Wanderer, it commemorates a specific place.
questions.explanation: The last sentence of passage B: 'Even The Ruin, which makes no such turn, offers its fallen city as an example of what fate does to all human work.' D paraphrases that. E is the trap for readers carrying passage A's frame into B: B says only 'perhaps Roman Bath,' a scholarly identification, and never says the poem commemorates or remembers the place. C is the opposite: 'makes no such turn.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement about The Ruin that passage B's author is committed to, using only what passage B says.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, paragraph 1, last sentence; paragraph 2, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Passage B says three things about The Ruin: it has no mourning speaker and no ubi sunt; it marvels at masonry of a city 'perhaps' Bath that wyrd has broken; and, despite making no religious turn, it offers the city 'as an example of what fate does to all human work.' Prephrase: the city is an example of a general fate. The hard part: E sounds like a fair inference from 'Roman Bath' but goes beyond what the passage says, and C reverses 'makes no such turn.'

choices.note: Out of scope. The passage gives no dates of composition for either poem and draws no conclusion from the missing questions.
Too strong. The author reports that the poem names wyrd but never infers a pagan outlook; the author's own claim concerns transience, not religion.
Opposite. The author says The Ruin 'makes no such turn.'
CORRECT. Passage B, last sentence: The Ruin 'offers its fallen city as an example of what fate does to all human work,' which is a general fate, not a remembered place.
Distortion. The passage says only 'perhaps Roman Bath,' a modern identification, and never says the poem commemorates a place; its last sentence treats the city as an example of a general fate.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Al-Jurjani showed that the Qur'an's inimitability lies chiefly in its metaphors, a conclusion that modern structuralist critics have independently reached.
Al-Jurjani's theory of construction, although developed to explain the Qur'an's inimitability, is best understood as an early version of structuralist linguistics.
Al-Jurjani located eloquence in grammatical construction, not in words or ideas alone, and his theory, though like modern ones, should be read in light of its purpose.
Al-Jurjani settled the dispute over wording and meaning by agreeing with al-Jahiz that a poet's merit lies in craft rather than in the ideas expressed.
Modern comparisons of al-Jurjani with Western critics have obscured the eleventh-century debates over the Qur'an's challenge, which were chiefly theological rather than literary.
questions.explanation: The passage sets out the wording-versus-meaning dispute, presents al-Jurjani's answer (nazm, construction according to grammatical meanings), reports the modern comparisons, and ends with the author's verdict: the resemblances are 'real,' but calling him a structuralist discards 'the question it was built to answer.' C has both halves. B is the view the author rejects, and E inflates the author's caution while dropping al-Jurjani's theory altogether.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: State the claim the whole passage supports, including the author's position in the last paragraph.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, last sentence; paragraph 2, sentence 3; paragraph 4, first and last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Map: P1 the dispute (wording vs. meaning) and its theological stakes; P2 al-Jurjani's answer, nazm, with examples; P3 modern comparisons (Abu-Deeb, Saussure, Brooks); P4 author: the resemblances are real, but al-Jurjani must be read in context and for his purpose. Prephrase: al-Jurjani put eloquence in construction; modern parallels exist but miss his aim. Reject choices that keep only one half or that adopt the view the author qualifies.

choices.note: Distortion. Al-Jurjani said readers who credited the verse's power 'to its metaphor alone' 'overlooked its construction,' and the passage reports no structuralist conclusion about the Qur'an.
Opposite of the author's conclusion. The last sentence says calling him 'a structuralist before his time' keeps his method 'while discarding the question it was built to answer.'
CORRECT. It joins paragraph 2's account of nazm (neither 'bare words' nor 'a bare idea') with paragraph 4's verdict that the resemblances are 'real' but leave out the end his comparisons 'served.'
Opposite. Al-Jurjani answered that 'both parties had looked in the wrong place'; he did not side with al-Jahiz's wording camp.

Too strong and half the story. The author grants that the resemblances 'are real' and does not say they obscured anything; the choice also leaves out al-Jurjani's theory, which takes up most of the passage.

questions.stem: According to the passage, al-Jurjani held that the order of sounds within a word
choices: follows the order of meanings in the mind of the speaker
determines whether a word pleases in one verse and grates in another
is the feature of the Qur'an's language that no human speaker can match
is arbitrary, unlike the order of words within an utterance
was the main concern of the critics who located excellence in wording
questions.explanation: The last sentence of paragraph 2: 'The order of sounds within a word is arbitrary, he added; the order of words follows the order of meanings in the mind.' D restates it. A attaches the second half of that sentence, which is about words, to sounds.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says al-Jurjani held about the order of sounds inside a word.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: A pure retrieval question: the passage contrasts two kinds of order in a single sentence. Sounds within a word: arbitrary. Words within an utterance: follow meanings in the mind. The trap is the choice that swaps the two.

choices.note: Shell game. The passage says this of 'the order of words,' not of sounds.
Distortion. The al-akhda' example shows that a word's merit depends on its setting; the passage never connects that to the order of its sounds.
Out of scope. Al-Jurjani located the Qur'an's power in construction, as with the verse about white hair; nothing ties inimitability to sound order.
CORRECT. Paragraph 2: 'The order of sounds within a word is arbitrary, he added; the order of words follows the order of meanings in the mind.'
Out of scope. The passage says al-Jahiz located merit in 'wording and craft' but never says that party was concerned with sound order within words.

questions.stem: The author mentions al-akhda' (second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that al-Jurjani preferred the poetry of al-Buhturi to the poetry of his older contemporary Abu Tammam
illustrate al-Jahiz's view that a poet's merit lies in wording rather than in meaning
give an example of a word whose meaning changed between the periods of two poets
demonstrate that metaphor matters less than syntax in the language of the Qur'an
illustrate al-Jurjani's claim that a word's merit depends on its setting, not on the word itself
questions.explanation: The example comes right after the claim it supports: 'Single words, he argued, are not ranked as bare words: the same word that delights in one verse burdens another, as al-akhda' ... pleases in a line of al-Buhturi and grates in a line of Abu Tammam.' One word, two settings, two verdicts. B gives the example to the wrong position-holder, al-Jahiz, whose view al-Jurjani is rejecting.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify the claim the al-akhda' example is there to support.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, sentence 1.

breakdown.analysis: The colon in sentence 1 introduces the evidence for 'Single words ... are not ranked as bare words.' The example holds the word constant and varies the verse, so the difference in merit has to come from the setting. Prephrase: proof that a word's value depends on context.

choices.note: Out of scope. The example says the word pleases in one line and grates in the other, not that one poet is better overall.
Wrong position-holder. Al-Jahiz located merit in wording; the example shows that a single word has no fixed merit, which is al-Jurjani's argument against both camps.
Out of scope. The passage says nothing about the word's meaning changing; the same word appears in two settings.
Wrong example. The point about metaphor and syntax comes from the Qur'anic verse about white hair, not from al-akhda'.
CORRECT. Paragraph 2: single words 'are not ranked as bare words: the same word that delights in one verse burdens another, as al-akhda' ... pleases ... and grates.'

questions.stem: In the second paragraph, the author uses the word "grammar" to refer to
choices: the rules that distinguish correct from incorrect usage in Arabic
the differences in meaning produced by choices among syntactic arrangements
the conventional pairing of sounds and senses that defines each word
the set of metaphors that critics before al-Jurjani had singled out for praise
the arrangement of ideas in a speaker's mind before they are put into words
questions.explanation: The passage defines its own term: 'By grammar he meant not rules of correctness but the meanings that syntactic choices carry: "Zayd muntaliq" and "al-muntaliq Zayd" differ in what they assert.' B paraphrases that. A is the everyday sense the passage explicitly rules out. E is the subtle trap: the passage does say word order 'follows the order of meanings in the mind,' but that is a separate claim, not what 'grammar' names.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Determine what 'grammar' means in this passage, which may differ from its ordinary sense.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, sentences 3 and 4, and the last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: When the LSAT asks about a word, the passage often defines it, and here it does: 'not rules of correctness but the meanings that syntactic choices carry,' illustrated by two arrangements of the same words that 'differ in what they assert.' Prephrase: the meaning carried by how a sentence is built. Watch for the ordinary sense (A) and for a neighboring idea in the same paragraph (E).

choices.note: Opposite. The passage says he meant 'not rules of correctness.'
CORRECT. Paragraph 2: 'By grammar he meant not rules of correctness but the meanings that syntactic choices carry,' illustrated by two orders of the same words that 'differ in what they assert.'
Shell game. The passage calls the order of sounds within a word 'arbitrary'; that is a contrast with grammar, not grammar itself.
Out of scope. Earlier readers praised the verse's metaphor, but al-Jurjani said they 'overlooked its construction,' which is where he locates its power.
Shell game. The passage says the order of words 'follows the order of meanings in the mind,' but 'grammar' names the meanings carried by syntactic choices, not ideas before they are expressed.

questions.stem: Which one of the following critical judgments would al-Jurjani, as described in the passage, be most likely to endorse?
choices: A line deserves praise chiefly because one of its words is unusually rare and sonorous.
A line deserves praise because its central idea is profound, however that idea is phrased.
Two lines deserve equal praise because a paraphrase of each would yield exactly the same statement.
A line deserves praise because putting a certain word first adds an emphasis another order would lose.
A line deserves blame because it repeats a metaphor that an earlier poet had already made famous.
questions.explanation: Al-Jurjani locates merit in nazm, the 'meanings that syntactic choices carry'; his examples compare orders of the same words ('Zayd muntaliq' and 'al-muntaliq Zayd') and show that the Qur'anic verse's construction conveys what the alternative 'does not.' D applies exactly that test to a new line. A puts merit in a single word, B in 'a bare idea that any paraphrase could carry,' and C treats paraphrase as the measure, all of which the passage says he rejected.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply al-Jurjani's criterion of eloquence, as the passage presents it, to five new judgments.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, sentences 1 through 5.

breakdown.analysis: The passage gives al-Jurjani's test in negative and positive form. Negative: merit is not in single words ('not ranked as bare words') and not in 'a bare idea that any paraphrase could carry.' Positive: merit lies in construction, in what a syntactic choice adds, shown by comparing alternative arrangements. Prephrase: praise a line for what its construction conveys that another construction would not.

choices.note: Contradicts the passage. Merit in a single word is the view he rejects: words 'are not ranked as bare words.'
Contradicts the passage. 'Nor does merit lie in a bare idea that any paraphrase could carry.'
Contradicts the passage. Judging lines by their paraphrase treats meaning apart from construction as the measure, which al-Jurjani denies.
CORRECT. This is his method: compare arrangements and credit what one construction conveys that another does not, as with 'Zayd muntaliq' and 'al-muntaliq Zayd' and the verse about white hair.
Out of scope. The passage says nothing about originality or borrowing among poets; and metaphor, in the verse he analyzes, is not where he locates merit.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the modern comparisons described in the third paragraph can most accurately be described as
choices: dismissive, because the comparisons rest on a misreading of what al-Jurjani actually wrote
qualified acceptance: the resemblances are genuine, but they leave out what his analyses were for
enthusiastic, because the comparisons reveal al-Jurjani as a forerunner of modern literary theory
neutral, since the author reports the comparisons without taking any position on their value
skeptical of the comparison with Saussure but fully persuaded by the comparison with the New Critics
questions.explanation: The last paragraph opens 'These resemblances are real, but...' and goes on to name two differences and to warn against calling him 'a structuralist before his time.' That is qualified acceptance. A is too negative (the author never says the comparisons misread the text), C ignores the caution, and E invents a split: the author treats all the resemblances together and objects to all of them on the same grounds.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize the author's own stance toward Abu-Deeb's and others' comparisons, at the right strength.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3 (how the comparisons are presented) and paragraph 4, sentences 1 and 4.

breakdown.analysis: Attitude questions turn on degree. The signal is 'These resemblances are real, but': a concession followed by a limit. The author then says the comparisons miss two things: the speaker's intention, and the evaluative and theological aim. Prephrase: they're partly right but leave something essential out. Eliminate the extremes and the neutral option, since the author takes a clear position.

choices.note: Too extreme. The author calls the resemblances 'real' and never says the comparisons misread al-Jurjani's texts; the objection concerns what they leave out.
CORRECT. 'These resemblances are real, but' Larkin 'was right to read al-Jurjani within' his century; calling him a structuralist discards 'the question it was built to answer.'
Opposite. The final sentence rejects calling him 'a structuralist before his time.'
Wrong. The author takes a clear position in paragraph 4, including the judgment that Larkin 'was right.'
Distortion. The author contrasts al-Jurjani with Saussure in particular, but grants that all 'these resemblances are real' and never says the Brooks comparison is complete.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's argument in the last paragraph?
choices: Saussure's linguistics deliberately sets aside both the intentions of individual speakers and any ranking of utterances as better or worse.
Abu-Deeb's 1979 study discusses al-Jurjani's treatment of metaphor at much greater length than it discusses his account of construction.
Several twentieth-century Arab critics regarded al-Jurjani as the founder of a distinctively Arabic tradition of literary theory and criticism.
Al-Jurjani's analyses of lines of poetry in the Dala'il are as detailed as his analyses of verses from the Qur'an.
Cleanth Brooks could not read Arabic and had no knowledge of al-Jurjani's work when he wrote about paraphrase.
questions.explanation: The author argues against calling al-Jurjani a structuralist on two grounds: Saussure's relations 'belong to an impersonal system' while al-Jurjani's belong to 'an utterance shaped by a speaker's intended meanings,' and al-Jurjani's comparisons served to show 'why one construction is superior to another.' If structuralist linguistics deliberately excludes both speaker intention and ranking, both differences are confirmed. E is the attractive trap: it sounds like a point against the comparison, but the author claims resemblance, not influence, so whether Brooks knew of al-Jurjani is irrelevant.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Calling al-Jurjani a structuralist before his time keeps his method while discarding the question it was built to answer.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: (1) Saussure's relations belong to an impersonal system; al-Jurjani's to an utterance shaped by a speaker's intended meanings. (2) His comparisons aimed to rank constructions and ultimately to show why the Qur'an's construction cannot be matched, an aim no structuralist would share.

breakdown.analysis: To strengthen, confirm the asserted disanalogies or close a gap. The argument assumes that structuralism really lacks what al-Jurjani has: speaker intention and evaluation. A fact establishing that would support both premises at once. Be wary of answers about influence (the author never claims any), about Abu-Deeb's emphasis, or about al-Jurjani's reputation.

choices.note: CORRECT. It confirms both of the author's disanalogies: Saussure excludes the speaker's intended meanings, and excludes the ranking of constructions that al-Jurjani's comparisons 'served' to establish.
Irrelevant. How Abu-Deeb divided his attention says nothing about whether al-Jurjani's method differs from structuralism in the ways the author claims.
Irrelevant. Al-Jurjani's standing as a founder of Arabic theory bears neither on his resemblance to structuralism nor on his purpose.
If anything weakens. Equal attention to poetry might suggest his method was not tied mainly to the Qur'anic question, which cuts against the claim that it was 'built to answer' that question.
Irrelevant. The author speaks only of resemblances ('may hear ... an anticipation'), not influence, so Brooks's ignorance of al-Jurjani neither helps nor hurts the argument.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Persian poems on the rose and the nightingale are in fact more original than Keats's ode, since their poets had to achieve individuality within a fixed set of images.
The Persian nightingale and Keats's nightingale differ chiefly in what they symbolize, the one standing for the soul and the other for the immortality of art.
The two traditions differ less in whether they rely on convention than in whether they acknowledge it, though part of the older contrast survives.
The familiar contrast between Persian convention and Romantic originality is mistaken, since both traditions depend to the same degree on inherited images.
Keats's ode shows that English Romantic poets, like later Persian poets, composed replies to their predecessors' poems within a shared formal frame.
questions.explanation: The passage lays out the Persian convention (P1), the Romantic nightingale and the common contrast drawn from it (P2), then says the contrast 'is real, but it is misdrawn' (P3) and relocates the difference in 'its acknowledgment' while conceding 'Something of the older contrast survives' (P4). C keeps all three moves. D is the trap: it drops the author's concession that the contrast is real and survives in part.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the claim the whole passage builds toward, including the author's qualification at the end.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, first sentence; paragraph 4, all three sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Map: P1 the Persian convention and its levels (Schimmel); P2 Keats's bird and the common contrast; P3 author: contrast real but misdrawn (Losensky; Keats's own borrowings); P4 the real difference is acknowledgment, though the Persian rose keeps settled meanings. Prephrase: the traditions differ, but not as convention vs. originality; they differ in whether convention is displayed or hidden, with one older difference left standing. Reject answers that make the author all-for or all-against the contrast.

choices.note: Too strong and out of scope. The author never ranks the traditions by originality; the point is that originality can exist within convention, not that Persian poems have more of it.
Distortion. The passage never says Keats's bird symbolizes the immortality of art, and the author's main claim is about the acknowledgment of convention, not a difference in symbols.

CORRECT. Paragraph 3: the contrast 'is real, but it is misdrawn'; paragraph 4: what differs 'is less the presence of convention than its acknowledgment,' and 'Something of the older contrast survives even so.'
Too strong. The author calls the contrast 'real' and says part of it 'survives'; nothing says the two traditions rely on inherited images to the same degree.
Shell game. The reply poems belong to Losensky's account of the Persian ghazal; the passage says Keats drew on inherited material, not that he wrote replies in a predecessor's meter and rhyme.

questions.stem: According to the passage, in Attar's Conference of the Birds the nightingale
choices: declines the journey because its love of the rose is enough for it
is wounded by the rose's thorn when it reaches for the flower it loves
stands for the divine beauty that the soul glimpses in the world
sets out toward the Simurgh but turns back after hearing the hoopoe's warning
argues to the hoopoe that the rose's beauty is too brief to be worth pursuing
questions.explanation: The last sentence of paragraph 1 says the nightingale 'declines the journey to the Simurgh... because love of the rose is enough for it.' A restates this. E gives the hoopoe's reply to the nightingale, and C gives the role the passage assigns to the rose.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Retrieve what the passage says about the nightingale in Attar's poem.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: One sentence answers it. Keep the speakers straight: the nightingale declines; the hoopoe replies that the rose is brief and unloving. Watch for answers that borrow details of the general convention (the thorn) or swap the roles of bird and rose.

choices.note: CORRECT. Paragraph 1, last sentence: the nightingale 'declines the journey... because love of the rose is enough for it.'
Shell game. The wounding thorn is part of the general convention described in paragraph 1, second sentence, not something the passage says happens in Attar's poem.
Reversal. In the mystical reading the nightingale is the soul and 'the rose the divine beauty it glimpses in the world.'
Distortion. The nightingale 'declines the journey'; the passage never says it sets out or turns back.
Wrong speaker. It is the hoopoe that 'replies that the rose's beauty is brief.'

questions.stem: The author mentions Coleridge's "The Nightingale" (third paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that Keats composed his ode as a reply to Coleridge's poem in the manner of a Persian ghazal poet
illustrate the Romantic poets' rejection of the melancholy associations that literary tradition gave the nightingale
provide an example of the European literary historians who dismissed later Persian poetry as derivative
suggest that Coleridge's poem, rather than Keats's ode, is the more original treatment of the nightingale
help support the claim that the Romantic nightingale had more precedent than it at first appears to have
questions.explanation: The Coleridge sentence follows 'Nor was the Romantic bird as unprecedented as it appears' and precedes the list of Keats's inherited material: it shows that the Romantic nightingale already had a literary history. B is the trap: Coleridge did argue with the melancholy bird, but the author cites that argument to show the bird had precedent, not to make a point about Romantic rejection of tradition.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the Coleridge reference does in the author's argument, not what it says.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, sentences four and five.

breakdown.analysis: Read the sentence before the reference: 'Nor was the Romantic bird as unprecedented as it appears.' The Coleridge poem and Keats's borrowings are the evidence for that claim. Prephrase: to show the Romantic nightingale had a tradition behind it. Traps restate the detail (Coleridge argued with tradition) as if it were the point.

choices.note: Too strong. The passage says only that Coleridge's poem came before Keats's ode; it never says Keats replied to it, and the reply form belongs to the Persian discussion.

True detail, wrong function. Coleridge did argue 'with the melancholy bird of literary tradition,' but the author uses that fact to show that the Romantic bird had precedents, which is nearly the opposite of a point about rejecting tradition.
Out of scope. The historians in paragraph 2 judged Persian poetry; Coleridge is mentioned as a poet who wrote about the nightingale, not as one of them.
Out of scope. The passage never compares the originality of Coleridge's and Keats's poems.

CORRECT. The reference supports paragraph 3's claim that the Romantic bird was not 'as unprecedented as it appears': Coleridge 'had argued with the melancholy bird of literary tradition before Keats wrote.'

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Keats's ode would be better understood if its nightingale were read as an allegory of the soul's longing for the divine.
A reader unaware of earlier uses of the rose and the nightingale would likely miss part of a Persian poet's achievement.
The European historians who found later Persian poetry derivative were right about its repetitiveness but wrong to count that as a defect.
The poets of the later Persian ghazal regarded individuality as unimportant compared with faithfulness to their predecessors.
The meaning of Keats's nightingale was largely determined in advance by the literary tradition from which he drew it.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the Persian poet 'displays mastery by turning a known image so that readers who know it notice the turn.' A reader without that knowledge would therefore miss the turn, which is part of the achievement. E is the opposite of the last sentence, which says Keats's bird 'means only what his poem makes it mean.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the passage's own claims support, without adding to them.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, sentences two and three; paragraph 4, second and third sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The author's specific claims: originality is 'a relation to precedent'; the Persian poet's mastery shows in a turn that 'readers who know it notice'; the Persian rose carries meanings 'settled before any poem begins,' while Keats's bird means 'only what his poem makes it mean.' The key will follow from one of these. Traps transfer the Persian features to Keats or credit the author with concessions he never makes.
