choices.note: Opposite. The last sentence says Keats's bird 'means only what his poem makes it mean'; the allegorical, mystical level belongs to the Persian rose and nightingale.

CORRECT. Paragraph 4: mastery is displayed 'by turning a known image so that readers who know it notice the turn.' A reader who does not know the earlier uses cannot notice the turn, so part of the achievement is lost on that reader.

Distortion. The author never grants that later Persian poetry was repetitive; paragraph 3 argues that individuality was 'measured in what a poet did within that shared frame,' which answers the charge rather than conceding it.
Opposite. On Losensky's account, as the author reports it, individuality was what poets displayed within the shared frame, so it was not unimportant to them.
Opposite. Keats drew on 'inherited material,' but the author's final sentence says his bird means 'only what his poem makes it mean,' unlike the Persian rose's settled meanings.

questions.stem: By "a relation to precedent rather than an escape from it" (third paragraph, third sentence), the author most probably means that originality
choices: requires a poet to reproduce an earlier poem's images as closely as the meter and rhyme permit
is achieved only by poets who eventually abandon the frame their predecessors established
depends on the poet's personal experience rather than on the models that literary tradition supplies
lies in how a poet reworks what earlier poets did, not in avoiding what they did
can be judged only by readers who know the circumstances in which a predecessor's poem was composed
questions.explanation: The phrase sums up Losensky's account in the previous sentence: poets replied to predecessors' poems and 'individuality was measured in what a poet did within that shared frame.' Originality, then, is how one reworks the precedent, not freedom from it (D). C states the Romantic idea of originality that the phrase is set against.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Interpret the phrase from the sentences around it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, sentences two and three.

breakdown.analysis: 'On this view' points back to the sentence before: replies in a predecessor's meter and rhyme, with individuality 'measured in what a poet did within that shared frame.' So 'relation to precedent' means doing something with earlier work, and 'escape' means getting free of it. Prephrase: originality is a poet's difference from his models, not freedom from them.

choices.note: Too strong. Keeping a predecessor's meter and rhyme is the frame; the passage locates originality in what the poet does within it, not in reproducing the earlier images closely.
Opposite. Abandoning the frame would be 'an escape' from precedent, the very idea the phrase rejects.
Wrong position-holder. Grounding originality in personal experience is the Romantic picture in paragraph 2, which the phrase is set against.
CORRECT. The previous sentence says 'individuality was measured in what a poet did within that shared frame,' so originality lies in how a poet reworks precedent rather than in escaping it.
Out of scope. The passage says nothing about knowing the circumstances in which earlier poems were written; the readers it mentions know earlier images, not biographies.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, which one of the following would most clearly exemplify the way, according to the author, that a Persian poet displays mastery?
choices: A poet introduces into the lyric a songbird that no earlier Persian poet had used, so that readers meet an image without any precedent.
A poet describes in vivid detail a particular nightingale he heard in his own garden one spring night, and his feelings as he listened to it.
A poet reproduces a famous predecessor's ghazal word for word, changing only the final line so that it bears his own pen name.
A poet prefaces his collection with a prose explanation of the mystical meanings of the rose and the nightingale for readers new to them.
A poet makes the nightingale, not the rose, the source of the familiar thorn's wound, a reversal readers of the convention will notice.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4: the Persian poet 'displays mastery by turning a known image so that readers who know it notice the turn.' E keeps the convention's known element (the wounding thorn) and turns it in a way only a reader of the convention would notice. B is the Romantic method the author contrasts with it: making an image 'seem to rise from his own experience.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply the author's description of Persian mastery to a new case.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, second sentence; paragraph 3, sentences two and three.

breakdown.analysis: The test has two parts: (1) the image must be known, part of the shared code; (2) the poet must turn it, so that informed readers notice the change. Check each choice against both. An image with no precedent fails (1); copying without change fails (2); a personal-experience poem is the Romantic method; explaining the convention isn't a turn at all.

choices.note: Fails the first condition. An image 'without any precedent' is originality as escape, which the author contrasts with the Persian relation to precedent.
Wrong method. This is the Romantic approach of paragraph 4, making an image 'seem to rise from his own experience,' as Keats's ode does.
Fails the second condition. A word-for-word copy keeps the frame but makes no turn that shows individuality; changing only the signature line is not reworking the image.
Irrelevant. A prose explanation of the convention's meanings helps new readers but involves no poetic turn of a known image.
CORRECT. The wounding thorn is a known element of the convention (paragraph 1), and moving it to the nightingale is a turn that 'readers who know it notice,' as paragraph 4 describes.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the contrast between Persian convention and Romantic originality described in the second paragraph can most accurately be described as
choices: qualified acceptance: it marks a real difference but misplaces it
firm endorsement: it accurately captures what separates the two traditions
complete rejection: it rests on a European prejudice against Persian poetry
reluctant agreement: it is right about later Persian poetry though unfair to Keats
detached neutrality: it is reported but neither accepted nor criticized
questions.explanation: The author says the contrast 'is real, but it is misdrawn if it implies that convention excludes originality,' relocates the difference in the acknowledgment of convention, and grants that 'Something of the older contrast survives even so.' That is qualified acceptance (A). C is the too-extreme trap a reader might pick after the critique in paragraph 3.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize the author's attitude precisely, including its degree.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, first sentence; paragraph 4.

breakdown.analysis: Two signals pull against each other: 'real, but... misdrawn' and 'Something of the older contrast survives.' The attitude is partial agreement with a correction. Eliminate the all-for, all-against and no-opinion choices, then check that the reason given fits the passage.

choices.note: CORRECT. The contrast 'is real' (paragraph 3) and part of it 'survives' (paragraph 4), but it is 'misdrawn' because the difference lies in 'acknowledgment' rather than in the presence of convention.
Too extreme. The author says the contrast is 'misdrawn,' so it is not endorsed as accurate.
Too extreme. The author calls the contrast 'real' and keeps part of it; the passage never attributes it to prejudice.
Distortion. The author does not agree with the verdict on later Persian poetry; paragraph 3 answers it with Losensky's account. Nor does the author say the contrast is unfair to Keats.
Opposite. The author takes a clear position in paragraphs 3 and 4.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Because most of the quatrains attributed to Khayyam are not his, FitzGerald's Rubaiyat is better regarded as an original English poem than as a translation.
No single verdict on FitzGerald's Rubaiyat suffices, partly because the Persian corpus he reshaped was already a composite rather than one author's work.
FitzGerald's condescension toward his Persian sources makes the Rubaiyat an Orientalist appropriation despite the poem's later popularity.
Zhukovsky's discovery of wandering quatrains showed that FitzGerald's manuscripts were unreliable, so that his version is inaccurate as a translation.
By placing its turn in the fourth line, the ruba'i allowed FitzGerald to convey Khayyam's thought in English without sacrificing its form.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph states the author's conclusion: 'Each verdict captures something, but none is adequate alone,' and the authenticity problem 'complicates any simple opposition' because FitzGerald's Khayyam 'was already a composite.' B states both parts. C is the trap: the author says the appropriation charge is 'weakest' when applied to the poem's effects.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the claim the passage builds toward, especially the author's verdict in the final paragraph.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, first and third sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Map: P1 publication history and the ruba'i form; P2 the authenticity problem; P3 FitzGerald's method and three verdicts (translation, English poem, appropriation); P4 author: none adequate alone; appropriation charge strong on the letter, weak on the effects; the composite source makes FitzGerald one more contributor, though an outsider. Prephrase: no one verdict works, partly because the original was itself a tradition.

choices.note: Wrong position-holder and too strong. Reading the work as an English poem is one of the three verdicts the author finds inadequate alone, and the passage never says 'most' of the quatrains are inauthentic.

CORRECT. Paragraph 4: 'Each verdict captures something, but none is adequate alone,' and the composite nature of the Khayyam corpus 'complicates any simple opposition between a faithful original and its English distortion.'
Wrong position-holder. This is the Orientalism critics' verdict; the author finds it 'weakest when directed at the poem's effects.'
Distortion. Zhukovsky's work shows that the corpus was mixed; the author uses this to complicate the faithful-or-distorted opposition, not to call the translation inaccurate.

Out of scope. The passage describes the ruba'i form and FitzGerald's use of it in paragraph 1, but that is background, not the point, and the passage makes no claim that he conveyed Khayyam's thought.

questions.stem: According to the passage, in the ruba'i form
choices: all four lines of the quatrain end on the same rhyme
the third line delivers the turn on which the quatrain ends
each line is composed in a meter equivalent to English iambic pentameter
the third line usually does not share the rhyme of the other lines
quatrains are arranged in sequences that move from dawn to nightfall
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: in the ruba'i 'the first, second, and fourth lines rhyme and the third usually does not.' D restates this. B moves the turn from the last line to the third, and E describes FitzGerald's arrangement, not the form.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Retrieve what the passage says about the ruba'i itself.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, fifth sentence; paragraph 3, first and second sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Separate what belongs to the Persian form (self-contained quatrain, lines 1, 2 and 4 rhyme, the third usually not, the last line delivers the turn) from what FitzGerald did (iambic pentameter, a dawn-to-nightfall sequence).

choices.note: Contradicted. The passage says the third line 'usually does not' rhyme.
Shell game. The third line is the unrhymed one; it is 'the last line, returning to the rhyme,' that 'delivers the poem's turn.'
Wrong source. Iambic pentameter is the meter FitzGerald used in English; the passage says nothing of the Persian meter.
CORRECT. Paragraph 1: 'the first, second, and fourth lines rhyme and the third usually does not.'
Wrong source. The dawn-to-nightfall sequence is FitzGerald's arrangement (paragraph 3); the passage calls the ruba'i 'a self-contained quatrain.'

questions.stem: The primary function of the second paragraph is to
choices: show that FitzGerald's source was of uncertain authorship, a point the author later uses to complicate the debate
argue that FitzGerald's version is unfaithful because the manuscripts Cowell supplied were corrupted by careless copyists
explain why the 1859 edition of the poem failed to find readers until a copy reached Rossetti
demonstrate that Khayyam wrote no poetry, so that every quatrain bearing his name belongs to someone else
provide support for Karlin's reading of the Rubaiyat as an English poem rather than a translation
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 shows that the Khayyam corpus was an 'accumulated tradition rather than a single author,' and the last paragraph draws on exactly this point: 'the problem of authenticity complicates any simple opposition between a faithful original and its English distortion.' A captures both the content and its later use. B is the trap: the paragraph calls the corpus composite, not corrupt, and it never judges FitzGerald unfaithful.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the second paragraph does in the passage as a whole.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, first and last sentences; paragraph 4, third sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The paragraph opens 'what FitzGerald was translating is less certain than it appears' and ends 'an accumulated tradition rather than a single author.' Ask where that pays off: paragraph 4's 'problem of authenticity.' Prephrase: it sets up the uncertainty about the source that the author later uses to blur the original-versus-distortion opposition.

choices.note: CORRECT. Paragraph 2 ends by calling FitzGerald's manuscripts 'an accumulated tradition rather than a single author,' and paragraph 4 uses 'the problem of authenticity' to complicate 'any simple opposition between a faithful original and its English distortion.'
Distortion. The paragraph says the corpus was enlarged by attribution, not corrupted by careless copying, and it makes no judgment that FitzGerald was unfaithful.
Out of scope. The sales history is in paragraph 1; paragraph 2 never addresses it.
Too strong. The passage says attributions appear only decades later and that scholars such as Dashti try to recover 'a small core of authentic poems,' which assumes Khayyam wrote some.
Wrong connection. Karlin appears in paragraph 3, and the author's own use of paragraph 2 is to judge all three verdicts inadequate alone, not to support Karlin's.

questions.stem: By "a wandering tradition" (last sentence of the passage), the author most probably means a body of poems
choices: that traveled from Persia to Victorian England through translation
whose themes lack any consistent direction or argument
whose attribution shifted among poets and which grew over time
composed by poets who lived as wanderers in the medieval Persian world
that were recited aloud from memory before anyone wrote them down
questions.explanation: 'Wandering' picks up Zhukovsky's 'wandering quatrains' in paragraph 2, 'poems ascribed to Khayyam in some manuscripts and to other poets in others,' and the same last paragraph calls the corpus 'a composite that generations of copyists had enlarged.' C captures both. A is the trap for a reader who knows the poem's later fame: geographical travel is not what the passage's word refers to.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Interpret the phrase from its context in the passage.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, third sentence; paragraph 4, third and fourth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Find the word's earlier use: Zhukovsky's 'wandering quatrains,' defined right there as poems whose ascription moves between Khayyam and other poets. The sentence before the phrase adds that the corpus was 'a composite that generations of copyists had enlarged.' Prephrase: a shifting, growing body of poems of uncertain authorship.

choices.note: Shell game with outside knowledge. The poem did travel to England, but the passage's 'wandering' comes from Zhukovsky's term for quatrains whose attribution moves, and FitzGerald is said to work 'from outside' this tradition, so the tradition is not the journey to England.
Out of scope. The passage says nothing about the themes of the quatrains lacking direction.

CORRECT. Paragraph 2 defines 'wandering quatrains' as poems 'ascribed to Khayyam in some manuscripts and to other poets in others,' and paragraph 4 calls the corpus 'a composite that generations of copyists had enlarged.'
Out of scope. Nothing in the passage describes the poets' way of life.
Unsupported. The passage discusses manuscripts and copyists, not oral transmission.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the author's position regarding the critics of Orientalism mentioned in the third paragraph?
choices: The author rejects their view entirely, on the grounds that FitzGerald's poem introduced Khayyam to English readers.
The author accepts their view and supports it with evidence that FitzGerald's manuscripts were inauthentic.
The author holds that they misread FitzGerald's letter, whose condescension was not meant seriously.
The author holds that they are right about the poem's effects on readers but wrong about the letter to Cowell.
The author finds their view more persuasive regarding FitzGerald's letter than regarding the poem's consequences.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4: 'The charge of appropriation is strongest when directed at the letter and weakest when directed at the poem's effects.' E paraphrases this exactly. D reverses it, and A overstates the author's reservation into a rejection.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pin down how the author's view relates to one group's view, including its degree.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, last sentence; paragraph 4, first and second sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The author grants that 'each verdict captures something' and then ranks where the appropriation charge holds: strongest for the letter, weakest for the effects. Prephrase: partial agreement, stronger on the letter than on the poem's consequences. Watch for the reversal and for all-or-nothing answers.

choices.note: Too strong. The author says each verdict 'captures something' and calls the charge 'strongest when directed at the letter,' so it is not rejected entirely.
Distortion. The passage calls the manuscripts an accumulated tradition, not inauthentic, and it uses that point to complicate all three verdicts, not to support this one.
Unsupported. The author nowhere suggests the condescension was not meant seriously; the charge is 'strongest' precisely when aimed at the letter.
Reversal. The author says the charge is 'strongest when directed at the letter and weakest when directed at the poem's effects.'
CORRECT. Paragraph 4, second sentence: the charge 'is strongest when directed at the letter and weakest when directed at the poem's effects.'

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the author's assessment of the charge of appropriation as applied to the poem's effects?
choices: FitzGerald, in other letters to Cowell, expressed deep admiration for several Persian poets, including Hafiz and Attar.
A small number of English scholars had read some of Khayyam's quatrains in Persian manuscripts before 1859.
Later research showed that Zhukovsky's list of wandering quatrains had included some poems that were in fact Khayyam's own.
Most readers drawn to Khayyam by FitzGerald took his sequence for the real Khayyam and dismissed closer translations as false.
Victorian reviewers who praised the Rubaiyat often singled out the poem's skill in rendering a Persian outlook in English verse.
questions.explanation: The author says the appropriation charge is 'weakest when directed at the poem's effects, since it was largely through FitzGerald that English readers came to know Khayyam at all.' That reasoning assumes that knowing Khayyam through FitzGerald brought readers toward the Persian poet. If those readers instead took FitzGerald's version for Khayyam and rejected closer translations (D), the poem's effects themselves extended the remaking the critics complain of. B is the tempting choice: a few earlier readers don't touch 'largely.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most undercuts the author's reason for calling the charge weakest when applied to the poem's effects.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, second sentence; paragraph 3, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Claim: the charge is weakest regarding effects. Reason: through FitzGerald English readers came to know Khayyam. Gap: that 'coming to know Khayyam' meant meeting the Persian poet rather than FitzGerald's remade one. Prephrase a weakener: the readers FitzGerald reached ended up with his Khayyam in place of the Persian one. Choices about the letter, the authenticity lists or a handful of earlier readers miss this gap.

choices.note: Irrelevant to the target. Admiration in other letters bears on FitzGerald's attitude, the letter-level charge, not on the poem's effects; if anything it softens the charge.
Too weak. A few earlier readers are compatible with English readers having come to know Khayyam 'largely' through FitzGerald.
Irrelevant. Revising Zhukovsky's list affects which poems are authentic, not whether the poem's effects on English readers were appropriative.

CORRECT. If the readers FitzGerald reached took his sequence for Khayyam and rejected closer versions, then the poem's effects themselves carried on the remaking of the Persian poet that the critics charge, undercutting the author's reason for calling the charge weakest there.
Irrelevant. Praise for rendering a Persian outlook says nothing about what readers came to know or believe about Khayyam as a result.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?
choices: A poem's publication history is recounted; a scholarly discovery is shown to discredit the poem; and three responses to that discovery are compared and ranked.
A poem's history and form are given; the identity of its source is questioned; rival assessments of it are presented; and the author weighs them.
A translator's method is described; the method is defended against an objection; the objection is traced to its source; and a new method of translation is proposed.
A poetic form is defined; its history in Persian literature is surveyed; its adaptation into English is criticized; and the author recommends a more faithful adaptation.
Three assessments of a poem are presented; evidence for each is reviewed; one of them is endorsed; and the remaining two are shown to rest on a common error.
questions.explanation: P1 gives the 1859 publication, reception and the ruba'i form; P2 questions what FitzGerald was translating; P3 describes his method and three verdicts; P4 weighs them ('none is adequate alone'). B tracks all four. E is the trap: the author endorses none of the three verdicts.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe the passage's paragraph-by-paragraph structure.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of each paragraph, and paragraph 4, first sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Label each paragraph: P1 history and form; P2 uncertain source; P3 method plus three verdicts; P4 author's weighing, with a qualified synthesis. Then match the sequence, checking every clause of each choice; half-right structures fail on one clause.

choices.note: Distortion. The authenticity problem does not 'discredit' the poem, and the three verdicts respond to FitzGerald's method, not to Zhukovsky's discovery; nor are they ranked.

CORRECT. P1 recounts history and form, P2 says the source 'is less certain than it appears,' P3 gives FitzGerald's method and three verdicts, and P4 weighs them: 'Each verdict captures something, but none is adequate alone.'
Half right at best. The passage describes a method, but it neither defends it against an objection nor proposes a new method of translation.
Distortion. The form is defined only briefly, no history of the form in Persian is surveyed, and the author recommends no other adaptation.
Wrong conclusion. The verdicts appear only in P3, and the author endorses none of them: 'none is adequate alone.'

sections.title: Reading Through Ideas 10: Haiku and the Imagist Image · Cathay and the Chinese Character · Eliot, al-Sayyab and the dying god · Ibn 'Arabi, Donne and the sacred love poem

passages.title: Haiku and the Imagist Image
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
In his 1914 essay "Vorticism," Ezra Pound recounted the making of a famous poem. After seeing beautiful faces in the Paris Métro, he wrote a thirty-line poem and destroyed it as work 'of second intensity'; six months later he wrote a poem half that length; a year later he arrived at what he called a "hokku-like sentence." Published in Poetry in 1913, "In a Station of the Metro" sets a line about faces in a crowd beside a second line, "Petals on a wet, black bough," with no verb. His explanation became an Imagist touchstone: "the 'one image poem' is a form of super-position, that is to say, it is one idea set on top of another."

Pound's model had exacting conventions. The hokku began as the opening verse of a haikai sequence, a chain of linked stanzas; only in the 1890s did Masaoka Shiki promote the independent verse under the name haiku. Its seventeen units fall into phrases of five, seven, and five, but the units are on, measures of sound length rather than syllables: Tōkyō, two syllables in English, counts as four on. A kigo, or season word, places the verse within a season and its accumulated associations, and a kireji, or cutting word, divides the verse into two parts whose relation the reader must supply. In Bashō's verse of 1686, furuike ya / kawazu tobikomu / mizu no oto (glossed word for word: an old pond; a frog jumps in; the sound of water), the frog is a season word for spring, and the cutting word ya sets the still pond apart from the sudden sound.

How much of this did Pound absorb? Yoshinobu Hakutani, in Haiku and Modernist Poetics (2009), argues that Imagism originated in haiku and that Pound learned of the hokku chiefly through the Japanese poet Yone Noguchi, who wrote hokku in English, rather than through F. S. Flint. On this account, super-position is Pound's name for the juxtaposition that the cutting word creates. Skeptics reply that Pound knew no Japanese and inherited a reception, shaped by Basil Hall Chamberlain's 1902 study of Bashō, that treated the hokku as a kind of epigram, valued it as a compressed image, and had little use for the season word.

Each side, I think, has hold of part of the truth. Pound grasped the structural core of the form: two elements placed side by side, their connection left unstated. But his two lines relate as image and figure. The petals stand for the faces, so the second line interprets the first. In Bashō's verse the pond and the splash are both actually present, and the cut joins two perceptions of a single scene rather than a thing and its metaphorical equivalent. The petals may evoke spring, yet nothing in Pound's poem works as a conventional season word, binding it to a shared calendar of associations; the vision remains Pound's own. He took the cut without the season, adopting juxtaposition as a technique of compression rather than as a discipline of attention. That partial reading was nonetheless productive: it gave English verse a device its own traditions lacked.

sources.author: Ezra Pound
sources.title: Vorticism
sources.note: Fortnightly Review, 1 September 1914; Pound's account of the Metro poem's drafts and his theory of the image. Source of the quotations "hokku-like sentence" and "the 'one image poem' is a form of super-position, that is to say, it is one idea set on top of another"; the poem line "Petals on a wet, black bough" is from 'In a Station of the Metro' (Poetry, April 1913).

sources.author: Yoshinobu Hakutani
sources.title: Haiku and Modernist Poetics
sources.note: Palgrave Macmillan; traces haiku from Bashō to Western modernism and argues that Pound's Imagism originated in haiku, with Yone Noguchi rather than F. S. Flint as Pound's main source on the hokku (paraphrased, not quoted).

sources.author: Basil Hall Chamberlain
sources.title: Bashō and the Japanese Poetical Epigram
sources.note: Transactions of the Asiatic Society of Japan; an influential early English account of Bashō that framed the hokku as an 'epigram', the reception the passage's skeptics point to (paraphrased).

passages.title: Cathay and the Chinese Character
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
In 1913 Mary Fenollosa entrusted Ezra Pound with the notebooks of her late husband, Ernest Fenollosa, an American scholar of East Asian art who had studied Chinese poetry with Japanese teachers. The notes gave word-by-word glosses of the poems and recorded the poets' names in their Japanese readings, which is why Li Bai appears in Pound's book as Rihaku. Pound knew no Chinese, yet the small volume he made from the notes, Cathay (1915), changed what English readers expected Chinese poetry to sound like; T. S. Eliot would later call Pound the inventor of Chinese poetry for our time.

The notebooks also contained an essay, which Pound published in 1919 as "The Chinese Written Character as a Medium for Poetry." Fenollosa held that the Chinese character is not an arbitrary sign but "a vivid shorthand picture of the operations of nature." In the sentence glossed "man sees horse," he claimed, the reader sees a man standing on his legs, an eye moving on running legs, and a horse on its four legs, so that the writing preserves the movement of the action it names. Poetry written in such characters, Fenollosa concluded, stays close to things and to the verbs that relate them, and Pound took the essay as the charter of what he came to call his ideogrammic method.

Sinologists have been severe. George Kennedy, in a 1958 essay, judged Fenollosa's account confused throughout, and John DeFrancis, in The Chinese Language: Fact and Fantasy (1984), listed the belief that characters represent ideas rather than sounds as the first of the myths about Chinese writing. Most characters, DeFrancis showed, are phonetic compounds, pairing an element that indicates meaning with one that indicates pronunciation; a literate reader takes them as signs for words of the spoken language, not as pictures. Fenollosa's etymologies, on this view, describe a script that no Chinese reader experiences.

Wai-lim Yip's Ezra Pound's Cathay (1969) does not defend the ideogram theory, but it argues that Pound captured genuine features of classical Chinese verse. The lines of that verse regularly omit the grammatical subject, mark no tense, and set images side by side without connectives. Pound's spare, paratactic English, Yip contends, preserves this mode of presentation better than translations that supply the subjects, tenses, and connectives English grammar seems to demand, and despite his errors Pound reached the original poets' concerns through what Yip calls "a kind of clairvoyance."

Yip's case is persuasive, but it shows that what Pound got right he got despite the theory rather than because of it. Parataxis and the absence of tense are features of syntax, and no picture theory of individual characters would reveal them. Nor did Pound preserve them consistently. A line in Li Bai's farewell poem, glossed word for word, reads floating cloud, wanderer's mind, with no verb or word of comparison; Pound's version, "Mind like a floating wide cloud," supplies the simile that the original leaves to the reader. Cathay is neither a vindication of Fenollosa nor a mere mistranslation, but an uneven achievement whose best moments rest on a sound perception of syntax.

sources.author: Ernest Fenollosa and Ezra Pound
sources.title: The Chinese Written Character as a Medium for Poetry
sources.note: Fenollosa's essay as edited and published by Pound (Little Review, 1919; book 1936; critical edition ed. Haun Saussy et al., Fordham, 2008); argues that characters picture natural processes, with the 'man sees horse' example. Source of the quotation "a vivid shorthand picture of the operations of nature."

sources.author: Wai-lim Yip
sources.title: Ezra Pound's Cathay
sources.note: Princeton University Press; argues that, whatever his errors, Pound caught the paratactic, tenseless, subject-dropping presentation of classical Chinese verse. Source of the quotation "a kind of clairvoyance"; Pound's line "Mind like a floating wide cloud" is from 'Taking Leave of a Friend' in Cathay (1915).

sources.author: John DeFrancis
sources.title: The Chinese Language: Fact and Fantasy
sources.note: University of Hawaii Press; the linguist's case against 'the ideographic myth', showing that Chinese characters are overwhelmingly phonetic compounds that write words of the spoken language (paraphrased).

sources.author: George A. Kennedy
sources.title: Fenollosa, Pound and the Chinese Character
sources.note: Yale Literary Magazine 126(5); the classic sinologist's critique of Fenollosa's essay, faulting its neglect of the phonetic component of characters (paraphrased).

passages.title: Eliot, al-Sayyab and the dying god
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Passage A

In the notes he appended to The Waste Land (1922), T. S. Eliot acknowledged that "the plan and a good deal of the incidental symbolism of the poem" were suggested by Jessie L. Weston's From Ritual to Romance (1920), and he named a second debt, to James Frazer's The Golden Bough. From Frazer came the dying and reviving gods of the eastern Mediterranean, Adonis, Attis, and Osiris, whose deaths and returns were believed to bring back the crops. From Weston came the argument that the medieval Grail romances preserved such a ritual in the figure of the Fisher King, a wounded ruler whose land lies barren until he is healed.

Eliot uses these materials chiefly by inversion. The poem's first line, "April is the cruellest month," treats the season of rebirth as an unwelcome disturbance of a comfortable numbness, and a later stanza asks of a corpse planted in a garden whether it has begun to sprout, as if the vegetation rite had dwindled into a macabre joke. Cleanth Brooks read the poem as organized by the paradox that true life comes only through a kind of death, and he found in its final section, where thunder speaks over a parched land, a real promise of renewal. The promise is there, but the poem does not keep it: rain is heralded and never falls, and near the close the speaker sits on the shore, the arid plain behind him, asking whether he shall at least set his lands in order. Eliot invokes the reviving god chiefly to measure a spiritual drought, not to end it.

Passage B

When Nazik al-Mala'ika and Badr Shakir al-Sayyab published their first poems in shi'r hurr, or free verse, in 1947, they broke with a form that had governed Arabic poetry for over a millennium: the line of two balanced hemistichs, sustained through an entire poem on one meter and one rhyme. The new verse kept the classical foot (taf'ila) but let each line hold as many feet as the sense required, and admitted shifting rhymes and refrains. That freedom soon carried a new mythology. Jabra Ibrahim Jabra, who in 1957 published an Arabic translation of the Adonis section of Frazer's The Golden Bough, gave wide currency to the Mesopotamian Tammuz, and the poets critics came to call the Tammuzis, al-Sayyab and Adunis among them, made the dying god central.

These poets knew Eliot's use of the myth, and al-Sayyab's "Rain Song" has often been read against The Waste Land. But the borrowing altered the myth's meaning. In al-Sayyab's poem, punctuated by the refrain matar ("rain"), the rain does fall; yet, the speaker says, not a year passes in Iraq without hunger. The barrenness is social, not natural. The poem's last stanza finds in each drop of rain the bud of a flower and a smile awaiting new lips in the world of tomorrow. For poets writing after the loss of Palestine in 1948 and amid struggles against colonial power, Tammuz promised that sacrifice would bring a people back to life. What Eliot used to measure a desolation, they used to prophesy an end to one.

sources.author: T. S. Eliot
sources.title: The Waste Land
sources.note: The poem itself; the quotation "the plan and a good deal of the incidental symbolism of the poem" is from the opening paragraph of Eliot's Notes (crediting Jessie L. Weston's From Ritual to Romance), and "April is the cruellest month" is the poem's first line, both as printed in the Project Gutenberg text of the 1922 edition.

sources.author: Jessie L. Weston
sources.title: From Ritual to Romance
sources.note: Argues that the Grail romances, with their wounded Fisher King and wasted land, preserve the remains of an ancient fertility ritual; the book Eliot named as the source of his poem's plan.

sources.author: Cleanth Brooks
sources.title: Modern Poetry and the Tradition
sources.note: Its chapter "The Waste Land: Critique of the Myth" is the classic New Critical reading, organizing the poem around the paradox of life through death and finding in it a qualified hope of renewal.

sources.author: Salma Khadra Jayyusi
sources.title: Trends and Movements in Modern Arabic Poetry
sources.note: The standard two-volume history of modern Arabic poetry, covering the free-verse movement of al-Mala'ika and al-Sayyab and the Tammuzi poets' use of the Tammuz-Adonis myth as a symbol of national resurrection.

passages.title: Ibn 'Arabi, Donne and the sacred love poem
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
In Mecca, where he lived in the first years of the thirteenth century, the Andalusian mystic Muhyiddin Ibn 'Arabi came to know Nizam, the learned daughter of a Persian scholar, and he later presented her as the inspiration for the poems of his Tarjuman al-Ashwaq (The Interpreter of Desires). The poems are built from the conventions of the classical Arabic love ode: the nasib, in which the poet halts at the traces of an abandoned campsite and remembers a beloved whose tribe has moved on; the camel litters carrying her away; the gazelles, doves, and desert place names of Arabia. Some readers took the collection for exactly what it appeared to be, the love poetry of a man of religion. Ibn 'Arabi answered them with a commentary, begun in Aleppo, that glosses the poems' images line by line as figures of divine knowledge and of the soul's longing for God.

John Donne seems to present the opposite case. In the sonnet that begins "Batter my heart, three-person'd God," the speaker begs God to overthrow him like a besieged town and ends with a frankly sexual paradox: he will never be "chaste, except you ravish me." No commentary is needed to show that this erotic language is a figure, since the poem names its addressee in its first line and speaks the vocabulary of Christian theology. It is tempting to conclude that the sacred meaning of Donne's sonnet lies in the poem, whereas that of Ibn 'Arabi's odes is supplied afterward by an interpreter, so that the commentary converts love poetry into mystical verse.

That conclusion is too simple on both sides. The Tarjuman itself signals that its love is not merely human. In one ode, in R. A. Nicholson's 1911 translation, the speaker's heart "has become capable of every form," a pasture for gazelles and a convent for monks, the pilgrim's Ka'ba and the tables of the Torah and the Qur'an, and he declares, "I follow the religion of Love." A beloved who can be all of these is not simply a woman in Mecca. Moreover, Sufi audiences had long heard ordinary love poetry as speaking of God, so the conventions Ibn 'Arabi used already carried that possibility. Conversely, Donne's paradox reads as devotion rather than blasphemy only for readers who know the long Christian tradition, rooted in allegorical readings of the Song of Songs, that pictures the soul as the bride of God.

Michael Sells, whose 2021 translation is the first complete English version since Nicholson's, insists that the poems are not simply versified doctrine. That warning is sound, but it does not show that the commentary imposes a foreign meaning on them. What the two cases suggest instead is that sacred meaning resides neither in the poem alone nor in its interpreter alone, but in conventions of reading that poet and audience share. Ibn 'Arabi's commentary made explicit, for readers who had forgotten such conventions or refused them, what Donne could still assume.

sources.author: Ibn al-'Arabi (ed. and trans. Reynold A. Nicholson)
sources.title: The Tarjumán al-Ashwáq: A Collection of Mystical Odes
sources.note: Nicholson's edition and literal translation, with an abridged version of Ibn 'Arabi's own commentary and his account of why he wrote it; the quotations "has become capable of every form" and "I follow the religion of Love" are from Nicholson's rendering of the ode on the heart's many forms (Royal Asiatic Society, London).

sources.author: Michael Sells (trans.)
sources.title: The Translator of Desires: Poems
sources.note: The first complete English translation since Nicholson's, with a facing Arabic text, per-poem commentary and Ibn 'Arabi's prefaces; Sells places the poems in the Arabic love-poetry tradition and argues they are not merely rhymed versions of Ibn 'Arabi's doctrines (Princeton University Press).

sources.author: John Donne (ed. Helen Gardner)
sources.title: The Divine Poems
sources.note: Gardner's Oxford edition of Donne's religious verse, including the Holy Sonnets; the quotations "Batter my heart, three-person'd God" and "chaste, except you ravish me" are from that sonnet (Holy Sonnet 14 in the traditional numbering), first printed in 1633.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Pound's "In a Station of the Metro" is best understood as an English haiku, since its two juxtaposed lines reproduce the effect that the cutting word creates in Bashō's verse.
Because Pound knew no Japanese and relied on a Western reception that treated the hokku as an epigram, his claim to have written a "hokku-like sentence" should not be taken seriously.
The conventions of the haiku, including its measure in on, its season word, and its cutting word, were largely lost when the form was adopted by English-language poets.
Pound took the haiku's unexplained pairing of two elements but not its way of relating them or its season word, a partial borrowing that still enriched English verse.
Hakutani's account of Pound's sources is more persuasive than that of the skeptics, because it explains the Metro poem's juxtaposition as a direct inheritance from the hokku.
questions.explanation: The author's view is in the last paragraph: each side 'has hold of part of the truth'; Pound 'took the cut without the season,' and his two lines relate 'as image and figure' rather than as two perceptions, yet the 'partial reading was nonetheless productive.' D states all three parts. A is Hakutani's view as the passage reports it, which the author accepts only in part; B is the skeptics' view pushed further than even they go.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall claim about what Pound took from the haiku.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, first sentence and last three sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Map: P1 Pound's account and his 'super-position' formula; P2 the haiku's elements, with Bashō's frog verse; P3 two positions (Hakutani: Imagism comes from haiku, super-position = the cut's juxtaposition; skeptics: Pound inherited a reductive Western reception); P4 the author: both partly right. Pound got the structural core (two elements, connection unstated) but related them as image and figure, without a season word; the partial reading was still productive. Prephrase: Pound borrowed the cut, not the season or Bashō's way of joining two perceptions, and that half-borrowing was valuable anyway.

choices.note: Wrong position-holder. This is roughly Hakutani's view as paragraph 3 reports it. The author says the Metro poem's lines relate 'as image and figure,' unlike Bashō's two perceptions, so the effect is not reproduced.
Too extreme, and the wrong position. The skeptics' points appear in paragraph 3, but the author credits Pound with grasping 'the structural core of the form' and calls his reading 'productive.'
Out of scope and too broad. The passage is about Pound's poem, not English-language haiku poets generally, and it never says the measure in on was lost by anyone.

CORRECT. Paragraph 4: Pound 'grasped the structural core,' but his lines 'relate as image and figure,' and he 'took the cut without the season'; still, 'That partial reading was nonetheless productive.'
Distortion. The author does not rank Hakutani above the skeptics; 'Each side, I think, has hold of part of the truth.' The author also denies that the juxtaposition works as it does in the hokku.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the kireji, or cutting word, in a haiku
choices: places the verse within a particular season and its accumulated associations
divides the verse into two parts and leaves their relation for the reader to supply
marks the boundaries between the three phrases of five, seven, and five on
links the opening verse of a haikai sequence to the stanza that follows it
turns the second part of the verse into a metaphor for the first part
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says a kireji 'divides the verse into two parts whose relation the reader must supply.' B restates that. A is what the passage says the kigo does, a shell game on the two Japanese terms; E is what the author says Pound's second line does, not what the cutting word does.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Retrieve what the passage says the cutting word does.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, fourth sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The passage defines two terms in one sentence: the kigo (season word) and the kireji (cutting word). Keep them apart. The cutting word divides the verse into two parts 'whose relation the reader must supply.'

choices.note: Shell game. This is the passage's definition of the kigo, the season word, from the same sentence.
CORRECT. Paragraph 2: a kireji 'divides the verse into two parts whose relation the reader must supply.'
Distortion. The passage says the verse has phrases of five, seven, and five on, but it never says the cutting word marks those phrase boundaries; it makes one cut that yields two parts.
Out of scope. The passage says the hokku was the opening verse of a linked sequence, but it says nothing about what links it to the next stanza.

Opposite of the author's contrast. Paragraph 4 says Pound's second line works as a metaphor for the first, while in Bashō's verse the cut joins two perceptions 'rather than a thing and its metaphorical equivalent.'

questions.stem: By "a discipline of attention" (fourth paragraph, second-to-last sentence), the author most probably means
choices: a strict adherence to the count of seventeen on in phrases of five, seven, and five
a habit of reducing a long first draft until only a single image remains
a willingness to let the reader rather than the poet determine what a poem means
a practice of selecting images that can stand as metaphors for a poet's private vision
a way of presenting things perceived together in one scene, within shared conventions
questions.explanation: The phrase is contrasted with 'a technique of compression' and sums up what Pound left out: Bashō's cut 'joins two perceptions of a single scene,' both 'actually present,' and the season word binds the verse to 'a shared calendar of associations.' E combines these. B describes compression, the very thing the phrase is contrasted with; D describes Pound's practice, the opposite of what is meant.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out what the phrase means from what the author contrasts it with.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, sentences 4-7.

breakdown.analysis: The sentence says Pound took 'the cut without the season,' using juxtaposition 'as a technique of compression rather than as a discipline of attention.' So the phrase names what Bashō's practice has and Pound's lacks. The preceding sentences supply it: both elements are 'actually present' as 'two perceptions of a single scene,' and the season word ties the verse to 'a shared calendar of associations' rather than a private vision. Prephrase: attending to what is really there together, inside a shared convention.

choices.note: Out of scope for the phrase. The passage notes the 5-7-5 measure in paragraph 2 but never connects it to what Pound failed to adopt; the contrast in paragraph 4 is about perception and the season word.
Opposite. Paring a draft down to one image is Pound's compression, the term the author sets against 'a discipline of attention.'
Distortion. Leaving the relation for the reader to supply is part of the cut, which the author says Pound did adopt, so it cannot be what he missed.
Opposite. Metaphor and a vision that 'remains Pound's own' are what the author says distinguish Pound's poem from Bashō's.

CORRECT. In Bashō's verse 'the pond and the splash are both actually present' as 'two perceptions of a single scene,' and the season word binds the verse 'to a shared calendar of associations.' That is what the phrase names.

questions.stem: The author's remark that in Bashō's verse "the pond and the splash are both actually present" (fourth paragraph) primarily serves to
choices: help distinguish the way the parts of Bashō's verse are related from the way the two lines of Pound's poem are related
show that Bashō's verse, unlike Pound's poem, contains a word that marks the season in which it is set
support Hakutani's claim that super-position is Pound's name for the juxtaposition created by the cutting word
suggest that Pound's poem would have been more faithful to the hokku if it had described an actual scene in the Métro
explain why the skeptics regard the Western reception of the hokku as having reduced the form to a compressed image
questions.explanation: The remark comes right after 'his two lines relate as image and figure. The petals stand for the faces,' and is followed by 'rather than a thing and its metaphorical equivalent.' Its job is the contrast in A. B confuses this point with the separate point about the season word, which the author makes in the next sentence.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the remark about Bashō's pond and splash does in the author's argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, sentences 2-4.

breakdown.analysis: Sentence 2: Pound's lines relate 'as image and figure.' Sentence 3: the petals stand for the faces. Sentence 4: in Bashō both things are 'actually present,' so the cut joins 'two perceptions of a single scene rather than a thing and its metaphorical equivalent.' The remark sets up a contrast in how the two parts relate. The season word is a second, separate difference, made in the next sentence.

choices.note: CORRECT. The remark contrasts Bashō's two perceptions of one scene with Pound's 'image and figure,' in which the petals 'stand for the faces.'
Shell game. The season-word difference is real, but the author makes it in the next sentence; this remark is about whether both parts are literally there.
Opposite. The remark marks a difference between Pound's juxtaposition and Bashō's, which qualifies Hakutani's equation rather than supporting it.
Unsupported. The author never says what Pound should have written. Pound's first line does describe faces in an actual crowd; the issue is that the second line is figurative.
Wrong paragraph and wrong party. The skeptics' view is in paragraph 3, and this remark is the author's own analysis, not an explanation of theirs.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about Hakutani's view that super-position is Pound's name for the juxtaposition created by the cutting word?
choices: It is mistaken, because Pound learned of the hokku through a Western reception that had little interest in the form's actual structure.
It is correct, because the Metro poem, like Bashō's verse, sets two elements side by side and leaves their connection unstated.
It identifies a structural feature Pound genuinely shared with the hokku but obscures a difference in how the juxtaposed elements relate.
It would be accurate if the petals in Pound's poem functioned as a conventional season word rather than merely evoking spring.
It cannot be evaluated without knowing whether Pound learned of the hokku from Noguchi or from Flint.
questions.explanation: The author agrees that Pound 'grasped the structural core of the form: two elements placed side by side, their connection left unstated,' which is what Hakutani's equation captures; but the author adds that Pound's elements relate 'as image and figure' while Bashō's are 'two perceptions of a single scene.' So the equation is half right, as C says. B is the trap: it states the half the author accepts and then calls the view simply correct, ignoring the difference the author goes on to draw.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Infer the author's assessment of one specific claim from paragraph 3.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, third sentence (the claim); paragraph 4, first four sentences (the author's response).

breakdown.analysis: Hakutani's claim: super-position = the juxtaposition the cut creates. The author: 'Each side, I think, has hold of part of the truth.' Pound has the core (two elements, connection unstated), which supports the claim as far as structure goes. But the relation is image-and-figure in Pound and two perceptions in Bashō, so calling them the same thing is too much. Prephrase: right about the structure, misses how the parts relate. Watch for choices that pick one side, and for one that swaps in the season-word point as if it were the only obstacle.

choices.note: Wrong position-holder. This is the skeptics' line, and the author grants that Pound did grasp the form's 'structural core,' so the claim is not simply mistaken.

Half right. The reason given is one the author accepts, but the author then shows that Pound's two elements relate differently ('image and figure'), so the author would not call the equation simply correct.

CORRECT. The author credits Pound with 'two elements placed side by side, their connection left unstated' but says his lines 'relate as image and figure,' unlike Bashō's 'two perceptions of a single scene.'
Distortion. The season word is a separate gap in the author's account; even with one, Pound's lines would still relate as image and figure, so fixing it would not make the equation accurate.
Irrelevant to the author's assessment. The author evaluates the claim by comparing the poems, not by settling the source question, and never suggests the source dispute must be resolved first.

questions.stem: Which one of the following short English poems would the author be most likely to regard as closest in method to Bashō's verse rather than to Pound's poem?
choices: Three lines of five, seven, and five English syllables comparing a widow's grief to snow that will not melt
Two lines in which a crowd of umbrellas is presented, without a verb, as a field of black mushrooms after rain
A single sentence in which the poet states that the cry of a gull reminds him of a friend who has died
Three lines that name the late autumn season and then explain why the season always makes the poet melancholy
Two lines setting the first frost on a garden path beside a dog's bark from the next farm
questions.explanation: On the author's account, Bashō's method joins two things 'both actually present,' 'two perceptions of a single scene,' with a season word and the relation left unstated. E has two literal perceptions, a seasonal marker (first frost), and no connective. B is the trap: it has Pound's verbless juxtaposition, but the mushrooms stand for the umbrellas, the 'image and figure' relation the author attributes to Pound.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply the author's contrast between Bashō's and Pound's methods to new poems.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, fourth and fifth sentences; paragraph 4, sentences 2-6.

breakdown.analysis: Pull out what marks Bashō's method on the author's account: (1) two parts, relation unstated (the cut); (2) both parts literally present, two perceptions of one scene; (3) a season word tying the verse to shared associations. Pound's method has (1) but replaces (2) with image-and-figure and lacks (3). Find the poem with all three. Beware poems that match the syllable count, since the passage says on are not English syllables and the author never treats the count as the decisive difference.

choices.note: Wrong criterion. Counting English syllables is not the passage's measure (on 'rather than syllables'), and comparing grief to snow is a figure, the feature the author links to Pound.
Tempting, but this is Pound's method: a verbless juxtaposition in which the second image stands for the first, as the petals 'stand for the faces.'
Fails the cut. The poet states the connection (it 'reminds him' of the friend), so nothing is left for the reader to supply.
Half right. It names a season, but explaining the poet's feeling states the relation the cut is supposed to leave open, and the vision stays private.
CORRECT. Two things actually present in one scene, a seasonal marker, and the relation left unstated: the features the author assigns to Bashō's verse and not to Pound's.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the author's claim that Pound "took the cut without the season"?
choices: Many readers of Pound's poem have taken its wet petals to suggest a rainy day in spring.
Pound wrote while composing the poem that the petals were meant to serve as a hokku-style season word for spring.
Several of the English-language hokku that Noguchi published included conventional Japanese season words.
Chamberlain's 1902 study of Bashō discussed the role of season words in some detail.
Pound later studied Japanese and translated several Nō plays from the notes of a Western scholar.
questions.explanation: The author's claim is that nothing in Pound's poem 'works as a conventional season word,' so he adopted the cut but not the season. Evidence that Pound deliberately built in a season word on the hokku model (B) cuts directly against that. A is the trap: the author already concedes 'The petals may evoke spring'; evoking a season is not functioning as a conventional season word. C and D concern Noguchi and Chamberlain, not what Pound did.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most undercuts the claim that Pound adopted the cutting word but not the season word.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, sixth and seventh sentences; paragraph 3, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The claim has two halves, but the 'without the season' half is the vulnerable one. The author's support: 'The petals may evoke spring, yet nothing in Pound's poem works as a conventional season word.' So a weakener must show that Pound's poem does use a season word in the hokku's way, not just that it suggests a season. Watch for the concession trap (the author already grants the evocation) and for facts about other people's knowledge, which don't touch what Pound did.

choices.note: Already conceded. The author grants that 'The petals may evoke spring'; readers' associations don't show the petals work as a conventional season word.
CORRECT. If Pound deliberately used the petals as a season word modeled on the hokku, the poem does take over the season-word convention, contrary to 'without the season.'
Out of scope. Even if Pound learned from Noguchi, what Noguchi's poems contained doesn't show that Pound's poem uses a season word.
Irrelevant to the claim. This would weaken the skeptics' account of the Western reception in paragraph 3, but the author's claim is about Pound's poem, not about what was available to him.
Out of scope. Pound's later study of Japanese has no bearing on whether the 1913 poem contains a season word.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Although Fenollosa misunderstood how Chinese characters work, his essay correctly identified the features of classical Chinese verse that Pound's Cathay preserves.
Pound's Cathay, which rests on Fenollosa's mistaken account of the Chinese character, is better understood as an original English work than as a translation.
Pound's Cathay unevenly captured real syntactic features of classical Chinese verse, successes that owe little to the ideogram theory.
Yip has shown that Pound's lack of Chinese did not prevent him from translating the poems of Li Bai more accurately than academic sinologists did.
The sinologists' criticisms of Fenollosa's essay have been answered by Yip's demonstration that classical Chinese verse omits subjects, tense, and connectives.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph gives the author's verdict: Pound got things right 'despite the theory rather than because of it,' he did not preserve parataxis 'consistently,' and Cathay is 'an uneven achievement whose best moments rest on a sound perception of syntax.' C states it. E misreads Yip's role: the passage says Yip 'does not defend the ideogram theory,' so he answers the sinologists on nothing; A gives Fenollosa's essay credit the author gives to syntax instead.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall verdict on Cathay and its relation to Fenollosa's theory.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 5, first sentence and last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Map: P1 the notebooks and Cathay's influence; P2 Fenollosa's ideogram theory; P3 sinologists' refutation; P4 Yip: the theory is wrong, but Pound caught real features of the verse (no subject, no tense, parataxis); P5 author: Yip is persuasive, but the successes came despite the theory, and Pound was inconsistent. Prephrase: Cathay got real syntax right, unevenly, and not because of the ideogram theory.

choices.note: Distortion. The author says no picture theory of characters 'would reveal' parataxis and absent tense, so Fenollosa's essay did not identify the features Pound preserved.

Unsupported. The author rejects 'mere mistranslation' and calls Cathay an 'achievement' resting on 'a sound perception of syntax,' but never reclassifies it as an original work rather than a translation; the Eliot remark is reported, not adopted.

CORRECT. Paragraph 5: Pound got things right 'despite the theory rather than because of it,' did not preserve these features 'consistently,' and Cathay is 'an uneven achievement' resting on 'a sound perception of syntax.'
Too strong. Yip says Pound's English preserves a 'mode of presentation' better than some translations, not that Pound was more accurate overall; the passage mentions Pound's 'errors.'
Wrong relationship. Yip 'does not defend the ideogram theory,' so his argument leaves the sinologists' criticism of it standing; it addresses a different question.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Li Bai's name appears in Cathay as Rihaku because
choices: Fenollosa's notes recorded the poets' names in their Japanese readings
Pound preferred names that would sound unfamiliar to English readers
Fenollosa had misidentified the author of the poems he glossed
Mary Fenollosa had transcribed her husband's notes into Japanese
Pound took the poems from a Japanese anthology rather than from Chinese texts
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: the notes 'recorded the poets' names in their Japanese readings, which is why Li Bai appears in Pound's book as Rihaku.' A restates it. B invents a motive for Pound; E confuses the source of the names with the source of the poems.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Retrieve the passage's stated reason for the name Rihaku.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The passage states the cause directly, with 'which is why.' The answer should be about Fenollosa's notes recording Japanese readings, nothing more.

choices.note: CORRECT. Paragraph 1: the notes 'recorded the poets' names in their Japanese readings, which is why Li Bai appears in Pound's book as Rihaku.'
Out of scope. The passage gives no motive of Pound's for the name; it attributes the form to the notes.
Unsupported. A Japanese reading of a name is not a misidentification; the passage says nothing about the wrong author.
Distortion. Mary Fenollosa 'entrusted' the notebooks to Pound; the passage never says she transcribed them.
Unsupported. Fenollosa studied with Japanese teachers, but the passage says Pound worked from Fenollosa's notes, not from a Japanese anthology.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that DeFrancis would be most likely to regard Fenollosa's analysis of the sentence glossed "man sees horse" as
choices: an accurate description of a small class of characters that Fenollosa wrongly took to be typical of the script
evidence that Fenollosa understood the meaning of the characters but misunderstood their pronunciation
a sound account of the characters' historical origins that has no bearing on how classical poems were composed
an attribution to readers of a pictorial experience of the characters that literate readers do not have
a reading that, although mistaken about the script, correctly captures the syntax of classical Chinese verse
questions.explanation: DeFrancis's view is that 'a literate reader takes them as signs for words of the spoken language, not as pictures,' and the paragraph concludes that Fenollosa's etymologies 'describe a script that no Chinese reader experiences.' Fenollosa's analysis says 'the reader sees' a man, an eye on legs, a horse; D names exactly that error. A and C import outside knowledge that some characters do descend from pictures, which the passage never attributes to DeFrancis; E is the author's and Yip's point about syntax, not DeFrancis's.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Infer DeFrancis's likely verdict on one specific example from paragraph 2.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, third sentence; paragraph 3, second and third sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Fenollosa's example is framed in terms of what 'the reader sees.' DeFrancis, as reported: most characters are phonetic compounds, and literate readers take characters 'as signs for words of the spoken language, not as pictures.' The paragraph's last sentence: these etymologies describe 'a script that no Chinese reader experiences.' So DeFrancis would say Fenollosa credits readers with seeing pictures they don't see. Stay within what the passage attributes to DeFrancis; a reader who knows that some characters began as pictographs may be drawn to A or C, but the passage gives DeFrancis no such concession.

choices.note: Beyond the passage. Some characters may in fact have pictorial origins, but the passage attributes no such concession to DeFrancis; it reports only that 'most' are phonetic compounds and that readers do not take characters as pictures.
Distortion. Nothing in the passage says Fenollosa erred about pronunciation while getting meaning right; DeFrancis's point is that characters write spoken words.
Unsupported. The passage never says DeFrancis accepts Fenollosa's etymologies as history; it says they 'describe a script that no Chinese reader experiences.'
CORRECT. Fenollosa says 'the reader sees' the pictures; DeFrancis holds that a literate reader takes characters 'as signs for words of the spoken language, not as pictures.'
Wrong position-holder. The point about syntax is Yip's and the author's; nothing ties DeFrancis to it, and the author says a picture theory of characters would not reveal syntax.

questions.stem: The author's discussion of a line from Li Bai's farewell poem (fifth paragraph) serves primarily to
choices: show that Pound misunderstood the meaning of the Chinese line he was translating
illustrate the claim that Pound did not consistently preserve the paratactic syntax of the originals
support Yip's contention that Pound's English preserves the mode of presentation of classical Chinese verse
demonstrate that Fenollosa's word-by-word glosses were less reliable than his essay on the written character
provide an example of a character whose pictorial form Fenollosa analyzed in his notes
questions.explanation: The example follows directly on 'Nor did Pound preserve them consistently': the Chinese line has 'no verb or word of comparison,' and Pound 'supplies the simile that the original leaves to the reader.' B states that role. C reverses it: the example qualifies Yip's contention rather than supporting it; A overstates the charge, since the author objects to the added simile, not to the meaning.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the Li Bai example does in the last paragraph.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 5, sentences 3-5.

breakdown.analysis: Sentence 3: 'Nor did Pound preserve them consistently.' Sentences 4-5: the Chinese line has no verb or comparative word; Pound's adds 'like.' So the example illustrates the inconsistency claim. Watch for the reversal (supporting Yip) and for answers that turn a syntactic point into a semantic one.

choices.note: Too strong. The author's objection is that Pound 'supplies the simile' the original leaves to the reader, a change of syntax, not a misunderstanding of what the line means.
CORRECT. It follows 'Nor did Pound preserve them consistently' and shows Pound adding a word of comparison the Chinese line lacks.
Opposite. The example qualifies Yip's case by showing a place where Pound's English did not preserve the parataxis.
Unsupported. The author relies on a word-by-word gloss to make the point; nothing in the passage questions the reliability of Fenollosa's glosses.
Out of scope. The author discusses the line's syntax; the passage says nothing about Fenollosa analyzing any character in this line.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Yip's argument can most accurately be described as
choices: skeptical, because Yip relies on intuitions about Pound that cannot be tested against the Chinese originals
wholly approving, because Yip shows that the sinologists' criticisms of Pound were mistaken
ambivalent, because Yip's argument supports both Fenollosa's theory and its critics
dismissive, because Yip overlooks the evidence that Pound's translations contain errors
largely favorable, but with reservations about how consistently Pound achieved what Yip credits him with
questions.explanation: The author calls Yip's case 'persuasive' and builds the verdict on Pound's 'sound perception of syntax,' but adds that Pound did not preserve these features 'consistently' and that his successes came 'despite the theory.' E captures the qualified approval. B is too extreme and misstates the target: the sinologists criticized Fenollosa's theory, which Yip does not defend; D is wrong because Yip himself acknowledges Pound's 'errors.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe the author's attitude toward Yip's argument, with its degree.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4 (Yip's argument); paragraph 5, first, third and last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: 'Yip's case is persuasive, but . . .': agreement with a qualification. The qualifications: the successes came despite the theory (a point Yip's case shows, not one against him) and Pound did not preserve parataxis 'consistently' (a real reservation). Prephrase: mostly positive, with a limit on how uniformly Pound did what Yip credits.

choices.note: Opposite in direction. The author calls the case 'persuasive' and tests it against a Chinese line, which shows the claims can be checked.
Too extreme, and misdirected. The author adds a reservation ('Nor did Pound preserve them consistently'), and the sinologists' criticisms concern Fenollosa's theory, which Yip does not dispute.
Distortion. Yip 'does not defend the ideogram theory,' so his argument does not support Fenollosa's theory.
Too extreme and factually off. The author is not dismissive, and Yip's argument acknowledges Pound's 'errors.'
CORRECT. 'Yip's case is persuasive,' yet Pound did not preserve these features 'consistently'; Cathay is 'an uneven achievement.'

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the relationship that the author sees between Fenollosa's theory and Pound's successes in Cathay?
choices: A navigator who trusts an accurate chart reaches harbor safely, though she misreads several of its symbols along the way.
A chemist whose theory of a reaction is correct produces poor results because his laboratory equipment is faulty.
A musician who has memorized a mistaken account of a composer's intentions plays the piece badly and blames the composer.
A traveler using a mistaken map reaches the right village by following the actual lie of the land, which the map does not show.
A student who has been taught an outdated grammar writes correct sentences only when she follows its rules exactly.
questions.explanation: The author holds that the ideogram theory is wrong, that Pound nonetheless got real things right, and that he got them 'despite the theory rather than because of it,' through 'a sound perception of syntax' that 'no picture theory of individual characters would reveal.' D matches: a wrong guide, a right result, and the result due to something the guide does not show. E is the reverse (success because of the flawed guide); A makes the guide accurate.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the structure of the author's view of theory and result to a new case.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 5, first and second sentences, and last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Abstract the relationship: (1) the guiding theory is mistaken (paragraph 3, accepted by the author); (2) the results are in part genuinely good; (3) the good results come from attending to something real that the theory does not reveal (syntax), 'despite the theory rather than because of it.' Find the choice with all three. Eliminate any where the guide is accurate, the result is bad, or the result comes from following the guide.

choices.note: Wrong first element. Here the chart is accurate; in the author's view Fenollosa's theory is mistaken.
Reversed. A correct theory with bad results is the opposite of a mistaken theory with partly good results.
Half right. The account is mistaken, but the result is bad and nothing real guides the musician to success.

CORRECT. A mistaken guide, a right result, and the result owed to something real the guide doesn't show: the author's 'despite the theory rather than because of it,' with syntax as the lie of the land.
Reversed. Success that comes only from following the flawed rules is success because of the guide, which the author denies.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim that what Pound got right in Cathay he got "despite the theory rather than because of it"?
choices: The glosses Pound worked from kept the word order and omissions of the Chinese lines, whatever Fenollosa thought of the characters.
Other modernist poets who accepted Fenollosa's account of the character also wrote in a spare, paratactic English.
Many sinologists who reject the ideogram theory agree that classical Chinese verse commonly omits subjects and tense.
DeFrancis estimated that well over four-fifths of Chinese characters are phonetic compounds.
Pound described several of the Cathay poems as attempts to apply the ideogrammic method he derived from Fenollosa's essay.
questions.explanation: If the syntax Pound reproduced reached him through glosses that preserved it independently of the pictorial analyses, then his successes had a source other than the theory, as the author claims. B would weaken the claim by linking the theory to paratactic style; E also points toward the theory as a cause. C supports Yip's premise that the features are real, which the author already accepts, without showing where Pound's grasp of them came from.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that best supports the claim that Pound's successes did not come from Fenollosa's theory.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 5, first and second sentences; paragraph 1, second sentence (the glosses).

breakdown.analysis: The claim is causal: the theory was not the source of what Pound got right. The author's support: parataxis and absence of tense are syntax, which a picture theory of characters would not reveal. A strengthener gives Pound an independent route to the syntax, or shows the theory couldn't have provided it. A weakener links the theory to the paratactic style. Answers that only confirm the theory is wrong, or that the features are real, don't address where Pound's success came from.

choices.note: CORRECT. It supplies an independent route: the glosses carried the Chinese syntax to Pound regardless of the pictorial analyses, so his paratactic successes need not owe anything to the theory.
Opposite. If poets who held the theory also wrote paratactically, that suggests the theory may have produced the style, weakening 'despite.'
Irrelevant truth. This confirms that the features Yip credits Pound with are real, which the author already accepts; it says nothing about how Pound came to reproduce them.
Premise restatement. More evidence that the theory is wrong about the script doesn't show that Pound's successes didn't come from it; a wrong theory can still prompt a good result.
Opposite. Pound's own statement that he was applying the method points toward the theory as a cause of his practice.

questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with
choices: explaining how Frazer's and Weston's anthropological theories were received by literary critics in English and in Arabic
the use poets made of a myth of a dying and reviving god and the significance they gave it
showing that the Arab free-verse movement owed its formal innovations to the example of Eliot's poetry
the debate over whether the endings of The Waste Land and "Rain Song" promise renewal
the reasons twentieth-century poets turned from traditional forms to free verse
questions.explanation: Passage A shows how Eliot used Frazer's dying gods and Weston's Fisher King and argues he used them 'to measure a spiritual drought'; passage B shows how al-Sayyab and the Tammuzis used Tammuz and argues they made it a prophecy of renewal. B covers both. D is the near-miss: only passage A discusses a critical debate (Brooks), and B never questions whether 'Rain Song' promises renewal.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the topic both passages are mainly about.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first and last sentences of each passage.

breakdown.analysis: Passage A: Eliot borrowed the dying-god myth (Frazer, Weston) and used it by inversion to measure desolation.
