Passage B: Arab free-verse poets borrowed the same kind of myth (Tammuz) and turned it into a promise of national rebirth. Common ground: poets' use of the myth and what they made it mean. Test each choice against both passages.

choices.note: Out of scope. Frazer and Weston are named as Eliot's and Jabra's sources, but neither passage discusses how critics received the anthropology itself.
CORRECT. Each passage describes a poet's or group's borrowing of the dying-and-reviving-god myth and then argues for what the myth means in their poems.

Distortion of passage B. B says the free-verse form came in 1947 and that the Tammuzis 'knew Eliot's use of the myth'; it never attributes the formal innovations to Eliot, and passage A says nothing about form.
Half right. Passage A does weigh Brooks's reading of Eliot's ending, but passage B states flatly how 'Rain Song' closes and debates nothing about it.
Passage B's first paragraph only. Passage A never discusses verse form at all.

questions.stem: According to passage A, the first line of The Waste Land
choices: alludes directly to the Fisher King whose land lies barren until he is healed
is an instance of the paradox Brooks identified, that true life comes only through death
was among the details Eliot said he took from Weston's account of the Grail romances
presents the return of the season associated with rebirth as something unwelcome
announces the rain that the poem's final section heralds but does not bring
questions.explanation: Passage A says the first line 'treats the season of rebirth as an unwelcome disturbance of a comfortable numbness.' D paraphrases that. B is the trap for readers who link Brooks's paradox to the line; the passage attributes the paradox to Brooks's reading of the poem as a whole, not to this line.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what passage A says about the poem's first line.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph of passage A, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The passage quotes 'April is the cruellest month' and says it treats rebirth's season as an unwelcome disturbance. The right answer will paraphrase 'unwelcome'. Watch for choices that attach other details from passage A (Fisher King, Brooks, the rain) to this line.

choices.note: Shell game. The Fisher King appears in the first paragraph as Weston's figure; the passage never connects him to the first line.
Tempting, since Brooks's paradox follows in the same paragraph. But the passage presents it as Brooks's reading of the whole poem and its final section, not as a description of the first line.
Distortion. Eliot's note credits Weston with 'the plan and a good deal of the incidental symbolism'; the passage never says the first line came from her.
CORRECT. 'Treats the season of rebirth as an unwelcome disturbance' is exactly this.
Shell game. The heralded rain belongs to the final section; nothing says the first line announces it.

questions.stem: The author of passage A refers to Cleanth Brooks's reading of The Waste Land primarily in order to
choices: introduce a reading whose observation the author grants but whose conclusion the author resists
provide authoritative support for the author's claim that Eliot used Frazer's and Weston's myths by inversion
show that critics have generally overlooked Eliot's debt to Weston and Frazer
illustrate how New Critical readers ignored the anthropological sources of Eliot's poem
concede that the poem's final section does in fact bring about the renewal that its opening refuses
questions.explanation: Brooks finds 'a real promise of renewal' in the final section; the author replies, 'The promise is there, but the poem does not keep it.' The author accepts that the promise exists and rejects the conclusion that the poem delivers renewal, as A says. E is the trap: the author concedes the promise, not the renewal.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify why the author brings in Brooks.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph of passage A, third and fourth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Map the paragraph: author's thesis (inversion) - Brooks's reading (paradox, promise of renewal) - author's reply ('The promise is there, but the poem does not keep it') - author's conclusion. Brooks is an opposing view the author partly accepts. Prephrase: to set up a reading the author qualifies.

choices.note: CORRECT. The author grants Brooks's point that a promise is present ('The promise is there') and resists his conclusion that the poem offers renewal ('the poem does not keep it').
Wrong function. Brooks's reading emphasizes renewal, which cuts against the inversion thesis; the author answers it rather than citing it as support.
Out of scope. Nothing about Brooks concerns Eliot's sources, and the passage says Eliot himself acknowledged them.
Out of scope and unsupported. The passage never says Brooks ignored Frazer or Weston, nor uses the label 'New Critical'.
Too strong. The author concedes that a promise is present, not that renewal is brought about; 'rain is heralded and never falls.'

questions.stem: In the context of passage B, the statement "The barrenness is social, not natural" (second paragraph, fourth sentence) is best understood to mean that
choices: al-Sayyab, unlike Eliot, wrote about an actual drought rather than about a symbolic one
the poem treats the Tammuz myth as a social custom rather than as a religious belief
the hunger the poem describes would come to an end if the rains that had failed for years were to return to Iraq
the free-verse form allowed al-Sayyab to address society more directly than classical poets had
the poem's hunger persists though the rain falls, and so has human rather than natural causes
questions.explanation: The preceding sentence says 'the rain does fall; yet... not a year passes in Iraq without hunger.' If hunger persists despite rain, its cause is not the weather but society, which is what E says. C reverses this: the rain has not failed.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out what 'barrenness is social, not natural' means in context.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, second paragraph, third and fourth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Read the sentence before: in 'Rain Song' the rain falls, yet Iraq is hungry every year. In the myth, barrenness is natural and ends when the god (and the rain) returns. Here rain is not the missing ingredient, so the cause lies in how society is ordered. Prephrase: hunger has human causes, since it continues despite the rain.

choices.note: Opposite. The passage says the rain does fall in al-Sayyab's poem, so there is no actual drought; the point is that hunger has a cause other than the weather.
Shell game. 'Social' is applied to the myth rather than to the barrenness; the passage says nothing about the myth as custom versus belief.
Reversal. The rain has not failed in the poem; it falls and hunger continues, which is why the barrenness is called social.
Out of scope. The free-verse form is discussed in the first paragraph and is not what this sentence is about.
CORRECT. Hunger continues though the rain falls, so the barrenness has human, social causes.

questions.stem: Which one of the following describes a contrast between The Waste Land as characterized in passage A and "Rain Song" as characterized in passage B?
choices: The former draws on Frazer's account of a dying god, whereas the latter draws instead on the Grail romances described by Weston.
The former contains a question about setting lands in order, whereas the latter closes with an appeal to Tammuz by name.
In the former the expected rain never arrives, whereas in the latter the rain arrives but does not end the deprivation.
The former treats renewal as a private, spiritual matter, whereas the latter treats it as impossible without the return of rain.
The former was written in free verse, whereas the latter retains the classical line of two hemistichs on a single rhyme.
questions.explanation: Passage A: 'rain is heralded and never falls.' Passage B: 'the rain does fall; yet... not a year passes in Iraq without hunger.' C states exactly that contrast. B is half right: A does report the question about setting lands in order, but passage B never says 'Rain Song' calls on Tammuz by name.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a difference between the two poems supported by both passages.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, second paragraph, last two sentences; passage B, second paragraph, third and fourth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Compare the rain in each poem. A: heralded, never falls. B: falls, but hunger remains. Every choice must be checked against both descriptions; many will get one side right.

choices.note: Unsupported. Passage B ties the Tammuz myth to Jabra's translation of Frazer and never mentions Weston or the Grail in connection with al-Sayyab.
Half right. The first half fits passage A, but passage B never says 'Rain Song' names Tammuz; it describes the last stanza as finding a flower's bud and a smile in each drop of rain.
CORRECT. A says the rain 'is heralded and never falls'; B says in al-Sayyab 'the rain does fall' yet hunger continues.
Half right and then opposite. A does call Eliot's drought spiritual, but B says al-Sayyab's barrenness is 'social, not natural,' so rain is not what renewal requires.
Reversed for 'Rain Song' and unsupported for Eliot. Passage B presents al-Sayyab as a founder of free verse, and passage A says nothing about Eliot's form.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship of passage B to passage A?
choices: Passage B traces a later borrowing of the kind of myth passage A examines and argues that it took on a hopeful meaning passage A denies it has in Eliot.
Passage B challenges passage A's account of Eliot's sources by showing that the Tammuz myth reached Eliot through Arabic rather than English scholarship.
Passage B supplies evidence that supports Brooks's reading of The Waste Land, which passage A rejects.
Passage B applies to Arabic poetry the method of inversion that passage A attributes to Eliot, and finds that the Arab poets inverted the myth just as Eliot did.
Passage B argues that the meaning of the dying-god myth depends on the form of the poem that uses it, a claim passage A implicitly rejects.
questions.explanation: Passage B's last sentence sums up the relation: 'What Eliot used to measure a desolation, they used to prophesy an end to one.' It describes a later borrowing (Tammuz, 1950s) and a reversal of the meaning passage A finds in Eliot, as A says. C is the trap: B finds hope in al-Sayyab, not in Eliot, so it gives no support to Brooks's reading of Eliot.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how passage B relates to passage A.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, second paragraph, first two sentences and last sentence; passage A, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: A: Eliot invokes the reviving god 'to measure a spiritual drought, not to end it.' B: the Tammuzis knew Eliot's use, borrowed the myth, and altered its meaning toward hope. So B is a later chapter in the borrowing, with the opposite meaning. Check each choice for what B actually claims about Eliot.

choices.note: CORRECT. B describes the Tammuzis' later borrowing and says they used the myth 'to prophesy an end to' the desolation Eliot measured, a hopeful meaning A says Eliot withheld.
Reversal and unsupported. B says the Arab poets knew Eliot and got Tammuz via Jabra's translation of Frazer; nothing says Eliot learned anything from Arabic scholarship.
Shell game. B's hope belongs to al-Sayyab's poem; about Eliot, B says he used the myth 'to measure a desolation,' which agrees with A rather than with Brooks.
Opposite. B says the borrowing 'altered the myth's meaning' toward renewal; it does not say the Arab poets inverted the myth as Eliot did.
Out of scope. B discusses free-verse form, but never argues that form determines the myth's meaning, and A says nothing about form.

questions.stem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Eliot's use of the dying-god myth was shaped by the political crises of the society in which he wrote.
Brooks was correct to find in the final section of The Waste Land a promise of renewal.
The Tammuzi poets misunderstood Eliot's use of the myth when they read it as a prophecy of renewal.
The Waste Land does not present the rebirth that the myth promises as something actually achieved.
The poems that drew on Frazer's dying gods were more original than the anthropology from which they borrowed.
questions.explanation: Author A: the poem 'does not keep' its promise; Eliot uses the god 'to measure a spiritual drought, not to end it.' Author B: 'What Eliot used to measure a desolation, they used to prophesy an end to one,' which implies Eliot did not prophesy or achieve renewal. Both support D. B is the trap: author A grants only that 'the promise is there' and rejects Brooks's conclusion; author B says nothing about Brooks.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim both authors would accept.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, last two sentences; passage B, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Look for overlap on Eliot, the one subject both authors address. A: renewal promised but not delivered. B: Eliot measured desolation; the Arab poets, by contrast, prophesied its end. Overlap: in Eliot, rebirth is not achieved. Be wary of choices that rely on one author only or attribute a view neither holds.

choices.note: Out of scope for both. Passage B ties political crisis to the Arab poets; neither passage attributes Eliot's use of the myth to politics, and A calls his drought 'spiritual'.
Wrong position-holder. Brooks's reading is what author A argues against ('the poem does not keep it'), and author B never mentions Brooks.
Distortion. Author B says the Tammuzis 'altered the myth's meaning,' a deliberate transformation; it nowhere says they misread Eliot, and author A says nothing about them.
CORRECT. A: 'the poem does not keep it'; B: Eliot used the myth 'to measure a desolation,' in contrast to poets who 'prophesy an end to one.'
Out of scope. Neither author compares the poems' originality with that of Frazer's or Weston's work.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Ibn 'Arabi's commentary on the Tarjuman al-Ashwaq imposed on conventional love poems a mystical meaning that the poems themselves do not contain.
Donne's sonnet, unlike Ibn 'Arabi's odes, contains its sacred meaning within the poem itself and so needs no interpreter or tradition to disclose it.
The view that one poem contains its sacred meaning while the other receives it from a commentator is misleading, since both depend on shared conventions of reading.
Sells is right that Ibn 'Arabi's poems are not simply versified doctrine, and so their sacred meaning must lie in the poems rather than in the commentary.
Sacred love poetry in both the Islamic and the Christian traditions derives ultimately from the allegorical readings of the Song of Songs that both traditions inherited.
questions.explanation: The passage sets up a tempting contrast (paragraph 2), calls it 'too simple on both sides' (paragraph 3), and concludes that sacred meaning lies 'in conventions of reading that poet and audience share.' C states that. B is the view the author rejects; D is Sells's point plus a conclusion the author explicitly declines to draw.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall claim.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last sentence of the second paragraph, first sentence of the third, and the last two sentences of the passage.

breakdown.analysis: Structure: paragraph 1 Ibn 'Arabi and his commentary; paragraph 2 Donne and the tempting contrast; paragraph 3 'too simple on both sides' with evidence each way; paragraph 4 Sells, then the author's conclusion about shared conventions. Prephrase: the 'in the poem vs. supplied by interpretation' contrast fails for both poets; meaning lives in shared conventions.

choices.note: Wrong position-holder. This is the tempting conclusion of paragraph 2 that the author calls 'too simple,' and the author says the commentary does not impose 'a foreign meaning'.
This is the half of the tempting contrast the author rejects: Donne's paradox reads as devotion 'only for readers who know' the bridal tradition.
CORRECT. The author rejects the in-the-poem/supplied-by-interpretation contrast for both poets and locates sacred meaning in shared conventions of reading.
Half right. The author accepts Sells's warning, but concludes that meaning lies 'neither in the poem alone nor in its interpreter alone,' not in the poems rather than the commentary.
Too strong and out of scope. The Song of Songs is mentioned only as the root of Donne's bridal tradition, not as the source of Islamic poetry.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Ibn 'Arabi's commentary on the Tarjuman al-Ashwaq
choices: reads the poems' images as figures of divine knowledge and of longing for God
was written at the request of Nizam, whom Ibn 'Arabi presented as the inspiration for the poems
was composed in Mecca shortly after the poems themselves were written
argues that the conventions of the nasib were invented by Sufi poets to speak of God
was the source from which Nicholson took the title and the arrangement of his 1911 translation
questions.explanation: The first paragraph's last sentence says the commentary 'glosses the poems' images line by line as figures of divine knowledge and of the soul's longing for God.' A paraphrases it. C is the trap: the passage says the commentary was 'begun in Aleppo,' while it was Ibn 'Arabi's acquaintance with Nizam that took place in Mecca.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says the commentary does.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph, last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The commentary is described once: an answer to readers who took the poems as love poetry, begun in Aleppo, glossing the images line by line as figures of divine knowledge and longing for God. Match that; reject choices that move Mecca or Nizam onto the commentary.

choices.note: CORRECT. This restates the passage's description of how the commentary glosses the images.
Shell game. Nizam is presented as the poems' inspiration; the passage says the commentary answered readers who took the poems as merely love poetry.
Shell game. Mecca is where Ibn 'Arabi met Nizam; the commentary was 'begun in Aleppo,' and the passage gives no timing for it.

Distortion. The passage calls the nasib a convention of the classical Arabic love ode and says Sufi audiences 'had long heard' such poetry as speaking of God; nothing says Sufis invented it, and this is the author's point, not the commentary's.
Unsupported. The passage gives no source for Nicholson's title.

questions.stem: The author's statement that "Sufi audiences had long heard ordinary love poetry as speaking of God" (third paragraph) serves primarily to
choices: explain why some readers took the Tarjuman for the love poetry of a man of religion
show that Ibn 'Arabi's commentary was unnecessary for the readers he wrote it to answer
suggest that Donne may have known, through intermediaries, the conventions of Sufi devotional poetry
support the claim that the sacred meaning of Ibn 'Arabi's odes was supplied by interpreters rather than by the poet
indicate that Ibn 'Arabi's conventions permitted a sacred reading before the commentary
questions.explanation: The sentence goes on: 'so the conventions Ibn 'Arabi used already carried that possibility.' It is one of the paragraph's reasons for calling the tempting contrast 'too simple': the sacred reading was available before the commentary, as E says. D reverses the sentence's role: it counts against the view that interpreters supplied the meaning.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the sentence about Sufi audiences does in the argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, first sentence and the sentence about Sufi audiences.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 3 opens: 'That conclusion is too simple on both sides.' Its first side: the Tarjuman is not merely supplied with sacred meaning afterward. Two reasons: the poems' own signals (the heart 'capable of every form') and the audience's long habit of hearing love poetry as about God. Prephrase: to show the conventions already allowed a sacred reading, so the commentary did not create it from nothing.

choices.note: Opposite effect. The sentence shows a sacred reading was available; it does not explain the critics' purely erotic reading.
Too strong. The author says the commentary 'made explicit' conventions for readers 'who had forgotten such conventions or refused them,' so it was not unnecessary for them.
Out of scope. The passage never connects Donne to Sufi poetry; Donne's conventions come from the Christian bridal tradition.
Reversal. This is the tempting conclusion the sentence is meant to undercut: the passage uses it to show meaning was not merely supplied afterward.
CORRECT. The sentence ends 'so the conventions Ibn 'Arabi used already carried that possibility,' which undercuts the idea that the commentary converted the poems.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Sells's view of Ibn 'Arabi's poems is best described as
choices: skepticism about whether the poems can be read apart from the commentary at all
agreement with the view, coupled with a denial that it supports a further inference
enthusiastic endorsement of the view as proof that the commentary distorts the poems it claims to explain
reluctant acceptance of the view on the strength of Sells's authority as a translator
disagreement grounded in the evidence of the commentary Ibn 'Arabi himself provided
questions.explanation: The author writes: 'That warning is sound, but it does not show that the commentary imposes a foreign meaning on them.' Agreement with Sells's claim, plus a refusal to draw a further conclusion from it: B. C is the overreach the author explicitly blocks.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize the author's stance on Sells.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, first two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Two signals: 'That warning is sound' (agreement) and 'but it does not show that...' (a limit on what follows). Prephrase: agrees, with a qualification about what it proves. Eliminate choices that are too negative or too positive.

choices.note: Too negative. The author calls Sells's warning 'sound'; nothing suggests the author doubts the poems can be read on their own.
CORRECT. 'That warning is sound' is agreement; 'it does not show that the commentary imposes a foreign meaning' denies a further inference.
Too extreme and opposite. The author denies precisely that Sells's point shows the commentary imposes a foreign meaning.
Distortion. The author's agreement is not reluctant and is not based on Sells's authority; the passage gives the author's own reasons in paragraph 3.
Opposite. The author agrees with Sells.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the author's claim about how readers understand the final paradox of Donne's sonnet?
choices: Readers unacquainted with Christian bridal imagery generally take the sonnet's closing paradox as devotional rather than blasphemous.
Some seventeenth-century readers who knew the allegorical readings of the Song of Songs nonetheless objected to Donne's language as indecorous and unfit for devotion.
Donne wrote erotic love poems earlier in his career that use military imagery similar to the besieged town of the sonnet.
Several of Donne's other religious poems address God directly in their opening lines.
Readers trained in the Christian bridal tradition are more likely than others to admire the sonnet's closing lines.
questions.explanation: The author claims Donne's paradox 'reads as devotion rather than blasphemy only for readers who know' the bridal tradition. If readers without that knowledge still read it as devotion, the 'only' claim fails: A. E is the opposite trap; it is consistent with, even supportive of, the author's claim.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most undercuts the author's claim about Donne's paradox.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The claim has a necessary-condition form: knowing the bridal tradition is required for the devotional reading. To weaken it, show the devotional reading without the knowledge. Watch for choices about readers who do know the tradition, which don't test the 'only'.

choices.note: CORRECT. The author says the paradox reads as devotion 'only' for readers who know the bridal tradition; readers without it who still read it as devotion contradict that.
Irrelevant to the claim. The author says knowing the tradition is necessary for a devotional reading, not that it guarantees approval; some knowing readers objecting is consistent with that.
Out of scope. Donne's earlier poems bear on his imagery, not on what readers need to know to read the paradox as devotion.
Irrelevant truth. It matches the passage's point about the sonnet naming its addressee, but says nothing about whether readers need the bridal tradition.
Opposite. If anything this fits the author's claim that the tradition shapes how the lines are received.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the role the author attributes to Ibn 'Arabi's commentary?
choices: A critic argues that a folk song's lyrics, which listeners have always taken literally, in fact encode a political message the songwriter intended.
A composer writes program notes that assign a narrative to a piece of instrumental music that had no narrative at all when it was first composed and performed.
A translator replaces the traditional images of a foreign poem with images more familiar to readers of the translation.
A scholar spells out, for a new audience, the symbolic meanings a genre's conventions carried for the audience the work was written for.
An editor removes from a poet's collection the poems that readers have found offensive, leaving only those whose religious meaning is plain.
questions.explanation: The author's last sentence: the commentary 'made explicit, for readers who had forgotten such conventions or refused them,' what the shared conventions already carried. D has the same structure: making explicit, for an audience lacking them, meanings the genre's conventions already held. B is the trap: it describes the commentary as the tempting view of paragraph 2 sees it, imposing a meaning the work lacked, which the author rejects.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the author's account of the commentary to a new case.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, last two sentences; third paragraph on the conventions.

breakdown.analysis: In the author's view the commentary does not invent meaning; it makes explicit a meaning the conventions already carried, for readers who had forgotten or refused those conventions. The analogue must (1) make meaning explicit, (2) meaning already carried by shared conventions, (3) for an audience lacking them. Reject analogues where meaning is added, replaced, or censored.

choices.note: Close but off on two counts: the meaning here is a hidden private intention rather than a convention shared by poet and audience, and listeners 'have always' read it otherwise, so it was never shared.
Tempting, but this is the view the author rejects: the program notes supply a meaning 'that had no story,' as the paragraph 2 conclusion says the commentary 'converts' the poems.
Out of scope. The commentary glosses the poems' images; it does not replace them.
CORRECT. Spelling out, for an audience that lacks them, meanings the genre's conventions already carried is what the author says the commentary did.
Distortion. The commentary interprets the poems rather than removing any of them.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the readers who took the Tarjuman al-Ashwaq for the love poetry of a man of religion
choices: were correct about what the poems themselves say but wrong about Ibn 'Arabi's intentions in writing them
did not apply a way of hearing love poetry that their own tradition made available
were persuaded by Ibn 'Arabi's commentary to read the poems as mystical verse
objected chiefly to the poems' references to the Ka'ba, the Torah, and the Qur'an
would have accepted the poems as mystical had they been written in the form of a sonnet
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says 'Sufi audiences had long heard ordinary love poetry as speaking of God,' and the last sentence says the commentary was for 'readers who had forgotten such conventions or refused them.' So these readers did not use a reading available in their tradition: B. C is unsupported: the passage never says the commentary changed their minds.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Infer what the passage implies about the Tarjuman's critics.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph, third and fourth sentences; third paragraph; last sentence of the passage.

breakdown.analysis: Connect the critics (paragraph 1) to the last sentence: the commentary was for readers who had forgotten or refused the conventions by which love poetry could speak of God. Prephrase: they didn't use the mystical reading their tradition made available. Stay within what is said; don't add outcomes.

choices.note: Distortion. The author argues that the poems themselves signal a love 'not merely human,' so the critics were not correct about the poems.
CORRECT. The commentary answered 'readers who had forgotten such conventions or refused them,' conventions by which Sufi audiences had 'long heard' love poetry as speaking of God.
Unsupported. The passage says the commentary answered them, not that it persuaded them.
Shell game. Those references appear in the ode the author cites as evidence of sacred meaning; nothing says the critics objected to them.
Out of scope. The sonnet appears only in the comparison with Donne; nothing suggests verse form would have changed the critics' reading.

sections.title: Reading Through Ideas 11: Said, Lewis and the question of Orientalism · Contrapuntal reading and Mansfield Park · Exile, Counterpoint and Darwish's Elegy · Said and the Idea of Late Style

passages.title: Said, Lewis and the question of Orientalism
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
Passage A

In Orientalism (1978), Edward Said argued that the European study of the Middle East and Islam could not be understood as a body of disinterested learning. Drawing on Michel Foucault's notion of a discourse, Said treated Orientalism not as a collection of individual scholarly opinions, each true or false, but as a system of statements, institutions, and habits of representation that governed what could intelligibly be said about the Orient at all. The tradition that took shape from the late eighteenth century onward, in philology and travel writing as much as in colonial administration, was best described, in Said's words, as "a Western style for dominating, restructuring, and having authority over the Orient." Knowledge and power were not merely adjacent: the authority to describe the Orient was itself a form of power over it, exercised above all by Britain and France through empire.

Said did not claim that every Orientalist was an agent of empire, or that any scholar could stand outside history; no scholar, he held, can be detached from the circumstances of his own life. His claim was that a scholar's work could be learned and still bear the discourse's marks, above all a fixed opposition between a rational, developing West and an unchanging, essentially different East, an East that was not free to answer for itself. Precisely because the scholarship was serious, it lent those assumptions the prestige of knowledge. To criticize Orientalism, then, was not to correct particular errors but to expose the conditions under which such errors had seemed to be knowledge.

Passage B

Bernard Lewis's 1982 reply, "The Question of Orientalism," began by asking readers to imagine Greek patriots denouncing the classical scholars of Europe for having appropriated and distorted the heritage of ancient Greece. The analogy was meant to show how strange the charge against Orientalism looked from within the scholarly tradition. For Lewis the word had long named a discipline: the philological study of the languages, texts, and history of the East, an inquiry that grew out of Renaissance humanism and was comparable to the study of Greek antiquity. Scholars, he allowed, are creatures of their time and have their biases; what marks scholarship is the effort to recognize such bias and correct it by the discipline's own methods. Lewis also charged that Said had selected his examples to suit his thesis, passing over the German scholarship that led the field in the nineteenth century, though Germany held no empire in the Arab lands. The term Orientalist, Lewis concluded, was now "polluted beyond salvation."

In the exchange that followed in the same journal, Said rejected the analogy with classical studies, insisting that the scholarship he examined had been bound up with the rule of the very peoples it described in a way that the study of ancient Greece had not. The exchange clarified where the two men actually differed. Neither held that scholarship is made in a vacuum. They disagreed over whether the circumstances of its making could be set aside when judging what it had found.

sources.author: Edward W. Said
sources.title: Orientalism
sources.note: Argues, drawing on Foucault's notion of discourse, that Western scholarship on the Orient was bound up with imperial power; the quotation 'a Western style for dominating, restructuring, and having authority over the Orient' is from its Introduction (confirmed in the Cambridge excerpt of the Introduction and multiple scholarly quotations).

sources.author: Bernard Lewis
sources.title: The Question of Orientalism (The New York Review of Books, June 24, 1982)
sources.note: Lewis's reply to Said, opening with the hypothetical of Greek patriots attacking classical scholarship and defending Orientalism as a philological discipline; the quotation 'polluted beyond salvation' is from the sentence 'The term Orientalist is by now also polluted beyond salvation' (NYRB text).

sources.author: Edward W. Said and Bernard Lewis
sources.title: Orientalism: An Exchange (The New York Review of Books, August 12, 1982)
sources.note: Said's letter answering Lewis, rejecting the classics analogy, and Lewis's rejoinder; the clearest statement of where the two disagreed.

passages.title: Contrapuntal reading and Mansfield Park
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
In Culture and Imperialism (1993), Edward Said proposed a way of reading the canonical European novel that he called contrapuntal, borrowing the term from music, in which independent melodic lines sound together. Looking back at the cultural archive, he wrote, we should reread it "not univocally but contrapuntally," holding in view both the metropolitan history that a novel narrates and the other histories, of colonized places and peoples, against which and together with which that history unfolds. The method does not ask whether a novel is about empire. It asks what the novel must take for granted in order to tell the story it does tell.

Said's best-known example is Jane Austen's Mansfield Park (1814). The Bertram family's English estate is sustained in part by Sir Thomas Bertram's property in Antigua, which in that period would have been a sugar plantation worked by enslaved people. Sir Thomas's voyage to Antigua lets disorder into his household, and his return restores order. Said read the parallel as more than plot: the novel's ideal of a well-governed home, he argued, is tied to, and financed by, the governance of a distant possession that Austen reduces to "a mere half dozen passing references to Antigua." Their brevity, for Said, was not evidence that empire mattered little to the novel but a sign of how completely it could be assumed. He insisted, too, that his purpose was not to dismiss Austen but to read her more fully.

Critics have pressed two objections. The first is that Said builds a large structure on a few sentences: a reader may grant that the Bertrams' income depends on Antigua without granting that the novel's moral order is an imperial one. The second, made by the literary historian Brian Southam and, from a feminist standpoint, by Susan Fraiman, is that Said underrates the novel's own awareness. When Fanny Price asks her uncle about the slave trade, she is met, in Austen's words, with "such a dead silence"; Southam argued that, read against the abolition debates of the years in which the novel is set, the silence registers the family's discomfort rather than the author's complacency. Fraiman charged that Said made Austen a flatly conservative figure and overlooked how her position as a woman writer complicated her relation to the order Sir Thomas represents.

Both objections have force, but they bear on different claims. Contrapuntal reading is at its strongest as an account of dependence: it can show, from evidence within the text, that the world of Mansfield Park rests on an economy the novel mentions only at its edges, and that showing is not undone by the fewness of the references. It is weakest as a verdict on attitude. Whether Austen endorsed, ignored, or quietly questioned that dependence is a separate matter, one the margins of the text cannot settle by themselves and that must be argued, as Southam and Fraiman argue it, from how the novel handles what it does say.

sources.author: Edward W. Said
sources.title: Culture and Imperialism
sources.note: Develops 'contrapuntal' reading of the cultural archive and, in the chapter 'Jane Austen and Empire', reads Mansfield Park's English estate against the Antigua plantation; the quotations 'not univocally but contrapuntally' (p. 51) and 'a mere half dozen passing references to Antigua' (p. 59) are from it, as quoted in published scholarship.

sources.author: Jane Austen
sources.title: Mansfield Park
sources.note: The novel itself; Fanny's question to Sir Thomas about the slave trade is met with 'such a dead silence' (Volume II, Chapter 3).

sources.author: Brian Southam
sources.title: The Silence of the Bertrams: Slavery and the Chronology of Mansfield Park (Times Literary Supplement)
sources.note: Dates the novel's action to the years after the 1807 abolition of the British slave trade and reads the Bertrams' silence as discomfort with their dependence on slavery, against Said's picture of Austen's complacency.

sources.author: Susan Fraiman
sources.title: Jane Austen and Edward Said: Gender, Culture, and Imperialism (Critical Inquiry 21.4)
sources.note: A feminist critique arguing that Said casts Austen as a flatly conservative figure and that his postcolonial reading neglects the gender politics of her position.

passages.title: Exile, Counterpoint and Darwish's Elegy
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Edward Said's essay "Reflections on Exile," first published in Granta in 1984, opens by warning against the appeal of its own subject: exile, he writes, is "strangely compelling to think about but terrible to experience." Said describes it as an unhealable rift between a person and a native place, and he treats the heroic and even triumphant episodes that literature records in exiles' lives as efforts to overcome a sorrow that can never finally be surmounted. Only after these concessions does he allow exile a compensation. Most people, he observes, are principally aware of a single culture and home; exiles are aware of at least two, and "this plurality of vision gives rise to an awareness of simultaneous dimensions," an awareness that, borrowing a term from music, he calls contrapuntal. The habits of the new place are lived against the memory of the old, and neither line absorbs the other.

The essay already names Mahmoud Darwish, whose poetry Said reads as a sustained attempt to turn the lyric of loss into a drama of return that is endlessly deferred. Two decades later the relation was reversed. After Said's death in 2003, Darwish wrote an elegy for his friend, "Tibaq," which Mona Anis translated as "Edward Said: A Contrapuntal Reading" and Fady Joudah later rendered as "Counterpoint." The Arabic title names the rhetorical figure of antithesis, the pairing of opposites, and the poem is built as an imagined conversation in which the dead critic speaks. "I am from there, I am from here, but I am neither there nor here," Said says in Anis's version. Rebecca Dyer has argued that the poem reworks the classical Arabic elegy so that Said's own contrapuntal method shapes the exchange: the elegist mourns his friend partly by reading as his friend taught.

It is tempting to conclude that criticism and poetry here form a single project, the essay supplying a concept that the poem then performs. The illumination is real but uneven. Said's essay teaches us to hear the poem's paired claims as counterpoint rather than contradiction: "from there" and "neither there nor here" sound together without resolving, as contrapuntal awareness requires. But an elegy is a consoling form; it gives the dead a voice and the mourners a shape for grief, and Said had insisted that exile's sorrow resists such shaping. In letting Said speak his exile with such poise, the poem risks making the terrible experience chiefly compelling to think about, the very slippage against which his opening sentence warns. Conversely, the poem can show what the essay could only assert, that contrapuntal awareness can be inhabited and not merely described; it cannot show that the essay's account of exile is true. Each clarifies the other's form; neither can settle the other's claims.

sources.author: Edward W. Said
sources.title: Reflections on Exile
sources.note: Said's essay (Granta 13, 1984; collected in Reflections on Exile and Other Essays, 2000) on exile as an unhealable rift whose one compensation is a 'contrapuntal' plurality of vision; the quotations 'strangely compelling to think about but terrible to experience' (its first sentence) and 'this plurality of vision gives rise to an awareness of simultaneous dimensions' are from it, and it describes Darwish's work as an effort to transform 'the lyrics of loss into the indefinitely postponed drama of return' (paraphrased in the passage).

sources.author: Mahmoud Darwish (trans. Mona Anis)
sources.title: Edward Said: A Contrapuntal Reading (Tibaq)
sources.note: Darwish's elegy for Said, an imagined conversation with him; Anis's translation appeared in Al-Ahram Weekly in 2004 and in Cultural Critique 67 (2007), and Fady Joudah's version, 'Counterpoint', is in If I Were Another (2009). The line 'I am from there, I am from here, but I am neither there nor here' is from Anis's translation.

sources.author: Rebecca Dyer
sources.title: Poetry of Politics and Mourning: Mahmoud Darwish's Genre-Transforming Tribute to Edward W. Said
sources.note: PMLA 122: reads 'Tibaq' as a reworking of the Arabic elegy (marthiya) in which Darwish uses Said's own contrapuntal method within the poem's imagined conversation to honor the friendship and comment on Said's politics.

sources.author: Judith Butler
sources.title: What Shall We Do Without Exile? Said and Darwish Address the Future (in Parting Ways: Jewishness and the Critique of Zionism)
sources.note: The 2010 Edward Said Memorial Lecture, a close reading of Darwish's elegy for Said and of exile as a condition from which to imagine a shared future; useful further reading on how the poem and Said's thought bear on each other.

passages.title: Said and the Idea of Late Style
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Criticism has long told a consoling story about the work artists produce at the end of their lives: age brings ripeness, and the last works gather a career's conflicts into serenity. Edward Said did not deny that such works exist; he cited Shakespeare's The Tempest and The Winter's Tale as examples of a late spirit of reconciliation. But On Late Style, assembled after his death in 2003 from lectures and drafts and published in 2006, pursues another possibility. What, Said asks, of artistic lateness "not as harmony and resolution but as intransigence, difficulty, and unresolved contradiction"?

His model was Theodor Adorno's essay of 1937 on Beethoven's late style. Adorno held that the late sonatas and quartets lack the roundness of ripe fruit; they are furrowed, even ravaged, and in them conventions stand bare, no longer absorbed into a unified whole. He refused to read this as a record of the composer's suffering or premonition of death, a psychological reading that, he thought, mistakes the work for a document. The fissures were formal, and his essay ends: "In the history of art late works are the catastrophes." Said took from Adorno the idea that lateness may be a refusal rather than a fulfillment, and then extended it far beyond Beethoven. Richard Strauss, whom Adorno despised, becomes late in Said's account because works such as the opera Capriccio, completed in 1941, retreat into eighteenth-century idioms deliberately out of step with their catastrophic moment. Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa, who began his only novel, The Leopard, late in life, and Jean Genet in his final works are read the same way: as artists at odds with their time and with audiences who expected them to settle.

Critics have doubted whether the category names anything real. Gordon McMullan, studying how the idea of "late Shakespeare" was invented, treats late style as a critical construct rather than a natural feature of genius in old age, and argues that the idea is "synecdochic of the biographical urge": we find lateness where we already know the artist was near death. Others object that any single late style flattens the varied ways people make art in old age into one story, whether of serenity or of defiance.

Said is better placed against these objections than his critics allow, though not entirely. He never claimed that all late works share a style; for him lateness was one possible stance among others, and his inclusion of Strauss shows that it need not coincide with anguish or with formal breakdown. Yet the further lateness is detached from chronology, the less it describes artists and the more it describes a way of reading them, one whose preference for the intransigent over the reconciled is Said's own. Understood as an interpretive stance rather than a law of artistic aging, the concept survives; it explains less than it seems to, but it lets us hear what a story of serenity would drown out.

sources.author: Edward W. Said
sources.title: On Late Style: Music and Literature Against the Grain
sources.note: Said's posthumous book (edited from his lectures and drafts, with an introduction by Michael Wood) on lateness as intransigence rather than serenity, with chapters on Beethoven, Strauss, Lampedusa, Genet and others; the quotation 'not as harmony and resolution but as intransigence, difficulty, and unresolved contradiction' is from its first chapter.

sources.author: Theodor W. Adorno
sources.title: Late Style in Beethoven (Spätstil Beethovens)
sources.note: Adorno's short essay arguing that Beethoven's late works are furrowed rather than ripe, that their bare conventions are formal rather than biographical facts, and that 'In the history of art late works are the catastrophes' (its last sentence, in Susan H. Gillespie's translation in Essays on Music, 2002).

sources.author: Gordon McMullan
sources.title: Shakespeare and the Idea of Late Writing: Authorship in the Proximity of Death
sources.note: A genealogy of the discourse of lateness from the eighteenth century through Adorno and Said, arguing that late style is a critical construct rather than a feature of genius in old age; the phrase 'synecdochic of the biographical urge' is from its introduction.

questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with
choices: determining whether the study of the Orient arose from Renaissance humanism or from colonial administration
the question of whether the political circumstances of European scholarship on the Orient compromise that scholarship
explaining how Foucault's notion of a discourse came to be applied to the study of the Middle East
comparing the treatment of the Orient by British and French scholars with its treatment by German scholars
evaluating whether classical scholarship distorted the heritage of ancient Greece
questions.explanation: Passage A presents Said's case that Orientalist knowledge was bound up with imperial power; passage B presents Lewis's defense of the discipline and ends by locating the disagreement in whether the circumstances of scholarship can be set aside when judging it. B covers both. D and E each pick up a detail from passage B alone.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the topic both passages address throughout.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of passage A; the last two sentences of passage B.

breakdown.analysis: Passage A: Said's charge that the scholarship is tied to power. Passage B: Lewis's defense, Said's reply, and the author's summary of the disagreement. Common subject: whether the context of Orientalist scholarship disqualifies it. Test each choice against both passages; the traps are details that appear in only one.

choices.note: Out of scope. Passage B mentions Renaissance humanism and passage A colonial administration, but neither tries to settle which one the study arose from; A lists administration alongside philology and travel writing.

CORRECT. Passage A argues that the scholarship was bound up with imperial power; passage B defends it and closes on exactly this disagreement: whether 'the circumstances of its making could be set aside when judging what it had found.'
Half right at most. Passage A mentions that Said drew on Foucault, but neither passage explains how that came about, and passage B never mentions Foucault.
Too narrow. German scholarship appears only in passage B, as one of Lewis's charges, and neither passage compares how the national traditions treated the Orient.
Shell game. Classical scholarship appears only as Lewis's analogy; neither passage evaluates whether classicists actually distorted Greek heritage.

questions.stem: Based on the passages, Said and Lewis would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: The European study of the Orient is best understood as a branch of Renaissance humanism.
Bias in European scholarship on the Orient can be corrected by the methods of that scholarship.
The study of ancient Greece offers an apt comparison for the European study of the Orient.
The term Orientalist can no longer serve as a neutral name for a field of scholarship.
The work of scholars is shaped to some degree by the times and circumstances in which they work.
questions.explanation: Passage A says Said held that no scholar 'can be detached from the circumstances of his own life'; passage B says Lewis allowed that scholars 'are creatures of their time,' and the last paragraph adds that 'Neither held that scholarship is made in a vacuum.' E is the shared ground. D is the trap: Lewis says the term is 'polluted beyond salvation,' and Said's book helped make it pejorative, but passage A never says Said thought the term unusable.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim both Said (as passage A presents him) and Lewis (as passage B presents him) are committed to.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, paragraph 2, sentence 1; passage B, paragraph 1, sentence 4, and paragraph 2, sentences 3-4.

breakdown.analysis: Agreement questions need textual support on both sides. Lewis concedes scholars are 'creatures of their time'; Said says no scholar can be detached from his circumstances. The disagreement is over what follows. Eliminate anything that is only Lewis's view (humanism, correcting bias by the discipline's methods, Greek analogy, polluted term).

choices.note: Lewis's view only. Passage A treats the tradition as a discourse bound up with power; nothing suggests Said would accept the humanism description.

Lewis's view, and Said would deny it: passage A says criticizing Orientalism was not 'to correct particular errors' but to expose the conditions under which errors 'seemed to be knowledge,' a problem correction within the discipline would not reach.
Opposite for Said. Passage B says Said 'rejected the analogy with classical studies.'
Plausible from outside knowledge, but unsupported for Said. Only Lewis says the term is polluted; passage A never reports Said's view of the word's usability.

CORRECT. Both concede the point: Said holds no scholar 'can be detached from the circumstances of his own life'; Lewis allows that scholars 'are creatures of their time.' Passage B confirms: 'Neither held that scholarship is made in a vacuum.'

questions.stem: In passage B, Lewis's statement that the term Orientalist was "polluted beyond salvation" (last sentence of the first paragraph) most probably means that the term
choices: had acquired associations that made it unusable as a neutral name for the scholarly discipline
had always carried connotations of imperial domination that scholars had failed to notice
referred to a discipline whose methods had been corrupted by political interests
had become too broad to distinguish philologists from other students of the East
could be restored to its earlier meaning only by the work of scholars themselves
questions.explanation: For Lewis the word 'had long named a discipline'; his complaint is that its meaning had been spoiled, so it could no longer serve that purpose. A says this. C is the trap: it attributes to Lewis Said's claim that the discipline itself was compromised, the very charge Lewis was answering.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out what Lewis means by calling the term polluted, from his position in passage B.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, paragraph 1, sentences 3 and 6.

breakdown.analysis: Lewis defends the discipline, so 'polluted' can't mean the discipline is corrupt; it is the word that has been spoiled, by the charges against it. 'Beyond salvation' means it can't be reclaimed. Prephrase: the label has picked up a bad meaning and can't be used neutrally anymore.

choices.note: CORRECT. Lewis says the word 'had long named a discipline'; 'polluted beyond salvation' says the word has been contaminated past repair, so it can no longer name that discipline neutrally.
Wrong position-holder. That the term always carried domination is closer to Said's view; Lewis says it 'had long named a discipline,' implying the pollution is recent.
Wrong position-holder. This is Said's charge against the discipline, which Lewis rejects; Lewis's complaint is about the word.
Out of scope. Nothing in passage B is about the term being too broad; Lewis's concern is contamination, not imprecision.
Opposite. 'Beyond salvation' says the term cannot be restored at all.

questions.stem: The author of passage B mentions Lewis's imagined Greek patriots (first sentence of passage B) primarily in order to
choices: provide evidence that classical scholarship, like Orientalism, served political ends
show that Lewis regarded the charge against Orientalism as a product of nationalist sentiment alone
introduce a criticism of Lewis that Said later developed in his reply
present an analogy meant to make the charge against Orientalism look implausible
illustrate how scholars who study a culture's past can recognize and correct their own biases
questions.explanation: The next sentence states the purpose: 'The analogy was meant to show how strange the charge against Orientalism looked from within the scholarly tradition,' and Lewis compares Orientalism to 'the study of Greek antiquity.' D says this. B is the near-miss: the analogy implies the charge looks strange, but nothing says Lewis thought it sprang from nationalism alone.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify why the Greek-patriots hypothetical appears in passage B.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, paragraph 1, sentences 1-3; paragraph 2, sentence 1.

breakdown.analysis: The author tells you directly in sentence 2: the analogy shows how strange the charge looks from within the tradition. Lewis then treats Orientalism as 'comparable to the study of Greek antiquity.' If no one would accept the charge against classicists, the parallel charge against Orientalists should look odd too. Watch for answers that turn the analogy against Lewis, or inflate it into a claim about motives.

choices.note: Opposite. Lewis uses the hypothetical to make the charge look absurd, not to concede that classical scholarship was political.
Too strong. The analogy suggests the charge seems strange from within scholarship; the passage never says Lewis traced the charge to nationalist sentiment 'alone.'
Distortion. The hypothetical is Lewis's own device; Said's reply rejected it rather than developing it.
CORRECT. Sentence 2: 'The analogy was meant to show how strange the charge against Orientalism looked from within the scholarly tradition,' and sentence 3 makes the two disciplines comparable.
Shell game. Correcting bias is a separate point Lewis makes two sentences later; the Greek hypothetical is about the charge, not about correction.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken the argument that passage B attributes to Lewis concerning German scholarship?
choices: German Orientalists of the nineteenth century were more often trained in classical philology than were their British and French counterparts.
Some British and French Orientalists of the nineteenth century openly opposed their governments' imperial policies.
German Orientalists took their central assumptions about the East from British and French scholarship produced in the service of empire.
Several German Orientalists of the nineteenth century were widely respected by scholars working in the Arab lands themselves.
Germany acquired colonies in Africa and the Pacific late in the nineteenth century, though none in the Arab lands.
questions.explanation: Lewis's point is that German scholarship 'led the field' without any German empire in the Arab lands, which seems to break the link between Orientalism and empire. If German scholars took their central assumptions from British and French work produced in the service of empire, the discourse passage A describes could reach scholars whose own country had no empire there, and the counterexample loses its force. E is the trap: it adds empire elsewhere, but Lewis's point concerns the Arab lands, and E concedes there was none.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Reconstruct Lewis's German-scholarship argument, then find the fact that most undercuts its force against Said.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, paragraph 1, sentence 5; passage A, paragraph 1, sentences 2-4.

breakdown.analysis: Lewis's argument: leading Orientalist scholarship existed without empire in the Arab lands, so Orientalism isn't explained by empire. Weaken it by showing the German work still depended on empire, or by showing that Said's thesis doesn't require each scholar's own country to rule. Passage A treats Orientalism as a discourse, a system of statements, not a set of national projects. A choice tying German assumptions to imperial British and French work does both.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Philological training says nothing about whether the scholarship was tied to empire; if anything it fits Lewis's picture of a philological discipline.
Opposite, if anything. Orientalists opposing empire would support Lewis's separation of scholarship from power, and the choice is about British and French scholars, not the German counterexample.

CORRECT. If the German scholars' central assumptions came from imperial British and French work, the lack of a German empire in the Arab lands no longer shows that leading Orientalist scholarship was free of the link to empire; the discourse reached them anyway.
Irrelevant. Being respected in the Arab lands doesn't show the work was independent of, or bound up with, imperial power.

Out of scope. Lewis's point concerns empire in the Arab lands, and this choice confirms Germany had none there; colonies elsewhere don't connect German Orientalism to rule over the peoples it studied.

questions.stem: Based on passage A, Said would most likely respond to Lewis's view that scholarship is marked by "the effort to recognize such bias and correct it by the discipline's own methods" (fourth sentence of passage B) by arguing that
choices: the discipline's methods may themselves share the assumptions whose effects they are meant to correct
scholars who study the Orient have rarely made any effort to recognize their biases
errors in Orientalist scholarship are best corrected by scholars from the Orient itself
the errors of individual Orientalists are too numerous to be corrected by any method
the discipline's methods were sound but were not applied consistently by British and French scholars
questions.explanation: Passage A says criticizing Orientalism 'was not to correct particular errors but to expose the conditions under which such errors had seemed to be knowledge,' and that even learned work bore the discourse's marks. Correction by the discipline's own methods would not reach assumptions that those methods themselves share. C is the trap: passage A says the East 'was not free to answer for itself,' but it never proposes Oriental scholars as the remedy.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Use what passage A says about Said's view to predict his answer to Lewis's point about correcting bias.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, paragraph 2, sentences 2-4; passage B, paragraph 1, sentence 4.

breakdown.analysis: Lewis: bias is individual and the discipline's methods can correct it. Said (A): the problem isn't particular errors but the conditions that made them seem to be knowledge, and serious scholarship lent those assumptions prestige. So the discipline's methods are part of what needs examining. Prephrase: the correcting tools carry the same assumptions.

choices.note: CORRECT. Passage A: the aim was 'not to correct particular errors but to expose the conditions under which such errors had seemed to be knowledge.' If the discipline's methods operate within those conditions, they share the assumptions they would be used to correct.
Unsupported. Nothing in passage A says Orientalists made no effort to recognize bias; Said's objection is to what correction could reach, not to whether it was attempted.
Goes beyond the passage. Passage A notes the East was 'not free to answer for itself,' but it doesn't propose who should correct the scholarship.
Distortion. Said's point concerns the conditions of knowledge, not the number of errors; passage A expressly says the critique is 'not to correct particular errors.'
Opposite. Passage A says learned, serious work still bore the discourse's marks; Said doesn't treat the methods as sound and merely misapplied.

questions.stem: According to passage A, Said held that the seriousness of Orientalist scholarship
choices: shows that many Orientalists were not agents of empire
made it possible for the discipline to correct its own biases
was a product of its reliance on philology rather than on travel writing
was rarely matched by the colonial administrators who used it
lent the prestige of knowledge to the discourse's assumptions
questions.explanation: Passage A, paragraph 2, sentence 3: 'Precisely because the scholarship was serious, it lent those assumptions the prestige of knowledge.' E restates it. A is the trap: passage A does say Said did not claim every Orientalist was an agent of empire, but it doesn't draw that from the scholarship's seriousness.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what passage A says about the effect of the scholarship's seriousness.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, paragraph 2, sentences 1-3.

breakdown.analysis: A straight retrieval: the sentence beginning 'Precisely because the scholarship was serious' answers it. Watch for a choice that pairs a true statement from the same paragraph with the wrong cause, and for Lewis's point about correcting bias attributed to Said.

choices.note: Shell game. Passage A does say Said didn't claim every Orientalist was an agent of empire, but it doesn't base that on the scholarship's seriousness.
Wrong position-holder. Correcting bias by the discipline's methods is Lewis's claim in passage B; Said says seriousness lent prestige to the assumptions.
Out of scope. Passage A lists philology and travel writing together; it never contrasts them or links seriousness to one of them.
Out of scope. Passage A never compares the seriousness of scholars and administrators.
CORRECT. Paragraph 2, sentence 3: 'Precisely because the scholarship was serious, it lent those assumptions the prestige of knowledge.'

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Said's contrapuntal reading of Mansfield Park has been refuted by critics who show that the novel's references to Antigua are too few to support his thesis.
Contrapuntal reading can show that Mansfield Park depends on a colonial economy but cannot by itself settle Austen's attitude toward it.
Southam and Fraiman show that Austen quietly questioned the slave economy on which the Bertrams' estate depended.
Said's contrapuntal method, borrowed from music, allows critics to determine what any canonical novel takes for granted about empire.
Mansfield Park is less concerned with empire than with the governance of the English household.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph gives the author's verdict: contrapuntal reading is 'at its strongest as an account of dependence' and 'weakest as a verdict on attitude,' which the margins of the text 'cannot settle by themselves.' B states both halves. C is the trap: it treats the critics' argument as proven, when the author says only that attitude must be argued 'as Southam and Fraiman argue it.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the claim the passage builds to, including the author's own qualified judgment in the last paragraph.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, all sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Map: P1 Said's method; P2 his Mansfield Park reading; P3 two objections; P4 the author sorts them: the method succeeds on dependence, not on attitude. Prephrase: good for showing the novel rests on Antigua, not enough to tell us what Austen thought of it. Expect traps that side wholly with Said or wholly with the critics.

choices.note: Opposite of the author's view. The author says the showing of dependence 'is not undone by the fewness of the references.'
CORRECT. Paragraph 4: the method is 'at its strongest as an account of dependence' and 'weakest as a verdict on attitude,' which the margins 'cannot settle by themselves.'
Too strong, and a wrong position-holder. The author reports Southam's and Fraiman's arguments without endorsing their conclusion; 'questioned' is one of three possibilities the author leaves open.
Too strong. The author limits what the method can show; 'determine what any canonical novel takes for granted' ignores that limit and generalizes beyond the passage.
Out of scope. No one in the passage claims this; even the first objection grants the dependence and disputes only what follows from it.

questions.stem: As described in the passage, reading a novel "contrapuntally" (second sentence of the first paragraph) involves
choices: attending only to the colonial histories that a novel leaves out
judging a novel by the political views of its author
comparing the structure of a novel to that of a piece of music with several parts
attending at once to the history a novel narrates and the histories it rests on
deciding whether a novel is primarily about empire or about domestic life
questions.explanation: The same sentence glosses the term: holding in view 'both the metropolitan history that a novel narrates and the other histories... against which and together with which that history unfolds.' D paraphrases it. A drops half the definition; E is what the passage says the method 'does not ask.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out what the passage says contrapuntal reading involves.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, sentences 1-4.

breakdown.analysis: The musical image (independent lines sounding together) and the gloss ('both... and') point to simultaneity: both histories at once. The third and fourth sentences add that it asks what a novel takes for granted, not whether it is 'about' empire.

choices.note: Half right. 'Only' drops the metropolitan history; the passage stresses 'both.'
Out of scope. The passage says nothing about judging by the author's politics; the last paragraph even separates the method from verdicts on attitude.
Distortion. The term is borrowed from music, but the method doesn't compare a novel's structure with a composition; the borrowed idea is lines sounding together.
CORRECT. The passage glosses the term as holding in view 'both the metropolitan history that a novel narrates and the other histories' against and with which it unfolds.
Opposite. 'The method does not ask whether a novel is about empire.'

questions.stem: The primary function of the fifth sentence of the second paragraph ("Their brevity... could be assumed.") is to
choices: concede that the scarcity of references to Antigua limits the scope of Said's reading of the novel
explain why Austen chose to say so little about Sir Thomas's plantation
give Said's reason for treating the scarcity of the references as significant
introduce the first of the objections discussed in the third paragraph
show that Said regarded empire as the novel's central subject
questions.explanation: The sentence tells us how Said read the 'mere half dozen passing references': their brevity is 'not evidence that empire mattered little' but 'a sign of how completely it could be assumed.' It turns an apparent weakness into support, so C. D is the trap: the first objection does concern the few references, but this sentence is Said's position, stated before the objections and answering that worry in advance.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify what the sentence about brevity does in the passage.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, sentences 4-5; paragraph 3, sentence 2.

breakdown.analysis: Sentence 4 quotes Said's own phrase 'a mere half dozen passing references.' A reader might take that as a weakness. Sentence 5 gives Said's answer: the brevity shows how much was assumed. Function: Said's reason for treating scarcity as significant.

choices.note: Opposite. The sentence is Said's, and it denies that brevity shows empire mattered little; it doesn't concede a limit.
Out of scope. The sentence concerns what the brevity signifies for Said, not Austen's reasons for writing it that way.
CORRECT. Said treats brevity not as 'evidence that empire mattered little to the novel but [as] a sign of how completely it could be assumed.'
Wrong position-holder. The first objection belongs to critics in paragraph 3; this sentence gives Said's own view, which anticipates it.
Distortion. The passage says the method 'does not ask whether a novel is about empire'; the sentence is about what the novel assumes, not its central subject.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward contrapuntal reading, as applied to Mansfield Park, can most accurately be described as
choices: confidence in what it shows about the novel's dependence on colonial wealth, with doubt that it can settle Austen's attitude
skepticism that it reveals anything about the novel that is not already evident from the novel's plot
admiration for its method combined with agreement with Fraiman that it misrepresents Austen as conservative
qualified approval of its conclusions about Austen's complacency, tempered by concern over its reliance on a few references
uncritical enthusiasm for its capacity to expose the imperial assumptions of canonical fiction
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says the method is 'at its strongest as an account of dependence' and that this 'is not undone by the fewness of the references,' while it is 'weakest as a verdict on attitude.' A captures both the confidence and the limit. D reverses where the author's confidence lies: the author defends the reliance on few references and doubts the verdict on attitude.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize the author's view of contrapuntal reading precisely, including where it is positive and where it is limited.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, sentences 1-4.

breakdown.analysis: Two parts: strongest on dependence (and the fewness objection fails there), weakest on attitude. Look for an answer with both, in the right places. Traps will put the doubt in the wrong place or adopt one critic's view outright.

choices.note: CORRECT. Paragraph 4: 'strongest as an account of dependence' and 'weakest as a verdict on attitude,' which the text's margins 'cannot settle by themselves.'
Too negative. The author credits the method with showing something from 'evidence within the text,' and the passage says Said read the plot's parallel as 'more than plot.'
Half right. The author says both objections 'have force' but doesn't endorse Fraiman's conclusion; Fraiman is cited as an example of how attitude must be argued.
Reversal. The author says the fewness of references does not undo the showing of dependence, and doubts precisely the method's verdicts on attitude, such as complacency.
Too extreme. The author marks a clear limit to the method in the last paragraph.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Southam's reading of the dead silence establishes that Austen opposed the slave trade.
A critic who grants that the Bertrams' income depends on Antigua must also grant that the novel's moral order is an imperial one.
The first objection to Said's reading succeeds in showing that the novel does not depend on a colonial economy.
That a novel rarely mentions a colonial possession does not by itself show that the possession is unimportant to the novel's world.
Contrapuntal reading is more reliable when applied to novels that refer frequently to empire than when applied to Mansfield Park.
questions.explanation: The author says contrapuntal reading can show that the novel's world 'rests on an economy the novel mentions only at its edges,' and that this showing 'is not undone by the fewness of the references.' D follows, hedged by 'by itself.' B is the trap: it states as necessary the very link the first objection says a reader may decline to draw, and the author never rejects that part of the objection.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the passage supports for the author, without going further than the text allows.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, sentence 2; paragraph 4, sentence 2.

breakdown.analysis: The author accepts the dependence point and rejects the idea that few references undo it. The author does not say whether dependence implies an imperial moral order, and leaves Austen's attitude open. A safe inference: few references don't show something is unimportant.

choices.note: Too strong. The author lists 'quietly questioned' as one possibility among three and says attitude must be argued; nothing says Southam established Austen's opposition.
Reversal of the objection the author lets stand. The first objection says a reader 'may grant' the dependence 'without granting' an imperial moral order, and the author never denies that.
Distortion. The first objection grants that the income depends on Antigua; it doesn't deny the dependence, and the author says the showing of dependence holds.
CORRECT. The author says that the showing of dependence 'is not undone by the fewness of the references.' The hedge 'by itself' keeps the claim within what the passage supports.
Unsupported comparison. The passage discusses only Mansfield Park and doesn't rank the method's reliability across kinds of novels.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, the author would regard which one of the following as the kind of claim that contrapuntal reading is best suited to establish?
choices: that a novelist privately disapproved of the colonial trade from which a character's fortune derives, since the novel mentions that trade only with evident reluctance
that a novel is primarily about empire, since its most important scenes take place in a colony
that a novelist was indifferent to colonial suffering, since the novel's references to the colony are brief
that a novel's moral vision is that of a colonial ruler, since its hero manages his estate as a governor manages a province
that a family's leisure in a novel is financed by a colonial mine, since details scattered through the novel show its income comes from the mine
questions.explanation: The author says the method is 'at its strongest as an account of dependence,' shown 'from evidence within the text,' and 'weakest as a verdict on attitude.' E is a claim of dependence drawn from textual details. C and A are claims about the novelist's attitude, which the author says the margins 'cannot settle by themselves'; D draws the moral conclusion the first objection says need not follow from dependence.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply the author's distinction between what contrapuntal reading does well and what it does poorly to new cases.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, sentences 3-4; paragraph 3, sentence 2; paragraph 4.

breakdown.analysis: Sort each choice: is it a claim about dependence shown from the text (strong), about the author's attitude (weak), about the novel's moral order (contested by the first objection), or about whether the novel is 'about' empire (not what the method asks)? Only one is a pure dependence claim.

choices.note: Attitude claim. Inferring private disapproval from the handling of the margins is exactly the verdict on attitude the author says the method cannot settle on its own.
Not the method's question. The passage says contrapuntal reading 'does not ask whether a novel is about empire.'
Attitude claim, and the trap a reader of Said's critics might pick: inferring indifference from brevity is a verdict on attitude, the method's weakest use.
Moral-order claim. The first objection, which the author says has force, holds that dependence does not by itself establish that a novel's moral order is imperial; this goes further than dependence.
CORRECT. A claim of economic dependence on something at the novel's edges, shown 'from evidence within the text': precisely what the author calls the method's strongest use.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen Southam's interpretation of the dead silence, as it is described in the passage?
choices: Elsewhere in the novel, the Bertram children often fall silent when the conversation turns to subjects that they find tedious.
In the years in which the novel is set, the conduct of slaveholders was a subject of heated public controversy in Britain.
