Fanny's question about the slave trade is the only explicit mention of that trade in the novel.
Sir Thomas's Antigua estate is described in less detail than any other place connected with the Bertram family.
Many readers in Austen's own time paid little attention to the novel's references to Antigua.
questions.explanation: Southam's reading depends on the context: 'read against the abolition debates of the years in which the novel is set,' the silence registers the family's discomfort. If slaveholders' conduct was heatedly disputed then, a slaveholder's family falling silent at the question is better explained by discomfort. A is the trap in the other direction: boredom is an alternative cause of the silence, so it weakens Southam's reading.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that makes Southam's reading of the silence, as discomfort in light of the abolition debates, more likely.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, sentences 3-4.

breakdown.analysis: Southam's claim: silence = family's discomfort, read against contemporary abolition debates, not author's complacency. Strengthen by making the topic one that would embarrass a slaveholding family at that time; weaken by offering another cause of the silence. Watch for facts that support Said's side rather than Southam's.

choices.note: Opposite. A habit of falling silent from boredom offers another explanation of the silence and so weakens the discomfort reading.

CORRECT. Southam's reading rests on the 'abolition debates of the years in which the novel is set'; if slaveholders' conduct was heatedly disputed then, a slaveholding family's silence at Fanny's question is more plausibly discomfort.
Irrelevant, or cuts toward Said. A single explicit mention fits Said's emphasis on how little the novel says; it doesn't tell us what the silence means.
Supports Said's side, not Southam's. Sparse description of the estate bears on the 'half dozen passing references,' not on the family's reaction to Fanny.
Irrelevant. How readers of the time attended to Antigua doesn't bear on why the Bertrams fall silent within the novel.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Darwish's elegy for Said is best understood as a poetic application of the theory of exile that Said developed in his 1984 essay.
Said's essay on exile cannot illuminate Darwish's elegy, because an elegy is a consoling form and Said held that exile's sorrow cannot be consoled.
Said's account of exile and Darwish's elegy for him clarify each other's form, though neither can confirm what the other claims.
Darwish's elegy improves on Said's essay by showing that contrapuntal awareness can be lived rather than merely described.
Said's essay and Darwish's elegy together show that exile, though terrible to experience, ultimately yields a valuable plurality of vision.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph rejects the 'single project' view, calls the illumination 'real but uneven,' gives one way the essay helps the poem and one way the poem helps the essay, and ends: 'Each clarifies the other's form; neither can settle the other's claims.' C restates that conclusion. A is the tempting view the author qualifies; D takes one half of the reciprocal point and inflates it into a ranking.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall conclusion about how Said's essay and Darwish's poem bear on each other.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, first two sentences and last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 1 lays out the essay; paragraph 2 the poem and Dyer's reading; paragraph 3 the author's verdict. The first sentence of paragraph 3 states a view only to qualify it ('It is tempting to conclude...'). Prephrase: they light each other up, but only partly, and neither proves the other. Watch for the tempting view itself, for a one-directional version, and for an answer that turns the author's caution into a denial.

choices.note: Wrong position-holder. This is the 'single project' view the author calls tempting and then qualifies as 'real but uneven.' A reader who knows the poem's title might pick it.

Too extreme. The author does note a tension between elegy and Said's view of sorrow, but says the essay 'teaches us to hear the poem's paired claims as counterpoint.' The illumination is uneven, not absent.
CORRECT. It matches the last sentence of the passage: 'Each clarifies the other's form; neither can settle the other's claims.' The hedged 'though' clause carries the author's qualification.
Half right. The passage says the poem 'can show what the essay could only assert,' but it immediately adds that the poem cannot show the essay is true, and never says the poem improves on the essay.

Out of scope. The passage reports Said's view that exile has a compensation, but the author's conclusion concerns how essay and poem illuminate each other, not a verdict that exile is ultimately valuable; the passage stresses Said's insistence on its sorrow.

questions.stem: The author mentions that the Arabic title of Darwish's poem names the rhetorical figure of antithesis (second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that Darwish's poem belongs to the classical Arabic elegiac tradition rather than to the vocabulary of Said's criticism
suggest that the English translations of the title misrepresent the way the poem's paired statements are arranged
explain why Darwish chose to cast his elegy as an imagined conversation in which the dead critic is given a voice
indicate that Darwish rejected the claim, made in Said's 1984 essay, that the sorrow of exile can never be surmounted
point to a feature of the poem's construction that parallels the awareness described in the first paragraph
questions.explanation: Antithesis is 'the pairing of opposites'; the first paragraph describes contrapuntal awareness as two lines lived together with neither absorbing the other, and the third paragraph hears the poem's 'paired claims' that way. The detail sets up that parallel. A is the trap: Dyer does connect the poem to the Arabic elegy, but the title detail is not used to set the poem against Said's vocabulary; the passage joins the two.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the detail about the title contributes to the passage's argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, fourth sentence; compare first paragraph, last two sentences, and third paragraph, third sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Function questions ask why the author includes something. Look at what the title detail connects to: 'pairing of opposites' echoes 'neither line absorbs the other' and anticipates 'the poem's paired claims.' Prephrase: it links how the poem is built to Said's idea of counterpoint.

choices.note: Distortion. The Arabic elegy is mentioned in Dyer's reading, and the passage says Said's method shapes the poem within it. Nothing sets tradition against Said's vocabulary; the passage presents them as working together.
Out of scope. The passage gives the translations without criticizing them; 'Counterpoint' and 'A Contrapuntal Reading' fit the parallel the author draws.
Shell game. The imagined conversation is mentioned in the same sentence, but the passage gives no account of why Darwish chose that form, and the title is not offered as the reason.
Out of scope. The passage never says Darwish rejected anything in Said's essay; the tension between elegy and sorrow is the author's own observation, in the third paragraph.
CORRECT. A figure of paired opposites mirrors an awareness in which two settings sound together without either absorbing the other, which the third paragraph applies to the poem's 'paired claims.'

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: The composure with which the poem gives voice to Said's exile is in some tension with a view Said himself expressed about exile.
Darwish's elegy succeeds as a poem only insofar as it accurately represents the argument of Said's essay.
Said's description of exile as a rift that cannot be healed was later abandoned in favor of his account of contrapuntal awareness.
An elegy that gave its subject a voice would be incapable of expressing grief.
Rebecca Dyer overstates the extent to which Said's critical method shapes Darwish's poem.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says Said 'had insisted that exile's sorrow resists such shaping,' and that 'In letting Said speak his exile with such poise, the poem risks making the terrible experience chiefly compelling to think about.' Poise in voicing exile is thus in tension with Said's own view. A hedges ('some tension') as the author does ('risks'). C is the trap for readers who see only the 'compensation' and miss that Said grants it only 'after these concessions.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the author's own claims support, without going further than they do.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, fourth and fifth sentences; first paragraph, second and third sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Inference questions reward staying inside the author's words. The author's worry is stated with 'risks,' so the right answer should be similarly modest. Check each answer against the third paragraph; reject anything about success criteria, abandonment, or a verdict on Dyer, none of which the passage gives.

choices.note: CORRECT. The poem lets Said speak his exile 'with such poise,' while Said 'had insisted that exile's sorrow resists such shaping'; the author says this 'risks' the slippage the essay warns against. 'Some tension' is exactly that strong.
Out of scope. The author discusses what the essay and poem clarify in each other, never a standard for the poem's success, and says the poem cannot even show the essay is true.

Distortion. The compensation comes 'only after these concessions' within the same essay; the passage gives no sign that Said abandoned the rift. Outside knowledge of Said's later work doesn't help here.
Too extreme. The author says an elegy gives 'the mourners a shape for grief'; voicing the dead is part of how it consoles, not something that makes grief inexpressible.
Out of scope. The author reports Dyer's argument without disputing it, and the third paragraph's own reading of the 'paired claims' is consistent with it.

questions.stem: In the context of the passage, the phrase "the very slippage against which his opening sentence warns" (third paragraph) refers to
choices: the substitution of a technical term borrowed from music for a direct description of exile
the tendency of translators to soften a poem's title when rendering it into another language
the shift from writing criticism about the experience of exile to writing poetry about it
the move from seeing exile as an ordeal to treating it chiefly as an object of fascination
the replacement of Said's sorrowful view of exile by a nationalist celebration of return
questions.explanation: Said's opening sentence contrasts exile as 'compelling to think about' with exile as 'terrible to experience,' and the author says the poem 'risks making the terrible experience chiefly compelling to think about.' The slippage is that shift, which D paraphrases. C is the trap: the passage moves between criticism and poetry, but that move is not what Said's sentence warns against.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out what 'slippage' refers to by connecting it to Said's opening sentence.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, fifth sentence; first paragraph, first sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Meaning-in-context: the phrase points back to 'his opening sentence,' so reread it. It sets thinking about exile against experiencing it. The sentence containing the phrase says the poem risks making the experience 'chiefly compelling to think about.' Prephrase: sliding from exile as suffering to exile as an interesting idea.

choices.note: Shell game. 'Contrapuntal' is a musical term in the passage, but Said's opening sentence says nothing about musical terms, and the author doesn't object to the term.
Out of scope. The passage gives two translations of the title without criticizing either.
Shell game. The passage does compare criticism and poetry, but the warning in Said's first sentence is about how exile is regarded, not about which genre treats it.
CORRECT. The opening sentence opposes 'compelling to think about' and 'terrible to experience'; the slippage is letting the first displace the second.
Out of scope. Nationalism appears nowhere in the passage; a reader who knows the essay's longer discussion of nationalism may supply it from outside.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Said regards the heroic and triumphant episodes that literature records in exiles' lives as
choices: evidence that exile can be overcome by sufficient creative effort
attempts to overcome a sorrow that cannot finally be surmounted
the source of the plurality of vision that exiles possess
examples of the contrapuntal awareness that exile makes possible
exaggerations introduced by writers who had not experienced exile
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says Said 'treats the heroic and even triumphant episodes that literature records in exiles' lives as efforts to overcome a sorrow that can never finally be surmounted.' B paraphrases it. A reverses the point: the efforts don't succeed.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says Said thinks of heroic episodes in exile literature.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: A straightforward detail. Locate 'heroic and even triumphant episodes' and read the rest of the sentence. The traps borrow later ideas from the same paragraph (plurality of vision, counterpoint) and attach them to the episodes.

choices.note: Opposite. The sorrow 'can never finally be surmounted'; the episodes are efforts, not evidence of success.
CORRECT. A close paraphrase of the second sentence of the first paragraph.
Shell game. Plurality of vision comes from being aware of 'at least two' cultures, not from the heroic episodes.
Shell game. Contrapuntal awareness is the compensation Said allows 'only after these concessions'; the episodes belong to the concessions.
Out of scope. The passage says nothing about who wrote these accounts or whether they exaggerate.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most closely analogous to the contrapuntal awareness described in the first paragraph?
choices: An interpreter living abroad who hears each remark at once in the language spoken and in her first language, neither replacing the other.
A composer who blends the folk melodies of his homeland and his adopted country into a single new style in which neither source can be distinguished.
A traveler who, after many years abroad, finds that she can no longer recall the customs and speech of the town where she grew up.
A scholar who studies a foreign culture intensively for a decade and then returns home to write about it from a coolly detached point of view.
An emigrant who follows the customs of his new country in public and those of his native country in private, keeping the two strictly apart.
questions.explanation: The passage defines contrapuntal awareness as 'an awareness of simultaneous dimensions': 'The habits of the new place are lived against the memory of the old, and neither line absorbs the other.' A has both elements, two at once and neither replacing the other. B is the near miss: two sources, but fused so that one absorbs the other. E keeps both but alternates them, so they are never simultaneous.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the case with the same structure as contrapuntal awareness: two settings present at once, neither absorbing the other.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph, last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Abstract the definition before reading the choices: (1) awareness of at least two settings, (2) at the same time, (3) without either absorbing the other. Then test each answer on all three. Fusion fails (3); forgetting fails (1); alternation fails (2); detached study is a different relation altogether.

choices.note: CORRECT. Both languages are present 'at once,' and neither version replaces the other, matching 'simultaneous dimensions' and 'neither line absorbs the other.'
Distortion. The two sources merge 'into a single new style'; in the passage neither line absorbs the other. A reader who equates counterpoint with harmony or blending falls here.
Opposite. Losing the memory of the old place leaves only one setting, the reverse of being aware of 'at least two.'
Out of scope. Studying a culture and then viewing it from a distance is neither exile nor simultaneous awareness; the two settings are not lived against each other.
Half right. Both cultures are kept, but in separate compartments and at separate times; the passage's awareness is of 'simultaneous' dimensions, with the new lived 'against' the old.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the view that criticism and poetry "form a single project" in the case of Said and Darwish can most accurately be described as
choices: firm rejection, on the grounds that Said's essay and Darwish's elegy have nothing important in common
enthusiastic endorsement, tempered only by doubts about the accuracy of the English translations
indifference, since the author is concerned only with the formal features of Darwish's poem and not with Said's claims
recognition that it captures a genuine relationship, with doubt that the relationship is as complete as it implies
reluctant acceptance, prompted by evidence that Darwish deliberately applied Said's critical method throughout the poem
questions.explanation: The author calls the view 'tempting' and then says 'The illumination is real but uneven,' going on to show that the essay and poem each clarify the other's form while neither can settle the other's claims. That is partial agreement with a limit, as D says. E is the trap: Dyer's reading is reported, but the author's verdict is qualified, not acceptance.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize the author's stance toward the 'single project' view, including its degree.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, first two sentences and last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Attitude questions turn on degree. 'Real' concedes something; 'uneven' limits it; the rest of the paragraph fills in both. Prephrase: partly right, but overstated. Eliminate the extremes first, then check the remaining answers' reasons against the passage.

choices.note: Too extreme. The author says the illumination is 'real' and shows how each clarifies the other's form.
Too extreme, and out of scope. 'Real but uneven' is not enthusiastic endorsement, and the passage never doubts the translations.
Distortion. The author takes a clear position on the view, and also discusses claims, not only form.
CORRECT. 'Real but uneven': the author grants a genuine relationship but argues it is incomplete, since 'neither can settle the other's claims.'
Distortion. The author's attitude is qualified, not acceptance, and the passage attributes the claim about Said's method to Dyer's argument, not to evidence of Darwish's intent.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Said showed that the late works of major artists, contrary to the received view, characteristically exhibit intransigence rather than serenity.
Said's idea of late style survives its critics' objections better as a way of reading works than as an account of how artists age.
Adorno's account of Beethoven's late style is more rigorous than Said's, because Said extended the idea to artists to whom it does not apply.
Critics have shown that late style is a construct produced by biographical interest, so Said's book tells us more about Said than about the artists he discusses.
Said's examples, including Strauss, Lampedusa and Genet, demonstrate that late style is found in literature as well as in music.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph gives the author's verdict: Said is 'better placed against these objections than his critics allow, though not entirely,' and the concept 'survives' when 'understood as an interpretive stance rather than a law of artistic aging.' B states that. A gives Said a universal claim the passage says he 'never claimed'; D adopts the critics' view, which the author partly answers.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall conclusion about Said's idea of late style.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, first and last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Map: P1 received view and Said's question; P2 Adorno and Said's extension; P3 critics; P4 author's partial defense with a cost. The main point lives in P4. Prephrase: Said's idea mostly survives the objections if taken as a way of reading, not a law about old age.

choices.note: Too strong. The fourth paragraph says Said 'never claimed that all late works share a style'; 'characteristically' turns his possibility into a rule.
CORRECT. It joins the partial defense ('better placed... though not entirely') to the condition under which the concept 'survives.'
Out of scope. The passage never ranks Adorno above Said or says the extension is misapplied; it presents the extension as Said's development of Adorno.

Too extreme and wrong position-holder. This pushes McMullan's objection to a conclusion the author resists; the author says only that the concept's preference for the intransigent is 'Said's own' and still defends it.
Detail, not main point. The examples appear in the second paragraph, and the passage's point is about the status of the category, not the range of arts it covers.

questions.stem: The author's discussion of Richard Strauss (second paragraph) serves primarily to
choices: show that Said accepted Adorno's judgments about which twentieth-century composers deserved serious critical attention
suggest that Said's category of late style applies more readily to composers than to novelists and playwrights
illustrate the serene kind of late work that Said acknowledged as existing alongside the intransigent kind
indicate the reach of Said's extension of Adorno's idea, which takes in an artist Adorno disdained
offer evidence that late style is a construct imposed on artists by critics who already know their biographies
questions.explanation: The paragraph says Said 'extended it far beyond Beethoven' and gives Strauss, 'whom Adorno despised,' as the first case: his late works are late because they 'retreat into eighteenth-century idioms deliberately out of step with their catastrophic moment.' D captures both points. C is the trap: Strauss's works are smooth rather than furrowed, but Said treats them as late in his intransigent sense, not as serene works.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the Strauss example contributes to the second paragraph.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, fifth and sixth sentences; fourth paragraph, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The sentence just before the Strauss example announces its job: Said 'extended it far beyond Beethoven.' Two features make Strauss a striking extension: Adorno's contempt for him, and lateness defined by being out of step with the time. The fourth paragraph uses the same example to show lateness 'need not coincide with anguish or with formal breakdown.'

choices.note: Opposite. Strauss is the composer 'Adorno despised,' yet Said counts him as late, so Said departed from Adorno's judgment.
Out of scope. Lampedusa and Genet follow 'read the same way'; nothing suggests the category fits music better.

Distortion. The serene kind is illustrated by The Tempest and The Winter's Tale in the first paragraph. Strauss becomes late because his works are 'out of step with their catastrophic moment,' Said's other kind.
CORRECT. Strauss shows the reach of Said's extension, to an artist Adorno despised and to a lateness defined by the works' relation to their moment.
Wrong position-holder. That is McMullan's objection in the third paragraph; the author uses Strauss in the fourth paragraph to defend Said.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Adorno rejected which one of the following?
choices: the view that Beethoven's late sonatas and quartets lack the roundness of ripe fruit
the claim that conventions appear bare, unabsorbed into a whole, in Beethoven's late works
the inclusion of Beethoven's late quartets among the composer's major achievements
the idea that an artist's lateness may be a refusal rather than a fulfillment
the reading of the late works' fissures as a record of suffering
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says Adorno 'refused to read this as a record of the composer's suffering or premonition of death.' E paraphrases it. A and B are views Adorno held, not ones he rejected.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says Adorno refused or rejected.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, second and third sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Detail question with an 'opposite' design: most choices are things Adorno affirmed. Find the verb 'refused' and read its object.

choices.note: Opposite. Adorno 'held that the late sonatas and quartets lack the roundness of ripe fruit.'
Opposite. In the late works 'conventions stand bare'; Adorno affirmed this.
Out of scope. The passage never says Adorno thought less of the late quartets.
Opposite. Said 'took from Adorno the idea that lateness may be a refusal,' so it was Adorno's idea.
CORRECT. He 'refused to read this as a record of the composer's suffering or premonition of death.'

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following statements about Adorno's essay and McMullan's objection?
choices: Adorno's approach sought to avoid the kind of reasoning that McMullan says underlies the idea of late style.
Adorno's essay on Beethoven is the principal target of McMullan's argument that late style is a critical construct.
McMullan's objection would apply to Adorno's essay with greater force than it applies to Said's book.
Adorno would have accepted McMullan's view that lateness is perceived only where an artist's biography is already known.
McMullan derived his account of the biographical urge from Adorno's criticism of psychological readings of Beethoven.
questions.explanation: McMullan says the idea is 'synecdochic of the biographical urge': 'we find lateness where we already know the artist was near death.' Adorno 'refused to read this as a record of the composer's suffering or premonition of death, a psychological reading that... mistakes the work for a document'; 'The fissures were formal.' So Adorno tried to avoid the biographical reasoning McMullan diagnoses. C is the near miss: the passage gives no basis for comparing how hard the objection hits Adorno versus Said, and Adorno's formal emphasis would if anything cut the other way.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Connect two parts of the passage the author does not explicitly link, and find what follows without going further.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, third and fourth sentences; third paragraph, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: This is a synthesis inference. Put McMullan's diagnosis (lateness is read through knowledge of the artist's approaching death) beside Adorno's stated method (reject the reading of late works as a record of suffering or premonition of death; the fissures are formal). The two are opposed in aim. The right answer says only that Adorno sought to avoid that reasoning, not that he succeeded, and not that McMullan targets or borrows from him. A reader who knows McMullan's book discusses Adorno may be tempted by B or E, which the passage doesn't support.

choices.note: CORRECT. Adorno rejected reading late works as 'a record of the composer's suffering or premonition of death,' which is the biographical inference McMullan attributes to the idea of late style. 'Sought to avoid' claims nothing about whether he succeeded.
Out of scope. The passage says McMullan studied 'how the idea of "late Shakespeare" was invented'; it never names Adorno as his principal target.

Unsupported comparison. The passage never weighs the objection against Adorno and Said separately; if anything, Adorno's insistence that the fissures were formal suggests he resisted the biographical reading.
Opposite. Adorno refused the biographical reading; nothing suggests he would endorse a view that ties lateness to knowledge of the artist's life.
Out of scope. The passage says nothing about where McMullan's ideas came from.

questions.stem: By "the less it describes artists and the more it describes a way of reading them" (fourth paragraph), the author most likely means that, as the concept of lateness is separated from chronology,
choices: it becomes impossible to determine which artists, if any, actually produced late works
it applies only to those artists whose biographies are unknown to their critics
it increasingly reflects the interpreter's preferences rather than facts about careers
it can no longer be applied to literature, since literary works are read rather than performed
it ceases to be of any use to critics and should therefore be abandoned
questions.explanation: The sentence continues: 'a way of reading them, one whose preference for the intransigent over the reconciled is Said's own.' Once lateness is not tied to when a work was made, what marks a work as late is the reader's preference, as C says. E is the too-extreme trap: the next sentence says the concept 'survives.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Interpret the phrase using the rest of its sentence and the sentence after it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, third and fourth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Read the full sentence: the phrase is glossed by 'one whose preference for the intransigent over the reconciled is Said's own.' The next sentence says the concept survives as 'an interpretive stance.' Prephrase: the label tells you more about the critic's tastes than about the artist's age.

choices.note: Too extreme. The author says the concept describes artists less, not that it becomes impossible to identify late works.
Distortion. Biography appears in McMullan's objection, not in this sentence; the author's point concerns the reader's preferences.
CORRECT. The 'way of reading' is one 'whose preference for the intransigent over the reconciled is Said's own'; the concept comes to express the interpreter's values.
Shell game. 'Reading' here means interpreting, not reading as opposed to hearing; the passage applies lateness to Lampedusa and Genet without difficulty.
Too extreme. The final sentence says the concept 'survives' and 'lets us hear what a story of serenity would drown out.'

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken McMullan's claim as it is presented in the passage?
choices: Some of Shakespeare's plays once thought to be late works have since been redated to earlier in his career.
Listeners told nothing about composers' lives or the dates of works reliably pick out composers' final works by form alone.
Many artists who lived into old age produced late works that critics describe as serene and reconciled rather than intransigent.
Said wrote much of On Late Style while he was seriously ill and aware that he might soon die.
Adorno's essay on Beethoven was written when Adorno himself was a relatively young man.
questions.explanation: McMullan's claim, as the passage gives it, is that late style is a construct of the biographical urge: 'we find lateness where we already know the artist was near death.' If listeners who know nothing of biography or chronology still pick out final works by form, then lateness is detectable without the biographical knowledge the claim says produces it. A is the trap: redating shows critics' labels can follow (mistaken) chronology, which fits McMullan.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that would most undermine the claim that lateness is perceived only because critics know the artist was near death.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Isolate the claim: perceived lateness depends on biographical knowledge. The strongest weakener removes the biographical knowledge and shows lateness is still perceived. Watch for answers that bear on Said's thesis (serene vs. intransigent) rather than McMullan's, and for facts about the critics' own lives, which don't test the claim.

choices.note: Opposite, roughly. If a play's 'lateness' was perceived only while it was thought late, that supports the view that lateness follows what critics believe about chronology.
CORRECT. Identifying final works without any biographical or chronological knowledge shows lateness can be found where no one 'already know[s] the artist was near death.'
Irrelevant to this claim. Serene late works bear on whether lateness is intransigent, Said's thesis, not on whether biography produces the perception of a late style.
Irrelevant, or slightly supportive. A critic's own illness might feed a biographical interest; it does nothing to show lateness is perceptible without biography.
Irrelevant. The age of the critic says nothing about whether perceived lateness depends on knowledge of the artist's approaching death.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?
choices: A received view and an alternative are introduced, the latter's source is traced, objections are reported, and it is then partly defended.
A theory is presented, the evidence for it is reviewed, and the theory is then rejected in light of objections that the author endorses.
Two rival accounts of a phenomenon are presented, and the author argues that each is correct about a different group of artists.
A concept is traced from its origins through its later development, and the author concludes that the later stages distorted its meaning.
An objection to a widely held theory is stated, the theory's defenders reply to it, and the author declines to choose between the two sides.
questions.explanation: P1 gives the consoling story and Said's question; P2 traces Adorno and Said's extension; P3 reports McMullan and other critics; P4 says Said is 'better placed... though not entirely' and that the concept survives as an interpretive stance. A follows each step. B gets the ending wrong: the author partly defends the theory.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the sequence of the four paragraphs to a description.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First sentence of each paragraph; fourth paragraph, first sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Label each paragraph before reading choices: received view + Said's alternative; Adorno + extension; critics; qualified defense. Then check each answer element by element; a single wrong element (rejected, declines to choose, distorted) eliminates it.

choices.note: CORRECT. Every element matches: consoling story and Said's question (P1), Adorno and the extension (P2), objections (P3), partial defense with a cost (P4).
Half right. The first steps fit loosely, but the author does not reject Said's idea; it 'survives' as an interpretive stance.
Distortion. Serenity and intransigence are both acknowledged by Said himself, not presented as rival accounts the author adjudicates artist by artist.
Distortion. The passage does trace Said's debt to Adorno, but the author never says Said's extension distorted Adorno's meaning.
Wrong order and wrong ending. The passage presents the theory before the objections, and the author takes a position in the last paragraph.

sections.title: Reading Through Ideas 12: What counts as the Thousand and One Nights? · Two islands: Hayy ibn Yaqzan and Robinson Crusoe · Dante and the Ladder of Muhammad · The Maqama and the Picaro

passages.title: What counts as the Thousand and One Nights?
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
The frame of the Thousand and One Nights is among literature's most economical devices. King Shahriyar, having discovered his wife's betrayal, resolves to marry a new bride each night and have her killed at dawn. Shahrazad, the vizier's daughter, volunteers to marry him and, with her sister Dunyazad's help, begins a tale each night that is left unfinished at daybreak, so that the king must spare her to hear the rest. Within her tales, characters tell further tales, often to ransom a life, so that storytelling becomes the means of survival the frame dramatizes. Yet what lies inside the frame has never been fixed. A ninth-century fragment shows that a book of a thousand nights already existed, and the tenth-century historian al-Mas'udi traced it to a Persian collection, the Hazar Afsan.

For Muhsin Mahdi, the question had a philological answer. His 1984 critical edition rests principally on a Syrian manuscript, probably of the fourteenth century, that Antoine Galland acquired around 1701; it contains only 282 nights and breaks off in the middle of a tale. Comparing manuscript families, Mahdi sought to recover the archetype from which the surviving copies descend, and he treated the later compilations that reached a full thousand and one nights by absorbing independent tales as accretions. He also showed that the Arabic manuscripts of Aladdin that surfaced after Galland were back-translations from the French. The reviewer Andras Hamori judged that Galland's manuscript "remains to this day the oldest and best witness to the 'original core.'"

The opposing view starts from Galland's own French translation, published from 1704 to 1717. Having exhausted his manuscript, Galland filled out later volumes with other material, including the so-called orphan tales, for which no earlier Arabic text is known. Several of these, Aladdin and Ali Baba among them, came from Hanna Diyab, a Maronite from Aleppo whom Galland met in Paris in 1709 and whose storytelling Galland noted in his diary. Diyab's memoir, preserved in the Vatican Library, has now been published, and Paulo Lemos Horta has argued that Diyab should be counted among the work's secret authors rather than treated as a mere informant. On this view the Nights was always an open collection, and tales told by a Syrian storyteller in Paris belong to it no less than tales copied by medieval scribes.

Each position captures something, but neither settles the question it is usually taken to settle. Mahdi's method can establish which text is oldest; it cannot establish that age confers identity on a work whose frame invites continuation, for a book in which the teller survives by always having another tale is ill served by a canon that closes at night 282. The open-collection view, in turn, risks dissolving the work: if everything ever told under Shahrazad's name belongs to it, the Nights becomes a label rather than a text. A better position separates the questions. The Galland manuscript is the best evidence of what the Nights was in medieval Syria; Diyab's tales are evidence of what it became. To call them inauthentic is to confuse a claim about origins with a claim about membership.

sources.author: Muhsin Mahdi (ed.)
sources.title: The Thousand and One Nights (Alf Layla wa-Layla) from the Earliest Known Sources
sources.note: The critical edition of the Syrian manuscript Galland acquired (Paris, BnF arabe 3609-3611; 282 nights, breaking off in the tale of Qamar al-Zaman), which reconstructs the manuscript tradition and shows the post-Galland Arabic Aladdin manuscripts to be back-translations; Andras Hamori's review of Mahdi's work in the Journal of the American Oriental Society says the manuscript "remains to this day the oldest and best witness to the 'original core'" (wording verified against the review's published excerpt).

sources.author: Paulo Lemos Horta
sources.title: Marvellous Thieves: Secret Authors of the Arabian Nights
sources.note: Argues that Hanna Diyab and other uncredited intermediaries should be recognized as authors of the Nights as Europe knows it, beginning with Diyab's role in the orphan tales Aladdin and Ali Baba.

sources.author: Hanna Diyab (tr. Elias Muhanna; ed. Johannes Stephan)
sources.title: The Book of Travels
sources.note: The Aleppan storyteller's own memoir, from the Vatican manuscript (Sbath 254), recounting his travels and his time in Paris, where he told Galland the tales that became Aladdin and Ali Baba.

sources.author: Robert Irwin
sources.title: The Arabian Nights: A Companion
sources.note: A standard introduction to the Nights' frame, manuscripts, Galland's translation and the orphan tales, and to the debate over Mahdi's search for an archetype.

passages.title: Two islands: Hayy ibn Yaqzan and Robinson Crusoe
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Passage A

Ibn Tufayl, a twelfth-century Andalusian philosopher and court physician to the Almohad ruler Abu Ya'qub Yusuf, presented Hayy ibn Yaqzan as an unveiling of the "Eastern" wisdom that Avicenna had alluded to. Its hero, whose name means "Alive, son of Awake," grows up alone on an equatorial island, nursed by a doe. When she dies, he dissects her body to find the cause and concludes that what animated her was not any organ but something that had departed from it. Passing through stages of seven years, he moves from the study of bodies to the heavens, reasons to a necessary and incorporeal Creator, and ends in ecstatic contemplation of that Being, all without language, teacher or scripture.

The tale's second half qualifies this triumph without retracting it. At about fifty, Hayy meets Absal, a devout man from a neighboring island governed by a revealed religion, who has come seeking solitude. Once Absal teaches him language, the two find that the religion's teachings are symbols of the truths Hayy reached unaided. When Hayy tries to teach the island's people directly, however, they reject him; he concludes that most people are best served by the law's symbols and returns to his island with Absal. The tale thus argues not that reason makes revelation superfluous but that the two converge, though only a few can follow reason to the end. Here lies the force of the thought experiment: an intellect stripped of custom and instruction discloses what reason itself can know of God.

Passage B

That Robinson Crusoe (1719) owes something to Hayy ibn Yaqzan has been argued since Antonio Pastor's The Idea of Robinson Crusoe (1930), and more recently by Samar Attar. The case rests largely on availability: Simon Ockley's English translation, titled "The Improvement of Human Reason, Exhibited in the Life of Hai Ebn Yokdhan," appeared in 1708. Skeptics reply that nothing shows Defoe read it and that the castaway Alexander Selkirk is a likelier model.

The deeper difference lies in what solitude is made to reveal. Crusoe arrives a grown man and salvages tools, grain and Bibles from the wreck; his knowledge of God comes from reading Scripture during an illness, not from reasoning about nature, and he reads his survival as providence. Ian Watt saw in the novel the economic individualism of a hero who counts, builds and owns; G. A. Starr and J. Paul Hunter placed it among Puritan spiritual autobiographies. Both readings point one way: Crusoe's ledger of evils and goods, by which he learns "to look more upon the bright side of my condition, and less upon the dark side," is a Protestant self-accounting. If Defoe borrowed Ibn Tufayl's island, he refurnished it: where Hayy finds that reason alone can reach God, Crusoe finds that a solitary self needs a Book and a providential reading of its fortunes. Yet neither island is as empty as it looks. Hayy's unaided reason retraces, stage by stage, the Avicennan philosophy his author already held, much as Crusoe's conversion follows the Puritan narratives Defoe knew. Solitude reveals chiefly what each author brings to it.

sources.author: Ibn Tufayl (tr. Lenn Evan Goodman)
sources.title: Ibn Tufayl's Hayy Ibn Yaqzan: A Philosophical Tale
sources.note: A standard English translation with introduction, presenting the tale's stages of self-taught discovery, the meeting with Absal and Salaman's island, and its Avicennan background.

sources.author: Samar Attar
sources.title: The Vital Roots of European Enlightenment: Ibn Tufayl's Influence on Modern Western Thought
sources.note: Argues for Ibn Tufayl's influence on early modern European thought, including a chapter on echoes of Hayy ibn Yaqzan (and Sindbad) in Robinson Crusoe; the passage quotes the title of Simon Ockley's 1708 translation, The Improvement of Human Reason, Exhibited in the Life of Hai Ebn Yokdhan, as recorded in library catalogues and the Project Gutenberg edition.

sources.author: Ian Watt
sources.title: The Rise of the Novel: Studies in Defoe, Richardson and Fielding
sources.note: Its chapter on Robinson Crusoe reads the novel as an expression of economic individualism; G. A. Starr's Defoe and Spiritual Autobiography (1965) and J. Paul Hunter's The Reluctant Pilgrim (1966) offer the competing religious reading.

sources.author: Daniel Defoe
sources.title: Robinson Crusoe
sources.note: The novel itself; the quotation "to look more upon the bright side of my condition, and less upon the dark side" is from Crusoe's reflections on his island life after his conversion (verified against standard editions).

passages.title: Dante and the Ladder of Muhammad
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
In 1919, in his address on entering the Royal Spanish Academy, the Arabist and Catholic priest Miguel Asín Palacios argued that Dante's Divine Comedy owed much of its design to Islamic accounts of the Prophet's night journey (isrāʾ) and ascension (miʿrāj). Asín set the poem beside successive versions of the miʿrāj legend and beside the mystical writings of Ibn ʿArabī, and he catalogued correspondences: an otherworld arranged in graded tiers, punishments fitted to particular sins, a guide who leads the traveler, and an ascent through the heavens to the divine presence. He did not claim that Dante had read any single Arabic text. His case was cumulative: so many resemblances, he held, could not be coincidental, and the Islamic culture of medieval Spain offered a plausible route into Italy.

The reception among Dante scholars was largely hostile. Critics objected that Asín drew his parallels from works scattered across several centuries, some of which no reader of Latin could have known, and that Christian vision literature supplied antecedents of its own. The most damaging objection, however, was that no channel of transmission was documented. In 1949 Enrico Cerulli and, independently, José Muñoz Sendino published the Liber scalae Machometi, the "Book of Muhammad's Ladder," a first-person account of the miʿrāj. At the order of Alfonso X of Castile, an Arabic original had been put into Castilian by a Jewish physician named Abraham and from Castilian into Latin and Old French; the French version is dated 1264, the year before Dante's birth. The Castilian is lost, but the Latin and French survive, and Cerulli showed that the book was known in fourteenth-century Italy, where Fazio degli Uberti cites it. Many hailed the text as the missing link in Asín's argument, and Maria Corti later proposed that Dante's teacher Brunetto Latini, sent by Florence as envoy to Alfonso's court in 1260, was the likely intermediary.

The discovery changes the question without settling it. It establishes what Asín could only assume: that an Arabic narrative of an otherworldly journey circulated in Latin Christendom within Dante's lifetime. It does not establish that Dante read it. Brunetto's embassy preceded the dated translations, and nothing Dante wrote mentions the book. Moreover, as Vicente Cantarino observed, the Liber itself is in an important sense the chief obstacle to Asín's thesis: it is a popular narrative of marvels, lacking the allegorical and mystical character on which Asín's most striking parallels depended. Nor does the poem's own treatment of Islam decide the matter. Dante places Muhammad in the eighth circle of Hell among those who in life were "seminator di scandalo e di scisma," but a poet can take material from a tradition he condemns, so this judgment is compatible both with borrowing and with ignorance.

What the evidence supports is narrower than Asín's thesis but broader than his critics' dismissal: the Comedy was composed in a Mediterranean world where Christian and Islamic narratives of ascent were in contact, and Dante could have known Islamic material, while the derivation of any particular feature of the poem from it remains unproven.

sources.author: Miguel Asín Palacios
sources.title: La escatología musulmana en la Divina Comedia
sources.note: Asín's address to the Real Academia Española arguing, from a cumulative catalogue of parallels with miʿrāj legends and Ibn ʿArabī, that Islamic eschatology shaped the Comedy; abridged in English as Islam and the Divine Comedy (trans. Harold Sunderland, 1926).

sources.author: Enrico Cerulli
sources.title: Il "Libro della Scala" e la questione delle fonti arabo-spagnole della Divina Commedia
sources.note: Vatican (Studi e Testi 150) edition of the Latin and Old French Liber scalae Machometi with a study of its circulation in Europe, including Fazio degli Uberti's citation; published the same year as José Muñoz Sendino's La Escala de Mahoma.

sources.author: Jan M. Ziolkowski (ed.)
sources.title: Dante and Islam
sources.note: Fordham collection that reprints Vicente Cantarino's 'Dante and Islam: History and Analysis of a Controversy' (1965), which judges the Liber's own character the greatest objection to Asín, and Maria Corti's essay on the Brunetto Latini channel.

sources.author: Dante Alighieri
sources.title: Divina Commedia: Inferno, canto XXVIII
sources.note: Source of the quotation 'seminator di scandalo e di scisma' (Inf. 28.35), describing the sowers of scandal and schism among whom Dante places Muhammad (Inf. 28.31); the Comedy was completed by Dante's death in 1321.

passages.title: The Maqama and the Picaro
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
The Arabic word maqāma derives from a root meaning "to stand"; it denoted first a place where one stands, then a gathering, and finally the discourse delivered before one. As a literary form it was created in the late tenth century by al-Hamadhānī, called Badīʿ al-Zamān, "the Wonder of the Age," and brought to its classical height in the early twelfth by al-Ḥarīrī of Basra. Each maqāma is a short episode in sajʿ, rhymed prose studded with verse. A narrator, ʿĪsā ibn Hishām in al-Hamadhānī and al-Ḥārith ibn Hammām in al-Ḥarīrī, arrives in some city and encounters an eloquent stranger who extracts money from his audience with a sermon, a lament or a feat of language; at the end, as a rule, the narrator recognizes the stranger as the same rogue, Abū al-Fatḥ al-Iskandarī or Abū Zayd al-Sarūjī, who has taken him in again. Al-Ḥarīrī pressed the display of virtuosity further, composing sermons of undotted letters only and a letter in which dotted and undotted letters alternate. The reader admires a performance that will prove a fraud. The form traveled: Judah al-Ḥarīzī rendered al-Ḥarīrī into Hebrew, and in al-Andalus writers such as al-Saraqusṭī composed maqāmas of their own.

That reach underlies the proposal that the maqāma lies behind the Spanish picaresque, beginning with the anonymous Lazarillo de Tormes (1554). Proponents point to a shared profile: an episodic, itinerant narrative; a hero who lives by his wits; satire of clerical greed and counterfeit piety, embodied in al-Hamadhānī's preaching rogue and in Lazarillo's miserly priest and fraudulent pardoner. James T. Monroe went further, reading al-Hamadhānī's work as itself a picaresque narrative, and centuries of Arabic and Hebrew maqāmas in Iberia seem to supply a route.

Skeptics answer with form. Lazarillo opens, "Pues sepa Vuestra Merced, ante todas cosas, que a mí llaman Lázaro de Tormes": the rogue tells his own life, from birth, to an addressee, and the episodes accumulate into an account of how he became what he is. In the maqāma the rogue is seen from outside by a narrator, and he reappears from episode to episode unchanged; the recurring recognition, not a life, organizes the collection. The maqāma's ornament, moreover, is the opposite of Lazarillo's plain speech. Jaakko Hämeen-Anttila, while allowing points of contact, judges that the maqāma was never well enough known to have shaped the picaresque significantly.

Both camps, though, treat descent as the only relation worth establishing. The skeptics' formal objections are real and tell against direct derivation, and on present evidence the claim of influence is unproven. But the comparison is illuminating whether or not it reveals a lineage. Each form puts a deceiver at its center and invites the reader to enjoy being deceived; they differ chiefly over whose voice carries the deception. The maqāma keeps the reader beside the dupe, astonished afresh at each unmasking, whereas Lazarillo takes the reader into the rogue's confidence.

sources.author: James T. Monroe
sources.title: The Art of Badīʿ az-Zamān al-Hamadhānī as Picaresque Narrative
sources.note: American University of Beirut study reading al-Hamadhānī's maqāmas, with their parody and trickster hero, as picaresque narrative.

sources.author: Jaakko Hämeen-Anttila
sources.title: Maqama: A History of a Genre
sources.note: Harrassowitz history of the genre from al-Hamadhānī and al-Ḥarīrī through its Hebrew and later forms; grants points of contact with the picaresque but doubts the maqāma was known well enough in Europe to have shaped it significantly.

sources.author: Anonymous
sources.title: La vida de Lazarillo de Tormes y de sus fortunas y adversidades
sources.note: Source of the quotation 'Pues sepa Vuestra Merced, ante todas cosas, que a mí llaman Lázaro de Tormes', the first sentence of the Tratado primero, where Lázaro begins his first-person life story to an unnamed addressee.

sources.author: al-Ḥarīrī (trans. Michael Cooperson)
sources.title: Impostures
sources.note: Library of Arabic Literature translation of al-Ḥarīrī's fifty maqāmas, each rendered in a different English style to convey the work's virtuosity and the con-man Abū Zayd's eloquence.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Mahdi's critical edition has shown that the orphan tales supplied by Hanna Diyab do not belong to the Thousand and One Nights.
The oldest manuscript shows what the Nights first was, but its age does not settle whether later tales like Diyab's belong to it.
Because the frame tale invites continuation, every tale ever told under Shahrazad's name is an equally authentic part of the Nights.
Galland's French translation, rather than any Arabic manuscript, should be regarded as the authoritative text of the Thousand and One Nights.
The publication of Hanna Diyab's memoir has established that he, rather than Galland, was the true author of Aladdin and Ali Baba.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph is the author's: the Galland manuscript 'is the best evidence of what the Nights was in medieval Syria; Diyab's tales are evidence of what it became,' and calling them inauthentic 'confuse[s] a claim about origins with a claim about membership.' B states both halves. A is Mahdi's side pushed to a conclusion the author rejects; C is the open-collection view, which the author says 'risks dissolving the work.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify the author's overall conclusion about what counts as the Nights.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The final paragraph, especially its last three sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 1 sets up the frame and the problem; paragraph 2 gives Mahdi's philological view; paragraph 3 gives the open-collection view; paragraph 4 is the author's middle position. Prephrase: the oldest text tells us origins, not membership, so neither camp wins outright.

choices.note: Wrong position-holder and too strong. This is the conclusion the author attributes to those who call Diyab's tales 'inauthentic' and then rejects as a confusion.
CORRECT. It keeps the concession to Mahdi (best evidence of the original) and the qualification (age does not settle membership), which is the author's distinction between origins and membership.
Opposite of the author's view. The author warns that if 'everything ever told under Shahrazad's name belongs to it, the Nights becomes a label rather than a text.'
Out of scope. No one in the passage proposes Galland's translation as the authoritative text; the author's 'best evidence' for the medieval work is the Arabic manuscript.

Too extreme and off-point. Horta argues Diyab should be counted 'among' the secret authors; the passage never says the memoir establishes sole authorship, and this is not the passage's point in any case.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the manuscript on which Mahdi's 1984 edition principally rests
choices: contains a full thousand and one nights, including the tales Galland later received from Diyab
was copied in Egypt from an earlier Persian collection known as the Hazar Afsan
was shown by Mahdi to be a back-translation of material originally written in French
breaks off partway through a tale after 282 nights
was acquired by Galland during his 1709 meetings with Hanna Diyab in Paris
questions.explanation: The second sentence of the second paragraph says the manuscript 'contains only 282 nights and breaks off in the middle of a tale.' D restates this. C attaches Mahdi's finding about the later Aladdin manuscripts to the wrong manuscript, and E confuses Galland's acquisition of the manuscript (around 1701) with his meeting Diyab (1709).

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about the manuscript behind Mahdi's edition.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Several manuscripts and dates are in play: the ninth-century fragment, the Syrian manuscript Galland acquired around 1701, the later compilations, and the post-Galland Aladdin manuscripts. Match the stem to the right one.

choices.note: Opposite. It contains 'only 282 nights'; reaching a full thousand and one is what the later compilations did, and the orphan tales have no earlier Arabic text.
Shell game. The passage calls the manuscript Syrian, and the Hazar Afsan is al-Mas'udi's report about the work's distant origin, not this manuscript's source.
Shell game. Mahdi showed that the Arabic manuscripts of Aladdin 'that surfaced after Galland' were back-translations, not this manuscript.
CORRECT. A paraphrase of 'it contains only 282 nights and breaks off in the middle of a tale.'
Wrong date and event. Galland acquired it 'around 1701'; he met Diyab in 1709.

questions.stem: The author mentions Mahdi's finding about the Arabic manuscripts of Aladdin (fourth sentence of the second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: indicate one basis for the view that Aladdin was not part of the Nights as the medieval manuscripts preserve it
suggest that Galland deliberately misrepresented the sources of the tales he added to the later volumes of his translation
show that Mahdi's method cannot distinguish between older and more recent versions of a tale
support the author's claim that the orphan tales belong to the Nights no less than the medieval tales do
explain why Hanna Diyab's memoir remained in the Vatican Library, unpublished, for so long
questions.explanation: The sentence belongs to the paragraph setting out Mahdi's philological case. Showing that the Arabic Aladdin manuscripts were translated from Galland's French removes the apparent evidence of a medieval Arabic Aladdin, so it supports the picture of Aladdin as outside the manuscript tradition. A says this. D gives the sentence to the open-collection view, and C is the opposite: the finding is an example of the method succeeding at dating.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the author reports the back-translation finding where it is.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, fourth sentence, read with the rest of that paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Ask whose argument the sentence serves. Paragraph 2 is Mahdi's paragraph; the back-translation finding shows that no genuine medieval Arabic Aladdin is known, which is part of the case for treating such tales as outside the original collection. The author's own later qualification does not change what the sentence does here.

choices.note: CORRECT. The finding removes what might have seemed Arabic evidence for Aladdin, supporting the view (developed in paragraph 2) that the tale lies outside the medieval tradition. The hedge 'one basis' fits.
Too extreme and out of scope. The passage says nothing about deliberate misrepresentation by Galland; the back-translations surfaced after him.

Opposite. Identifying back-translations is a case of the method distinguishing later from earlier texts; the author's later doubt concerns whether age settles identity, not whether the method can date texts.
Wrong position-holder. That claim belongs to the open-collection view in paragraph 3, and the author never endorses it in those terms; the sentence serves Mahdi's case.
Out of scope. The memoir is discussed in paragraph 3 and is unconnected to the Aladdin manuscripts.

questions.stem: By "a claim about membership" (last sentence of the passage), the author most probably means a claim about
choices: which scholars are qualified to decide disputes over the text of the Nights
whether Hanna Diyab was a member of the community of Arabic storytellers
how many nights a manuscript must contain to count as a complete copy
the period and place in which a particular tale was first composed
whether a given tale is properly regarded as part of the Nights
questions.explanation: The author contrasts 'a claim about origins' (where and when a tale arose, which the Galland manuscript best attests) with 'a claim about membership' (whether a tale belongs to the work). E is the second. D describes the claim about origins, the other half of the contrast.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Interpret the phrase from its contrast with 'a claim about origins.'

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last two sentences of the passage, and the 'age confers identity' sentence earlier in the paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The paragraph separates two questions: what the Nights was (origins, answered by the oldest manuscript) and what belongs to it (identity or membership). The phrase names the second question.

choices.note: Out of scope. The paragraph is about tales and the work, not about which scholars may judge.
Shell game. 'Membership' here concerns tales in a collection, not a person in a community.
Too narrow and off-target. Completeness by count is never the issue; the author's point is that membership is not settled by the 282-night manuscript.
Opposite half of the contrast. This is what 'a claim about origins' concerns.
CORRECT. Membership is whether a tale belongs to the work, the question the author says age and origin cannot settle by themselves.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: The later compilations that reach a full thousand and one nights are more faithful to the spirit of the frame tale than the Galland manuscript is.
Hamori's assessment of the Galland manuscript is mistaken, because no manuscript can preserve an original core.
Showing that a tale has no medieval Arabic source does not by itself show that the tale is not part of the Nights.
Horta's argument about Diyab is persuasive only if Diyab composed the orphan tales himself rather than retelling tales he had heard.
Mahdi's attempt to recover an archetype was misguided, since the Nights never existed as a fixed text in any period.
questions.explanation: The author grants that Mahdi's method shows 'which text is oldest' but denies that 'age confers identity,' and concludes that calling Diyab's tales inauthentic 'confuse[s] a claim about origins with a claim about membership.' So absence of a medieval source settles origins, not membership: C. E is the trap for readers who take the author to side with the open-collection view; the author instead calls the Galland manuscript 'the best evidence of what the Nights was in medieval Syria.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement that follows from the author's own position, not from Mahdi's or the open-collection view.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Final paragraph, especially 'it cannot establish that age confers identity' and the last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The author's distinction does the work: origin questions (oldest text, earliest source) differ from membership questions. Any statement that treats origin evidence as settling membership, in either direction, is not the author's. Watch for answers that turn the author's partial criticism of Mahdi into total rejection.

choices.note: Out of scope comparison. The author says the frame invites continuation but never ranks the later compilations as more faithful than the manuscript.
Distortion. The author accepts that the manuscript is the 'best evidence' of the early work; the objection is to what age is taken to prove, not to Hamori's judgment.

CORRECT. The author's claim that origins and membership are different questions means a tale's lacking a medieval source does not on its own exclude it, though the hedge 'by itself' leaves room for other grounds.
Out of scope. The author never conditions Horta's argument on whether Diyab invented or retold the tales.

Too extreme. The author does say 'what lies inside the frame has never been fixed,' but treats the Galland manuscript as evidence of 'what the Nights was in medieval Syria,' which concedes that the archetype project tells us something real; the criticism is limited to inferring identity from age.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the distinction the author draws in the last paragraph?
choices: A historian argues that because a folk song's oldest recording is the most reliable one, every later recording of the song should be disregarded.
A critic holds that a play's first draft shows its original conception, but that scenes added in later productions may still belong to it.
A musicologist maintains that any piece ever performed under a composer's name must be included in the composer's collected works.
An editor decides that a novel's final published version supersedes all earlier drafts, since the author approved it last.
A librarian concludes that a manuscript's value depends entirely on its age, so that the oldest copy of a text is always the most valuable.
questions.explanation: The author separates what the oldest text shows (how the work began) from what may belong to it (membership), allowing that later additions can belong. B has the same structure for a play. A and E make age decisive, the inference the author rejects; C is the open-collection extreme the author warns 'risks dissolving the work.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Map the author's origins-versus-membership distinction onto a new case.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Final paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Abstract the structure: the earliest text is the best evidence of the original; that does not by itself exclude later additions from the work; but not everything associated with the name belongs automatically. The right analogy keeps the first two features and doesn't commit to the third extreme.

choices.note: Opposite. Disregarding all later versions because the oldest is most reliable is the age-confers-identity inference the author rejects.
CORRECT. The earliest draft is evidence of the original conception (origins), while later scenes may still belong to the play (membership), which is the author's distinction.
Wrong position-holder. This mirrors the open-collection extreme, which the author criticizes for turning the work into 'a label rather than a text.'
Out of scope. Authorial approval of a final version is a different criterion and keeps only one version, unlike the author's two-question approach.
Opposite and too extreme. Making value depend 'entirely' on age matches the inference the author denies.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim that Diyab's tales are evidence of what the Nights became?
choices: Galland's diary shows that he heard several tales from Diyab that he never chose to include in any volume of his translation.
Some manuscripts of the Nights copied before 1700 contain tales that are absent from the Galland manuscript that Mahdi edited.
Diyab's memoir describes his travels in France in considerable detail but mentions Galland only briefly.
Within a century of Galland's translation, Aladdin and Ali Baba were widely retold and printed as tales of the Thousand and One Nights.
Mahdi's dating of the Galland manuscript to the fourteenth century has been disputed by other scholars, who place it later.
questions.explanation: The claim is that Diyab's tales show what the Nights 'became': that the work, as later transmitted and received, came to include them. Evidence that they were widely retold and printed as part of the Nights supports this. B concerns other pre-1700 tales, not Diyab's; E bears on the manuscript's age, which is irrelevant to what the work later became.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that best supports the claim that Diyab's tales became part of the work.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Final paragraph, the sentence contrasting what the Nights 'was' and what it 'became.'

breakdown.analysis: 'Became' points to the work's later history and reception. The best support shows the tales actually being taken up as part of the Nights after Galland. Beware answers about Diyab's life or about the manuscript's date.

choices.note: Irrelevant, or slightly the opposite. Tales Galland left out are, if anything, ones that did not become part of the published Nights.
Out of scope. Other pre-1700 tales concern the medieval tradition's variety, not Diyab's tales or the work's later development.
Irrelevant. How much the memoir says about Galland does not bear on whether the tales became part of the Nights.
CORRECT. Widespread retelling and printing of the tales as tales of the Nights is direct evidence that the work came to include them.
Irrelevant truth. Whether the manuscript is fourteenth or fifteenth century affects the origins question, not what the work later became.

questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with
choices: establishing whether Defoe actually read Ockley's translation before writing Robinson Crusoe
explaining how Ibn Tufayl's tale was transmitted from Arabic into European languages
what a narrative of a solitary islander is meant to show about how a person comes to know God
the claim that reason makes revealed religion unnecessary for the few who can follow it to the end
how the economic individualism of the early eighteenth century shaped the English novel
questions.explanation: Passage A ends with what the solitary intellect 'discloses' about knowledge of God; passage B turns on 'what solitude is made to reveal' and contrasts Hayy's reason with Crusoe's 'Book and a providential reading.' C covers both. A is only the first paragraph of passage B; D is a claim passage A explicitly denies.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the concern the two passages share.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last sentences of passage A; second paragraph of passage B.

breakdown.analysis: A shared-concern question: discard anything that fits only one passage. A analyzes Hayy's route to God and its limits; B compares it with Crusoe's. The common thread is what each island story reveals about knowing God.

choices.note: Only passage B, and only its first paragraph; passage A never mentions Defoe.
Only passage B touches transmission (Ockley's translation), and only in passing.
CORRECT. Each passage asks what solitude on an island reveals: A, natural reason reaching God; B, a self that needs Scripture and providence.
Opposite of passage A, which says the tale argues 'not that reason makes revelation superfluous but that the two converge.'
Only passage B, and only as one critical reading (Watt's) among others.

questions.stem: According to passage A, Hayy's dissection of the doe leads him to conclude that
choices: what had given her life had left her body and was not any of its organs
the cause of her death lay in a defect of one of the organs he examined
all living things are composed of the same material elements
knowledge gained through the senses cannot lead to knowledge of God
he must seek out other beings like himself in order to learn the truth
questions.explanation: Passage A says he 'concludes that what animated her was not any organ but something that had departed from it.' A paraphrases this. B is the natural assumption about a dissection, which the passage contradicts.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Retrieve what the dissection episode leads Hayy to conclude.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, first paragraph, third sentence.

breakdown.analysis: A straight detail question; the trap is assuming what a dissection usually finds (a diseased organ) instead of what the passage says.

choices.note: CORRECT. A restatement of 'what animated her was not any organ but something that had departed from it.'
Opposite. He concludes the animating principle was 'not any organ.'
Out of scope. The passage says nothing about common material elements.
Opposite in spirit. His study of bodies is the first stage of a path that does reach God.
Out of scope. He reaches his conclusions alone; he meets Absal decades later by chance.

questions.stem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over whether
choices: Ibn Tufayl's hero is presented as reaching knowledge of God without the aid of scripture
Ockley's translation of Hayy ibn Yaqzan appeared before Robinson Crusoe was written
Crusoe's knowledge of God depends on his reading of Scripture
Ibn Tufayl's tale presents revealed religion as superfluous
the stages of Hayy's discovery disclose what reason itself can know of God
questions.explanation: Passage A's author says the thought experiment's force is that 'an intellect stripped of custom and instruction discloses what reason itself can know of God.' Passage B's author answers that 'neither island is as empty as it looks': Hayy's reason 'retraces... the Avicennan philosophy his author already held,' so 'solitude reveals chiefly what each author brings to it.' That is E. A is a point of agreement (B: 'Hayy finds that reason alone can reach God'), and B, C and D are each addressed by only one passage.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a question on which both authors take a position, and opposite positions.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last sentence of passage A; last three sentences of passage B.

breakdown.analysis: For a disagreement question, the key must be a point both authors address. Both describe Hayy as reaching God without scripture, so that is agreement. The real clash is over what the island experiment shows: A says it discloses what reason itself can know; B says the island is 'furnished' with its author's philosophy.

choices.note: Agreement, not disagreement. A says 'without language, teacher or scripture'; B says 'Hayy finds that reason alone can reach God.'
Only passage B addresses the translation's date; passage A is silent, so no disagreement can be inferred.
Only passage B discusses Crusoe; passage A never mentions him.
Passage A denies this ('not that reason makes revelation superfluous'), but passage B takes no position on Ibn Tufayl's view of revelation, so there is no clash.

CORRECT. A affirms that the stripped intellect discloses what reason can know; B holds that Hayy's reason retraces what Ibn Tufayl 'already held' and that solitude 'reveals chiefly what each author brings to it.'

questions.stem: The reference to Alexander Selkirk (first paragraph of passage B) serves primarily to
choices: show that Defoe could not have drawn on Ockley's translation
present part of a skeptical reply to the claim that Defoe drew on Hayy ibn Yaqzan
identify the source from which Ockley learned of Ibn Tufayl's tale
support Pastor's and Attar's argument that Robinson Crusoe is modeled on an earlier castaway
illustrate the author's own view that Defoe's island is refurnished rather than borrowed
questions.explanation: The sentence reads: 'Skeptics reply that nothing shows Defoe read it and that the castaway Alexander Selkirk is a likelier model.' Selkirk is offered by the skeptics as an alternative model, part of their reply. A turns 'likelier' into 'could not'; D gives the skeptics' point to the influence camp.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why Selkirk is mentioned.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, first paragraph, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The paragraph moves from the influence claim (Pastor, Attar, Ockley's availability) to 'Skeptics reply.' Selkirk sits inside the reply.

choices.note: Too strong. Skeptics call Selkirk a 'likelier model'; nothing in the passage rules out Defoe's having read Ockley.
CORRECT. Selkirk is the skeptics' alternative model, offered alongside the point that 'nothing shows Defoe read it.'
Out of scope. The passage says nothing about how Ockley learned of the tale.
Wrong position-holder. Pastor and Attar argue for Hayy's influence; Selkirk is raised against them.
Wrong position-holder and shell game. The 'refurnished' claim is the author's, in the next paragraph, and it concerns what solitude reveals, not Selkirk.

questions.stem: Passage B's statement that Crusoe salvages Bibles from the wreck and comes to know God by reading Scripture relates to passage A primarily in that it
choices: confirms passage A's claim that knowledge of God can be reached without instruction
parallels Hayy's discovery of the animating principle through dissecting the doe
undermines passage A's claim that Ibn Tufayl wrote with knowledge of Avicenna's work
contrasts Crusoe's route to God with Hayy's, which proceeds without language, teacher or scripture
shows that Defoe's hero, like Absal in passage A, arrives on the island already holding a revealed religion
questions.explanation: Passage A stresses that Hayy reaches God 'all without language, teacher or scripture'; passage B notes that Crusoe's 'knowledge of God comes from reading Scripture during an illness, not from reasoning about nature.' The detail sets up the contrast: D. E is the attractive trap: passage B says Crusoe arrives with salvaged Bibles but locates his knowledge of God in his later reading, not in a religion he already held.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Relate a detail in passage B to what passage A says about Hayy.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, end of first paragraph; passage B, second paragraph, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Prephrase: Crusoe gets to God through a book; Hayy explicitly does not. The detail is a point of contrast.

choices.note: Opposite. Crusoe's knowledge comes from Scripture, which is instruction of a kind, so it does not confirm unaided knowledge.
