Shell game. Both involve something physical (a wreck, a body), but salvaging Bibles is not a discovery by reasoning about nature; the passage calls it the opposite.
Out of scope. Neither passage disputes Ibn Tufayl's knowledge of Avicenna; passage A states it and passage B relies on it.
CORRECT. The detail marks the difference between Crusoe's scriptural route and Hayy's route 'without language, teacher or scripture.'
Distortion. Passage B places Crusoe's knowledge of God in his reading 'during an illness' on the island, not in a faith held on arrival; the analogy to Absal is not drawn.

questions.stem: The author of passage B would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Even if Defoe knew Ockley's translation, his novel does not share the conclusion Hayy ibn Yaqzan draws from solitude.
The evidence now available shows that Defoe never read Ockley's or any other version of Ibn Tufayl's tale.
Watt's economic reading of Robinson Crusoe is incompatible with the religious reading offered by Starr and Hunter.
Crusoe's conversion owes little to the Puritan narratives with which Defoe was familiar.
Ibn Tufayl's tale has no philosophical value, since its hero merely repeats his author's beliefs.
questions.explanation: The author of passage B leaves the influence question open ('If Defoe borrowed Ibn Tufayl's island') but insists that he 'refurnished it: where Hayy finds that reason alone can reach God, Crusoe finds that a solitary self needs a Book.' So borrowing, if it happened, does not carry Hayy's thesis with it: A. B overstates the skeptics' point; C contradicts 'Both readings point one way'; E inflates the author's claim that Hayy's reason retraces Avicenna into a dismissal the author never makes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the author of passage B is committed to, staying within what the passage says.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, second paragraph, especially the 'If Defoe borrowed' sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The author is noncommittal on whether Defoe read Ockley and firm on the difference in what solitude reveals. The key will combine those: grant the possible borrowing, deny the shared thesis. Avoid answers that settle the influence question or inflate the 'empty island' point.

choices.note: CORRECT. The conditional 'If Defoe borrowed... he refurnished it' says that even granting the borrowing, Crusoe's island reveals something different from Hayy's.
Too strong. The skeptics say only that 'nothing shows Defoe read it'; the author keeps the possibility open with 'If.'
Opposite. The author says 'Both readings point one way.'
Opposite. The author says Crusoe's conversion 'follows the Puritan narratives Defoe knew.'
Too extreme. Saying Hayy's reason 'retraces' Avicennan philosophy is a claim about what the thought experiment shows, not a verdict that the tale is worthless.

questions.stem: Passage A's account of Hayy's meeting with Absal bears on passage B's contrast between Hayy and Crusoe in which one of the following ways?
choices: It undermines the contrast, since Hayy, like Crusoe, ultimately comes to base his knowledge of God on a revealed scripture.
It shows that passage B mistakenly treats Ibn Tufayl as hostile to revealed religion.
It suggests that Defoe must have known Ibn Tufayl's tale, since both heroes come to accept a revealed religion.
It is irrelevant to the contrast, since passage B concerns only the first half of Ibn Tufayl's tale.
It is consistent with the contrast, since revealed teaching there confirms, rather than supplies, what Hayy already knew.
questions.explanation: Passage A says that when Absal teaches Hayy language, 'the two find that the religion's teachings are symbols of the truths Hayy reached unaided.' Revelation thus confirms rather than produces Hayy's knowledge, which fits passage B's contrast ('Hayy finds that reason alone can reach God'; Crusoe 'needs a Book'). A is the trap: it treats agreement with scripture as dependence on it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Decide whether the Absal episode supports, undermines or is neutral to passage B's contrast.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, second paragraph, sentences 2–4; passage B, 'where Hayy finds that reason alone can reach God, Crusoe finds that a solitary self needs a Book.'

breakdown.analysis: The episode might look like Hayy finally getting a scripture, like Crusoe. But the order matters: Hayy reached the truths first and recognized the religion as symbols of them. Crusoe's knowledge comes from his reading. So the contrast survives.

choices.note: Distortion. Hayy recognizes the religion's teachings as symbols of 'the truths Hayy reached unaided'; his knowledge is not based on them.
Out of scope. Passage B never calls Ibn Tufayl hostile to revealed religion; it says only that Hayy reaches God by reason alone.
Too strong and out of scope. Neither passage infers influence from this, and the resemblance claimed is itself inaccurate, since Hayy's knowledge does not come from the religion.
Distortion. Passage B's contrast concerns how Hayy reaches God, which the Absal episode bears on directly; nothing limits passage B to the first half.
CORRECT. The meeting shows revelation agreeing with what Hayy had already reached, so passage B's claim that Hayy reached God by reason alone, unlike Crusoe, stands.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The publication of the Liber scalae Machometi in 1949 confirmed Asín Palacios's thesis that the Divine Comedy was modeled on Islamic accounts of the Prophet's ascension.
Asín Palacios's critics were right to dismiss his thesis, because the parallels he identified were drawn from texts that no reader of Latin could have known.
The Liber scalae shows that Islamic miʿrāj material was available in Dante's world, not that any feature of the Comedy derives from it.
Dante's placement of Muhammad among the sowers of scandal and schism demonstrates that Dante was unfamiliar with Islamic accounts of the otherworld.
Brunetto Latini's embassy to the court of Alfonso X provides the most plausible route by which Islamic eschatology could have reached Dante.
questions.explanation: The third and fourth paragraphs give the author's verdict: the discovery 'establishes' that the narrative 'circulated in Latin Christendom within Dante's lifetime' but 'does not establish that Dante read it,' and 'the derivation of any particular feature of the poem from it remains unproven.' C states both halves. A is the view of those who 'hailed' the text; B adopts the critics' dismissal, which the author calls too broad.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify the author's overall conclusion about the 1949 discovery and Asín's thesis.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraphs 3 and 4, especially the first sentence of paragraph 3 and the whole of paragraph 4.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 1 states Asín's thesis, paragraph 2 gives the hostile reception and the 1949 discovery with its enthusiastic reading, and paragraphs 3–4 give the author's middle position. Prephrase: the Liber proves Islamic material was available, not that Dante used it. Expect one trap for each extreme and one that promotes a detail.

choices.note: Wrong position-holder. This is how 'many' read the discovery ('the missing link'); the author says it 'changes the question without settling it.'
Too extreme, and the author's view is the opposite. The author calls the evidence 'broader than his critics' dismissal,' and the 'no reader of Latin' objection concerns only 'some' of Asín's texts.
CORRECT. It joins what the discovery establishes (availability within Dante's lifetime) to what it does not (derivation of any particular feature), which is the author's stated position.
Distortion. The author says this judgment 'is compatible both with borrowing and with ignorance,' so it demonstrates neither.
Wrong position-holder and detail. The Brunetto route is Corti's proposal, and the author weakens it by noting that the embassy 'preceded the dated translations.'

questions.stem: According to the passage, Asín Palacios's argument for Islamic influence on the Comedy
choices: rested on the accumulated weight of many resemblances rather than on proof that Dante had read a particular text
depended principally on a Castilian translation of an Arabic account that Asín had located at the court of Alfonso X
identified Brunetto Latini as the person through whom Dante learned of Islamic accounts of the otherworld
was accepted by most Dante scholars until the publication of the Liber scalae in 1949
treated the Comedy's condemnation of Muhammad as evidence that Dante had studied Islamic sources
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says Asín 'did not claim that Dante had read any single Arabic text. His case was cumulative: so many resemblances, he held, could not be coincidental.' A restates this. B and C attach later discoveries and Corti's proposal to Asín.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about the nature of Asín's argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last two sentences of paragraph 1.

breakdown.analysis: Detail questions reward going back to the text. The answer is a paraphrase of 'His case was cumulative.' Watch for choices that move later scholars' evidence back onto Asín.

choices.note: CORRECT. Paraphrases 'He did not claim that Dante had read any single Arabic text. His case was cumulative.'
Shell game. The Castilian translation belongs to the 1949 discovery story; the passage says the Castilian 'is lost' and that Asín lacked a documented channel.
Wrong position-holder. The Brunetto proposal is attributed to Maria Corti, 'later.'
Opposite. The passage says 'the reception among Dante scholars was largely hostile.'
Out of scope. The condemnation of Muhammad is discussed by the author in paragraph 3, not as part of Asín's case, and the author says it decides nothing.

questions.stem: In the second paragraph, the phrase "the missing link in Asín's argument" most probably refers to
choices: a lost Arabic original from which both the Liber scalae and the Comedy were independently derived
evidence of a route by which Islamic accounts could have reached Christian Europe
a passage in Dante's writings that acknowledges an Islamic source for the Comedy
a set of parallels between the Comedy and Ibn ʿArabī's mystical writings that Asín had overlooked
proof that the resemblances Asín catalogued could not have arisen from Christian vision literature
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 calls the absence of a documented 'channel of transmission' the 'most damaging objection,' then reports a text showing that an Arabic miʿrāj account was translated into Latin and French and known in Italy. The 'missing link' is that channel. E confuses it with a different objection the discovery does not answer.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out what the Liber was supposed to supply in Asín's argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third sentence of paragraph 2 sets up the phrase.

breakdown.analysis: Meaning-in-context questions are answered by the surrounding sentences, not by the phrase's general use. The sentence just before the discovery names the gap: 'no channel of transmission was documented.' Prephrase: the documented route.

choices.note: Distortion. The Arabic original is the source of the Liber, not a common source of the Liber and the Comedy; the passage never proposes such a shared ancestor.
CORRECT. The 'most damaging objection' was that 'no channel of transmission was documented,' and the Liber, translated in Castile and cited in Italy, was taken to supply that channel.
Opposite of the passage. The author says 'nothing Dante wrote mentions the book.'
Out of scope. Ibn ʿArabī belongs to Asín's original comparisons in paragraph 1; the Liber adds a new text, not overlooked parallels.
Shell game. The Christian-antecedents objection appears in paragraph 2, but the Liber answers the transmission objection, not this one.

questions.stem: The author discusses Dante's placement of Muhammad in the eighth circle of Hell (third paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: support the critics' contention that Dante could not have borrowed from a tradition he regarded as heretical
show that Dante's knowledge of Islam came from Christian polemical sources rather than from Islamic texts
suggest that the Liber scalae was known in Italy before Fazio degli Uberti cited it
illustrate the allegorical and mystical character that Cantarino found lacking in the Liber scalae
set aside a consideration that seems relevant but favors neither side
questions.explanation: The sentence opens 'Nor does the poem's own treatment of Islam decide the matter' and ends that the judgment 'is compatible both with borrowing and with ignorance.' Its job is to neutralize an apparent piece of evidence. A is the tempting trap: it is the inference the author explicitly blocks ('a poet can take material from a tradition he condemns').

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Determine why the author brings up Dante's treatment of Muhammad.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last two sentences of paragraph 3.

breakdown.analysis: Function questions turn on signal words. 'Nor does…decide the matter' tells you the author is disposing of evidence, not using it. A reader who knows that Dante condemns Muhammad may expect the detail to count against influence; the passage says it counts neither way.

choices.note: Opposite. The author rejects this inference: 'a poet can take material from a tradition he condemns.' The passage also never attributes this contention to the critics.
Out of scope. The passage says nothing about Christian polemical sources for Dante's knowledge of Islam.
Shell game. Italian circulation and Fazio are in paragraph 2 and are unrelated to the canto.
Distortion. Cantarino's point concerns the Liber's character; the canto illustrates nothing about it.
CORRECT. The author raises the detail only to say it 'does not decide the matter,' being 'compatible both with borrowing and with ignorance.'

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: The Liber scalae lacks enough resemblance to the Comedy for the 1949 discovery to be of any value in assessing Asín's thesis.
The 1949 publication answered one objection to Asín's thesis but left open whether Dante used the text.
Cantarino's observation about the Liber scalae shows that Asín's thesis is less plausible than it was before 1949.
Had Brunetto Latini's embassy taken place after 1264, the Liber scalae would be proven to be a source of the Comedy.
The critics' objection that Christian vision literature supplied antecedents was refuted by the discovery of the Liber scalae.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 calls the undocumented channel 'the most damaging objection,' and paragraph 3 says the discovery 'establishes what Asín could only assume' about circulation but 'does not establish that Dante read it.' B follows. D is the trap: a later embassy would remove one difficulty, but the author also notes that 'nothing Dante wrote mentions the book,' so it would still not prove use.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the author's own claims support, without going beyond them.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, first three sentences; paragraph 2 for the objection the discovery addressed.

breakdown.analysis: Prephrase from the author's sentence 'changes the question without settling it': one gap (a channel) is filled; another (actual use) remains. Test each choice against both halves, and watch for choices that turn a weakening into a refutation or a removed obstacle into proof.

choices.note: Too extreme. The author says the discovery 'establishes what Asín could only assume,' so it is of value; Cantarino's point limits it but does not cancel it.
CORRECT. The documented channel answers the 'most damaging objection,' while the author says the discovery 'does not establish that Dante read it.'

Unsupported comparison. Cantarino identifies an obstacle within the Liber, but the author says the discovery established something Asín 'could only assume,' so the thesis is not shown to be weaker than before 1949.

Reversal of necessary and sufficient. A later embassy would remove one chronological difficulty, but the passage gives other reasons (no mention by Dante, Cantarino's point) why use would remain unproven.
Out of scope. The Liber answers the transmission objection; nothing in the passage says it refutes the claim about Christian antecedents.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim that Dante's judgment on Muhammad "is compatible both with borrowing and with ignorance"?
choices: Other passages of the Comedy show respect for certain Muslim philosophers.
The Latin version of the Liber scalae was more widely copied than the Old French version.
Fazio degli Uberti, who cites the Liber scalae, expressed hostility toward Islam in his Dittamondo.
Several Christian vision narratives earlier than the Comedy describe journeys through the circles of hell.
Medieval Christian poets who condemned Islam generally avoided material they knew to be of Islamic origin.
questions.explanation: The author's claim rests on the principle that 'a poet can take material from a tradition he condemns.' C supplies a direct case: Fazio drew on the very Liber and, on this supposition, condemned Islam, so hostility and use coexisted in Dante's own milieu. E is the opposite: it would make condemnation a sign of non-borrowing. A changes the subject to Dante's attitude, a trap for readers who know Dante's Limbo.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that best supports the idea that condemning Islam is consistent with borrowing from Islamic material.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last sentence of paragraph 3.

breakdown.analysis: The claim needs support for its 'borrowing' half: evidence that hostility to Islam and use of Islamic material went together. The best answer shows that combination as close to Dante's situation as possible. Beware answers that are true-sounding but concern Dante's attitude or the transmission of the text.

choices.note: Irrelevant to the claim, and it plays on outside knowledge. Respect for Muslim philosophers would bear on Dante's attitude toward Islam generally, not on whether condemnation and borrowing can coexist.
Irrelevant truth. Which version circulated more concerns transmission, not the compatibility of hostility with borrowing.
CORRECT. A writer of Dante's century and region who used this very text while condemning Islam is a direct instance of what the author says is possible.

Irrelevant to the claim. Earlier Christian journeys through hell bear on the critics' point about Christian antecedents for the poem's structure, not on whether condemning Muhammad is compatible with borrowing from Islamic sources.
Opposite. If condemning poets avoided Islamic material, Dante's condemnation would count as evidence against borrowing, undermining the author's claim.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the author's assessment of the significance of the 1949 discovery?
choices: A historian concludes that because a novelist's book closely resembles an earlier play, the novelist must have attended a performance of it.
A historian argues that a composer could not have been influenced by a foreign musical style because the composer criticized that style in print.
A historian discovers that a painter's letters mention a certain engraving and concludes that the engraving influenced the painter's work.
A historian dismisses all claimed parallels between two philosophers because the earlier philosopher's work was never translated.
A historian finds that a treatise was available where an architect trained but denies that this shows he consulted it.
questions.explanation: The author says the Liber shows that the text 'circulated in Latin Christendom within Dante's lifetime' but 'does not establish that Dante read it.' E has the same structure: access shown, use not shown. A and C infer use; B mirrors the inference the author rejects about Dante's condemnation of Muhammad.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Abstract the author's reasoning about the discovery, then find the scenario with the same structure.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, first three sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Strip the content: new evidence shows that a source was available in the subject's world; the author concludes that availability is established but use is not. The right analogue must have both halves, availability shown and the inference to use withheld.

choices.note: Opposite structure. It infers use from resemblance alone, which is closer to the enthusiasts' reasoning than to the author's caution.
Wrong part of the passage. This mirrors the inference from condemnation to non-borrowing that the author rejects in paragraph 3, not the assessment of the discovery.
Disanalogous. Here the subject himself mentions the source, which the author says is precisely what is missing ('nothing Dante wrote mentions the book'), and the historian infers influence.
Too extreme, and the wrong position. This resembles the critics' wholesale dismissal, which the author calls too narrow, not the author's assessment.
CORRECT. Availability in the subject's milieu is established while use is expressly left unproven, exactly the author's treatment of the Liber.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The maqāma is the direct ancestor of the Spanish picaresque, as its shared episodic structure and its satire of counterfeit piety demonstrate.
Because the maqāma is narrated by a witness rather than by the rogue, it has nothing of value to teach readers of the picaresque.
Al-Ḥarīrī's virtuosity in rhymed prose surpassed that of al-Hamadhānī and made his maqāmas known throughout Iberia.
Although influence of the maqāma on the picaresque has not been shown, comparing the two forms clarifies how each handles its deceiver.
The debate over the origins of the picaresque cannot be resolved until scholars agree on the meaning of the term maqāma.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph states the author's position: 'on present evidence the claim of influence is unproven,' but 'the comparison is illuminating whether or not it reveals a lineage,' because the forms differ 'over whose voice carries the deception.' D captures both halves. A is the proponents' view at full strength; B turns the skeptics' point into a wholesale dismissal the author rejects.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify the author's overall conclusion about the maqāma–picaresque comparison.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 1 describes the maqāma, paragraph 2 the case for influence, paragraph 3 the case against, and paragraph 4 the author's reframing. Prephrase: influence unproven, comparison still worthwhile.

choices.note: Wrong position-holder, too strong. This is the proponents' claim, which the author says is 'unproven.'
Too extreme. The author accepts the formal difference but says the comparison is 'illuminating.'
Detail, distorted. Al-Ḥarīrī 'pressed the display of virtuosity further,' but the passage never says his work was known 'throughout Iberia,' and this isn't the point.
CORRECT. It joins the author's two claims: influence 'unproven,' and the comparison 'illuminating' for how each form handles 'whose voice carries the deception.'
Out of scope. The etymology of maqāma opens the passage as background; no one in it ties the debate to the term's meaning.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which one of the following is true of the narrator of a maqāma?
choices: He is the rogue himself, recounting his own adventures to an addressee.
He meets the eloquent stranger in some city and at the end recognizes him as the rogue.
He changes from episode to episode as he learns to see through the rogue's disguises.
He delivers the sermons and laments with which the audience is persuaded to part with money.
He is named ʿĪsā ibn Hishām in both al-Hamadhānī's and al-Ḥarīrī's collections.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: the narrator 'arrives in some city and encounters an eloquent stranger…; at the end, as a rule, the narrator recognizes the stranger as the same rogue.' B restates this. A describes Lazarillo's narrator, and E misassigns ʿĪsā ibn Hishām to both authors.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says the narrator does.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The fourth sentence of paragraph 1.

breakdown.analysis: A detail question: go back to the sentence that describes the narrator's role. Several wrong answers borrow features of the rogue or of Lazarillo.

choices.note: Shell game. This describes Lazarillo ('the rogue tells his own life… to an addressee'), the contrast the skeptics draw.
CORRECT. Matches 'arrives in some city and encounters an eloquent stranger… at the end, as a rule, the narrator recognizes the stranger as the same rogue.'
Distortion. The passage says the rogue 'has taken him in again' each time, and stresses that the rogue reappears unchanged; nothing says the narrator learns.
Wrong character. The stranger, not the narrator, extracts money 'with a sermon, a lament or a feat of language.'
Detail error. ʿĪsā ibn Hishām is al-Hamadhānī's narrator; al-Ḥarīrī's is al-Ḥārith ibn Hammām.

questions.stem: The author quotes the opening of Lazarillo de Tormes (third paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: illustrate a formal feature that skeptics contrast with the maqāma
provide evidence that the author of Lazarillo knew the Hebrew maqāmas of Iberia
show that Lazarillo, like the maqāma, was addressed to a patron who commissioned it
exemplify the plain style that proponents of influence regard as derived from sajʿ
demonstrate that Lazarillo's narrator, like Abū Zayd, deceives the person he addresses
questions.explanation: The paragraph begins 'Skeptics answer with form,' and the quotation is followed by 'the rogue tells his own life, from birth, to an addressee,' contrasted with the maqāma, where 'the rogue is seen from outside by a narrator.' A names this. D misassigns the plain style to proponents and reverses its relation to sajʿ, which the passage calls 'the opposite.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Determine why the quotation appears where it does.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, first two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Function questions turn on the paragraph's purpose. The topic sentence, 'Skeptics answer with form,' tells you the quotation is evidence for the skeptics' formal contrast: first-person life story versus a rogue seen from outside.

choices.note: CORRECT. The quotation shows the first-person address ('a mí llaman Lázaro de Tormes') that skeptics set against the maqāma's outside narrator.
Opposite. The quotation is used against influence, and the passage says nothing about the author of Lazarillo's reading.
Out of scope. The passage mentions no patron for either form; 'Vuestra Merced' is simply the addressee.
Wrong position-holder and reversal. Plain speech is a skeptics' point, and they call the maqāma's ornament 'the opposite' of it.
Unsupported. The passage never says Lázaro deceives his addressee; this imports a reading from outside the passage.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following statements about al-Hamadhānī's maqāmas?
choices: Their narrator is the same throughout the collection, but their rogue is a different figure in each episode.
They were known to the author of Lazarillo de Tormes through Judah al-Ḥarīzī's Hebrew rendering.
Their rogue's sermons are presented as sincere expressions of piety that the narrator misjudges.
Their sajʿ was simpler than al-Ḥarīrī's because al-Hamadhānī avoided verse.
Their reader, like their narrator, typically learns the stranger's identity only at the end of an episode.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the narrator recognizes the stranger 'at the end,' and paragraph 4 says 'the maqāma keeps the reader beside the dupe, astonished afresh at each unmasking.' Together these support E. B is the trap for a reader who knows Iberian history: the passage names al-Ḥarīzī's translation (of al-Ḥarīrī, not al-Hamadhānī) but never links it to Lazarillo.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Combine statements in the passage to find what must be (or is very likely) true of al-Hamadhānī's maqāmas.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, fourth sentence; paragraph 4, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Inference questions reward combining two statements. Paragraph 1 places the recognition at the end of the episode; paragraph 4 says the reader stays 'beside the dupe' and is 'astonished afresh at each unmasking.' Eliminate choices that rely on outside knowledge or misplace a detail.

choices.note: Opposite. The narrator recognizes 'the same rogue,' Abū al-Fatḥ al-Iskandarī, who 'reappears from episode to episode unchanged.'
Out of scope. Al-Ḥarīzī rendered al-Ḥarīrī, not al-Hamadhānī, and the passage never says what the author of Lazarillo read; Hämeen-Anttila even doubts the form was well known.
Opposite. The stranger 'extracts money' and the 'performance [is] known to be a fraud.'
Unsupported. Both writers' maqāmas are 'rhymed prose studded with verse'; nothing says al-Hamadhānī avoided verse.
CORRECT. The narrator recognizes the rogue 'at the end,' and the reader is kept 'beside the dupe, astonished afresh at each unmasking.'

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the proponents of maqāma influence on the picaresque can most accurately be described as
choices: dismissive of the parallels they identify, which the author regards as superficial
fully persuaded by their case, though aware that it remains controversial
unconvinced by their claim of derivation, while valuing the comparison they draw
indifferent to their conclusions, since the author regards the debate as trivial
hostile to their methods, which the author regards as ignoring the maqāma's Hebrew tradition
questions.explanation: The author says 'on present evidence the claim of influence is unproven' and that the skeptics' objections 'tell against direct derivation,' yet 'the comparison is illuminating whether or not it reveals a lineage.' C has both halves. A goes too far: the author builds on the parallels (a deceiver at the center) rather than dismissing them.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize the author's view of those who argue for influence.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4.

breakdown.analysis: Attitude questions punish extremes. The author rejects the proponents' conclusion ('unproven') but keeps their comparison. Prephrase: skeptical about descent, appreciative of the comparison.

choices.note: Too extreme. The author says the comparison is 'illuminating,' and the shared deceiver at the center is one of the proponents' parallels.
Opposite. The author says the claim of influence is 'unproven' and the skeptics' objections 'are real.'
CORRECT. 'Unproven' and 'tell against direct derivation' on one hand; 'illuminating whether or not it reveals a lineage' on the other.
Too extreme. The author faults both camps but finds the question worth a paragraph of analysis; nothing suggests the debate is trivial.
Distortion. The proponents themselves cite 'Arabic and Hebrew maqāmas in Iberia'; the author's criticism is that both camps treat descent as the only relation worth establishing.

questions.stem: Which one of the following discoveries, if it were made, would most directly answer the skeptics' formal objection as the passage presents it?
choices: a Castilian maqāma in which the rogue narrates his own life from birth to an addressee
a Castilian translation of al-Ḥarīrī's maqāmas made in the fifteenth century and preserved in a Spanish monastery
evidence that the author of Lazarillo de Tormes could read Arabic
a Hebrew maqāma from al-Andalus whose rogue is a greedy priest who feigns piety
a maqāma by al-Saraqusṭī in which the narrator fails to recognize the rogue at the end
questions.explanation: The skeptics' formal objection is that Lazarillo is a rogue's first-person life told 'from birth, to an addressee,' whereas the maqāma's rogue is 'seen from outside by a narrator.' A maqāma narrated by the rogue in exactly that way, circulating in Spain, answers the formal objection directly. B and C answer the separate question of availability (Hämeen-Anttila's point), not the formal one; D supports a thematic parallel the skeptics never contested.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify the skeptics' formal objection, then find the discovery that removes it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, first three sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Separate the skeptics' two arguments: form (first-person life versus outside narrator, plain versus ornate) and availability (the maqāma not well enough known). The stem asks only about form. The best answer supplies a maqāma with Lazarillo's narrative arrangement.

choices.note: CORRECT. It supplies a maqāma with the very feature the skeptics say the form lacks, a rogue's own life from birth told to an addressee, and places it in Spain.
Wrong objection. This answers Hämeen-Anttila's doubt about how well known the form was, not the formal difference.
Wrong objection. Ability to read Arabic bears on access, and even with access the formal difference would remain.
Irrelevant to the objection. Satire of counterfeit clerical piety is a parallel the proponents already cite; the skeptics' objection concerns narrative form.
Partially relevant at best. Removing the final recognition loosens one feature, but the rogue would still be seen from outside, so the central formal objection stands.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?
choices: A literary form is described; its origins are traced to an earlier tradition; the author defends that genealogy against critics.
Two genres are compared; the author argues that one descends from the other; an objection is raised and answered.
A form is described; a claim about its influence is presented, then objections; the author assesses the claim and finds another value in the comparison.
A hypothesis about a genre's origins is stated; evidence for it is evaluated; the author concludes that the hypothesis is false.
The history of a word is traced; its meaning is applied to two genres; the author concludes that the genres share a common ancestor.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 describes the maqāma; paragraph 2 presents the influence claim; paragraph 3 gives the skeptics' objections; paragraph 4 judges the claim 'unproven' and argues that the comparison is 'illuminating' anyway. C tracks all four. D is the near miss: 'unproven' is not 'false.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match each paragraph to its job.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The topic sentence of each paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Map the passage: description (¶1), proponents (¶2), skeptics (¶3), the author's reframing (¶4). The key must include all four moves and get the author's verdict at the right strength.

choices.note: Wrong direction. The passage traces the maqāma forward to a proposed descendant, and the author doesn't defend the genealogy.
Wrong position-holder. The descent claim is the proponents', and the author does not answer the skeptics' objection but accepts it as 'real.'
CORRECT. Description, influence claim, objections, and the author's two-part assessment, in that order.
Too strong. The author calls the claim 'unproven,' not false, and the passage does not start with the hypothesis.
Distortion. The etymology is background in the first sentence only, and the author never posits a common ancestor.

tests.name: Reading Through Ideas 5
tests.source: Original RC passages written for LSAT Trainer from real scholarship (philosophy, epistemology, etymology, poetry, literature, history, mathematics, Islamic thought, law, economics and politics), with sources for further reading on every passage. Every key was confirmed by a blind solver and every passage checked for accuracy. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

sections.title: Reading Through Ideas 13: Conrad, Achebe, and Salih's reversal · Where the Arabic novel came from · The Thirty Birds and the Pilgrim · Rostam, Sohrab and Arnold

passages.title: Conrad, Achebe, and Salih's reversal
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Passage A

Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness (1899) is a story told within a story. An unnamed narrator on the Thames recalls how a seaman named Marlow described his voyage up an African river in search of Kurtz, a company agent whose professed idealism has decayed into savage domination and whose dying words are "The horror! The horror!" Long read as an indictment of imperial greed, the tale was challenged in a 1975 lecture by the Nigerian novelist Chinua Achebe. Conrad, he argued, used Africa as mere setting and backdrop for a European's moral crisis; the novella "projects the image of Africa as 'the other world,' the antithesis of Europe and therefore of civilization." Its Africans scarcely speak.

Conrad's defenders reply that Achebe confuses author with narrator. Cedric Watts, answering Achebe in 1983, argued that the tale's irony is aimed at its European characters and that, by the standards of its day, it was unusually anti-imperialist and anti-racist. Achebe had anticipated this move: nothing in the novella, he said, supplies an alternative frame of reference from which to judge Marlow.

The defense, however, answers a charge Achebe was not chiefly making. His point was less that Conrad held repugnant opinions than that the novella grants Africans no point of view at all. By reversing the direction of the gaze, making a European classic the object of African scrutiny, the lecture did more than invert Conrad's picture: it stepped outside the terms on which the novella was built, and it made plain that Heart of Darkness is one side of a conversation that African and Arab novelists had already joined.

Passage B

Tayeb Salih's Season of Migration to the North (1966) answers Conrad by reversing his route. Its unnamed narrator returns to his village on the Nile after seven years of study in England and meets Mustafa Sa'eed, a stranger whose past he slowly uncovers. A prodigy from Khartoum, Mustafa went north to London and made the imperial capital his own dark continent: several women he seduced with invented tales of a sensual East took their own lives, and he killed his English wife. He casts himself as an invader, "a drop of the poison which you have injected into the veins of history."

Critics such as Edward Said and Saree Makdisi have read the novel as an oppositional rewriting of Conrad, the colonized subject voyaging into the metropolis. Yet the reversal is the novel's subject more than its solution. Mustafa's conquest depends on the very fantasies of the East that empire produced; he can invert the colonizer's journey only by playing the part that journey scripted for him. Nor does the novel let the narrator stand outside the pattern. Educated in England and now a government official, he finds in Mustafa a double he can neither disown nor fully understand, and the book ends with him floundering in the Nile, crying out for help. Byron Caminero-Santangelo has accordingly urged critics to abandon a purely oppositional model for one in which Salih transforms Conradian elements rather than simply inverting them. Writing back, in this novel, remains written in the empire's terms.

sources.author: Chinua Achebe
sources.title: An Image of Africa
sources.note: The Massachusetts Review 18.4, the printed version of Achebe's February 1975 Chancellor's Lecture at the University of Massachusetts Amherst (later revised as 'An Image of Africa: Racism in Conrad's Heart of Darkness'); source (in the essay's standard text, also in the revised version) of the quotation that the novella 'projects the image of Africa as "the other world," the antithesis of Europe and therefore of civilization,' and of the argument that Conrad offers no alternative frame of reference for judging Marlow.

sources.author: Cedric Watts
sources.title: 'A Bloody Racist': About Achebe's View of Conrad
sources.note: The Yearbook of English Studies 13; the first full rebuttal of Achebe, arguing that the tale's irony targets its Europeans and that by the standards of its time it was unusually anti-imperialist and anti-racist.

sources.author: Tayeb Salih (trans. Denys Johnson-Davies)
sources.title: Season of Migration to the North
sources.note: English translation (Heinemann) of the 1966 novel first serialized in the Beirut journal Hiwar; source of Mustafa Sa'eed's self-description as 'a drop of the poison which you have injected into the veins of history.'

sources.author: Byron Caminero-Santangelo
sources.title: Legacies of Darkness: Neocolonialism, Joseph Conrad, and Tayeb Salih's Season of Migration to the North
sources.note: ARIEL 30.4; argues that the oppositional model of intertextuality assumed by Said and Makdisi should give way to an account of how Salih transforms Conradian elements, including in a critique of neocolonial elites.

passages.title: Where the Arabic novel came from
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Literary histories long told the story of the modern Arabic novel as one of import. During the nahda, the Arab cultural revival of the nineteenth century, translators and journalists in Cairo and Beirut introduced European fiction to a growing readership, and Arab writers, on this account, eventually learned to imitate it. Many critics fixed the genre's starting point at Zaynab (1913), Muhammad Husayn Haykal's tale of love and thwarted desire in the Egyptian countryside, written while he studied law in France and first published under a pseudonym meaning an Egyptian peasant. Earlier fiction, including Jurji Zaydan's historical romances, was classed as didactic or merely entertaining: a prelude to the true novel rather than a part of it.

Revisionist scholars have attacked both the date and the story it supports. Elliott Colla has argued that Zaynab's crowning as the first Arabic novel owed less to its literary merits than to later efforts to build a national canon, and others have pushed the starting line back as far as Ahmad Faris al-Shidyaq's Leg over Leg (1855). Others stress continuity of form. Muhammad al-Muwaylihi's Hadith 'Isa ibn Hisham, serialized from 1898, borrows its narrator from the maqamat of the tenth-century writer al-Hamadhani, episodes in rhymed prose, and has him guide a pasha risen from the grave through modern Cairo. The sira, or popular heroic epic, and the anecdotal prose of adab supplied further narrative models. Roger Allen has treated al-Muwaylihi's work as a bridge between classical narrative and modern fiction, and Muhsin al-Musawi has gone further, insisting on the unbroken continuity of Arabic letters against the old picture of a long post-classical decline.

Sabry Hafez rejects the terms of the dispute. In The Genesis of Arabic Narrative Discourse (1993) he declines both to derive modern narrative from the maqama and to treat it as a Western import, shifting attention from literary forms to the social changes that produced a new reading public with a world view of its own. Neither a borrowed model nor an inherited one, he holds, explains why new narrative forms arose when they did.

Each account captures part of the record. The import account is right that the realist novel had European models. Naguib Mahfouz's Cairo Trilogy (1956-57), a chronicle of a merchant's family between the world wars, is thoroughly realist, and in his 1988 Nobel lecture Mahfouz, having described himself as born "in the lap of" Pharaonic and Islamic civilization, added: "Then I drank the nectar of your rich and fascinating culture." But the import account is wrong to conclude that the older forms were inert. Al-Muwaylihi chose the maqama for a satire of modern manners, and Mahfouz, decades after the Trilogy, reworked the Thousand and One Nights in Arabian Nights and Days (1982) and the classical travel narrative in The Journey of Ibn Fattouma (1983). Continuity scholars, for their part, risk treating any extended prose narrative as a novel in waiting. What the record shows is less a lineage than a repertory, on which writers drew as their purposes required. Continuity, in this sense, is better understood as something writers made than as something they inherited.

sources.author: Sabry Hafez
sources.title: The Genesis of Arabic Narrative Discourse: A Study in the Sociology of Modern Arabic Literature
sources.note: Saqi Books; rejects both the maqama-lineage and the Western-import accounts of modern Arabic narrative and traces its genesis to social change and the rise of a new reading public with its own world view.

sources.author: Elliott Colla
sources.title: How Zaynab Became the First Arabic Novel
sources.note: History Compass 7.1; argues that Zaynab's status as the 'first' Arabic novel was a later construction tied to building a national literary canon rather than a verdict on its literary merits.

sources.author: Roger Allen
sources.title: The Arabic Novel: An Historical and Critical Introduction
sources.note: Manchester University Press (2nd ed. Syracuse, 1995); the standard English survey of the genre's emergence and development, by the scholar who also wrote the study of al-Muwaylihi's Hadith 'Isa ibn Hisham, A Period of Time.

sources.author: Naguib Mahfouz
sources.title: Nobel Lecture
sources.note: Read on Mahfouz's behalf at the Swedish Academy on 8 December 1988 (English text at nobelprize.org); source of the quotations 'in the lap of' (of the Pharaonic and Islamic civilizations) and 'Then I drank the nectar of your rich and fascinating culture.'

passages.title: The Thirty Birds and the Pilgrim
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Farid al-Din 'Attar, a poet of Nishapur in northeastern Iran, composed The Conference of the Birds (Mantiq al-Tayr) late in the twelfth century. Its title, "the speech of the birds," echoes the Qur'anic account of Solomon, who was taught that speech, and its guide is the hoopoe, Solomon's messenger in the Qur'an. The hoopoe summons the birds of the world to seek their king, the Simorgh. One by one they excuse themselves: the nightingale cannot leave its love for the rose; the parrot wants only the water of immortality. The hoopoe answers each with anecdotes, among them the long tale of Shaykh San'an, a revered master who abandons his devotions for love of a Christian girl. Those who set out must cross seven valleys: quest, love, knowledge, detachment, unity, bewilderment, and finally poverty and annihilation. Only thirty birds arrive, and the climax turns on a pun, for in Persian si morgh means "thirty birds." Gazing at the Simorgh, the thirty see themselves; the Simorgh, speaking as a mirror, tells them that whoever comes sees only himself in it, and that had more come, more would have been reflected.

For English readers the obvious comparison is John Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress (1678), in which Christian, burdened by sin, flees the City of Destruction despite his family's pleas: he "put his fingers in his ears, and ran on, crying, Life! life! eternal life!" Both works narrate the soul's journey to God through a landscape of trials, and comparatists commonly conclude that they part where they end. Bunyan's pilgrim arrives at the Celestial City still Christian, a particular person welcomed by a God who remains wholly other; Attar's birds discover that seeker and sought were never two, and fana, the Sufi term for the final valley's annihilation, names the passing away of the self.

This contrast captures something real but exaggerates on both sides. Attar's mirror is a careful image: a reflection is not the thing reflected, and a reader who takes the pun as a declaration that the birds are God ignores that the Simorgh shows each visitor only what that visitor brings. Sufi theorists, moreover, as Annemarie Schimmel explains, paired fana with baqa, subsistence in God, so that what passes away is the self's illusion of independence rather than the creature as such. Nor is Bunyan's self simply preserved. Christian's burden falls from him at the cross through no effort of his own, and the dream closes with a warning that confidence in one's own standing can fail at the very threshold: "there was a way to hell, even from the gates of heaven."

The deeper difference lies in what each pilgrim learns at the journey's end. Bunyan's arrives at a gate and is received by a grace that comes from beyond himself; Attar's discover that what they sought was mirrored in their own seeking. Each allegory demands that the self be emptied. They disagree about whether, once emptied, it stands before its Lord or finds His reflection.

sources.author: Farid ud-Din Attar (trans. Afkham Darbandi and Dick Davis)
sources.title: The Conference of the Birds
sources.note: The Penguin Classics verse translation, which renders Attar's rhymed couplets as English rhymed couplets, with an introduction; the passage's account of the hoopoe, the birds' excuses, Shaykh San'an, the seven valleys and the Simorgh's mirror speech follows the poem in paraphrase (no line of the translation is quoted).

sources.author: John Bunyan
sources.title: The Pilgrim's Progress
sources.note: The Christian allegory compared here; both quotations, "put his fingers in his ears, and ran on, crying, Life! life! eternal life!" (Christian's flight from the City of Destruction) and "there was a way to hell, even from the gates of heaven" (the Ignorance episode that closes Part I), come from its text, checked against standard online editions.

sources.author: Annemarie Schimmel
sources.title: Mystical Dimensions of Islam
sources.note: The classic survey of Sufism, which explains the paired stations of fana (passing away of the self) and baqa (subsistence in God) and treats Attar's epics; the source of the passage's account of fana and baqa.

sources.author: Hellmut Ritter (trans. John O'Kane, ed. Bernd Radtke)
sources.title: The Ocean of the Soul: Man, the World and God in the Stories of Farid al-Din 'Attar
sources.note: The English translation of Ritter's monumental Das Meer der Seele (1955), the standard study of Attar's thought, with chapters on extinction and union with the divine; read it for how Attar's anecdotes, Shaykh San'an's among them, carry his theology.

passages.title: Rostam, Sohrab and Arnold
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Ferdowsi of Tus completed the Shahnameh, or Book of Kings, about 1010. Its roughly fifty thousand couplets carry Iran's story from the first mythical king to the fall of the Sasanian dynasty to the Arab conquerors in the seventh century, preserving in Persian verse a body of pre-Islamic myth and history. The poem is often praised as well for its scarcity of Arabic words. The orientalist E. G. Browne, sampling verses from a single episode, put the Arabic element at four or five percent and took it for deliberate avoidance. Mohammad Djafar Moïnfar's complete count found 706 words of Arabic origin; he attributed their relative rarity not to aversion but to the poem's subject matter and style, and, as John Perry adds, the epic's meter itself restricted which loanwords could fit.

The episode Browne sampled is the poem's most famous: the tragedy of Rostam and Sohrab. Rostam, Iran's greatest champion, spends one night with Tahmineh, a princess of Samangan, and leaves a token for their child. Sohrab grows up to lead a Turanian army into Iran, hoping to find his father. When they meet, Sohrab asks whether his opponent is Rostam, and Rostam denies it. When Sohrab throws him, Rostam saves himself by claiming that custom forbids killing a man at his first fall; at their next bout Rostam stabs his son, and recognizes the token too late. The king, Kay Kavus, wary of so formidable a pair, delays sending the remedy that might have saved Sohrab.

English readers have known the story chiefly through Matthew Arnold's "Sohrab and Rustum" (1853). Arnold had no Persian and worked largely from Sainte-Beuve's review of Jules Mohl's French translation; of Mohl's book itself, he admitted, he had not "been able to obtain sight." His blank verse, studded with extended similes in the Homeric manner, has encouraged readers to treat the Shahnameh as Iran's Iliad, and scholarship has pursued the parallel too: Olga Davidson, applying methods developed for Homeric epic, argued that Ferdowsi drew on a living oral tradition, a thesis other specialists contest, insisting on his written sources.

Reza Taher-Kermani has argued that, despite Arnold's indirect access to Ferdowsi, his rendition "remains unusually faithful to its original," and much of the plot does survive. Yet the alterations are telling. Arnold moves the episode from the reign of the weak Kay Kavus to that of the great Kay Khosrow, and he has Rustum, hard-pressed, shout his own name, so that the stunned Sohrab falters and is speared. Ferdowsi opens the tale by brooding on the injustice of death, but he assembles the catastrophe from human choices: a father's lie, his trick, a king's suspicion. Arnold, closing on the river Oxus flowing on toward the Aral Sea, makes it a tragedy of fate watched by indifferent nature. He kept the story; what he altered was where its blame resides.

sources.author: Reza Taher-Kermani
sources.title: The Persian Presence in Victorian Poetry
sources.note: Its chapter on 'Sohrab and Rustum' traces Arnold's indirect access to Ferdowsi through Sainte-Beuve's review of Mohl and argues that his rendition "remains unusually faithful to its original" despite its diversions (the quotation is from that chapter's summary).

sources.author: John R. Perry
sources.title: Šāh-nāma iii. Arabic Words (Encyclopaedia Iranica)
sources.note: Reports E. G. Browne's four-to-five-percent estimate from verses of the Sohrab episode and Moïnfar's complete count of 706 Arabic-origin words (Le vocabulaire arabe dans le Livre des rois de Firdausī, 1970), with Moïnfar's explanation from subject matter and style and the constraint of the motaqāreb meter.

sources.author: Matthew Arnold
sources.title: Sohrab and Rustum: An Episode
sources.note: Arnold's blank-verse adaptation, in Homeric style, ending on the Oxus; the quoted admission that "of M. Mohl's book itself I have not been able to obtain sight" comes from Arnold's own note on his sources (Malcolm's History of Persia and Sainte-Beuve's review).

sources.author: Olga M. Davidson
sources.title: Poet and Hero in the Persian Book of Kings
sources.note: Applies comparative methods developed for Homeric and other oral epic to argue that the Shahnameh rests on a living oral poetic tradition, a thesis contested by scholars such as Mahmoud Omidsalar who stress Ferdowsi's written sources.

questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with
choices: the question of whether Conrad himself intended Heart of Darkness to serve as a critique of European imperialism
the biographical sources of Conrad's and Salih's differing attitudes toward the empires of their day
the ways in which African and Arab novelists have imitated Conrad's narrative technique
how later writers have answered Heart of Darkness and its colonial point of view
the critical reception of Season of Migration to the North among Western academic scholars
questions.explanation: Passage A is about Achebe's response to Conrad and its defenders; passage B is about Salih's novel as an answer to Conrad ('answers Conrad by reversing his route'). D covers both. A is the trap for a reader who knows the Achebe controversy: Conrad's intention is at issue only in passage A's second paragraph, and passage B never raises it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the topic the two passages share.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, last sentence of the third paragraph; passage B, first sentence.

breakdown.analysis: A: Achebe's lecture and its critics, ending with the lecture making plain that the novella is 'one side of a conversation that African and Arab novelists had already joined.' B: Salih's novel 'answers Conrad.' Prephrase: how later writers answer Heart of Darkness. Check each choice against both passages, not just one.

choices.note: Half the pair. Whether Conrad's irony makes the tale anti-imperialist is debated in passage A, but passage B never discusses Conrad's intentions.
Out of scope. Neither passage discusses either writer's life as a source of his views.
Distortion. Passage B describes Salih reversing and transforming Conrad, not imitating his technique, and passage A discusses Achebe's lecture, not novelists' technique.
CORRECT. Achebe's lecture (A) and Salih's novel (B) are both responses to Conrad's novella and its view from the colonizer's side.
Too narrow. Said, Makdisi and Caminero-Santangelo appear only in passage B, and passage A says nothing about the reception of Salih's novel.

questions.stem: According to passage A, Watts argued that Heart of Darkness
choices: supplies an alternative frame of reference from which readers can judge Marlow
directs its irony at its European characters
grants its African characters a point of view of their own
should be read primarily as a record of Conrad's own experiences in Africa
was less critical of imperialism than its first readers believed
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says Watts 'argued that the tale's irony is aimed at its European characters.' B restates this. A is the shell game: the phrase 'alternative frame of reference' comes from Achebe's anticipatory reply in the next sentence, and the passage never attributes a claim about it to Watts.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what passage A attributes to Watts.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, second paragraph, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Watts made two claims: the irony targets the Europeans, and the tale was unusually anti-imperialist and anti-racist for its time. Read the sentence and keep it apart from Achebe's position in the sentence that follows.

choices.note: Shell game. The 'alternative frame of reference' wording belongs to Achebe, who says the novella lacks one. Watts's defense is consistent with this idea, but the passage does not say he argued it.
CORRECT. 'The tale's irony is aimed at its European characters' is a direct paraphrase of what Watts argued.
This is what the third paragraph says the novella fails to do ('grants Africans no point of view at all'), and nothing attributes the opposite claim to Watts.
Out of scope. The passage says nothing about Conrad's biography.
Opposite. Watts held that, by the standards of its day, the tale was 'unusually anti-imperialist.'

questions.stem: The author of passage A would most likely describe the defense of Conrad presented in the second paragraph as
choices: a decisive refutation of the charge Achebe brought against the novella
irrelevant, because Watts misreads the relation between Marlow and the frame narrator
persuasive with respect to Marlow but not with respect to Conrad himself
evidence that Achebe's lecture has had no lasting influence on the reading of Conrad
a reply to a charge other than the one Achebe chiefly made
questions.explanation: The third paragraph opens: 'The defense, however, answers a charge Achebe was not chiefly making.' Achebe's main point was that the novella 'grants Africans no point of view at all,' not that Conrad held repugnant opinions, which is what the author-versus-narrator defense addresses. E paraphrases this. B is the near miss: the author does say the defense misses its target, but never says Watts misreads the frame, and calling the defense 'irrelevant' overstates the claim.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify the author's evaluation of Watts's defense.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, third paragraph, first two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The author does not say the defense is false. The author says it is aimed at the wrong charge: whether Conrad held bad views (an author-versus-narrator issue) rather than whether the book gives Africans a point of view. Prephrase: it answers a different charge.

choices.note: Too extreme. The author goes on to credit Achebe's lecture with doing 'more than invert Conrad's picture.'
Partly right in spirit, but the passage never says Watts misreads the frame, and 'irrelevant' is stronger than 'answers a charge Achebe was not chiefly making.'
Invented distinction. The author does not divide the defense into a persuasive part and an unpersuasive part.
Opposite. The author credits the lecture with stepping outside Conrad's terms and making plain that the novella is 'one side of a conversation.'
CORRECT. The defense deals with Conrad's opinions; Achebe's main charge concerned the novella's denial of an African point of view.

questions.stem: In passage B, the statement that "the reversal is the novel's subject more than its solution" (second paragraph, second sentence) most probably means that
choices: the novel scrutinizes its inversion of Conrad's journey rather than offering it as an escape
Salih set out to resolve a problem that Conrad's novella had left unresolved
the plot of the novel is organized around Mustafa's journey to London rather than around the narrator's return home
the reversal of Conrad's route is a minor element of the novel that critics have exaggerated
Said and Makdisi did not notice that the novel reverses the route of Conrad's novella
questions.explanation: The sentences that follow explain the claim: Mustafa 'can invert the colonizer's journey only by playing the part that journey scripted for him,' and 'Writing back, in this novel, remains written in the empire's terms.' So the novel makes the reversal something to examine, not an escape route. That is A. D is the trap: it reads 'more than its solution' as a downgrading, but calling the reversal the novel's 'subject' makes it central, not minor.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Interpret the quoted sentence in context.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, second paragraph, sentences 2 to 4 and the last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: 'Yet' marks a contrast with Said and Makdisi's 'oppositional rewriting.' A solution would be the reversal as an answer to empire; a subject is the thing the novel scrutinizes. The next sentences show the reversal reproducing imperial fantasy. Prephrase: the novel looks hard at the reversal instead of treating it as the answer.

choices.note: CORRECT. The novel scrutinizes the reversal and shows it trapped in empire's terms rather than presenting it as a way out.
Shell game on 'solution.' The passage never says Salih aimed to solve a problem in Conrad; it says the reversal is not a solution.
Literal misreading of 'subject' as plot focus. The sentence concerns what the novel does with the reversal, not whose story is told.
Opposite. Calling the reversal the novel's 'subject' makes it central.
Contradicts the passage. Said and Makdisi read the novel as a rewriting of Conrad, which presupposes seeing the reversal; the author disagrees with what they make of it.

questions.stem: Passage B mentions that the novel ends with the narrator "floundering in the Nile, crying out for help" primarily in order to
choices: suggest that the narrator finally rejects the education he received in England
indicate that the narrator's account of Mustafa's life cannot be trusted
support the claim that the narrator, too, is caught in the pattern
show that the novel ends with Mustafa Sa'eed's death by drowning
contrast the narrator's eventual moral clarity with the self-deception that Mustafa never overcomes
questions.explanation: The detail follows 'Nor does the novel let the narrator stand outside the pattern,' and comes with the narrator's finding in Mustafa 'a double he can neither disown nor fully understand.' It is evidence for that claim, as C says. D is the trap for a reader who knows the novel, in which Mustafa vanishes in the river; but this sentence is about the narrator, and the passage says nothing about Mustafa's end.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Determine why the author mentions the novel's final scene.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, second paragraph, sentences 4 and 5.

breakdown.analysis: Look at the claim the detail supports. The sentence before it says the narrator is not allowed to 'stand outside the pattern'; the detail shows him not in control, unable to escape. Prephrase: it shows the narrator caught too.

choices.note: Unsupported. The passage gives no sign that the narrator rejects his English education; it stresses that he cannot disown his double.
Out of scope. The passage never questions whether the narrator's account is reliable.
CORRECT. It is evidence for 'Nor does the novel let the narrator stand outside the pattern.'
Wrong person. The floundering figure is the narrator, and the passage says nothing about how Mustafa dies.
Opposite. The narrator is shown confused and in danger, not morally clear, and he cannot fully understand Mustafa.

questions.stem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over whether
choices: reversing a colonial narrative's direction can free a work from that narrative's assumptions
Heart of Darkness has become one side of a continuing exchange with the writers who answer it
Conrad's novella gives its African characters little opportunity to speak
Salih treats the crimes Mustafa Sa'eed commits in London with sympathy
Achebe's 1975 lecture directly influenced the novels that later Arab writers produced
questions.explanation: Passage A says that by reversing the gaze the lecture 'stepped outside the terms on which the novella was built.' Passage B says Mustafa's reversal depends on empire's fantasies and that 'Writing back, in this novel, remains written in the empire's terms.' That is a direct clash, as A states. B is the agreement trap: both authors treat Conrad's novella as answered by later writers.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim on which the two authors take opposite positions.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, third paragraph, last sentence; passage B, second paragraph, second, third and last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: For a disagreement, each author needs a stated view and the two views must conflict. A: reversal escapes the original's terms. B: reversal stays within them. Eliminate choices that only one author addresses or that both accept.

choices.note: CORRECT. Author A says that by reversing the gaze Achebe's lecture 'stepped outside the terms' of Conrad's novella; author B says the novel's reversal 'remains written in the empire's terms.'
Both agree. A says the novella is now 'one side of a conversation'; B opens with Salih's novel answering Conrad.
Only passage A addresses this ('Its Africans scarcely speak'); passage B takes no position.
Neither author says whether Salih treats Mustafa sympathetically.
Neither author claims Achebe influenced Arab novelists. Passage A says African and Arab novelists had already joined the conversation; it never says the lecture shaped their novels.

questions.stem: Based on passage B, its author would most likely respond to the claim in passage A that the lecture "stepped outside the terms on which the novella was built" by pointing out that
choices: Achebe's lecture, unlike Salih's novel, was a work of criticism rather than of fiction
a reversal can rely on the very images it aims to overturn, as Mustafa's conquest does
Conrad's novella already contains a reversal of its own, since Marlow tells his story on the Thames after his return from Africa
Watts was right that Heart of Darkness was unusually anti-imperialist for its time
Said and Makdisi share Achebe's view that Conrad's novella denies the Africans it depicts any point of view of their own
questions.explanation: Passage B's central argument is that Mustafa's reversal 'depends on the very fantasies of the East that empire produced' and so 'remains written in the empire's terms.' Applied to passage A's claim, that argument would say reversing direction does not by itself escape the original's terms. B states this. A is the irrelevant-truth trap: the difference between criticism and fiction is real, but passage B gives no reason to think it matters, and it would not rebut the claim.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply passage B's reasoning to a claim made in passage A.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, third paragraph, last sentence; passage B, second paragraph, sentence 3 and the last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Passage B's author thinks reversal stays inside the empire's terms because the reverser must use the images empire produced. Prephrase: 'reversal doesn't automatically escape; it can rely on what it reverses.' Then find the choice that carries that reasoning over.

choices.note: Irrelevant truth. Passage B never suggests that the difference between criticism and fiction bears on whether a reversal escapes the original's terms.
CORRECT. This is passage B's own reason for denying that reversal escapes the empire's terms, applied to A's general claim.
Out of scope. Passage B says nothing about the structure of Marlow's telling.
Wrong position-holder. Watts appears only in passage A, and passage B takes no view of his defense.
Unsupported. Passage B says Said and Makdisi read Salih's novel as an oppositional rewriting; it says nothing about their view of Conrad's Africans.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Zaynab should no longer be regarded as the first Arabic novel, since earlier works have an equal or stronger claim to that title.
The modern Arabic novel derives from the maqama and other classical forms rather than from European fiction.
The rise of the modern Arabic novel is best explained by the emergence of a new reading public rather than by any literary model.
The Arabic novel had European models, but its writers also chose to draw on older Arabic forms.
Mahfouz's later turn to traditional forms shows that he came to regard his earlier realism as an imitation of European fiction.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph gives the author's verdict: 'Each account captures part of the record.' The import account is right about the realist novel's European models but wrong that older forms were 'inert,' and continuity is 'something writers made.' D states both halves. B and C are wrong position-holder traps: B is the continuity scholars' view and C is Hafez's.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: State the passage's overall claim.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The fourth paragraph, first sentence and last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The passage sets out three views (import, continuity, Hafez's sociology) and then the author's qualified synthesis in the fourth paragraph. The main point should keep both sides of the author's verdict: European models are real, and older forms were taken up deliberately.

choices.note: Too narrow. The dating dispute is one point in the second paragraph; the author's conclusion is about how the genre relates to its sources.
Wrong position-holder. This is roughly the continuity view, which the author criticizes for risking 'treating any extended prose narrative as a novel in waiting.'
Wrong position-holder. This is Hafez's position from the third paragraph, not the author's conclusion.
CORRECT. It joins 'the realist novel had European models' with the author's claim that writers drew on older forms 'as their purposes required.'
Distortion. The passage never says Mahfouz regretted or disowned his realism; it uses his career to show that both kinds of resource were available.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Hadith 'Isa ibn Hisham
choices: was the first work of Arabic fiction to appear in serialized form
takes its narrator from a classical collection of narratives in rhymed prose
was first published under a pseudonym
was identified by Colla as the earliest true Arabic novel
was modeled on the European historical romance that Zaydan popularized
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says al-Muwaylihi's work 'borrows its narrator from the maqamat of the tenth-century writer al-Hamadhani, episodes in rhymed prose.' B paraphrases this. C and D are shell games that attach details from elsewhere in the passage (Zaynab's pseudonym; Colla's argument about the 'first' novel) to al-Muwaylihi.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage states about al-Muwaylihi's work.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, fourth sentence; fourth paragraph, sixth sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Go back to the sentence that names Hadith 'Isa ibn Hisham: serialized from 1898, narrator taken from al-Hamadhani's maqamat, a resurrected pasha in modern Cairo. Watch for details that belong to Zaynab or to Zaydan.

choices.note: Too strong. The passage says it was serialized, not that it was the first serialized work of Arabic fiction.
CORRECT. Its narrator is borrowed 'from the maqamat of the tenth-century writer al-Hamadhani, episodes in rhymed prose.'
Shell game. The pseudonym belongs to Haykal's Zaynab.
Shell game. Colla is cited for an argument about Zaynab's reputation; the passage never says he crowned al-Muwaylihi's work, and the 'first novel' alternative it names is Leg over Leg.
Opposite in spirit. The work is presented as evidence of continuity with classical forms, and historical romance is associated with Zaydan.

questions.stem: The primary function of the third paragraph is to
choices: present a view that rejects an assumption common to the two earlier accounts
offer evidence that supports the continuity account against the objections raised by proponents of the import account
introduce the conclusion that the author defends in the remainder of the passage
qualify Colla's claim about the role of nationalism in Zaynab's reputation
explain why Mahfouz turned to older narrative forms in the decades after he completed the Cairo Trilogy
questions.explanation: Hafez 'rejects the terms of the dispute': he declines both the maqama derivation and the import thesis and says 'neither a borrowed model nor an inherited one' explains the timing. Both earlier accounts assume the question is which literary model the novel came from; Hafez rejects that shared assumption, as A says. C is the trap: the author's own view comes in the fourth paragraph and differs from Hafez's.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe the role of the paragraph on Hafez.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, especially the first and last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The first paragraph gives the import account and the second the continuity account. The third does not side with either; it changes the question from models to social conditions. Prephrase: a third view that rejects what both share.

choices.note: CORRECT. Both earlier accounts locate the novel's origin in a literary model, imported or inherited; Hafez denies that either model explains it.
Hafez rejects the continuity account too ('declines both to derive modern narrative from the maqama and to treat it as a Western import').
Wrong position-holder. The author's conclusion is the 'repertory' view in the fourth paragraph, which keeps literary models in play.
Colla is not mentioned in the third paragraph, and the paragraph does not address Zaynab's reputation.
Mahfouz first appears in the fourth paragraph.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Mahfouz's realist fiction, including the Cairo Trilogy, owed comparatively little to the European novel.
No meaningful relation exists between the classical maqama and the forms of modern Arabic fiction that followed it.
The import account's chief error lies in the date it assigns to the first Arabic novel.
Hafez's account fully explains why later novelists returned to inherited forms.
An older form's resemblance to the novel does not by itself prove descent.
questions.explanation: The author warns that continuity scholars 'risk treating any extended prose narrative as a novel in waiting' and prefers 'a repertory' to 'a lineage.' That supports E: resemblance alone does not establish descent. C is the trap: the passage reports the dating dispute, but the author's criticism of the import account is that it wrongly treats older forms as 'inert.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the author's views support.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, sentences 5 to 8.

breakdown.analysis: The author criticizes each side. The import account is wrong that older forms were inert. The continuity account risks seeing a novel in every long narrative. The author also prefers 'repertory' to 'lineage.' Look for a modest choice that follows from one of these.

choices.note: Contradicts the passage. The author says 'the realist novel had European models' and cites the Trilogy as the example.
Too extreme. The author treats al-Muwaylihi's use of the maqama as real evidence that older forms were not 'inert.'
Distortion. The author's stated objection to the import account is that it treats older forms as 'inert,' not its dating.
Unsupported. The author does not apply Hafez's account to later novelists, and 'fully' is far stronger than anything in the passage.
CORRECT. This follows from the warning against treating 'any extended prose narrative as a novel in waiting' and the preference for 'repertory' over 'lineage.'

questions.stem: In the last sentence of the passage, the author's statement that continuity is "something writers made" rather than "something they inherited" most probably means that
choices: the inherited forms had disappeared completely before the nahda and had to be invented again
later Arab novelists rejected the forms their predecessors had used
writers forged links to older forms by choosing to use them
the craft of individual novelists matters more than the literary traditions in which those novelists were educated
Arab novelists of the nahda were the first writers in Arabic to compose extended narratives in rhymed prose
questions.explanation: The sentence before calls the record 'a repertory, on which writers drew as their purposes required,' and the examples show writers choosing old forms: al-Muwaylihi 'chose the maqama,' and Mahfouz 'reworked' the Nights. Continuity that writers 'made' is continuity they chose, as C says. A takes 'made' too literally; the passage never says the old forms had vanished.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Interpret the contrast between 'made' and 'inherited.'

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, sentences 6 to 9.

breakdown.analysis: 'Inherited' suggests a lineage that carries writers along; 'made' suggests writers' own choices. The 'repertory' sentence and the verbs 'chose' and 'reworked' settle it. Prephrase: writers chose to connect themselves to older forms.

choices.note: Too extreme and literal. The forms were available to be drawn on; nothing says they had vanished.
Opposite. The writers drew on older forms rather than rejecting them.
CORRECT. It matches 'a repertory, on which writers drew as their purposes required' and the examples of choosing and reworking.
