Out of scope. The sentence is about how continuity arises, not a ranking of craft against education.
Contradicts the passage, which places rhymed prose in al-Hamadhani's tenth-century maqamat.

questions.stem: Which one of the following would best exemplify continuity in the sense described in the last two sentences of the passage?
choices: A modern critic reclassifies a medieval collection of maqamat as an early example of the novel, since both are extended prose narratives.
A realist novelist, late in her career, shapes a novel on a classical travel narrative to serve aims realism did not suit.
A nahda journalist translates a popular French romance into Arabic for the readers of a Cairo newspaper.
A scholar shows that the plot of a nineteenth-century Arabic novel was borrowed from a European source.
A storyteller in a coffeehouse recites episodes of a heroic sira exactly as they were set down in older manuscripts.
questions.explanation: The author's sense of continuity is a 'repertory, on which writers drew as their purposes required': a writer chooses an older form for a present purpose, as Mahfouz did with The Journey of Ibn Fattouma. B fits exactly. A is the strongest trap because it involves an old form and the novel, but it is the very move the author warns against, 'treating any extended prose narrative as a novel in waiting.' E is continuity as mere inheritance, which the author sets aside.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply the author's notion of continuity to new cases.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, last three sentences and the Mahfouz example before them.

breakdown.analysis: Continuity as 'made': a writer, for a purpose of their own, chooses and reworks an older form. Not a critic relabeling old texts (the error the author names), not passive repetition (mere inheritance), and not import.

choices.note: The trap. This is a critic treating an older narrative as 'a novel in waiting,' which the author identifies as the continuity scholars' risk, not as continuity writers made.
CORRECT. A writer drawing on an inherited form 'as her purposes required,' parallel to Mahfouz's Journey of Ibn Fattouma.
This is the import account's picture of the nahda, with no older Arabic form involved.
Borrowing from a European source illustrates import, not continuity with Arabic forms.
Unchanged recitation is continuity as inheritance; nothing is chosen or reworked for a new purpose.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's position in the last paragraph?
choices: Early modern writers who used maqama devices had absorbed them unawares, not chosen them.
Some nahda translators adapted European novels freely, altering plots and names, instead of translating them exactly.
Zaynab was written before several of the works now proposed as earlier novels were rediscovered by scholars.
Mahfouz read widely in European fiction, in Arabic translation and in English, before writing the Cairo Trilogy.
Early readers of Arabian Nights and Days recognized at once its debt to the Thousand and One Nights.
questions.explanation: The author claims that continuity is 'something writers made,' a repertory 'on which writers drew as their purposes required,' as when al-Muwaylihi 'chose the maqama.' If the writers who used maqama devices did so unknowingly and saw no tradition they were choosing, continuity would look inherited after all. A does this. D is the opposite trap: it supports the author's concession that 'the realist novel had European models.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most undermines the author's synthesis.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, especially the sixth sentence and the last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The core of the author's position is that writers deliberately chose and reworked older forms. To weaken it, show that the use of older forms was not chosen. Facts about translation practice, dating or Mahfouz's reading do not touch that claim.

choices.note: CORRECT. If maqama devices were absorbed unawares rather than chosen, the claim that continuity was 'something writers made' loses its support.
Irrelevant. How freely translators worked does not bear on whether novelists chose older Arabic forms.
Irrelevant to the last paragraph. It concerns the dating dispute, not the author's account of continuity.
Supports the author's concession that the realist novel 'had European models.'
Consistent with the author's view. Recognizing the debt to the Nights fits a deliberate reworking.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Attar's Conference of the Birds and Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress, though often compared, have little in common, since one dissolves the self and the other preserves it.
The usual contrast between the two allegories as dissolving versus preserving the self is overstated, though they do differ in what their pilgrims learn about the divine.
The pun with which Attar's poem ends shows that the birds are identical with the Simorgh, a conclusion that Bunyan's allegory explicitly rejects.
Bunyan's allegory, like Attar's, teaches that the self must be annihilated, so the standard contrast between the two works should be reversed.
Attar's poem can be properly understood only in light of the Sufi doctrine of baqa, a doctrine that comparatists have consistently neglected in favor of the doctrine of fana.
questions.explanation: The passage describes Attar's poem, reports the comparatists' contrast (Bunyan preserves the self, Attar dissolves it), says that contrast 'captures something real but exaggerates on both sides,' and relocates the difference to what each pilgrim learns at the end. B has both halves. D is the trap for readers who stop at paragraph 3: the author says Bunyan's self is not 'simply preserved,' not that it is annihilated, and the author keeps a real difference rather than reversing the contrast.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the claim the passage builds toward, including the author's own refinement in the last paragraph.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, first sentence; paragraph 4, first sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Map: P1 Attar's poem and the si morgh pun; P2 the Bunyan comparison and the usual contrast (Bunyan keeps the self, Attar dissolves it); P3 author: the contrast exaggerates on both sides (the mirror; fana paired with baqa; Christian's burden and the gate of hell); P4 the deeper difference is what each pilgrim learns. Prephrase: the standard contrast is overdrawn, but the works still differ on whether the emptied self meets its Lord or finds His reflection. Watch for answers that keep only the usual contrast or only the critique.

choices.note: Wrong position-holder and too strong. This is the comparatists' contrast pushed further ('little in common'); the author says both works narrate the soul's journey and both demand that the self be emptied.
CORRECT. Paragraph 3 says the contrast 'captures something real but exaggerates on both sides'; paragraph 4 locates 'the deeper difference' in what each pilgrim learns at the journey's end.

Opposite. The author argues that reading the pun as 'a declaration that the birds are God' ignores what the mirror image implies; nor does the passage say Bunyan's allegory explicitly rejects anything of Attar's.

Too strong. The author says Bunyan's self is not 'simply preserved' and that each allegory demands the self be emptied, but never says Bunyan teaches annihilation or that the contrast should be reversed; a difference remains.
Half right and too narrow. Baqa is one point in paragraph 3's critique, and 'only' overstates it; the answer also leaves out Bunyan and the author's final account of the difference.

questions.stem: The primary function of the second sentence of the third paragraph is to
choices: offer evidence that Attar intended his poem as a reply to Christian accounts of the soul's journey
concede that the comparatists' contrast accurately characterizes the ending of Attar's poem
explain why the birds' journey must pass through seven valleys rather than reaching the Simorgh directly
challenge one interpretation of the poem's climax by drawing out an implication of the image Attar uses
suggest that the pun on si morgh matters less to the poem than the anecdotes the hoopoe tells
questions.explanation: The sentence argues that 'a reflection is not the thing reflected' and that a reader who takes the pun 'as a declaration that the birds are God' ignores that the mirror shows each visitor only what it brings. That is a challenge to one reading of the climax, built from what the mirror image implies: D. B is the trap: the sentence comes right after the author grants that the contrast 'captures something real,' but the sentence itself is the first step of the 'exaggerates' half, not a concession.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the sentence does in the author's argument, not what it says.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, first and second sentences; paragraph 1, last sentence (the mirror speech).

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 3 opens with a thesis: the contrast is real but exaggerated 'on both sides.' The second sentence begins the Attar side of the case: the mirror image itself tells against reading the pun as identity. Prephrase: it uses the logic of the mirror to undercut the identity reading of the ending. Eliminate answers that turn it into a concession or that bring in intentions the passage never mentions.

choices.note: Out of scope. Nothing in the passage says Attar wrote in response to Christian works; the Bunyan comparison is the comparatists' and the author's, and Bunyan wrote five centuries later.
Opposite. The sentence attacks the part of the contrast that applies to Attar (that seeker and sought 'were never two'); the concession is in the first sentence, and only in general terms.
Irrelevant. The seven valleys are listed in paragraph 1, but the sentence concerns the mirror at the journey's end, not why the journey has stages.

CORRECT. 'A reflection is not the thing reflected' draws out an implication of the mirror, and it is aimed at 'a reader who takes the pun as a declaration that the birds are God,' one interpretation of the climax.
Shell game. The sentence mentions the pun, but it reinterprets it rather than ranking it below the anecdotes; the anecdotes appear only in paragraph 1.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Bunyan's allegory is less concerned than Attar's with the dangers that beset the soul on its journey.
Because the usual comparison between Attar and Bunyan is misleading, the two works are better studied apart.
Both works present a pilgrim's confidence in its own independence as something that must be overcome.
Readers familiar with Sufi doctrine are especially likely to take the pun on si morgh as a declaration of identity with God.
The annihilation of the final valley in Attar's poem is best understood as the destruction of the creature as such.
questions.explanation: For Attar, the author says what passes away in fana is 'the self's illusion of independence'; for Bunyan, the burden falls 'through no effort of his own' and the closing warning is that 'confidence in one's own standing can fail.' Paragraph 4 sums up: 'Each allegory demands that the self be emptied.' C paraphrases that common ground. B is the tempting overreach: the author corrects the comparison but plainly finds it illuminating, since the passage ends by refining it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the one statement the author's own claims support, without going beyond them.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, third through fifth sentences; paragraph 4, third sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Inference questions reward a modest paraphrase of what the author says. The author's view: the contrast is overdrawn, both works require the self to be emptied, and the real difference is what the pilgrim learns. Prephrase something about common ground between the two works. Eliminate answers that rank the works, abandon the comparison, or reassert the reading the author rejects.

choices.note: Unsupported comparison. The passage says both works pass 'through a landscape of trials' and never ranks their concern with danger; Bunyan's closing warning about the 'way to hell' suggests the opposite if anything.
Too extreme. The author refines the comparison rather than rejecting it; the whole last paragraph states the 'deeper difference' that the comparison reveals.

CORRECT. Attar: what passes away is 'the self's illusion of independence'; Bunyan: the burden falls 'through no effort of his own,' and 'confidence in one's own standing can fail.' Hence 'Each allegory demands that the self be emptied.'
Reversal. The author invokes Sufi theory (fana paired with baqa) against the identity reading; nothing suggests that knowing the doctrine makes the reading more likely.
Opposite. The author says that what passes away is the self's illusion of independence 'rather than the creature as such.'

questions.stem: By "a careful image" (third paragraph, second sentence), the author most probably means that Attar's mirror
choices: was chosen to conceal the poem's real teaching from readers who might object to it
is described with unusual visual detail at the poem's climax
appears only sparingly, being reserved for the end of the journey
reflects Attar's caution about how the poem would be received by Christians
is exact in what it implies about the birds and the Simorgh
questions.explanation: The phrase is followed by a colon and its explanation: 'a reflection is not the thing reflected,' and the mirror shows 'each visitor only what that visitor brings.' 'Careful' therefore means exact in its implications: the image says something definite about the birds' relation to the Simorgh. A and D read 'careful' as 'cautious,' a sense the context does not support.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Use the words after the colon to fix what 'careful' means here.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Meaning-in-context questions turn on the sentence's own explanation. After the colon the author spells out what the image implies: reflection, not identity. Prephrase: the image is exact, chosen so that it implies a definite relation. Eliminate the everyday senses of 'careful' (cautious, sparing, detailed) that the colon does not support.

choices.note: Wrong sense of the word. 'Careful' here concerns what the image implies, not concealment; the passage says nothing about hiding a teaching from objectors.
Distortion. The passage gives no description of the mirror's visual detail; 'careful' refers to the logic of the image, not its vividness.
Wrong sense of the word. Nothing in the passage says how often the image appears, and frequency is not what the colon explains.
Out of scope. The passage never mentions Christian readers of Attar or any caution on his part; the Christian comparison is the modern comparatists'.
CORRECT. The colon explains the phrase: 'a reflection is not the thing reflected,' and the mirror shows each visitor 'only what that visitor brings.' The image is exact about the relation.

questions.stem: The passage attributes each of the following to Attar's poem EXCEPT:
choices: a guide who is Solomon's messenger in the Qur'an
birds that decline the journey out of attachment to something else
a dream within which the whole journey is narrated
a tale about a revered master who abandons his devotions
a sequence of valleys ending in poverty and annihilation
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 names the hoopoe as Solomon's messenger (A), the nightingale's and parrot's excuses (B), the tale of Shaykh San'an (D) and the seven valleys ending in 'poverty and annihilation' (E). The dream belongs to Bunyan: in paragraph 3, 'the dream closes with a warning.' C attaches a detail of the other work to Attar's.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Check each choice against the description of Attar's poem; the one not attributed to it is the answer.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1 for Attar; paragraph 3, fifth sentence for the dream.

breakdown.analysis: EXCEPT detail questions are checked choice by choice. Four details sit in paragraph 1. The dream appears only in the Bunyan discussion, which makes this a shell-game test: a real detail from the passage attached to the wrong work.

choices.note: Attributed. Paragraph 1: 'its guide is the hoopoe, Solomon's messenger in the Qur'an.'
Attributed. Paragraph 1: the nightingale 'cannot leave its love for the rose'; the parrot 'wants only the water of immortality.'
CORRECT. The dream is Bunyan's: 'the dream closes with a warning' (paragraph 3). The passage says nothing of a dream frame in Attar's poem.
Attributed. Paragraph 1: Shaykh San'an, 'a revered master who abandons his devotions for love of a Christian girl.'
Attributed. Paragraph 1 lists seven valleys ending with 'poverty and annihilation.'

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's argument against the usual contrast as that argument applies to Attar's poem?
choices: The theorists who paired fana with baqa held that after fana God alone subsists, nothing of the creature.
In The Pilgrim's Progress, those who enter the Celestial City are given new garments before they are welcomed.
Many of the poem's readers in Persian regard the pun on si morgh as essentially playful rather than doctrinal.
In Attar's poem, the Simorgh states that the number of birds who arrive determines the number reflected in it.
Many of the birds who begin the journey in Attar's poem perish in the valleys long before reaching the Simorgh.
questions.explanation: Against the claim that Attar's birds simply dissolve, the author offers two supports: the mirror image, and the Sufi pairing of fana with baqa, read as meaning that what passes away is 'the self's illusion of independence rather than the creature as such.' If the theorists who held that pairing meant that only God subsists and nothing of the creature remains, that second support turns against the author: A. D is the trap: it restates the mirror speech the author relies on, so it strengthens rather than weakens.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Isolate the author's reasons for saying the contrast exaggerates the Attar side, then find the fact that undercuts one of them.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, second and third sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The scope is limited to Attar, so answers about Bunyan are out. The author's Attar argument has two premises: (1) a reflection is not the thing reflected; (2) fana is paired with baqa, so only the illusion of independence passes away. A weakener attacks a premise or the inference. Prephrase: show that baqa does not preserve the creature after all, or that the mirror really does mean identity.

choices.note: CORRECT. The author uses baqa to argue that what passes away is the self's illusion 'rather than the creature as such.' If those theorists meant that nothing of the creature remains, the doctrine supports the usual contrast instead.
Out of scope. The stem limits the question to Attar's poem; a detail about Bunyan's Celestial City does not touch the author's reasons about Attar, and if anything bears on the Bunyan half.
Irrelevant. Calling the pun playful neither restores the identity reading nor undercuts the mirror or baqa arguments; if anything it lowers the doctrinal weight the usual contrast puts on the pun.
Opposite. This restates the mirror speech from paragraph 1, which supports the author's point that the Simorgh 'shows each visitor only what that visitor brings.'
Irrelevant. How many birds fail on the way says nothing about what happens to the self of those who arrive.

questions.stem: Which one of the following pairs of situations is most analogous to the difference the author identifies in the last paragraph between what Bunyan's and Attar's pilgrims learn?
choices: One traveler reaches a famous oracle and receives counsel; another reaches a different oracle and receives contrary counsel.
One applicant is admitted to a school after an examination; another applicant fails the same examination and is turned away.
One climber reaches a summit by a long and difficult route; another reaches the same summit quickly by an easier route.
One searcher is welcomed at a friend's door; another, seeking a famous teacher, finds the qualities she sought displayed in her own search.
One pilgrim makes the whole journey alone; another sets out in a large company, most of whose members turn back before the end.
questions.explanation: The author's difference: Bunyan's pilgrim 'is received by a grace that comes from beyond himself'; Attar's birds 'discover that what they sought was mirrored in their own seeking.' D pairs a welcome from another at a door with a discovery that the object sought was displayed in the searcher's own search. B is the trap built from the Ignorance episode: it contrasts admission with rejection, which is a difference in outcome, not in what is learned about the relation to what was sought.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: State the abstract difference in the last paragraph, then match its structure, not its surface.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Abstract the relation. Case 1: the seeker arrives and is received by someone other than himself. Case 2: the seeker arrives and learns that what was sought was reflected in the seeking itself. Prephrase: one is welcomed by another; the other discovers the goal in herself. Ignore surface features (alone vs. in company, routes, success vs. failure).

choices.note: Both cases involve counsel from an external source; neither has the recognition that what was sought was present in the seeking.

Wrong distinction. Admission versus rejection mirrors Christian versus Ignorance within Bunyan, not the difference between Bunyan's and Attar's pilgrims; both applicants are judged by an external authority.
Wrong distinction. The contrast is between routes to the same goal, whereas the author's contrast concerns what the arrival reveals.
CORRECT. The first is received by another 'from beyond himself'; the second discovers that what she sought was 'mirrored in [her] own seeking.'

Surface feature. Attar's company of birds, most of whom drop out, and Bunyan's single pilgrim resemble this pairing, but the author's difference is about what each learns at the end, not how many travel.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The Shahnameh preserves pre-Islamic Iranian history in a Persian deliberately purged of Arabic, a feature that Arnold's English adaptation could not reproduce.
Because it was based on secondhand sources, Arnold's "Sohrab and Rustum" departs so far from Ferdowsi that it should not be read as an adaptation of the Shahnameh.
Arnold's adaptation retains much of Ferdowsi's tragedy of Rostam and Sohrab, but its changes move the cause of the catastrophe from human choices to fate.
The resemblance between Arnold's poem and Homeric epic confirms that Ferdowsi, like Homer, drew on a living oral tradition.
Unlike Arnold, Ferdowsi presents the death of Sohrab as entirely the product of human choices, with no role for fate or the injustice of death.
questions.explanation: The passage introduces the Shahnameh, tells the Rostam and Sohrab story, describes Arnold's sources and Homeric manner, then gives the author's verdict: Arnold is largely faithful, but his changes shift 'where its blame resides' from human choices to 'a tragedy of fate.' C states it. E is the near-miss: the author grants that Ferdowsi 'opens the tale by brooding on the injustice of death,' so 'no role for fate' is too strong.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the claim the last paragraph argues for and the rest of the passage sets up.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, first, fourth, fifth and last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Map: P1 the Shahnameh and the Arabic-words debate (background); P2 Ferdowsi's version of the tragedy, with its lie, trick and royal delay; P3 Arnold's sources and Homeric style, and the Iliad parallel; P4 author: largely faithful, but the changes relocate blame. Prephrase: Arnold kept the plot but changed where the blame lies. Watch for answers built from paragraph 1 or 3 alone, and for overstatements of either side of the qualified verdict.

choices.note: Wrong position-holder and out of focus. 'Deliberately purged' is Browne's view, which the passage counters with Moïnfar's; and the passage never discusses whether Arnold could reproduce Ferdowsi's vocabulary.
Too extreme. The author agrees that 'much of the plot does survive' and calls the poem a rendition of the story; the objection concerns specific alterations, not the whole.
CORRECT. 'Much of the plot does survive. Yet the alterations are telling': Ferdowsi 'assembles the catastrophe from human choices,' while Arnold 'makes it a tragedy of fate.'
Distortion and wrong position-holder. Davidson's oral thesis is reported as contested, not confirmed, and the resemblance of Arnold's style to Homer is evidence of nothing about Ferdowsi.
Too strong. The author says Ferdowsi 'opens the tale by brooding on the injustice of death' and only then assembles the catastrophe from human choices.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Moïnfar attributed the relative rarity of Arabic words in the Shahnameh to
choices: Ferdowsi's aversion to the language of the Arab conquerors
the restrictions that the epic's meter placed on loanwords
Ferdowsi's reliance on oral rather than written sources
the small sample of verses on which earlier estimates had been based
the subject matter and style of the poem
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: Moïnfar 'attributed their relative rarity not to aversion but to the poem's subject matter and style.' E. B is the trap: the meter point is introduced with 'as John Perry adds,' so it is Perry's addition, not what the passage reports as Moïnfar's explanation.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the sentence that reports Moïnfar's explanation, and keep it separate from the views next to it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, fourth sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Three people speak in paragraph 1: Browne (deliberate avoidance), Moïnfar (subject matter and style), Perry (the meter). A detail question that lists all three views tests whether you keep track of who said what.

choices.note: Wrong position-holder. Deliberate avoidance is Browne's explanation; Moïnfar's was 'not to aversion.'
Wrong position-holder. The meter point is introduced with 'as John Perry adds'; the passage does not attribute it to Moïnfar.
Out of scope. Oral and written sources come up only in paragraph 3, in connection with Davidson, not Moïnfar.
Distortion. The passage notes that Browne sampled a single episode and that Moïnfar made a complete count, but it does not say Moïnfar explained the rarity by the size of Browne's sample.
CORRECT. Paragraph 1: Moïnfar 'attributed their relative rarity not to aversion but to the poem's subject matter and style.'

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following statements about Browne's estimate and Moïnfar's count?
choices: Moïnfar found a considerably larger proportion of Arabic words in the poem than Browne had estimated.
Moïnfar's figure rested on the whole poem, whereas Browne's was generalized from verses of a single episode.
Browne's estimate excluded words that Moïnfar classified as being of Arabic origin.
Moïnfar agreed with Browne that the scarcity of Arabic words reflects a deliberate choice, though not an aversion.
Browne's estimate was based on the most famous episode because that episode contains the fewest Arabic words.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says Browne put the Arabic element at four or five percent 'sampling verses from a single episode,' and calls Moïnfar's a 'complete count.' B follows directly. A is the trap for readers who know Moïnfar's percentages: the passage gives Moïnfar's result only as 706 words, a figure in different units from Browne's percentage, so no comparison of proportions can be drawn from the passage.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Compare what the passage says about how each figure was reached, and infer no further than that.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, third and fourth sentences; paragraph 2, first sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The passage gives Browne's method (a sample from one episode, which paragraph 2 identifies as the Rostam and Sohrab story) and his figure (four or five percent), and Moïnfar's method (a complete count) and his figure (706 words). The numbers are in different units, so the safe inference concerns method, not size. Prephrase: one is a sample of one episode, the other a full count.

choices.note: Unsupported. Browne gives a percentage and Moïnfar, as reported, a count of 706 words; the passage offers no basis for comparing proportions. Outside knowledge of Moïnfar's percentages is exactly what this trap exploits.
CORRECT. Browne was 'sampling verses from a single episode'; Moïnfar made a 'complete count.'
Unsupported. The passage says nothing about how either scholar classified particular words.
Opposite. The passage sets them against each other: Browne 'took it for deliberate avoidance,' while Moïnfar attributed the rarity 'not to aversion but to' subject matter and style.
Unsupported causal claim. The passage says only that Browne sampled the episode that is the poem's most famous; it gives no reason for his choice and no ranking of episodes by Arabic content.

questions.stem: The author refers to Olga Davidson's argument (third paragraph, last sentence) primarily in order to
choices: show that the Homeric parallel suggested by Arnold's style has a disputed scholarly counterpart
provide evidence that Arnold's Homeric manner faithfully reproduced the style of Ferdowsi's own verse
refute the view of other specialists that Ferdowsi relied chiefly on written sources
explain why Arnold was unable to obtain a copy of Mohl's French translation
support Taher-Kermani's claim that Arnold's rendition is faithful to its original
questions.explanation: The sentence says Arnold's Homeric verse 'has encouraged readers to treat the Shahnameh as Iran's Iliad, and scholarship has pursued the parallel too,' then reports Davidson's oral-tradition thesis as one 'other specialists contest.' A captures both the extension of the parallel and its contested status. C is the trap: the author reports Davidson's thesis and the opposing insistence on written sources without taking a side.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Ask why the author brings Davidson in at this point, given what comes just before.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Context: Arnold's Homeric similes invite the 'Iran's Iliad' comparison; 'scholarship has pursued the parallel too' introduces Davidson, and 'a thesis other specialists contest' frames her view as disputed. Prephrase: to show the Homeric comparison has a scholarly version, which is contested. Watch for answers that make the author endorse either side.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Scholarship has pursued the parallel too': Davidson applied 'methods developed for Homeric epic,' and her thesis is one 'other specialists contest.'
Distortion. The passage calls Arnold's similes Homeric, not Ferdowsian, and Davidson's argument concerns Ferdowsi's sources, not Arnold's style.
Too strong. The author reports Davidson's thesis and notes that others 'contest' it, insisting on written sources; the author refutes neither side.
Irrelevant. Arnold's lack of access to Mohl's book is mentioned earlier in the paragraph but has nothing to do with Davidson.
Shell game. Taher-Kermani's claim comes in paragraph 4 and concerns Arnold's fidelity to the plot; Davidson's argument concerns Ferdowsi's sources.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Taher-Kermani's claim about Arnold's fidelity can most accurately be described as
choices: dismissive, on the grounds that a poet without Persian could not have been faithful to Ferdowsi
wholly approving, since the author regards Arnold's departures from Ferdowsi as superficial
reluctantly accepting, because Arnold himself admitted that he never saw Mohl's translation
accepting, with the reservation that a few departures change the story's meaning
uncertain, since the author finds the evidence about Arnold's sources too incomplete to judge
questions.explanation: The author grants the claim ('much of the plot does survive') and then qualifies it: 'Yet the alterations are telling,' ending with the judgment that Arnold 'altered... where its blame resides.' D captures acceptance with a substantial reservation. B is the trap for readers who stop at the concession; the author calls the departures 'telling,' not superficial.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pin down both the agreement and the 'Yet' that follows it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, first two sentences and last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Attitude questions on the LSAT usually reward the qualified option. Here the author agrees ('does survive') and then turns ('Yet'). Prephrase: agrees about the plot, but thinks the few changes matter a great deal. Eliminate the extremes and any answer that rests the attitude on the wrong reason.

choices.note: Too extreme and the wrong reason. The author agrees that 'much of the plot does survive' and never argues that ignorance of Persian ruled out fidelity.
Too extreme. The author calls the alterations 'telling' and argues that they relocate the blame; they are not superficial.

Wrong reason. Arnold's admission about Mohl explains his indirect access, which Taher-Kermani's claim already allows for ('despite Arnold's indirect access'); it is not the basis of the author's attitude, and 'reluctant' is not supported.
CORRECT. 'Much of the plot does survive. Yet the alterations are telling'; Arnold changed 'where its blame resides.'
Unsupported. The author reaches a confident judgment about the alterations and expresses no doubt about the evidence.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the author's claim about the effect of Arnold's alterations?
choices: Arnold's poem repeatedly compares the two combatants at length to storms, eagles and other natural forces.
Most English readers in the nineteenth century knew no version of the story of Rostam and Sohrab other than Arnold's.
In Arnold's poem the dying Sohrab blames Rustum's refusal to reveal his name, and Rustum accepts the blame.
Arnold moved the episode to Kay Khosrow's reign because one of his sources assigned it to that reign.
Ferdowsi's prologue to the episode dwells on the apparent injustice of death striking the young.
questions.explanation: The author claims that Arnold's changes turn a catastrophe 'assembled from human choices' into 'a tragedy of fate,' shifting 'where its blame resides.' If Arnold's own poem has Sohrab blame Rustum's concealment and Rustum accept the blame, then human choice stays at the center of Arnold's version and the claim about its effect fails: C. D is the trap: it explains why Arnold made a change, but the author's claim concerns the change's effect, whatever its motive.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify the claim exactly (an effect on where the blame lies), then find the fact that shows the effect did not occur.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, last three sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Claim: in Ferdowsi the catastrophe is built from human choices; in Arnold it becomes fate watched by nature, so Arnold changed where the blame resides. To weaken it, show that blame for human choices remains prominent in Arnold's version. Watch for answers about motive, about readers, or about details the author has already conceded.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Similes comparing the fighters to natural forces would, if anything, fit the author's picture of a tragedy set within nature; they do not restore human blame.
Irrelevant. How many readers knew only Arnold's version bears on his influence, not on where his poem places the blame.

CORRECT. If Arnold's Sohrab blames Rustum's concealment and Rustum accepts the blame, the blame in Arnold's version still rests on human choices, against the claim that he made it 'a tragedy of fate.'
Motive, not effect. The author's claim is about what the alterations do to the story; a source-based reason for the change leaves that effect untouched.
Already conceded. The author grants that 'Ferdowsi opens the tale by brooding on the injustice of death' and still finds the catastrophe assembled from human choices.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, which one of the following adaptations would the author regard as most closely resembling Arnold's treatment of the story?
choices: A film of a tragedy that cuts the scene in which a ruler's jealousy delays a rescue and ends on a river flowing past the battlefield.
A translation of an ancient epic that preserves every episode and speech but replaces its archaic diction with modern idiom.
A retelling of a legend that adds a scene in which a king confesses that his suspicion caused a hero's death.
A prose version of a verse epic, made directly from the original language by a scholar who knows it well.
A stage version of a legend that keeps the plot entirely intact but moves the action from the ancient world to a modern city.
questions.explanation: On the author's account, Arnold kept the plot but removed human culpability (moving the story away from the weak Kay Kavus, whose suspicion delays the remedy) and closed on the indifferent Oxus, turning the story into 'a tragedy of fate watched by indifferent nature.' A does both: it cuts a ruler's culpable delay and ends on nature moving on. C is the opposite trap: it adds royal blame rather than removing it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: State what, for the author, defines Arnold's treatment, then find the adaptation with the same features.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, last sentence; paragraph 4, third through last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Abstract Arnold's treatment: (1) much of the plot kept; (2) the human sources of blame, especially the king's suspicion, removed or softened; (3) the ending turned to fate and indifferent nature. The analogue must change where blame lies. Eliminate changes of diction, medium or setting that leave the blame where it was.

choices.note: CORRECT. Cutting the ruler's jealous delay parallels moving the story away from Kay Kavus, whose suspicion delays the remedy; the closing shot of the river parallels Arnold's ending on the Oxus.
Wrong feature. A change of diction alters style, not where the story places blame; the author's point about Arnold concerns the latter.
Opposite. Adding a king's confession increases human, royal blame, the reverse of what the author says Arnold did.
Wrong feature. Working from the original language reverses Arnold's situation (he 'had no Persian'), and nothing suggests a shift in blame.
Wrong feature. Moving the setting while keeping the plot intact changes nothing about where the catastrophe's causes lie.

sections.title: Reading Through Ideas 14: Two ways of seeing in My Name Is Red · Averroes and the theater he never saw · Is The Tale of Genji a novel? · The Arab historian of Don Quixote

passages.title: Two ways of seeing in My Name Is Red
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Orhan Pamuk's My Name Is Red (1998) is set in Istanbul in the winter of 1591, where miniaturists of the sultan's workshop are secretly illustrating a book in the manner of the Venetian masters. Due for the thousandth year of the Hegira, it is to end with a portrait of the sultan himself, painted as the Venetians paint a particular man. Enishte Effendi, who oversees it, was dazzled by such portraits in Venice. It troubles Master Osman, head of the workshop, for whom the tradition descending from the Persian master Bihzad depicts the world as God sees it, from above and in its essential forms, not as it appears to one observer in one place. Perspective, on this view, is less a technique than a presumption: it puts a single human eye where God's should be.

Pamuk stages this dispute as a murder mystery. The novel opens with a gilder speaking from the afterlife: "I am nothing but a corpse now, a body at the bottom of a well." A fellow miniaturist killed him for threatening to denounce the book as blasphemous. Each of the fifty-nine chapters has a single narrator. Some are characters; others are a dog, a tree, a counterfeit gold coin, Death and the color red, voiced by a coffeehouse storyteller who speaks for drawings hung beside him. The tree, glad not to have been drawn in the Frankish manner, declares, "I don't want to be a tree; I want to be its meaning." The plot turns on style itself. The tradition counts a signature, or any trait that marks an individual hand, as a flaw, yet the murderer is finally exposed by just such a trait, a peculiar way of drawing horses' nostrils that he had not known was his.

Critics have divided over what the novel makes of this conflict. Erdağ Göknar, its English translator, reads Pamuk's fiction as a body of "secular blasphemies": by setting Ottoman, Islamic and Sufi contexts against the secular nation-state's account of itself, it restores to view a heritage the Turkish republic had set aside. Other critics object that, whatever its sympathies, the novel keeps the opposition of East and West in place, treating each as a self-contained whole. Pamuk himself, interviewed in 2002, said the familiar Western and Eastern accounts of a clash between the two were both mistaken.

None of these readings quite describes how the novel handles its question. It never settles whether God's view or one man's view is the truer way to see. Its form instead concedes something to each: a novel of first-person chapters gives every voice, human or not, a single point of view, which is the very principle of the Venetian portrait, while its most memorable voices speak for the miniaturists' conviction that what a picture owes the world is meaning rather than appearance. What the novel does judge is the attempt to settle the matter by force. The killings, and the zealots' raid that silences the storyteller, are what it plainly condemns. Its impartiality is real, but it is impartiality between ways of seeing, not between argument and violence.

sources.author: Orhan Pamuk (trans. Erdağ Göknar)
sources.title: My Name Is Red
sources.note: English translation (Knopf, 2001) of Benim Adım Kırmızı (1998); source of the two quotations, the opening line "I am nothing but a corpse now, a body at the bottom of a well" and the tree's "I don't want to be a tree; I want to be its meaning," checked against multiple quotations of Göknar's text.

sources.author: Erdağ Göknar
sources.title: Orhan Pamuk, Secularism and Blasphemy: The Politics of the Turkish Novel
sources.note: Routledge study of all Pamuk's novels arguing that fiction confronting the nation-state (devlet) with Ottoman, Islamic and Sufi contexts (din) produces "secular blasphemies" (the term quoted in the passage, from the book's own summary of its thesis).

sources.author: Orhan Pamuk, interviewed by Elizabeth Farnsworth
sources.title: Orhan Pamuk: Bridging Two Worlds (PBS NewsHour)
sources.note: Interview on My Name Is Red in which Pamuk says the common Western and Eastern views of a 'clash' are both mistaken; paraphrased, not quoted, in the passage.

passages.title: Averroes and the theater he never saw
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
In Jorge Luis Borges's story "Averroes's Search" (1947), the twelfth-century philosopher of Córdoba, at work on a commentary on Aristotle's Poetics, is halted by two words he cannot interpret: tragedy and comedy. They recur throughout the treatise, and nothing in the Arabic poetry he knows corresponds to them. Borges surrounds him with clues he cannot read. Below his window, children are playing: one, standing on another's shoulders, pretends to be a muezzin, the boy beneath him serves as the minaret, and a third, kneeling, is the congregation. That evening a traveler describes a performance he saw in China, in which masked men on a terrace represented a story, and his listeners cannot grasp what he describes. Averroes returns to his manuscript and writes that Aristotle gives the name tragedy to panegyrics and comedy to satires. In an afterword Borges turns the irony on himself: Averroes, imagining drama without knowing what a theater is, was no more absurd than Borges, imagining Averroes from a few pages of Renan, Lane and Asín Palacios.

The confusion is historical, though it began before Averroes. He knew no Greek and worked from the Arabic version of Abu Bishr Matta (d. 940), itself made from a Syriac translation, which had already rendered tragedy and comedy as madih and hija', praise and invective, two established genres of Arabic verse. The Arabic tradition, moreover, counted the Poetics among Aristotle's works on logic. Averroes's Middle Commentary nonetheless became the principal route by which the Poetics reached Latin Europe, through a Latin version made in 1256.

Renan, Borges and the Moroccan critic Abdelfattah Kilito have treated the commentary, in Rebecca Gould's phrase, as "an exemplary case of the failure of translation," though Kilito blamed the conditions of transmission rather than Averroes himself. Charles Butterworth, whose 1986 English translation remains standard, reads the work on its own terms, as a philosopher's account of what is praiseworthy in Greek poetics and both praiseworthy and blameworthy in Arabic poetry. Dimitri Gutas, reviewing that translation, countered that it neglects the decisive influence of the garbled Arabic version on Averroes's understanding. Gould goes furthest. Taking seriously Averroes's stated aim, to set out the rules of poetry common to all or most nations, she argues that praise and blame gave him "a useful means of conceiving literary form outside the confines of a single literary tradition."

Gould's account of the commentary's purpose is persuasive, but it does not dissolve Borges's point. Averroes was not trying to reconstruct the Athenian stage; he was seeking rules that could govern the poems of many peoples, and for that purpose praise and blame, which the Poetics itself uses in tracing poetry's origins, served him well. Yet a comparative framework can compare only what it can perceive, and enactment by actors, which is what separates drama from narration, lay outside his. The children in the courtyard are Borges's emblem of that blind spot. The afterword, however, implies that the lesson was never about Averroes alone. What the story ironizes is any reader's confidence in having grasped another culture, including that of the reader who smiles at Averroes's mistake.

sources.author: Jorge Luis Borges
sources.title: La busca de Averroes (Averroes's Search)
sources.note: First published in Sur (1947), collected in El Aleph (1949); the story of Averroes failing to grasp 'tragedy' and 'comedy', with the afterword naming Renan, Lane and Asín Palacios (paraphrased, not quoted).

sources.author: Charles E. Butterworth (trans.)
sources.title: Averroes' Middle Commentary on Aristotle's Poetics
sources.note: Princeton University Press translation with introduction and notes, presenting the commentary as showing what is praiseworthy in Greek poetics and both praiseworthy and blameworthy in Arabic poetics; Dimitri Gutas's review article 'On Translating Averroes' Commentaries' (JAOS 110, 1990) faults it for neglecting the garbled Arabic version's influence.

sources.author: Rebecca Ruth Gould
sources.title: The Poetics from Athens to al-Andalus: Ibn Rushd's Grounds for Comparison
sources.note: Modern Philology 112.1: argues the praise/blame rendering was a productive comparative tool rather than a failure; both quotations ("an exemplary case of the failure of translation" and "a useful means of conceiving literary form outside the confines of a single literary tradition") are from its abstract.

passages.title: Is The Tale of Genji a novel?
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Murasaki Shikibu's The Tale of Genji, written by a lady-in-waiting at the Heian court in the early eleventh century, runs to fifty-four chapters. It follows Genji, an emperor's son reduced to commoner rank, through love affairs, exile and a return to power, and then, after his death, turns to a bleaker generation at Uji. Since Arthur Waley's English translation (1925–33), the work has often been introduced to Western readers as the world's first novel, and Waley encouraged the description. In the chapter "Fireflies," Genji finds a young woman absorbed in tales and, after teasing her, defends them: the official histories, he says, record only part of what happened, while tales supply the rest. Waley's Genji declares, "I have a theory of my own about what this art of the novel is." The word Waley rendered as "novel" was monogatari: a tale, a telling of things.

Proponents of the label point to what the Genji does with consciousness. Its characters remember, regret and misread one another, and early choices return to govern later lives: Genji's secret affair with his father's consort Fujitsubo, who resembles his dead mother, produces a son who becomes emperor, and Genji spends years pursuing women who recall her. Long before any comparison with Europe arose, Motoori Norinaga, the eighteenth-century scholar of native learning, accounted for the same depth in his own terms. In his commentary of 1799 he rejected the long tradition of reading the tale as Buddhist allegory or as moral instruction that rewards good and punishes evil, and argued that its purpose was to make readers know mono no aware, the capacity to be moved by things.

Critics of the label answer that it imposes a European genre on a different form. Haruo Shirane's The Bridge of Dreams (1987) treats the Genji as a work that, for all its resemblance to the psychological novel, was not conceived as a single whole but grew in stages, circulating in installments among a small aristocratic audience, and Shirane reads it against the conventions of earlier tales and of court poetry that this audience knew. Some 795 poems are woven into its prose, and much of its emotional life passes through them. To call such a work the first novel, on this view, is to make it the forerunner of a form that emerged centuries later elsewhere, and to prize it chiefly for anticipating that form.

The critics are right about the word "first," which converts a resemblance into a line of descent that the evidence cannot support; no European novelist read Murasaki before the form was long established. But it does not follow that the resemblance is an artifact of the label. Norinaga, who knew nothing of the European novel, located the work's power in the same attention to feeling that Western readers later praised, and he did so by refusing to subordinate the tale to doctrine. The psychological depth is the Genji's own; what is borrowed is only the story that makes it a beginning. Genji's argument in "Fireflies" claims for tales not priority but a kind of completeness, a claim the work sustains without the label.

sources.author: Haruo Shirane
sources.title: The Bridge of Dreams: A Poetics of "The Tale of Genji"
sources.note: Stanford University Press study arguing that the Genji, though resembling a psychological novel, grew in stages and must be read against the tale and poetic conventions its court audience knew.

sources.author: Murasaki Shikibu, trans. Arthur Waley
sources.title: The Tale of Genji
sources.note: The first full English translation (6 vols., 1925–33), which presented the work to Western readers as a novel; source of the quoted line from the 'Fireflies' chapter, 'I have a theory of my own about what this art of the novel is.'

sources.author: Motoori Norinaga
sources.title: Genji monogatari tama no ogushi (The Tale of Genji: A Little Jeweled Comb)
sources.note: Norinaga's commentary arguing that the tale aims to make readers know mono no aware, against Buddhist and moral-didactic readings.

sources.author: Thomas Harper and Haruo Shirane (eds.)
sources.title: Reading The Tale of Genji: Sources from the First Millennium
sources.note: Anthology in translation of a thousand years of Genji commentary, including Norinaga, for reading the critical tradition in its own words.

passages.title: The Arab historian of Don Quixote
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
In the eighth chapter of Don Quixote (1605), Cervantes's narrator abandons his hero in mid-combat, sword raised against a Basque squire, because, he says, his source breaks off. In the ninth he finds the rest. In the Alcaná, Toledo's market street, he sees a boy selling old notebooks to a silk merchant, recognizes the script as Arabic, and finds a Morisco, one of the Muslims compelled to convert to Christianity or their descendants, to translate them. The notebooks prove to be the history of Don Quixote written by Cide Hamete Benengeli, "historiador arábigo," an Arab historian. From then on the novel presents itself as that chronicle in translation, and Cide Hamete is cited, praised and doubted until the last page of Part II (1615).

One long-standing reading treats the device as parody. Romances of chivalry presented themselves as ancient chronicles recovered by chance and translated; Garci Rodríguez de Montalvo claimed that his sequel to the Amadís de Gaula, the Sergas de Esplandián, had been found in a stone tomb beneath a hermitage near Constantinople. Cervantes, whose prologue announces that his book aims to destroy the authority of such romances, gives the convention a deflating home: his precious manuscript is waste paper bought for small change in a market. Critics in this line, E. C. Riley among them in Cervantes's Theory of the Novel (1962), treat Cide Hamete chiefly as an instrument through which Cervantes reflects on the relations between history and fiction, and between truth and verisimilitude.

Other critics insist that the choice of an Arab historian cannot be merely formal. Cervantes wrote when Spain's Moriscos were suspected of practicing Islam in secret; between the publication of the two parts they were expelled from the kingdom, and Part II gives a long hearing to Ricote, Sancho's Morisco neighbor, who returns in disguise to lament his exile. María Rosa Menocal, in The Ornament of the World (2002), reads the scene in the Alcaná, with its Arabic text, its Morisco translator and its Toledan setting, as a nostalgic invocation of convivencia, the coexistence of Muslims, Jews and Christians that Spain had lost.

Each reading captures something, but the narrator's words complicate both. He warns that if anything can be objected to the history's truth, it is that its author was an Arab, "siendo muy propio de los de aquella nación ser mentirosos," since lying is characteristic of that nation. The parody reading treats this as a joke about unreliable chroniclers; the Morisco reading tends to pass over it in favor of the device's nostalgic resonance. Yet the slur is the hinge of the device. A book that would expose the false histories of chivalry rests its own claim to truth on a witness the narrator's culture held to be a liar, rendered into Castilian by a convert it held to be suspect. Cervantes need not have mourned a lost past to make that witness carry his novel's central question; he needed only to see that the question of who could be trusted to tell the truth had become, in his Spain, a question about its Muslims. That is less than Menocal claims, but more than parody explains.

sources.author: Miguel de Cervantes
sources.title: El ingenioso hidalgo don Quijote de la Mancha
sources.note: Part I, chapter 9 is the source of both quotations: the manuscript's attribution to Cide Hamete Benengeli, 'historiador arábigo,' and the narrator's warning 'siendo muy propio de los de aquella nación ser mentirosos.'

sources.author: E. C. Riley
sources.title: Cervantes's Theory of the Novel
sources.note: Classic study setting Cervantes's ideas on prose fiction against Renaissance theory, with central chapters on history and fiction and on verisimilitude and the marvellous.

sources.author: María Rosa Menocal
sources.title: The Ornament of the World: How Muslims, Jews, and Christians Created a Culture of Tolerance in Medieval Spain
sources.note: Its chapter 'Somewhere in La Mancha' reads the Toledo manuscript scene, with its Arabic text and Morisco translator, as an evocation of Spain's lost convivencia.

sources.author: Garci Rodríguez de Montalvo
sources.title: Amadís de Gaula
sources.note: The most famous Spanish romance of chivalry. Montalvo's prologue presents its sequel, the Sergas de Esplandián, as a book found in a stone tomb under a hermitage near Constantinople: the convention Cervantes deflates.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: My Name Is Red ultimately sides with Master Osman's tradition, presenting perspective as a presumption that puts a human eye where God's should be.
My Name Is Red leaves open which of two ways of seeing is truer, drawing on both in its form, while plainly condemning efforts to settle the question by force.
Critics have misread My Name Is Red as a novel about East and West, when it is in fact a murder mystery whose solution turns on the nature of artistic style.
Göknar's reading of My Name Is Red as restoring a set-aside Ottoman heritage is more persuasive than the objection that the novel preserves the opposition of East and West.
My Name Is Red shows that the miniaturists' ideal of an anonymous style refutes itself, since the murderer is exposed by a trait of his own individual hand.
questions.explanation: The author's thesis is in the last paragraph: the novel 'never settles whether God's view or one man's view is the truer way to see,' its form 'concedes something to each,' and what it 'does judge is the attempt to settle the matter by force.' B states all three parts. A gives Master Osman's view (paragraph 1) to the novel, the trap for a reader who knows the book's elegiac tone.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall claim about how the novel treats the conflict it depicts.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, which follows 'None of these readings quite describes how the novel handles its question.'

breakdown.analysis: Paragraphs 1 and 2 set out the two ways of seeing and the novel's form; paragraph 3 gives critics' readings; paragraph 4 gives the author's own: impartial between ways of seeing, not between argument and violence. Prephrase: the novel doesn't pick a side aesthetically, uses both, but condemns violence.

choices.note: Wrong position-holder. 'Perspective... is less a technique than a presumption' is Master Osman's view ('on this view'). The author says the novel 'never settles' the question.

CORRECT. It matches 'never settles whether God's view or one man's view is the truer way to see,' 'concedes something to each,' and 'what the novel does judge is the attempt to settle the matter by force.'
Distortion. The author never says critics misread the novel as being about East and West, and the murder plot is presented as how Pamuk 'stages this dispute,' not as a replacement for it.
Wrong comparison. The author says 'None of these readings quite describes' the novel and does not rank Göknar's above the objection.

Too strong. The nostrils episode is an irony the author notes, but the author says the novel never settles the question; claiming the novel shows the ideal refutes itself is a verdict the passage denies.

questions.stem: The author mentions the way the murderer draws horses' nostrils (last sentence of the second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: provide evidence that the miniaturists secretly preferred the Venetian manner to their own tradition
show that Master Osman's account of the Bihzad tradition is historically inaccurate
explain why the gilder threatened to denounce the illustrated book as blasphemous
illustrate the claim that the novel's plot turns on the question of style
demonstrate that the tradition's view of signatures as flaws is one the novel finally rejects
questions.explanation: The sentence before it announces the point: 'The plot turns on style itself.' The nostrils detail is the example: a tradition that counts individual traits as flaws has its murderer exposed by one. D names that role. E is the trap: it turns an irony into a verdict, but the last paragraph says the novel 'never settles' between the two ways of seeing.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the nostrils detail does in the paragraph.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, last two sentences: 'The plot turns on style itself' followed by the tradition's view of signatures and the murderer's exposure.

breakdown.analysis: Function questions are answered by the sentence that frames the detail. Here the frame is the topic sentence 'The plot turns on style itself.' Prephrase: an example of the plot hinging on individual style.

choices.note: Out of scope. Nothing says the miniaturists secretly preferred the Venetian manner; the murderer did not even know the trait was his.
Out of scope. The passage never assesses the historical accuracy of Osman's account.
Shell game. The gilder's threat is mentioned earlier in the paragraph, but the nostrils detail concerns how the murderer is exposed, not why the gilder acted.
CORRECT. The detail exemplifies 'The plot turns on style itself': the trait that the tradition counts as a flaw is what betrays the killer.
Too strong. The irony is real, but the author's last paragraph says the novel 'never settles' the question, so the detail is not offered as the novel's rejection of the tradition.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about the readings described in the third paragraph?
choices: Göknar is mistaken in holding that the novel engages Ottoman, Islamic and Sufi contexts.
The objection that the novel keeps East and West in place is refuted by Pamuk's remarks in 2002.
Pamuk's remarks deserve more weight than the critics' readings, since they reveal his intentions.
The readings all fail because they attend to the novel's historical setting rather than its plot.
None of the readings fully accounts for the way the novel's form draws on both traditions.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph opens 'None of these readings quite describes how the novel handles its question' and then gives the author's alternative: the form 'concedes something to each.' So the author thinks the readings miss that feature (E). B is the trap for a reader who takes the author's own word as decisive; the passage reports Pamuk's remark among the readings and does not use it to refute anyone.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's view of the critics' positions.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3 for the readings; the first three sentences of paragraph 4 for the author's response.

breakdown.analysis: 'Not quite' is a qualified rejection: the readings are incomplete, not simply wrong. What they miss is the author's own point about form. Prephrase: they don't capture how the novel's form uses both sides.

choices.note: Too strong. The author never disputes that the novel engages these contexts; 'not quite' describes an incomplete reading, not a false one.
Wrong position-holder. The passage reports Pamuk's 2002 remark but never uses it to refute the objection, and the author says none of the readings quite describes the novel.
Out of scope. The author says nothing about weighing an author's intentions against critics' interpretations.
Distortion. The author's complaint concerns how the novel handles its question, especially its form, not a neglect of plot in favor of setting.
CORRECT. 'None of these readings quite describes how the novel handles its question,' and what the author then supplies is that the form 'concedes something to each.'

questions.stem: By "presumption" (last sentence of the first paragraph), the author most probably means
choices: a claim to a standpoint that is not properly one's own
an assumption adopted provisionally until evidence can confirm it
a pictorial convention that makes images resemble their subjects
a belief the Venetian masters held without being aware of it
an expectation that viewers will recognize the person depicted
questions.explanation: The colon explains the word: perspective 'puts a single human eye where God's should be.' A presumption here is an overstepping, taking a place that isn't one's own. B is the familiar sense of 'presumption' (a working assumption), the trap for a reader who doesn't read past the colon.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Decide what 'presumption' means in its sentence.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, last sentence: 'less a technique than a presumption: it puts a single human eye where God's should be.'

breakdown.analysis: The word is contrasted with 'technique' and defined by the clause after the colon. Prephrase: arrogance, usurping God's viewpoint.

choices.note: CORRECT. The sentence glosses the word: perspective 'puts a single human eye where God's should be,' taking a standpoint that is not man's to take.
Common-meaning trap. 'Presumption' can mean a provisional assumption, but nothing here concerns evidence; the colon describes an overreach.
Opposite. The sentence says perspective is 'less a technique than a presumption,' so the word is contrasted with a convention or technique.
Distortion. The sentence gives Master Osman's judgment of perspective, not a claim about what the Venetians were or were not aware of.
Shell game. Portraits of 'a particular man' come up earlier, but recognizing a sitter is not what the colon says the presumption consists in.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the chapters narrated by a dog, a tree, a counterfeit gold coin, Death and the color red are
choices: spoken by the murdered gilder from the afterlife
more favorable to the Venetian manner than the chapters narrated by characters
voiced by a storyteller who speaks for drawings displayed beside him
the chapters in which the murderer's identity is finally revealed
the novel's only departures from first-person narration
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says these narrators are 'voiced by a coffeehouse storyteller who speaks for drawings hung beside him.' C restates it. A borrows the gilder who 'speaks from the afterlife' in the opening chapter, a shell game.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Retrieve what the passage says about the non-human narrators.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, fourth sentence.

breakdown.analysis: A pure detail question: find the sentence and match a paraphrase. Watch for choices that attach nearby details to the wrong subject.

choices.note: Shell game. The gilder speaks from the afterlife in the opening chapter; the non-human narrators are voiced by the storyteller.
Opposite. The one example given, the tree, is glad not to have been drawn the Frankish way, and the author says these voices speak for the miniaturists' conviction.
CORRECT. 'Voiced by a coffeehouse storyteller who speaks for drawings hung beside him.'
Unsupported. The murderer is exposed by the nostrils detail; the passage does not say in which chapters.
Contradicts the passage. Each chapter 'has a single narrator,' and the last paragraph calls the whole a 'novel of first-person chapters'; these chapters are not described as departures.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously undermine the author's interpretation of the novel in the last paragraph?
choices: Several of the novel's human narrators, Enishte among them, express open and lasting admiration for the Venetian portraits.
The novel's ending treats the Venetian manner as a clear advance and Osman's loyalty to tradition as self-deception.
The zealots who raid the coffeehouse are depicted in the novel as sincere in their beliefs.
Pamuk has said that Persian miniatures were his chief inspiration in conceiving the novel.
Some of the novel's narrators speak in only one chapter and never appear in others.
questions.explanation: The author claims the novel 'never settles whether God's view or one man's view is the truer way to see.' If its ending declared the Venetian manner a clear advance and Osman self-deceived, the novel would settle exactly that, so B undermines the thesis. C is the trap: sincere zealots can still be condemned for using force, so it doesn't touch the claim.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most damages the author's reading.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4: the novel 'never settles' the question; it condemns force; its 'impartiality is real.'

breakdown.analysis: The author's reading has two parts: impartial between ways of seeing, condemning violence. A strong weakener shows the novel taking an aesthetic side, or not condemning violence. Prephrase: the novel takes sides after all.

choices.note: Consistent with the passage. Enishte already admires the portraits; characters' views are not the novel's verdict.
CORRECT. A novel that ends by presenting one way of seeing as a clear advance and the other as self-deception has settled the question the author says it 'never settles.'
Irrelevant to the gap. Depicting the zealots as sincere is compatible with condemning their raid; the author says the novel condemns 'the attempt to settle the matter by force,' not insincerity.
Out of scope. A source of inspiration says nothing about whether the finished novel takes sides.
Irrelevant. How often a narrator appears does not bear on whether the novel judges between the two ways of seeing.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the relationship the author describes, in the last paragraph, between the novel's form and the two traditions it depicts?
choices: A historian narrates a war between two kingdoms entirely from the victor's archives, noting in a preface that the loser's records are lost.
A composer writes a piece in a traditional form and then publishes an essay arguing that the form is now obsolete.
A painter trained in one school abandons it midway through her career and adopts the methods of a rival school.
A playwright stages a debate between two schools of theater and has a narrator announce at the end which school has won.
A dramatist writes a play wholly in soliloquies, one school's favored device, but gives the best of them to defenders of a rival school.
questions.explanation: The author says the novel's first-person form embodies 'the very principle of the Venetian portrait' while 'its most memorable voices speak for the miniaturists' conviction,' and that it never settles between them. E has the same shape: the form belongs to one school, the most eloquent content argues for the other, and no verdict is given. D is the near miss: it stages both sides, but announcing a winner is what the novel does not do.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the structure of the form/content relationship to a new case.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, third sentence: 'Its form instead concedes something to each...'

breakdown.analysis: Abstract the relationship: (1) the work's structure follows one side's principle; (2) its strongest voices advocate the other side; (3) no verdict. The key must have all three; each trap drops one.

choices.note: Fails part 2. Drawing entirely on one side's sources gives the other side no voice at all.
Fails part 3. The essay gives a verdict against the form, which the novel never does.
Wrong structure. A sequential conversion from one school to another isn't the two at once within one work.
Fails part 3. Having a narrator announce the winner settles the question the author says the novel 'never settles.'
CORRECT. The form follows one school's principle while the most eloquent voices argue for the rival school, and no winner is named, which is the double concession the author describes.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Borges's story shows that Averroes's commentary on the Poetics was a failure of translation, though the failure began with Abu Bishr Matta rather than with Averroes.
Gould has shown that the scholars who regarded Averroes's commentary as a failure of translation were mistaken, and Borges's story should be read accordingly.
Though the commentary served its comparative aim better than Borges's story allows, the story's irony marks a real limit, one shared by Averroes's judges.
Averroes misread tragedy and comedy because the Arabic tradition classified the Poetics as a work of logic rather than a work on poetry.
Scholars disagree about the merits of Averroes's commentary, and their disagreement cannot be resolved without a more accurate translation of the Arabic text.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph gives the author's view: Gould is 'persuasive' about the commentary's purpose, which praise and blame 'served... well,' 'but it does not dissolve Borges's point,' and the lesson applies to 'any reader,' including 'the reader who smiles at Averroes's mistake.' C states both halves. B is the trap: it takes Gould's side entirely, against 'it does not dissolve Borges's point.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall claim.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, which evaluates the positions laid out in paragraphs 1 to 3.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 1: Borges's story. Paragraph 2: the real history. Paragraph 3: scholars' views. Paragraph 4: the author's qualified judgment. Prephrase: the commentary succeeded on its own terms, but Borges is right about a limit that applies to us too.

choices.note: Wrong position-holder. 'Failure of translation' is the view of Renan, Borges and Kilito; the author says praise and blame 'served him well.'
Too strong. The author finds Gould persuasive about purpose but says her account 'does not dissolve Borges's point.'
CORRECT. It combines the concession to Gould (the categories 'served him well') with the limit ('enactment by actors... lay outside his') and the afterword's turn to 'any reader.'
Distortion. The classification among works on logic is background in paragraph 2; the passage never says it caused the rendering, which it traces to Abu Bishr's version.
Out of scope. The passage never calls for a new translation, and the author does reach a judgment.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the rendering of tragedy and comedy as praise and invective
choices: had already appeared in the Arabic version from which Averroes worked
was introduced by Averroes because he could not read the Syriac translation
was corrected in the Latin version of the commentary made in 1256
was first identified as a mistranslation by Butterworth
was adopted by Averroes in opposition to Abu Bishr's version
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: Averroes 'worked from the Arabic version of Abu Bishr Matta..., which had already rendered tragedy and comedy as madih and hija'.' A restates it. B is the trap for a reader who remembers the Syriac link and that Averroes 'knew no Greek' but misses 'already.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Retrieve what the passage says about the source of the rendering.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, first two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The word 'already' locates the rendering before Averroes. Prephrase: it was in Abu Bishr's Arabic version.

choices.note: CORRECT. Abu Bishr's version 'had already rendered tragedy and comedy as madih and hija'.'
Distortion. Averroes 'knew no Greek' and used the Arabic version, but the rendering was already there; he did not introduce it.
Unsupported. The passage mentions the 1256 Latin version only as a route to Europe, not as a correction.
Wrong position-holder. The passage says nothing of Butterworth identifying the mistranslation; he reads the work 'on its own terms.'
Opposite. Averroes followed the Arabic version's rendering, not opposed it.

questions.stem: The author refers to "the children in the courtyard" (fourth sentence of the last paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: suggest that Averroes could have understood drama had he paid closer attention to life in Córdoba
show that Borges's story is historically inaccurate in its portrayal of Averroes
support Gould's claim that praise and blame let Averroes conceive literary form beyond a single tradition
indicate that Arabic culture had a form of drama that Averroes deliberately ignored
connect a detail of Borges's story to the specific limitation the author finds in Averroes's framework
questions.explanation: The preceding sentence says 'enactment by actors... lay outside' Averroes's framework; the next calls the children 'Borges's emblem of that blind spot.' The reference ties the story's scene to that limitation (E). A is the trap: it reads the scene as a missed opportunity Averroes could have seized, but the author speaks of a framework's blind spot, not a lapse of attention.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the reference to the children does in the last paragraph.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, third and fourth sentences; the scene itself is in paragraph 1.

breakdown.analysis: 'That blind spot' points back to the previous sentence. Prephrase: the scene illustrates the limit the author has just conceded.

choices.note: Distortion. The author speaks of what a framework 'can perceive,' not of inattention Averroes could have corrected.
Out of scope. The author calls the scene Borges's 'emblem,' not a historical error.
Opposite. The reference illustrates the limit of the framework, which qualifies Gould's account rather than supporting it.
Too strong. The children play at a call to prayer; the passage does not say Arabic culture had a drama that Averroes deliberately ignored.
CORRECT. 'The children in the courtyard are Borges's emblem of that blind spot,' the blind spot being enactment by actors.

questions.stem: The author's position regarding Gould's argument is best described as
choices: full endorsement, since Gould shows that Averroes's framework accommodated every feature of Greek drama
rejection, on the grounds that Averroes never stated an aim of comparing the poetry of different nations
agreement with her conclusion but not her evidence, which the author thinks relies too much on Butterworth
acceptance of her account of the commentary's aim, with the view that a limit Borges dramatizes remains
skepticism, because Gould, like Renan and Kilito, treats the commentary as a failure of translation
questions.explanation: 'Gould's account of the commentary's purpose is persuasive, but it does not dissolve Borges's point': acceptance of the aim, plus a remaining limit (D). A is the trap for a reader who registers 'persuasive' and 'served him well' but not the 'Yet' sentence about enactment lying outside the framework.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize the author's stance toward Gould.

setup.label: Where to look
