setup.text: Paragraph 4, first three sentences; Gould's argument is in the last two sentences of paragraph 3.

breakdown.analysis: Classic qualified agreement: 'persuasive, but.' Prephrase: right about purpose, not the whole story.

choices.note: Too strong. The author says enactment by actors 'lay outside' the framework, so it did not accommodate every feature of drama.
Contradicts the passage. Paragraph 3 reports Averroes's 'stated aim, to set out the rules of poetry common to all or most nations,' and the author accepts it.
Unsupported. The author never says Gould relies on Butterworth.
CORRECT. 'Persuasive' about purpose, 'but it does not dissolve Borges's point': the blind spot remains.
Wrong position-holder. 'Failure of translation' is the view Gould argues against, not hers.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following claims about Kilito and Gould?
choices: Both regard Averroes's rendering of tragedy and comedy as a deliberate interpretive choice.
Neither treats the handling of tragedy and comedy as a personal failing of Averroes's.
Both believe that Borges's story misrepresents the historical Averroes.
Both rely on Butterworth's translation in reaching their conclusions.
Neither believes that the Arabic version of the Poetics contained errors.
questions.explanation: Kilito treats the commentary as a failure of translation but 'blamed the conditions of transmission rather than Averroes himself'; Gould argues praise and blame were 'a useful means,' so for her there is no failing at all. Different reasons, same result: neither faults Averroes personally (B). A is the trap: it holds for Gould, but Kilito, grouped with Renan and Borges, treats the commentary as a failure, not a choice.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage supports about both critics at once.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, first sentence (Kilito) and last two sentences (Gould).

breakdown.analysis: Agreement questions about two opponents: look for the narrow point they share. Kilito: failure, but not Averroes's fault. Gould: not a failure. Overlap: not Averroes's personal fault. Each wrong choice is true of at most one of them, or of neither.

choices.note: Half right. True of Gould, but Kilito is among those who treat the commentary as 'an exemplary case of the failure of translation.'
CORRECT. Kilito blamed 'the conditions of transmission rather than Averroes himself,' and Gould sees the rendering as a useful means, not a failing.
Unsupported. Kilito is grouped with Borges in seeing failure, and nothing says Gould thinks Borges misrepresents Averroes.
Out of scope. The passage does not say what translation either critic used.
Contrary to the passage. Kilito blames the conditions of transmission, which implies that the transmitted text was flawed, and Gould is not said to deny errors.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen Gould's argument as the passage describes it?
choices: Averroes uses praise and blame to bring out shared features of Greek and Arabic poems that had seemed unrelated.
Abu Bishr Matta's Arabic version of the Poetics contains many errors besides its rendering of tragedy and comedy.
Borges relied on Renan's account of Averroes more heavily than on any other source in writing the story.
The Latin version of the commentary made in 1256 was widely read by European scholars of the following century.
Averroes never witnessed a dramatic performance of any kind, either in Córdoba or elsewhere.
questions.explanation: Gould argues that praise and blame gave Averroes 'a useful means of conceiving literary form outside the confines of a single literary tradition.' Evidence that he actually used them to connect Greek and Arabic poems is direct support (A). B is the trap: it supports Gutas's emphasis on the 'garbled Arabic version,' which bears on Averroes's understanding, not on the usefulness Gould claims.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that best supports Gould's claim.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Gould's claim is about usefulness for comparison across traditions. A strengthener shows the categories doing comparative work. Prephrase: Averroes successfully compares poems across traditions with them.

choices.note: CORRECT. It shows praise and blame working as 'a useful means of conceiving literary form outside the confines of a single literary tradition.'
Opposite direction. More errors in the Arabic version support Gutas's point about its 'decisive influence' and the failure reading, not Gould's.
Irrelevant. Borges's sources bear on the story, not on whether the categories were useful to Averroes.
Irrelevant. The commentary's later readership does not show that the categories served comparison.
Irrelevant, or slightly against. It bears on the blind spot the author concedes, not on the usefulness Gould claims.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Borges's story can most accurately be described as
choices: dismissive of it as a misleading caricature of a major philosopher's work
admiring of it as an accurate historical record of how the commentary came to be written
appreciative of its insight into a limit of understanding, though it slights the commentary's achievement
neutral, reporting its content without evaluating its significance
ambivalent, since the author cannot decide whether Averroes or Borges is the more absurd figure
questions.explanation: The author says praise and blame 'served him well' for his purpose, so the story's picture is incomplete, yet Borges's point is not dissolved and its lesson applies to 'any reader.' C captures both sides. A is too extreme: the author keeps Borges's point and builds the conclusion on his afterword.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize the author's attitude toward the story.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4 throughout, especially 'it does not dissolve Borges's point' and the last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Mixed but leaning respectful: Borges is right about a limit and about readers, but the commentary achieved more than the story credits. Rule out extremes and 'neutral.'

choices.note: Too extreme. The author says Gould's account 'does not dissolve Borges's point' and ends by endorsing the story's lesson.
Distortion. The author never treats the story as a historical record; it is fiction with an afterword about its own scanty sources.
CORRECT. The story's insight survives ('does not dissolve Borges's point'), but the commentary's categories 'served him well' for a purpose the story does not credit.
Wrong. The author evaluates the story directly in the last paragraph.
Distortion. The afterword compares Averroes's absurdity with Borges's; the author shows no indecision about it and uses it to draw the lesson.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The Tale of Genji should be understood as a monogatari shaped by court poetry and serial circulation, and comparing it with the European novel obscures its real character.
Although calling the Genji the first novel wrongly implies a lineage, the psychological depth that prompted the label is a genuine feature of the work.
Norinaga's account of mono no aware has been superseded by modern scholarship that reads the Genji against the conventions known to its first audience.
Waley misled Western readers by rendering monogatari as "novel," and the Genji's reputation as the first novel rests largely on that mistranslation.
The debate over whether the Genji is a novel is resolved once it is recognized that the European novel descends from tales like those Genji defends.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph gives the author's view in two halves: the critics are right that 'first' turns a resemblance into an unsupported 'line of descent,' but 'it does not follow that the resemblance is an artifact of the label'; 'the psychological depth is the Genji's own.' B states both halves. A is the critics' view from paragraph 3, which the author accepts only in part.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify the author's overall claim about calling the Genji 'the first novel.'

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, which evaluates the proponents (paragraph 2) and critics (paragraph 3).

breakdown.analysis: Paragraphs 2 and 3 set out the two sides; paragraph 4 splits the difference. Prephrase: the critics win on 'first,' but the novel-like depth is real, not a product of the label. Watch for an answer that simply adopts one side.

choices.note: Wrong position-holder. This is the critics' view from paragraph 3. The author agrees only about 'first' and denies that the resemblance is an artifact of the label, so the author does not think the comparison simply obscures the work.
CORRECT. The first clause matches 'converts a resemblance into a line of descent that the evidence cannot support'; the second matches 'The psychological depth is the Genji's own.'
Out of scope and opposite in spirit. The passage never says Norinaga has been superseded; the author uses Norinaga as evidence in paragraph 4.
Too extreme. The passage says Waley 'encouraged the description' and notes the original word, but never calls his rendering a mistranslation or says the reputation rests on it.
Opposite. The author denies any line of descent: 'no European novelist read Murasaki before the form was long established.' A reader who assumes world literature is one lineage may pick this.

questions.stem: The author mentions Norinaga's commentary (last two sentences of the second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that Japanese scholars accepted the European classification of the Genji before Western critics did
provide evidence that the Genji was read in its own time chiefly as a work of moral instruction
introduce the objection that the label "novel" imposes foreign categories on a Japanese work
indicate that the quality proponents cite had been recognized without reference to Europe
suggest that the depth of the Genji's characters derives from Buddhist teachings about the transience of feeling
questions.explanation: The sentences open 'Long before any comparison with Europe arose' and say Norinaga 'accounted for the same depth in his own terms.' Their job is to show that the depth proponents cite was recognized independently of the European frame, which the author later uses ('Norinaga, who knew nothing of the European novel...'). D says this. E is the trap for a reader who associates mono no aware with Buddhist transience; the passage says Norinaga rejected the Buddhist reading.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the author brings in Norinaga in paragraph 2.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, last two sentences; then paragraph 4, third sentence, where the author reuses the point.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 2 gives the proponents' evidence (consciousness, memory). Norinaga is introduced with 'Long before any comparison with Europe arose' and 'in his own terms.' Prephrase: the depth was seen independently of the novel comparison. Paragraph 4 confirms this is the point the author needs.

choices.note: Distortion. Norinaga wrote 'long before any comparison with Europe arose' and 'knew nothing of the European novel,' so he could not have accepted a European classification.
Distortion. The passage says Norinaga rejected 'the long tradition' of reading the tale as moral instruction; it does not say how the work was read in its own time.
Wrong paragraph. The objection about foreign categories is the critics' view, introduced in paragraph 3; Norinaga's commentary appears among the proponents' evidence.

CORRECT. 'Long before any comparison with Europe arose' and 'in his own terms' show that the depth was recognized independently, which paragraph 4 uses against the idea that the resemblance is an artifact of the label.

Outside knowledge and opposite. The passage says Norinaga rejected 'reading the tale as Buddhist allegory'; nothing says the characters' depth derives from Buddhist teaching. A reader who knows mono no aware is often linked to impermanence may be tempted.

questions.stem: By "what is borrowed is only the story that makes it a beginning" (fourth sentence of the last paragraph), the author most probably means that
choices: the account casting the Genji as a genre's origin comes from European literary history, not from the work itself
Murasaki Shikibu took the plot of the Genji from earlier tales whose conventions her court audience already knew
Waley borrowed the vocabulary of the European novel to translate an aesthetic concept that has no English equivalent
the Genji's psychological depth was later borrowed by European novelists who read the work in translation
the critics of the label have borrowed Norinaga's account of the work while rejecting his conclusions about it
questions.explanation: The sentence contrasts what is 'the Genji's own' (its psychological depth) with what is 'borrowed': the 'story that makes it a beginning,' i.e., the narrative of being 'first,' which the first sentence of the paragraph says 'converts a resemblance into a line of descent.' That lineage story belongs to the European novel's history, not to the Genji. A says this. B is a shell game on 'earlier tales' from paragraph 3.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Interpret the phrase 'what is borrowed is only the story that makes it a beginning.'

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, first and fourth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The semicolon sets 'the Genji's own' (depth) against 'borrowed' (a story). The 'story that makes it a beginning' points back to 'first' and 'line of descent.' Prephrase: the 'first novel' narrative is imported from outside; the depth is not.

choices.note: CORRECT. The 'story' is the lineage narrative implied by 'first,' and it is borrowed from the history of the European form rather than found in the Genji, whose depth is 'its own.'
Shell game. Paragraph 3 mentions 'earlier tales,' but the author's sentence concerns a story about the work, not a plot Murasaki took from others.
Distortion. Waley rendered monogatari, a genre term, as 'novel'; the passage never says he translated an untranslatable aesthetic concept, and 'story' does not mean a word choice.
Contradicts the passage, which says 'no European novelist read Murasaki before the form was long established.'
Out of scope. The passage never says the critics use Norinaga's account at all.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the critics described in the third paragraph can most accurately be described as
choices: dismissive, because their historical approach ignores the work's psychological depth
wholehearted agreement with their view that the novel comparison misrepresents the work
skepticism about their account of how the Genji was composed and circulated
neutrality, since the author declines to evaluate the merits of their arguments
agreement on the word "first" but not on whether the label creates the resemblance
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 opens 'The critics are right about the word "first"' and then turns: 'But it does not follow that the resemblance is an artifact of the label.' That is partial agreement, which E describes. B is the too-strong trap; A is too negative.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize the author's stance toward the critics of the 'first novel' label.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, first two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Look for the signal words: 'are right about' (agreement) and 'But it does not follow' (limit). Prephrase: agrees with them on 'first,' resists the further step that the resemblance is illusory.

choices.note: Too negative. The author says 'the critics are right' about 'first' and never faults their historical approach.
Too strong. The agreement is limited to 'first'; the author then says the resemblance is not 'an artifact of the label.'
Unsupported. The author never disputes Shirane's account of the work's growth in stages and installments.
Opposite. The author explicitly evaluates them: 'The critics are right about the word "first."'
CORRECT. 'The critics are right about the word "first"' plus 'it does not follow that the resemblance is an artifact of the label' is qualified agreement.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: A literary work can be fruitfully compared with works of a later genre only if it influenced the development of that genre.
Norinaga's interpretation of the Genji was correct in each respect in which it departed from earlier readings of the work.
A feature a work shares with a later genre need not have been read into it by those who apply that genre's label.
The Genji's embedded poetry matters less to its emotional life than its depiction of characters' memories and regrets.
Waley's translation of "Fireflies" distorts Genji's argument by turning a claim about completeness into a claim about priority.
questions.explanation: The author denies any line of descent yet insists 'it does not follow that the resemblance is an artifact of the label,' citing Norinaga, who saw the depth without knowing the European novel. So a shared feature need not be projected by those who apply the genre label. C states this general principle. E is a distortion: the author says Genji's argument claims completeness, but never says Waley's translation distorts it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the author's reasoning in paragraph 4 commits the author to.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, first three sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The author separates two claims: (1) the Genji is the origin of the novel (rejected) and (2) the Genji genuinely shares novel-like depth (accepted), and argues (2) survives without (1). Prephrase: resemblance can be real even without descent and even though the label is foreign.

choices.note: Opposite. The author holds that the resemblance is real even though there is no 'line of descent,' so comparison does not require influence.
Too strong. The author endorses Norinaga's attention to feeling and his refusal to subordinate the tale to doctrine, but says nothing about every respect of his reading.
CORRECT. The author holds that the Genji's depth is real and was seen by Norinaga, who knew nothing of the novel, so it is not an 'artifact of the label' applied by those who call the work a novel.
Out of scope. The author never ranks the poetry against the depiction of memory; paragraph 3's claim that 'much of its emotional life passes through' the poems goes unchallenged.
Distortion. The author contrasts priority and completeness to describe Genji's argument, not to criticize Waley's translation of it.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Shirane treats the Genji as a work that
choices: anticipated the European psychological novel in its treatment of memory and desire
was conceived as a single whole and only later divided into separate chapters
grew in stages and circulated in installments among a small aristocratic audience
owes its emotional power chiefly to the Buddhist themes of its later chapters
was written for anonymous readers who knew little of the conventions of court poetry
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says Shirane treats the Genji as a work that 'was not conceived as a single whole but grew in stages, circulating in installments among a small aristocratic audience.' C restates this. B reverses it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Retrieve what the passage says about Shirane's account of the Genji.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: A straight detail question: find Shirane's sentence and match it. Watch for answers that reverse it or import the proponents' views.

choices.note: Wrong position-holder. Anticipating the novel is what the proponents stress; Shirane's account is offered by the critics, who object to prizing the work 'for anticipating that form.'
Reversal. Shirane holds that it 'was not conceived as a single whole.'
CORRECT. This paraphrases 'grew in stages, circulating in installments among a small aristocratic audience.'
Out of scope. The passage mentions Buddhist readings only as a tradition Norinaga rejected, and says nothing about the Buddhist themes of later chapters.
Opposite. Shirane reads the work 'against the conventions of earlier tales and of court poetry that this audience knew.'

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the author's argument that the Genji's resemblance to the novel is not an artifact of the label?
choices: Several Japanese tales written before the Genji show little interest in the inner lives of their characters.
Norinaga's commentary was not known to Western readers or translators until well into the twentieth century.
Some modern Japanese scholars also describe the Genji as a novel when writing for Japanese readers.
Waley later said that he had chosen the word "novel" in part to attract a wider readership.
Norinaga's mono no aware meant chiefly a reader's being moved by poignant scenes and poems, not characters' inner lives.
questions.explanation: The author's evidence that the resemblance is real is that Norinaga 'located the work's power in the same attention to feeling that Western readers later praised.' If Norinaga's mono no aware concerned the reader's emotional response to moments and poems rather than the characters' interiority that proponents cite (paragraph 2), then he was not praising 'the same' thing, and the independent confirmation disappears. E does this. B is the trap: it looks relevant but, if anything, strengthens the independence of Norinaga's view.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most undermines the author's reason for thinking the resemblance is genuine.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, second and third sentences; paragraph 2 for what the proponents mean by depth.

breakdown.analysis: Argument: Norinaga, ignorant of the novel, praised 'the same attention to feeling' Western readers praised; so the resemblance is not created by the label. Gap: that Norinaga's 'feeling' and the proponents' 'consciousness' are the same thing. Attack the sameness.

choices.note: Irrelevant or slightly strengthening. If earlier tales lacked inner lives, the Genji's depth is more distinctive; this does not touch whether Norinaga saw the same quality.
Opposite. Western ignorance of Norinaga makes his view more clearly independent, which supports the author.
Irrelevant. Who else uses the label says nothing about whether the resemblance is real or projected.
Irrelevant truth. Waley's motive for the word bears on the label's origin, which the author already treats as borrowed, not on whether the depth is the Genji's own.
CORRECT. It breaks the link between Norinaga's 'attention to feeling' and the characters' interiority that proponents and Western readers praise, removing the author's independent evidence.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Cervantes's Arab historian is best understood as a parody of the found manuscripts of chivalric romance, and political readings of the figure lack textual support.
Cervantes used the scene in the Alcaná chiefly to express nostalgia for the coexistence of Muslims, Jews and Christians that Toledo had once known.
The narrator's slur against Arabs shows that Cervantes shared his culture's distrust of the Moriscos, a fact both major readings of the novel overlook.
Neither the parody reading nor the Morisco reading suffices, since the narrator's slur ties the novel's concern with truth to suspicion of Spain's Muslims.
Critics disagree about Cide Hamete chiefly because Cervantes's treatment of the Moriscos changed between the publication of Part I and Part II.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says each reading 'captures something' but the narrator's words 'complicate both'; the slur is 'the hinge of the device,' tying the question of who can be trusted to tell the truth to 'a question about its Muslims'; this is 'less than Menocal claims, but more than parody explains.' D captures that. C is the trap: it turns the narrator's slur into Cervantes's own belief, which the author never says.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify the author's overall thesis about Cide Hamete Benengeli.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, especially its first, fourth and last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 1 describes the device, paragraphs 2 and 3 give the parody and Morisco readings, and paragraph 4 builds a middle position on the narrator's slur. Prephrase: both readings are partial; the slur shows that the novel's question about truth is also a question about Spain's Muslims.

choices.note: Wrong position and too strong. This is the parody reading; the author says the account offered is 'more than parody explains.'
Wrong position-holder. This is Menocal's reading; the author's view is 'less than Menocal claims' and denies that Cervantes need have 'mourned a lost past.'
Distortion. The author speaks of what 'the narrator's culture' held, not Cervantes's own beliefs, and does not say the readings overlook a fact about Cervantes.
CORRECT. It combines the verdict on both readings ('complicate both,' 'less than Menocal claims, but more than parody explains') with the author's claim about the slur as 'the hinge of the device.'
Out of scope. The passage mentions the expulsion between the two parts but never says Cervantes's treatment of the Moriscos changed or that this explains the critical disagreement.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which one of the following is true of the manuscript the narrator finds in the ninth chapter?
choices: It was offered to the narrator by the Morisco who later translated it.
It contained a different account of the battle broken off in the eighth chapter.
It was being sold by a boy to a silk merchant when the narrator saw its script.
It was said to have been found in a stone tomb near Constantinople.
It was written in Castilian by an author who claimed Arab descent.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: the narrator 'sees a boy selling old notebooks to a silk merchant, recognizes the script as Arabic, and finds a Morisco... to translate them.' C restates this. D is the shell game: the stone tomb belongs to Montalvo's Amadís in paragraph 2.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Retrieve the circumstances of the manuscript's discovery.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, third and fourth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Find the discovery scene and match the details exactly; beware details borrowed from paragraph 2.

choices.note: Distortion. The boy was selling the notebooks; the narrator then 'finds a Morisco' to translate them.
Unsupported. The narrator finds 'the rest' of the story; nothing says it gave a different account.
CORRECT. The passage says he 'sees a boy selling old notebooks to a silk merchant, recognizes the script as Arabic.'
Shell game. The stone tomb near Constantinople is Montalvo's claim about Amadís de Gaula in paragraph 2.
Contradicts the passage. The script is Arabic and the author is 'historiador arábigo'; a translator is needed.

questions.stem: The author mentions Montalvo's claim about his sequel to Amadís de Gaula (second sentence of the second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: illustrate the convention that the parody reading takes Cervantes to be mocking
show that Cervantes borrowed the found-manuscript device from Arabic sources
contrast the solemnity of chivalric romance with the humor of Cervantes's prologue
support Menocal's view that the Toledo scene evokes a lost multicultural past
establish that early readers took found-manuscript claims to be literally true
questions.explanation: The sentence before it says romances of chivalry 'presented themselves as ancient chronicles recovered by chance and translated'; Montalvo's tomb is the example. The next sentence says Cervantes gives 'the convention a deflating home.' So the example illustrates the convention the parody reading says Cervantes mocks: A. D attaches the example to the wrong reading.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the Montalvo example appears in paragraph 2.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, sentences 1 to 3.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 2 sets out the parody reading. Sentence 2 gives a concrete instance of the chivalric 'found chronicle' convention; sentence 3 shows Cervantes deflating it. Prephrase: it is an example of what is being parodied.

choices.note: CORRECT. It exemplifies the convention ('ancient chronicles recovered by chance and translated') that Cervantes is said to deflate with waste paper bought 'for small change.'
Out of scope. Montalvo is a Castilian romancer, and nothing suggests the device came from Arabic sources.
Distortion. The contrast drawn is between the romances' grand discovery and Cervantes's waste paper, not with the humor of his prologue.
Wrong position. The example belongs to the parody reading in paragraph 2, not to Menocal's reading in paragraph 3.
Unsupported. The passage says nothing about whether readers believed such claims.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the author's criticism of the Morisco reading?
choices: It exaggerates how far Cervantes's contemporaries suspected the Moriscos of practicing Islam in secret.
It passes over the narrator's slur against the Arab historian and claims more about Cervantes than is needed.
It treats Cide Hamete chiefly as an instrument for reflecting on history and fiction rather than on Spain's Muslims.
It fails to recognize that found manuscripts were a convention of the chivalric romances Cervantes mocked.
It relies on episodes from Part II of the novel while ignoring the scene in the Alcaná in Part I.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says 'the Morisco reading tends to pass over' the slur 'in favor of the device's nostalgic resonance,' and that the author's account 'is less than Menocal claims' because Cervantes 'need not have mourned a lost past.' B states both criticisms. C is the parody reading's view, Riley's 'instrument,' attached to the wrong school.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify what the author faults in the Morisco reading.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, third, sixth and seventh sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The author gives two criticisms: it 'tends to pass over' the slur, and it claims more (nostalgic mourning) than needed. Prephrase: ignores the slur and overreaches about Cervantes's nostalgia.

choices.note: Unsupported. The author accepts that Moriscos were 'suspected of practicing Islam in secret' and builds on it.
CORRECT. 'Tends to pass over it in favor of the device's nostalgic resonance' plus 'less than Menocal claims' and 'need not have mourned a lost past.'
Wrong position-holder. Treating Cide Hamete 'chiefly as an instrument' for reflecting on history and fiction is the parody critics' approach (paragraph 2).
Unsupported. The author never says Morisco critics are unaware of the chivalric convention; the convention belongs to the parody reading's argument.
Opposite. Menocal's reading centers on the scene in the Alcaná.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, which one of the following works would most closely exemplify the function the author attributes to Cide Hamete in the last paragraph?
choices: A satirical novel attributes its whole story to a celebrated court historian whose reputation for accuracy all of the novel's readers accept.
A novel set in a city once shared by several religious communities lingers affectionately over the ruins of their meeting places.
A mock-epic claims to translate an ancient poem discovered in a ruined temple, in order to ridicule the pretensions of heroic verse.
A historical novel corrects official accounts of a war by drawing on testimony from veterans whom the government has honored.
A novel from a time of suspicion toward a minority credits its account to a member of that minority, whom the narrator calls untrustworthy.
questions.explanation: The author says the book 'rests its own claim to truth on a witness the narrator's culture held to be a liar,' so that the question of who can be trusted to tell the truth becomes a question about a suspected minority. E reproduces both elements: a source from a distrusted minority, flagged as untrustworthy, in a time of suspicion toward that group. C is the trap: it fits the parody reading, which the author thinks does not explain enough.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply the author's account of Cide Hamete's function to a new case.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, fifth and sixth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Abstract the author's account: (1) the work's claim to truth rests on a source (2) from a group the surrounding culture distrusts, (3) so the question of reliable testimony becomes a question about that group. Find the case with all three.

choices.note: Opposite. The witness is trusted; the author's point depends on a witness 'held to be a liar.'
Wrong reading. Affectionate lingering over a lost multicultural past matches Menocal's nostalgic reading, which the author says claims too much, and there is no question of a source's truth.
Half right. This is the parody function, deflating a genre's found-manuscript convention, but the source is not from a distrusted group; the author says the device does 'more than parody explains.'
Opposite. Honored veterans are trusted witnesses, and there is no suspected minority.

CORRECT. The account rests on a member of a suspected minority whom the narrator tells readers to distrust, so truth and the minority's standing become one question, as with the 'historiador arábigo.'

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?
choices: A device is described; two readings of it follow; a detail both underweight supports an account drawing on each.
A literary device is described; its historical origins are traced; two critics' evaluations of it are compared, and the earlier evaluation is endorsed.
Two interpretations of a novel are presented; the evidence for each is weighed; both are rejected in favor of a reading drawn from the novel's prologue.
A scene is summarized; a long-standing interpretation of it is defended against a recent challenge; the challenge is shown to rest on a misreading.
A historical event is described; its effect on a novel is traced; two critics are shown to disagree about whether the novelist approved of the event.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 describes Cide Hamete; paragraphs 2 and 3 give the parody and Morisco readings; paragraph 4 uses the narrator's slur, which the parody reading treats as 'a joke' and the Morisco reading 'tends to pass over,' to propose an account that is 'less than Menocal claims, but more than parody explains.' A matches. B is half right: it starts well but the author endorses neither reading.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe the order and role of the passage's parts.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First sentence of each paragraph; paragraph 4 throughout.

breakdown.analysis: Map: P1 device; P2 reading one; P3 reading two; P4 overlooked detail and a middle position. Check each answer against all four parts.

choices.note: CORRECT. Device (P1), two readings (P2, P3), a detail both underweight (the slur) used for a middle account that keeps something from each (P4).
Half right. The passage opens with the device, but it does not endorse either reading; the author's account goes beyond parody and falls short of Menocal.
Distortion. The readings are not rejected outright ('Each reading captures something'), and the author's account rests on the ninth chapter's slur, not the prologue.
Distortion. No reading is defended against a challenge, and nothing is called a misreading.
Out of scope. The expulsion is mentioned, but the passage is organized around a device, and no critic is said to discuss Cervantes's approval of the expulsion.

questions.stem: In saying "That is less than Menocal claims" (last sentence of the passage), the author most probably means that the author's own account
choices: rests on less textual evidence from the novel than Menocal's reading does
does not require crediting Cervantes with a longing for a lost coexistence
denies that the scene in the Alcaná alludes to Spain's Muslims in any way
concerns fewer episodes of the novel than Menocal's reading does
concedes that Cide Hamete is primarily a parody of chivalric romance
questions.explanation: The preceding sentence explains the comparison: 'Cervantes need not have mourned a lost past to make that witness carry his novel's central question.' Menocal's reading is 'a nostalgic invocation of convivencia'; the author's account drops the nostalgia. B says this. C overshoots: the author's account still makes the device 'a question about its Muslims.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Interpret 'less than Menocal claims.'

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, sixth and seventh sentences; paragraph 3, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: 'Less' is defined by the previous sentence: the author's account doesn't need Cervantes to have 'mourned a lost past,' which is the heart of Menocal's 'nostalgic invocation.' Prephrase: it drops the nostalgia but keeps the link to Spain's Muslims.

choices.note: Wrong sense of 'less.' The comparison concerns what is claimed about Cervantes, not the quantity of evidence; the author in fact adds evidence (the slur).
CORRECT. 'Need not have mourned a lost past' removes exactly the nostalgic element of Menocal's 'nostalgic invocation of convivencia.'
Too extreme. The author keeps the connection to Spain's Muslims: the question of truth 'had become... a question about its Muslims.'
Wrong sense of 'less.' Nothing concerns the number of episodes discussed.
Opposite. The same sentence says the account is 'more than parody explains.'

sections.title: Reading Through Ideas 15: The hard problem and the unity of the subject · Fine-tuning and the many-universes reply · Moral Realism and the Darwinian Dilemma · What the Readiness Potential Shows

passages.title: The hard problem and the unity of the subject
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
In 1995 David Chalmers drew a distinction that has organized the field ever since. The "easy problems" of consciousness, he argued, concern functions: how a system discriminates stimuli, integrates information, and reports on its own states. However difficult in practice, these yield to cognitive science, since to explain a function is to specify a mechanism that performs it. The hard problem is different. Even with every such mechanism in hand, a question would remain: "Why is the performance of these functions accompanied by experience?" The question is not new. Avicenna asked his readers to imagine a man created in full maturity, suspended in the air with his senses veiled and his limbs held apart, and argued that such a man would affirm his own existence while affirming that of no part of his body. What is new is the pressure the question now exerts on a science that has otherwise explained so much.

One response denies that anything is left to explain. Keith Frankish's illusionism holds that phenomenal consciousness is illusory: experiences "do not really have qualitative, 'what-it's-like' properties." The hard problem gives way to what Frankish calls the illusion problem: explaining why experiences seem to have such properties. Critics reply that the view relocates the difficulty rather than dissolving it, since a seeming appears to be precisely the kind of thing whose existence was in question.

A second response, championed by Philip Goff in Galileo's Error (2019), runs the other way. Physics, Goff observes, describes only what matter does, its dispositions and mathematical structure, and is silent about what matter intrinsically is. Galileo made mathematical physics possible by setting sensory qualities outside its domain and relocating them in the minds of observers; Goff proposes instead that consciousness is the intrinsic nature of matter itself, present in rudimentary form in its fundamental constituents. The cost is the combination problem: how could countless tiny subjects of experience compose a single subject, such as a human being, whose experience is given to it as one? Goff treats it as a research task, not a refutation.

Dualists, and the theistic philosophers who extend their case, read the difficulty as evidence. If the unity of a subject cannot be assembled from parts, perhaps it was never composed of them, as Avicenna's thought experiment was meant to display: a self known to itself without reference to anything with parts. J. P. Moreland adds that if consciousness cannot be derived from physical structure, its lawlike correlation with brain states itself calls for explanation, which theism supplies more naturally than naturalism. This line needs care. The floating man shows at most that the self can be conceived without the body, and physicalists press the gap between the conceivable and the actual against every such argument, ancient or modern. Yet the combination problem supplies what conceivability alone cannot: an independent reason, arising within the panpsychists' own program, to think that a subject's unity is not a sum. Whether a unity known only from within can be explained by anything known only from without may be the question that outlasts every response.

sources.author: David J. Chalmers
sources.title: Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness
sources.note: The Journal of Consciousness Studies paper that separates the 'easy problems' of explaining cognitive functions from the hard problem of experience; source of the quotation "Why is the performance of these functions accompanied by experience?" (p. 202).

sources.author: Keith Frankish
sources.title: Illusionism as a Theory of Consciousness
sources.note: Journal of Consciousness Studies target article arguing that phenomenal consciousness is illusory and replacing the hard problem with the 'illusion problem'; source of the quotation that experiences "do not really have qualitative, 'what-it's-like' properties."

sources.author: Philip Goff
sources.title: Galileo's Error: Foundations for a New Science of Consciousness
sources.note: A book-length case for panpsychism: physics tells us what matter does, not what it is, and Galileo's exclusion of sensory qualities from physics left consciousness outside science; it treats the combination problem as a task for a new science of consciousness.

sources.author: J. P. Moreland
sources.title: Consciousness and the Existence of God: A Theistic Argument
sources.note: Argues that irreducible consciousness, and its regular, law-like correlation with physical states, is better explained by theism than by naturalism, and criticizes rivals including panpsychism.

passages.title: Fine-tuning and the many-universes reply
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
Physicists describe the universe with a handful of constants whose values their theories leave unfixed: the strengths of the fundamental forces, the masses of the elementary particles, the energy density of empty space. In A Fortunate Universe (2016), the cosmologists Geraint Lewis and Luke Barnes survey what happens, according to our best theories, when these values are varied. Across much of the range, the result is a universe with no stable atoms, no long-lived stars, or no structure at all; the life-permitting values occupy a strikingly small region. The two authors agree about the physics but differ over its interpretation, as philosophers have for decades.

Robin Collins has given the design inference a careful probabilistic form. It rests on what he calls the prime principle of confirmation, "a general principle of reasoning which tells us when some observation counts as evidence in favor of one hypothesis over another": an observation supports whichever of two hypotheses renders it more probable. A life-permitting universe is not improbable if a designer intended life, Collins argues, but is enormously improbable on what he terms the atheistic single-universe hypothesis, so fine-tuning favors design over that alternative. The comparison is deliberately restricted: the argument does not claim to favor design over every rival.

The rival most often proposed is a multiverse, an ensemble of universes across which the constants vary. If the ensemble is large enough, some life-permitting universe is to be expected, and, as Brandon Carter's anthropic principle reminds us, observers can find themselves only in such a universe. Ian Hacking (1987) objected that inferring many universes from the character of ours commits an inverse gambler's fallacy, like a gambler who walks in on a double six and concludes that the dice must have been rolled many times before. Hacking aimed the charge at John Wheeler's model of a universe that passes through successive cycles; Roger White (2000) extended it to universes existing side by side. Our evidence, White argues, is not that some universe is life-permitting but that this one is, and the existence of other universes does nothing to make this one more likely to be life-permitting.

Defenders of the multiverse answer that the analogy fails: the gambler could have walked in on any roll, whereas we could not have existed in a universe hostile to life, so our observing this universe is not independent of its being life-permitting. White's allies reply that selection explains why we observe a life-permitting universe, not why the universe we observe is one. The exchange is unsettled, but it shows at least that the multiverse does not neutralize fine-tuning as cheaply as its proponents once supposed. The design inference carries its own unpaid debt, however. Its probabilities presuppose a measure of how likely each possible value of a constant is, and where the possible values have no natural bound, none is obvious. A classical theist might regard that debt with some equanimity, since for Aquinas the argument from order never depended on improbable settings. For anyone arguing from probabilities, though, the deeper question is whether "How probable was our universe?" has an answer at all.

sources.author: Geraint F. Lewis and Luke A. Barnes
sources.title: A Fortunate Universe: Life in a Finely Tuned Cosmos
sources.note: Two cosmologists survey how varying the forces, particle masses and cosmological constant would leave a sterile universe, then set out their differing views of what the fine-tuning means.

sources.author: Robin Collins
sources.title: A Scientific Argument for the Existence of God: The Fine-Tuning Design Argument
sources.note: In Michael J. Murray, ed., Reason for the Hope Within; states the design inference through the 'prime principle of confirmation' and compares theism with the 'atheistic single-universe hypothesis'; source of the quotation "a general principle of reasoning which tells us when some observation counts as evidence in favor of one hypothesis over another."

sources.author: Ian Hacking
sources.title: The Inverse Gambler's Fallacy: The Argument from Design. The Anthropic Principle Applied to Wheeler Universes
sources.note: Mind 96: 331-340; names the inverse gambler's fallacy (inferring many prior rolls from one double six) and charges Wheeler's oscillating-universe explanation of fine-tuning with it.

sources.author: Roger White
sources.title: Fine-Tuning and Multiple Universes
sources.note: Noûs 34: 260-276; extends Hacking's charge to coexisting universes, arguing that our evidence is that this universe is life-permitting, which other universes do not make more probable.

passages.title: Moral Realism and the Darwinian Dilemma
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Robust moral realism, the view that there are moral truths independent of anyone's beliefs or desires and irreducible to natural facts, was out of favor for much of the twentieth century. Its recent revival owes much to Russ Shafer-Landau's Moral Realism: A Defence (2003) and to Derek Parfit's On What Matters (2011), which argued that there are irreducibly normative truths about reasons and that, like mathematical truths, they can be known through reasoning without our standing in causal contact with them.

Sharon Street's "A Darwinian Dilemma for Realist Theories of Value" (2006) posed the challenge that has organized the debate since. Natural selection, she argued, has had an enormous influence on the content of human evaluative attitudes: we judge that we have reason to care for our children, and creatures who judged otherwise would have left fewer descendants. The realist must say how these influences relate to the independent truths realism posits. If there is no relation, then most of our evaluative judgments are "off track due to the distorting pressure of Darwinian forces," and realism collapses into skepticism. If there is a relation, the realist must claim that selection favored ancestors who grasped the truth. But this tracking account, Street argued, is scientifically inferior to its rival: the hypothesis that such judgments were favored because they prompted reproductively advantageous behavior explains the same data more economically, without positing evaluative truths.

In reply, Shafer-Landau argued that many well-supported moral beliefs were not shaped by evolutionary pressures and can be used to assess the rest. David Enoch and Erik Wielenberg offer third-factor replies: if survival and flourishing are, by and large, good, then selection aimed only at fitness would also tend to point us toward the good, without ever tracking it directly. Such replies remove the appearance of a miracle, but they do so by relying on moral premises, the very beliefs the debunker has impugned. That reliance need not be vicious, since we vindicate perception only by perceiving. Yet it leaves the deepest question untouched: why should the order of natural causes and the order of moral reasons be aligned at all?

Here theistic philosophers claim an advantage. If the source of the moral order is also the source of the creatures who know it, the alignment is no coincidence but an intention. Aquinas held that the light of natural reason by which we discern good and evil is "nothing else than an imprint on us of the Divine light," and the Islamic notion of fitra, the original disposition with which humans are created, makes a comparable claim. The reply deserves a hearing, for it supplies what realism needs: an explanation of the correlation rather than a denial that one is required. But it cannot be adopted merely to rescue realism. It earns its place only if theism is credible on independent grounds and if providence can be shown to work through selection rather than around it. The realist is left with a question that is not only ethical: whether the fact that we know anything about what matters is itself evidence about what kind of world we inhabit.

sources.author: Sharon Street
sources.title: A Darwinian Dilemma for Realist Theories of Value
sources.note: Philosophical Studies 127: argues that realists must either deny any relation between evolutionary influences and evaluative truth (skepticism) or posit a tracking relation that is scientifically worse than the adaptive-link explanation; source of the quotation "off track due to the distorting pressure of Darwinian forces" (from the paper's abstract).

sources.author: Derek Parfit
sources.title: On What Matters
sources.note: Two-volume defense of irreducibly normative truths about reasons, which Parfit treats as knowable by reasoning, on the model of mathematical and logical truths, without causal contact (paraphrased, not quoted).

sources.author: Russ Shafer-Landau
sources.title: Evolutionary Debunking, Moral Realism and Moral Knowledge
sources.note: Journal of Ethics and Social Philosophy 7(1): reconstructs the debunking argument and replies that many well-supported moral beliefs are immune to evolutionary influence and can be used to assess the rest (paraphrased); his book Moral Realism: A Defence (2003) is the fuller statement of his realism.

sources.author: Thomas Aquinas
sources.title: Summa Theologiae, I-II, q. 91, a. 2
sources.note: Written c. 1271; argues that natural law is the rational creature's participation in the eternal law; source of the quotation "nothing else than an imprint on us of the Divine light" (English Dominican Province translation).

passages.title: What the Readiness Potential Shows
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
In 1965 Hans Kornhuber and Lüder Deecke reported that voluntary movements are preceded by a slow buildup of electrical activity over the scalp, which they named the Bereitschaftspotential, or readiness potential. In 1983 Benjamin Libet and his colleagues asked when, relative to this buildup, a person becomes aware of intending to move. Their subjects flexed a wrist whenever they felt the urge and reported, by noting the position of a spot revolving on a clock face, when they first became aware of the wish. For spontaneous acts, the averaged readiness potential began roughly 550 milliseconds before movement, while reported awareness came only about 200 milliseconds before it. They concluded that the cerebral initiation of a spontaneous, freely voluntary act "can begin unconsciously." Libet himself left room for conscious control, suggesting that awareness arrives in time to veto an act already under way, but many commentators drew the starker lesson that the brain decides before we do.

Critics questioned the reliability of the clock reports, but the most consequential challenge concerned what the readiness potential is. Libet and his popularizers assumed that it reflects preparation, a decision already in progress. In 2012 Aaron Schurger, Jacobo Sitt, and Stanislas Dehaene proposed another account. In a task where nothing favors one moment over another, they suggested, the brain need only let ongoing, random fluctuations in neural activity accumulate until they cross a threshold, at which point movement follows. Because researchers average recordings aligned to the moment of movement, fluctuations that happened to drift upward before each crossing sum to a smooth ramp. On this model, "the precise moment at which the decision threshold is crossed leading to movement is largely determined by spontaneous subthreshold fluctuations in neuronal activity." The decision, if the word applies, occurs at the crossing, not half a second earlier.

Schurger's model does not vindicate free will; it removes one reason to doubt it. What both readings share is a feature of the task. Libet's subjects had no reason to move at one instant rather than another, so what they performed is what philosophers call picking rather than choosing: selecting among options that no consideration distinguishes. Al-Ghazali argued, in The Incoherence of the Philosophers, that a man offered two dates alike in every respect will still take one, since it belongs to the will to single out a thing from its like. The new model suggests how a brain might manage such a selection, but this is not the kind of choice on which responsibility is thought to rest. A 2019 study by Uri Maoz and colleagues found readiness potentials before arbitrary decisions about charitable donations but largely not before deliberate ones.

The experiments thus establish less than has been claimed on either side. That neural events precede and accompany action is something any view that does not divorce mind from body should expect. Whether the reasons a person weighs make a difference to what that person does is a question that a study of an arbitrary flick of the wrist cannot reach. If noise settles what does not matter, the question worth asking is what settles what does.

sources.author: Benjamin Libet, Curtis A. Gleason, Elwood W. Wright, and Dennis K. Pearl
sources.title: Time of Conscious Intention to Act in Relation to Onset of Cerebral Activity (Readiness-Potential): The Unconscious Initiation of a Freely Voluntary Act
sources.note: Brain 106: the clock experiment, finding readiness-potential onset several hundred milliseconds before reported awareness of the wish to act; source of the quotation "can begin unconsciously" (abstract).

sources.author: Aaron Schurger, Jacobo D. Sitt, and Stanislas Dehaene
sources.title: An Accumulator Model for Spontaneous Neural Activity Prior to Self-Initiated Movement
sources.note: PNAS 109(42): models the readiness potential as the movement-locked average of stochastic fluctuations accumulating to a threshold; source of the quotation beginning "the precise moment at which the decision threshold is crossed" (abstract).

sources.author: Uri Maoz, Gideon Yaffe, Christof Koch, and Liad Mudrik
sources.title: Neural Precursors of Decisions That Matter: An ERP Study of Deliberate and Arbitrary Choice
sources.note: eLife 8: finds readiness potentials before arbitrary donation decisions but largely absent before deliberate ones, suggesting Libet-style findings do not generalize to decisions that matter.

sources.author: Marcel Brass, Ariel Furstenberg, and Alfred R. Mele
sources.title: Why Neuroscience Does Not Disprove Free Will
sources.note: Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews: argues that Libet-style tasks, which involve arbitrary picking rather than deliberate choosing, pose no serious challenge to free will.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Recent responses to the hard problem have shown that consciousness can be explained once its supposed qualitative properties are recognized as illusory.
Each leading response to the hard problem has a cost, and one such cost lends the dualist view of the subject some independent, though not conclusive, support.
Illusionism and panpsychism both fail because each relocates the difficulty of consciousness rather than resolving it, so that dualism is the only position left standing.
Avicenna's floating man argument establishes the distinctness of the self from the body more convincingly than any argument advanced in the contemporary debate.
The combination problem shows that panpsychism must be abandoned, although the hard problem itself may yet turn out to be an illusion of the kind Frankish describes.
questions.explanation: The passage presents the hard problem, then illusionism (with the critics' reply) and panpsychism (with the combination problem), and ends with the author's qualified judgment: the dualist line 'needs care,' yet the combination problem supplies 'an independent reason' to think a subject's unity is not a sum. B states both the survey and the hedge. C is the trap: it borrows the critics' phrase about illusionism, applies it to panpsychism, and overstates the conclusion.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify the author's overall claim, not the view of any one figure.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, especially 'This line needs care' and the sentence beginning 'Yet the combination problem supplies.'

breakdown.analysis: Paragraphs 2 and 3 each give a response and its cost. Paragraph 4 lets dualists read one cost as evidence, then qualifies twice: the floating man proves only conceivability, but the combination problem gives an independent reason. Prephrase: the responses each pay a price, and one price modestly favors dualism.

choices.note: Wrong position-holder. This is Frankish's view; the author reports a critics' objection to it and never endorses it.
CORRECT. 'Each leading response... has a cost' covers paragraphs 2 and 3; 'some independent, though not conclusive, support' matches 'an independent reason' together with 'This line needs care.'

Shell game and too strong. 'Relocates the difficulty' is the critics' charge against illusionism only, and the author never says dualism is the only position left; the last sentence leaves the question open.
Opposite. The author says the floating man 'shows at most that the self can be conceived without the body,' a limit on its force.

Distortion. Goff treats the combination problem as 'a research task, not a refutation,' and the author draws from it a point about unity, not a verdict that panpsychism must go; the author also never endorses illusionism.

questions.stem: The author refers to Avicenna's thought experiment in the first paragraph primarily in order to
choices: suggest that Chalmers drew his distinction between easy and hard problems from medieval sources
show that the hard problem can be answered by introspection rather than by the methods of cognitive science
illustrate one of the easy problems of consciousness with a case in which the senses supply no information
indicate that Chalmers's question is old while preparing a contrast with what gives it force today
establish at the outset that the self is distinct from the body, a conclusion the rest of the passage then defends
questions.explanation: The thought experiment follows 'The question is not new' and precedes 'What is new is the pressure the question now exerts on a science that has otherwise explained so much.' It shows the question's age and sets up the contrast with its present force. E is the trap for a reader who knows the floating man as an argument for the soul: the author later says it shows 'at most' conceivability.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the author brings in Avicenna in paragraph 1.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The sentences just before and after the Avicenna sentence in paragraph 1.

breakdown.analysis: The example is framed by 'The question is not new' and 'What is new is....' Its job is historical: the question is old, and the novelty lies elsewhere. Prephrase: to show the question predates Chalmers.

choices.note: Out of scope. The passage says the question is old, not that Chalmers took his distinction from Avicenna.
Out of scope. Nothing says introspection answers the hard problem; the passage leaves the hard problem open.
Shell game. The easy problems are about functions such as discrimination and report; the floating man concerns self-awareness without the senses, not a function.
CORRECT. 'The question is not new' introduces the example, and 'What is new is the pressure the question now exerts' supplies the contrast.
Too strong and against the passage. The author later says the floating man 'shows at most that the self can be conceived without the body'; the passage does not defend dualism outright.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the illusion problem is the problem of explaining
choices: why experiences appear to have qualitative properties
why the performance of certain functions is accompanied by experience
how a system discriminates stimuli and reports on its own states
how many small subjects of experience could compose a single subject
why those who study consciousness wrongly conclude that it is illusory
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 defines it: 'what Frankish calls the illusion problem: explaining why experiences seem to have such properties,' that is, qualitative, 'what-it's-like' properties. A restates this. B is the trap: it is Chalmers's hard problem, which the illusion problem replaces.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the passage's definition of the illusion problem.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, third sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Each paragraph names a different problem: the easy problems and the hard problem (paragraph 1), the illusion problem (paragraph 2), the combination problem (paragraph 3). The traps swap them. Prephrase: why experiences seem to have qualitative properties.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Explaining why experiences seem to have such properties,' where 'such properties' are the qualitative, 'what-it's-like' properties just mentioned.
Wrong problem. This is Chalmers's hard problem, quoted in paragraph 1; the illusion problem is what it 'gives way to.'
Wrong problem. These are among the easy problems of paragraph 1.
Wrong problem. This is the combination problem facing panpsychism in paragraph 3.
Reversal. Illusionists hold that consciousness in the phenomenal sense is illusory; the problem is to explain why it seems otherwise, not why people think it illusory.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Avicenna's floating man, considered as an argument that the self is distinct from the body, can most accurately be described as
choices: dismissive, because it depends on a medieval conception of the soul that the contemporary debate has abandoned
enthusiastic, because it anticipates the hard problem and also resolves it
noncommittal, since the author reports the thought experiment without evaluating it
skeptical, because the combination problem shows that it rests on a false premise
appreciative of what it displays but doubtful that it alone establishes its conclusion
questions.explanation: The author says the thought experiment was meant to display 'a self known to itself without reference to anything with parts,' a point the author connects to the unity of the subject, but also that it 'shows at most that the self can be conceived without the body.' E captures both. D is the trap: the author thinks the combination problem helps the dualist, supplying 'what conceivability alone cannot.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Judge how the author evaluates the floating man as an argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, from 'as Avicenna's thought experiment was meant to display' through 'what conceivability alone cannot.'

breakdown.analysis: Two signals: the author uses the floating man to state what dualists say about unity, then limits it: 'shows at most... can be conceived.' The combination problem is offered as a supplement. Prephrase: it shows something real but cannot carry the conclusion alone.

choices.note: Too extreme and unsupported. The author calls the gap a problem for 'every such argument, ancient or modern,' not a defect peculiar to medieval thought, and still credits what the thought experiment displays.
Too extreme. The author limits its force ('at most') and calls the hard problem a question that may outlast every response.
Wrong. Paragraph 4 evaluates it explicitly: 'This line needs care. The floating man shows at most....'
Reversal. The combination problem is presented as supporting the dualist reading, 'what conceivability alone cannot' supply, not as refuting the floating man.
CORRECT. Appreciative: it displays 'a self known to itself without reference to anything with parts.' Doubtful: it 'shows at most that the self can be conceived without the body.'

questions.stem: Based on the passage, Goff would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Galileo's exclusion of sensory qualities from physics has prevented physics from accurately describing how matter behaves.
Consciousness first arises when physical systems become complex enough to integrate information.
A complete description of matter's dispositions and mathematical structure would leave open what matter intrinsically is.
The combination problem shows that a human being's experience is not in fact given to it as a unity.
Physics has no legitimate contribution to make to a future science of consciousness.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: physics 'describes only what matter does, its dispositions and mathematical structure, and is silent about what matter intrinsically is.' C follows directly. A is the trap: the passage says Galileo's move 'made mathematical physics possible'; Goff's complaint concerns what physics leaves out, not its accuracy about behavior.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement Goff's view, as reported, supports.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, second and third sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Goff's view has two parts: physics captures only what matter does, and consciousness is matter's intrinsic nature. Prephrase: physics, even complete, does not say what matter is in itself.

choices.note: Distortion. The passage says Galileo's move 'made mathematical physics possible'; nothing says physics describes behavior inaccurately.
Opposite. Goff holds that consciousness is present 'in rudimentary form in its fundamental constituents,' not that it arises only at a level of complexity.
CORRECT. Physics 'is silent about what matter intrinsically is,' a silence that no completion of its account of dispositions and structure removes.
Unsupported. The passage treats the unity of human experience ('given to it as one') as the datum panpsychism must explain, and Goff treats the problem as a research task.
Too extreme. Goff's view supplements physics with an account of matter's intrinsic nature; nothing says physics has no role.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the author's claim in the last paragraph that the combination problem supplies an independent reason to think that a subject's unity is not a sum?
choices: The obstacles to explaining how many subjects compose one arise equally for wholes, such as tables, that plainly are composed of parts.
Avicenna intended his thought experiment to show that the soul is aware of itself even when it has no awareness of the body.
Most panpsychists, Goff among them, regard the combination problem as a task for future research rather than as a refutation of their view.
Physicalists reject every conceivability argument on the grounds that what can be conceived need not be actual.
Some naturalists hold that the correlation between consciousness and brain states needs no further explanation.
questions.explanation: The author infers from panpsychism's difficulty in combining subjects that a subject's unity may not be compositional. If the same difficulty attends every case of composition, including ones where composition is not in doubt, then the difficulty says nothing special about subjects, and the inference loses its force. C is the trap: the passage already reports Goff's attitude, and a theorist's confidence does not show the problem is no evidence.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most undercuts the inference from the combination problem to the non-compositional unity of the subject.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, 'Yet the combination problem supplies what conceivability alone cannot...'; paragraph 3 for the problem itself.

breakdown.analysis: The argument: panpsychists cannot explain how many subjects make one; so a subject's unity is probably not built from parts. The gap: the failure might reflect a general puzzle about composition rather than anything about subjects. Prephrase: the same difficulty arises where composition is certain.

choices.note: CORRECT. If the obstacle arises even for wholes, such as tables, plainly composed of parts, it cannot be evidence that subjects are not composed of parts, which is the point the author draws from it.
Irrelevant, and if anything consistent with the passage, which says the floating man was meant to display a self known without reference to anything with parts.
Premise restatement. The passage already says Goff 'treats it as a research task, not a refutation'; the panpsychists' optimism does not show that the problem is not evidence about unity.
Irrelevant. This objection targets conceivability arguments, which the author has already set aside; the author's point is that the combination problem supplies a different kind of reason.
Out of scope. This concerns Moreland's argument about correlation, not the author's claim about the unity of the subject.

questions.stem: In saying that, according to critics, illusionism "relocates the difficulty rather than dissolving it" (last sentence of the second paragraph), the author most probably means that those critics hold that
choices: illusionism moves the hard problem out of philosophy and into cognitive science, where it can be solved
illusionism solves the easy problems of consciousness but leaves the hard problem untouched
illusionism grants that experiences have qualitative properties but denies that those properties are physical
the illusion problem is harder to solve than the hard problem, so that illusionism is a step backward
explaining why experiences seem a certain way may require the very thing illusionism denies exists
questions.explanation: The critics' reason follows the phrase: 'a seeming appears to be precisely the kind of thing whose existence was in question.' So the illusion problem would require explaining seemings, which are the very item illusionism denies. E says this. C is the trap for readers who confuse illusionism with views that deny only that qualitative properties are physical; the passage says flatly that experiences 'do not really have' them.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Interpret 'relocates the difficulty rather than dissolving it' using the rest of its sentence.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, last sentence, especially the 'since' clause.

breakdown.analysis: The 'since' clause is the gloss: the illusion problem asks about seemings, and a seeming looks like the thing whose existence was in question. The difficulty reappears in a new place. Prephrase: the problem returns as a problem about seemings.

choices.note: Distortion. 'Relocates' is about the difficulty reappearing elsewhere, not about a change of discipline; and nothing says it can then be solved.
Out of scope. The critics' point concerns the illusion problem, not the easy problems.
Opposite. Illusionism, per the passage, holds that experiences 'do not really have qualitative... properties' at all.
Too strong. The critics say the difficulty reappears, not that it becomes harder.
CORRECT. Paraphrases the 'since' clause: a seeming is 'precisely the kind of thing whose existence was in question.'

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: argue that fine-tuning provides conclusive evidence of design once the multiverse hypothesis has been set aside
defend the multiverse hypothesis against the charge that it commits an inverse gambler's fallacy
trace a debate over what fine-tuning shows and identify unresolved difficulties confronting both of the main interpretations
explain the physical processes by which small changes in the constants would prevent the formation of atoms and stars
show that probabilistic arguments about the universe are meaningless and that classical theism should therefore be preferred
questions.explanation: The passage sets out the physics, Collins's design inference, the multiverse rival with Hacking's and White's objection, and the reply; it then says the exchange 'is unsettled' and that the design inference 'carries its own unpaid debt.' C covers both. A is the trap for a reader sympathetic to design: the author says the debt remains unpaid.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: State what the passage as a whole is doing.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, which evaluates both sides.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 1 gives the data; paragraph 2 the design inference; paragraph 3 the multiverse and its critics; paragraph 4 weighs both and ends with a question. Prephrase: to survey the debate and show neither side is home free.

choices.note: Too strong. The author says the design inference 'carries its own unpaid debt' and calls the deeper question open.
Opposite in part. The author reports the defense but also that White's allies reply and that the multiverse does not neutralize fine-tuning 'as cheaply as its proponents once supposed.'
CORRECT. 'The exchange is unsettled' marks the multiverse side's difficulty, and the 'unpaid debt' marks the design side's.
Too narrow. Only paragraph 1 concerns the physics, and it reports results rather than explaining processes.
Too extreme. The author asks whether the probability question 'has an answer at all'; it does not assert that such arguments are meaningless or recommend classical theism.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Collins's version of the design inference
choices: claims that fine-tuning favors design over one particular alternative, not over every alternative
holds that a life-permitting universe could not exist at all unless some designer intended life
relies on the claim that the multiverse hypothesis commits an inverse gambler's fallacy
was formulated in response to the evidence surveyed by Lewis and Barnes
holds that an observation supports whichever of two hypotheses was proposed first
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: fine-tuning 'favors design over that alternative,' the atheistic single-universe hypothesis, and 'the argument does not claim to favor design over every rival.' A restates this. C is the trap: the passage gives that objection to Hacking and White, not Collins.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about Collins's argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Collins compares two hypotheses via the prime principle of confirmation, and the passage stresses that the comparison is 'deliberately restricted.' Prephrase: design beats the atheistic single-universe hypothesis, and that is all it claims.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Fine-tuning favors design over that alternative' together with 'the argument does not claim to favor design over every rival.'
Too strong. Collins says a life-permitting universe is 'enormously improbable,' not impossible, on the rival hypothesis.
Wrong position-holder. The inverse gambler's fallacy charge belongs to Hacking and White in paragraph 3.
Out of scope. The passage gives no date or occasion for Collins's argument and does not connect it to Lewis and Barnes's book.
Distortion. The principle concerns which hypothesis 'renders it more probable,' not which came first.

questions.stem: Which one of the following inferences is most analogous to the inference that, according to White, is fallacious?
choices: A woman hears that someone has won a lottery that need not have a winner and concludes that the lottery probably sold a great many tickets.
A hiker finds fresh footprints on a deserted beach and concludes that someone walked there earlier that morning.
A gambler who has lost several rolls in a row concludes that a winning roll is now more likely than usual.
A woman learns that her own ticket has won a lottery that need not have a winner and concludes that the lottery probably sold a great many tickets.
A scientist observes a rare mutation in one sample and concludes that the mutation is present in every sample.
questions.explanation: White distinguishes the evidence that some universe is life-permitting, which many universes would make likely, from the evidence that this one is, which other universes do not make more likely. In D the evidence concerns her own ticket, and the number of other tickets sold does nothing to make her ticket more likely to win. A is the trap: there the evidence is that someone won, which many tickets really would make more likely, the counterpart of 'some universe is life-permitting.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the structure of the inference White calls fallacious.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: White's point turns on 'some' versus 'this one': many trials raise the chance that some trial succeeds, not the chance that a particular trial does.
