questions.explanation: The sentence opens with the claim it supports, 'Psychology is then irrelevant to our persistence,' and gives the fetus and the vegetative state as cases where we exist without psychological continuity. A. E is the trap for readers who know the fetus case as a problem in the literature; here it supports animalism.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain why the fetus example appears.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, sentence 4.

breakdown.analysis: The colon after 'irrelevant to our persistence' introduces examples: you existed as a fetus with no mental life; you could survive without one. Prephrase: examples showing that we persist without psychological continuity.

choices.note: CORRECT. The example follows the colon after 'Psychology is then irrelevant to our persistence' and illustrates that claim.
Out of scope. The passage says nothing about moral status.
Wrong position. The example supports Olson's biological view against the psychological approach Parfit shares.
Out of scope. The passage does not connect Olson to immaterial souls.
Opposite. The example supports animalism; it is a problem for psychological views.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the account of the human being that Aquinas developed can most accurately be described as
choices: unreserved endorsement of it as the long-sought resolution of the debate over personal identity
detached interest in it as a historical alternative that the author declines to assess
qualified sympathy: it is credited with exposing a doubtful assumption but faces open problems
skepticism, on the grounds that its reliance on resurrection undermines its credibility as philosophy
admiration for the consolation it offers, combined with doubt that its central arguments succeed
questions.explanation: The author says Aquinas's view 'questions that framing' and that it 'suggests' a better account of the fear of death, but also that it 'must still explain how a form can exist without the matter it informs' and that Thomists 'divide.' Sympathy with qualification: C. A is the trap: the author's sympathy is real, but the acknowledged problems rule out 'unreserved.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize the author's attitude toward Aquinas's account.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, sentences 2, 5 and 6.

breakdown.analysis: Positive signals: 'questions that framing,' 'Olson is right,' 'it suggests.' Limits: 'must still explain,' 'Thomists divide.' Prephrase: favorable, with open problems acknowledged.

choices.note: Too extreme. The author notes it 'must still explain' a central difficulty.
Wrong. The author evaluates it, crediting it with questioning a shared framing.
CORRECT. It credits the view with questioning the framing Parfit and Swinburne share and concedes that it must still explain how a form exists without its matter.
Opposite. The author presents hope in resurrection as following from the view and does not treat it as a defect.
Distortion. The author's interest is in the view's arguments about what we are, not its consolation; the doubts concern an open problem, not the failure of its arguments.

questions.stem: Suppose that an injury destroys all of a woman's memories and permanently transforms her character, while her body continues to live and function normally. Based on the passage, which one of the following is most strongly supported?
choices: Swinburne would hold that she has ceased to exist, since her psychology has not continued.
Olson would hold that she has ceased to exist, although the organism that was her body continues.
Parfit would hold that she has kept everything that matters in survival, since her brain and body persist.
Aquinas, as the author presents him, would hold that her soul has separated from her body.
Olson would hold that she survives, while Parfit's view implies that much of what matters has been lost.
questions.explanation: Olson: 'Psychology is then irrelevant to our persistence' and we are organisms, so she survives. Parfit: what matters is 'psychological connectedness and continuity,' which the injury destroys. E. A is the trap: a reader who knows dualism stresses the mind may assume Swinburne ties identity to psychology, but the passage says his identity is a further fact not settled by 'every physical and psychological fact.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply each thinker's view, as the passage gives it, to a case of psychological discontinuity with bodily continuity.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, sentence 4; paragraph 2, sentences 2 to 5; paragraph 3, sentence 2.

breakdown.analysis: The case separates psychology from the organism. Olson tracks the organism; Parfit tracks psychological relations; Swinburne tracks a soul not fixed by either. Prephrase: Olson says she survives; Parfit says what matters is lost.

choices.note: Wrong position. For Swinburne identity is a further fact, not settled by psychological facts, so loss of psychology does not entail she has ceased to exist.
Opposite. On Olson's view we are organisms and psychology is irrelevant to persistence, so she survives.
Opposite. For Parfit what matters is psychological connectedness and continuity, which the injury destroys.
Out of scope. The passage gives no basis for saying her soul separates while her body lives; for Aquinas the soul is the body's form.
CORRECT. Olson's biological criterion keeps her in existence, while Parfit's 'what matters' is the psychological relation the injury has severed.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?
choices: Three views are presented with some of their implications; an older view is then offered that questions an assumption two of them share, despite difficulties of its own.
A single thought experiment is described, three competing interpretations of it are evaluated in turn, and the interpretation judged best is defended against objections.
A traditional view of the self is described, modern challenges to it are summarized in turn, and the traditional view is then reaffirmed without any qualification.
Two opposing theories of the self are contrasted, and a third theory is introduced that reconciles them by combining their central claims.
A view of personal identity is presented, objections to it are raised and rebutted, and the practical consequences of the view are then drawn out.
questions.explanation: Paragraphs 1 to 3 give Parfit, Olson and Swinburne with consequences for survival, desert and death; paragraph 4 finds the framing Parfit and Swinburne share, offers Aquinas's view against it, and notes it 'must still explain' a problem. A. D is the trap: Aquinas's view does not combine two theories' claims; it questions a shared assumption, and there are three prior views.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how the passage is organized.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The opening sentence of each paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Track the paragraphs: Parfit; Olson; Swinburne; then the author's critique of the Parfit-Swinburne framing via Aquinas, with a caveat. Prephrase: three views, then an older view that challenges a shared assumption, with a caveat.

choices.note: CORRECT. It matches the sequence: three views with implications, then Aquinas's view questioning 'that framing' Parfit and Swinburne share, with problems acknowledged.
Distortion. The divided-brain case appears in two paragraphs, but the passage is not organized around interpreting one experiment, and the author defends none of the three views.
Wrong order and too strong. The older view comes last, and it is not reaffirmed without qualification.
Half right. A later view is introduced, but it questions a shared assumption rather than combining claims, and there are three earlier views, not two.
Wrong structure. No single view is presented, objected to and rebutted.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Wykstra's CORNEA principle shows that no instance of suffering can reasonably be said even to appear pointless, so Rowe's argument cannot get started.
Skeptical theism answers Rowe's argument fully, since both of the objections raised against it rest on a confusion about the nature of human moral duty.
Skeptical theism can answer the charge that it undermines moral obligation, but it has not yet shown that its humility has a principled limit.
The Qur'anic story of Moses establishes that human beings remain obligated to prevent suffering even in cases where God is justified in permitting it.
Rowe's argument and Wykstra's reply together show that the problem of evil cannot be settled without an appeal to what God has revealed.
questions.explanation: The author defends skeptical theism against the moral-paralysis objection ("mistakes the kind of humility at issue") but calls the wider-skepticism objection "harder" and says the needed line has been "drawn but not yet secured." C captures both halves. B is the tempting half-right answer: it extends the author's rebuttal of the first objection to the second, which the author explicitly does not do.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: State the point the whole passage builds to, including the author's qualified verdict.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The fourth paragraph: the author rejects the first objection and concedes the second is unresolved.

breakdown.analysis: The first three paragraphs are background: Rowe's argument, Wykstra's reply, two objections. The author speaks only in the last paragraph, and the verdict is split: objection one fails, objection two remains open. The main point must carry both halves; an answer that gives skeptical theism a complete win or a complete loss is too extreme.

choices.note: Distortion and too strong. CORNEA limits when one may claim that suffering appears pointless given theism; the passage never says no suffering can appear pointless, and the author never says Rowe's argument cannot start.
Half right. The author does say the first objection mistakes the kind of humility at issue, but calls the second 'harder' and says skeptical theism's line is 'not yet secured.'
CORRECT. This matches the author's two verdicts: the moral-paralysis objection is answered, while the line that would stop wider skepticism has been 'drawn but not yet secured.'

Too narrow and too strong. The story is offered as an illustration that 'classical traditions anticipated' the distinction; it supports one step, it is not the passage's main point, and the author does not claim it 'establishes' anything.
Out of scope. Revelation figures only in the worry about whether God might deceive us; the passage never claims the debate requires an appeal to revelation.

questions.stem: The author mentions a parent's purposes and a one-month-old infant (second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: explain why, on Wykstra's view, our not discerning a justifying good is what theism predicts
show that suffering inflicted for a good purpose can appear pointless to those who undergo it
suggest that human beings will eventually come to understand the goods for whose sake God permits suffering
concede that Rowe's fawn example appeals to the emotions rather than to evidence
argue that God's relation to human beings is in every respect like that of a parent to a child
questions.explanation: The analogy supports Wykstra's claim that, if theism is true, God's reasons would lie beyond our grasp, so that 'failing to see such goods is then just what theism predicts.' A states that role. B is the trap: it describes what parent cases often illustrate in everyday thought, but the passage uses the analogy to make a point about the gap in understanding, not about the experience of the sufferer.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what job the parent-infant comparison does in Wykstra's reply.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third and fourth sentences of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The sentence containing the analogy says God's goods would lie as far beyond our grasp as a parent's purposes lie beyond an infant's; the next sentence draws the consequence: failing to see them is what theism predicts. So the analogy illustrates the size of the cognitive gap that makes our failure to see unsurprising.

choices.note: CORRECT. The analogy sets up the next sentence: 'Failing to see such goods is then just what theism predicts, and so is no evidence against it.'
Distortion. The passage says nothing about the infant suffering or about how suffering appears to the one who undergoes it; the point is the gap between the parent's purposes and the infant's grasp.
Out of scope. Nothing in the passage predicts that humans will eventually understand; the analogy stresses how far beyond us the goods lie.
Wrong position-holder and out of scope. Wykstra does not dismiss the fawn case as emotional; he challenges the inference from 'appears pointless' to 'is pointless.'
Too strong. The analogy is about one respect, the reach of understanding; nothing claims the relation is alike 'in every respect.'

questions.stem: According to the passage, Almeida and Oppy argued that if skeptical theism is correct, then
choices: we could not reasonably judge that God would never deceive us
Rowe's fawn example would provide stronger evidence against theism than Rowe himself claimed
the goods we know of would turn out to be representative of the goods there are
a person who prevents suffering would be morally blameworthy for doing so
we would lack grounds for judging whether we ourselves ought to prevent a given evil
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says Almeida and Oppy argued that 'if we cannot judge whether a given evil serves some unseen good, we cannot judge whether we ourselves should prevent it.' That is E. A is the wider-skepticism objection, which the passage assigns to 'others,' not to Almeida and Oppy.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Retrieve what the passage attributes to Almeida and Oppy specifically.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second sentence of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The third paragraph contains two objections from two sources. Almeida and Oppy: we could not judge whether we should prevent an evil. 'Others': we could not judge that God would never deceive us. Match the stem's named critics to their own objection.

choices.note: Wrong position-holder. This is the 'wider skepticism' pressed by 'others' in the last sentence of the third paragraph, not Almeida and Oppy's argument.
Out of scope. Almeida and Oppy's argument is about the consequences of skeptical theism for moral reasoning, not about the strength of Rowe's evidence.
Opposite. Skeptical theism denies that we have reason to think the known goods are representative; Almeida and Oppy draw consequences from that denial.

Too strong. Their claim is that we could not judge whether to intervene, so the bystander 'would have to allow that intervening might forfeit a greater good'; not that intervening would be blameworthy.
CORRECT. The passage: 'we cannot judge whether we ourselves should prevent it.'

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Moses was mistaken, by the moral standards he had been given, to protest the acts of the servant of God.
An agent can be obligated to prevent an evil even if God would be justified in permitting that same evil.
Defenders of skeptical theism have shown that humility about God's reasons for permitting evil does not extend to God's reasons for speaking.
Rowe's argument fails because the fawn's suffering in fact served a good that no human could discern.
A human agent's duty to prevent an evil depends on an assessment of every consequence that preventing it would have.
questions.explanation: The author says 'a skeptical theist can therefore hold that God may permit what she must still prevent,' because a human's duty is set by what she can know and the standards she has been given. B paraphrases that. C is the trap for readers who track only the author's sympathy for skeptical theism: the author says that line has been 'drawn but not yet secured.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the author's own claims support, without going beyond them.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First two sentences of the fourth paragraph; its last two sentences for what the author has not granted.

breakdown.analysis: The author's view has two parts: the duty point (human duty is indexed to human knowledge, so God may permit what we must prevent) and the open question about wider skepticism. Test each choice against both. Several choices reverse the author (A, E) or overstate a claim the author leaves open (C) or never makes (D).

choices.note: Opposite. The author stresses that Moses is faulted only for impatience and that the knowledge justifying the acts was 'not a license for Moses to act on'; the story is used to show the protest was in keeping with the standards Moses had.
CORRECT. This restates 'a skeptical theist can therefore hold that God may permit what she must still prevent.'
Too strong, and contrary to the passage. The author says that line has been 'drawn but not yet secured.'
Too strong. The author never claims the fawn's suffering in fact served any good; the defense concerns what we can know, not what is the case.
Opposite. The author says a human agent's duty is set by what she can know, 'not by a reckoning of every consequence the world contains.'

questions.stem: In the first sentence of the third paragraph, the claim that "this humility proves too much" most nearly means that
choices: skeptical theists claim more confidence about God's purposes than their own principle permits them
the humility required by CORNEA is excessive only when applied to cases of intense suffering
skeptical theism demands more of human knowledge than any human being could supply
the reasoning that blocks Rowe's inference would also block judgments skeptical theists need
skeptical theism shows that Rowe's argument is unsound but cannot show that theism is true
questions.explanation: An argument 'proves too much' when, if it worked, it would also establish conclusions its own proponents reject. The paragraph then gives two such conclusions: we could not judge whether to prevent evils, and could not judge that God would never deceive us. D captures that. E is the trap: it describes a real limitation of a defense, but not the sense of 'proves too much,' which is about unwanted extra consequences.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Interpret the phrase from how the rest of the paragraph develops it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The rest of the third paragraph, which spells out what the humility would also undermine.

breakdown.analysis: Prephrase from context: the critics show that the same skepticism, if accepted, would also wipe out moral judgments about prevention and trust in God's truthfulness, things a skeptical theist wants to keep. 'Proves too much' therefore means the reasoning overreaches into territory its users need intact.

choices.note: Opposite. The objection is that skeptical theists' humility is too sweeping, not that they are too confident.
Out of scope. The objection extends the humility to bystander cases and divine speech; nothing confines the problem to intense suffering.
Distortion. The objection is not that skeptical theism requires impossible knowledge; it is that it denies us knowledge we need.
CORRECT. Both examples that follow are judgments the skeptical theist wants to keep, moral judgments about preventing evil and trust that God does not deceive, which the same humility would undercut.
Irrelevant truth at best. This names a different limitation of a purely defensive reply; 'proves too much' concerns unwanted further consequences, which the paragraph then lists.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken Wykstra's reply to Rowe as the passage describes it?
choices: Many people who reflect on cases like the fawn's report that the suffering appears to them to be pointless.
Parents frequently act for purposes that their infants are incapable of grasping.
Some goods that might justify permitting suffering are goods that human beings would recognize if they were pointed out.
Rowe later developed versions of his argument that do not rely on the case of the fawn.
If God exists, God would have strong reason to make the goods served by suffering humanly discernible.
questions.explanation: Wykstra's reply depends on the claim that, if theism is true, God's justifying goods would likely lie beyond our grasp; only then does CORNEA's condition fail, so that our failing to see them is 'what theism predicts.' E denies that link: if God would make such goods discernible, then on theism we would likely see them, and not seeing them becomes evidence after all. C is the trap: it sounds as if it brings the goods within reach, but recognizing a good once it is pointed out is compatible with our being unable to discern it unaided, which is what CORNEA asks about.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most undercuts Wykstra's reply.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph: CORNEA, and the claim that on theism the goods 'would likely lie' beyond our grasp.

breakdown.analysis: Wykstra's reply has two steps: (1) CORNEA: 'it appears there is no good' is licensed only if, were there a good, we would likely discern it; (2) on theism, the goods would likely lie beyond us. Attack step 2: anything giving reason to think that on theism the goods would be discernible restores Rowe's inference.

choices.note: Premise restatement. Wykstra does not deny that the suffering appears pointless in the ordinary sense; his reply concerns whether that appearance is evidence. More reports of the appearance leave his point untouched.
Opposite. This supports the parent-infant analogy on which Wykstra relies.

Irrelevant truth. Being able to recognize a good once shown it does not mean we would likely discern it on our own in cases like the fawn's, which is what CORNEA turns on; and 'some goods' leaves the rest beyond us.
Out of scope. Rowe's later versions are not part of the reply described, and the fact that the argument can be restated says nothing about whether Wykstra's reply works.

CORRECT. This denies the step 'if theism is true, the goods would likely lie beyond our grasp': if God would make such goods discernible, then on theism we would likely see them, and failing to see them is again evidence against theism.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward skeptical theism is most accurately described as
choices: qualified support, persuaded it survives one objection but doubtful that it has met another
unreserved endorsement of it as the most successful of the available responses to the evidential problem of evil
detached neutrality, presenting its arguments and its critics' without taking a position
reluctant rejection, on the grounds that its humility leads to moral paralysis
skepticism about its premises combined with admiration for its classical antecedents
questions.explanation: The author defends skeptical theism against the moral-paralysis objection ('mistakes the kind of humility at issue') but concedes the wider-skepticism objection is 'harder' and that the needed line is 'not yet secured.' That is qualified support, A. C is the trap for readers who notice that the first three paragraphs are reportorial; the fourth paragraph is first-person and takes sides.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize the author's attitude, with its degree.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The fourth paragraph, especially 'I think' and 'The second objection is harder.'

breakdown.analysis: Look for evaluative language. 'The first objection, I think, mistakes...' is a defense; 'The second objection is harder' and 'not yet secured' are reservations. The right answer must be positive but qualified.

choices.note: CORRECT. The author rebuts the moral-paralysis objection but says the line needed against wider skepticism has been 'drawn but not yet secured.'
Too extreme. The author's reservations about the second objection rule out unreserved endorsement, and the passage never ranks responses to Rowe.
Opposite. The fourth paragraph is in the first person and takes a position on each objection.
Opposite. The author rejects the moral-paralysis objection, the very ground this choice gives for rejection.
Distortion. The author does not doubt skeptical theism's premises, and the classical story is used as support for the author's own point, not admired apart from it.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: argue that Schellenberg's hiddenness argument fails because the inquirers it describes are in fact resistant
compare the treatment of divine hiddenness in Christian and Islamic thought
trace the development of Schellenberg's argument from its first formulation to its later revisions
present an argument and two replies, then question an assumption that all three share
defend the view that a relationship with God can exist without any belief at all
questions.explanation: The passage lays out Schellenberg's argument, Murray's appeal to freedom (with Schellenberg's answer), and the appeal to the will (with its critics), then argues that 'both responses... leave in place Schellenberg's assumption that belief comes first' and questions that assumption. D describes that design. A is the trap: it attributes to the author the Pascal-Moser line, which the author treats as facing an objection and then sets aside.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe what the passage as a whole is doing.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First sentences of each paragraph; the first two sentences of the fourth.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 1: the argument. Paragraphs 2 and 3: two responses, each with a reply. Paragraph 4: the author identifies a shared assumption and questions it, explicitly saying 'This does not refute the argument.' The purpose statement needs all of that and must not claim more than the author does.

choices.note: Wrong position-holder. This is the second response's line, which the passage says 'must deny that the sincere inquirer is really nonresistant'; the author neither adopts it nor claims the argument fails.
Out of scope. Pascal and Moser are not presented as a Christian tradition to be compared with al-Ghazali; the passage compares no traditions.
Too narrow. The later recasting is mentioned in one sentence; most of the passage concerns responses and the author's challenge.
CORRECT. The fourth paragraph's first sentence names the shared assumption, and the rest of the passage questions it while conceding that 'this does not refute the argument.'
Too strong. The author says a relationship 'might begin before belief' and leaves the question open; no claim is made that it can exist without any belief at all.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Schellenberg answered the appeal to freedom by contending that
choices: morally significant choice does not require any distance between God and human beings
a person can believe that God exists and still resist a relationship with God
the prospect of divine judgment would not in fact affect human behavior
nonbelief is reasonable only when it does not result from a person's turning away
evidence of God is offered only to those who are willing to be transformed
questions.explanation: The second paragraph: 'Schellenberg answered that belief that God exists does not compel a relationship: one may believe and still resist.' That is B. D is the trap: it echoes Schellenberg's later notion of nonresistant nonbelief from the first paragraph, but it is not his answer to the freedom objection.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Retrieve Schellenberg's reply to Murray's line.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last sentence of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The passage states the reply directly. Watch for choices that use real ideas from elsewhere in the passage (the nonresistance premise, Moser's purposive availability) attached to the wrong question.

choices.note: Distortion. Schellenberg's reply does not deny that freedom requires something; it denies that granting belief would override freedom.
CORRECT. 'Belief that God exists does not compel a relationship: one may believe and still resist.'
Out of scope. The reply does not dispute whether judgment would affect behavior; it says belief alone does not force a relationship.
Shell game. This draws on the first paragraph's description of nonresistant nonbelief, Schellenberg's later recasting of his premise, not his answer to the appeal to freedom.
Wrong position-holder. This is Moser's view from the third paragraph.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that the critics mentioned in the last sentence of the third paragraph would most likely hold that the response they criticize
choices: depends on a claim about inquirers' inner dispositions that others cannot readily check
misrepresents Pascal's view of the relationship between light and obscurity
succeeds against Schellenberg's 1993 formulation but not against his later one
concedes that sincere inquirers are nonresistant and thereby grants Schellenberg's key premise
shows that evidence of God is equally available to all who seek it
questions.explanation: The critics say the response 'must deny that the sincere inquirer is really nonresistant, a claim about another person's heart that is hard to confirm from outside.' A paraphrases that. D reverses it: the response must deny nonresistance, not concede it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Infer the critics' view of the Pascal-Moser response from the one sentence describing it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last sentence of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The critics' point has two parts: the response commits itself to saying the sincere inquirer is not really nonresistant, and that is a claim about another's heart that is hard to verify. The answer should paraphrase this ('inner dispositions' for 'heart', 'cannot readily be checked' for 'hard to confirm from outside').

choices.note: CORRECT. 'A claim about another person's heart that is hard to confirm from outside' is a claim about inner dispositions that others cannot readily check.
Out of scope. The critics raise nothing about Pascal's view; Moser is said to develop Pascal's thought, and no one disputes the reading.
Out of scope. The passage never says which formulation the response answers or how it fares against each.
Opposite. The critics' point is that the response must deny that sincere inquirers are nonresistant.
Opposite. The response holds that evidence 'may be withheld from those unwilling to be changed,' so it is not equally available.

questions.stem: The author's discussion of al-Ghazali in the fourth paragraph functions primarily to
choices: provide evidence that sincere inquirers who find nothing must in fact be resisting God
illustrate the appeal to freedom discussed in the second paragraph with an example from another tradition
show that classical thinkers had already refuted the argument from hiddenness
suggest that certainty about divine things cannot be reached by any means
offer an account on which knowledge of God follows practice rather than preceding it
questions.explanation: The author introduces al-Ghazali right after naming the assumption that 'belief comes first' and says it 'deserves more scrutiny'; al-Ghazali regarded the surest knowledge of divine things as 'reached through disciplined practice rather than a premise from which practice starts.' He is a counter-model to the belief-first assumption, E. C is the trap: the author explicitly says 'This does not refute the argument.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the author brings in al-Ghazali at this point.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The fourth paragraph, from the naming of the assumption to 'If something like this is right.'

breakdown.analysis: Context: the author has just identified the belief-first assumption and called for scrutiny. Al-Ghazali's account reverses the order (practice leads to knowledge), and the next sentence draws the moral: a relationship might begin before belief. So the reference supplies an alternative to the assumption.

choices.note: Wrong position-holder. That inquirers must be resisting is the claim the second response is committed to; the author's point via al-Ghazali is that the seeker might already be in the relationship, not that he is resisting.
Shell game. Freedom was the subject of Murray's response, which the author says leaves the belief-first assumption in place; al-Ghazali is used against that assumption, not to illustrate Murray.
Too strong. The author says plainly, 'This does not refute the argument.'
Opposite. Al-Ghazali's account describes certainty being reached, through a light God cast into his breast and through practice.

CORRECT. Al-Ghazali regarded such knowledge as reached through practice 'rather than a premise from which practice starts,' which is offered as an alternative to the assumption that 'belief comes first.'

questions.stem: Which one of the following situations most clearly illustrates the possibility the author raises in the fourth paragraph?
choices: A man who is convinced that his neighbor exists nonetheless refuses every invitation the neighbor extends.
A student comes to believe that a famous author is alive only after the author answers one of her letters, and then begins a correspondence.
A woman unsure whether her lost brother is alive writes him letters she cannot send, and grows more attentive toward him.
A traveler gives up searching for a guide he has been told about, concluding that the guide does not exist.
A child believes in a benefactor on the testimony of others but forms no attitude toward the benefactor.
questions.explanation: The author's possibility is that 'a relationship might begin before belief, in attention, longing, or the search itself,' raising the question whether 'one can be in a relationship with someone whose existence one doubts.' In C, the woman doubts her brother is alive yet her attention and longing shape an orientation toward him: something relationship-like begins before belief. B is the main trap: it shows belief coming first and the relationship following, which is exactly Schellenberg's order.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Map the author's abstract possibility onto a concrete case.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last four sentences of the fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Prephrase: someone who does not believe (or doubts) that a person exists, yet attends to, longs for, or searches for that person in a way that could count as the start of a relationship. Eliminate cases where belief comes first (A, B, E) and cases where searching ends without any such orientation (D).

choices.note: Wrong idea. This is belief without relationship, the case Schellenberg uses against the appeal to freedom, not relationship before belief.
Reversal. Belief comes first here and the correspondence follows: the order the author questions.
CORRECT. She doubts her brother's existence, yet her attention and longing toward him grow: a relationship-like orientation that begins before belief.
Opposite. The search ends in disbelief and withdrawal; nothing of the relationship is present.
Wrong idea. The child has belief but no relationship, which says nothing about relationship preceding belief.

questions.stem: As it is used in the first paragraph, the phrase "nonresistant nonbelief" refers to
choices: a failure to believe in God that does not result from the person's own turning away
a refusal to enter a relationship with God despite believing that God exists
nonbelief that persists even after a person has been given decisive evidence
the belief that God exists combined with resistance to God's will
nonbelief that is reasonable because no argument for God's existence is sound
questions.explanation: The passage defines the phrase in apposition: 'nonresistant nonbelief, nonbelief not produced by the person's own turning away.' A paraphrases that. B and D describe belief combined with resistance, the case Schellenberg raises in the second paragraph, not nonbelief.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Use the passage's own gloss to interpret the phrase.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fifth sentence of the first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The phrase is glossed immediately after it appears. Match the gloss; then check that the answer is about nonbelief (not belief) and about its source (not its reasonableness on other grounds).

choices.note: CORRECT. The passage: 'nonbelief not produced by the person's own turning away.'
Shell game. This is the believing-but-resisting case from the second paragraph, the opposite of nonbelief.
Out of scope. The passage says nothing about decisive evidence being given; the hiddenness argument presupposes it has not been.
Opposite. This describes belief, not nonbelief, and adds resistance, which the phrase excludes.
Distortion. The phrase is defined by the absence of resistance, not by the failure of arguments for God's existence.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen Schellenberg's answer to the appeal to freedom?
choices: Many sincere inquirers report that they would welcome a relationship with God if God existed.
Morally significant choices are possible only when the consequences of choosing are not fully known.
People who come to believe that God exists usually also come to love God.
People fully convinced that someone exists often refuse any relationship with that person.
Threats of punishment influence behavior more strongly than promises of reward do.
questions.explanation: Schellenberg's answer rests on the claim that belief that God exists 'does not compel a relationship: one may believe and still resist.' D supports the general point that belief in a person's existence leaves one free to refuse a relationship. C is the opposite trap: if belief usually brings love, granting belief looks closer to compelling the relationship, which helps the appeal to freedom.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that best supports Schellenberg's reply to Murray's line.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last sentence of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Schellenberg's reply: granting belief would not override freedom, because belief does not compel a relationship. Support comes from evidence that believing someone exists leaves the relationship up to the believer. Watch for choices that bear on the original argument rather than on this reply, or that help Murray instead.

choices.note: Out of scope for this reply. This bears on whether inquirers are nonresistant (the first and third paragraphs), not on whether belief compels relationship.
Opposite. This supports the appeal to freedom: if choice needs uncertainty, granting belief might undercut it.
Opposite. If belief typically brings love, belief looks more like it compels the relationship, which weakens Schellenberg's answer.
CORRECT. This supports the general claim the answer rests on: believing that a person exists does not compel a relationship with that person.
Irrelevant truth. Murray's line appeals to threatened judgment, but comparing threats with rewards does not touch whether belief compels relationship.
